stories.title: Million-dollar donations boost fundraising for 24 Sussex renovation
stories.summary: A handful of wealthy donors have made sizable commitments toward the project’s $50-million goal
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Listen to this article

Learn more about audio

The majority of money raised from the public for the renovation of 24 Sussex Dr. has come from a wealthy class of donors who have contributed between $1-million and $5-million, according to the foundation in charge of the effort.

Thousands of Canadians have made smaller donations toward the renovation of the prime ministerial residence, but roughly 61 per cent of the $8.2-million raised so far has come from a small group the foundation is calling “legacy” donors.

Teresa Marques, the president and chief executive officer of the Rideau Hall Foundation, which is managing the fundraising, said the foundation is grateful for every donation it receives.

“There are very few opportunities for Canadians to contribute personally to a project of national significance that will still matter generations from now,” she said in a statement.

The foundation is trying to raise $50-million as part of a federal government plan to renovate the historic building.

Twenty-four Sussex Dr., which was built in the 1860s and adapted into a prime ministerial residence as of 1951, fell, over the decades, into such disrepair that Justin Trudeau and his family were unable to move in when Mr. Trudeau became prime minister in 2015.

The Trudeaus moved into the Rideau Cottage residence on the grounds of Rideau Hall, the property that serves as the official home and working space for the governor-general. Prime Minister Mark Carney now lives at Rideau Cottage.

Meanwhile, 24 Sussex Dr. was left empty and, in 2023, gutted by the National Capital Commission. The commission had furnishings, finishes and other interior components removed.

In June, Mr. Carney announced a fundraising effort, run by the foundation, to finance the renovation of 24 Sussex Dr., and a contest led by the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada to find a proponent to redesign the building that nine prime ministers have lived in since 1951. A winner is to be announced by next Canada Day.

The foundation’s listed legacy donors are Ed and Fran Clark; Stephen Dent and Janet Maclaren; Heather Ryan and L. David Dubé Foundation; the Sixty Three Foundation; and Roger and Jenny Hardy of the Hardy Family Foundation.

Mr. Clark is a former CEO of TD Bank Group, who is known, along with his wife, Fran, for philanthropic endeavours. Mr. Dubé of Saskatoon is an Order of Canada recipient cited for his philanthropic work, and the president and CEO of the Concorde Group Corp. He has supported causes through the foundation he established with his wife, Ms. Ryan. The Sixty Three Foundation is a Toronto-based charitable organization associated with Prem Watsa, founder and CEO of Fairfax Financial Holdings.

Vancouver-based Roger Hardy is the CEO and chairman of Hardy Capital, and co-founder and former CEO of Coastal Contacts Inc., an online eyewear retailer. He is also involved with the Hardy Family Foundation charity organization, where his wife, Jenny Hardy, is the managing director.

In an interview, Mr. Hardy said he became engaged with the 24 Sussex Dr. effort after a family visit to Ottawa last year that included a stop at the beleaguered property.

Mr. Hardy, who grew up in nearby Kanata, Ont., brought his children to see 24 Sussex Dr. in the summer of 2025 and was struck by its state of decline.

“I think we were just disappointed, frankly, that there wasn’t more there,” he said.

“That’s sort of where I think my journey began,” Mr. Hardy said, adding he was surprised that the residence was not in a good state. “I don’t think I was really up to speed that no one had lived there.”

He declined to be specific about how much money he had given to the 24 Sussex Dr. project. “I’m in that legacy category, so more than a million,” Mr. Hardy said of his donation.

The Rideau Hall Foundation has a policy against releasing detailed donation information.

“In keeping with our donor recognition principles, we publicly acknowledge donors within the applicable giving range rather than disclosing individual gift amounts,” spokesperson Allison MacLachlan said in a statement.

“Every contribution matters, regardless of its size. Major gifts can provide significant momentum, but broad participation is equally important because it reflects the collective support of Canadians,” she said. According to the foundation, the median gift it has received is $100.

Mr. Hardy has also joined the Council for 24 Sussex, a group of volunteers who are working to encourage Canadians to support the 24 Sussex Dr. project.

Mr. Hardy said he wants to help raise awareness about the rebuilding project. “Not everyone in B.C. is probably familiar with it,” he said. “It’s not at the top of their awareness right now.”

Mr. Hardy said he watched the Prime Minister’s June announcement describing his plan for dealing with the residence, which Mr. Carney has said he does not plan to move into.

“Frankly, I thought it was good that he said he wasn’t going to live there just because it makes it less political,” he said. “From my standpoint, it’s more iconic for all Canadians, iconic for all parties, whatever they May be.”

The foundation has capped donations at $5-million, and is only accepting donations from Canadian citizens or permanent residents. Charitable organizations can also make donations, but corporations cannot.

All eligible donors receive charitable tax receipts for their donations.

Mr. Hardy said he wants to help raise awareness about the rebuilding project. “Not everyone in B.C. is probably familiar with it,” he said. “It’s not at the top of their awareness right now.”
Mr. Hardy said he watched the Prime Minister’s June announcement describing his plan for dealing with the residence, which Mr. Carney has said he does not plan to move into.

“Frankly, I thought it was good that he said he wasn’t going to live there just because it makes it less political,” he said. “From my standpoint, it’s more iconic for all Canadians, iconic for all parties, whatever they May be.”

The foundation has capped donations at $5-million, and is only accepting donations from Canadian citizens or permanent residents. Charitable organizations can also make donations, but corporations cannot.
All eligible donors receive charitable tax receipts for their donations.

stories.title: ‘Just horrific’: Canadian alleged bag tag switch victims trapped in New Zealand for 14 months
stories.summary: A husband and wife flew from Toronto’s Pearson International Airport on Air Canada to Auckland, New Zealand, in January 2025 but were stopped when one of their luggage tags was found on a bag containing 15 kilograms of methamphetamine.
stories.author: Jack Hauen, Avery Haines
stories.content:
It was supposed to be a two-week trip.

A husband and wife flew from Toronto’s Pearson International Airport on Air Canada to Auckland, New Zealand, in January 2025 but were stopped when one of their luggage tags was found on a bag containing 15 kilograms of methamphetamine.

The couple spent five weeks in a New Zealand prison and another 13 months on bail in a monitored facility that they had to pay for.

They are now clients of Toronto lawyer Paul Miller, who has been approached by almost two dozen alleged victims of bag tag switching who flew through Pearson International Airport.

If you have information about corruption at Canadian airports, reach out to avery.haines@bellmedia.CA and jack.hauen@bellmedia.CA , or jackhauen.33 on Signal.

Miller said the wife was denied her pain medication, and both had to wear ankle bracelets while on bail.

The husband lost his job in the skilled trades, said Cassandra De Marco, an associate lawyer who works with Miller.

“Obviously, the mental anguish that [they] went through is just horrific,” Miller said.

Their trial took about two weeks. The decision took far less time.

“From what they have told me … the jury was out for less than five minutes and the case was thrown out,” Miller said.

But the couple couldn’t return to Canada right away because the price of a last-minute plane ticket was astronomical, he said.

So they spent another three weeks in New Zealand before it was financially feasible to leave, Miller said.

“That feeling, I can’t imagine,” he said. “I’m sure they were feeling like, are they being watched? You know, do the police believe they are not drug dealers?”

Their arrest took place just nine days after Toronto man Tommy Moyeen was also arrested for importing meth at the same Auckland airport.

Both cases involve allegations of bag tag switching. But while the couple are now back home in Canada, Moyeen was sentenced to nearly 10 years in jail .

Moyeen has been behind bars in New Zealand for almost two years. In a phone call from prison, he said his appeal will rely heavily on W5’s research from two documentaries — Trafficked: The Airport Conspiracy and “ That’s Not My Bag .”

How bag tag switching works

W5 has identified dozens of cases of tag switching at Pearson .

A corrupt worker will smuggle a bag of drugs into an airport, take the tag off an unsuspecting passenger’s luggage and attach it to the drug bag.

A courier is waiting at the destination to pick up the drug suitcase. But if it’s intercepted by security, the innocent passenger is left to explain themselves

W5’s latest investigation triggered an explosion of Google searches about the scheme and how Canadians can protect themselves.

Google Trends screenshot

From Pearson to Prison: Toronto man faces 15 years in Albania after luggage tag switch

Federal government moves to overhaul airport security after CTV News investigation

Around the world, drug cases keep leading back to bag tags

Pearson bag tag victims say they were ignored. Now they’re fighting back

After years of bag tag switching, one man says he has the fix

More alleged victims come forward after W5 investigation

Miller represented 11 alleged victims of bag tag switching when W5’s latest documentary on the scheme premiered just over a week ago. Since it aired, that number has nearly doubled to 21 confirmed and potential clients.

They have been accused of smuggling drugs from Toronto into countries around the world — the latest batch includes Brazil, Aruba, Germany, Sri Lanka, Australia, the Dominican Republic and New Zealand.

They differ in age, sex, race and the airlines they flew, including Air Canada, WestJet, Air Transat and Cathay Pacific.

But all of them went through Pearson airport.

This week has been “a little crazy,” said Miller, who has practiced personal injury law for 25 years.

“The stories are so disturbing — about people spending a lot of time in prison and under house arrest, going to trials,” he said.

“A couple clients have said, thankfully, the documentary helped them not go to jail,” he added.

Some legal cases are ongoing and not all the facts are known. Miller said he’s been researching each case to weed out the ones trying to use the scheme as a get-out-of-jail-free card.

“But I think for the most part, everyone is very legit, honest, and concerned about what happened to them and others,” he said.

Trapped in the Caribbean for 100 days

Miller is now representing Zach Crawford and Cassandra DiPietro, who were only supposed to be in the Dominican Republic for five days.

The couple was sitting on the tarmac looking forward to heading home to St. Catharines after their first vacation together when an agent escorted them off the plane. A half-dozen drug control officers then took them to an interrogation room and then a detention centre with barbed wire and armed guards, the St. Catharines Standard reported in July 2025.

Crawford and DiPietro spent more than three months in the Dominican Republic, both in prison and out on bail, desperately fighting to get home.

Faced with expensive legal bills, the pair drained their line of credit, maxed out credit cards and had to remortgage their home, the Standard reported.

It’s an example of how quickly lives can be turned upside down by tag switching, Miller said.

“I mean, we’re not talking about 17-year-old kids being arrested. We’re talking about people with careers, a life here.”

Alleged tag switching victims seeking up to $1M

Miller said he had to turn away at least one prospective client because the limitation period had expired. You have two years from when you first find out about the incident — likely the day you’re first detained — to launch legal action, he said.

At least three of his clients say the airlines have offered them some form of compensation, including a $300 flight credit for a woman who was questioned in Barbados, $2,000 for a couple who were detained for 12 hours at Pearson, and about $22,000 for a woman who was imprisoned in the Philippines for 24 days — about half of what she says the ordeal cost her in legal fees and upended travel plans.

Miller said he’s seeking somewhere in the ballpark of $100,000 to $1 million per client.

Several airlines involved in tag switching cases previously told W5 they take security seriously and that many other organizations are involved in baggage handling. They declined to say who is liable for bags that are tampered with.

The Greater Toronto Airports Authority, which runs Pearson, previously told W5 that it “does not direct or oversee baggage security,” and pointed to federal agencies and police.

All of Miller’s cases will get underway before the end of the year, he said.

He said he’s been in talks with one airline so far and expects another call in the next week or two.

“And we’ll get an idea, I think, from that case, how other airlines are going to approach this,” he said.

Miller said he hopes the publicity will encourage more people to come forward — potentially at other airports, too.

“There is no way this is just confined to Pearson,” he said.

stories.title: Why daily cannabis use in Canada just topped daily alcohol use for adults under 50: 'A generational shift'
stories.summary: The study in the Canadian Medical Association Journal also found daily use in under-35s exceeds daily cigarette smoking.
stories.author: Omar Mosleh
stories.content:
Bret Simpson smokes cannabis near Monarch Park last week. He said legalization made a big difference on stigma within his social group.

Sophie Bouquillon/Toronto Star

Sophie Bouquillon/Toronto Star[](https://www.thestar.com/news/gta/why-daily-cannabis-use-in-canada-just-topped-daily-alcohol-use-for-adults-under-50-a-generational-shift/article_e5d9348b-2a3a-41a2-97a1-c630412b1886.html)

ByOmar Mosleh Staff Reporter

Daily cannabis use has surpassed daily drinking among Canadian adults under 50, in what researchers are calling a “generational shift” with long-term health implications.

A study published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, led by researchers at North York General and McMaster University, found that 5.7 per cent of Canadian adults ages 18 to 49 reported daily cannabis use, or roughly 1.81 million people. In contrast, the data showed 5.2 per cent reported drinking alcohol daily, while 8.5 per cent were smoking cigarettes daily.

Senior author Dr. Daniel Myran said the findings are significant because there are risks associated with long-term daily use of cannabis. He said the trend signals a need for governments and public health authorities to tailor their messaging and regulations to ensure young people who otherwise wouldn’t start using cannabis don’t start because of how accessible and increasingly acceptable it is.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

“It’s a real generational shift in what substances people are using ... Even if we’re just more accurately capturing current use right now, the prevalence of use is really high,” said Myran, who is the Cheesbrough Research Chair at North York General, a clinician scientist and associate professor at the University of Toronto’s Department of Family and Community Medicine.

Depression and anxiety nearly tripled between 2013 and 2023, McMaster researchers find.

The researchers pulled the data from nearly 100,000 respondents to the 2023-24 Canadian Community Health Survey. They are calling for stronger warnings on product packaging about the risks of regular cannabis use, stricter rules and enforcement around promotion, and targeted prevention strategies to reduce usage in younger adults, youth and people vulnerable to mental illnesses.

With a legal market, “if the government should choose, there are a variety of levers that they could pull to start mitigating harms related to cannabis use,” Myran said.

Daily cannabis use now also exceeds daily cigarette smoking in people under 35. Men 25 to 34 were the most likely to use daily, at 11 per cent, compared to 2.9 per cent who said they drink daily and eight per cent who smoke tobacco regularly. Among women in that cohort, 6.8 per cent reported daily cannabis use compared to 1.2 per cent who drink daily and 4.5 per cent who smoke tobacco daily.

“We were expecting there to be huge overlap between people who use cannabis daily, tobacco daily and alcohol daily … there’s much less overlap than you would think,” Myran said.

While legalization is one major driving force, there are other factors. Researchers credit long-term tobacco control policies and changing social norms for a decline in cigarette smoking among younger adults, while cannabis has seen greater availability and social acceptance since legalization.

“I think that there is essentially a consensus in society that tobacco use is harmful, and that we desire it to be as low as possible,” Myran said.

“That is not the societal view that we have for alcohol and cannabis,” adding that cannabis use is associated with “individual liberties, recreation and enjoyment”.

The study found that 41 per cent of adults who reported daily cannabis use started after legalization in 2018. Adults ages 18 to 24 were most likely to report they started post-legalization (85.4 per cent).

Bret Simpson, a daily cannabis user, experimented a few times in high school but didn’t start using regularly until a few years before legalization, when grey market stores became more common. Now he sticks to sanctioned stores, which he finds more reliable.

Simpson said stigma around cannabis use has “changed massively” in his social circle, adding that once it became legal, he no longer felt he had to “try to like escape down an alley” to get high.

“I had a history of never letting on to my employer or family that I was doing any sorts of drugs at all,” Simpson said. “And then that changed pretty much overnight with legalization.”

Daily cannabis use was more common among people with mood disorders (14.7 per cent) and anxiety (12.2 per cent) compared to people who didn’t report any mental health issues. Myran said that could be because people are using cannabis to self-medicate for their symptoms, or cannabis use could be contributing to anxiety and depression.

Long-term daily cannabis use has been strongly linked to anxiety and depression, and emerging evidence suggests it could be a risk factor for lung disease, heart attacks and strokes, depending on the method of consumption. Evidence on cancer risk is limited and mixed, and researchers say we need stronger data on the harms of using cannabis regularly.

The study examined over 1,000 adults and found that the effects of heavy cannabis use may be long-lasting.

Smoking is still the primary method of consumption for daily cannabis users, with 3.9 per cent of respondents saying they smoked daily compared to 1.8 per cent who said they used products like vapes or edibles.

“One of the arguments (for legalization) was people are going to start doing non-combustible methods, and it’s going to be better for their lung health … that doesn’t seem to be what’s occurring,” Myran said.

Mike Dunn, owner of 1922 Cannabis Retail in Moss Park, said he has seen growth in demand for products that are easier to consume such as pre-rolled joints, edibles and vapes.

“Potency is less and less of a question over the six years we’ve been open,” Dunn said. “If anything it’s the opposite, with more people asking for lower THC and lighter products.”

Myran said he’s concerned with the prevalence of high-potency THC products, which he said are more closely linked to addiction and mental health problems, as well as being concerned with how cannabis is promoted. A previous study he co-authored found widespread violations of the Cannabis Act on retailer websites, including “inducement-related content,” endorsements or testimonials, content that appeals to youth and health or cosmetic benefit claims, all of which are prohibited.

Myran noted it’s not uncommon for stores to also advertise prices and promotions on the sidewalk, which is prohibited.

Dunn, who noted his store does not advertise prices outside the shop, said “the rules are already strict. They need to be enforced evenly, so the stores following them aren’t competing with the ones that don’t.”

Simpson said he agrees cannabis shouldn’t be promoted so as to entice youth, but sees the normalization and promotion of alcohol as more problematic.

“I can only buy one ounce of weed (at a store), but I can go to the LCBO and buy enough alcohol to kill myself four times over. I find that quite silly.”

Omar Mosleh is a Toronto-based reporter covering social issues for the Star. Reach him here:omarmosleh@thestar.ca.

Daily cannabis use has surpassed daily drinking among Canadian adults under 50, in what researchers are calling a “generational shift” with long-term health implications.

A study published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, led by researchers at North York General and McMaster University, found that 5.7 per cent of Canadian adults ages 18 to 49 reported daily cannabis use, or roughly 1.81 million people. In contrast, the data showed 5.2 per cent reported drinking alcohol daily, while 8.5 per cent were smoking cigarettes daily.

Senior author Dr. Daniel Myran said the findings are significant because there are risks associated with long-term daily use of cannabis. He said the trend signals a need for governments and public health authorities to tailor their messaging and regulations to ensure young people who otherwise wouldn’t start using cannabis don’t start because of how accessible and increasingly acceptable it is.
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

“It’s a real generational shift in what substances people are using ... Even if we’re just more accurately capturing current use right now, the prevalence of use is really high,” said Myran, who is the Cheesbrough Research Chair at North York General, a clinician scientist and associate professor at the University of Toronto’s Department of Family and Community Medicine.
Depression and anxiety nearly tripled between 2013 and 2023, McMaster researchers find.

The researchers pulled the data from nearly 100,000 respondents to the 2023-24 Canadian Community Health Survey. They are calling for stronger warnings on product packaging about the risks of regular cannabis use, stricter rules and enforcement around promotion, and targeted prevention strategies to reduce usage in younger adults, youth and people vulnerable to mental illnesses.
With a legal market, “if the government should choose, there are a variety of levers that they could pull to start mitigating harms related to cannabis use,” Myran said.

Daily cannabis use now also exceeds daily cigarette smoking in people under 35. Men 25 to 34 were the most likely to use daily, at 11 per cent, compared to 2.9 per cent who said they drink daily and eight per cent who smoke tobacco regularly. Among women in that cohort, 6.8 per cent reported daily cannabis use compared to 1.2 per cent who drink daily and 4.5 per cent who smoke tobacco daily.
“We were expecting there to be huge overlap between people who use cannabis daily, tobacco daily and alcohol daily … there’s much less overlap than you would think,” Myran said.

While legalization is one major driving force, there are other factors. Researchers credit long-term tobacco control policies and changing social norms for a decline in cigarette smoking among younger adults, while cannabis has seen greater availability and social acceptance since legalization.
“I think that there is essentially a consensus in society that tobacco use is harmful, and that we desire it to be as low as possible,” Myran said.
“That is not the societal view that we have for alcohol and cannabis,” adding that cannabis use is associated with “individual liberties, recreation and enjoyment”.

The study found that 41 per cent of adults who reported daily cannabis use started after legalization in 2018. Adults ages 18 to 24 were most likely to report they started post-legalization (85.4 per cent).

Bret Simpson, a daily cannabis user, experimented a few times in high school but didn’t start using regularly until a few years before legalization, when grey market stores became more common. Now he sticks to sanctioned stores, which he finds more reliable.
Simpson said stigma around cannabis use has “changed massively” in his social circle, adding that once it became legal, he no longer felt he had to “try to like escape down an alley” to get high.
“I had a history of never letting on to my employer or family that I was doing any sorts of drugs at all,” Simpson said. “And then that changed pretty much overnight with legalization.”

Daily cannabis use was more common among people with mood disorders (14.7 per cent) and anxiety (12.2 per cent) compared to people who didn’t report any mental health issues. Myran said that could be because people are using cannabis to self-medicate for their symptoms, or cannabis use could be contributing to anxiety and depression.

Long-term daily cannabis use has been strongly linked to anxiety and depression, and emerging evidence suggests it could be a risk factor for lung disease, heart attacks and strokes, depending on the method of consumption. Evidence on cancer risk is limited and mixed, and researchers say we need stronger data on the harms of using cannabis regularly.
The study examined over 1,000 adults and found that the effects of heavy cannabis use may be long-lasting.

Smoking is still the primary method of consumption for daily cannabis users, with 3.9 per cent of respondents saying they smoked daily compared to 1.8 per cent who said they used products like vapes or edibles.

“One of the arguments (for legalization) was people are going to start doing non-combustible methods, and it’s going to be better for their lung health … that doesn’t seem to be what’s occurring,” Myran said.
Mike Dunn, owner of 1922 Cannabis Retail in Moss Park, said he has seen growth in demand for products that are easier to consume such as pre-rolled joints, edibles and vapes.
“Potency is less and less of a question over the six years we’ve been open,” Dunn said. “If anything it’s the opposite, with more people asking for lower THC and lighter products.”

Myran said he’s concerned with the prevalence of high-potency THC products, which he said are more closely linked to addiction and mental health problems, as well as being concerned with how cannabis is promoted. A previous study he co-authored found widespread violations of the Cannabis Act on retailer websites, including “inducement-related content,” endorsements or testimonials, content that appeals to youth and health or cosmetic benefit claims, all of which are prohibited.
Myran noted it’s not uncommon for stores to also advertise prices and promotions on the sidewalk, which is prohibited.

Dunn, who noted his store does not advertise prices outside the shop, said “the rules are already strict. They need to be enforced evenly, so the stores following them aren’t competing with the ones that don’t.”
Simpson said he agrees cannabis shouldn’t be promoted so as to entice youth, but sees the normalization and promotion of alcohol as more problematic.
“I can only buy one ounce of weed (at a store), but I can go to the LCBO and buy enough alcohol to kill myself four times over. I find that quite silly.”

stories.title: Ottawa recruiting commissioners for wrongful-conviction review body
stories.summary: Ottawa - The federal government is beginning recruitment for its independent Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The federal government is beginning recruitment for its independent Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission — though some are questioning why it has taken two years to begin the process.

The federal government made the announcement in a news release Monday and said that recruiting commissioners is the next step in building a team to examine possible wrongful convictions.

stories.title: How Canada can make itself harder for Trump to bully, according to Harvard economists
stories.summary: Ricardo Hausmann and Eric Protzer say reducing U.S. leverage requires new markets abroad — and economic reforms at home
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — With a trade war still brewing with the U.S., Ottawa is grappling with Canada’s prosperity being so dependent on economic integration with its southern neighbour.

Economists Ricardo Hausmann, director of Harvard’s Growth Lab and a political economy professor at the Harvard Kennedy School, and Eric Protzer, a researcher at the Harvard Growth Lab, wrote “Canada After America” to explain how Canada could become less vulnerable to U.S. economic pressure — and how it requires fixing weaknesses in Canada’s own economy. National Post asked both men for their insights on how Canada can develop greater economic resilience.

Ricardo Hausmann: I think Canada needs optionality so that it cannot be exploited. If you can walk away, you can’t be held up, right? So the idea is that Canada’s strategy changes the payoffs to U.S. behaviour.

Monday - Saturday Free

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

For example, suppose Canada exported only oil, and it could decide if it sends the oil to the U.S. or to somewhere else. Some minor decision. It’s the same oil. You don’t really care where it goes. It doesn’t really change your life. But it’s the industries that are highly reliant on access to the U.S. market that become hostage. So in part, those industries should have more options, and then you have to develop industries that give you more options.

Now, suddenly you are in an economy that has options; then the U.S. will want to deal with you, but they won’t be able to exploit you because the moment they start exploiting you, you have options. The U.S., after all, is 13 per cent of global imports. There’s a whole world out there.

As we say in the book, if the U.S. didn’t exist, Canada would look like Australia, and Australia is a happy place.

Hausmann: So we looked at industries that are what we call remoteness-resilient, industries that can source their inputs from far away and they can sell their wares far away because distance is less of an issue for them.

The ones we developed in the book were pharma, medical devices, aerospace, as examples of industries that have that characteristic. And the opposite example is industries like the car industry, the auto industry, that are super reliant on very tightly connected value chains, geographically connected value chains.

So it’s not that Canada’s car industry is highly connected to the U.S.; it’s that Ontario’s car industry is highly connected to Michigan and the Great Lakes. It’s more regional.

Hausmann: You have to assume that many things could happen in the U.S. You don’t want the economy to be that vulnerable to eventual returns of problems.

Eric Protzer: So in this other book that I’ve co-authored with Paul Somerville, “Reclaiming Populism,” we make the argument that countries with low social mobility are structurally vulnerable to populism, because you have few opportunities that are easily reachable from a precarious economic position. So when a shock hits, it’s very difficult to adjust.

People perceive the United States to be the land of opportunity, but that’s not empirically true. It, in fact, has some of the worst social mobility of any developed country.

So going forward, there’s vulnerability.

Hausmann: I think Trump is the setting, is the emergency, is the need to rethink.

And then we ask ourselves, “Why is it that a country that has such spectacular science, such excellent universities, and such generous innovation grants — why does it punch so low in innovation?” And that uncovered a bunch of other things that have nothing to do with Trump.

So we found there are these remoteness-resilient industries. They look promising. They look doable. Why have they not happened? And our answer is partly that they have not happened because the policy framework is not ideal.

Protzer: Generally, we’ve got a little bit of a “small is beautiful” approach to innovation. And in most industries in Canada, we’ve actually got a reasonably healthy pipeline of startups, but we have persistently struggled to scale those companies up.

That’s true in most sectors, but interestingly, there’s a major exception. It’s a very revealing exception, and it’s software and ICT.

It’s also systematically true that in the most successful innovating countries, it is the big companies that do the lion’s share of private sector R&D. So that inability to scale is really crucial, and the information that the software exception gives us is important because software is an industry that is not especially intensive in regulatory overhead or capital requirements to scale.

And those are two areas where Canada has somewhat notoriously struggled for quite a while.

Protzer: If you’re a new pharma company in Canada and you’re trying to do drug development, you have to go and get separate approvals from different hospitals in most of the country, and that increases your cost of drug development massively.

If you’ve then got your actual pharmaceutical developed and you want to bring that to market, you then go through this very lengthy procurement process that in Canada can take years, whereas in other high-income countries that do this really well, it can take a matter of months.

Canada has these steps that it does one after another, whereas other countries do them in parallel, all at the same time. So it’s much faster.

Protzer: My perception is that, in Canada, the big sticking point has been politics.

Think of the prospect of getting an oil pipeline through British Columbia. Logistically, it would have worked, and it could have been done during the global commodity supercycle. It’s just that there was disagreement: Alberta really wanted to do it, and British Columbia had very serious environmental concerns. So what are you going to do?

Hausmann: You have to have the ability to move your resources to where they’re demanded, and there’s plenty of global demand for them.

So there are many things that Canada can do with its resources. But interestingly, 80 per cent of the population growth in Canada, as we mention in the book, is happening in the 10 largest cities. And they’re not about natural resources.

So Canada needs another policy that enables those cities to be sources of value creation.

Hausmann: It’s that question of optionality. The U.S. is not the biggest importer of many of the things Canada exports. The world oil market is above a hundred million barrels, and Canada produces five.

There’s plenty of demand for oil in the world. There’s plenty of demand for wood and paper products in the world. There’s plenty of demand for agricultural products in the world.

All things being equal, you would want to sell in the U.S. and save yourself the transportation cost. But if the only thing that the U.S. can threaten you with is a slightly higher transportation cost, they don’t really have leverage over you.

But it’s the kind of industries that, if you don’t sell to the U.S., you don’t exist, that make you vulnerable.

Hausmann: Canada has a 35 per cent subsidy rate on R&D for small firms and 15 per cent for big firms. You have those R&D subsidies take the form of tax credits for big firms, and not grants.

And now tax credits means that you are able to deduct the R&D expenditure from your taxes, but that presumes that you’re making profits.

But also that you have a much lower rate of support for bigger firms than for smaller firms, and that means that the moment you grow enough, you lose the intensity of the support and some companies prefer to stay small.

Hausmann: We’re not proposing subsidies. That is, Canada is giving subsidies to sort of like sunset industries, where they’re playing defense.

Canada is a very, very small player in pharma. And in pharma, what you need is to come up with new drugs and come up with new medical devices.

So that’s our point: it’s the next big thing, not the things that used to be big and that are not and are now in trouble.

Hausmann: All the capabilities in metalworking that go into the car industry could potentially be repurposed for gas turbines. And gas turbines also are remoteness-resilient. You can sell them in many parts, and you can buy inputs broadly.

So gas turbines are one of the ones that we pointed out as being remoteness-resilient, and they are in super short supply in the world right now. Maybe Canada can repurpose some of its existing capacity in auto parts in that direction.

Hausmann: It’s much more chemistry than mechanics. So, it would be a transformation and not just a change of nationality. It’s a change of technology, sources of comparative advantage, technology areas that are involved, and so on. But it also talks about developing optionality.

Hausmann: Well, diversification itself reduces risk and gives you optionality. But this is in part also a message to the U.S. that if the U.S. thinks that its main adversary in the world is China, and it treats its main allies the way it does, it inevitably weakens its hand in dealing with China.

So part of the message is, we have options. Don’t push us too much because we have options. And that itself is what makes the U.S. strategy counterproductive to the U.S.

Hausmann: We think that Canada’s housing problems are growth problems. As good things happen in a city, and if any of the things that we say need to happen happen, you’re going to have more demand for labour in the city.

But if you don’t build more houses, then that demand for labour is going to translate into more demand for housing, no supply of housing, and just more expensive housing.

And then the industries that didn’t get the good shocks are going to feel that they need to pay their workers so that they can afford the housing, but they can’t, and so they shrink, and instead of all of these good things generating growth, it generates gentrification. The culprit is the elasticity of the supply of housing. It’s about how responsive housing supply is to housing demand.

Hausmann: If this strategy is followed, I would observe, number one, more income accruing to Canada out of its natural resources and agriculture. More income accruing to Canada out of its aerospace, pharma, medical device industries, and so on, that are going to touch other communities.

You have a lot of aerospace in Quebec. You have a lot of medical devices in the Waterloo-Kitchener area. And potentially elsewhere. You have a lot of natural resources in Alberta. You have potentially an interesting tech hub in Vancouver. So you would have different provinces participating in interesting ways and in new opportunities.

You would be a country where there would be fewer incentives for the U.S. to see how you can be exploited, and more incentives for the U.S. to see how they can partner with you. You would face a more manageable external environment.

Based in the U.S. capital region, Tracy Moran has covered Canada-U.S. relations for National Post since 2025. She previously reported on international news for DW, USA Today, Gzero Media and several online magazines. She holds a master’s degree in international affairs from George Washington University.

stories.title: High levels of toxic forever chemicals found near Newfoundland site, study finds
stories.summary: Residents downstream from St. John’s airport sue federal government, alleging contaminants fouled drinking water
stories.author: Patrick White, Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
More than two decades after firefighters last sprayed flame-dousing foam at a Newfoundland practice facility, high concentrations of toxic forever chemicals linked to those foams are still turning up several kilometres away, according to a new Memorial University paper.

The research, published earlier this month in the journal Environmental Science & Technology, appears to bolster the claims of residents living downstream of the St. John’s International Airport who are suing the federal government, alleging the chemicals have fouled their drinking water.

“The contamination the researchers found was significantly more widespread than even we had recognized,” said Ed Sheerr, one of the lead plaintiffs in a proposed class-action lawsuit on behalf of roughly 700 households in the area.

The lawsuit argues that per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) originating from the airport training facility have contaminated local well water, imperiling residents’ health and cratering property values. The plaintiffs are asking for immediate remediation and compensation for losses.

Transport Canada, the federal agency responsible for the site, has acknowledged using PFAS-laden foams but in a statement of defence, it has denied that any PFAS migrated from the airport to drinking water wells. The agency declined to comment on the results of the published scientific paper.

Transport Canada spokesperson Sau Sau Liu wrote in an e-mail that given the proposed class-action lawsuit “involving the Government of Canada, and out of respect for the judicial process, Transport Canada will not comment on matters before the court.”

Memorial researchers began sampling local water in December 2024, after learning that Transport Canada wasn’t testing private wells outside a designated subdivision near the airport where PFAS had been found.

“We got involved because we wanted to better understand the issue and provide free testing for folks who wanted that,” said Karl Jobst, a Memorial chemistry professor who worked on the study, which was led by PhD student Emmanuel Tolefe.

The researchers found the highest concentrations of PFAS in foams that naturally form on surface waters near the airport, with measurements reaching 2,000,000 nanograms per litre (ng/L), orders of magnitude higher than Health Canada drinking water guidelines of 30 ng/L.

Water samples near the airport were far lower, but still exceeded the federal guidelines, ranging from 318 to 2,302 ng/L.

Concentrations declined with distance from the airport, but levels remained well above drinking-water standards more than four kilometres away.

Researchers detected the chemicals in 32 of 42 private wells sampled. In seven of those wells, the PFAS levels exceeded the Health Canada guideline.

“It is concerning when these compounds are detectable above Health Canada’s drinking water guideline,” said Dr. Jobst, “They set that guideline for a reason.”

PFAS refers to a family of more than 6,000 synthetic chemicals. Prized for their resistance to heat, water and oil, they have been a common additive in non-stick cookware, waterproof clothing and stain-resistant furniture since the 1950s.

In more recent years, PFAS have been linked to kidney and testicular cancer, metabolic disruption, immune suppression, pregnancy complications and other adverse health effects.

One member of the chemical family, PFOS, was also a major component of fire-fighting foams used at the airport between 1982 and 2004.

The authors found that PFOS made up 62 per cent of the PFAS detected near the defunct practice facility.

Transport Canada has been delivering bottled water to Mr. Sheerr and other residents whose water exceeds the Health Canada threshold.

A Globe and Mail analysis last year found that eight communities across six provinces are in a similar position, relying on the federal government for bottled water to replace natural sources contaminated by PFAS.

Across the country, Ottawa has identified 86 federal properties where PFAS has fouled the groundwater.

The Memorial study could be a template for other communities seeking to map the spread of PFAS from contaminated sites. The researchers used novel spectrometry methods that allowed them to identify both well-known, regulated PFAS and those that are not readily identifiable using analyses.

Mr. Sheerr says he hopes the study will convince the government to work with residents rather than deny responsibility.

“Right now, every single day, I’m impacted by this,” he said. “We have to use bottled water for everything. And we’re not alone. There’s hundreds of families dealing with this and we just wanted to see it rectified.”

stories.title: There's been a 'generational shift' from daily drinking to daily cannabis use: study
stories.summary: Toronto - A new study says daily cannabis use has surpassed daily drinking in what the authors call a "generational shift" in substance use.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A new study says daily cannabis use has surpassed daily drinking in what the authors call a “generational shift” in substance use.

The research, published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, estimates that 1.8 million people in Canada use cannabis on a daily basis.

Using data from Statistics Canada, the researchers found that adults younger than 50 are more likely to use cannabis than drink alcohol every day.

But that trend stops at age 65, when alcohol becomes the preferred choice for people using substances daily.

In people under 35, using cannabis is more common than smoking cigarettes on a daily basis, especially among women.

Lead author André McDonald says it’s unhealthy to use any of these substances every day, but the results suggest more public health efforts need to focus on cannabis.

“If you’re using cannabis daily, that’s really strongly associated with cannabis use disorder,” said McDonald, who is a postdoctoral fellow at the Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research at McMaster University in Hamilton.

“Then there’s also, you know, if you’re smoking it every day, you’re being exposed to that smoke. It’s similar to cigarette smoking where that could pose risks to your lung health.”

McDonald said the study found about two-thirds of people using cannabis every day are smoking it rather than using edibles.

There hasn’t been as much research about the health effects of cannabis as there has been for alcohol and cigarettes, he said, but noted there’s some evidence linking it to psychotic disorders, as well as mood and anxiety disorders.

Addictions researcher Jibran Khokhar, who was not involved in the study, said the relationship between cannabis and mental health is a “chicken or egg question that we’re still trying to answer.”

One theory is that genetics or neural circuitry make people susceptible to both a mental disorder and excessive cannabis use, said Khokhar, who is the Canada Research Chair in translational neuropsychopharmacology at Western University in London, Ont.

Another theory is that using cannabis, especially when the brain is developing, could cause the mental disorder, he said.

Yet another variable is the fact that some people with mental health issues use cannabis to self-medicate.

“Be it real or not, and the jury’s still out on it, but a lot of people believe that cannabis helps them manage their symptoms.”

The study used data from 99,920 respondents to Statistics Canada’s 2023/2024 Canadian Community Health Survey.

McDonald said he would expect the same trends in daily cannabis use to continue if the survey was done today.

“If we kind of project forward, if these trends were to continue as they age, we would expect to see that in middle age, you know, in 10 to 15 years, that cannabis is going to become the predominant substance of choice for middle-aged people at that point,” he said.

“And so when you’re thinking about population health long-term, cannabis is kind of becoming more of an important priority.”

Limitations of the research included the fact that the survey responses are self-reported and could be affected by stigma that persists, even though cannabis has been legal in Canada since 2018, the study said.

The research also didn’t differentiate between daily cannabis use for medical and non-medical purposes.

Daily substance use by the numbers

The authors found that 5.7 per cent of adults reported daily cannabis use, representing about 1.8 million people in Canada.

They found that 5.2 per cent reported daily alcohol use and 8.5 per cent reported smoking cigarettes every day.

But much more pronounced differences showed up when the data was broken down by age group and gender.

Among men aged 25 to 34, 10.8 per cent reported using cannabis daily, compared to 2.9 per cent who said they drank alcohol every day and eight per cent who smoked daily.

Among women in that age group, 6.8 per cent used cannabis every day, 1.2 per cent drank alcohol and 4.5 per cent smoked cigarettes.

Among women aged 18 to 24, 6.6 per cent used cannabis every day, compared to less than one per cent who said they drank alcohol every day. Two per cent said they smoked cigarettes daily.

The authors said there was a similar pattern among men in that age group.

Among people 65 years of age and older, 13 per cent of men and 6.7 per cent of women drank alcohol daily. Only 3.3 per cent of older men and 2.3 per cent of older women used cannabis every day.

People who identified as gender diverse had the highest prevalence of cannabis use, with 22.6 per cent reporting they used it daily.

Two per cent of gender-diverse people said they drank alcohol every day and 9.7 per cent said they smoked daily.

—With files from Hannah Alberga

stories.title: Daily cannabis use more common among Canadian adults than daily alcohol consumption, study finds
stories.summary: Health experts warn regular consumption carries risks, such as developing psychosis
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Daily cannabis use is more common than alcohol among Canadian adults, and it is equal to or exceeds daily cigarette use among those younger than 35, says a new study in The Canadian Medical Association Journal.

The findings, released on Monday, were included in an examination of daily cannabis, alcohol and tobacco use. It involved nearly 100,000 respondents to the 2023-2024 Canadian Community Health Survey, a nationally representative survey of individuals age 18 and older.

“This study suggests a generational shift in substance use behaviours has taken place, which will likely have long-term implications for population health,” said lead author André McDonald, a psychiatric epidemiologist and Canadian Institutes of Health Research postdoctoral fellow at McMaster University’s Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research.

A study published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal says adults younger than 50 are more likely to use cannabis than drink alcohol on a daily basis. The Canadian Press

The research offers new insight on the impacts of cannabis legalization in Canada. It has been eight years since the country became the first major industrialized nation to legalize and regulate cannabis access for non-medical purposes in October 2018.

While cannabis use for adults has now been legal for a number of years, health experts say regular consumption carries risks, such as developing psychosis and schizophrenia. As well, a growing body of evidence suggests cannabis May be a risk factor for chronic disease.

Daniel Myran, a senior author of the study who is also the Cheesbrough research chair at North York General Hospital, said one of the most surprising findings was a substantial number of people who use cannabis daily do not drink alcohol or smoke cigarettes every day.

He said it is commonly assumed that regular cannabis smoking goes hand-in-hand with tobacco use, but this did not appear to be the case for almost two-thirds of those who use cannabis daily.

The study was funded through an award given to Dr. Myran through the Terry Fox Research Institute.

Researchers found daily cannabis use was the highest among males aged 25 to 34 years at 10.8 per cent, exceeding both daily alcohol use at 2.9 per cent and cigarette use at 8 per cent.

Opinion: Canada’s illegal cannabis problem was exported to Europe. Can we work together to stub it out?

A similar pattern was observed among females aged 25 to 34 years, for whom daily cannabis use 6.8 per cent, exceeding daily alcohol use at 1.2 per cent and to a lesser extent, daily cigarette use at 4.5 per cent, according to the study.

Previous research has examined changes in cannabis use over time, particularly in the context of its legalization in Canada in 2018. Most have found trends of increased use. By contrast, the research focused on daily use which its authors said is strongly associated with dependence, mental health problems and other adverse outcomes.

Among people aged 18 to 24 years, the study found daily cannabis use substantially exceeded both daily alcohol and cigarette use. For females in this age bracket, daily cannabis use, at 6.6 per cent, was markedly higher than alcohol use at 0.4 per cent. Cigarette use was 2 per cent, with similar patterns observed among male respondents.

“Declining cigarette use among younger people reflects sustained tobacco-control policies, changing social norms, reduced product appeal and accessibility and greater awareness of harms,” it added.

“Concurrent increases in cannabis use are consistent with its increasing availability, social acceptability, and normalization in the post legalization era.”

The research found that three in five who use cannabis daily did not report concurrent daily cigarette use and that nine in 10 did not report concurrent daily alcohol use.

Dr. Myran said one of the arguments for legalization and increasing the variety of products on the market was that it would shift people away from smoked cannabis to other forms of use, such as edibles, that May lower the risk for heart or lung disease or cancer.

However, the study’s findings do not support that hypothesis: 68 per cent of people who use cannabis daily reported that they smoke it.

The authors believe further research is needed to quantify the health impacts of changing substance use patterns because a significant proportion of those using cannabis daily started to do so after it became legal.

The research offers new insight on the impacts of cannabis legalization in Canada. It has been eight years since the country became the first major industrialized nation to legalize and regulate cannabis access for non-medical purposes in October 2018.

While cannabis use for adults has now been legal for a number of years, health experts say regular consumption carries risks, such as developing psychosis and schizophrenia. As well, a growing body of evidence suggests cannabis May be a risk factor for chronic disease.

Daniel Myran, a senior author of the study who is also the Cheesbrough research chair at North York General Hospital, said one of the most surprising findings was a substantial number of people who use cannabis daily do not drink alcohol or smoke cigarettes every day.
He said it is commonly assumed that regular cannabis smoking goes hand-in-hand with tobacco use, but this did not appear to be the case for almost two-thirds of those who use cannabis daily.
The study was funded through an award given to Dr. Myran through the Terry Fox Research Institute.
Researchers found daily cannabis use was the highest among males aged 25 to 34 years at 10.8 per cent, exceeding both daily alcohol use at 2.9 per cent and cigarette use at 8 per cent.
Opinion: Canada’s illegal cannabis problem was exported to Europe. Can we work together to stub it out?

A similar pattern was observed among females aged 25 to 34 years, for whom daily cannabis use 6.8 per cent, exceeding daily alcohol use at 1.2 per cent and to a lesser extent, daily cigarette use at 4.5 per cent, according to the study.

Previous research has examined changes in cannabis use over time, particularly in the context of its legalization in Canada in 2018. Most have found trends of increased use. By contrast, the research focused on daily use which its authors said is strongly associated with dependence, mental health problems and other adverse outcomes.

Among people aged 18 to 24 years, the study found daily cannabis use substantially exceeded both daily alcohol and cigarette use. For females in this age bracket, daily cannabis use, at 6.6 per cent, was markedly higher than alcohol use at 0.4 per cent. Cigarette use was 2 per cent, with similar patterns observed among male respondents.
“Declining cigarette use among younger people reflects sustained tobacco-control policies, changing social norms, reduced product appeal and accessibility and greater awareness of harms,” it added.
“Concurrent increases in cannabis use are consistent with its increasing availability, social acceptability, and normalization in the post legalization era.”
The research found that three in five who use cannabis daily did not report concurrent daily cigarette use and that nine in 10 did not report concurrent daily alcohol use.

Dr. Myran said one of the arguments for legalization and increasing the variety of products on the market was that it would shift people away from smoked cannabis to other forms of use, such as edibles, that May lower the risk for heart or lung disease or cancer.
However, the study’s findings do not support that hypothesis: 68 per cent of people who use cannabis daily reported that they smoke it.

The authors believe further research is needed to quantify the health impacts of changing substance use patterns because a significant proportion of those using cannabis daily started to do so after it became legal.

ByJason Miller Crime Reporter

Two men convicted in the 2023murder of a Canadian animation pioneer Daniel Langlois and his partnerDominque Marchand in the Caribbean island nation of Dominica have been sentenced to spend the remainder of their “whole life” in prison by a judge Monday.

Even though the case meets the mark of the “worst of the worst” killings in Dominica, Justice Sejilla McDowall said in the High Court of Justice in the island’s capital Roseau on Monday, she opted not to seek the death penalty, the maximum available punishment, noting that the defendants have no previous convictions, showed positive traits and displayed good prospects for rehabilitation.

She added it was an “unprovoked attack” of two respected people, which had “chilling community impact.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

Americans Jonathan Lehrer, 60 and Robert Snyder Jr., 66, were both found guilty of murder by a

“I’m satisfied in this case that the whole life sentence is appropriate,” she said.

Americans entrepreneur Jonathan Lehrer, 60, Robert Snyder Jr., 66, were both found guilty of murder by a jury in July. Both convicts listened on from the prisoners box inside the court Monday while flanked by security personnel.

Court documents revealed that both victims were known for their charitable work in their adopted home and just a month before the murder, Langlois had received a meritorious service award from the president of Dominica.

Langlois and Marchand were found dead in a burnt-out SUV not far from the off-grid mountaintop resort they owned on the island on Dec. 1, 2023. Four days later Lehrer and Snyder Jr., who was purportedly working for Lehrer as a mechanic, were arrested.

The state’s case was premised on the allegation that it was a “contract killing,” and that Lehrer hired Snyder to kill them, according to court filings.

Snyder was said to be a hit man who, armed with a licenced firearm belonging to Lehrer, who shot Langlois and Marchand as they returned to their home.

Special prosecutor Keith Scotland had argued that the “callousness” of the offenders makes it the “worst of the worst,” and that it was particularly aggravating that the men ambushed two victims, shot and burned them before attempting to conceal the bodies.

“It was planned and cold-blooded,” Scotland told the Star.

“This matter is appropriate for a whole life sentence,” the Scotland argued in sentencing submissions obtained by the Star.

More to come.

Jason Miller is a Toronto-based reporter for the Star covering crime and justice. Reach him on email: jasonmiller@thestar.ca or follow him on X: @millermotionpic.

stories.title: Cold case homicide solved using DNA evidence
stories.summary: London, ON (November 23, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section have solved the 1968 homicide of 16-year-old Jacqueline “Jackie” Dunleavy following an extensive review of historical evidence and the use of modern forensic DNA technology and Forensic Investigative Genetic Genealogy.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 23, 2026) –Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section have solved the 1968 homicide of 16-year-old Jacqueline “Jackie” Dunleavy following an extensive review of historical evidence and the use of modern forensic DNA technology and Forensic Investigative Genetic Genealogy.

Through the careful preservation and re-examination of evidence collected nearly six decades ago, investigators have identified Michael Joseph Moore, who was 25 years old at the time, as the individual responsible for Jackie’s murder.

Moore died on March 3, 2018, before he was identified through this investigation. As a result, no criminal charges can be laid.

At the time of Jackie’s murder, Moore had been living in London for less than a year. He was born in Ireland in 1942 and emigrated to Canada in January 1967. He moved into an apartment on Springbank Drive in May 1967. He was white, around six feet tall and had dark hair. Typically, he was clean shaven, but he would sometimes grow out a beard when he was on vacation.

“I want to acknowledge the tremendous work of our Major Crime Section and the investigators, forensic specialists, and partner agencies, the Ontario Provincial Police and Toronto Police Service, who contributed to this outcome.,” said Chief Thai Truong of the London Police Service. “Their collective efforts reflect the professionalism, persistence, and commitment that serious investigations demand.”

On Tuesday, January 9, 1968, Jackie was working at the Stanley Variety Store on Stanley Street near Wharncliffe Road. She finished her shift at approximately 6:30 p.m. and was last seen leaving the store on foot.

At approximately 8 p.m. that evening, three youths found Jackie on the grounds of Katherine Harley School, now known as the location of Matthews Hall, ON Oxford Street. Emergency responders attended, and Jackie was pronounced deceased.

The investigation determined that Jackie had been murdered. While she had suffered a head injury, the cause of death was determined to be strangulation.

Jackie was 16 years old and a Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School.

At the time, investigators conducted an extensive homicide investigation. Numerous leads were pursued, witnesses were interviewed, and forensic evidence, including biological material, was collected and carefully preserved. Despite those efforts, the person responsible was not identified, and the case remained unsolved.

Over the years, generations of investigators continued to review the case as new investigative opportunities emerged. This included being part of Project Angel, a joint London Police Service and Ontario Provincial Police project that ran from 1997 to 2001. More recently, members of the Major Crime Section undertook a comprehensive review of the investigation, re-examining historical evidence and exploring advances in forensic science.

“The investigators who worked on Jackie’s homicide in 1968 did everything they could with the investigative and forensic tools available to them at the time,” said Detective Sergeant Micah Bourdeau of the London Police Service Major Crime Section. “The evidence they carefully collected and preserved ultimately allowed investigators decades later to continue that work. This investigation shows the importance of preserving evidence and continuing to revisit historical cases as new technology becomes available.”

Using modern forensic techniques, additional DNA testing and analysis was conducted on preserved evidence.

“Through specialized forensic testing conducted by Othram, investigators were able to identify distant genetic relatives associated with the unknown suspect's DNA profile," said Detective Mike Budzyn of the London Police Service Major Crime Section and the current lead investigator. "Working with our partners at the Toronto Police Service, genealogical research was then used to construct family trees and narrow the investigation toward a potential suspect. Our investigators conducted additional interviews, gathered new evidence, and obtained DNA samples for comparison. Those samples were submitted to the Centre of Forensic Sciences for analysis. Based on the evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met. Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged in relation to Jackie’s murder.”

The decision to publicly identify Moore was not made lightly. It followed careful consideration of the evidence, the public interest and the responsibility of the London Police Service to be transparent about the outcome of an investigation that had remained unresolved for nearly six decades.

While criminal proceedings are no longer possible due to Moore’s death, that does not diminish the strength of the evidence or the confidence investigators have in the conclusion reached through this investigation. Publicly identifying Moore provides an accurate historical record and answers that Jackie’s family and the community have sought for decades.

The London Police Service recognizes the important contributions of the Centre of Forensic Sciences, Othram Laboratories, the Toronto Police Service and the Ontario Provincial Police. The DNA profile that ultimately assisted investigators was also connected to earlier work completed through Project Angel. These partnerships, along with advances in forensic science and the work of generations of investigators, played an important role in moving the investigation forward.

While the investigation has identified the person responsible for Jackie’s murder, investigators recognize there May still be people with historical information. Hearing the name Michael Joseph Moore, or learning information about him today, May bring back memories for people who knew him, had contact with him or were familiar with him during that time. Information that May not have seemed significant at the time could have meaning today.

Anyone with information related to this investigation, or who believes they May have relevant historical information, is encouraged to contact the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

He moved into an apartment on Springbank Drive in May 1967. He was white, around six feet tall and had dark hair. Typically, he was clean shaven, but he would sometimes grow out a beard when he was on vacation.

“I want to acknowledge the tremendous work of our Major Crime Section and the investigators, forensic specialists, and partner agencies, the Ontario Provincial Police and Toronto Police Service, who contributed to this outcome.,” said Chief Thai Truong of the London Police Service. “Their collective efforts reflect the professionalism, persistence, and commitment that serious investigations demand.”

On Tuesday, January 9, 1968, Jackie was working at the Stanley Variety Store on Stanley Street near Wharncliffe Road. She finished her shift at approximately 6:30 p.m. and was last seen leaving the store on foot.

At approximately 8 p.m. that evening, three youths found Jackie on the grounds of Katherine Harley School, now known as the location of Matthews Hall, ON Oxford Street. Emergency responders attended, and Jackie was pronounced deceased.
The investigation determined that Jackie had been murdered. While she had suffered a head injury, the cause of death was determined to be strangulation.
Jackie was 16 years old and a Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School.

At the time, investigators conducted an extensive homicide investigation. Numerous leads were pursued, witnesses were interviewed, and forensic evidence, including biological material, was collected and carefully preserved. Despite those efforts, the person responsible was not identified, and the case remained unsolved.

Over the years, generations of investigators continued to review the case as new investigative opportunities emerged. This included being part of Project Angel, a joint London Police Service and Ontario Provincial Police project that ran from 1997 to 2001. More recently, members of the Major Crime Section undertook a comprehensive review of the investigation, re-examining historical evidence and exploring advances in forensic science.

“The investigators who worked on Jackie’s homicide in 1968 did everything they could with the investigative and forensic tools available to them at the time,” said Detective Sergeant Micah Bourdeau of the London Police Service Major Crime Section. “The evidence they carefully collected and preserved ultimately allowed investigators decades later to continue that work. This investigation shows the importance of preserving evidence and continuing to revisit historical cases as new technology becomes available.”
Using modern forensic techniques, additional DNA testing and analysis was conducted on preserved evidence.

“Through specialized forensic testing conducted by Othram, investigators were able to identify distant genetic relatives associated with the unknown suspect's DNA profile," said Detective Mike Budzyn of the London Police Service Major Crime Section and the current lead investigator. "Working with our partners at the Toronto Police Service, genealogical research was then used to construct family trees and narrow the investigation toward a potential suspect. Our investigators conducted additional interviews, gathered new evidence, and obtained DNA samples for comparison. Those samples were submitted to the Centre of Forensic Sciences for analysis. Based on the evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met. Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged in relation to Jackie’s murder.”

The decision to publicly identify Moore was not made lightly. It followed careful consideration of the evidence, the public interest and the responsibility of the London Police Service to be transparent about the outcome of an investigation that had remained unresolved for nearly six decades.

While criminal proceedings are no longer possible due to Moore’s death, that does not diminish the strength of the evidence or the confidence investigators have in the conclusion reached through this investigation. Publicly identifying Moore provides an accurate historical record and answers that Jackie’s family and the community have sought for decades.

The London Police Service recognizes the important contributions of the Centre of Forensic Sciences, Othram Laboratories, the Toronto Police Service and the Ontario Provincial Police. The DNA profile that ultimately assisted investigators was also connected to earlier work completed through Project Angel. These partnerships, along with advances in forensic science and the work of generations of investigators, played an important role in moving the investigation forward.

While the investigation has identified the person responsible for Jackie’s murder, investigators recognize there May still be people with historical information. Hearing the name Michael Joseph Moore, or learning information about him today, May bring back memories for people who knew him, had contact with him or were familiar with him during that time. Information that May not have seemed significant at the time could have meaning today.
Anyone with information related to this investigation, or who believes they May have relevant historical information, is encouraged to contact the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Understanding Canada’s commitment to the $100 million Nato Innovation Fund
stories.summary: The Nato Innovation Fund is a multi-sovereign venture capital fund that invests in technology, industries and start up businesses connected to security and defense.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - The Nato Innovation Fund is a multi-sovereign venture capital fund that invests in technology, industries and start up businesses connected to security and defense.

Canada is contributing more than $100 million and is now one of 25 Nato-allied nations that form the fund’s membership.

“Opening new opportunities for investment in Canadian startups and innovation funds,” said Defence Minister David McGuinty, when describing the fund while speaking the at the Halifax International Security Forum. McGuinty also announced defence businesses in Canada will have access to more than €1 billion, more than $1.5 billion which is managed by the fund.

“We have the talent, we have the technology and partnerships to lead,” said McGuinty. “And today we are giving Canadian innovators greater access to the capital and the opportunities they need to succeed.”

McGuinty also suggested, Canada joining the Nato Innovation Fund is designed to diversity and strengthen its defence partnerships with European allies.

“And that should be significant,” said retired navy commander and defence analyst Ken Hansen.

Hansen said as Canada’s relationship with the U.S. continues to be strained, the federal government is shifting its focus to overseas partnerships, beyond its existing transactions and agreements with south of the border.

“The Prime Minister has been plain about how he sees the Canada-U.S. relationship, especially when it comes to defense,” said Hansen. “He does not want to be limited, and he does not want to be sandwiched.”

The U.S. is not a part of the Nato Innovation Fund -- in fact Canada is the only North American member of the fund

Democratic Virginia Sen. Andy Kim suggested this as another example of the gap widening between the countries.

“We don’t want partners to be working around us,” said Kim. “We want them to be working with us.”

Hansen predicted the fund will eventually support a multitude of Canadian businesses, entrepreneurs and defence contractors.

“This should be seed money for more good things,” Hansen said, and added it is a move aimed at enhancing Canada’s security, while pivoting away from the U.S. and building new defence partnerships.

November 22, 2026 at 6:43 p.m.

The U.S. and Canada are “fairly close” to signing a trade deal, Washington’s chief trade negotiator has said.

In an interview with Fox News on Sunday morning, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said both sides have made “a lot of progress” toward “finding a landing zone.”

Greer’s comments followed what he called a “bipartisan” consensus that Canada seeking deeper economic ties with China was a “concern.”

Canada is “actually having a little bit of a rapprochement on trade with China,” he said, citing Canada’s decision to lower tariffs on Chinese vehicles, steel and aluminum. In January, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that Canada would allow domestic imports of up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a reduced tariff rate of 6.1 percent, down from 100.

“Our view is this: this goes a little bit backwards,” Greer said, explaining that the differences came down to policy.

“We’re trying to manage North American trade in auto steel and aluminum; they’ve always been more inclined to free trade and open trade,” he said.

“We’re more inclined to fixing the challenges of globalization,” while Canada is more interested in “doubling down,” he added.

“I think it’s a philosophical difference, and we’re trying to square the circle between their economy and ours, because we are close — we are integrated.”

Greer had neared a trade deal with Canada in August on a swath of goods, including steel, aluminum and autos. But the deal was scuppered after a last-minute intervention by U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department oversees Section 232 national security tariffs imposed on those three imports.

U.S. tariffs on Canadian vehicles are set to double from 25 to 50 per cent in January, putting thousands of jobs at risk. As National Post previously reported, Carney has suggested Canada could seek investment from Chinese automakers to protect the sector.

Still, Greer noted in the interview that talks were “constructive” and that Canada remains a close trade partner.

“The vast majority of goods going back and forth between Canada and the United States still are duty-free, still supporting a lot of jobs on both sides of the border,” he said. “So it’s a more positive story, I think, than people realize.”

Greer concluded that the U.S. wants “to make sure that we’re protecting the North American economy while also landing at a deal that’s good for the United States and good for Canada.”
