stories.title: Ontario Liberals to name new leader after weeks of voting, months of campaigning
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario Liberals are getting ready to name their new party leader, with results from members' ranked ballots set to be revealed later today.
stories.author: Allison Jones and Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Former MP Navdeep Bains eked out a narrow victory Saturday to become the next Ontario Liberal leader, pledging to focus now on uniting the party and getting it in fighting shape for the next election.

Bains received 50.3 per cent of the vote on the third and final ballot at the party’s leadership convention, just a few points ahead of his next closest competitor, provincial caucus member and former hospital executive Lee Fairclough, who received 49.7 per cent of the vote.

After the results were announced in front of a crowd of more than 1,000 Liberals gathered in downtown Toronto, Bains took to the stage thanking his fellow contestants.

Ontario Liberals have selected Navdeep Bains as their new leader, emerging as victor less than one percentage point ahead of his next closest competitor, provincial caucus member Lee Fairclough. After receiving 50.3 per cent of the vote on the third and final ballot at the party’s leadership convention, Bains took to the stage and thanked his fellow contestants. (Nov. 21, 2026)

“This May be the end of a leadership race, ladies and gentlemen, but this is just the beginning of our campaign to replace Doug Ford and the (Progressive) Conservative Party of Ontario,” he said.

Bains is likely to face several hurdles on that road, including not having a seat in the legislature. His two predecessors were also without a seat and some party members had suggested during this race that it was time to select a leader who already has a voice in Queen’s Park.

He suggested at a media availability later in the day that he does want to seek a seat, but does not yet have a plan for when and where.

“I’ll definitely be running, and the determination around the exact location will be made at the appropriate time,” he said.

From outside the party, Bains is likely to face opposition attacks based on his past with the Justin Trudeau federal government. Progressive Conservative cabinet minister Graham McGregor, speaking at the leadership event as an observer, congratulated Bains but gave a preview of the narrative critics are looking to build.

“Certainly, in my region in Peel, we remember well when he was one of the biggest supporters of Justin Trudeau, not only as prime minister but when he was running for Liberal leader in the first place,” McGregor said.

“So we know that connection very well. I think Ontarians know that well.”

Bains conceded that the next several years before an election that May happen as late as 2030 won’t be easy.

“It’s going to be hard,” he said. “It’s going to be really, really hard. But we’re in it together.”

Bains is new to provincial elected office, but previously represented Mississauga ridings federally as a Liberal MP for 13 years, and served as federal minister of innovation, science and industry.

Before entering politics he was a senior financial analyst at Ford Motor Company, and after leaving Parliament in 2021, he worked as an executive at Cibc and later at Rogers Communications.

He spoke in his victory speech about his family, in particular his parents, who moved to Ontario 50 years ago from a small village in Rajasthan in India. His dad learned cabinet-making as a trade and his mother worked the night shift at a factory, he said.

This province provided opportunities for his parents and for himself, Bains said, and he worries that those same opportunities are no longer available.

“One in four people in my community of Mississauga visit the food bank, who have a job, who have multiple jobs, who play by the rules and are falling further and further behind,” he said. “The reason why that is, is because Doug Ford and the Conservatives have abandoned the fight, they are not in it for the people.”

Bains becomes the party’s third leader since former premier Kathleen Wynne resigned following the party’s sweeping defeat in the 2018 election.

Steven Del Duca was chosen as leader in 2020 but resigned two years later after a disappointing election result, and Bonnie Crombie served as leader from late 2023 until early this year, when she left following a weak leadership vote at an annual general meeting.

This leadership race started with five contestants and ended with four, as housing advocate Eric Lombardi dropped out partway through. Former government staffer Dylan Marando finished last, with 9.3 per cent of the vote on the first ballot.

He was dropped for the second ballot, ON which provincial caucus member and former bank executive Stephanie Bowman finished last, with 15.7 per cent.

In a speech before the results were announced, Bowman said that at the end of the day, some people in the room would be disappointed.

“Of course they will, but I’m asking you to keep showing up, keep working for our party and our province,” she said. “We came into this room as four teams. We must leave as one.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.

stories.title: B.C.’s new government must make the province an easier place to grow a modern economy
stories.summary: Too many of the province’s best and brightest are moving elsewhere to build their companies
stories.author: Dan Burgar
stories.content:
Dan Burgar is the founder and CEO of Frontier Collective.

David Eby’s own-goal election call has given British Columbians a new government and a chance for bold action to fix B.C.’s economy.

In Vancouver, voters also opted for change in electing Pete Fry as mayor.

Premier Lorne Doerkson, a B.C. Conservative sworn in on Friday, deserves credit for his focus on economic issues. He will now have serious work to do.

Decades of bipartisan neglect has led to a budget deficit of $13.3-billion atop ever-increasing debt. We are years behind in implementing a real innovation agenda to build an economy that will dig us out of the hole.

The province had been coasting on its worthy foundations of resources, real estate and a very talented population. But we cannot count on major federal projects to carry the entire resource sector, property is in a downturn and the population growth that papered over economic cracks is finished.

I’ve spent the last decade building innovation ecosystems with Frontier Collective, and I’m seeing an accelerating number of very talented workers and company founders leaving for places that make it easier to start a business and attract the risk capital they need to scale up.

If we don’t invest now in growth and keeping our best companies and people here, amid one of the biggest technological revolutions ever, we risk becoming a place where great companies are born but create wealth somewhere else.

B.C. should be backing our best people, leading at the technological frontier and creating conditions for companies to make long-term bets.

A successful innovation economy will require, above all, a new approach. What’s holding us back? Let’s begin in Vancouver.

Municipal decisions are more important than we think. Mr. Fry should speed up and liberalize permitting and zoning for innovation, lab and advanced manufacturing space. Delays mean lost opportunities.

Vancouver city council has already debated reviving and accelerating a central technology and innovation hub to serve as the centre of gravity for its ecosystem. This is a kind of “third space” where deal-making happens, people collaborate on prototypes in shared labs, and teams from different industries create new product and service crossovers to mutual benefit.

Newlab in Brooklyn and Station F in Paris are great entrepreneur-run (not government-run) examples to look to. It’s the kind of engine and flywheel setup that’s powered by in-person collaboration that just can’t happen over Zoom. The next council should move beyond debate and create the conditions for it to happen, while encouraging a pro-business environment everywhere.

Our inability to build enough affordable housing drives high costs that ripple throughout the economy, one of the main reasons for top talent and founders leaving (or not even considering) B.C.

Much municipal funding for day-to-day spending on infrastructure comes from development charges and permit fees that, together, can add many thousands of dollars to the cost of each new housing unit. Do new leaders (and voters) have the courage to reform municipal taxation, unlock much-needed new housing and bring down housing costs?

City and provincial procurement should also give local startups the “anchor” customer they May need to go from zero to one, powering local jobs and economies instead of giant foreign vendors. We must make municipal and provincial procurement a legitimate first-customer pathway for B.C. startups. City-owned land is another growth lever that can be powered up for mixed-use leases and development with little upfront spending.

On the provincial side, continuing to delay more serious investment will cost us talent, companies and capital deployed elsewhere. Retaining and scaling B.C.-founded companies must be an explicit economic development goal with measurable outcomes.

Voters should ask our new provincial government what they will do to work with municipalities to drive down the cost and complexity that gets in the way of people finding or building places to live and work.

A new government cannot turn B.C. into Silicon Valley overnight, nor should it, but it can turn B.C. into an easier place to start and grow the companies of the future.

Key questions: How fast can a company start? Can it hire the best people from anywhere? Can it access capital? And can it scale up without moving to Seattle, San Jose or Toronto?

The new Conservative government also has an opportunity to link our resource, energy and innovation sectors thanks to B.C.’s clean power advantage for AI and computer centres. Innovation need not happen in silos; better connecting B.C. tech companies with the resource sector and its wealth of experience will lead to more profitable and greener resource projects.

The window of opportunity to put our economy on firmer footing is only a few years, not decades, and every cycle we wait costs us the founders and companies we most want to keep.

British Columbians have voted for change. It is now up to our new leaders to deliver and be bold in this existential moment for B.C.

stories.title: Ucp’s direction is a battleground as Smith fails to purge separatists from party
stories.summary: The party’s future is expected to be a major focus at next week’s annual meeting – the first post-referendum
stories.author: Matthew Scace, Carrie Tait
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has failed to purge separatists from the United Conservative Party’s leadership ranks, a month after decreeing that officials within her organization must be committed to federalism.

Further, Ms. Smith’s demand that all local party presidents stop advocating for Alberta’s secession has aggravated independence advocates and free-speech absolutists ahead of the Ucp’s annual meeting next weekend in Calgary.

“We are bitterly divided,” Vince Byfield, once one of Ms. Smith’s most reliable supporters, said at a UCP forum this week.

Ms. Smith has begged her fellow conservatives to focus on winning the 2027 provincial election, which she said will require abandoning the quest for secession given that 75 per cent of Albertans rejected the idea in a referendum last month.

She first encouraged Albertans to drop the issue in a televised address after the vote, and again the next day when she told UCP members that separatist agitators were no longer welcome in the party. In late October, her party asked all candidates in the Ucp’s coming board elections to sign a pledge committing to respect the referendum results. It has recently expanded that request to its 87 constituency association presidents.

But many of the movement’s leaders are prominent players in the UCP and believe most party members want the organization to continue pushing for separation.

The Premier’s inability to quell dissent means UCP members will, once again, battle over the party’s direction and focus at what is expected to be a raucous annual meeting. The organization has sold roughly 7,000 tickets to the event, where members will elect eight people to the party’s provincial board, which influences the Ucp’s strategy, policies and politics.

While the candidates are largely split between two slates, their histories reveal deeper divisions within the party. Mr. Byfield is challenging incumbent Patrick Malkin, a senior official in the Premier’s office, for a vice-president position. Both men first won spots on the provincial board in the fall of 2022, as part of a populist wave that just weeks prior had helped Ms. Smith become party leader.

Now, Mr. Malkin is on the Team Unity slate backing Ms. Smith, and Mr. Byfield is informally aligned with the separatist cluster of candidates.

Dozens of UCP members gathered on Wednesday evening at a private Christian academy in south Calgary for an event dubbed the “Cowtown Showdown,” to hear board candidates make their pitch.

TJ Schmidt, who is running against a Team Unity candidate for a vice-president position, compared the party’s proclivity for infighting to an Olympian with an immune system prone to illness.

“It pits about half the cells in the body against the other half,” he told the crowd. “That strength is still there for that athlete, but it’s turned inwards to fight itself.”

At the end of October, the UCP stripped boisterous independence leader Jeffrey Rath of his membership. At the Ucp’s annual meeting last year, Mr. Rath whipped up the crowd in support of secession; the audience booed Ms. Smith when she responded by touting Alberta’s renewed relationship with Ottawa.

Mr. Rath’s removal gave credibility to Ms. Smith’s post-referendum promise to focus on the 2027 election. Party members, including separatist sympathizers, cheered his removal.

However, large pockets within the party have rejected Ms. Smith’s broader housecleaning effort.

Earlier this month, the UCP demanded its 87 constituency association presidents respect and abide by the results of October’s referendum question on separation, effectively ordering them to stop publicly pushing for independence. The deadline elapsed without full compliance.

Fifteen presidents openly defied Ms. Smith by releasing a letter stating the dictate exceeded the party’s power. The signatories include Mitch Sylvestre, a key separatist organizer who fiercely supported the Premier in the past.

Ms. Smith has yet to specify – let alone mete out – consequences for refusing to comply. Instead, she said last week that she would continue her persuasion campaign.

The party brass has not yet discussed repercussions, according to UCP president Rob Smith, who defended the organization’s decree. “Is it not reasonable to actually expect those individuals to recognize, respect and abide by a decision that was made by 75 per cent of Albertans?”

Mr. Smith, who is not up for re-election this year and is not related to the Premier, declined to share his position on separation, but said he is “satisfied that the issue has been laid to rest.”

Asked whether he believes the secession conversation is over within the UCP, Mr. Smith said: “In the short term, it is.”

UCP spokesman Dave Prisco backed the Premier’s diplomatic approach to dissent.

“We’re going to work with people respectfully,” he said in an e-mailed statement.

The outcome of October’s referendum question on separation raised the stakes in the fight for control over the Ucp’s provincial board and the makeup of its constituency associations. Ms. Smith could face a leadership review if two-thirds of the provincial directors vote in favour of a special general meeting, or if 22 of 87 constituency associations call for one.

Board candidates running with the Team Unity slate launched an e-mail blitz this week.

“We must stand united behind our party’s leader, Danielle Smith and her call to respect the results of the recent referendum and, as a party, commit to a strong Alberta within a United Canada,” Ken Engler, a candidate for the party’s chief financial officer, said in an e-mail.

Mr. Engler, who did not acknowledge an interview request, was first elected treasurer in 2022, after serving as Ms. Smith’s CFO during her leadership campaign. He does not currently sit on the board.

While the UCP expects record crowds at its annual meeting, and the voting booths will only be open for five hours, Mr. Engler encouraged prospective attendees to be in the main convention hall for Saturday’s keynote address.

“Hear Premier Smith speak and cheer her on.”

stories.title: ‘A wake-up call’: Experts raise alarm over drone incursions at Canadian military bases
stories.summary: A series of drone incursions over Canadian military bases should serve as a wake-up call for the federal government, defence experts say, as questions remain about the country’s ability to detect and defend against the growing threat.
stories.author: Jeremie Charron
stories.content:
A series of drone incursions over Canadian military bases should serve as a wake-up call for the federal government, defence experts say, as questions remain about the country’s ability to detect and defend against the growing threat.

CTV News has learned there have been at least seven drone incursions over Canadian military bases since 2024, including incidents in which counter-drone technologies struggled or failed to detect the aircraft.

Whether any of the incidents were considered hostile or involved malicious intent remains unclear.

“This is a wake-up call,” said retired Maj.-Gen. David Fraser, a CTV military analyst. “I think Canadians should be concerned and asking questions.”

Fraser said the threat posed by drones is evolving rapidly, raising concerns about Canada’s ability to keep pace.

“The world is more dangerous than it ever has been,” he said. “Drone technology is evolving much more rapidly than, in fact, what it appears. Canada can keep up.”

The Department of National Defence declined to comment on the specific incidents, citing operational security.

However, the department said it has “procurement activities planned to support the continued evolution and enhancement of its approach to countering UAS (drone) threats.”

In July, the federal government launched its Defence Drone Initiative, earmarking $2.3 billion for the effort in Budget 2026.

Some counter-drone systems have been deployed at military bases and ports, but Canada’s overall drone defence capabilities remain limited.

Conservative defence critic James Bezan says the government has failed to equip the military with the technology needed to address the threat.

“By not having that technology in place that actually works to deal with the counter-drone efforts that we need to have across this country is a failure of the government,” Bezan said.

He argues every military installation needs the ability to protect personnel and infrastructure from potential surveillance or attacks.

“Every one of our wings and bases across this country need to have the technology to protect our aviators, our sailors, our soldiers to ensure that they’re not being spied on,” he said.

“We need to ensure that counter-drone technology is at the forefront to ensure that we’re protecting both the soldier in theatre as well as our bases and our infrastructure across this country.”

Al Viger, a former Canadian army member who now leads Vancouver-based technology company Caseway AI, develops software for counter-drone systems.

He says Canada needs to move quickly to ensure the technology it purchases can effectively address the threat.

“We need to find a way to act really fast and to make sure the things that we’re buying are actually useful, that they work,” Viger said.

He also added that counter-drone rules tied to federal laws in Canada have a great impact on the extent to which drone’s can be countered in the country.

“We actually have the laws to enable us to intercept the drones, to shoot down the drones,” said Viger.

“This technology does exist, and it can be bought,” he added. “From a tech perspective, absolutely, this could be deployed very fast. Politically, probably non-Canada.”

Fraser also cautions against becoming complacent as drone technology continues to advance, arguing Canada needs a strategy that prioritizes both procurement and innovation.

“You should never have the complacency to think that it’s good enough,” he said. “We need to anticipate and adapt and have a procurement strategy and innovation strategy that’s going to get the latest equipment and get it into the hands of the people who need it to protect our infrastructure, including the military.”

Defence experts and the political opposition are urging the government to make drone and counter-drone capabilities a higher priority, warning that the threat is evolving faster than Canada’s ability to respond.

stories.title: The exorcist: Alleged cult leader says she can drive out demons
stories.summary: Liana Shanti, the spiritual teacher ordered to pay three Canadians $56 million for defamation, has posted her first public exorcism video.
stories.author: Derek Miller, Avery Haines
stories.content:
An American alleged cult leader who was ordered to pay three Canadians more than $56 million in a defamation case claims she is an exorcist and that a former supporter’s son will soon be possessed by a demon.

Liana Shanti, whose legal name is Liane Wilson, is an online Hawaii-based spiritual teacher who says she has performed several exorcisms. An exorcism is a religious ceremony that purports to drive out demons from people who are possessed by them.

This week on an online publishing platform, she wrote that she’s performed the controversial religious rites over the past 10 years. She says all of those were done one-on-one and in private.

Alleged cult leader claims COVID vaccines opened the door to demons

“[T]oday I did something I have never done in my life…I filmed and posted my first Anointed Deliverance video on Instagram…an exorcism,” says her post.

In the video she refers to, posted on Tuesday, Liana Shanti isn’t performing a ritual on another person, but is being filmed in a room on her own speaking directly to camera.

“I now revoke every form of access for every demon that tried to enter you through the mRNA technology,” she says in an apparent reference to the COVID-19 vaccine. Shanti has long railed against the vaccines, repeating conspiracy theories that say they are dangerous and calling them part of “Satan’s plan.”

Claims former student is ‘possessed’

Shanti’s recent postings on exorcism take direct aim at a Canadian former-follower.

Amanda Brady from Regina was a student of Liana Shanti for eight years. She now believes she was under the influence of a cult leader and testified against her at her August defamation trial in Honolulu.

Liana Shanti claims to have performed five exorcisms on one of Amanda Brady’s children and now says that the child will be in “Full Demonic Posession [sic]” “within three years.”

“I saw the face of the demon in [the child],” says the Instagram post. “The child has no control. This demon is growing stronger. Daily.”

Shanti also writes that “the demon” she refers to “fully occupies Amanda herself.”

In a phone interview with W5, Amanda Brady says the online attacks were expected and she refuses to let them hurt her.

“I really don’t put any weight into what she’s saying because she can be so cruel and she’s so vindictive and all of this is coming from a place of rage and anger,” she says. “She’s not out there right now doing God’s work and anybody who believes that is sorely mistaken.”

Brady adds that she believes Liana Shanti is attacking her to send a message to her current students.

“All of this is to intimidate those who are still there to make sure that they know what’s going to happen to them if they leave,” she says.

“She’s trying to intimidate me. She’s trying to intimidate every other woman from the community who’s watching this from speaking,” she says.

The message from Jesus

In her online blog , Liana Shanti tells the story of performing her very first exorcism – which she also calls a “deliverance” - on an Australian woman 10 years ago. She writes that the woman complained about having nightmares and “weird, negative thoughts.”

“I knew instantly it was a demonic energy,” she writes. “Since the age of two I have been able to see and feel the presence of demons.”

She writes that she was reluctant to perform the exorcism but was convinced by Jesus.

“I kept saying to Jesus… I do not know how. I do not know how to do this. I have never done this. I do not know how. And Jesus said… YOU DO,” she writes.

She says the moment the demon was cast out, the Australian woman told her that a gust of wind blew through her room and knocked over an essential oil diffuser.

Shanti claims the cause of the “demonic possession” was the husband’s pornography habit.

Driving out demons is not the only supernatural power that Liana Shanti claims to have.

In the W5 documentary, Fake Filtered Cult Leader , former students say the spiritual teacher claimed to be psychic and would repeatedly state that followers had been sexually abused as children. She then encouraged them to publicly “out” the alleged abusers and cut off all contact with them.

Many believed her and with devastating results, including family breakups.

Followers shared several screenshots of those so-called psychic confirmations with W5.

Shanti suggests W5 reporter May have been sexually abused

As an example of how quickly and cavalierly Shanti makes suggestions of past childhood sexual abuse, after the W5 documentary aired, Shanti took to Instagram to write about W5 correspondent and managing editor, Avery Haines.

Shanti wrote that one of the motives for W5 investigating the alleged cult May be that Avery “has deeply repressed CSA (childhood sexual abuse} from around age 4 and is doing this to reaffirm her own denial.”

In August, a Hawaii-jury found that Liana Shanti, aka Liane Wilson, defamed three Canadians from Saskatchewan for calling them Satanists, child abusers and pedophile supporters. The jury awarded the trio C$56 million. That money has not been paid out and Shanti says she plans to appeal.

Shanti has publicly stated that she will litigate her “facts” about the Canadians, and other former followers online. She has continued to post allegations similar to what the jury found to be defamatory.

content_blocks.text: An American alleged cult leader who was ordered to pay three Canadians more than $56 million in a defamation case claims she is an exorcist and that a former supporter’s son will soon be possessed by a demon.

Liana Shanti, whose legal name is Liane Wilson, is an online Hawaii-based spiritual teacher who says she has performed several exorcisms. An exorcism is a religious ceremony that purports to drive out demons from people who are possessed by them.
This week on an online publishing platform, she wrote that she’s performed the controversial religious rites over the past 10 years. She says all of those were done one-on-one and in private.
Alleged cult leader claims COVID vaccines opened the door to demons
“[T]oday I did something I have never done in my life…I filmed and posted my first Anointed Deliverance video on Instagram…an exorcism,” says her post.
In the video she refers to, posted on Tuesday, Liana Shanti isn’t performing a ritual on another person, but is being filmed in a room on her own speaking directly to camera.

“I now revoke every form of access for every demon that tried to enter you through the mRNA technology,” she says in an apparent reference to the COVID-19 vaccine. Shanti has long railed against the vaccines, repeating conspiracy theories that say they are dangerous and calling them part of “Satan’s plan.”

content_blocks.caption: Liana Shanti says a former student’s child will soon be possessed.

content_blocks.text: Claims former student is ‘possessed’
Shanti’s recent postings on exorcism take direct aim at a Canadian former-follower.

Amanda Brady from Regina was a student of Liana Shanti for eight years. She now believes she was under the influence of a cult leader and testified against her at her August defamation trial in Honolulu.
Liana Shanti claims to have performed five exorcisms on one of Amanda Brady’s children and now says that the child will be in “Full Demonic Posession [sic]” “within three years.”
“I saw the face of the demon in [the child],” says the Instagram post. “The child has no control. This demon is growing stronger. Daily.”
Shanti also writes that “the demon” she refers to “fully occupies Amanda herself.”
In a phone interview with W5, Amanda Brady says the online attacks were expected and she refuses to let them hurt her.

“I really don’t put any weight into what she’s saying because she can be so cruel and she’s so vindictive and all of this is coming from a place of rage and anger,” she says. “She’s not out there right now doing God’s work and anybody who believes that is sorely mistaken.”
Brady adds that she believes Liana Shanti is attacking her to send a message to her current students.
“All of this is to intimidate those who are still there to make sure that they know what’s going to happen to them if they leave,” she says.
“She’s trying to intimidate me. She’s trying to intimidate every other woman from the community who’s watching this from speaking,” she says.

In her online blog , Liana Shanti tells the story of performing her very first exorcism – which she also calls a “deliverance” - on an Australian woman 10 years ago. She writes that the woman complained about having nightmares and “weird, negative thoughts.”
“I knew instantly it was a demonic energy,” she writes. “Since the age of two I have been able to see and feel the presence of demons.”
She writes that she was reluctant to perform the exorcism but was convinced by Jesus.
“I kept saying to Jesus… I do not know how. I do not know how to do this. I have never done this. I do not know how. And Jesus said… YOU DO,” she writes.
She says the moment the demon was cast out, the Australian woman told her that a gust of wind blew through her room and knocked over an essential oil diffuser.
Shanti claims the cause of the “demonic possession” was the husband’s pornography habit.
Driving out demons is not the only supernatural power that Liana Shanti claims to have.

In the W5 documentary, Fake Filtered Cult Leader , former students say the spiritual teacher claimed to be psychic and would repeatedly state that followers had been sexually abused as children. She then encouraged them to publicly “out” the alleged abusers and cut off all contact with them.
Many believed her and with devastating results, including family breakups.
Followers shared several screenshots of those so-called psychic confirmations with W5.

stories.title: Downtown Eastside housing workers resist B.C. non-profit's facial recognition plans
stories.summary: Vancouver - The union representing workers at a Downtown Eastside housing non-profit in Vancouver is resisting a plan to implement facial recognition technology for employees.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The union representing workers at a Downtown Eastside housing non-profit in Vancouver is resisting a plan to implement facial recognition technology for employees.

Cupe Local 5536, representing B.C. harm reduction workers, sent a letter to members earlier this month outlining its opposition to the PHS Community Service Society’s plan to introduce “a facial recognition-based punch clock.”

The letter, obtained by The Canadian Press, says the employer has suggested workers would need to scan their faces each time they arrive or leave work and when they take and return from breaks.

It says the use of facial recognition is “debasing,” and that normalizing artificial intelligence or biometric surveillance in harm reduction would be “reckless and dangerous,” calling on the society to abandon its plans.

The union’s recently elected president, Devin Lefebvre, declined to comment before a meeting with the employer’s leadership on November 19.

Micheal Vonn, the society’s CEO, says the organization’s current manual payroll system needs an urgent upgrade after a series of errors, and the new “touch-free” system would use facial recognition, but photos taken of employees’ faces would be deleted immediately.

Vonn said in an interview that the technology would be used for authentication, and doesn’t involve any type of biometric surveillance.

“It is exactly the kind of technology that many people now use to access their phones and other devices.”

Vonn, a lawyer and former policy director of the BC Civil Liberties Association, said she’s “deeply interested” in privacy matters and that the union’s resistance campaign came before it was briefed on new system.

Union members have shown up to work wearing buttons declaring their opposition to facial recognition, and the letter said the technology’s “implementation must be stopped, (and) PHS needs to abandon its plans.”

Vonn said the union’s concerns and conclusions about the technology were premature and overblown, and the button campaign was inappropriate and based on misinformation.

“We are not looking to put this technology in place to catch people out who are five minutes late on their shift or any of those things,” she said. “We have very good and compelling reasons why we want to automate the system.”

Vonn said they’re looking to implement the new system as soon as possible because “sooner would obviously be better for everything relating to the accuracy of the system and ensuring that we pay people appropriately.”

She said everyone working in the supportive housing and harm reduction sector faces deep challenges in “deeply antagonistic times,” while homelessness and the toxic drug crisis persist.

“We have very few friends at this juncture in our world,” she said.

“Everybody’s in favour of supportive housing as long as it’s on Mars. We have very little social licence, and every day is a freaking battle.”

Vonn said on Friday that the meeting with the union dealt with a series of questions and employees’ concerns. Lefebvre was not available for comment on Friday afternoon.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026

stories.title: Vietnamese farmed lobsters ate Canada’s lunch, now southwest Nova Scotia is coming back for China’s market
stories.summary: Since tariffs were lowered in March, Canadian lobster slowly gaining back some lost ground
stories.author: Erin Valois
stories.content:
When China lowered its tariffs on Canadian lobster in March, exporters found Vietnamese farmed lobster had claimed much of its market share.

As exporters push to slowly regain lost ground in the critical Chinese market, the industry received good news earlier this month when Canada and China agreed to a two-year extension until the end of 2028 of the favourable market access provided under the preliminary joint arrangement for Canadian canola meal, peas, lobsters and crab.

Without that agreement in place, the 25 per cent tariff on Canadian lobster imports to China would have returned on Jan. 1.

For the Canadian and Chinese governments, it's bigger than Nova Scotia's lobster industry — the 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian agricultural and seafood products were levied March 1, 2025, in response to Canadian tariffs on their electric vehicles.

That was on top of a seven per cent "most favoured nation" tariff into China, bringing the total tariff to 32 per cent.

The United States, meanwhile, only had a 17 per cent tariff on their lobster heading to China.

The impact was immediate. According to the United States Department of Agriculture's Foreign Service, American lobster exports to China grew by 25 per cent in 2025 to a total value of US$200 million.

At the same time, Canadian exports dropped by 43 per cent year-over-year to $348 million.

Meanwhile, total market share for North American lobster shrank as spiny lobster farmed in Vietnam made massive inroads, rising 114 per cent to $764 million from 2024 to 2025.

That's expected to continue. According to analysts, in the first six months of 2026 Vietnam exported 11,790 tonnes of farmed spiny lobster to China worth US$548.6 million, a 44.1 per cent increase in export value over the same period in 2025.

"At first, people thought Vietnamese lobster was just eating Canada's lunch — they were rapidly expanding production, selling more (lobster) and at higher prices," said American seafood analyst John Sackton.

"In my view, yes, Vietnam's a competitor, but it's the tariffs that are the bigger issue."

Sackton doesn't see the expansion of Vietnamese spiny lobster into China as catastrophic for Canadian exports. The Chinese long preferred the tropical spiny lobster, which doesn't have big claws, imported largely from Vietnam and Australia.

In recent years, a massive push toward farming the spiny lobster took over Vietnamese estuaries. The method sees tiny juvenile lobsters caught in the wild and raised in cages, reaching market size in under a year.

But since the Chinese tariffs were lowered in March, Canadian lobster has been slowly gaining back some lost ground.

Meanwhile, it has an advantage over American lobster, which still has a 17 per cent tariff.

Geoff Irvine, executive director of the Lobster Council of Canada, said that through the tariff battles the industry has been able to expand live exports to the European Union, South Korea and other Asian countries.

"Demand is higher for processed products, with the vast majority going to the U.S.: raw tales, whole in-shell cooked, lobster meat," said Irvine.

"Three-quarters of lobster is now sold frozen or processed, where it was 55 per cent traditionally."

Demand in the United States is steady.

"Right now in the U.S., live lobster prices are smack dab in the middle of five-year averages, neither higher nor lower than they used to be," said Sackton.

"It's very hard to say what the picture will look like at the end of November. It's after the U.S. election, and we don't know how that will affect spending. I think the takeaway I have is right now the live lobster prices are quite stable. In both Maine and Canada there's been a decline in landings, which has helped support the price."

stories.title: Navdeep Bains wins Ontario Liberal leadership on third ballot
stories.summary: Third Ontario Liberal leader in six years without a seat in the legislature faces Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives.
stories.author: Rob Ferguson; Robert Benzie; Moira Welsh
stories.content:
Ontario Liberals are banking on new leader Navdeep Bains — a key architect of Justin Trudeau’s sweep to power more than a decade ago — working his magic again.

The former federal industry minister’s win Saturday marks the third time in six years the provincial party has elected a boss without a seat in the legislature to battle face-to-face with Premier Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives.

A turban-wearing Sikh elected five times as an MP in Mississauga and Brampton, Bains, 49, becomes the first racialized leader of a major party in the province.

Ontario Liberals have selected Navdeep Bains as their new leader, emerging as victor less than one percentage point ahead of his next closest competitor, provincial caucus member Lee Fairclough. After receiving 50.3 per cent of the vote on the third and final ballot at the party’s leadership convention, Bains took to the stage and thanked his fellow contestants. (Nov. 21, 2026)

His narrow third-ballot victory over two MPPs and a former policy adviser is a bet that he can bring the organizational skills that helped the federal Liberals leapfrog from third place to first in 2015 to a struggling provincial party.

“What an honour,” a jubilant Bains told more than 1,000 cheering Liberals at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre, standing with his wife and daughters.

He won 50.3 per cent of the vote to 49.7 per cent for runner-up Lee Fairclough, 53, the MPP for Etobicoke-Lakeshore.

“We are a united party. When we heard the results, you know what Lee said to me, ‘I’ve got your back,’” added the accountant who left federal politics in 2021 and was a senior executive for Rogers and Cibc before entering the leadership race in May.

To win, Bains overcame concerns that the third-place Ontario Liberals have failed to connect with voters, in part because the last two leaders, Steven Del Duca and Bonnie Crombie, didn’t win seats in the 2022 and 2025 elections.

Ford has never faced a full-time Liberal leader in the legislature.

But Bains, a Mississauga resident and married father of two daughters, refused to commit to where he would run — either in a byelection or in a general election expected in 2029 or 2030.

“I’ll definitely be running and the determination around the exact location will be made at the appropriate time,” he said, emphasizing he does not want one of the 14 Liberal MPPs in the 124-member house to resign to trigger a byelection.

Bains, mindful he is a political pioneer in Ontario, also downplayed concerns of intolerance in the electorate.

“There’s a lot of hate and negativity out there, and I’ve met a few mean-spirited people, but I can tell you right now, ON balance, people are very generous, very kind, and very thoughtful, and that’s the positivity we need to harness.”

He ran a classic front-runner campaign, sticking to vague policy promises and a mantra of improving “opportunities” for Ontarians to avoid giving Ford’s Tories ammunition for attack ads later.

Bains, who pledged to make affordability concerns his main focus, had support from a wide array of prominent figures in the federal and Ontario Liberal spheres, although the only MPP to endorse him was Andrea Hazell (Scarborough-Guildwood).

The Bay Street veteran was the fundraising leader throughout the race, garnering at least $808,456 in donations over $200 according to Elections Ontario figures as of Friday — well ahead of his three rivals.

Fairclough raised $604,531 while MPP Stephanie Bowman, 59 (Don Valley West), who finished third, had $507,229 and last-place candidate Dylan Marando, 39, a former policy aide who has never held elected office, was well back at $190,869.

Marando worked for Trudeau and former premiers Dalton McGuinty and Kathleen Wynne during their years in power.

Prior to the results being announced, Bowman appealed for party unity.

“No grudges, no one takes their marbles and goes home,” she implored.

“We came into this room as four teams; we must leave as one.”

Fairclough echoed that sentiment immediately after her razor-thin defeat.

“At the end of the day, we are all a Liberal team, so I am 100 per cent behind the person who won this. It was close … but now we need to unite; we need to focus on defeating Doug Ford,” she said.

On the first ballot, Bains was at 44.1 per cent to 33.7 per cent for Fairclough, 12.9 per cent for Bowman and 9.3 per cent for Marando.

Ontario Liberals have turned to former industry minister Navdeep Bains — who helped Justin Trudeau rebuild the federal party more than a decade ago — as their new leader.

On the second, Bains was at 46.1 per cent, to 38.2 per cent for Fairclough and 15.7 per cent for Bowman.

The Ontario Liberals have been trying to make a comeback since their crushing 2018 defeat by Ford after almost 15 years in government under McGuinty and Wynne.

While it has more recently enjoyed second place in most public opinion polls behind Ford and his PCs despite not having a full-time leader, the party sits behind the Official Opposition NDP led by Marit Stiles with 27 seats. The Tories have 79 seats.

In the absence of a leader with a seat, Liberal MPP John Fraser (Ottawa South) has served as the party’s parliamentary leader, grilling Ford in the legislature’s question period.

Fraser had some advice for the new leader last week.

“You need to have a plan to get a seat … because the last two leaders didn’t.”

Citizenship and Multiculturalism Minister Graham McGregor, a Brampton MPP, congratulated Bains, but signalled the Tories’ planned line of attack.

“As a Trudeau minister, he supported the carbon tax and the policy of prime minister Trudeau at the time,” said McGregor, an observer at the Liberal convention.

“I’ve been hearing from residents in my community in Brampton, and we know Nav, right, and we remember when Nav was one of the most ardent supporters of Justin Trudeau,” he said.

Ford, for his part, was gracious in his congratulatory message to Bains.

“Ontario families are counting on us to work collaboratively and put province over party so we can stand up to tariffs, protect workers and make life more affordable. I look forward to continuing that work,” he said.

That was in sharp contrast to 2023 when the premier pointedly failed to publicly congratulate Crombie for her victory over Nate Erskine-Smith.

Not that the Liberals made any mention of their former leader, who resigned in January and returned them to official party status in last year’s election, during their three-hour program of speeches and tributes.

Crombie returned the favour by posting a photo of her and her grandchild, smiling on a beach on Saturday.

“Beach time with my favourite person,” she wrote.

stories.title: Man sentenced to prison in one of Canada’s largest fentanyl busts
stories.summary: In February, Nicholas Traviss, 30, plead guilty to six charges including trafficking, discharging a firearm, along with other weapons related offences.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
In February, Nicholas Traviss, 30, plead guilty to six charges including trafficking, discharging a firearm, along with other weapons related offences.

The court heard that in November 2024 he was involved in a home invasion style break-in at an apartment on Simcoe Street in downtown London.

A shot was fired but no one inside the unit was injured.

As London Police tracked Traviss back to a Jacksway Crescent apartment in the north end, they got inside and seized 13 kilograms of fentanyl with a street value of $2.4 million.

Along with that, they also found firearms along with more than $37,000 in cash.

At the sentencing hearing before Justice Bruce Thomas, Federal Crown Vincenzo Mazza told the court, “Mr. Traviss had a record setting amount of fentanyl.”

Mazza went on to describe how the drug ruins thousands of lives, “In 2024, London recorded 54 fentanyl related deaths.”

Justice Thomas responded, “The gravity of loss of life directly linked to fentanyl is not lost on me.”

Mazza asked that Traviss who is already in custody receive a sentence of 24 to 26 years in prison on the drug conviction.

The provincial Crown asked for a total of 12 years for the home invasion and shooting to be served concurrently.

Defence lawyer Melody Izadi asked the judge not to impose an unduly harsh sentence citing his difficult upbringing, “A sentence of 15 years is significant and it addresses the severity of the charges.”

In the end, Justice Thomas sentenced Traviss to 20 years and with credit for time served he has 16 years remaining behind bars.

stories.title: More beds, but even more need: Shelters prepare for winter program as London’s homelessness numbers hit new high
stories.summary: London’s revamped Winter Response to Homelessness is preparing to open more overnight spaces, but amid a growing crisis there’s uncertainty about whether everyone who needs a warm space will get one.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
London’s revamped Winter Response to Homelessness is preparing to open more overnight spaces, but amid a growing crisis there’s uncertainty about whether everyone who needs a warm space will get one. “I am very pleased that the city announced it early, and (shelters) plan to be fully open across the city Dec.

1, and there is a coordinated approach with service providers so that it is an every night approach, largely,” explained Sarah Campbell, executive director of Ark Aid Street Mission. When city council approved the winter response in the summer, the scale of London’s homelessness crisis had been relatively stable, but the previous two months saw numbers hit highs never before experienced in London.

According to the city’s online dashboard, roughly 2,200 to 2,300 unique individuals interacted with frontline services each month from January to August. That number climbed to 2,388 in September and 2,534 in October—a net increase of 146 people in a single month.

A question from CTV News asking city hall to explain what might be causing the record-setting surge was not specifically answered in an emailed response Friday afternoon. Campbell acknowledges it could put additional pressure on shelters, “We could be looking at more people coming to us (this winter), and we May find ourselves tight on space.” Unlike last winter, the Boyle Community Centre will not be utilized as a cold weather emergency shelter.

Instead, council allocated $5.8 million for existing shelters to provide an additional 238 spaces every night between Dec. 1 and March 31, plus another 29 spaces will open when temperatures fall below -15 C or the wind chill drops below -20 C.

Ark Aid plans to use its two existing locations and is now unlikely to temporarily rent a third. The 20 to 40 beds initially envisioned for that third shelter will instead be divided between The Ark and Cronyn-Warner House, as well as other frontline shelters.

“The truth is we had a hard time securing a third location this year,” admitted Campbell. ”That’s the first time in six-years, but it’s happened. We were being specific to an area of the city, and we’re continuing to be in talks with some churches just in case we need some of that expansion space.” Peak demand experienced last winter was 240 individuals at the Winter Response to Homelessness emergency shelters.

This year shelters will create a total of 267 additional overnight spaces, 27 more than last winter’s peak demand, but London’s Unique Client Count has risen by more than 300 people since last winter. “I think when we see these new numbers about homelessness, this is an important number to track, because when people are new to homelessness they have some resources initially, maybe they can stay with a friend for a little while, maybe they can manage in various ways, but over time this is when the crisis becomes really intense for people,” Campbell said.

City staff commit to track the situation as the winter progresses. “The City will monitor demand and availability with local providers throughout the winter. If demand exceeds available spaces, we’ll work with providers to assess options and keep City Council informed,” wrote Jonathan John, the City of London’s director of Housing Stability Services.

Campbell says the municipal funding will only provide nighttime spaces this winter, participating shelters and frontline agencies will still depend on the generosity of Londoners for everything else. “One thing is, if you’ve cleaned out your closet and you have any winter gear at all, please donate to the organization of your choice.

At Ark Aid if we have more, (then) we share with others. But the truth is, we always run out,” she said. “The second thing is come and volunteer with us. You know, get your hands involved. We need people on the ground,” Campbell added.

“The third thing would be make a donation to one of these organizations. There’s always gaps to be filled.” The City of London’s full statement: “Last winter, many warming spaces opened only during extreme cold conditions.

On the busiest night, 240 people used those spaces, exceeding planned capacity. This year, 238 Winter Response spaces will be available every night from December 1 to March 31, with 29 more opening during extreme cold conditions.

That gives people more reliable options for coming indoors throughout the entire duration of the winter season. In addition, 419 year-round emergency shelter beds, respite beds and transitional housing spaces will continue to operate throughout the winter months.

Together, year-round shelters, respite programs, transitional housing and seasonal services will provide 657 spaces this winter and 686 during extreme cold conditions. The City and its partners will continue helping people move from shelters into housing this winter, which can free up shelter spaces for others who need them.

In addition, the Canada-Ontario Housing Benefit and other rent supplements will help people find or keep housing. Federal reimbursement through the Unsheltered Homelessness and Encampments Initiative also allowed Council to reinvest $350,000 in outreach, daytime drop-ins and access to showers and other basic needs.

If demand exceeds available spaces, we’ll work with providers to assess options and keep City Council informed. This year’s Winter Response represents an investment of $5,784,775, including $3,632,500 in municipal funding and $2,152,275 in federal funding.

Like other major cities across Canada, London continues to face a shortage of deeply affordable and attainable housing. The City is working closely with federal and provincial partners on long-term solutions to expand access to housing.”

stories.title: Kelowna city hall faces more transparency questions after wage hike kept quiet
stories.summary: While the former council was kept apprised of the negotiations, residents were not given a public announcement before the vote.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
A nearly 12 per cent wage increase for City of Kelowna staff, approved just days before the Oct. 17 municipal election but announced publicly afterward, is raising questions about transparency in how city council communicates with taxpayers.

The agreement was ratified on October 19, two days after the municipal election.

While the former council was kept apprised of the negotiations, residents were not given a public announcement before the vote.

Many learned about the wage hike through local media reports.

“Taxpayers shouldn’t be learning how much stuff costs from reporters. This kind of transparency should really be the bare minimum standard for cities,” said Gage Haubrich, a director with the Canadian Taxpayers Federation.

Haubrich added the city should have let residents know in advance what was being considered and the financial implications.

“At bare minimum it should be a news release,” he said.

Stuart Leatherdale, the city’s lead negotiator for the agreement and general manager of people and protective services, says the City had an understanding with Cupe at the beginning of negotiations not to involve the media.

That understanding remained in place through the bargaining process and ratification.

Leatherdale acknowledged the public’s criticism over the lack of an announcement.

“I think it’s a fair comment, and I’ll accept that from the general public,” Leatherdale said.

Leatherdale explained that the city has issued news releases about labour agreements in the past, but those announcements were made jointly with the union.

“Normally, when we have done that in the past, it’s by joint agreement. We both put that statement out,” he said. “We just never did get to making that agreement this time around.”

The city instead issued a subsequent “For the Record” news release disputing information published in media reports and providing additional context about negotiations.

It is part of a growing collection of after-the-fact statements on the city’s website, including a recent release in which the city manager defended the municipality’s record on transparency.

Sean Holman, a journalism professor at the University of Victoria, says the city’s approach points to a broader communication problem.

“It is a symptom of a communication problem. It is the symptom of a bureaucratic public relations process that is afraid of sharing facts with the media and by extension with the public,” Holman said. “Constant massaging of image actually does not serve government in the long run. It actually simply makes the government appear less trustworthy.”

When Global News requested interviews Friday about the broader issue of transparency and communication, neither the mayor, city manager, or anyone else from city hall was available to meet the daily news deadline for an on-camera interview.

The issue comes as Kelowna’s re-elected mayor has vowed to improve communication with residents, but how that commitment will translate into changes at city hall remains to be seen.

“It’s an incredibly adversarial approach that the city is taking,” Holman said. “What they should be doing is providing facts in a timely manner to journalists, so we can report on stories in a timely manner to the public who we serve, just like the city is supposed to serve.”

stories.summary: Treasury Department names alleged ’Ndrangheta leaders and several GTA businesses, including funeral homes, in new sanctions order
stories.author: Colin Freeze, Eric Reguly
stories.content:
The United States Department of the Treasury has announced financial sanctions against alleged senior members of an Italian mafia group based in the Toronto region, as well as associated businesses in the city, such as funeral homes.

The department announced the sanctions this week against the ‘Ndrangheta, a family-based crime group that started centuries ago in Italy and now believed to operate in dozens of countries. American officials issued a statement that singled out the Toronto faction of the crime group and alleged it directs drug trafficking, money laundering, murder and other crimes in Canada, the United States, Italy and elsewhere.

“The ‘Ndrangheta locale that operates in the Greater Toronto Area in Canada has strengthened in recent years, becoming so powerful that they dictate events in Italy from across the ocean,” the U.S. Treasury Department statement says.

The allegations contained in the Treasury Department statement have not been tested in court.

The department named several Canadian families as key players in ‘Ndrangheta operations. The new sanctions order identifies three Toronto-area funeral parlours and a limousine service as alleged mafia fronts.

The financial order is being touted as the latest example of President Donald Trump ’s efforts to dismantle the hemisphere’s drug traffickers and cartels. “The ’Ndrangheta frequently partner with Mexican and South American drug trafficking organizations,” the U.S. statement said.

Within Canada, York Regional Police and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have long struggled to contain the ‘Ndrangheta. The U.S. Treasury Department thanked both forces for information that supported the new sanctions.

The new U.S. Treasury listings are not known to be accompanied by any known new criminal charges in either Canada or the United States. Canadian police and the U.S. Department of Justice did not respond to requests for comment.

But a U.S. sanctions listing is a powerful denunciatory tool that can result in asset seizures south of the border. And it May also block people and businesses from doing commerce with the designated people and entities.

The U.S. government has produced an organizational chart of alleged Canadian ‘Ndrangheta members centred in and around Toronto.

The statement identifies the alleged leaders of the Toronto faction as Angelo and Cosimo Figliomeni, brothers Rocco Remo Commisso and Francesco Commisso, and also Vincenzo ‘Jimmy’ DeMaria. They are alleged to participate in a Camera di Controllo – “a collegial body of the ‘Ndrangheta that decides on important questions concerning the organization and settles disputes, even outside of Toronto,” according to the U.S. Treasury statement.

The U.S. Treasury org chart also alleges that Canada’s newer ‘Ndrangheta generation is headed by Luigi Vescio Senior, a 55-year-old who is said to control three funeral businesses and a limousine service in the Toronto area.

A woman at one of the entities, Fratelli Vescio Funeral Homes, declined to answer The Globe’s questions by phone Friday. She asked for questions about all businesses to be relayed by e-mail instead. There was no response to e-mailed questions.

A published Nov. 19 order by the U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control seeks to block financial transactions with the funeral businesses.

Police in Canada have spent decades investigating the ‘Ndrangheta. The Treasury Department statement notes that Rocco Remo Commisso was convicted in Canada in 1981 for conspiracy to commit murder and again in 1984 in connection with a bombing that killed one person.

The Trump administration has been expanding its use of sanctions in other countries. Last year, it sanctioned reputed Canadian members of the drug gang allegedly controlled by Ryan Wedding , the former Olympic snowboarder now jailed on allegations he ordered murders of several Canadians.

Earlier this month, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned eight Canadian money services businesses alleging they are providing an economic lifeline to the state of Iran and its Revolutionary Guards Corp.

The ‘Ndrangheta’s origins are in Calabria, the “toe” of Italy, in what was part of Greater Greece in ancient times. Their name comes from the Greek word for “bravery” or “manliness.” They are considered the wealthiest and most powerful of Italy’s four main mafia organizations.

Among Italy’s ‘Ndrangheta families, power is almost always passed down from father to son over generations.

The ‘Ndrangheta came into prominence in the late 1800s and specialized in brutish, yet unsophisticated acts of extortion, banditry and robbery.

stories.title: World leaders gather in Halifax for international security forum
stories.summary: The Halifax International Security Forum is a showcase of military experts and strategic leaders from more than 70 countries. The three-day event will take place in downtown Halifax this weekend, for its 18th year.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - The Halifax International Security Forum is a showcase of military experts and strategic leaders from more than 70 countries. The three-day event will take place in downtown Halifax this weekend for its 18 th year.

Canada’s military and its global and domestic responsibilities will be closely examined at length, over the weekend through a series of seminars and meetings.

“This is more than just a security forum,” said Peter Van Praagh, the president of the forum. “We want to make sure we gather good ideas to put into decision-makers’ heads.”

“Canada is making historic investments in defence, rebuilding our industrial capacity, and we are working with our allies to deliver the capabilities that we need, and that we need to share,” said Canada’s Defence Minister David McGuinty.

In his remarks to open the security forum, McGuinty clarified the government’s stance on military cadets, following reports that Ottawa would be implementing cutbacks to cadet programming in Canada . The budget for the programs this year was approximately $265 million.

McGuinty said no core changes are coming to the cadet program and cited recent growth across the country.

“In the past three years, we have seen a 59 per cent increase in the number of people joining the cadet movement,” said McGuinty. “It is astonishingly encouraging.”

The 2026 version of the Halifax International Security Forum comes at a time when tariff and trade tensions have strained Canada’s relationship with the U.S.

Van Praagh said the war with Ukraine will be a major topic over the weekend, and U.S. President Donald Trump’s meeting on Thursday in Shenzhen, China with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, have already sparked reactions from those attending this event.

“People are going to want to talk about that,” said Van Praagh. “We are keeping Ukraine front and centre even though it’s been five years and what happens in Ukraine really is fundamental to Canadian security because Russia is testing the entire international system.”

No members of Trump’s administration are attending the security forum.

Dalhousie University International Development Studies Professor Robert Huish suggested that members of the Trump administration May have stayed away to avoid criticisms.

“Let us not forget that Mr. Trump has opened a war in Iran, and he’s declared victory many times and he’s still within the quagmire of it,” said Huish.

Global food security is also a prominent theme at the forum. Experts will examine international shipping routes around the world, like the Strait of Hormuz, the Panama Canal and Gibraltar. Having those areas and potential shipping choke points secured, is crucial so food can be transported to countries that need it.

stories.title: Man sentenced in U.S. murder plot that officials say has links to slaying of Canadian Sikh leader
stories.summary: Nikhil Gupta sentenced to 19 years in prison for attempt to arrange contract killing of political activist
stories.author: Greg Mercer, Mike Hager
stories.content:
A U.S. judge has sentenced an Indian man to more than 19 years in prison for trying to arrange a contract killing hire that U.S. and Canadian officials allege was part of a broader, government-backed assassination campaign run by India’s spy agency – including the 2023 killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia.

Nikhil Gupta, 55, was sentenced in New York on Friday after previously pleading guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering, in a failed plot against Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a political activist and attorney who holds Canadian and American citizenship.

Mr. Pannun, a vocal critic of the Indian government, leads a Sikh organization that advocates for the secession of Punjab, a state in northern India, to create a breakaway country called Khalistan. U.S. court documents alleged a plot to kill the activist was foiled by American authorities in May 2023, when Mr. Gupta contacted an undercover officer who he thought was a hit man, and was caught arranging an advance of $15,000 cash for Mr. Pannun’s murder.

U.S. prosecutors allege Mr. Gupta was recruited by his co-accused, Vikash Yadav, who they say was working for India’s foreign intelligence service, the Research and Analysis Wing, to arrange the assassination of multiple Khalistan activists. In phone messages contained in court records, the pair discussed targets in California, Pakistan, Nepal and Canada, as well as Mr. Pannun.

The Indian government has denied any involvement in either the plot against Mr. Pannun or Mr. Nijjar’s killing.

“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in a Manhattan courthouse that was surrounded by heavy security, Sikh protestors and media. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”

U.S. court filings said Mr. Gupta had a background in international narcotics and weapons trafficking, and that he agreed to help Mr. Yadav in exchange for having criminal charges against him in India dropped. He apologized to Mr. Pannun, while his family listened through an internet hookup from India.

Mr. Pannun, in a lengthy speech to the court, described Mr. Gupta as “just a foot soldier acting at the behest” of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist who has opposed the independence movement.

“I do not stand before you for my personal safety because my life belongs entirely to my people,” he said.

Mr. Gupta’s case has been closely watched by law enforcement officials in Canada investigating a rise in allegations of transnational repression against Sikhs. Mr. Nijjar, a prominent Khalistani separatist and Sikh leader, was killed by masked gunmen outside his temple in Surrey, B.C., in June 2023.

His slaying strained relations between Canada and India, after former prime minister Justin Trudeau told Parliament there was credible allegations linking the shooting to agents of the Indian government. Four Indian men, who entered Canada on student visas, are awaiting trial in the B.C. Supreme Court.

Jody Thomas, Canada’s former national security advisor, said on Friday that the U.S. evidence “lays bare the links to the murder of Mr. Nijjar.”

“The sentencing of Mr. Gupta is reassuring to see and it confirms the Canadian position that this was a part of a broader campaign that unfortunately was successfully executed in Canada,” she said.

India has consistently denied it targeted Sikh separatists, and described Mr. Yadav as rogue operator who is no longer employed by the government. In May, India’s High Commissioner Dinesh Patnaik told The Globe the RCMP was investigating “fantasy allegations” and said Mr. Yadav can’t answer to the charges against him in the U.S. because he’s disappeared.

In 2024, the RCMP announced it was probing multiple homicides and violent acts targeting pro-Khalistan communities in Canada that it alleged were linked to New Delhi. The Globe reported in March that law enforcement and national security officials were previously briefed on reports that Indian consular staff in Vancouver helped supply information related to Mr. Nijjar’s assassination.

Canada ultimately expelled six Indian diplomats, including the then-high commissioner, as part of a dispute that quickly escalated into a tit-for-tat diplomatic crisis that Prime Minister Mark Carney is now trying to repair as part of new trade talks.

Prosecutors alleged Mr. Yadav sent Mr. Gupta a video clip showing Mr. Nijjar’s bloody body slumped in a vehicle, and then sent him the street address for Mr. Pannun’s residence in New York. Mr. Gupta, who replied that he wished he had personally killed Mr. Nijjar, later sent the same video to the undercover officer, and told him “we have so many targets.”

In a statement sent after the sentencing, Mr. Pannun called on Ottawa to use evidence from his case to seek justice in the Nijjar trial, which isn’t expected to begin until 2028.

“The Carney government must now use the evidence submitted by the U.S. Department of Justice to prosecute those responsible,” he said about Mr. Nijjar’s assassination, adding that includes pursuing Mr. Yadav and “members of his network in Canada, including Indian consular officials who provided logistical support for Nijjar’s assassination.”

The RCMP said it couldn’t comment on its continuing investigation into Mr. Nijjar’s death, including “the potential relevance of foreign judicial proceedings to Canadian investigations, co-operation with international partners, or investigative steps involving any named individual.”

Pritpal Singh, a California-based Sikh leader who said the FBI warned him his life was in danger just days after Mr. Nijjar’s assassination, urged officials to do more to prosecute those who directed the killing of Sikh dissidents.

“Follow the evidence to everyone who ordered, financed or enabled what we regard as India’s global assassination program targeting Sikhs in the diaspora,” he said in a statement.

With a report from Associated Press
paragraphs: A U.S. judge has sentenced an Indian man to more than 19 years in prison for trying to arrange a contract killing hire that U.S. and Canadian officials allege was part of a broader, government-backed assassination campaign run by India’s spy agency – including the 2023 killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia.

Nikhil Gupta, 55, was sentenced in New York on Friday after previously pleading guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering, in a failed plot against Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a political activist and attorney who holds Canadian and American citizenship.

Mr. Pannun, a vocal critic of the Indian government, leads a Sikh organization that advocates for the secession of Punjab, a state in northern India, to create a breakaway country called Khalistan. U.S. court documents alleged a plot to kill the activist was foiled by American authorities in May 2023, when Mr. Gupta contacted an undercover officer who he thought was a hit man, and was caught arranging an advance of $15,000 cash for Mr. Pannun’s murder.

U.S. prosecutors allege Mr. Gupta was recruited by his co-accused, Vikash Yadav, who they say was working for India’s foreign intelligence service, the Research and Analysis Wing, to arrange the assassination of multiple Khalistan activists. In phone messages contained in court records, the pair discussed targets in California, Pakistan, Nepal and Canada, as well as Mr. Pannun.
The Indian government has denied any involvement in either the plot against Mr. Pannun or Mr. Nijjar’s killing.

“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in a Manhattan courthouse that was surrounded by heavy security, Sikh protestors and media. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”

U.S. court filings said Mr. Gupta had a background in international narcotics and weapons trafficking, and that he agreed to help Mr. Yadav in exchange for having criminal charges against him in India dropped. He apologized to Mr. Pannun, while his family listened through an internet hookup from India.

Mr. Pannun, in a lengthy speech to the court, described Mr. Gupta as “just a foot soldier acting at the behest” of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist who has opposed the independence movement.
“I do not stand before you for my personal safety because my life belongs entirely to my people,” he said.

Mr. Gupta’s case has been closely watched by law enforcement officials in Canada investigating a rise in allegations of transnational repression against Sikhs. Mr. Nijjar, a prominent Khalistani separatist and Sikh leader, was killed by masked gunmen outside his temple in Surrey, B.C., in June 2023.

His slaying strained relations between Canada and India, after former prime minister Justin Trudeau told Parliament there was credible allegations linking the shooting to agents of the Indian government. Four Indian men, who entered Canada on student visas, are awaiting trial in the B.C. Supreme Court.
Jody Thomas, Canada’s former national security advisor, said on Friday that the U.S. evidence “lays bare the links to the murder of Mr. Nijjar.”
“The sentencing of Mr. Gupta is reassuring to see and it confirms the Canadian position that this was a part of a broader campaign that unfortunately was successfully executed in Canada,” she said.

India has consistently denied it targeted Sikh separatists, and described Mr. Yadav as rogue operator who is no longer employed by the government. In May, India’s High Commissioner Dinesh Patnaik told The Globe the RCMP was investigating “fantasy allegations” and said Mr. Yadav can’t answer to the charges against him in the U.S. because he’s disappeared.

In 2024, the RCMP announced it was probing multiple homicides and violent acts targeting pro-Khalistan communities in Canada that it alleged were linked to New Delhi. The Globe reported in March that law enforcement and national security officials were previously briefed on reports that Indian consular staff in Vancouver helped supply information related to Mr. Nijjar’s assassination.

Canada ultimately expelled six Indian diplomats, including the then-high commissioner, as part of a dispute that quickly escalated into a tit-for-tat diplomatic crisis that Prime Minister Mark Carney is now trying to repair as part of new trade talks.

Prosecutors alleged Mr. Yadav sent Mr. Gupta a video clip showing Mr. Nijjar’s bloody body slumped in a vehicle, and then sent him the street address for Mr. Pannun’s residence in New York. Mr. Gupta, who replied that he wished he had personally killed Mr. Nijjar, later sent the same video to the undercover officer, and told him “we have so many targets.”
In a statement sent after the sentencing, Mr. Pannun called on Ottawa to use evidence from his case to seek justice in the Nijjar trial, which isn’t expected to begin until 2028.

“The Carney government must now use the evidence submitted by the U.S. Department of Justice to prosecute those responsible,” he said about Mr. Nijjar’s assassination, adding that includes pursuing Mr. Yadav and “members of his network in Canada, including Indian consular officials who provided logistical support for Nijjar’s assassination.”

The RCMP said it couldn’t comment on its continuing investigation into Mr. Nijjar’s death, including “the potential relevance of foreign judicial proceedings to Canadian investigations, co-operation with international partners, or investigative steps involving any named individual.”

Pritpal Singh, a California-based Sikh leader who said the FBI warned him his life was in danger just days after Mr. Nijjar’s assassination, urged officials to do more to prosecute those who directed the killing of Sikh dissidents.
“Follow the evidence to everyone who ordered, financed or enabled what we regard as India’s global assassination program targeting Sikhs in the diaspora,” he said in a statement.
