stories.title: Quebec pledges to unveil a road map for phasing out fossil fuels
stories.summary: Environmental groups praised the Parti Québécois government for its commitment
stories.author: Stéphane Blais
stories.content:
Quebec has pledged to create a road map for its transition away from fossil fuels, sparking a wave of congratulations from environmental organizations.

Jean Lemire, the Quebec government’s envoy for climate change and northern issues, announced the commitment for a “just and orderly transition away from fossil fuels this year,” in a news release at the United Nations climate change summit.

Quebec shared the news as part of its membership in the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance, an international alliance of states and governments collaborating on phasing out fossil fuel production.

“Achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 requires a clear commitment to phasing out fossil fuels. Quebec has already banned fossil fuel exploration and production,” Lemire said in the release on Wednesday.

Quebec has served as co-chair of the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance since 2023.

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres recently called on members of the alliance to each develop a road map for phasing out oil and gas.

The office of the new Environment Minister, Jean Pellerin, declined to comment on the announcement.

Environmental groups praised the Parti Québécois government for its commitment.

“Minister Jean Pellerin’s term is off to a strong start. With this commitment, Quebec is planning for the future, while Canada is becoming increasingly mired in the fossil fuels of the past,” said Caroline Brouillette, executive director of Climate Action Network Canada.

“We can be proud to see Quebec taking such a leadership role in the transition away from fossil fuels,” said Alice-Anne Simard, executive director of environmental organization Nature Québec.

The environmental law organization, Centre québécois du droit de l’environnement, also congratulated the newly elected PQ government.

The organization had announced on Wednesday that it was filing a lawsuit to the Superior Court against the Quebec government over the postponement of its 2030 greenhouse gas emissions target.

“This ambition must also translate into ambitious targets, concrete measures, and a governance framework that is up to the challenge. Our climate lawsuit . . . serves as a reminder that the government must fulfill its obligations in the fight against climate change,” wrote executive director Geneviève Paul.

Charles-Edouard Têtu, climate policy analyst at Équiterre, encouraged the federal government to take notes from Quebec’s promise.

“The announcement of the road map to phase out fossil fuels is a breath of fresh air after spending the week listening to Mark Carney ’s government try to make us believe it takes the climate crisis seriously,” said Têtu.

The Carney government also confirmed it was granting its final approval to a deepwater offshore oil project called Bay du Nord, off the coast of Newfoundland on Friday. The project’s proponent, Equinor, is expected to make a decision about whether to proceed with the $14-billion venture early next year.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government has said it hopes Bay du Nord won’t be the last oil and gas development in its territory offshore.

But federal officials and the Canadian oil and gas industry appeared to have little to say on Friday about Quebec’s new commitment.

Environment and Climate Change Canada said it needed more time to provide a statement about the Quebec pledge.

An oil and gas industry lobby group also declined a request for an interview.

“We will have to wait for the government’s announcement details before offering any comments,” wrote a spokesperson for the Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers, in an e-mail.

Denmark launched its own road map during the summit, while Spain, Portugal, Luxembourg, Chad and Brazil announced plans to develop road maps, said the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance press release.

These countries join Finland, which launched its road map early in the summit, and France, Germany and the Netherlands, which published such road maps earlier this year.

stories.title: Tenants ordered to vacate ‘state-of-chaos’ apartment building in central Edmonton
stories.summary: Stadium Plaza tenants were released from their leases at the 'state-of-chaos apartment building' that's become overrun by squatters and has no heat due to copper pipe theft.
stories.author: Jasmine King, Karen Bartko
stories.content:
A problem apartment building in central Edmonton has been emptied of its residents after the courts found evidence of suspected gang activity, drug use, squatting and copper pipe thefts.

People living at Stadium Plaza on 86 Street, near 112 Avenue, were moving their worldly belongings out on Friday.

Paige Parenteau had been living at the problem property in the Parkdale neighbourhood near Commonwealth Place for the past 10 months.

She, along with dozens of other tenants, were evicted after an Alberta judge released them from their leases and said they must move out by noon on Nov. 20.

“I stayed till the last day because some people, they had nowhere to go, and I wanted to make sure they were ok,” Parenteau said.

While the living conditions were horrible, some residents said they had nowhere else to turn.

“This was like living in a homeless shelter. It really was,” Parenteau said, adding people were regularly breaking into a side door and causing problems.

Justice Michael Lema made the eviction decision a week ago on Nov. 13. Court documents state that rental payments had largely dried up at the “state-of-chaos apartment building.”

Of 78 rental units at Stadium Plaza, 22 were occupied by people whose lease agreements had expired, two who never had one and 12 people with valid agreements.

The owner stopped making mortgage payments this past January and legal proceedings began.

“The receiver was appointed on Aug. 25, 2026. It has collected only approximately $13,000 of an estimated $90,000 of rent collectively due since then,” read the decision from Justice Lema.

They noted the building was plagued with problems: inoperable elevators, gang activity, destruction of suites and eventually, the loss of heating due to copper pipe thefts.

The building is relatively new, having been built in 2022-2023 at a cost of around $12.3 million . Lema noted its construction was plagued by problems, “as reflected in the registration of various construction liens.”

The building has fared no better since opening, Lema said, noting the following issues:

Less-than-full occupancy

Unleased suites being occupied by squatters

Illegal-drug-related activities occurring in certain suites and in public areas

Flooding rendering the elevators inoperable

Ongoing destruction of or damage to the main entrance and the entrances of various suites

Graffiti reflecting gang activity in the building

Excessive noise (day and night)

Effectively daily attendance by police

Eventually the loss of heat via ongoing thefts of copper piping throughout the building

Global News spoke with three residents who lived in Stadium Plaza on Friday. All said they had been assaulted, had their units broken into, and feared for their life.

One man who didn’t share his name said he was attacked with a knife and bear sprayed by random people who entered the building.

It was hard to shower or use the washroom because he was constantly worried about someone breaking in, he said.

Parenteau had similar experiences.

“The night this happened to me,” she said, gesturing to a large, fading green and purple bruise on her jaw and cheek and mark near her eye, “I think I was inside my apartment sleeping and I didn’t lock my door.

“I woke up in an ambulance.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I woke up in an ambulance."

Parenteau said she had to get dental work done and couldn’t open her eye because of the random assault.

“That’s pretty extreme, to neglect a building that much where your tenants are getting hurt.”

Due to the pipe thefts and other damage, repairs on the heating system could cost around $461,000 and would take months to fix — right as winter weather is arriving.

One resident who spoke at the court proceedings told the judge she has been coping, in part, with space heaters and by boiling water while looking for a new place to live.

The receiver of the property said the repairs were not possible with the building occupied, which is part of the reason residents were told to leave.

“I find that no reasonable tenant would be willing to remain as a tenant in an unheated apartment building from mid-November to mid-February (at minimum) in Edmonton,” read Justice Lema’s decision.

The eviction has left some residents in limbo, unable to afford to move to a new rental.

“I was off the street, so I had to stay there til I found another spot,” one tenant said. “Because the owners aren’t around, there’s no damage deposit to be given back to go get a new place.”

While residents acknowledge not every problem could’ve been avoided, they hope others living in similar situations have a better ending than they did.

“If a tenant has an issue, sometimes it’s exaggerated; I understand that, and it gets annoying when it’s repetitive, but this… really needed some attention,” Parenteau said. “I’m very curious as to how closely the relationships are monitored between social workers, welfare workers and the landlords they connect with.”

The judge also brought up what appeared to be a lack of public health inspections, noting the building has never been declared unfit for human habitation.

“I note, in closing, the continuing absence of a section 62 order under the Public Health Act and query how an apartment building lacking heating, apparently not remediable for last three months i.e. until mid-February, can be regarded, even implicitly, as fit for habitation,” Lema said.

While she says she will be ok, Parenteau worries about the people she shared walls with.

“I am very concerned for some of my neighbours — I cared so much about them and I really hope they are doing ok.”

stories.title: B.C. nurses get 3% annual wage increases through 2029 in arbitration ruling
stories.summary: Decision has left nurses feeling ‘gravely disappointed’ after they asked for 8% annually, union president says
stories.author: Ashley Joannou
stories.content:
Arbitrators have imposed annual wage increases of three per cent through to 2029 for British Columbia’s more than 60,000 nurses, a decision their union president says has left nurses feeling “gravely disappointed” after they asked for eight per cent annually.

The decision ends a fractious dispute between the provincial government and the BC Nurses’ Union that included strike action with nurses briefly refusing non-essential overtime this summer.

The binding decision from special mediators Vince Ready and Amanda Rogers was issued Wednesday and only covered compensation after contract language on violence in the workplace, nursing duties and nursing shortages was resolved through earlier mediation.

Union president Adriane Gear said in an interview Friday that the deal imposed on nurses “falls incredibly short” of what members wanted, leaving them “gravely disappointed with the outcome.”

“Our collective bargaining round was constrained by a mandate that didn’t allow for nurses to actually feel valued and respected for what they bring to the health-care system,” she said.

The three per cent pay increase is in line with pay allowances set by government for public sector workers in the province and is retroactive to 2025.

Gear said the increase is the same that was offered in a tentative deal that was rejected by 67 per cent of voting members in May 2026, leading to job action for several days in early July where nurses stopped non-essential overtime or doing non-nursing duties, such as answering phones or processing doctors’ orders.

She said a provincial government mandate requires that wage increases not be higher than three per cent and that if the nurses had been able to negotiate more, other unions would have also received pay increases because of “me-too agreements” signed with the government.

“When we were offered the arbitration, we were told that that was the only way we could have our compensation considered because the arbitrators are not constrained by the mandate or the me-too (agreements,)” she said, describing trying to bargain under the mandate like swimming with your arms tied behind your back.

The new deal will now take seven years for nurses to get to highest pay scale starting in April 2027, down from a previous 10-year grid, and nurses who have 10 years of work experience will get an extra 50 cents per hour, effective the first pay period following April 1, 2028.

The 45-page written decision said the smaller grid brings nurses to the top rate three years sooner, while preserving a progression through the middle years of a nurse’s career.

It said that in order to meet the province’s first phase of nurse-to-patent ratio promises, about 10,500 additional nurses will be required and evidence suggests that nurses under 35 are most likely to leave the profession.

Gear said the new grid means the starting wage for nurses in B.C. is among the highest in the country, but beyond year four, not much has changed. She called the 50-cent increase at 10 years “kind of just insulting.”

The two sides spent about seven months at the bargaining table before reaching a tentative agreement in May 2026 that was rejected by the nurses.

Gear said nurses in the province feel unheard or unvalued and the work conditions remain poor, with up to 6,000 vacancies at one time.

“They got it right in terms of how do we recruit new nurses? But (the deal) falls extremely short, devastatingly short, in terms of retaining nurses that have been holding the system together,” she said.

stories.title: Cadbury chocolate bar recalled due to undeclared pistachio
stories.summary: Food and snack maker Mondelez Canada has issued a recall of Cadbury Dairy Milk Oreo Candy bars due to undeclared pistachio, which can cause serious or life-threatening allergic reactions.
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) says food and snack maker Mondelez Canada has issued a national recall of Cadbury Dairy Milk Oreo Candy bars due to undeclared pistachio, which can cause serious or life-threatening allergic reactions.

The federal agency says 14.5 gram individual treat-size bars are being recalled, along with boxes of 45 and 90 count Favourites Fun Treats Treat Size Bars bearing the best before dates of January 3, 2027 and January 4, 2027.

The box of 45 bears the UPC code 0 61200 01984 1 while the box of 90 has the UPC code 0 61200 01986 5.

It’s unclear whether anyone has been hospitalized, but the Cfia says the recall was triggered after someone suffered a reaction after consuming the product.

“Do not consume recalled products to which you are allergic or sensitive as they May cause a serious or life-threatening reaction,” the Cfia said in a release issued Friday. “Recalled products should be thrown out or returned to the location where they were purchased.”

The latest recall comes on the heels of a similar one issued in July when an alert was issued for Cadbury’s Dairy Milk Oreo candy bar due to the presence of pistachio, which wasn’t declared on the label.

stories.title: The holiday train got rolling and could soon be in a community near you
stories.summary: A holiday classic is now on track, delivering cheer and picking up donations in communities across Canada. The Cpkc Holiday Train made its first stop in Montreal-West, where a large crowd gathered as a freight full of the spirit of the season pulled in.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Montreal - A holiday classic is now on track, delivering cheer and picking up donations in communities across Canada. The Cpkc Holiday Train made its first stop in Montreal-West, where a large crowd gathered as a freight full of the season’s spirit pulled in.

The Holiday Train project got rolling 28 years ago and this year two trains will make stops in 182 communities in Canada and the United States. When the locomotive and rail cars decorated with colourful lights arrive at a station, one of the wagons opens up and is transformed into a stage.

The Toronto-based band Magic! is among the artists on board for the first leg of the journey, delivering hit songs like “Rude,” and a newly released holiday tune called “As Long As We’re Together.”

“We’ve played beaches, we’ve done skiing lodges, we’ve done arenas and festivals, and the Holiday Train is a Canadian tradition,” says frontman Nasri Atweh. “We’re Canadian boys, we want to be part of giving back and we want to have fun.”

Niloo Morati was at the train station with her five-year-old daughter Harper. She says experiencing the show on rails is now a staple of the holidays.

“I find that with all the technology and everything around us it is really important to build family traditions and to have opportunities like this to spend time with family and neighbours,” Morati says.

‘It’s about giving back’

Along with the spirit of the season, the train’s voyage comes with a deeper message. Spectators are encouraged to donate or bring non-perishable goods to the show. Since 1999, the train has collected $20 million and 2.5 million kilograms for local food banks.

“It’s about giving back to communities where we operate and about bringing awareness to food insecurity,” says Cpkc Director of Government Affairs, André Hannoush.

Money and goods collected in Montreal-West are headed to food bank Moisson Montreal. Its director of philanthropy, Matias Duque, says the donation comes as needs are growing.

“Times are tough, with the high cost of living,” he says. “We didn’t used to see people who are working coming to food banks, now we do. We see more students, more older adults as well, so there is more demand. So, there is a lot of bad news, but there is good news as well. We are making a difference.”

Four-year-old Aidan and his dad Gabe Lewis brought canned goods.

“It’s always important to me to make sure that we learn to share and to think about how we can give when we have so much,” says Lewis.

Magic!’s performance on the ride delivered a sprinkle of holiday spirit to a landscape where no snowflake has fallen yet.

Montreal is experiencing an unusually warm season. Many spectators welcomed the balmy temperatures, but Shwetha Nair was disappointed. She is visiting family in Quebec from India and had snow on her Christmas wish list.

But she says the show was a beautiful gift.

“It was awesome, I am probably more hyped for this than the snow now,” she says.

The schedule for the holiday train is on the Cpkc website .

stories.title: What role can Canada play in global security as world leaders gather in Halifax?
stories.summary: The Halifax International Security Forum is a showcase of military experts and strategic leaders from more than 70 countries. The three-day event will take place in downtown Halifax this weekend, for its 18th year.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - The Halifax International Security Forum is a showcase of military experts and strategic leaders from more than 70 countries. The three-day event will take place in downtown Halifax this weekend for its 18 th year.

Canada’s military and its global and domestic responsibilities will be closely examined at length, over the weekend through a series of seminars and meetings.

“This is more than just a security forum,” said Peter Van Praagh, the president of the forum. “We want to make sure we gather good ideas to put into decision-makers’ heads.”

“Canada is making historic investments in defence, rebuilding our industrial capacity, and we are working with our allies to deliver the capabilities that we need, and that we need to share,” said Canada’s Defence Minister David McGuinty.

In his remarks to open the security forum, McGuinty clarified the government’s stance on military cadets, following reports that Ottawa would be implementing cutbacks to cadet programming in Canada . The budget for the programs this year was approximately $265 million.

McGuinty said no core changes are coming to the cadet program and cited recent growth across the country.

“In the past three years, we have seen a 59 per cent increase in the number of people joining the cadet movement,” said McGuinty. “It is astonishingly encouraging.”

The 2026 version of the Halifax International Security Forum comes at a time when tariff and trade tensions have strained Canada’s relationship with the U.S.

Van Praagh said the war with Ukraine will be a major topic over the weekend, and U.S. President Donald Trump’s meeting on Thursday in Shenzhen, China with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, have already sparked reactions from those attending this event.

“People are going to want to talk about that,” said Van Praagh. “We are keeping Ukraine front and centre even though it’s been five years and what happens in Ukraine really is fundamental to Canadian security because Russia is testing the entire international system.”

No members of Trump’s administration are attending the security forum.

Dalhousie University International Development Studies Professor Robert Huish suggested that members of the Trump administration May have stayed away to avoid criticisms.

“Let us not forget that Mr. Trump has opened a war in Iran, and he’s declared victory many times and he’s still within the quagmire of it,” said Huish.

Global food security is also a prominent theme at the forum. Experts will examine international shipping routes around the world, like the Strait of Hormuz, the Panama Canal and Gibraltar. Having those areas and potential shipping choke points secured, is crucial so food can be transported to countries that need it.

stories.title: 25 new prosecutors half to what is needed to make ‘meaningful change’ on Manitoba Crown workloads
stories.summary: The provincial government is adding several Crowns over three and a half years, but one attorney says it's still far off from meaningful change.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
The provincial government is adding several Crowns over three and a half years, but one attorney says it’s still far off from meaningful change.

The Manitoba Association of Crown Attorneys announced the province is hiring 25 new prosecutors over three and a half years on Monday, and the organization is withdrawing its grievance filed against the government in April 2023. Fifteen new support workers will also be hired.

The number of Crowns that will be hired is half of what is needed, said Ben Wickstrom, vice-president of the Manitoba Association of Crown Attorneys.

“We’ve said that 50 is what we think would have a really meaningful impact on our workload,” said Wickstrom. “So, 25 is some distance from that, but it certainly is a step in the right direction.”

The plan is to have five new Crowns hired before the end of the fiscal year, which is in April 2027, said Wickstrom. They intend to hire six in 2028, seven in 2029, and another seven in 2030.

The organization has long been advocating for more resources to help with Crown workloads.

The amount of cases disposed in the system went up 22 per cent from 2020 to 2023, according to Manitoba Provincial Court Annual Reports. In 2020-21, there were 32,194 cases disposed and 39,503 in 2022-23.

Manitoba Justice Minister Matt Wiebe points the finger to the previous government on the overburdened court.

But another issue is retaining Crowns in the province.

“The question for us is obviously going to be ‘can we recruit and retain the people into these positions?’ It has been an ongoing challenge, and we’ve noted that there’s real retention problems,” said Wickstrom, noting the compensation isn’t competitive with other jurisdictions.

Legal counsel salaries in Manitoba range from $97,800 to around $200,000, according to the Manitoba Association of Crown Attorneys’ pay scale effective March 2021 to March 2027.

A person charged with an offence is given the right to be tried in a “reasonable time” as the time frame ranges from 18 to 30 months depending on the court, according to the Canadian Charter of Right and Freedoms.

Fifteen cases were stayed for unreasonable delay from 2018 to 2023, according to numbers from the province of Manitoba. The number of delay motions has also fluctuated since 2018 from 19 to 23 in 2025. There were 43 delay motions filed in 2024.

“You have to get work done on a more compressed timeline,” said Wickstrom.

Cait Alexander, an intimate partner violence survivor, said her former partner nearly beat her to death in 2021, but his charges were thrown out under Jordan’s rule.

“I would rather have physical violence committed against me than engage in that system,” said Alexander. “This is the norm. The norm is that the criminal court system is failing victims.”

She said more resources are needed in the court to minimize harm for survivors.

“Fund the court system on all levels, so that survivors aren’t waiting years,” she said. “It’s not just me. It’s tens and tens of thousands of victims.”

This comes as the court is slashing multiple sittings in rural locations in April 2027.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association is suing the provincial government for stagnant underfunding for Legal Aid Manitoba.

The number of Crowns that will be hired is half of what is needed, said Ben Wickstrom, vice-president of the Manitoba Association of Crown Attorneys.

content_blocks.text: “We’ve said that 50 is what we think would have a really meaningful impact on our workload,” said Wickstrom. “So, 25 is some distance from that, but it certainly is a step in the right direction.”
content_blocks.html: “We’ve said that 50 is what we think would have a really meaningful impact on our workload,” said Wickstrom. “So, 25 is some distance from that, but it certainly is a step in the right direction.”

content_blocks.text: The plan is to have five new Crowns hired before the end of the fiscal year, which is in April 2027, said Wickstrom. They intend to hire six in 2028, seven in 2029, and another seven in 2030.
The organization has long been advocating for more resources to help with Crown workloads.

The amount of cases disposed in the system went up 22 per cent from 2020 to 2023, according to Manitoba Provincial Court Annual Reports. In 2020-21, there were 32,194 cases disposed and 39,503 in 2022-23.
Manitoba Justice Minister Matt Wiebe points the finger to the previous government on the overburdened court.
But another issue is retaining Crowns in the province.

“The question for us is obviously going to be ‘can we recruit and retain the people into these positions?’ It has been an ongoing challenge, and we’ve noted that there’s real retention problems,” said Wickstrom, noting the compensation isn’t competitive with other jurisdictions.
Legal counsel salaries in Manitoba range from $97,800 to around $200,000, according to the Manitoba Association of Crown Attorneys’ pay scale effective March 2021 to March 2027.
Overworked court on tighter deadlines

A person charged with an offence is given the right to be tried in a “reasonable time” as the time frame ranges from 18 to 30 months depending on the court, according to the Canadian Charter of Right and Freedoms.

stories.title: Staples customers’ personal information compromised in website hack
stories.summary: The company said the hack happened between Nov. 1 and Nov. 5, during which the party had access to “certain customer personal information.”
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Staples Canada ULC said it has become aware of a possible data breach after an unknown party gained “unauthorized access” to the staplesprint.CA website.

The company said the hack happened between Nov. 1 and Nov. 5, during which the party had access to “certain customer personal information.”

“The personal information impacted included name, email address, shipping address, billing address, order summary, and encrypted password,” Adrian Lang, chief people and legal officer at Staples, said in a message to customers.

“No financial information was exposed,” she said.

Lang said Staples “promptly excluded the threat actor from our system and secured all accounts.”

She said customers who were potentially impacted will be prompted to reset their password upon their next login.

“While we believe the risk to you is low, we encourage you to regularly change passwords, use unique passwords for different websites, and remain vigilant about unsolicited emails that ask you to provide personal information.”

She said customers will be updated once the company learns more about the incident.

stories.title: Crown closes its case at murder trial of man charged with setting his best friend on fire
stories.summary: As the second week of the murder trial looking into the death of a London man who was set on fire came to a close, the Crown called its final witness in the case.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
As the second week of the murder trial looking into the death of a London man who was set on fire came to a close, the Crown called its final witness in the case.

Clive Hubbard from the Ontario Fire Marshal’s Office testified that he showed up to the strip plaza located at Admiral Drive and Trafalgar Street just hours after Jonathan Graham, 29, was set on fire on July 12, 2022.

He said he inspected a white Jeep Compass which belonged to the victim along with a nearby charred area of grass and a Bic lighter that was discovered.

In the Jeep there was gas on the driver side seat. “Gasoline was introduced to the interior of the motor vehicle,” said Hubbard.

However he said, “There was no evidence of fire in and around the vehicle, no charring, no scorching.”

Hubbard testified that the Bic lighter was located near two dumpsters. He said either a lighter or match could have been the ignition source for the fire, “At some point the vapours of gasoline were ignited, the clothing was then ignited...then to the ground.”

As for where the fire started, Hubbard concluded, “In my opinion the origin of the fire happened somewhere between the Jeep and the area of charred grass.”

Graham was rushed to hospital with severe burns. He died from thermal injuries.

The court has heard that Graham and his best friend got into a fight on that July night while out at a nearby after hours hangout.

It’s the Crown’s theory that they would eventually meet up at the strip plaza and that an angry Joudrey doused Graham with gasoline from a Pepsi bottle before setting him on fire.

Charged with first degree murder, Joudrey has pled not guilty.

Hubbard was the last witness called by the Crown.

stories.title: ‘I thought I died’: Survivor of deadly Tsawwassen Mills crash on long road to recovery
stories.summary: B.C. freelance videographer Kevin Li was setting up his equipment at Tsawwassen Mills Mall on Truth and Reconciliation Day, Sept. 30.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Julie Nolin
stories.content:
B.C. freelance videographer Kevin Li was setting up his equipment at Tsawwassen Mills Mall on Truth and Reconciliation Day, Sept. 30.

He is still recovering from life-changing injuries and trying to get his life back together.

Li was hit by a truck outside the mall that morning. Two people died at the scene and one person passed away in hospital about two weeks later .

“I got there about 30, 40 minutes before the event was about to start,” Li told Global News.

He said he saw wilapiya (Barb Joe) and Virginia Splockton chatting as they were getting set to unveil the House Post, carved by Joe’s son’s team.

“I set up and then it was really, really quiet,” Li said.

“And all of a sudden, I felt something hit me from the left side, almost like a big body check. But it wasn’t a body check; it was a pickup truck. It hit me; my body had twisted, my head had stayed still.”

Joe and Splockton were killed.

Li said that when it happened, time stopped and he wasn’t sure if he was going to make it.

“I asked myself, do I have my will done? I said yes. I asked myself, did I spend enough time with my daughter? I said, yes. And then the third thing was, did I do enough with my life? And I said yes,” he said.

“And it went black and I’d found peace. I thought I died. I honestly did.”

But when Li opened his eyes, everything was blurry. He didn’t know where he was or what had happened.

“I laid still on the ground and I heard, ‘Mom, stay with me, don’t go yet,’ Li said.

“And it was horrific.”

Li said he knew his life would never be the same.

“While I’m on the ground, I asked, ‘How am I gonna take care of my kid? How am I going to take care of my parents when they get older? Why should they have to take of me?’

“How am I supposed to take care of my parents and my kid?”

Li said at events he has attended since the Lapu Lapu Day tragedy , in which an SUV drove into a crowd of people, killing 11 people and injuring dozens more, organizers have installed temporary barricades.

Li says his life has changed “because of some guy that drove through us, because of the mall and not being able to put boulders on for a public gathering.”

In a statement, Tsawwassen Mills said they recognize the “profound impact” the incident had on the families and community.

“The safety and well-being of everyone at Tsawwassen Mills remain our highest priority. We understand the concerns raised regarding protective barriers and take them seriously,” they said.

“Given the sensitive nature of this incident, we are not in a position to comment on specific safety measures or potential changes at this time.”

Li said that before the incident he was getting in the best shape of his life – training for Hyrox and taking scuba lessons.

“And to have all of that stopped, to lying there on the ground and thinking, ‘How am I gonna ever pick up my daughter again? How am I going to take care of my parents when they get older? Why should they have to take of me?” he added.

Li is now recovering at home, but he says his nightmare is not over.

He has been battling with Icbc and WorkSafeBC.

“Why is nobody held accountable for this?” Li said.

Police have not released the driver’s name in the case, but previously stated that it is possible that the driver experienced a medical event prior to the collision.

“Initially, Icbc didn’t even want to even pay for my equipment that was bulldozed by the pickup truck,” Li said.

“I lost two cameras, three lenses, two tripods and a lot of other peripherals that was at retail around 20 something to $30,000. They didn’t want to pay for it. Why? Because the person had an unforeseen medical issue, which is not covered by Icbc.

“So you want me to get back to work, but you won’t replace my equipment. And so, I mean, I’m victimized again and again.”

But Li said the community stepped up to help take care of him and he is so grateful for his family, the Tsawwassen First Nation and friends who brought him food and checked up on him every day.

“That’s what really carried me because for a long time I kept it secret because I didn’t want to rely on anybody else,” he said.

“A lot of my friends actually didn’t know. And it was very, very dark and I felt very invisible, especially having to deal with Icbc. The first thing I had to do after surgery was to file an Icbc claim and all that paperwork that trailed afterwards and to realize, oh, you gotta do a WorkSafe claim now.”

A friend set up a GoFundMe for Li , which exceeded its goal in about 24 hours.

Li said he is now learning about gratitude and healing and trying to move forward while his body recovers, even though every day is a challenge.

“I want people to know that people don’t think this can happen to them, but they also don’t think that it can’t happen to them,” he said.

“Treasure every day and have gratitude for waking up in the morning and being able to take a shower without bath seats and bars and everything like that and being to do daily activities without pain.

“I had no idea how good I had it until after this accident.”

stories.title: Let’s not shame Doug Ford for his French
stories.summary: His face plant was spectacular, but Canada is not truly bilingual
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
John Diefenbaker’s French was dire. Though he was a stirring orator, he never learned the language and spoke it haltingly when he served as prime minister in the 1950s and 1960s. Audiences would wince when, jowls shaking, he would say: “ Mesdames et messieurs, permettez-moi de vous adresser quelques mots dans la langue française .”

But he was a master of tongues compared with Doug Ford. The Ontario Premier was in Montreal this week addressing the chamber of commerce. In the spirit of friendship between neighbouring provinces, he decided to try out his French. It did not go well.

Obviously nervous, staring fixedly and a little desperately at his teleprompter, he staggered through his own “ quelques mots ,” mispronouncing most of them. When he said that Ontario and Quebec should “ travaillons ensemble ,” it came out as something like “tryon sambla.” When he wished “ longue vie ” to Quebec, Ontario and Canada, he rendered the “vie” like the via in Via Rail.

Most people who grew up in Canada can at least put together a few words of French. Mr. Ford spoke almost as if he had never heard the language, even though he has repeatedly mentioned working on his French skills since becoming Premier in 2018.

Not since John Travolta introduced singer and actress Idina Menzel as the “wickedly talented, one and only, Adele Dazeem” at Hollywood’s Academy Awards has someone committed such a massive face plant. As they say in Quebec, “ il s’est planté royalement .”

Ford’s opponents in Ontario jumped all over him for it. NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the episode was embarrassing and “a little insulting” to French-speaking Ontarians. Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser felt it was “not something to laugh about” (though just about everyone did, including Mr. Ford’s Montreal audience). Mr. Fraser said he had heard someone suggest that what the Premier did to the French language was a hate crime, though he himself thought that was exaggerating. Oh, just a tiny bit.

Mr. Ford was apologetic about his fractured français , telling his listeners that the prospect of giving the speech had kept him awake at night. In the midst of one of his heroic attempts to form a French sentence, he stopped to say, “I’m really messing this one up.”

In truth, nobody expects to hear a guy like Mr. Ford to speak good French. He grew up in a Toronto suburb and, like many people in English Canada, never had much call to use the language of Champlain.

The plain fact is that though Canada May be a bilingual country by law, in practice it is not. More than half a century has passed since the enactment of the Official Languages Act ushered in the era of government-backed bilingualism. Yet less than one in five Canadians are truly bilingual – one in 10 outside of Quebec.

The bilingualism we do have – highway signs, labelling, proficiency requirements for civil servants – is mainly symbolic. If the aim of this noble gesture was to discourage separatism by making French Canadians feel fully included in the Canadian family, it has failed spectacularly. Successive nationalist governments of Quebec have devoted themselves to enforcing official unilingualism within its borders.

Yes, anglophones who aspire to high national office are expected to speak at least passable French. Good. About 20 per cent of Canadians have French as their mother tongue. Quebec is an important battleground in federal elections and any prime minister must deal with the Quebec question. We have evolved since Dief was the chief.

Politicians at lower levels are another question. Some are bilingual. Manitoba’s charismatic NDP Premier Wab Kinew speaks French. So does Naheed Nenshi, the former mayor of Calgary who leads the NDP in Alberta. Many others do not.

Mr. Ford stands out only for the level of his inability. But it seems wrong to blame him for it. Some people are just not good at languages. Many of us in English Canada are ashamed of our French, especially if we visit Quebec. At least he tried.

Mr. Ford was properly sheepish when asked later about his big fail in Montreal. As he put it, “Man, I need French lessons, big time.”

stories.title: Calgary man pleads guilty to threatening to kill PM Carney in YouTube posts
stories.summary: A man has admitted to posting online threats to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Calgary — A Calgary man admitted in court Friday to posting an online threat to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Jamie Dacosta pleaded guilty to a charge of threatening to kill the prime minister as well as offences involving a city business and its staff.

The 31-year-old was arrested in September after the RCMP’s Integrated National Security Enforcement Team learned of a threat on YouTube.

“We are going to Ottawa. If you can’t afford the gas, someone will help you pay for gas,” said Dacosta, in a YouTube post that was played in court.

“We’re gonna go kick in the door and bust out the four-four. You heard me. We’re gonna go slaughter Mark Carney – the clown and his carnival. This ain’t a circus no more, punk. We’re coming for you and your children.”

In another post, Dacosta threatened to slit the prime minister’s throat and harm his family.

Dacosta’s last post was made a few days before Carney was scheduled to visit Red Deer, north of Calgary. Police quickly made an arrest.

Sitting in court, Dacosta yawned and laughed as his posts were shown in court.

A judge was told that Calgary police had warned Dacosta back in March after he posted in a TikTok video that he was going to mutilate Carney and kill one of the prime minister’s children.

Defence lawyer Adriano Iovinelli asked the court for a pre-sentence report. He also acknowledged his client’s comments were alarming.

“He didn’t try to put them under someone else’s IP address. He made it very clear this is me, this is what I’m saying and I’ll say it again and again,” Iovinelli told reporters outside of court.

“This really screams out that there is some sort of mental illness and my client should be assessed.”

Dacosta also admitted to uttering threats, extortion and mischief at a tire shop, where he was seen on video smashing windows with an axe.

The case is back in court on Feb. 4.

Iovinelli said that gives the Crown prosecutor time to find out if Carney wishes to give a victim impact statement for sentencing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

Bill Graveland, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Stellantis agrees to continue talks about retaining ownership of plant
stories.summary: Automaker is paying $135-million a year to maintain idle Brampton plant, Doug Ford says
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Automaker Stellantis NV Stla-N has agreed to keep talking with government and union officials about retaining ownership of its plant in Brampton, Ont., and will send an official from Europe to continue negotiating next week.

The company idled its Brampton plant in 2023 and recently announced its sale to armoured-car maker Roshel Inc. This touched off a crescendo of worry and outcry over the future of Canadian automaking in the face of a trade war with the United States.

Stellantis is paying $135-million a year just to maintain the idle Brampton plant, plus hundreds of millions on federal greenhouse-gas emissions taxes, Ontario Premier Doug Ford told reporters on Friday evening in Toronto. His comments followed a meeting with Stellantis Canada president Trevor Longley, federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Unifor national president Lana Payne.

Mr. Ford said talks are expected to continue next week.

“That’s where we can mitigate [taxes], buy a little more time and focus on what we can put into the plant,” Mr. Ford said, describing the meeting as challenging but productive.

Ms. Payne said the sale of the plant has not closed and it’s still possible to stop it from being finalized, but there remains “a mountain to climb here.”

“The sale needs to be reversed and the company was adamant that it was going ahead,” Ms. Payne said.

She said the emissions taxes paid in Canada amount to an “own goal” that automakers face. This is on top of tariffs when shipping to their most important market, the United States.

Mathis Denis, a spokesman for Ms. Joly, declined to say what offers were made to Stellantis, saying, “We will not stand for the sale to happen.” Mr. Ford and Ms. Payne also declined to provide details.

In a statement, Stellantis said it remains “committed to continuing constructive discussions.”

About 2,200 Brampton Stellantis workers remain on layoff benefits. The plant was being retooled for the Jeep Compass but Stellantis assigned that production to a plant in Illinois after the U.S. imposed 25-per-cent tariffs on imported cars.

Stellantis and Roshel say the plant could be used for automotive and defence production but have provided no details.

The automaker is struggling to make a profit and faces excess capacity at its global manufacturing facilities.

Speaking to reporters earlier on Friday, Ms. Joly repeated the government’s threat to take the company to court and recoup “hundreds of millions” of dollars in taxpayers’ financial aid to Stellantis if the plant is sold.

This includes the money given to the company under a 2022 agreement for work on the Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., as well as an EV battery plant in Windsor in which the company is no longer involved. However, Ms. Joly said, “if they decide to protect the workers we can work together.”

The exact amount the government is seeking is $831-million, according to a source familiar with the discussions. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the person because they are not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.

Stellantis has offered to repay $24-million, the amount it says it received to retool the Brampton plant.

stories.title: Military to continue avalanche control in B.C.'s Rogers Pass
stories.summary: Rogers Pass - Parks Canada says military support for avalanche control along a major highway corridor in southeastern British Columbia will continue, at least for now, in an apparent reversal of a decision to end the program next year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Rogers Pass - Parks Canada says military support for avalanche control along a major highway corridor in southeastern British Columbia will continue, at least for now, in an apparent reversal of a decision to end the program next year.

Artillery shells have been fired to set off slides along the Trans-Canada Highway, which winds through Rogers Pass in Glacier National Park, for more than 60 years.

stories.title: 70 units ready in Saint John tiny home community as N.B. combats homelessness
stories.summary: Seventy new homes are now ready for tenants at a tiny home community in Saint John, N.B., as the city continues to tackle chronic homelessness.
stories.author: Reeti Rohilla
stories.content:
Seventy new homes are now ready for tenants at a tiny home community in Saint John, N.B., as the city continues to tackle chronic homelessness.

Officials unveiled the units at the Sunnyside Tiny Home Community, ON the city’s east side, Friday.

“The safe, warm house is really just the beginning. It’s housing first not housing only,” said Marcel LeBrun, founder of 12 Neighbours, which was contracted to deliver on-site support services to residents.

Housing Minister David Hickey says the province has committed to reducing chronic homelessness by 40 per cent, with a target date of 2028-29.

“As of this month, there are now 332 chronically homeless individuals living in Saint John, part of the total of 1,095 chronically homeless people across the province,” he said.

Mayor Donna Reardon says the crisis caught the city off guard.

“Homelessness has come on the city like a tsunami. And we had no playbook for it. We didn’t know what we were doing. We knew we needed to approach it from a human rights perspective,” she said.

Despite some concerns from nearby residents, city council unanimously approved rezoning the land last year.

Ottawa is contributing more than $11.7 million and the province is committing $5 million to the project.

United Way Maritimes is aiming to build 500 homes in the Maritimes by 2031. In Saint John, the first residents are expected to move into the Sunnyside community in December.

“About 14 individuals have been selected. In the next couple of weeks we’ll be starting to interview those individuals and select the people who will be in that first sort of wave,” said Alexya Heelis, vice-president of community relations at United Way Maritimes.

The community will have around-the-clock staffing, that will connect residents with health care, recovery and employment services.

— with a file from Rebecca Lau

stories.title: Arbitration ends B.C. nurses labour dispute with 3% wage increases, smaller pay grid
stories.summary: Vancouver - An arbiter has imposed annual wage increases of three per cent through to 2029 for British Columbia's more than 60,000 nurses, much lower than the eight per cent through to 2028 that the union wanted.
stories.author: Ashley Joannou The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Arbitrators have imposed annual wage increases of three per cent through to 2029 for British Columbia’s more than 60,000 nurses, a decision their union president says has left nurses feeling “gravely disappointed” after they asked for eight per cent annually.

The decision ends a fractious dispute between the provincial government and the BC Nurses’ Union that included strike action with nurses briefly refusing non-essential overtime this summer.

The binding decision from special mediators Vince Ready and Amanda Rogers was issued Wednesday and only covered compensation after contract language on violence in the workplace, nursing duties and nursing shortages was resolved through earlier mediation.

Union president Adriane Gear said in an interview Friday that the deal imposed on nurses “falls incredibly short” of what members wanted, leaving them “gravely disappointed with the outcome.”

“Our collective bargaining round was constrained by a mandate that didn’t allow for nurses to actually feel valued and respected for what they bring to the health-care system,” she said.

The three per cent pay increase is in line with pay allowances set by government for public sector workers in the province and is retroactive to 2025.

Gear said the increase is the same that was offered in a tentative deal that was rejected by 67 per cent of voting members in May 2026, leading to job action for several days in early July where nurses stopped non-essential overtime or doing non-nursing duties, such as answering phones or processing doctors’ orders.

She said a provincial government mandate requires that wage increases not be higher than three per cent and that if the nurses had been able to negotiate more, other unions would have also received pay increases because of “me-too agreements” signed with the government.

“When we were offered the arbitration, we were told that that was the only way we could have our compensation considered because the arbitrators are not constrained by the mandate or the me-too (agreements,)” she said, describing trying to bargain under the mandate like swimming with your arms tied behind your back.

The new deal will now take seven years for nurses to get to highest pay scale starting in April 2027, down from a previous 10-year grid, and nurses who have 10 years of work experience will get an extra 50 cents per hour, effective the first pay period following April 1, 2028.

The 45-page written decision said the smaller grid brings nurses to the top rate three years sooner, while preserving a progression through the middle years of a nurse’s career.

It said that in order to meet the province’s first phase of nurse-to-patent ratio promises, about 10,500 additional nurses will be required and evidence suggests that nurses under 35 are most likely to leave the profession.

Gear said the new grid means the starting wage for nurses in B.C. is among the highest in the country, but beyond year four, not much has changed. She called the 50-cent increase at 10 years “kind of just insulting.”

The two sides spent about seven months at the bargaining table before reaching a tentative agreement in May 2026 that was rejected by the nurses.

Gear said nurses in the province feel unheard or unvalued and the work conditions remain poor, with up to 6,000 vacancies at one time.

“They got it right in terms of how do we recruit new nurses? But (the deal) falls extremely short, devastatingly short, in terms of retaining nurses that have been holding the system together,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Politics Insider: A Conservative cabinet in B.C.
stories.summary: Lorne Doerkson was sworn in as the province’s 38th premier
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

British Columbia ’s first Conservative cabinet in nearly a century was sworn in today, installing a largely untested group of ministers who are now tasked with delivering on an ambitious platform centred on greater affordability, a stronger economy and easing health-care strains.

From Victoria, Andrea Woo reports that Lorne Doerkson was sworn in as the province’s 38th premier by Lieutenant-Governor Wendy Cocchia in a ceremony at Government House, alongside a streamlined cabinet of 18 ministers and six ministers of state.

The new cabinet includes: Attorney-General Caroline Elliott; Finance Minister Peter Milobar; Health Minister Ryan Peterson; Public Safety Minister and Solicitor General Jessy Sahota; Social Development Minister and Deputy Premier Claire Rattée; Minister of Indigenous Relations and Reconciliation Scott McInnis; Minister of Energy, Mines and Petroleum Resources Larry Neufeld; and Transportation and Infrastructure Minister Trevor Halford.

The smaller cabinet is consistent with Doerkson’s broader campaign commitment to streamline government and reduce non-essential spending. The NDP cabinet after the 2024 election comprised 23 ministers and four ministers of state.

This is the daily Politics Insider newsletter, curated by

. It is available exclusively to our digital subscribers. You can sign up for more than 20 other newsletters on

Ontario Liberal Party to name new leader Saturday: The party is looking to rebuild after three consecutive election losses, with the goal of presenting a serious alternative to Premier Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives in the next election.

Ottawa open to three-player telecom sector, sources say : Privately, politicians and civil servants have signalled to industry executives the government is no longer wedded to a four-player structure and is open to a three-company oligopoly in Canada.

Carney government plans to conclude trade deal with Taiwan: Prime Minster Mark Carney’s government says it intends to complete a trade agreement with the self-governing democracy of Taiwan even as Ottawa rekindles relations with China after a deep freeze.

Ford’s Oakville assembly plant reopens after more than two years: The plant will make heavy-duty pickup trucks, defying the trade war and offering hope for the future of Canadian automaking.

Prime Minister’s Day : Mark Carney, who returned from a four-country trip on Thursday, did not have any public events scheduled for today.

Party Leaders : Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre held a news conference on Parliament Hill. No schedules were available for other party leaders.

Ministers on the Road:

In Halifax, Defence Minister David McGuinty hosted the annual Halifax International Security Forum.

In Sault Ste. Marie, Ont., Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon , with Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Singh Sarkaria, announced investments to support trade diversification across Canada

In Oakville, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly , with Ontario Premier Doug Ford as well as Ivan Boykin, president and CEO of Ford Motor Company of Canada and Unifor National President Lana Payne, announced funding to support auto manufacturing in the Ontario town.

On Saturday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will begin a tour of the Gulf region through next Thursday to boost trade and seek new investment. The stops are in Doha, which is the capital of Qatar, and Abu Dhabi and Dubai in the United Arab Emirates.

Rideau Hall Skating : The Rideau Hall skating rink , which dates back to 1872, will be open to the public as of Saturday until March 27, weather permitting. Visitors have to bring their own skates.

“Canada has been very difficult for this country for 50 years. For some reason, they feel emboldened, and we can’t let them feel that way anymore. ... With that being said, we’re working on making a deal that’s fair.” – U.S. President Donald Trump during a news conference at the White House today.

Ontario Liberals are naming a new leader today. Ontario’s third premier was also a Liberal, and the longest-serving premier in the province’s history. Who was he?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Donors have started giving up on Pierre Poilievre, and a leader who can’t fundraise can’t last

It is no small thing to ask a would-be donor to part with his or her money for a political cause, and compared to last year, tens of thousands of donors have given up on the Poilievre-led Conservative one. It may take a new leader to bring them back. — Robyn Urback, columnist

Canada’s film and television industry is being left in familiar territory : the dark

There are three things that members of Canada’s film and television industry have become experts in over the past half-decade: producing the kind of buzzy, headline-grabbing content that goes global; waiting; and then waiting some more. — Barry Hertz, film editor and deputy arts editor

Straightlaced Carney is rattling the U.S. with his China reset - and it is unlikely comedy gold

Mr. Carney is a quintessential Canadian do-gooder, who is playing by the rules. Officials of the current U.S. administration seem have a deep commitment to misunderstanding that. — Rita Trichur, columnist

Got a news tip that you’d like us to look into? E-mail us at tips@globeandmail.com . Need to share documents securely? Reach out via SecureDrop .

The answer to today’s question: Oliver Mowat, who was premier for 24 years , from 1872 to 1896, when he was appointed to the Senate. In 1897, he left Ottawa to become the lieutenant governor of Ontario. He died in April 1903, aged 82.

stories.title: Renters’ advocacy group wants seat at the table when it comes to National Housing Strategy
stories.summary: Renters’ advocacy group Acorn took its message to the streets of London Friday, calling for a seat at the table as the federal government shapes the National Housing Strategy.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Renters’ advocacy group Acorn took its message to the streets of London Friday, calling for a seat at the table as the federal government shapes the National Housing Strategy.

About a dozen members of the local chapter marched from Victoria Park to the Hyman Street constituency office of London Centre MP Peter Fragiskatos.

Fragiskatos was not on site, but the group left a letter for him and Prime Minister Carney in the mailbox.

They’re calling for federal housing funding to be tied to national standards including rent-controls, an end to no-cause evictions, and a ban on using federal funds for projects that demolish existing affordable housing.

“Luxury units and high-priced units, those prices are coming down because no-one can afford them. But affordable housing units that our members can afford, and the general public can afford- these are being demolished and the rents continue to rise,” said Acorn London Chapter Chairperson Claire Wittnebel.

stories.title: NHL linesman Matt Pavelich was a peacemaker during a wild era of on-ice lawlessness
stories.summary: He wore the striped jersey for 23 seasons with the National Hockey League, from 1956 to 1979, and was the first of his profession to be enshrined in the Hockey Hall of Fame
stories.author: Tom Hawthorn
stories.content:
Matt Pavelich skated in more Stanley Cup Finals series than Dave Keon, Gordie Howe, Bobby Hull, Jean Béliveau or Frank Mahovlich.

Unlike those star players, he never got his name engraved on hockey’s storied trophy, though his brother did.

Mr. Pavelich, who has died at 92, served as a linesman for 23 seasons in the National Hockey League , becoming the first of his profession to be enshrined in the Hockey Hall of Fame.

He worked the blue lines in 21 finals, including 19 consecutive from 1961 until retirement in 1979.

Tall, with jet-black hair unprotected by a helmet, and, later, sporting a soup-strainer mustache, Mr. Pavelich was a familiar figure for a generation who saw him on Hockey Night in Canada and other televised games.

Linesmen are on-ice officials in striped jerseys responsible for such quotidian duties as icings, offsides and face-offs. Along with routine chores, they also have the unenviable responsibility of serving as hockey’s bouncers, breaking up fights between players.

Mr. Pavelich survived the era of wild, rock ’em, sock ’em hockey of the 1970s when the Big Bad Bruins of Boston and Philadelphia’s Broad Street Bullies engaged in assorted melees, donnybrooks and bench-clearing brawls, a period of lawless mayhem akin to professional wrestling, only without choreography and a script.

“Now we have maybe one fight every 10 games,” he once told the Busted Lip Podcast , whose host included his youngest son. “In my day, they used to have 10 fights in one game.”

The act of skating between two brawlers demands bravery, strength and timing. Doing so before gloves are dropped means perhaps an uneasy peace is maintained. Doing so before the fighters have tired risks the peacemaker being on the receiving end of a haymaker.

“If two guys go at it and they’re even-Steven, we let them go at it until they’ve punched themselves out,” he told the magazine writer Earl McRae in 1971. “We step in when it’s obvious one guy has the advantage and someone is going to get hurt.”

The linesman suffered cuts and scratches, as well as numerous bruises. He once needed six stitches on the inside of his mouth when he inadvertently “walked into a punch” thrown by Bobby Hull.

In one 1963 game, Mr. Pavelich intervened too quickly during a fight between Lou Fontinato of the Montreal Canadiens and Earl Ingarfield of the New York Rangers. He took a punch to the jaw and collapsed face first on the ice, as the skaters continued to wrestle and throw punches.

“I must have been out cold for a couple of minutes,” Mr. Pavelich told the Montreal Gazette eight years later. “And you know what Ingarfield and Fontinato were doing when I came to? Both claimed credit for knocking me out.”

For the record, it was a right from Mr. Fontinato that felled the linesman. In the player’s defence, Mr. Ingarfield had pulled his sweater over his head and he was swinging wildly.

In a game a month before his retirement, Mr. Pavelich was left dazed after being accidentally punched in the back of the head by the ironically named Larry Playfair, whose intended target was the face of opponent Al Secord. Only 46 seconds after play resumed, the hapless linesman was called on to separate tough guy Dennis O’Brien from Dave (The Hammer) Schultz, whose rap sheet was as long as the Saskatchewan winters from which he emerged.

Though he himself never played a game of junior or professional hockey, Mr. Pavelich’s own hardscrabble origins provided a street education in the fistic arts. In a 1961 game in Kingston, Mr. Pavelich and goaltender Jack McCartan, a recent winner of an Olympic gold medal, threw punches during an argument after the final buzzer. The league president reported Mr. Pavelich “said there were a couple of blows traded – but most of them couldn’t break a pane of glass.”

Matthew Ivan Pavelich was born on March 12, 1934, in Gold Park, a Northern Ontario gold mining town of 300 people about seven kilometres from Wawa. The family received a silver loving cup in honour of his being the first baby born in the community. He was one of four children born to the former Zora Stilin, known as Rose, from a Croatian family in Sault Ste. Marie, Ont., and Mate Pavelich, a Croatian immigrant gold miner who took Matthew as his English name.

Shortly after Matt’s third birthday, his father suffered a grievous facial injury on the job. He was drilling in the Parkhill mine when the act set off an unexploded stick of dynamite left behind by another crew. His face and head were peppered by rock fragments, causing him to lose an eye and be blinded in the other. He also suffered a hand injury.

On Boxing Day in 1938, he died by suicide, according to a correspondent’s report for the Daily Clarion, a Toronto-based pro-union newspaper. He was 42. His widow remarried another Croatian immigrant, Davorin Krmpotich, known as Martin, and the family settled in Sault Ste. Marie, where Matt was raised in a blended family.

Older brother Marty Pavelich debuted in the NHL during the 1947-48 season, going on to win four Stanley Cup championships with the Detroit Red Wings. A year later, Matt Pavelich exchanged a hockey stick for a whistle.

“I was only 14 and had just got off the bus at an outdoor rink in the Soo,” he told Dave Waddell of the Windsor Star in 2011. “They didn’t have a referee, so they asked me. I didn’t have my skates with me, so I ran up and down the ice in my boots with these little tykes.”

He decided to become an on-ice official because the speed and agility he displayed on skates was lost once he had to hunch over a hockey stick.

He was the first member of his family to graduate from high school, though he twice ran away from home to join a travelling carnival when it passed through the Soo.

At age 20, he became a referee for the Northern Michigan Intermediate League, a tough circuit where his car tires were slashed and he needed a police escort for some games. He made his NHL debut at Boston Garden on Oct. 11, 1956, a 4-4 tie with the Toronto Maple Leafs. The legendary Red Storey worked as the referee, while Doug Davies was the other linesman.

That season, he and his brother made NHL history by being the first pair from one family to have a player and an on-ice official in the same game. By coincidence, the Skov brothers – Art, a linesman who later became a referee, and Glen, a linemate of Marty’s on the Red Wings – matched the brothers’ feat later that same season.

When assigned a game with the Red Wings, Mr. Pavelich always arranged for the other linesman to handle Marty during hostilities.

While his brother retired from hockey after the 1956-57 season, Mr. Pavelich continued a career that would see him handle 1,727 regular-season games, including 14 as a referee. He also worked 245 playoff games, as well as 10 All-Star Games and the 1976 Canada Cup tournament.

One of his most memorable games pitted the felonious Flyers against the Soviet Red Army in an exhibition game in Philadelphia on Jan. 11, 1976. After referee Lloyd Gilmour did not call a penalty on a check thrown by Ed Van Impe that left Valery Kharlamov in a pile on the ice (a “dying swan routine,” the linesman said afterward), the Soviet team refused to resume play. The referee called them for delay of game and they left the ice, as a television audience heard Bob Cole make one of the most famous calls in the history of hockey broadcasting: “They’re going home! They’re going home! Yeah! They’re going home.”

The Soviets were coaxed back onto the ice, reportedly after being reminded they had yet to be paid for Super Series ’76 exhibitions.

Later in the game, won handily by the Flyers, 4-1, Mr. Pavelich broke up a confrontation between Reggie Leach and Boris Alexandrov, grabbing their sticks. “That’s enough,” he said. The Soviet player pushed the linesman, swearing at him in Russian. The linesman, who spoke Croatian and knew a smattering of Russian, shocked the player by getting the referee to assess a two-minute penalty for unsportsmanlike conduct.

The linesman missed the occasional game over the years from what he suspected were heart problems. The ailment was eventually diagnosed as a hiatal hernia, a stomach and esophagus issue which can manifest as chest pain. Mr. Pavelich remained on the ice until 1979 before spending 15 seasons as a supervisor of officials for the NHL, serving as a mentor for those who wear the striped sweater, a fraternity jocularly known as zebras.

He continued in a supervisory role for Junior B and C games in the Ontario Hockey Association into his late 70s.

Mr. Pavelich, a longtime resident of Windsor, Ont., died on Oct. 30. He leaves his wife, the former Dragica Stipaničić, whom he met in his father’s birthplace of Senj, a coastal town in Croatia on the Adriatic Sea. They were married in Yugoslavia in 1964. He also leaves a daughter, Carol Brown, and sons Matthew and Mark Pavelich, as well as four grandchildren, two great-grandchildren, and a brother, Ronald Krmpotich.

He was predeceased by two sisters and two brothers, including Marty Pavelich, who died in 2024 at age 96.

What turned out to be the linesman’s final NHL game was played on May 21, 1979, as the Montreal Canadiens won their fourth consecutive Stanley Cup by beating the visiting New York Rangers by 4-1 to take the series in five games.

In the dying seconds, a Rangers player dumped the puck into the Montreal end, where goaltender Ken Dryden reached down to pick it up in his trapper. “A lovely souvenir of a special occasion,” he later said, “my final game.”

Mr. Pavelich raced to the goalie as the final horn sounded, asking for the puck.

“Matt, it’s my last game,” Mr. Dryden said, sharing a secret only his wife knew.

“Ken, it’s my last game, too,” Mr. Pavelich replied. “And I think I have more seniority than you.”

As Canadiens players mobbed their goalie, he turned his catching glove over to let the puck fall into the linesman’s bare hands.

Mr. Dryden, then aged 31, asked the linesman, then 45, to leave the puck for him in his will. The linesman agreed. As it turned out, the goalie preceded the official in death by a little more than a year.

stories.title: December sentencing in Holmesville murder case in jeopardy
stories.summary: The planned sentencing of a 15-year-old Huron County boy for first degree murder in the violent murder of an 11-year-old girl in Holmesville May not happen before the end of the year.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The planned sentencing of a 15-year-old Huron County boy for first degree murder in the violent murder of an 11-year-old girl in Holmesville May not happen before the end of the year.

Appearing virtually in a Goderich courtroom Friday, the teen murder suspect heard that “inconsistencies” between what was reported in a recent psychiatric assessment of the suspect, and what was revealed in court during a June court hearing has prompted the Crown to seek a second opinion.

They are seeking a forensic psychiatrist to evaluate the Nov. 13 psychiatric assessment of the 15-year-old suspect. The Crown is also interested in potentially cross examining those that completed the most recent psychiatric assessment.

It’s not clear if all that can be completed before the planned Dec. 14 to 17 sentencing hearing.

Court heard an 11-year-old girl was stabbed to death in a wooded area near the former Holmesville Public School on July 2, 2024. The suspect who was 13 years old at the time and was known to the victim, sexually assaulted and then stabbed the girl more than 70 times after she refused his sexual advances.

Court heard that the suspect then called 911, saying the victim had been abducted by three men in a van. He was taken into custody, shortly thereafter, and charged with first degree murder. On June 2, 2026, he pleaded guilty to first degree murder.

He faces a maximum sentence of 10 years. Six years served in custody, four years served under supervision in the community, under strict conditions. By the end of this month, the suspect will have already spent 29 months, or 2.5 years behind bars which can count against this sentence.

The next court date in this case is Dec. 8. Sentencing could still proceed on Dec. 14 to 17, if the issues surrounding the Crown’s concerns regarding “inconsistencies” in the suspect’s psychiatric assessment report, and evidence heard in court can be resolved.

stories.title: Supreme Court to issue landmark ruling on Quebec’s Bill 21 next week
stories.summary: Case centres on province’s secularism law and the power of governments to override wide swaths of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada will deliver its landmark ruling in the Quebec secularism case on Nov. 27.

In a brief announcement on Friday, the country’s top court said the ruling will be issued next Friday at 9:45 a.m. Ottawa time.

The hotly political case is rooted in foundational questions about Canada’s Constitution and the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Seven judges of the top court heard the appeal over four days in March, one of the longest hearings in the history of the Supreme Court.

The decision is the biggest in the court’s recent history and one of the most important Charter rulings ever. The Supreme Court’s judgment is in part a reckoning with the political compromises of the early 1980s that helped achieve the patriation of the Constitution from Britain in 1982 and the inclusion of the Charter in the Constitution.

At issue in the Quebec secularism case at the Supreme Court is the province’s Bill 21. Passed in 2019, the law prohibits many public-sector workers in the province, including teachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols (such as a hijab or a cross) on the job. The provincial government shielded Bill 21 from court challenges with Section 33 of the Charter, the notwithstanding clause, which allows legislatures to override many of the rights in the Charter.

Quebec’s goal is secularism but some people believe Bill 21 violates freedom of religion and is a state attack on minorities. The notwithstanding clause requires renewal every five years and Quebec did so in 2024. Bill 21 was also twice upheld by the lower courts in Quebec, in 2021 and 2024, both times because of the notwithstanding clause.

The clause, which went mostly unused for decades, has become popular in recent years among some conservative-led provinces. Quebec’s Bill 21 in 2019 was a demarcation point. Alberta used the clause in four laws last year, one to end a teachers’ strike and the other three to restrict the choices of transgender youth.

The Bill 21 case at the Supreme Court intensified federal-provincial political fissures. The federal Liberal government, and numerous advocacy groups, in March argued that the judges should impose additional limits on the notwithstanding clause. Ottawa asserted that the clause’s extended use to override rights effectively eliminates rights and rewrites the Constitution.

Quebec insists its political autonomy is in peril and at the Supreme Court the province vied against six groups of appellants who argued Bill 21 should be struck down. The federal government, as well as some appellants and intervenors, want the court to endorse what are called judicial declarations, where a superior trial court could rule that a law protected by the notwithstanding clause violates Charter rights, even as that law is allowed to stand.

Quebec parried the fusillade of arguments aimed at taking down Bill 21 and rejected the idea of judicial declarations.

“It is not up to the court to answer a political question that does not concern the courts,” Quebec government lawyer Isabelle Brunet argued at the Supreme Court in March.

Ontario, Alberta and Saskatchewan, all conservative led, sided with Quebec. The NDP in B.C. and Manitoba were open to judicial declarations but did not support limits on the notwithstanding clause. (B.C. in October elected a Conservative government .)

In late 1981 an agreement to formalize the notwithstanding clause in the Charter was a key compromise to bridge a political divide at the time, as Pierre Trudeau sought to patriate the Constitution and enact the Charter of Rights. Many provincial leaders felt the Charter could usurp legislators, with courts striking down laws.

The federal government has never invoked the clause, through decades of Liberals and Conservatives in power.

The Nov. 27 date for the Bill 21 judgment had been widely viewed as likely by court watchers, after Chief Justice Richard Wagner in June at his annual news conference said the judges aimed to publish the ruling before the end of Justice Sheilah Martin’s tenure on the top court. She retired at the end of May but has six months, until the end of November, to participate in judgments.
