stories.title: Alberta tweaks carbon capture incentive program to allow grants during construction
stories.summary: The change to cover 12 per cent of eligible capital costs is meant to better align provincial policy with the federal Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage Tax Credit.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
The Alberta government has tweaked its carbon capture and storage incentives so that some funds are available during construction, instead of only once a project starts up.

Under the Alberta Carbon Capture Incentive Program , companies can receive grants covering 12 per cent of eligible capital costs for certain projects, including in the oil and gas, petrochemical and power industries.

The change is meant to better align the provincial policy with the federal Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage Tax Credit.

“Alberta is already a global leader in carbon capture and storage, and we want to build on that advantage,” Brian Jean, the provincial energy and minerals minister, said in a news release late Thursday.

“Strengthening Accip and better aligning it with federal support will help accelerate projects to ensure that industries, such as oil and gas, remain sustainable for decades and continue to contribute to the province’s prosperity.”

The announcement comes as Alberta, Ottawa and the five biggest oilsands producers work to hammer out final agreements on moving the Pathways project forward while at the same time enabling oilsands production growth.

Pathways would transport carbon dioxide captured from various oilsands sites via pipeline to an underground storage hub near Cold Lake, Alta., where the greenhouse gas would be prevented from entering the atmosphere.

The governments and industry players had aimed to announce definitive agreements around Nov. 15, but company executives have recently signalled they’re willing to take the time necessary to get the right deal.

Under a federal-provincial energy accord signed a year ago, Pathways’ advancement is a condition for the proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast getting Ottawa’s support, and vice versa.

Pathways is being developed by the Oil Sands Alliance, which includes Cenovus Energy Inc., Canadian Natural Resources Ltd., Suncor Energy Inc., Imperial Oil Ltd. and ConocoPhillips Canada.

The alliance said that Pathways will have the capacity to transport and store about six million tonnes per year of captured CO2 by the mid-2030s. The parties are aiming for another 10 million tonnes of reductions by 2045.

That’s a significant scale-back from the 22 million tonnes of emissions by 2030 they had earlier targeted.

stories.title: The holiday train delivers cheer as it picks up donations across Canada
stories.summary: A holiday classic is now on track, delivering cheer and picking up donations in communities across Canada. The Cpkc Holiday Train made its first stop in Montreal-West, where a large crowd gathered as a freight full of the spirit of the season pulled in.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Montreal - A holiday classic is now on track, delivering cheer and picking up donations in communities across Canada. The Cpkc Holiday Train made its first stop in Montreal-West, where a large crowd gathered as a freight full of the season’s spirit pulled in.

The Holiday Train project got rolling 28 years ago and this year two trains will make stops in 182 communities in Canada and the United States. When the locomotive and rail cars decorated with colourful lights arrive at a station, one of the wagons opens up and is transformed into a stage.

The Toronto-based band Magic! is among the artists on board for the first leg of the journey, delivering hit songs like “Rude,” and a newly released holiday tune called “As Long As We’re Together.”

“We’ve played beaches, we’ve done skiing lodges, we’ve done arenas and festivals, and the Holiday Train is a Canadian tradition,” says frontman Nasri Atweh. “We’re Canadian boys, we want to be part of giving back and we want to have fun.”

Niloo Morati was at the train station with her five-year-old daughter Harper. She says experiencing the show on rails is now a staple of the holidays.

“I find that with all the technology and everything around us it is really important to build family traditions and to have opportunities like this to spend time with family and neighbours,” Morati says.

‘It’s about giving back’

Along with the spirit of the season, the train’s voyage comes with a deeper message. Spectators are encouraged to donate or bring non-perishable goods to the show. Since 1999, the train has collected $20 million and 2.5 million kilograms for local food banks.

“It’s about giving back to communities where we operate and about bringing awareness to food insecurity,” says Cpkc Director of Government Affairs, André Hannoush.

Money and goods collected in Montreal-West are headed to food bank Moisson Montreal. Its director of philanthropy, Matias Duque, says the donation comes as needs are growing.

“Times are tough, with the high cost of living,” he says. “We didn’t used to see people who are working coming to food banks, now we do. We see more students, more older adults as well, so there is more demand. So, there is a lot of bad news, but there is good news as well. We are making a difference.”

Four-year-old Aidan and his dad Gabe Lewis brought canned goods.

“It’s always important to me to make sure that we learn to share and to think about how we can give when we have so much,” says Lewis.

Magic!’s performance on the ride delivered a sprinkle of holiday spirit to a landscape where no snowflake has fallen yet.

Montreal is experiencing an unusually warm season. Many spectators welcomed the balmy temperatures, but Shwetha Nair was disappointed. She is visiting family in Quebec from India and had snow on her Christmas wish list.

But she says the show was a beautiful gift.

“It was awesome, I am probably more hyped for this than the snow now,” she says.

The schedule for the holiday train is on the Cpkc website .

stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada to issue decision on Quebec's secularism law next week
stories.summary: Montreal - The Supreme Court of Canada will issue a landmark decision next Friday on Quebec’s secularism law, known as Bill 21.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Supreme Court of Canada will issue a landmark decision next Friday on Quebec’s secularism law, known as Bill 21.

The court heard arguments earlier this year from groups that support and oppose the law, which prohibits civil servants in positions of authority, including teachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols on the job.

stories.title: Nova Scotia marks Transgender Day of Remembrance with flag raising and poetry
stories.summary: The annual occasion honours transgender and gender-diverse people whose lives were lost to anti-transgender violence and hatred.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
About 50 people, including provincial politicians from all major parties, gathered in front of Nova Scotia’s legislature on Friday to mark Transgender Day of Remembrance.

The annual occasion honours transgender and gender-diverse people whose lives were lost to anti-transgender violence and hatred.

Nova Scotia NDP member Lisa Lachance hosted a ceremony that featured poetry readings by Halifax artist Asiah Sparks.

Sparks says the occasion calls for people to honour those who weren’t given the chance to safely live their lives authentically.

Lachance, who is Nova Scotia’s first openly gender-queer member of the legislature, says rates of violence against queer and trans people continue to rise, and it’s crucial allies do what they can to make the lives of trans people safer.

Statistics Canada data released in March says hate crimes targeting gender identity or expression increased for the fourth consecutive year in 2024, with 139 police-reported incidents.

The rate of hate crimes experienced by transgender and gender-diverse people since 2020 has nearly tripled.

stories.title: Saskatoon appeals board rules oversized million-dollar home can remain
stories.summary: Saskatoon's Development Appeals Board is granting a variance for a multimillion dollar Nutana home, allowing it to stay built despite being too tall under city bylaws.
stories.author: Chris Carr
stories.content:
Saskatoon’s Development Appeals Board is granting a variance for a multimillion dollar Nutana home, allowing it to stay built despite being too tall under city bylaws.

“It is certainly a relief for them,” said Kim Anderson, a lawyer who has been representing Curtis Kelln in the matter. Kelln bought the property at 833 University Dr. in 2025 from the estate of the previous owner who died unexpectedly. Much of the home had already been framed under a building permit issued in 2022.

However, Kelln was unaware the home exceeded the city’s zoning height limit by 1.8 metres.

Even though the city conducted nine building and framing inspections between 2022 and 2026, the height issue was never flagged. Anderson said his client relied in good faith on the city-issued permits.

“The height of the building is something that would normally have been inspected and caught,” Anderson said.

The homeowners argued the 9.68 metres total height of the house should be allowed because the circumstances were exceptional, the requested variance was minor and granting it would not unfairly affect the neighbours.

In the decision, the Development Appeals Board agreed, saying in part, “granting a 1.8 metre height variance to recognize the as-built structure under these exceptional, circumstances does not confer special privilege that would be denied to another applicant in identical circumstances.”

And there was a lot at stake. A professional opinion found if the variance was denied, the only viable option would be to tear down and rebuild. That’s because removing the top floor alone was estimated to cost just over a million dollars, roughly the value of the home itself.

Robert Clipperton with the Nutana Community Association sympathized, but still opposed the variance.

“By exceeding the size restrictions, it goes against the neighbourhood preservation theme.”

He’s worried the decisions could set a precedent.

“So, the concern is if you allow one house that is four and half feet that are taller than they should be, what happens to the next one?” Clipperton asked.

Anderson thinks that is very unlikely, given how unusual the circumstances are in Kelln’s case.

That said, the final chapter May still be written.

“We need to continue to struggle on this. I don’t know whether we still end up appealing the decision to the Saskatchewan appeals board, or not,” Clipperton said.

The October appearance before the board was the second appeal made by Kelln. Two other areas of the house, including a sidewall, have since been brought into compliance. An exterior wall has also since been removed.

“Essentially, when we returned with the second appeal, we were making a substantially smaller ask, than we did the first time around,” said Anderson.

“And given the direction and comments we’d received from the board on the first appeal we thought we had a good chance of finding favour and certainly upon our review, the decision it seems that that smaller ask did make the difference.”

stories.title: ‘Cash is king’: Why money is a popular holiday present for many Canadians
stories.summary: With holiday shopping season in full swing and Black Friday approaching, more than a quarter of Canadians say they would much get cash than a present, according to a survey.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Who doesn’t love unwrapping a holiday present? More than a quarter of Canadians, apparently, who would rather open an envelope full of cash instead, a new survey shows.

With holiday shopping season in full swing and Black Friday approaching, more than a quarter of Canadians (27 per cent) say they would much rather their friends, family and loved ones gave them cash than a present, a new survey from EQ Bank shows.

“We all have memories of being really excited about opening a present, opening it with glee and finding something you didn’t want, like a pair of socks,” said Leslie Logan, senior financial planner at TD Wealth.

Younger Canadians are more likely to prefer cash, with 41 per cent of those aged 18 to 34 preferring money, compared to only 12 per cent of those over the age of 55.

The social taboo around giving someone cash, whether for the holidays or for a wedding, is ending, Logan said.

“My mother would be aghast if she received an envelope full of cash, but nowadays it’s more normal to receive cash,” she said.

Receiving cash saves many the stress of returning a present they don’t like or ending up with something they won’t use and gives the recipient more flexibility.

“Cash is king,” Logan said.

Another 11 per cent said they prefer gift cards.

Of the 27 per cent who prefer cash, 14 per cent said they would use it for covering everyday expenses. This points to a holiday shopping squeeze, with more than a third (35 per cent) saying they are in a worse financial position than they were last holiday season.

More than half (57 per cent) said they plan to reduce, postpone or skip at least one holiday expense to afford the holidays this year.

Cash comes in handy in a pinch like this, Logan said.

“Instead of buying GTA VI, you pay your credit card bill,” she said.

Seven per cent said in the EQ Bank survey that they prefer cash because they can use it to buy something they like, while six per cent said they would use that money to save or invest.

An alternative to cash is buying someone a financial product or contributing to a savings account.

“If you’re giving to grandchildren, an Resp (Registered Education Savings Plan) for their future post-secondary education is a great option,” Logan said.

For helping an adult, topping up their Tax-Free Savings Account (Tfsa) can also help. If your loved one is an aspiring homeowner, contributing to their First Home Savings Account can also go a long way, Logan said.

However, if your loved one finds financial products overwhelming, it can help to take them to a bank or financial advisor and help set them up with a new investment account, she said.

Even a contribution as small as $50 or $25 can compound over a long period of time and help start an investment habit.

“This Christmas you could give the gift of financial literacy,” Logan said.

stories.title: Rancher says Alberta well cleanup fund a positive step — but litany of concerns remain
stories.summary: Energy companies would initially hand over up to $50,000, followed by incremental payments across 10 years, with the funds attached to each well regardless of ownership changes.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Alberta legislation that would require oil and gas companies to pay upfront for the eventual cleanup of each well seems positive on the surface, but much will depend on how it’s implemented and enforced, says a rancher and landowner advocate.

“It looks good on paper,” Bill Heidecker, president of the Alberta Surface Rights Federation, said Thursday. “We got lots of questions on how it will actually work.”

The legislation introduced as part of a broader bill Wednesday would require companies to make an initial payment of up to $50,000 followed by yearly incremental payments over a 10-year period, with the funds attached to each well regardless of any ownership changes.

The new rules in the Energy, Environment and Utilities Statutes Amendment Act, 2026, are expected to apply to wells drilled after April 1, 2027.

The backlog of thousands of wells that have yet to be properly closed remains an ongoing issue.

Heidecker has a cattle ranch near Coronation, Alta., in the eastern part of the province, and says there are a “couple dozen” wells on his land — some producing and some not.

Dealing with the industry has been a “constant headache,” he said. Heidecker wants assurances companies will be held to their obligations.

“There are a lot of laws and regulations on the books that haven’t been enforced to the degree they should have,” he said.

It’s also unclear what the rules are for energy infrastructure beyond wells, such as pipelines, he said. And he wants more detail on the formula to calculate the cost of well cleanup — is it based on today’s costs or future projected ones? What if there are multiple well bores stemming from one pad? — as well as how to prioritize which wells are cleaned up first.

“We’ve seen that in the existing cleanup, the companies tend to clean up the easy, simple ones and they’re leaving the difficult, expensive ones lower down on the list,” he said.

“So we welcome this, of course, but we’re reserving judgment until we see what actually happens.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "So we welcome this, of course, but we're reserving judgment until we see what actually happens."

Heidecker’s group sent a letter to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith last week expressing “profound dissatisfaction” with her government’s handling of energy policy and landowner rights, listing off a litany of concerns around both current development and inactive infrastructure.

It urged landowners to withhold consent for oil and gas development on their properties and not voluntarily sign new leases.

Heidecker said the call for resistance remains, despite the province taking a “step in the right direction” with the proposed upfront closure funding.

“There’s so many other things they need to address,” he said. Those matters include a lack of firm cleanup deadlines, unpaid municipal taxes and inadequate enforcement.

Meanwhile, an environmental think-tank offered qualified praise for the move.

The new rules would be “an important and positive step toward ensuring industry meets its legal responsibility to clean up after itself,” said Amanda Bryant, manager of the oil and gas program at the Pembina Institute.

But she said to be successful, the new rules should include minimum thresholds for how much financial security is set aside for cleanup.

“Additional action is needed to address existing inactive and orphan wells, such as implementing enforceable timelines for well closure, charging an inactive well fee, or increasing the orphan well levy charged to industry to reflect the scale of the cleanup work ahead,” Bryant said.

Wells are deemed orphans when there is no entity legally responsible for their cleanup, for instance when their owner goes bankrupt. Such wells become the responsibility of the non-profit Orphan Well Association, which is funded through an industry fee.

The Orphan Well Levy for the 2026-27 fiscal year is $154.56 million.

The well association has pegged total cleanup costs of its inventory at $1.66 billion. Landowner advocates say the current levy isn’t high enough to address the scale of the backlog, and some have raised concern about the health and environmental effects of potential contamination from improperly managed wells.

Heidecker’s group is part of a lawsuit filed in September by landowners challenging what they call the Alberta Energy Regulator’s “chronic underfunding” of the Orphan Well Levy, the amount of which is determined by the Alberta government based on the regulator’s recommendation.

The latest monthly numbers from the Orphan Well Association say there are 7,328 wells waiting to be decommissioned, which involves permanently dismantling equipment so that the site is safe.

Another 9,258 sites are in need of reclamation, which means restoring the land so it’s similar to its original state.

In the 2025-26 fiscal year, the combined cost of decommissioning and reclaiming a well was more than $56,000.

Brian Jean, Alberta’s energy and minerals minister, said the cost of putting funds into the new Resource Asset Closure Assurance and Stewardship Fund shouldn’t have a negative impact on industry.

He figures the funds would amount to an initial one per cent of the cost of drilling the well, plus another one per cent from the incremental payments over the following decade.

He told reporters Thursday that as companies become more efficient and find ways to drive down the cost, “frankly, there are good opportunities to make money.”

Under the legislation, companies would be able to unlock the funds — which would have accrued compound interest over the years — once reclamation is complete.

Jean said if companies don’t put down the deposit, they can’t get a licence to drill.

“It’s a cost of doing business,” he said.

“The truth is that it’s a very innovative approach. It’s a one-of-a-kind approach, the first in the world, and it’s going to work.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "The truth is that it's a very innovative approach. It's a one-of-a-kind approach, the first in the world, and it's going to work."

stories.title: ‘Waste to opportunity’: Saskatchewan government to expand bioenergy in north
stories.summary: Premier Scott Moe said Friday's announcement will support the power grid and forestry sector to prepare both for the future demands they are projected to see.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The Saskatchewan government is looking to expand its generation of biofuel-sourced electricity to support a growing electrical grid.

The province committed to assessing the potential for additional bioenergy power generation Friday, a move Premier Scott Moe said builds upon an existing agreement between the Meadow Lake Tribal Council (Mltc) and a provincial Crown corporation.

The Mltc Bioenergy Centre produces enough carbon-neutral power for approximately 7,000 houses and sells that electricity to SaskPower, according to a Saskatchewan government news release.

“Electricity demand is projected to increase by 40 per cent by 2035, and that number can move significantly one way or the other. And (it is) expected to more than double by the year 2050. That’s significant growth,” Moe said at a news conference in Prince Albert.

“Meeting that demand will require Saskatchewan to continue to consider every available option.”

The project will max out at 100 megawatts of electricity production. Moe said that amount supports Saskatchewan’s growing electrical needs and forestry sector.

“Today is about opportunities for future partnerships by taking an agreement that is working in this province with Meadow Lake Tribal Council and making it available to other communities across the province,” he added.

Bioenergy is produced with waste known as biomass, including forestry residue, agricultural residue and processing byproducts, according to the Natural Resources Canada website.

To produce energy, those products are broken down into combustible synthetic gas, that gas is then cleaned, conditioned and prepared until it has the chemical makeup required to produce energy.

“It turns our forestry and agricultural byproducts into a very valuable resource generating power for our families and for our jobs,” Moe told reporters.

Bioenergy can be renewable, though Natural Resources Canada notes that whether it falls under that umbrella depends on the rate of regeneration in relation to the rate of consumption.

Three bioenergy projects – including the one with Meadow Lake Tribal Council and landfill gas projects in Regina and Saskatoon – are currently operating in Saskatchewan.

Bioenergy can also act as a complimentary base energy source, in combination with intermittent power providers, such as wind or solar power, according to Moe.

“Turning waste into opportunity, that’s what we’ve been doing in this province for over a century now,” the premier said. “For Saskatchewan’s forestry sector, that opportunity is particularly impactful and, I think, timely. And very, very important.

“The forest industry is an economic anchor.”

Moe pointed to the province’s plan to spend $2.5 million on protecting its forestry industry as U.S. tariffs continue hitting the sector.

“Although 94 per cent of our Saskatchewan exports, our economy, is absent of those tariffs. The six per cent that is touched by those tariffs is touched 100 per cent. And the forestry industry is no exception,” he said.

Mltc Tribal Chief Jeremy Norman told reporters that unlike solar and wind power, biomass will exist so long as forests and agricultural production does. He said the Mltc Bioenergy Centre has been able to practice environmental stewardship while boosting the local economy.

stories.title: Trump says Canada feeling 'emboldened' but he's seeking a 'fair' trade deal
stories.summary: Washington - U.S. President Donald Trump says Canada is feeling "emboldened" but his administration is working on a trade deal "that's fair."
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Washington - U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday Canada is feeling “emboldened” but his administration is working on a trade deal “that’s fair.”

In a wide-ranging news conference at the White House, the president said he spoke with Prime Minister Mark Carney on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific economic summit in Shenzhen, China, and described the Canadian leader as “very nice.”

Trump then turned to his repeated claims about Canada ripping off the United States and being frustrating to deal with on the trade file.

“For some reason they feel emboldened and we can’t let them feel that way anymore,” Trump said.

It wasn’t clear exactly what the president was referring to — the historically close Canada-U.S. relationship or the midterm elections which saw American voters issue a clear rebuke of Trump’s trade policy and sweeping tariff campaign.

Trump’s trade war with Canada rapidly escalated after negotiations broke down in August. The president hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs and banned imports of others, prompting Ottawa to respond with retaliatory duties.

Trump also signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and spent days posting images on social media disparaging Canada.

The Trump administration’s tone on Canada softened somewhat after the Republican shellacking in the midterm elections.

On Nov. 12, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said “we want to have a deal that makes sense for them and for us.”

“Part of it means protecting our supply chains and getting them here, but also making accommodation when possible,” Greer said.

Trump said Friday that when Canada’s trade deficit with the United States is down to zero, he’ll be ready to talk. That trade deficit is driven by U.S. consumption of oil and energy products, which Trump also has said he wants to increase.

The president repeated Friday the claim that Carney wants to “build a Keystone pipeline for us” — likely a reference to the Prairie Connector pipeline that would reuse Keystone XL infrastructure.

Carney on Wednesday said a “very good trade arrangement” with the United States is possible but Canada won’t just sit around and wait. Carney has embarked on a mission to reduce Canada’s reliance on the United States, including signing trade deals last week with the Philippines and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations group.

“We’d like to do a deal. If the U.S. doesn’t want to do a deal, we’re busy,” Carney said in an interview during the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.

Canada’s Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette has said Canada must prepare for a world where a tariff-free arrangement May no longer be possible.

The objective is to “get to the lowest rate of tariff on the narrowest basket of goods with the most preferential access for Canadian businesses and Canadian workers,” Charette told MPs during a meeting Tuesday of the House of Commons international trade committee in Ottawa.

Democrats have indicated ending the trade war with Canada will be among their top priorities when they take control of Congress in January — but they could struggle to achieve the supermajority they need to override the president’s veto.

Canada will also need to continue working with the Trump administration to renew the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, better known as Cusma.

Trump did not renew Cusma in July, triggering a rolling annual review for up to a decade — at which point the agreement will expire if the three countries cannot agree on an extension.

During Friday’s nearly 90-minute press briefing where Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the president also said companies that build artificial intelligence data centres in other countries will be hit with “a tremendous tax.”

“We’re not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen,” Trump said. “And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”

Trump said he hadn’t yet told his own officials about his plan and offered no details. Throughout the president’s second term he has suggested tariffs and punishments for a wide range of actions that have never materialized.

Unease over the fast pace of data centre development in the U.S. also helped Democrats win big in the midterm elections.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026

— With files from The Associated Press

Bay du Nord oil project clears final regulatory hurdle, awaits Equinor's next move

stories.title: Bay du Nord oil project clears final regulatory hurdle, awaits Equinor's next move
stories.summary: ST. John's - Equinor's proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project has cleared its final regulatory hurdle in Newfoundland and Labrador.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - A proposal for Canada’s first deepwater oil project has cleared its final regulatory hurdle as the Newfoundland and Labrador government awaits the owner’s next move.

Canada and Newfoundland and Labrador’s joint energy regulator approved Equinor’s development plan for Bay du Nord earlier this month. On Friday, officials from both governments gathered in St. John’s, N.L., to say they’d accepted that approval.

All that’s left now is for Equinor to make a final decision to proceed with the $14-billion venture, and that decision is expected early next year, said Premier Tony Wakeham. And though climate scientists are urging governments to turn away from fossil fuels, the Newfoundland and Labrador government hopes Bay du Nord won’t be the last oil and gas development in its territory offshore.

“We are talking to companies and countries all over the world who have an interest in coming here,” Lloyd Parrott, the provincial energy minister, told reporters. “We do things different than they do in the rest of the world, and we do things better.”

The federal government approved Bay du Nord in the spring of 2022, but Equinor still had to submit its development plan to the joint Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Energy Regulator for scrutiny. The Norway-based company submitted the plan in May, and it was approved by Nov. 4, according to the province.

Friday’s announcement about Bay du Nord came as a United Nations climate summit — known as COP31 — began to wrap up in Turkey. This year’s talks came amid urgent warnings that the planet is sure to overshoot the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial temperatures.

The Quebec government also pledged at the summit to create a road map to transition away from fossil fuels as part of its membership in the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance — a group of states and governments collaborating to phase out oil and gas production.

Joanne Thompson, the federal fisheries minister, said Canada is working to build up clean energy resources, but traditional energy sources — such as oil and gas — are needed in the meantime.

“This is how we control our destiny, how we are able to work toward our goal, but understanding that we need at this point to still have both conventional and clean energy,” she told reporters in St. John’s.

Bay du Nord would be the first deepwater oil development in Canada, and farther from shore than any other oil project on Earth. Equinor would drill wells more than a kilometre below the surface of the ocean, in waters about 500 kilometres northeast of St. John’s.

The company expects to extract more than 400 million barrels of oil, with first oil expected in 2031.

Equinor is the majority owner and operator of Bay du Nord. British oil giant Shell recently announced it was buying a 30-per-cent share of the project and the Newfoundland and Labrador government is considering purchasing a 10-per-cent stake.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

— with files from The Associated Press

“This is how we control our destiny, how we are able to work toward our goal, but understanding that we need at this point to still have both conventional and clean energy,” she told reporters in St. John’s.

Bay du Nord would be the first deepwater oil development in Canada, and farther from shore than any other oil project on Earth. Equinor would drill wells more than a kilometre below the surface of the ocean, in waters about 500 kilometres northeast of St. John’s.
The company expects to extract more than 400 million barrels of oil, with first oil expected in 2031.

Equinor is the majority owner and operator of Bay du Nord. British oil giant Shell recently announced it was buying a 30-per-cent share of the project and the Newfoundland and Labrador government is considering purchasing a 10-per-cent stake.

stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada upholds conviction for aggravated sexual assault
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada says a judge made a clear legal error when he required evidence that a complainant in a sexual assault case communicated her lack of consent to the accused man.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Supreme Court of Canada says a judge made a clear legal error when he required evidence that a complainant in a sexual assault case communicated her lack of consent to the accused man.

In a ruling today, the top court says there is no legal requirement to communicate non-consent to sexual contact.

Bevin Kerry Degale was charged with aggravated sexual assault after his then-girlfriend emerged from a van in a state of extreme distress and told people she had been raped.

Neither the complainant nor the accused testified during the trial in Ontario court.

The trial judge acquitted Degale but the Ontario Court of Appeal set aside the acquittal and substituted a conviction.

The Supreme Court affirmed the appeal ruling, saying there is no reasonable doubt that the accused knew of — or was at least wilfully blind or reckless about — the lack of consent.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Russian missiles landing in Poland a 'deliberate' strategy: McGuinty
stories.summary: Halifax - Defence Minister David McGuinty says objects believed to be Russian cruise missiles and a drone which landed in Poland today are part of Russia's "deliberate" strategy to expand its incursions in the Baltic region.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - Defence Minister David McGuinty said Friday Russia is deploying a “deliberate” and “sophisticated” hybrid war campaign in eastern Europe after Poland reported Russian incursions into its airspace.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an “intentional provocation” on Friday after two suspected cruise missiles and a drone entered his country’s airspace.

A few hundred Canadians are stationed in Europe as part of Operation Unifier, which is helping to train Ukrainian security forces. McGuinty told reporters on the sidelines of the Halifax International Security Forum that Canadian armed forces personnel are all safe.

Poland said the objects landed not far from where some European troops were holding a military exercise. McGuinty would not comment on the location of Canadian troops in Poland at the time of the incursion.

There are no immediate reports of injuries or damage from Russian air incursions in Poland.

Tusk said the incident happened while Russia was carrying out a major nighttime bombardment of Ukraine.

Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the development in Poland a “grave violation” of that country’s airspace.

“This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine,” Rutte wrote on X.

There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the missiles and suspected drone, or on Friday’s drills.

McGuinty suggested Friday that the reported Polish incursion would fit the wider pattern of Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine.

“Other countries have also seen these occurrences, some of which have been explained, many of which have not been explained,” he said.

“The prosecution of the war by the Russians, in terms of hybrid warfare, is sophisticated. It’s deliberate. It is reaching into neighbouring countries.”

European troops were taking part Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began Nov. 9 in southeastern Poland. Forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine to stabilize the country and rebuild its military.

U.S. President Donald Trump discussed the war at a summit in China on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff.

Another Trump envoy, his son-in-law Jared Kushner, told European leaders that the United States believes Russia is “comfortable” with Nato-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine.

Russia’s nighttime attack on Ukraine came hours after Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes this week on a bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. The bridge is vital to Moscow’s war effort.

McGuinty had just returned Friday from Brussels, where he attended a meeting of the coalition of nations supporting Ukraine. He confirmed Friday that Trump called into the meeting from Air Force One and “spoke for several minutes,” but he did not share details of what the president said.

Bloomberg, Politico and other international outlets have reported that Trump highlighted the financial and human costs of the conflict during the call and urged countries to pull back their funding for Ukraine’s defence.

McGuinty said leaders in the room left “more united” in their support for Ukraine.

The minister cited Canada’s promised contributions to postwar security guarantees for Ukraine but did not provide details about what form that could take.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

— written by Craig Lord in Ottawa with files from Devin Stevens in Halifax and The Associated Press

stories.title: Lorne Doerkson sworn in as B.C. Premier, unveils pared-down cabinet
stories.summary: Smaller Conservative cabinet is consistent with the new leader’s commitment to streamline government, reduce non-essential spending
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
British Columbia ’s first Conservative cabinet in nearly a century was sworn in Friday, tasking a mix of political veterans, former municipal leaders and newcomers to provincial politics to deliver on an ambitious platform centred on greater affordability, a stronger economy and easing health care strains.

Lorne Doerkson was sworn in as the province’s 38th premier by Lieutenant-Governor Wendy Cocchia at a ceremony at Government House in Victoria, alongside a reduced cabinet of 18 ministers and six ministers of state.

The new cabinet includes two people who ran for the party leadership earlier this year. Peter Milobar, who was first elected as a BC Liberal MLA in 2017 and has served as the Opposition finance critic, has been named finance minister. Caroline Elliott, who has made repealing the province’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act a central focus of her campaign, was named attorney-general. This is her first term as an MLA.

Among other cabinet ministers who are newcomers to the legislature are tech entrepreneur Ryan Peterson as Minister of Health; former Central Saanich councillor Cathie Ounsted as Minister of Local Government, Housing, Sport and Culture; and police officer Jessy Sahota as Minister of Public Safety and Solicitor-General.

Claire Rattée, first elected in 2024, has been named Social Development Minister and Deputy Premier.

Mr. Doerkson congratulated the new ministers and told attendees – who included former Conservative leader John Rustad and former premier Christy Clark – that they accept their responsibilities with humility, gratitude and a deep sense of purpose.

“Together we will work tirelessly for every single British Columbian,” he said. “We will honour the trust that has been placed in us and help build an even stronger future for this province and this extraordinary place that we call home.”

Andrew Reeve, a senior public affairs consultant at Earnscliffe and former BC Liberal press secretary, said Mr. Doerkson would have had to balance several considerations in assembling his cabinet, including members’ sector-specific experience, regional representation and the interpersonal dynamics within his caucus.

The appointments also offer clues about how the new Premier intends to approach some of the government’s most consequential files.

Mr. Reeve said Mr. Milobar’s appointment as finance minister was widely expected, given his “incredible grasp on the province’s finances and budgeting.” He’ll be tasked with managing the province’s projected $13.8-billion deficit.

“This is a pick that indicates a clear preference for ability and experience in this highest-profile portfolio,” Mr. Reeve said.

Mr. Peterson, who was also former chair of the Business Council of B.C., was given the health portfolio because of his business background.

“This is a massive ministry with $40-billion of expense, and I’m convinced that Ryan’s the fellow for the job,” Mr. Doerkson told reporters after the ceremony. Mr. Doerkson has previously said his government would slash health care administration while maintaining front-line workers.

Ms. Rattée, who has spoken openly about her past struggles with drug addiction and homelessness, received a standing ovation as she was named deputy premier – an appointment that she said left her surprised, honoured and overwhelmed.

“I hope that this just reminds anyone who’s struggling – anybody who might feel like they aren’t qualified for a position like this, but wants to try and make a difference – that if you put your mind to it, anything is possible,” she told reporters after the ceremony.

As Attorney-General, Ms. Elliott will be tasked with some of the province’s thorniest legal challenges, including its appeal of the landmark Cowichan Tribes Aboriginal title ruling.

Greg Lyle, president of Innovative Research Group, said Ms. Elliott’s appointment “sends a clear message on their approach to Indigenous issues.”

It’s expected that Ms. Elliott will work to repeal Dripa alongside new Minister of Indigenous Relations and Reconciliation Scott McInnis, who said Friday that he has spent the last two years developing good personal and professional relationships with First Nations and that he looks forward to continuing that work.

The smaller cabinet is consistent with Mr. Doerkson’s broader campaign commitment to streamline government and reduce non-essential spending. The NDP cabinet after the 2024 election comprised 23 ministers and four ministers of state.

Other ministerial appointments include Larry Neufeld (Energy, Mines and Petroleum Resources), Trevor Halford (Transportation and Infrastructure) and Ian Paton (Agriculture).

Mr. Doerkson said his government will forgo a fall legislative session to give members time to familiarize themselves with their portfolios. However, it will immediately pursue several measures that don’t require legislative changes, including a “repeal” of the optional teaching resource Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity, commonly called Sogi, with more to be announced next week, Mr. Doerkson said.

The BC Teachers’ Federation said it is unclear on what that means in practice, given that Sogi is not part of any curriculum.

“There seems to be a misunderstanding of what Sogi is and the new government has never really been able to articulate what they want to repeal or what they will replace it with,” the union said in a statement provided by its director of media relations, Amy Smart. “At the end of the day, teachers need resources to support students to feel safe and accepted.”

Meanwhile, Mr. Milobar said he would provide more information in coming days on an independent review into the province’s books.

A briefing with Mr. Doerkson on the matter included the phrase, “It’s a massive mess that we’re inheriting,” Mr. Milobar told reporters. “So that is why we’re going to be down to business right away.”

As well, Mr. Doerkson recommitted to raising the province’s personal income tax exemption level to $32,000, from $13,216, in the spring legislative session, which would save most workers $1,000 a year.

“My hope – don’t hold me to this – is that that will be dated back to Jan. 1, but I’m not sure of the intricacies of doing that,” the Premier said.

Peter Milobar, who was first elected as a BC Liberal MLA in 2017 and has served as the Opposition finance critic, has been named finance minister. Caroline Elliott, who has made repealing the province’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act a central focus of her campaign, was named attorney-general. This is her first term as an MLA.

Among other cabinet ministers who are newcomers to the legislature are tech entrepreneur Ryan Peterson as Minister of Health; former Central Saanich councillor Cathie Ounsted as Minister of Local Government, Housing, Sport and Culture; and police officer Jessy Sahota as Minister of Public Safety and Solicitor-General.
Claire Rattée, first elected in 2024, has been named Social Development Minister and Deputy Premier.

Mr. Doerkson congratulated the new ministers and told attendees – who included former Conservative leader John Rustad and former premier Christy Clark – that they accept their responsibilities with humility, gratitude and a deep sense of purpose.

“Together we will work tirelessly for every single British Columbian,” he said. “We will honour the trust that has been placed in us and help build an even stronger future for this province and this extraordinary place that we call home.”

Andrew Reeve, a senior public affairs consultant at Earnscliffe and former BC Liberal press secretary, said Mr. Doerkson would have had to balance several considerations in assembling his cabinet, including members’ sector-specific experience, regional representation and the interpersonal dynamics within his caucus.
The appointments also offer clues about how the new Premier intends to approach some of the government’s most consequential files.

Mr. Reeve said Mr. Milobar’s appointment as finance minister was widely expected, given his “incredible grasp on the province’s finances and budgeting.” He’ll be tasked with managing the province’s projected $13.8-billion deficit.
“This is a pick that indicates a clear preference for ability and experience in this highest-profile portfolio,” Mr. Reeve said.
Mr. Peterson, who was also former chair of the Business Council of B.C., was given the health portfolio because of his business background.

“This is a massive ministry with $40-billion of expense, and I’m convinced that Ryan’s the fellow for the job,” Mr. Doerkson told reporters after the ceremony. Mr. Doerkson has previously said his government would slash health care administration while maintaining front-line workers.

Ms. Rattée, who has spoken openly about her past struggles with drug addiction and homelessness, received a standing ovation as she was named deputy premier – an appointment that she said left her surprised, honoured and overwhelmed.

“I hope that this just reminds anyone who’s struggling – anybody who might feel like they aren’t qualified for a position like this, but wants to try and make a difference – that if you put your mind to it, anything is possible,” she told reporters after the ceremony.
As Attorney-General, Ms. Elliott will be tasked with some of the province’s thorniest legal challenges, including its appeal of the landmark Cowichan Tribes Aboriginal title ruling.
Greg Lyle, president of Innovative Research Group, said Ms. Elliott’s appointment “sends a clear message on their approach to Indigenous issues.”

It’s expected that Ms. Elliott will work to repeal Dripa alongside new Minister of Indigenous Relations and Reconciliation Scott McInnis, who said Friday that he has spent the last two years developing good personal and professional relationships with First Nations and that he looks forward to continuing that work.

The smaller cabinet is consistent with Mr. Doerkson’s broader campaign commitment to streamline government and reduce non-essential spending. The NDP cabinet after the 2024 election comprised 23 ministers and four ministers of state.
Other ministerial appointments include Larry Neufeld (Energy, Mines and Petroleum Resources), Trevor Halford (Transportation and Infrastructure) and Ian Paton (Agriculture).

Mr. Doerkson said his government will forgo a fall legislative session to give members time to familiarize themselves with their portfolios. However, it will immediately pursue several measures that don’t require legislative changes, including a “repeal” of the optional teaching resource Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity, commonly called Sogi, with more to be announced next week, Mr. Doerkson said.
The BC Teachers’ Federation said it is unclear on what that means in practice, given that Sogi is not part of any curriculum.

“There seems to be a misunderstanding of what Sogi is and the new government has never really been able to articulate what they want to repeal or what they will replace it with,” the union said in a statement provided by its director of media relations, Amy Smart. “At the end of the day, teachers need resources to support students to feel safe and accepted.”
Meanwhile, Mr. Milobar said he would provide more information in coming days on an independent review into the province’s books.

A briefing with Mr. Doerkson on the matter included the phrase, “It’s a massive mess that we’re inheriting,” Mr. Milobar told reporters. “So that is why we’re going to be down to business right away.”

As well, Mr. Doerkson recommitted to raising the province’s personal income tax exemption level to $32,000, from $13,216, in the spring legislative session, which would save most workers $1,000 a year.
“My hope – don’t hold me to this – is that that will be dated back to Jan. 1, but I’m not sure of the intricacies of doing that,” the Premier said.

stories.title: Scotties Tournament of Hearts will be played in Vernon, B.C., in 2028
stories.summary: Vernon - The Scotties Tournament of Hearts will return to British Columbia in 2028, with Vernon hosting the Canadian women’s curling championship for the first time.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vernon - The Scotties Tournament of Hearts will return to British Columbia in 2028, with Vernon hosting the Canadian women’s curling championship for the first time.

Curling Canada announced Friday that the tournament will run Feb. 11-20 at Kal Tire Place.

The arena hosted the 2008 women’s world championship, where Canada’s Jennifer Jones won gold.

It will be the 10th Tournament of Hearts held in B.C. and the first since Kerri Einarson won her fourth straight Canadian title in Kamloops in 2023.

Next year’s event will be held in Charlottetown, P.E.I., with the winner earning a spot in Vernon as Team Canada.

The 2028 winner will represent Canada at the world championship March 17-26 in Truro, N.S., and return to the 2029 Scotties as defending champion.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

NHL player's wife, Lauren Kyle McDavid, shared home reno details on Instagram but denied any move to the Maple Leafs

Connor McDavid and then-fiancé Lauren Kyle on the red carpet before the 2023 NHL Awards at Bridgestone Arena on June 26, 2023, in Nashville, Tennessee. (Bruce Bennett / Getty Images)

November 20, 2026 at 1:58 p.m.

Connor McDavid, the 29-year old centre and captain for the Edmonton Oilers, is putting down roots in Toronto. But don’t expect him to swap his Oilers jersey for one for the Maple Leafs any time soon.

McDavid and his wife, Lauren Kyle McDavid, were married in 2024 in Muskoka, and they own a cottage in that Ontario region as well as a home in Edmonton.

This week, Lauren shared on an Instagram post news that they had bought another home in the Toronto area. Connor’s hometown is Newmarket, just north of the city.

View this post on Instagram

“So I just arrived in Toronto,” Lauren says at the start of a two-minute video on Instagram. “I’m here for the weekend to go to the game and see some family, but also to go check on our house. We’re doing a renovation here.”

She adds: “We bought a place in the summer and hoping for it to be all reno’d by next summer. It’s a lot of work and a lot to do.”

In a previous story, National Post reported that McDavid has three properties, each with a sauna. If this is indeed their third, that means there is one here too.

“Connor and I love the routine … it feels meditative,” Lauren told Architectural Digest recently of the sauna experience, adding their typical routine consists of two 15-minute sessions in the heat, followed by a two- to three-minute dip in the cold plunge or in the lake if they’re at their cottage.

The latest video doesn’t show much of the exterior of the property, though we do get a glimpse of an imposing metal gate and a curved, wooded drive before the view cuts to inside, where Lauren lays out some staining samples for a dark wood-panelled room.

“This is room one that’s getting stained,” she says. “We’re turning this into a little bit more of a brown, kind of mink colour.” She adds: “This will be my office.”

Lauren’s LinkedIn profile says she completed her Bachelor’s degree in Interior Architecture from Ryerson University. She owns Kyle & Co. Design Studio. She also founded Sports Club Atelier, a sportswear brand featuring hockey-inspired merchandise.

It was in that capacity that she shut down any idea that the new home purchase might be linked to a change in team affiliation for her husband, who is having a strong year with the Oilers.

During a video in which she modelled several NHL-themed items, she at one point donned a Maple Leafs sweater.

“This is one of the Toronto sweaters,” she said. “It’s a nice powdery blue.” She then added: “I’m just wearing this for show. We’re not going to Toronto. I’m sorry to break it to you.”

Connor is currently signed to a two-year, $25-million contract that expires at the end of the 2027-28 season, at which point he’ll be an unrestricted free agent. He has played with the Oilers since first being drafted in 2015.

He was in Toronto for a game against the Leafs last Saturday night at Scotiabank Arena, which the Oilers won 1-0, with McDavid collecting an assist on the sole goal by teammate Evan Bouchard.

Toronto’s losing streak reached eight games Thursday with a 4-3 loss at home to the Los Angeles Kings. Their record in this dubious category is 10 losses in a row, set during the 1966-67 season.

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

Connor McDavid and then-fiancé Lauren Kyle on the red carpet before the 2023 NHL Awards at Bridgestone Arena on June 26, 2023, in Nashville, Tennessee. (Bruce Bennett / Getty Images)
November 20, 2026 at 1:58 p.m.
Connor McDavid, the 29-year old centre and captain for the Edmonton Oilers, is putting down roots in Toronto. But don’t expect him to swap his Oilers jersey for one for the Maple Leafs any time soon.
McDavid and his wife, Lauren Kyle McDavid, were married in 2024 in Muskoka, and they own a cottage in that Ontario region as well as a home in Edmonton.
This week, Lauren shared on an Instagram post news that they had bought another home in the Toronto area. Connor’s hometown is Newmarket, just north of the city.
View this post on Instagram

“So I just arrived in Toronto,” Lauren says at the start of a two-minute video on Instagram. “I’m here for the weekend to go to the game and see some family, but also to go check on our house. We’re doing a renovation here.”
She adds: “We bought a place in the summer and hoping for it to be all reno’d by next summer. It’s a lot of work and a lot to do.”

In a previous story, National Post reported that McDavid has three properties, each with a sauna. If this is indeed their third, that means there is one here too.

The latest video doesn’t show much of the exterior of the property, though we do get a glimpse of an imposing metal gate and a curved, wooded drive before the view cuts to inside, where Lauren lays out some staining samples for a dark wood-panelled room.

stories.title: What Canadians need to know about the recent tech outages and emergency preparedness alerts
stories.summary: Is AI to blame? And do we really need to start panic-buying water again?
stories.author: Arisa Valyear
stories.content:
Widespread tech outages affecting Microsoft, Apple, the U.S. Federal Aviation Agency and National Security Agency, and even supermarket fridges over the past month have sent ripple effects across the globe, spurring generalized unrest, stock-market turbulence and a renewed focus on emergency preparedness.

Countries including Japan and Britain have recently pushed national campaigns encouraging residents to plan ahead for unexpected events, such as extreme weather and cyberattacks. Britain’s “Be Ready” checklist includes stocking up on water, food, hygiene items, as well as communication technology such as a battery-powered radio and back-up chargers for devices.

In the United States, consumers have reportedly been flocking to retailers because of these outages, with social media videos showing shoppers stocking up on essentials such as water and toilet paper. Costco’s comparable sales (excluding fuel) rose more than 8 per cent last month and up to 12 per cent during the last week of October, according to a report from Mizuho, a global financial institution. The analysts say “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media” have contributed to increased sales of emergency goods and that the pace of growth held into nearly November.

Costco Canada did not respond to a request for comment when asked whether they had also seen an uptick in sales of essential goods including canned food, water and toilet paper. Metro representative Stephanie Bonk said sales and orders on those items indicated “business as usual,” though Loblaw spokesperson Candace Beres reported seeing “some higher-than-usual demand in the last few days” in an e-mailed statement to The Globe. Walmart Canada and Sobeys did not respond to a request for comment.

Nonetheless, Google searches for “emergency preparedness” and “emergency essentials” spiked in November across Canada, with people looking for advice on what to include in an emergency kit, the best types of food to store and which canned goods to stock. On Reddit, one user posted in a Canada Costco thread asking others to explain the sudden surge in bottled water purchases witnessed at their location. A Facebook user posted in an “Ask Calgary” group earlier this month , writing “why are people hoarding cases of water?”

“Panic buying,” read one response. Another flagged the city’s water restrictions and a third user pointed to a range of causes, including climate instability, rising geopolitical tensions and cyberattacks, as well as infrastructure failures.

The federal government has an emergency kit checklist that suggests Canadians stock basic supplies (can opener, first aid kit), important documents (passports, insurance information), medical items (baby formula, prescription medications) and more in the event of “natural disasters, pandemics, cyber incidents and terrorism.” The kit should be designed to last at least 72 hours, according to the documentation, and should account for living without power or tap water. A date stamp on the checklist web page shows it was last updated in April of this year.

Public Safety Canada spokesperson Tim Warmington said in an e-mail that the recommendations on their Get Prepared website “builds on previous advice and is updated to reflect best practices.”

The website is “not focused on any particular type of risk” and is intended to help Canadians prepare for “a broad range of hazards and emergencies that could temporarily disrupt essential services” that include wildfires, floods, prolonged internet outages, extended power outages and critical infrastructure disruptions.

Most of the recent outages have been tied to issues or bugs with internal software updates. The U.S. government, as well as Microsoft, Apple and others, have said there is no evidence that the disruptions were linked to a cyberattack. Microsoft directly said its outage was not caused by “AI/agents.”

“Even if it’s not the direct result of an autonomous agent, it’s probably still tied to what’s going on with AI development,” said Brett Caraway, an associate professor at the University of Toronto and interim director of the school’s Institute of Communication, Culture, Information and Technology.

“A lot of the upgrades are happening as a preemptive response to security vulnerabilities that are being identified by AI, and I think they’re being rolled out quickly and probably not in a controlled, systematic fashion that would have been done previously.”

In an era of increased data breaches , AI hacks and agents going rogue , are these outages becoming the new normal? “I think everybody’s anxiety is running high because of all the doomer discourse coming out of the AI sector,” Prof. Caraway said. “But we’ll probably continue to see greater levels of instability. There’s a growing realization that the internet is becoming more dynamic and less secure.”

He pointed to data security practices including enabling two-factor authentication and using password-management applications as solutions Canadians can take to keep themselves protected.

When it comes to panic-buying water and essential goods, he said a certain level of preparedness is likely warranted. “I withdrew some money recently in the event that my banking system goes down and I can’t access my credit or debit accounts.”

Evan Light, an associate professor at the University of Toronto who specializes in artificial intelligence, information policy and data privacy, said backing up digital address books and looking into products such as eSIM cards can also help during potential outages.

“I think people should be prepared to be without the luxuries we’re used to, including drinking water and the internet, for example. These outages have shown how vulnerable our systems really are.”

Last week, for example, some companies, schools and hospitals were without communication software for prolonged periods of time when Microsoft’s entire suite of products ranging from e-mail to instant messaging went dark. In September, 911 services across Canada were down as the system grappled with a temporary lapse.

But Prof. Light believes data security shouldn’t rest on the shoulders of Canadians alone. “All of us use third parties to store our data. Those places should be trustworthy and secure, but that takes the government to step in and make sure the systems are regulated and are treated as essential services.”

With reports from Reuters and The Associated Press

stories.title: Police didn't consider key factors in Francique arrest plan, inquest hears
stories.summary: A coroner's inquest into the fatal shooting of a Black man by a police officer is hearing that police did not anticipate several factors, including the man's previous victimization.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Police did not anticipate several factors in planning out the arrest of a Black man who was then fatally shot during the operation, a coroner’s inquest heard Friday.

Peel regional police Det. Jason Sweeting, a supervisory officer in the investigation, testified that the arrest plan for Jamal Francique did not account for how quickly the 28-year-old would walk from his home to his car.

Officers were waiting for Francique to leave his home in a Mississauga, Ont., townhouse complex on the evening of Jan. 7, 2020, and planned to block his vehicle to arrest him before he got in the car, the detective said.

Instead, Francique entered his vehicle and put it in motion, Sweeting said.

Officers in unmarked cars and on foot rushed to contain his car, and one of the officers on foot fired four gunshots, the inquest has heard. One of the bullets struck the left side of Francique’s head, jurors have heard.

Francique’s car then smashed into the pillar of a nearby garage, the inquest heard.

Sweeting previously testified that paramedics were told to stand by since police hadn’t cleared Francique’s car as safe to approach.

The inquest has heard Francique didn’t receive medical care until after a tactical unit arrived about 20 minutes later and removed him from the car. He died in hospital days later.

Police had been observing Francique for days after receiving a tip that he had a gun and was trafficking drugs, the inquest has heard. They did not, however, find any evidence to corroborate those allegations, jurors heard.

Officers then determined to arrest him for breaching the conditions of his bail, which included house arrest.

Under questioning from a lawyer representing Francique’s father, the detective agreed there was no urgency to arrest Francique on the alleged bail breach, a non-violent offence. Police had also not received any information to suggest he would not comply if placed under arrest, he said.

“So without having any supporting basis for doing so, you acted in a manner that suggested you had reasons to believe he would flee or not comply with an arrest,” Sabrina Shillingford said.

“The plan was to reduce that possibility and take that possibility away, had he decided that was an option,” Sweeting replied.

Shillingford suggested police had other alternatives, such as contacting Francique’s sureties or serving him with a notice to appear in court.

“You would agree that it would be irregular for seven officers to converge on somebody, some of whom had their guns drawn, for a breach of that nature. Is that fair?” she asked. Sweeting agreed.

Asked if officers were aware that Francique was a victim of a shooting following an ambush in 2017, Sweeting said it “rings a bell.”

The detective agreed that the plan hinged on an “element of surprise” to keep control of the situation as the arrest was being made.

“You’d agree that somebody who had been a previous victim of a crime wherein they were ambushed and shot at May be more susceptible to fleeing in such circumstances, is that fair?” Shillingford asked.

“Yeah, possibly,” Sweeting said.

Dmitriy Pak, counsel for Francique’s partner, suggested police planned all along to arrest Francique inside his car, since that would allow them to search the vehicle for drugs or a gun — something they would not have grounds to do if he was arrested before getting to his vehicle.

“That’s not what happened and that was not the plan,” Sweeting said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

Officers in unmarked cars and on foot rushed to contain his car, and one of the officers on foot fired four gunshots, the inquest has heard. One of the bullets struck the left side of Francique’s head, jurors have heard.
Francique’s car then smashed into the pillar of a nearby garage, the inquest heard.
Sweeting previously testified that paramedics were told to stand by since police hadn’t cleared Francique’s car as safe to approach.
The inquest has heard Francique didn’t receive medical care until after a tactical unit arrived about 20 minutes later and removed him from the car. He died in hospital days later.

Police had been observing Francique for days after receiving a tip that he had a gun and was trafficking drugs, the inquest has heard. They did not, however, find any evidence to corroborate those allegations, jurors heard.
Officers then determined to arrest him for breaching the conditions of his bail, which included house arrest.

Under questioning from a lawyer representing Francique’s father, the detective agreed there was no urgency to arrest Francique on the alleged bail breach, a non-violent offence. Police had also not received any information to suggest he would not comply if placed under arrest, he said.
“So without having any supporting basis for doing so, you acted in a manner that suggested you had reasons to believe he would flee or not comply with an arrest,” Sabrina Shillingford said.
“The plan was to reduce that possibility and take that possibility away, had he decided that was an option,” Sweeting replied.
Shillingford suggested police had other alternatives, such as contacting Francique’s sureties or serving him with a notice to appear in court.
“You would agree that it would be irregular for seven officers to converge on somebody, some of whom had their guns drawn, for a breach of that nature. Is that fair?” she asked. Sweeting agreed.
Asked if officers were aware that Francique was a victim of a shooting following an ambush in 2017, Sweeting said it “rings a bell.”
The detective agreed that the plan hinged on an “element of surprise” to keep control of the situation as the arrest was being made.

“You’d agree that somebody who had been a previous victim of a crime wherein they were ambushed and shot at May be more susceptible to fleeing in such circumstances, is that fair?” Shillingford asked.
“Yeah, possibly,” Sweeting said.

Dmitriy Pak, counsel for Francique’s partner, suggested police planned all along to arrest Francique inside his car, since that would allow them to search the vehicle for drugs or a gun — something they would not have grounds to do if he was arrested before getting to his vehicle.
“That’s not what happened and that was not the plan,” Sweeting said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Calgary Mayor Farkas says he believes revisions coming to Alberta bike lane bill
stories.summary: Calgary - Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas says the Alberta government appears to have fumbled a bill that would allow the province to bulldoze bike lanes and download the cost onto cities.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said Friday that the Alberta government appears to have fumbled a bill that would allow the province to bulldoze bike lanes and download the cost onto cities.

The proposed legislation, tabled Thursday, would give Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen the authority to order the removal of municipal bike lanes.

The bill dictates municipalities would need to pick up the tab.

Farkas said Premier Danielle Smith’s office promised him otherwise and that the bill put forward is a “premature draft version.”

“My understanding and speaking with the premier’s office is that was a mistake. The provincial government will fully pay for any change orders that are required,” Farkas said outside city council chambers.

“The premier’s office has told me that under no circumstances will municipalities be paying for this and I take that to the bank.”

In response, the transportation ministry didn’t directly address the mayor’s claims or confirm whether it’s planning to introduce amendments to the bill.

In an emailed statement, Dreeshen said the province would work with municipalities to both limit future bike lanes in busy areas and deal with “problem” ones.

“This is about better collaboration with cities to ensure we’re making responsible, evidence-based transportation decisions that protect road capacity and make sure transportation networks work for everyone,” he said.

Dreeshen said Thursday that the bill came in response to concern that some bike lanes reduce road capacity and parking, increase congestion and can get in the way of emergency vehicles.

He said the goal is for bike lanes to be removed when road maintenance is already scheduled in the same location so that it’s cheaper, but added Edmonton and Calgary have extensive budgets for bike lanes while the province does not.

Farkas said Friday the bill states bike lanes will be forbidden unless approved by the transportation minister but that’s not how he expects the legislation would work.

“I understand that to be an oversight and a mistake in terms of the legislation, and I fully expect that there’s future amendments that will be coming.”

Farkas said he believes the province is looking to address some of the concerns municipalities have, as both levels of government look at affordable transportation options.

Cycling advocates say removing bike lanes would make roads more deadly for cyclists.

Jack Mason, infrastructure lead for the non-profit Bike Calgary, said he feels safer on his daily bike commute in a bike lane and separated from vehicle traffic rather than having to mingle with cars.

“I mean, Safe and Sensible Roads Act? This bill is neither safe nor sensible,” he said Friday.

“It’s going to have an easily foreseeable deleterious effect on safety on roads in Alberta, and Albertans will die as a result.”

Bike Edmonton is urging Alberta to scrap the legislation, calling it misguided, impractical and an overstep into municipal politics.

In a Friday statement, it said cycling is a way to cheaply move around the city as the cost of living increases. It pointed to a 2012 study that found there were much fewer cyclist injuries in areas with bike infrastructure.

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said Thursday that the legislation would force property tax increases and undermine local governments.

Removing lanes installed in the city in the last decade could cost $150 million, he said.

Knack said the actions of Smith’s United Conservative Party government don’t match the promises it made face to face.

“Their words mean nothing to me anymore,” he said.

A Thursday technical briefing for reporters with department officials also created confusion over the scope of the bill.

Officials said the responsibility of paying for bike lane removal isn’t addressed in the proposed legislation but, upon publication, the bill says municipalities must pay.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

— With files from Lisa Johnson in Edmonton

Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks at an announcement for a new deal on the Churchill Falls and Gull Island hydro-electric projects Aug. 17, 2026. At left is Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham and at right is then-Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette. (Keith Gosse/The Telegram)

Catherine Lévesque

November 20, 2026 at 1:25 p.m.

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney likes to tout the recent Churchill Falls agreement as proof can Canada can be an energy superpower, but the newly elected Parti Québécois government could be a squeaky wheel in advancing the project.

Quebec’s Minister of Economic Development, Innovation and Energy, Stéphane Paquet, raised some eyebrows last week when he told Montreal radio station 98,5FM that the project was not “set in stone” and hinted there could be some changes.

“Give us time to analyze it properly. And upon analysis — yes, there are things we do not agree with. So, we are going to go back and work with our friends in Newfoundland to ensure that certain clauses included therein are satisfactory to everyone,” he said.

A spokesperson for Paquet said he would not be granting interviews or answering written questions on the Churchill Falls agreement for the time being.
