The idea of going back to the drawing board once more has already been shot down by Tony Wakeham, the premier of Newfoundland and Labrador, who told legislators this week that he has made his position clear to Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

In a statement to National Post, Wakeham said the current Churchill Falls agreement is a “win-win-win” for Newfoundland and Labrador, the federal government and Quebec.

“It is entirely reasonable for a new government to review an agreement of this magnitude, but the material terms negotiated between the parties are reflected in the Definitive Cooperation and Implementation Agreement (Dcia) and I don’t intend to renegotiate them,” he said.

“Our focus remains on completing the necessary steps to implement the agreement.”

The current iteration of the agreement was announced with great fanfare on Aug. 17, days before the start of the electoral campaign in Quebec, with Carney, Wakeham and former Quebec premier Christine Fréchette all praising the terms of the deal.

It promises to boost energy production at the existing Churchill Falls hydroelectric facilities significantly, as well as commits to build a long-debated new production facility at nearby Gull Island. It also includes an onshore wind energy project.

Carney called it the largest renewable energy investment in Canada’s history. “It is the equivalent of 18 Hoover Dams in America, at its current operating capacity,” he said.

The premiers however confirmed that much of the current agreement is non-binding until the deal is completely finalized and approved, likely by the end of the year.

Pierre-Olivier Pineau, a professor specialized in energy policy at HEC Montréal, said Paquet was not wrong to say that the terms agreed by all three parties are not set in stone because the Dcia is an agreement in principle and not a contract.

“It is certain that there have already been so many delays and restarts in the negotiations — largely due to political shifts — that every new party that comes to power, naturally wants to introduce its own vision and interests,” he said.

“And, for better or worse, they May well disagree with certain elements of the agreement-in-principle they have inherited,” he said.

In some ways, what the PQ government is doing is no different than when Wakeham was elected in 2025, promising to review a 2024 deal that was signed between former N.L. Premier Andrew Furey and former Quebec Premier François Legault.

A report given to the government of Newfoundland and Labrador concluded the 2024 deal was not in the province’s best interests and negotiations restarted on both sides.

Pineau said he sees an opportunity for the Quebec government to tweak certain aspects of the current agreement when finalizing the contract in the coming months.

“If it is simply a matter of drafting a contract that requires certain details to be specified — since some aspects May need fine-tuning — then adjustments can certainly be made when transitioning from the initial agreement to the formal contract,” he said.

The current framework is set to end upon the signing of a definitive agreement or on March 31, 2027, unless the parties mutually decide to extend or waive the deadline.

The PQ previously told National Post over the summer that if elected, it would look into redrafting any deal to include further compensation for the province’s historic loss of the territory of Labrador roughly one century ago.

But during the election period, St-Pierre Plamondon was a bit more measured in its response, saying his party had no interest in tearing up the deal for the sake of it.

Pineau said the PQ should think carefully about starting a new round of negotiations on Churchill Falls.

“It’s true that, for the Péquistes, there’s a certain sense of a ‘clean slate’ regarding all this. But for the general public, this has been a topic of discussion for a long time,” he said, noting that this would be the second renegotiation since the 2024 agreement.

“The public isn’t really all that interested, and it would only lead to further weariness and cynicism.”

stories.title: Beal Gives Back campaign returns to support London organizations
stories.summary: The initiative aims to address social issues in the community by collecting donations for Ark Aid Mission and the London Food Bank.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
London’s Beal Secondary School has launched its second annual Beal Gives Back campaign.

The initiative aims to address social issues in the community by collecting donations for Ark Aid Mission and the London Food Bank.

“It’s our job to try to make the community a better place to live for all of us,” teacher Harry Gorman said.

The campaign runs from Nov. 30 to Dec. 14 and will see students collect food and other donations for the two organizations.

Last year’s campaign raised more than $6,000 and collected more than 3,000 winter items for Ark Aid.

Grade 10 student Grace Yoo said organizers hope this year’s effort will help people struggling with food insecurity in the community.

stories.title: Museum London staff back strike action ahead of conciliation
stories.summary: Workers at Museum London have voted overwhelmingly in favour of strike action as contract negotiations between the museum and their union continue.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Workers at Museum London have voted overwhelmingly in favour of strike action as contract negotiations between the museum and their union continue.

About 30 full-time and part-time employees represented by Cupe Local 217.02 voted 95 per cent in favour of a strike mandate, according to the union. The bargaining unit includes workers in a range of roles, including curatorial services, programming and events, graphic design and finance.

The union said employees have experienced years of wage freezes or annual increases of about one per cent and are seeking improvements as part of a new collective agreement.

“Members have fallen behind year over year,” bargaining unit chair Krista Hamlin said in a statement issued by the union. Hamlin said workers are concerned about wages amid other investments made by the museum.

The vote does not mean a strike will occur, but gives the union a mandate to take job action if negotiations fail to produce an agreement.

The union and Museum London are scheduled to enter conciliation on Nov. 30.

stories.title: N.B. government in talks with Quebec firm about restarting idled Nackawic pulp mill
stories.summary: Fredericton - The New Brunswick government says it's in talks with a Quebec-based forest products company about restarting the AV Nackawic pulp mill that was shut down earlier this month, resulting in hundreds of layoffs.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Fredericton - The New Brunswick government says it’s in talks with a Quebec-based forest products company about restarting the AV Nackawic pulp mill that was shut down earlier this month, resulting in hundreds of layoffs.

Provincial Natural Resources Minister John Herron issued a statement Friday saying government officials were talking to Arbec Forest Products Inc., based in Saint-Léonard, Que.

ByAdam Radwanski Business Columnist,andRob Ferguson Queen’s Park Bureau

This weekend, Ontario Liberals will make one of the most consequential decisions in the party’s recent history.

After eight years in opposition, two failed leadership tenures and three consecutive Doug Ford majority governments, members will choose the politician they believe can finally return the party to power.

The race ends this Saturday, when voters will pick one of the four candidates — former federal minister Navdeep Bains, MPPs Lee Fairclough and Stephanie Bowman, and former political staffer Dylan Marando — who have gamely traversed the province, visiting ridings where their party’s membership is sometimes in the single digits.

To make sense of the results, join business columnist Adam Radwanski and Queen’s Park reporter Rob Ferguson on Monday, Nov. 23 at 11:15 a.m. for a live Q&A in the comments.

The live Q&A will take place in the comment section below. There is no live stream video. Adam and Rob will instead respond to questions by replying to individual comments.

To ask a question, log into our site or app and submit you query via the comment section. When your question is answered, there will be a button below your comment that says “Show reply.” Click to see the reporter’s response.

Any reader can ask a question as long as they are registered and logged in to the Star. Nonregistered readers can still view the live chat.

Like all conversations on the Star, questions and comments are subject to moderation and the Star’s Code of Conduct.

Ontario’s police watchdog says it has reasonable grounds to believe the officer committed criminal offences in the April 16 incident.

The Special Investigations Unit says an officer driving an unmarked OPP vehicle that morning was stopped partially in a live lane of traffic while trying to merge onto Highway 11.

The SIU says there was a collision involving a school bus and a dump truck.

He’s due in court on Dec. 8.

In seven surveys conducted since 2013, most Canadians says a debate about abortion is unnecessary, according to Research Co.

An anti-abortion activist protest outside the U.S. Supreme Court on June 27, 2022. The court overturned the landmark 50-year-old Roe v Wade decision, erasing a federal right to abortion. (Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images)

November 20, 2026 at 12:22 p.m.

Almost three in five Canadians (58 per cent) believe there is no point in re-opening the abortion debate, while fewer than three in ten (28 per cent) think debate is overdue, according to a new poll from Research Co.

The survey results reflect marked differences between Canadians and Americans in their views on abortion.

In contrast to Canada, more than two in five Americans (45 per cent) think there should be further debate about abortion, while just over a third (34 per cent) think there is no point in restarting the discussion.

“In seven different surveys conducted since July 2013, majorities of Canadians have indicated that a debate about abortion is unnecessary,” Mario Canseco, president of Research Co. said in a statement accompanying the survey results. “In the United States, the proportion of residents who think the issue is settled is significantly lower,” he added.

When asked whether abortion should be legal, almost half of Canadians (49 per cent) said the procedure should be legal under any circumstances. That’s unchanged from a Research Co. poll in conducted in August 2025. A third (37 per cent) of Canadian would only allow it under certain circumstances. Just 6 per cent of Canadians think abortion should be illegal in all circumstances.

That differs from the U.S. The poll showed almost half of Americans (46 per cent), think abortion should only be legal under certain circumstances. A third of Americans (33 per cent) would allow the procedure under any circumstances, while 10 per cent would make it illegal no matter what the circumstances.

Meanwhile, fewer than one in five Canadians and Americans (18 per cent and 16 per cent, respectively) think there should be greater restrictions than there are now for abortion.

A third of Americans (34 per cent) are of the view that abortion should be allowed only in cases where rape or incest has occurred, or to save the woman’s life. One in five Canadians (20 per cent) share that view. Low percentages of both Canadians (9 per cent) and Americans (13 per cent) believe the procedure should be restricted to instances involving saving the woman’s life.

In Canada, 57 per cent of Quebecers, 54 per cent of women and 53 per cent of those aged 55 and over support legal abortion under any circumstances, along with majorities of those who voted for the NDP (67 per cent) or the Liberals (56 per cent) in last year’s federal election.

In the United States, legal abortion under any circumstances is endorsed by 36 per cent of women, 36 per cent of residents of the northeast section of the country, and 40 per cent of Americans aged 18 to 34. Democrats are significantly more likely to hold this view (47 per cent) than Independents (34 per cent) or Republicans (21 per cent).

Almost half of Canadians (47 per cent) are of the view that the health-care system should bear the cost of abortions whenever they are requested, while more than a third (36 per cent) believe the health-care system should only fund abortions in the event of medical emergencies. Only 7 per cent believe the health-care system should cease funding for abortions.

This survey was conducted between Oct. 29 and Oct. 31 among 1,003 adults in Canada and 1,001 adults in the United States. The data has been statistically weighted according to Canadian and American census figures for age, gender and region. The margin of error—which measures sample variability—is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, for each country.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

One in five Canadians (20 per cent) share that view. Low percentages of both Canadians (9 per cent) and Americans (13 per cent) believe the procedure should be restricted to instances involving saving the woman’s life.

In Canada, 57 per cent of Quebecers, 54 per cent of women and 53 per cent of those aged 55 and over support legal abortion under any circumstances, along with majorities of those who voted for the NDP (67 per cent) or the Liberals (56 per cent) in last year’s federal election.

In the United States, legal abortion under any circumstances is endorsed by 36 per cent of women, 36 per cent of residents of the northeast section of the country, and 40 per cent of Americans aged 18 to 34. Democrats are significantly more likely to hold this view (47 per cent) than Independents (34 per cent) or Republicans (21 per cent).

Almost half of Canadians (47 per cent) are of the view that the health-care system should bear the cost of abortions whenever they are requested, while more than a third (36 per cent) believe the health-care system should only fund abortions in the event of medical emergencies. Only 7 per cent believe the health-care system should cease funding for abortions.

This survey was conducted between Oct. 29 and Oct. 31 among 1,003 adults in Canada and 1,001 adults in the United States. The data has been statistically weighted according to Canadian and American census figures for age, gender and region. The margin of error—which measures sample variability—is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, for each country.

stories.title: City of Montreal backtracks and appoints executive responsible for systemic racism
stories.summary: Montreal - Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada has named a councillor responsible for racism and discrimination at its executive committee following a cabinet shuffle.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The shuffle comes after a councillor and member of the executive committee, Chantal Gagnon, announced she was leaving the Ensemble Montreal party in a radio interview Friday morning.

In a news release, Martinez Ferrada’s cabinet announced that the Côte-des-Neiges—Notre-Dame-de-Grâce borough mayor, Stéphanie Valenzuela, will be responsible for racism and discrimination. She will also oversee social cohesion and the status of women.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Toronto Marlies reflect on the meaning behind their Calder Cup Championship

Image 10Image 11

“Today, we are strengthening a team that shares a common vision for a stronger, more inclusive, and more prosperous city,” Martinez Ferrada says in the news release. “I am pleased to be able to count on passionate, skilled colleagues who are deeply rooted in their communities to advance our priorities and continue building the Montreal of tomorrow.”

The announcement comes a few days after Martinez Ferrada said her executive already had someone overseeing diversity and inclusion and did not need an additional position.

City councillor Josué Corvil will continue to be the executive responsible for diversity and inclusion after the shuffle.

Concerns about racism have been a hot topic at city hall since June when Police Chief Fady Dagher announced the dismantling of a patrol unit in a multicultural neighbourhood of the city over allegations of racism and criminal misconduct.

The Opposition at City Hall had requested at Monday’s council meeting that the administration name an executive responsible for systemic racism and discrimination.

At the time, Martinez Ferrada said the issue of racism and discrimination is a personal priority, which she also tackles in her capacity as mayor.

Ericka Alneus, the interim leader of the Opposition, says Valenzuela’s appointment is “excellent news.”

“Now that the appointment has been made, we expect action, not just a title,” she said in a statement sent to The Canadian Press.

The city is expected to present its latest budget next week.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Police launch Festive Ride program to prevent impaired driving
stories.summary: With the holidays fast approaching, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) have increased sobriety checkpoints as a p...
stories.author: Ryan Baynton
stories.content:
With the holidays fast approaching, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) have increased sobriety checkpoints as a part of the annual Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere (Ride) program, police said Thurday.

Launched Thursday, the Festive Ride program aims to keep impaired drivers off the road. This year alone, 35 people have died in crashes that involved alcohol or drugs, and OPP have charged 9,300 motorists with impaired driving.

“Impaired driving remains one of the most preventable threats to road safety,” said Ontario solicitor general Michael Kerzner. “As we travel throughout the holiday season, I encourage all drivers to make responsible choices and never get behind the wheel impaired. Together, we can help ensure that all Ontarians enjoy the season safely

Over the past 10 years, 610 people have died as a result of impaired driving on OPP-controlled roads, the agency said in a statement issued Thursday.

OPP encourages people to drive sober, plan ahead if your attending a party and to call 9-1-1 if you suspect someone is driving under the influence.

“The message remains clear: impaired driving is not an accident, it is a choice and one that can have tragic consequences,” said OPP commissioner Thomas Carrique. “Never drive impaired. We all share a responsibility to abide by the laws intended to keep our roads safe.”

The festive Ride campaign runs from Nov, 19, 2026 until Jan 1, 2027.

stories.title: Bronfmans make major donation of glassworks and endowment fund to National Gallery
stories.summary: The donation consists of 56 works of modern and contemporary glass by artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
'If you have enough money, you’re going to find someone to do whatever you want.' — Dr. Ian MacArthur, a plastic surgeon

The donation consists of 56 works of modern and contemporary glass by artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia

From left, a Tiffany Studios lamp, c. 1900; a Daum lamp, c. 1905; a Theodore B. Starr Company vase, c. 1900; and a Tiffany Studios vase from 1905, ON display at the National Gallery of Canada. The Starr vase is a gift of Léon Simard of Westmount, Que. The others are from the Bronfmans. (Handout / National Gallery of Canada)

November 20, 2026 at 12:07 p.m.

The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) has received a major donation from Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman, that it says “will significantly transform the NGC holdings and set the stage for a new chapter in decorative arts and design.”

In a press release on Friday, the NGC said the donation consists of 56 works of modern and contemporary glass together with an endowment fund. The works are by artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. A selection of them are currently on view at the gallery in Ottawa through April 30.

The gallery said the endowment will enable the creation of a new curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design.

“For more than a century, members of the Bronfman family have championed cultural initiatives in Canada and around the world,” said Jean-François Bélisle, CEO and director of the NGC. “This promised gift builds on that legacy and opens an important chapter for decorative arts and design at the gallery.”

Charles Bronfman, who turned 95 this year, is a member of the Bronfman family whose father, Samuel, founded Distillers Corporation Limited and purchased the Seagam Company, which became the world’s largest liquor distilling firm. His second wife, Andrea, died in 2006.

“My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass-making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Bronfman said in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”

The donation includes glass that has been blown, moulded, fused, engraved, sculpted and enamelled, and features works of Art Nouveau, Arts and Crafts, Modernism and Art Deco styles. It includes early works by Louis Comfort Tiffany (whose father founded Tiffany & Co.), French artist Emile Gallé, and the French art studio Daum.

“What I find so compelling about glass is its extraordinary versatility,” said Anabelle Kienle Ponka, a senior curator at the gallery. “It can be sculptural, functional, decorative and also conceptual.”

She added: “The gift gives the Gallery a bold new platform for future acquisitions, research and public engagement with glass and to shape new conversations around the field.”

stories.title: Ontario, Ottawa commit $250-million for new port in Sault Ste. Marie
stories.summary: Ford government says the project will fill gap in province’s trade infrastructure
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario and the federal government say they’re committing $250-million to help build a new port in Sault Ste. Marie on the north shore of the Saint Marys River.

The province says the project will see the construction of two docking berths, a transload yard to transfer cargo from ships to rail, and other infrastructure to move goods between northern and southern Ontario, Quebec and overseas markets.

Ottawa is providing $125-million through the Trade Diversification Corridors Fund, a $5-billion fund aimed at doubling non-U.S. exports, while the province makes up the difference through a repayable financing loan.

In a news release, the province says the new port will serve as a gateway in the Great Lakes and support mining, steelmaking and critical mineral development in northern Ontario, including the Ring of Fire region.

The Hamilton-Oshawa Port Authority leads development of the project, which aims to be online by 2029 and reach full capacity by 2031.

The port authority signed a partnership last year with Sault Ste. Marie to advance the transportation hub and the city committed $15-million to the project in July.

The province says the project will see the construction of two docking berths, a transload yard to transfer cargo from ships to rail, and other infrastructure to move goods between northern and southern Ontario, Quebec and overseas markets.

stories.title: ‘GTA VI’ actor with Canadian ties says it’s ‘surreal’ to be part of game
stories.summary: Edwina Rai, who appears in the video game as supporting character Katerina Rosselli, said she first auditioned in April 2022 without even knowing what the project was.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
An actor with ties to Canada says it’s “surreal” to play a part in ‘ Grand Theft Auto VI .’

Edwina Rai, who appears in the video game as supporting character Katerina Rosselli, said she first auditioned in April 2022 without even knowing what the project was.

Rai, whose husband is from Quebec, told Global News Friday it wasn’t until her third audition that things started to click.

“I’m not a gamer. I knew the game, but it didn’t hit me how big it was until I started following on Instagram the memes about (how) we got this before GTA VI, we got that before GTA,” she said.

“So now, it’s really, like, hitting hard. I don’t know, it feels amazing. But like I said, it feels surreal. It’s, like, not real yet.”

Rockstar Games kept much of the cast behind its blockbuster video game under wraps before launch Thursday, including the performers behind protagonists Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval.

Now that players are roaming Vice City and the wider fictional state of Leonida, actors who spent years bound to secrecy are revealing themselves.

Rai shared her role in the franchise’s sixth installment in an Instagram post.

“I’m happy that finally we can get the word out because you can’t imagine how hard it was to tell my friends, ‘I’m working on this, but I can’t tell you,’” she told Global News.

“A lot of people were preparing the post for like weeks in advance. I was just like, ‘I’ll get to it tomorrow’ because I was, like, very stressed about it, so I would just keep pushing it. But eventually, last minute I put in what happened and then I just like posted it.”

Grand Theft Auto VI has been hotly anticipated for over a decade as Rockstar and the developer’s parent company, Take-Two Interactive, ran into multiple delays, including during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Rai said she splits her time between New York and Montreal, and that this is her first video game.

“I wasn’t sure about it at the beginning, like before we got to it, but then I’m like, this is so much fun. I’d love to do more games for sure, absolutely,” she said.

“I’m very grateful to Rockstar and to everybody who embraced me and had me be part of this. It’s like amazing.”

— with files from Ariel Rabinovitch and The Associated Press

stories.title: Expert insight: Art Gallery of Ontario’s exhibition showcases power and glory of Black style
stories.summary: Western professor Cornel Grey says appearance can express reverence for an occasion and regard for those with whom we share it.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
For some, the lesson in needing to look presentable to society began with a reprimand about scuffed shoes. For others, it was a warning about stray hairs, an untidy hairline, trousers that needed pressing or a last-minute stain. A parent was often ready to send you back to the mirror, unwilling to let you leave looking as though nobody at home had taken the time to care for you.

Behind these admonitions was an uneasy mixture of affection and discipline. Taking pride in one’s appearance communicated dignity, but it also reflected the demands of respectability in a world where Black people have often worked exceptionally hard for recognition routinely afforded to others.

No one needed to grow up attending church to appreciate the ethic of “Sunday Best.” Rooted in traditions of dressing for worship, the practice reflects a collective belief that appearance can express reverence for an occasion and regard for those with whom we share it.

At the opening of the Art Gallery of Ontario’s “Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style,” the crowd understood the assignment. Attendees arrived dressed to impress, bringing sartorial flair to the celebration.

Conceived and curated by a transnational team, including AGO curator Julie Crooks and fashion historian Jason Cyrus, with Amanda Bock and Clare Sauro, “Sunday Best” brings together garments, photographs and personal effects spanning Black diasporic life from the 1880s to the present.

Displays of church fashion recall generations of Black women and the splendour of dress for Sunday worship. Elsewhere, the distinctive uniforms of the Black Panther Party are on display, a nod to the role clothing and fashion play in political organizing.

The exhibition also honours Black dandies, alongside those who have challenged conventions of gender through the way they dress.

Among them are Toronto-based trans soul singer Jackie Shane and the late fashion icon André Leon Talley, a long-time editor at Vogue magazine, whose styles helped to expand the possibilities of Black self-presentation.

The exhibition also contains references to ballroom culture that show how Black traditions of dress and performance have been inherited and reimagined for self-expression and communal recognition.

The exhibition traces how Black styles and cultural practices travel through migration. Visitors May recognize traces of traditions from their own families. A hat May evoke an auntie preparing for church, a family photograph the sober pride of relatives posing for a formal portrait.

The curators bring these expressions of Black life together, drawing connections between diverse traditions.

The exhibition arrives amid renewed public attention to Black fashion. Last year, New York’s Met Gala put Black dandyism on the global stage with its theme, “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style.”

“Sunday Best” contributes to this conversation by showcasing the communal rituals that give style meaning. The exhibition calls attention to the pressures under which Black people have fashioned themselves.

In an iconic 1956 photograph, Gordon Parks depicts Joanne Thornton Wilson and her niece Shirley Anne Kirksey standing beneath a neon “Colored Entrance” sign outside a department store, in Mobile, Alabama. Their elegant and dignified dress contrasts with the indignity of segregation.

For generations, dressing well could be understood as a defence against racial scrutiny or a means of improving one’s social standing. But no degree of sartorial excellence could guarantee protection from discrimination. The demands of respectability also placed constraints on those whose expressions of gender or sexuality challenged accepted conventions.

Covers of Ebony magazine on display offer another perspective. As a Black-led publication, Ebony helped cultivate images of Black beauty and achievement in the United States that spoke to how Black communities understood themselves, free from the stereotypes and expectations of mainstream audiences.

Across these histories, the attention given to one’s appearance carried meanings beyond the judgments of others. Dressing for worship could express reverence, just as a carefully chosen outfit might bring pleasure or communicate regard for others.

The Sunday best tradition thus emerges as an ethic of dignity and care, fostered within Black communities even when those qualities went unrecognized by the wider society.

The exhibition’s treatment of Black queerness unsettles the presumed divide between church traditions and ballroom culture. Black churches have held complicated relationships with queer people, offering spaces for artistic expression alongside experiences of exclusion. Through these church communities, Black queer people have inherited styles and sensibilities they continue to reinvent.

Consider drag performer Kennedy Davenport’s viral appearance on The Pit Stop. Reacting to another queen’s outfit, she sang: “Black stockings, white shoes, shouldn’t be allowed in the church.” Her playful critique drew on the rules of Black church fashion, finding humour in a set of esthetic rules passed down through generations.

Black queer performers have also helped shape gospel music and traditions of Black religious life, including in spaces where their sexuality was not fully accepted.

In “Sunday Best,” the proximity of church fashion to ballroom culture highlights how these traditions inform one another. Through inventive clothing and performance, ballroom turns resourcefulness into glamour, creating spaces where beauty and ambition earn recognition.

In the exhibition, everyday grooming tools share space with dresses and photographs. Hairbrushes evoke the private rituals behind a public appearance. Many of these belongings have survived for decades.

In her book Ordinary Notes, writer and scholar Christina Sharpe describes regard as “a habit of care.” She says: “It is appreciation and esteem. It is the right of repair.” Her words invite us to consider the attention given to these belongings and the lives they represent.

The curators extend this ethic of care to bring these histories together. From garments and paintings to archival photographs and moving images, their staging treats Black cultural expression as worthy of preservation and public appreciation. Behind the displays lies the painstaking labour of conservation, ensuring these materials will encountered by new generations.

Black artists have long struggled for recognition in Canadian institutions, giving moments like these added weight. In 2019, the AGO hosted “The Feast”, marking 30 years since the groundbreaking exhibition “Black Wimmin: When and Where We Enter.” The gathering brought 100 Black women and gender-nonconforming artists and cultural workers into Ago’s Walker Court.

At the opening of “Sunday Best,” the carefully dressed crowd offered another expression of this cultural legacy. Across the gallery, objects once worn with pride had been kept with care, their stories deserving of the same attention.

_Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style is on view at the Art Gallery of Ontario until Feb. 28, 2027._Image 1: The Conversation

Cornel Grey, Assistant Professor in Department of Gender, Sexuality, and Women’s Studies, Western University

In the exhibition, everyday grooming tools share space with dresses and photographs. Hairbrushes evoke the private rituals behind a public appearance. Many of these belongings have survived for decades.

In her book Ordinary Notes, writer and scholar Christina Sharpe describes regard as “a habit of care.” She says: “It is appreciation and esteem. It is the right of repair.” Her words invite us to consider the attention given to these belongings and the lives they represent.

The curators extend this ethic of care to bring these histories together. From garments and paintings to archival photographs and moving images, their staging treats Black cultural expression as worthy of preservation and public appreciation. Behind the displays lies the painstaking labour of conservation, ensuring these materials will encountered by new generations.

Black artists have long struggled for recognition in Canadian institutions, giving moments like these added weight. In 2019, the AGO hosted “The Feast”, marking 30 years since the groundbreaking exhibition “Black Wimmin: When and Where We Enter.” The gathering brought 100 Black women and gender-nonconforming artists and cultural workers into Ago’s Walker Court.

At the opening of “Sunday Best,” the carefully dressed crowd offered another expression of this cultural legacy. Across the gallery, objects once worn with pride had been kept with care, their stories deserving of the same attention.
_Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style is on view at the Art Gallery of Ontario until Feb. 28, 2027._Image 1: The Conversation

stories.title: Supreme Court sharpens focus on issue of consent in sexual-assault cases
stories.summary: In two rulings, court says there is no legal requirement to communicate non-consent to sexual contact
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada has sharpened the legal focus on the issue of consent in sexual assault cases, and in one of two related judgments the top court underlined the fact that there is no legal requirement to communicate nonconsent to sexual contact.

The two rulings on Friday aim to bring additional clarity to the increasingly complicated nature of sexual-assault trials.

But one of the rulings also highlighted a split among the nine judges of the Supreme Court about how the Criminal Code should be interpreted when Crown prosecutors are seeking to prove fault in a sexual assault case.

Both cases – one from Ontario, the other from Alberta – were among the final rulings for Justice Sheilah Martin, who retired in May and can participate in judgments until the end of this month. Her work on issues of consent in sexual assault cases is among her legacies from her eight-plus years on the Supreme Court.

In the Ontario case a provincial trial judge acquitted Bevin Kerry Degale of aggravated sexual assault in 2023. The Ontario Court of Appeal in 2024 overturned that ruling and entered a conviction for the crime.

The Supreme Court on Friday unanimously upheld his conviction.

The court, however, split 5-4 on legal reasoning, with the majority judgment written by Chief Justice Richard Wagner and Justice Mary Moreau.

Chief Justice Wagner and Justice Moreau spoke of “a proper application of well-settled law” and that the court “cannot discover new ‘pathways’ to proving the fault element of an offence absent legislative change.”

Justice Martin wrote concurring reasons on behalf of the other four judges, agreeing with Mr. Degale’s conviction but differing sharply on how the court should interpret the Criminal Code. Her reasons, even as they did not garner a majority, were seen by legal experts as something of a tour-de-force at the end of her Supreme Court tenure.

Lawyer Howard Krongold of AGP LLP in Ottawa, who represented Mr. Degale, said that while his client lost, the majority decision is essential, as it represented a reaffirmation of bedrock legal principles such as proof beyond a reasonable doubt in difficult cases of sexual assault.

He added that the majority of five judges, led by the Chief Justice, indicated that any changes to sexual assault law should happen on Parliament Hill.

“Criminal law should not be expanded in the courts,” Mr. Krongold said in an interview Friday. “The court was clear about its limited role.”

Justice Martin’s extensive reasons were more than double the length of the majority judgment and included a Charter of Rights and Freedoms analysis. She sought to address what she called persisting uncertainty, stretching back decades, over the relationship between the fault element in sexual assault and “the so-called ‘defence’ of honest but mistaken belief in communicated consent.”

She stated that consent cannot be implied from silence, passivity or ambiguous behaviour.

“In this respect, the law has moved from a ‘no means no’ framework to an ‘only yes means yes’ understanding of consent,” Justice Martin wrote.

The divide at the court centred on a section of the Criminal Code that speaks about “reasonable steps . . . to ascertain that the complainant was consenting.”

The majority decision strongly de-emphasized the importance of that provision, said Janine Benedet, a law professor at the University of British Columbia who is an expert in sexual assault law. She was also co-counsel with UBC law professor Isabel Grant for the Vancouver Rape Relief Society, an intervenor in both of the cases decided Friday.

“This May be a case where Parliament May have to look at this, if they think Justice Martin’s view of things is correct,” Prof. Benedet said in an interview. “What Justice Martin would have confirmed is the reasonable steps provision is important and the accused doesn’t get to say: ‘How was I supposed to know that she didn’t consent.’”

Prof. Benedet also predicted that the majority ruling that de-emphasized the reasonable steps provision will lead to more acquittals on charges of sexual assault.

The other case decided on Friday began in Alberta, where Jordan Bilinski was acquitted of sexual assault after a superior court jury trial in 2023. In 2025, the Alberta Court of Appeal overturned that ruling and ordered a new trial.

The Supreme Court, by a 7-2 margin, rejected Mr. Bilinski’s appeal and upheld the order for a new trial. Justice Martin wrote the majority judgment for this case. A key message from the court was that judges at trial must instruct juries on consent in sexual-assault cases and that the judge’s failure at Mr. Bilinski’s 2023 trial to properly explain to the jury “communicated consent” justified a new trial.

The top court heard the Degale and Bilinksi appeals on May 21 and 22, at the end of the spring session. The hearings marked the last days on the bench for Justice Martin.

Justice Martin joined the Supreme Court of Canada from Alberta in late 2017, when former chief justice Beverley McLachlin retired. Before the May 22 hearing began, Chief Justice Wagner saluted her work, in particular in the areas of criminal law and Charter cases.

Justice Wagner praised her “careful attention to individual rights and a strong sense of responsibility to the law,” as well as her “contagious enthusiasm.”

As of Dec. 1, Justice Martin’s name will be marked with an asterisk on judgments from other cases on which she sat before retiring, as having taken “no part in the judgment.” There May be more than a dozen of such asterisks in pending judgments – an unusually high figure in the court’s long history.

stories.title: Fanshawe students excited for Grand Theft Auto VI
stories.summary: Grand Theft Auto fans around the world prepared for Thursday's launch of the most anticipated video game in hi...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
Grand Theft Auto fans around the world prepared for Thursday’s launch of the most anticipated video game in history. And many Fanshawe College students are among them.

Vice City, the sixth installment in the GTA franchise has been 13 years in the making. Fan anticipation for GTA VI has already driven $2 billion dollars in pre-order sales for the game that will be available on Xbox and PlayStation 5.

Some Fanshawe students were ready to dive into the game’s ultra-realistic graphics.

“Oh yeah, I’m so excited to play it, I’ve been waiting years for it,” said student Logan Teather. “Just looking at the faces in the trailers and just like how the lights kind of mix in with all the objects.”

First-year Journalism-Multimedia student Nick Lima said he didn’t mind waiting until after launch.

“I’ll probably get it within the next couple of months when it goes on sale, and overall, I’m just excited about the new features,” Lima said.

Others were experiencing delays due to a lack of capability or an experience with what every gamer tends to fear.

“My PS4 broke, so unfortunately, I cannot play GTA VI,” said Luke Turner, a second-year police foundations student. “However, if I did have a working device, I 100 percent would have bought GTA VI.”

The next installment in the GTA franchise is set to release on Nov, 19 and will be considered not just the biggest release in video game history, but in media history.

stories.title: 'Most ambitious since Avro': Ottawa defence startup unveils partners for Scout drone
stories.summary: Ottawa - Eliot Pence, the hard-charging founder of Canadian defence company Dominion Dynamics, has a message for the industry's leading contractors around the world: We're coming for your lunch.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Eliot Pence, the hard-charging founder of Canadian defence company Dominion Dynamics, has a message for the industry’s leading contractors around the world: We’re coming for your lunch.

The fledgling Ottawa-based startup unveiled twelve partnerships with established defence players in Canada on Friday for developing its Scout drone, an uncrewed “loyal wingman” reliant on artificial intelligence that could pair with fighter jets and fly alongside them.

Dominion is planning to compete in an anticipated future procurement to supply the federal government with autonomous collaborative platforms. It’s bringing a made-in-Canada pitch to the competition at a time when Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is focused on acquiring sovereign capabilities and building up domestic industries.

“The intention here is for it to be the most ambitious air platform since the Avro in Canada,” Pence told The Canadian Press.

Avro Canada was a post-World War II aerospace manufacturer known mainly for its CF-105 Arrow, a highly regarded but short-lived interceptor jet.

Dominion’s project has been in the works since his company’s inception some 18 months ago. Pence is quickly assembling plans for a supply chain that would be mostly domestic.

Dominion’s early development partners include Pratt and Whitney Canada — it plans to use PW300-type engines in its drones — Telesat, Top Aces, North Aircraft Industries, PV Labs, SRC Can, Thales Canada and Altitude Aerospace.

Pence’s company would build the drone and its systems for handling data communication, sensors and intelligence, and turn to these other companies for expertise in areas such as operator training, avionics and landing gear.

Dominion also announced a stand-alone partnership with Canadian satellite operator Telesat this week to make antennas designed for Arctic use. They would connect uncrewed military hardware systems to Lightspeed, Telesat’s planned low-Earth satellite network.

The federal government awarded a $17 million contract to Dominion Dynamics this week. The 24-month contract was awarded to the company to build a remotely controlled marine drone that can survey the ocean floor to detect, locate and identify underwater mines.

The federal government’s website said the drone will allow the Royal Canadian Navy to conduct missions by providing near real-time transmission of data while keeping personnel and crewed vessels outside of threat areas.

With Canada’s current CF-18 Hornet fighter jets expected to reach the end of their service lives by 2032, Ottawa has started acquiring advanced F-35 stealth fighters made by Lockheed Martin, although the jets are not yet based in Canada.

Shortly after taking office in early 2025, Carney’s government launched a review of Ottawa’s plan to purchase a fleet of 88 F-35s.

Saab, the Swedish defence manufacturer that was a runner-up in Canada’s fighter jet competition, has said it could set up a manufacturing hub in Canada for its Gripen fighter jets if Ottawa chooses to put in a bulk order for those aircraft.

Pence said Dominion’s drones would work with either the F-35 or the Gripen, and with other platforms like the early warning and control aircraft Canada wants to acquire.

These companies and other large legacy defence firms are developing similar kinds of drones they can sell alongside their crewed platforms.

Pence said he believes all of these companies are at the same starting line, since the technology is so new. And he’s betting that offering a Canadian-made drone designed for the vast and harsh Arctic environment gives his company an edge.

“We are building for the specific Arctic problem set and nobody else is doing that,” he said.

“There are very specific problems we’re seeking to solve for the Rcaf — range, Arctic ruggedization, gravel runway takeoff, short runways.”

paragraphs: Ottawa - Eliot Pence, the hard-charging founder of Canadian defence company Dominion Dynamics, has a message for the industry’s leading contractors around the world: We’re coming for your lunch.

The fledgling Ottawa-based startup unveiled twelve partnerships with established defence players in Canada on Friday for developing its Scout drone, an uncrewed “loyal wingman” reliant on artificial intelligence that could pair with fighter jets and fly alongside them.

Dominion is planning to compete in an anticipated future procurement to supply the federal government with autonomous collaborative platforms. It’s bringing a made-in-Canada pitch to the competition at a time when Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is focused on acquiring sovereign capabilities and building up domestic industries.
“The intention here is for it to be the most ambitious air platform since the Avro in Canada,” Pence told The Canadian Press.
Avro Canada was a post-World War II aerospace manufacturer known mainly for its CF-105 Arrow, a highly regarded but short-lived interceptor jet.
Dominion’s project has been in the works since his company’s inception some 18 months ago. Pence is quickly assembling plans for a supply chain that would be mostly domestic.

Dominion’s early development partners include Pratt and Whitney Canada — it plans to use PW300-type engines in its drones — Telesat, Top Aces, North Aircraft Industries, PV Labs, SRC Can, Thales Canada and Altitude Aerospace.

Pence’s company would build the drone and its systems for handling data communication, sensors and intelligence, and turn to these other companies for expertise in areas such as operator training, avionics and landing gear.

Dominion also announced a stand-alone partnership with Canadian satellite operator Telesat this week to make antennas designed for Arctic use. They would connect uncrewed military hardware systems to Lightspeed, Telesat’s planned low-Earth satellite network.

The federal government awarded a $17 million contract to Dominion Dynamics this week. The 24-month contract was awarded to the company to build a remotely controlled marine drone that can survey the ocean floor to detect, locate and identify underwater mines.

The federal government’s website said the drone will allow the Royal Canadian Navy to conduct missions by providing near real-time transmission of data while keeping personnel and crewed vessels outside of threat areas.

With Canada’s current CF-18 Hornet fighter jets expected to reach the end of their service lives by 2032, Ottawa has started acquiring advanced F-35 stealth fighters made by Lockheed Martin, although the jets are not yet based in Canada.
Shortly after taking office in early 2025, Carney’s government launched a review of Ottawa’s plan to purchase a fleet of 88 F-35s.

Saab, the Swedish defence manufacturer that was a runner-up in Canada’s fighter jet competition, has said it could set up a manufacturing hub in Canada for its Gripen fighter jets if Ottawa chooses to put in a bulk order for those aircraft.
Pence said Dominion’s drones would work with either the F-35 or the Gripen, and with other platforms like the early warning and control aircraft Canada wants to acquire.
These companies and other large legacy defence firms are developing similar kinds of drones they can sell alongside their crewed platforms.

Pence said he believes all of these companies are at the same starting line, since the technology is so new. And he’s betting that offering a Canadian-made drone designed for the vast and harsh Arctic environment gives his company an edge.
“We are building for the specific Arctic problem set and nobody else is doing that,” he said.
“There are very specific problems we’re seeking to solve for the Rcaf — range, Arctic ruggedization, gravel runway takeoff, short runways.”
Pence said he expects the government will launch a procurement competition for autonomous platforms in 2028 or 2029.
He said he intends to have the Dominion Scout flying in late 2028.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario, Ottawa committing $250 million to help fund new port in Sault Ste. Marie
stories.summary: Sault STE. Marie - Ontario and the federal government say they're committing $250 million to help build a new port in Sault Ste. Marie on the north shore of the Saint Marys River.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Sault STE. Marie - Ontario and the federal government say they’re committing $250 million to help build a new port in Sault Ste. Marie on the north shore of the Saint Marys River.

The province says the project will see the construction of two docking berths, a transload yard to transfer cargo from ships to rail, and other infrastructure to move goods between northern and southern Ontario, Quebec and overseas markets.

stories.title: Cadets Canada parents, instructors speak out against activity pause
stories.summary: The Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) says that, starting Nov. 21, all cadet activities across the country will be paused, except for the core weekly parades.
stories.author: Emma Crawford
stories.content:
By Marija Robinson

Posted November 20, 2026 11:18 am.

Programs that once helped kids’ dreams take flight are now being grounded.

Thanks to an ongoing fiscal review, the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) says that, starting Saturday, Nov. 21, all cadet activities across the country will be paused, except for the core weekly parades.

That means for the 12- to 18-year-old youths enrolled, there won’t be any more weekend trips to museums, playing in the band, practicing survival skills, or learning to fly planes.

Patrick Shea used to teach teens to fly.

“I call it some of the most rewarding experiences of my life, and frankly some of the scariest experiences of my life,” Shea said.

He says that from the perspective of the Canadian Armed Forces, the cuts are understandable.

“Their job is to defend this country,” he said.

“They don’t see the cadets as directly contributing to the defence of this country.”

This is not something he agrees with, and he says the CAF has underestimated how much Canadians care about cadets.

A petition to reverse the decision gained close to 5,000 signatures in just hours.

One of those who signed it is parent Lesia Payne, whose oldest son has been working towards getting his pilot’s licence with his squadron in Vernon, B.C. This could now be at risk.

“In order to get the training that you need for those activities, those are all extracurricular programs that are in addition to the weekly training nights,” Payne said.

Speaking about the benefits of the programming, Shea says it gives kids experiences that many of them would otherwise never access.

“A good chunk of them, their parent is working two jobs to keep the child clothed and fed. So travelling and organized sports is not necessarily something that they can expect. This program gives them that.”

The benefits of cadet programs aren’t just anecdotal, either.

A report published by the federal government in March found that for every $1 spent on a cadet, the social return on investment ranges from $19.85 to $41.15.

“How can you not think that is a spectacular return on your money?” Shea said.

The CAF says this pause on activities will last until at least March 2027, though there’s concern that will get extended.

“These kids are only 16 years old once,” Shea said.

“You can’t just postpone these activities for a couple of years and see if they can do it then, because they age out of this program by 19.”

stories.title: Recent flooding damages dikes in B.C.'s Pemberton Valley: dyking district
stories.summary: Pemberton, British Columbia - The Pemberton Valley Dyking District says repair costs to its dikes after this month's torrential rain and flooding will be "significant."
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
About 50 to 60 homes in the Village of Pemberton have been “badly affected” by this month’s torrential rain and flooding with repairs to the community’s dikes expected to cost millions of dollars, the mayor said.

“Our whole diking system has taken on probably about $5 -to $6 million in damage just from this event,” Mike Richman said in an interview Friday.

“Our banking infrastructure survived the flood quite well, but if we got hit with another event in this condition, we would not survive it in the same way.”

Richman’s comments came after the Pemberton Valley Dyking District said repair costs to its dikes after the flooding from a series of storms will be “significant.”

The district manages 44 kilometres of dikes around the community in B.C.‘s Sea to Sky region and said its infrastructure “took a fairly good beating” in the flooding that prompted an evacuation alert for all of Pemberton as rivers swelled with heavy rains.

Its update on social media said work is underway to assess the full extent of the damage from the first major storms of the season and once that’s done it must tally the cost of repairs.

The district said the immediate focus is repairs that “impact our ability to withstand another rain event or pose a public safety risk.”

On top of the damage to the dikes, Richman said the village’s fire department training base was under about half a metre of mud.

Richman said when B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson visited the village last week, he also raised concerns about the Pemberton Creek Bridge on Highway 99, which serves as a key crossing southwest of the village.

The bridge is the only way out of the community to the south and is too low, he said, adding that the only way out to the north “consistently floods in high water events.”

“We were about two to three inches from having that bridge wash out last weekend, and if that happens, that means we are stuck both from the north end and the south end,” said Richman.

The district said it’s planning to apply for provincial disaster financial assistance, but not all flood or emergency events qualify and it must plead its case.

Jeremy Valeriote, the re-elected Green MLA who represents the area, says the region is in “urgent need” of funding for emergency readiness and sent a request to Doerkson.

Valeriote’s letter says the village was “only a few hours of rainfall away from full-scale disaster,” and there’s an urgent need for B.C. to get serious about preparing for an emergency.

“As you establish your new government, my request is simple: emergency readiness and response needs to be a top priority, with an all-of-government approach centred in the premier’s office,” the letter to Doerkson says

“These devastating emergency events do not respect bureaucratic boundaries or political positions on climate action,” it says.

His requests include emergency funding for repairs and upgrades to Pemberton’s diking system, replacement or resizing culverts and bridges to mitigate flooding and approval of disaster financial assistance to affected residents and businesses.

Valeriote said in an interview on Friday that $6 million repairs fees could “bankrupt” the village’s dyking district.

“I will say it could have been a lot worse if there were three or four more hours of rain. It would have been a full-scale disaster. The entire community probably would have had to be evacuated,” said Valeriote.

The series of storms earlier this month drenched southwestern B.C., where flood advisories spanned several regions, and four people died in as many days in rivers near Squamish, about 90 kilometres south of Pemberton.

The dyking district said it has done some emergency repairs on a culvert in Pemberton Creek and is in the process of removing log jams.

“For the larger repairs like Miller Weir and some yet to be quantified dike damage, we will have to see how this process moves as we go.”

Richman said the community has been through a tough six months, after a wildfire in July ahead of the latest flooding.

He said they are doing what they can but can’t recover without help.

“We need the province and the federal government to step up and and support us.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

On top of the damage to the dikes, Richman said the village’s fire department training base was under about half a metre of mud.

Richman said when B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson visited the village last week, he also raised concerns about the Pemberton Creek Bridge on Highway 99, which serves as a key crossing southwest of the village.
The bridge is the only way out of the community to the south and is too low, he said, adding that the only way out to the north “consistently floods in high water events.”
“We were about two to three inches from having that bridge wash out last weekend, and if that happens, that means we are stuck both from the north end and the south end,” said Richman.
The district said it’s planning to apply for provincial disaster financial assistance, but not all flood or emergency events qualify and it must plead its case.
Jeremy Valeriote, the re-elected Green MLA who represents the area, says the region is in “urgent need” of funding for emergency readiness and sent a request to Doerkson.
Valeriote’s letter says the village was “only a few hours of rainfall away from full-scale disaster,” and there’s an urgent need for B.C. to get serious about preparing for an emergency.

“As you establish your new government, my request is simple: emergency readiness and response needs to be a top priority, with an all-of-government approach centred in the premier’s office,” the letter to Doerkson says
“These devastating emergency events do not respect bureaucratic boundaries or political positions on climate action,” it says.

His requests include emergency funding for repairs and upgrades to Pemberton’s diking system, replacement or resizing culverts and bridges to mitigate flooding and approval of disaster financial assistance to affected residents and businesses.
Valeriote said in an interview on Friday that $6 million repairs fees could “bankrupt” the village’s dyking district.

“I will say it could have been a lot worse if there were three or four more hours of rain. It would have been a full-scale disaster. The entire community probably would have had to be evacuated,” said Valeriote.

The series of storms earlier this month drenched southwestern B.C., where flood advisories spanned several regions, and four people died in as many days in rivers near Squamish, about 90 kilometres south of Pemberton.
The dyking district said it has done some emergency repairs on a culvert in Pemberton Creek and is in the process of removing log jams.
“For the larger repairs like Miller Weir and some yet to be quantified dike damage, we will have to see how this process moves as we go.”
Richman said the community has been through a tough six months, after a wildfire in July ahead of the latest flooding.
He said they are doing what they can but can’t recover without help.
“We need the province and the federal government to step up and and support us.”

stories.title: Joly, Stellantis officials set for latest showdown on Friday
stories.summary: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is set to meet with representatives of Stellantis, the Ontario government and Unifor again today behind closed doors. The sit-down comes as Joly says the automaker can either keep its Brampton, Ont. plant open rather than selling it to defence contractor Roshel, or face a multimillion-dollar lawsuit from the federal government…
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Industry Minister Mélanie Joly met with representatives of Stellantis, the Ontario government and Unifor on Friday afternoon behind closed doors.

“This was a challenging meeting that we just had, but a productive meeting as well,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford told reporters after it wrapped.

The sit-down came as Joly said the automaker could either keep its Brampton, Ont., plant open rather than completing its sale to defence contractor Roshel, or face a multimillion-dollar lawsuit from the federal government.

“They need to protect the workers. If not, we’ll get our money back,” Joly told reporters earlier in the day during a separate announcement.

“If they go ahead and sell the plant, well then they will face legal recourses from the Government of Canada of hundreds of millions of dollars. And if they decide actually to protect their workers and not sell the plant, then we can work together.”

The automaker said its global CEO, Antonio Filosa, and Stellantis Canada president and CEO Trevor Longley were to represent the company during the meeting. Ford and Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli were there, while Unifor national president Lana Payne was also set to take part.

Payne said afterwards that while Stellantis did not waver on its decision to sell the plant, substantial proposals were presented, and discussions will continue with company executives next week.

“In this moment, it is imperative that governments not cede ground in this increasingly brittle trade war started by President Trump. There can be no scenario where Canada and Ontario lose an auto assembly plant, and governments must do everything they can to protect autoworkers and the Canadian auto industry,” Payne said in a statement.

Last week, the federal government served Stellantis with a notice of default on its 2022 funding agreement, in which Ottawa committed up to $529 million to help Stellantis retool its Brampton and Windsor facilities to produce electrified vehicles.

A letter from Joly said Stellantis breached conditions of the commitment by halting Jeep Compass production in Brampton, failing or refusing to identify a replacement vehicle, not maintaining any production at the facility and closing the plant.

Joly’s letter said Stellantis has 30 days to demonstrate it will “correct these conditions” or she will declare that the company is in default of its obligations. It warned that if Stellantis remains in breach of its conditions, the company could face penalties including a requirement to repay all or part of the funding it has received, plus interest.

But Stellantis has said it intends to repay only $24 million in federal government support received for the Brampton facility’s retooling plan.

Joly’s office said she was not planning to speak with media after it concluded. Roshel was not invited to participate.

Fedeli and Ford answered some reporter questions after the meeting, where Fedeli said the difference between operating in the United States and Canada came up.

Citing Stellantis figures, Ford said it costs about $135 million a year to keep the plant going when it’s not operational. He said keeping jobs in the province was his priority.

“We were very clear: we don’t want that facility to be closed or sold. We don’t want kits coming, not just from China but anywhere in the world. We want production there,” Ford said.

Fedeli also said the discussion was productive, despite concerns raised by the automaker.

“Today was a positive meeting, in respect that we put some options on the table, we’ve shown them a way that they can keep the building warm … keep it open and look for products in the future,” he said.

“But they kept going back to the fact that it’s the tariffs, it’s the greenhouse gas emission costs that the Americans don’t have, that we have in Canada, so we’re on two different playing fields.”

Stellantis said after the meeting it was open to further talks.

“The future of our Canadian operations and our employees remained the focus of today’s second meeting with representatives of the Canadian and Ontario governments and Unifor,” spokesperson LouAnn Gosselin said in an emailed statement.

“We remain committed to continuing constructive discussions.”

Speaking in Ottawa earlier on Friday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said the promised terms of the agreement with Stellantis must be enforced.

“Right now, we’re getting the worst of both worlds. We’re not getting the jobs, but we are getting the costs, where the workers are losing their paycheque and Canadians are losing their tax dollars. So, it’s up to the government to deliver the jobs that they force taxpayers to fund.”

He went on to say that investment-friendly government policies are a better way to support the auto sector long-term and don’t require “coming to offer them a crutch” when companies struggle.

“Here’s a plan,” Poilievre said. “Get rid of the industrial carbon tax. Stop Beijing from dumping its vehicles in our country. Speed up permits and negotiate an auto pact with the United States that requires automakers produce one car in Canada for every one they sell here. That is how we will re-industrialize and produce automobiles without the necessity of government handouts and bailouts.”

Last week, Joly said she was still in “solution mode” to prevent the Stellantis facility’s sale to Roshel, a Brampton-based armoured vehicle manufacturer, and that Ottawa has offered an “aggressive package” that it hopes can convince Stellantis to change course.

Fedeli has said there are supports available to Stellantis if it can “buy some time” rather than moving forward with the sale, which is expected to close before the end of this year.

A retooling began at the Brampton plant in early 2024, however the automaker paused its plan to produce the Jeep Compass there in February 2025 — one month after U.S. President Donald Trump retook office and began issuing tariffs on imports from Canada and other countries.

Stellantis later announced it was moving Jeep Compass production to Illinois, leaving more than 2,000 workers laid off and the Brampton plant idled indefinitely.

Roshel has said its plans for the site have the potential to create more than 2,000 jobs as production ramps up, and that laid-off workers would receive first priority consideration as hiring takes place.

— With files from Maan Alhmidi in Oakville, Ont., David Baxter in Ottawa and Allison Jones in Toronto.

stories.title: Ford Super Duty pickup trucks begin rolling out after retool at Oakville, Ont., plant
stories.summary: The retool was part of a $5-billion spend, with funding also dedicated toward Ford's first stamping plant in Canada.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

Posted November 20, 2026 11:00 am.

Last Updated November 20, 2026 11:20 am.

The plant is reopened and trucks are already rolling out.

Now, Ford Motor Co. hopes its Oakville, Ont., assembly complex can help it drive growth and demonstrate the automaker’s commitment to Canadian manufacturing for the long haul.

Friday marks the official relaunch of the site following a major transformation to prepare for production of the F-Series Super Duty pickup truck. The milestone is the culmination of two years of construction.

“It was absolutely immense,” said Bev Goodman, president and CEO of Ford of Canada, in an interview.

“We did take it down to the studs effectively. Everything that was in the plant came out.”

The retool was part of a $5-billion spend, with funding also dedicated toward Ford’s first stamping plant in Canada. Stamping is a process where flat metal sheets are moulded into specific shapes. A new building went up on a previously empty piece of land, where all panels and body parts that go into the truck are stamped. Other funding was allocated to Ford’s Windsor facilities, including its Essex engine plant which is being expanded to support production of its 7.3-litre engine line.

Ford announced its plan to assemble the Super Duty trucks at the Oakville plant in July 2024, saying the move would add capacity of up to 100,000 additional units and create nearly 2,000 jobs at the facility. The company also builds Super Duty vehicles at its plants in Kentucky and Ohio, but it needed a third site to “meet customer demand,” said Goodman.

She said Oakville made perfect sense after production of the Lincoln Nautilus and Ford Edge came to an end at the facility.

“When we make investments, we do make them for the long term,” she said.

“None of us know what the trade environment is going to look like. But we do know that Canada is a significantly important part of Ford globally.”

Ford already began shipping vehicles out of the facility two weeks ahead of schedule, Goodman said.

Premier Doug Ford, federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Unifor national president Lana Payne were scheduled to be on hand Friday to celebrate the reopening, which comes a few months after Ford employees ratified a new collective agreement.

Payne had praised the retool during summer contract negotiations with the company, which Unifor selected as its target to open the pattern bargaining process with the auto sector. Deals have been reached with Ford and General Motors, but contract talks with Stellantis remain at a standstill after that company sold its Brampton, Ont., manufacturing plant to defence contractor Roshel.

“The talks were very collaborative,” said Goodman.

The three-year agreement included wage increases and job security. It also renewed a no-closure agreement and program commitments at all Ford facilities.

Transforming the site to build pickup trucks marked a shift from initial plans to produce electric vehicles in Oakville. Ford had previously announced a $1.8-billion transformation of the facility into a hub for EV manufacturing, including vehicle and battery pack assembly. After planning to start EV production at the plant in 2025, the company pushed that back to give the consumer market more time to develop and allow for further development of EV battery technology.

Changing gears to Super Duty production meant some employees would return to work a year earlier than expected.

Other automakers have also halted EV project plans in Canada amid sluggish demand.

Earlier this year, Honda Motor Co. froze development on its $15-billion electric vehicle complex in Alliston, Ont., after last year pausing those plans and saying it would review where the EV market was before deciding the future of the project. General Motors ended production of its BrightDrop electric delivery van last year.

Goodman said demand for Super Duty trucks remains “surprisingly resilient,” as they serve “a specific need.”

“It is highly utilized by our commercial customers, people who need their trucks for their farms, to be upfit into an ambulance, to work on construction sites and so on. It is a very different marketing proposition and approach than what you see if you’re trying to sell a Bronco Sport to a first-time buyer,” she said.

“We do take different marketing approaches on that basis. We really focus in on the capability of this truck, which is really what matters to the users of these vehicles.”

For automakers like Ford, it’s been a bumpy couple of years, punctuated by tariffs and a broader trade war between Canada and the United States.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in recent days that trade talks with the U.S. are making progress, but Ottawa won’t accept a deal that doesn’t allow for a viable auto sector. That came three months after Canada pulled out of trade talks with the U.S. due to last-minute demands from Washington that included a hit to Canada’s auto sector.

Vehicles made in Canada are currently tariffed at 25 per cent, minus U.S. content in them. In August, President Donald Trump threatened to hike tariffs on all vehicles, auto parts and steel from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. 1.

“At the end of the day, this industry is … an integrated industry across North America. It has been for decades,” said Goodman.

“It is what makes us efficient and it is what enables us all to compete against competitors from other markets. Our discussions with governments on both sides of the border is really about advocating for policy that supports and also strengthens that connected, integrated North American auto industry. It’s been successful for decades and we need to get back to that.”

Ford and other automakers are monitoring new competitors in the Canadian market.

Chinese electric vehicles have been entering Canada this year after a deal was struck, allowing up to 49,000 Chinese EVs per year at a 6.1 per cent tariff instead of the 100 per cent tariff that was in place. By 2030, half of those imported vehicles are to cost less than $35,000 and would account for less than three per cent of the domestic auto market.

“It is absolutely something that’s on our mind,” said Goodman, adding the quota — meant to match the number of vehicles imported from China in 2023 before the tariffs — will help manage the impacts for now as Ford seeks a “level playing field as Chinese vehicles … come to market.”

“We really do believe that the government needs to make sure that we have trade policies that protect the long-term competitiveness of our industry,” she said.

“That means we’ve got to identify and put in place safeguards that will help protect against unfair trade practices, but also clear rules for connected vehicles as a means to really protect customers’ data and privacy as well as thinking about national security concerns.”
