stories.title: Gordon Lightfoot’s band carries on without the man
stories.summary: Autumnal residencies by the late balladeer at Toronto’s Massey Hall had been a semi-regular ritual in his later years
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Gordon Lightfoot performed the last of his more than 170 concerts at Massey Hall on Nov. 27, 2021. The autumnal residencies by the late balladeer at the historic Toronto venue had become a semi-regular ritual in his later years. This Saturday, his old bandmates play the room without the man.

The gales of November may come early, but the Lightfoot Band is right on time.

The Sundown singer was 84 years old when he died on May 1, 2023 . Eight months later, his band played a pair of shows at Toronto’s El Mocambo club with American Andy Mauck handling “the legend lives on” vocals. Since then, Mauck, bassist Rick Haynes (with Lightfoot for 55 years), drummer Barry Keane (with Lightfoot for 48 years) keyboardist Mike Heffernan (joined in 1980) and new guitarist Bill Bell (who has toured with Tom Cochrane and Andy Kim) have played more than 70 shows in Canada and the United States.

Before the Tragically Hip’s Gord Downie died of brain cancer, he encouraged his bandmates to keep the group going after this death. Thus far they have declined to do so. As for Lightfoot’s band carrying on without the star attraction, the subject was never brought up.

“We didn’t expect to lose him when we did,” Haynes says, speaking with his rhythm section partner Keane in a pair of floor seats near the stage at Massey Hall recently. “He always came back.”

By the fall of 2022, Lightfoot was suffering from emphysema. On a swing through Western Canada he was sitting down during the concerts. His final show was in Winnipeg on Oct. 30 of that year.

“He was a man who took so much pride in his performances,” Keane says. “It took a lot of courage to be on stage as a lesser form of himself. I could see people were listening with their memories more than the actual performances.”

Performing without Lightfoot now gives the band a chance to open things up a bit. They tackle the epic seven-minute long Canadian Railroad Trilogy , which Lightfoot didn’t perform toward the end of his career. Also, 1968’s The Circle is Small and 1971’s Summer Side of Life have been reintroduced into the setlist.

When Queen, the Who and Bruce Springsteen toured after the death of prominent band members, they incorporated archival photos and video images of the deceased musicians into the live performances. The Lightfoot Band doesn’t resort to that gimmickry.

“We talked about it, but it felt a little cheesy,” Keane says. “Cashing in on his image, that’s not us.”

They’re cashing in on his music, though, and they’re not the only ones doing it.

Singer-guitarist John Stinson fronts Classic Lightfoot Live, a tribute band based in Aurora, Ont. They have a concert in Kitchener, Ont., on Dec. 4. Rather brazenly, the act’s website claims to be the “finest possible Gordon Lightfoot concert experience since 2014.”

But Lightfoot was still alive and kicking in 2014, and for years afterward. Are they saying Classic Lightfoot Live is better than Lightfoot was himself?

Pretty much.

“At that time, Gordon’s voice was tailing off,” Stinson says. “And for all his fantasticness, he didn’t try to replicate the recordings on stage. I’ve tried to do that over the years.”

The musicians in Classic Lightfoot Live include Bob Doidge, who produced Lightfoot’s 2004 album Harmony and co-produced 1998’s A Painter Passing Through . Lightfoot’s bass-playing nephew Steve Eyers is also in the band. On the website it says “It doesn’t get much more authentic” than him.

It does, though. Bassist Haynes has been with Lightfoot since Trudeaumania and he played on Lightfoot’s 1969 live album Sunday Concert , recorded at Massey Hall.

“Tribute bands when the actual artist is still alive never quite sat right with me,” Haynes says. As for authenticity, he and Keane played on the original recordings that cover bands such as Classic Lightfoot Live attempt to replicate. “Gordon wrote the songs, but we were part of the creative process,” Haynes says.

But what does the legacy act Lightfoot Band give fans that the tribute bands don’t? History − Haynes, Keane and a Heffernan have a combined 146 years of experience performing, recording and doing “what you don’t confess” on the road with Lightfoot.

“We tell stories,” Keane says. “And because we were with the man, there’s a joy of playing the songs we played with him. None of the other bands can say that and give that. We’re the real deal.”

The Lightfoot Band plays Massey Hall on Nov. 21 .

stories.title: Ford’s Oakville assembly plant reopens after more than two years
stories.summary: About 2,000 people have returned to work at the plant west of Toronto, which makes Ford’s F-Series Super range
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Ford Motor Co.’s F-N assembly plant in Oakville, Ont., shuttered for more than two years, has reopened to make heavy-duty pickup trucks, defying the trade war and offering hope for the future of Canadian automaking.

More than 2,000 people have returned to work at the plant west of Toronto, which makes Ford’s F-Series Super Range of large pickups for Canadian, U.S. and global markets.

Detroit-based Ford spent $5-billion on the plant, retooling the assembly line and building a new stamping shop on site for body panels. The federal and Ontario governments contributed $464.5-million and $295-million, respectively, to the total.

“Today is a big day for Ford and for Canada,” said Bev Goodman, Ford Canada’s chief executive officer, at a ceremony to mark the plant’s reopening on Friday.

Brad Walker, a 14-year Ford employee who assembles dashboards on the trucks, said he was glad to be back at work and never doubted the plant would reopen, given the customer demand.

Brent Hogenbirk, who started at the plant 30 years ago and conducts tests of finished trucks, has been back at work since May as the plant began ramping up production. “It was hard,” he said of the almost two years on layoff.

Premier Doug Ford and Industry Minister Mélanie Joly were among the speakers to hundreds of auto workers and Ford officials in an event marked by celebration and flashes of Canadian economic nationalism.

Mr. Ford’s mention of U.S. President Donald Trump, who has targeted much of Canada’s economy with tariffs, drew boos from the assembled crowd.

Lana Payne, national president of Unifor, which represents about 40,000 auto workers in Canada, a sector that has been battered by U.S. tariffs, called the plant’s reopening “nothing short of an industrial rebirth for Canada” and an “act of resistance” amid the trade war with the United States. She said the plant was a “lighthouse in some very dark times.”

Ms. Joly echoed Ms. Payne’s resistance comment and thanked all Canadians in these “tough days of dealing with American tariffs.”

“Ford’s decision to invest in Oakville is a signal to the world that Canada is open for business,” Ms. Joly said. “Canada is competitive, and Canada is the place to build autos in North America.”

Ford’s Oakville plant, which used to make the Edge, closed in 2024 to be retooled for an electric car . Ford scrapped that plan amid slowing demand for EVs and began work to make the trucks, including the F-250, F-350 and F-450, which are all used in construction, agriculture and for other commercial purposes.

The work on the plant continued even after the U.S. last year widened its tariff policy to include the very trucks made in Oakville.

In an interview, Ms. Goodman said the reopening of the plant underlines Ford’s commitment to manufacture in Canada, dating back 122 years to a town near Windsor, Ont. The Oakville plant opened in 1953.

“This investment in this moment is really about staying true to our commitments,” Ms. Goodman said. “That’s a commitment to manufacturing here in Canada as well as to building new capabilities and supporting jobs here in Canada.”

Including the smaller F-150, the F-Series trucks were bestselling vehicles in Canada and the United States in 2025, beating the Toyota RAV-4, according to DesRosiers Automotive Consultants Inc.

The Oakville plant made 3,488 trucks in October, and has the capacity to make 100,000 a year. Some of the trucks will use the 7.3-litre V8 gasoline engine made at Ford’s plant in Windsor. Ford recently announced a US$500-million investment at the engine plant.

“So what’s really cool here is you’re going to have a vehicle built in Oakville with engines from Windsor,” said Flavio Volpe, head of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association.

Mr. Volpe said the plant’s reopening signals the automaker believes Canada and the U.S. will eventually eliminate tariffs and abide by the terms of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

“It’s a very public bet that they think they’ll have tariff peace between Canada and the U.S.” he said.

Oakville production will supplement output at Ford’s Super Duty plants in Kentucky and Ohio.

Canadians bought more than 138,000 F-series trucks in 2025, outselling the nearest truck competitors combined, the GMC Sierra and Chevrolet Silverado, according to DesRosiers.

“The capacity that we’re adding here at Oakville to our system will allow us to meet that demand,” Ford’s Ms. Goodman said, “and it will give us the ability to deliver to our customers more configurations and shorten our order time for the trucks to get to customers.”

She spoke of the plant’s transformation over the past two years, from an almost empty factory and site, to the construction of the new stamping shop’s structure and the now-full employee parking lot.

“Seeing the activity over that time period with the folks who were transforming the plant, and now to have the employees back working full-time is just something to be really proud of,” Ms. Goodman said.

Ms. Goodman said the company committed to Oakville production before the U.S. announced tariffs on heavy-duty trucks in October 2025. Ford supports renewal of the Usmca that, before Mr. Trump’s tariffs, allowed automotive and other goods to cross the border tariff-free.

“Our investments are long-term,” she said. “And they underscore that Canada is very, very important in our global Ford plan, but it’s also importantly a reflection of the capability of our team and the demonstration of the quality that they can build here.”

When asked why Ford did not delay the plant’s restart in the face of tariffs, Ms. Goodman said, “We made a commitment to our employees and made a commitment to our business, and we’ve retained those commitments, which is important to Ford.”

'We have heard the concerns raised by cadets, families, and communities across Canada about changes to planned cadet activities,' said Defence Minister David McGuinty

Canada's Defence Minister David McGuinty listens at a doorstep during the summit of the so-called "Coalition of the Willing", a group of Ukraine's most significant allies and supporters, at the chancellery in Berlin on November 19, 2026. (ODD Andersen / AFP via Getty Images)

November 20, 2026 at 10:55 a.m.

Defence Minister David McGuinty says he’s asked for a funding review of Canada’s military cadet program, in the wake of a decision to put many cadet training activities on hold until April 2027 because of a fiscal belt-tightening initiative.

Cadets across the country have been told they’d be allowed to continue to have weekly training nights that focus on drill, uniform inspections and leadership, but that other training had been put on hold.

“We have heard the concerns raised by cadets, families, and communities across Canada about changes to planned cadet activities,” McGuinty said Friday in a written statement posted to social media.

McGuinty points out that the budget for cadets this year is $265 million, “which is an increase from last year and previous years.”

He has asked officials to review cadet funding, “and will ensure the cadet community is kept informed as that work progresses.”

McGuinty notes in his statement that the cadet program “has grown by 59 per cent in recent years. We have significantly increased funding to support its continued growth and are continually working with program leadership to evaluate and respond to evolving priorities and needs.”

stories.title: The Iran war is still going on. So why have gas prices fallen?
stories.summary: As of Friday morning, the Canadian Automobile Association recorded the national average for gas prices at 144.4 cents per litre, almost 30 cents lower from late October.
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
Gas prices in Canada are finally falling.

As of Friday morning, the Canadian Automobile Association recorded the national average for gas prices at 144.4 cents per litre.

That’s almost 30 cents-per-litre lower since late October, when the average sat at 171.3 cents per litre, and a 46 cents-per-litre drop since the year’s highest price, recorded in May at 190.4 cents per litre.

“Oil prices have come down to their lowest level in about two months,” former Cibc World Markets chief economist Jeff Rubin told CTV’s Your Morning on Friday.

He attributed the drop to a significant decrease in global demand and supply diversification.

“On the supply side, they’re diverting oil flows from the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. “(And) higher oil prices raise supply, but they also kill demand and the world’s consuming about almost four million barrels a day less than it was before the war started because of the higher oil prices.”

Supply up, demand down

The war between the U.S., Iran and Israel, which began in February, has choked one of the world’s most important shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz , by damaging refineries, offshore oil platforms and processing facilities, stranding tankers and forcing suppliers to rethink routes, adding weeks to delivery time.

Approximately eight million barrels of oil are transported through the Hormuz strait, Rubin said. “But there are another five or six (million) that are getting through other routes.”

“Middle Eastern producers have been relatively successful at finding ways of getting their product to world markets, bypassing the straits.”

The U.S. has also increased its oil production to almost 14 million barrels a day , he added.

“Refineries are running at 96 per cent capacity,” he said. “So yes, inventories have increased.

Thursday’s meeting between the U.S., China and Russia, out of which the leaders of all three nations pledged to stabilize energy flows , could also have implications, he said.

“China’s got the most to gain from that because China’s the largest energy importer,” Rubin said. “(And) will the Trump administration put pressure on Zelenskyy not to target Russian diesel installations. These are all certainly factors that could affect the ultimate outcome.”

On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials confirmed strikes on two refineries in Russia’s Krasnodar region . Together the refineries process around 95 million barrels of oil a year and supply Russian forces in southern and eastern Ukraine.

Ukraine has consistently struck refineries in Russia, aiming to hurt its oil sector, a mainstay of the country’s economy.

stories.title: Melanie Joly, Doug Ford to announce supports for Canada’s auto industry
stories.summary: Stellantis, the parent company of Jeep, announced earlier this month a deal to sell its Brampton, Ont. vehicle assembly plant to defence manufacturer Roshel.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Industry Minister Melanie Joly and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are set to announce new supports for Canada’s auto manufacturing sector, which is reeling from U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

In addition to federal and provincial officials, Joly’s office said she and Ford will be accompanied by Ford Motor Company of Canada CEO Ivan Boykin and Unifor National President Lana Payne.

This comes as Stellantis , the parent company of Jeep and other automotive brands, announced earlier this month a deal to sell its Brampton, Ont., vehicle assembly plant to Canadian defence and armoured vehicle manufacturer Roshel.

Last week, Joly said the CEO will meet with Ontario and Ottawa officials to work on “remedies for breach.”

The financial terms of that agreement have not been made public, and although there have been questions about whether some Stellantis workers May be grandfathered into Roshel’s operations, no specifics have been provided.

That deal came as contract talks between Stellantis and the union representing more than 9,000 of its workers in Canada remain at an impasse.

Joly said the automaker must repay “hundreds of millions of dollars” to Ottawa after it failed to restore jobs at its idled plant.

If those funds are not paid back, the government will sue the company, she said following a high-stakes meeting with the company last week.

“I’m fed up, workers are fed up and Canadians are fed up. This is happening at a time when other automakers are doubling down on Canada and investing in their plant,” she said.

Joly sent the automaker a letter dated Nov. 12 that says Stellantis is in default of a 2022 federal funding agreement because it halted Jeep Compass production at the plant, failed or refused to identify a replacement vehicle, did not maintain any production at the facility, and closed the plant.

Stellantis has 30 days to demonstrate it will “correct these conditions,” Joly’s letter states, or face penalties, which could include terminating the funding deal and requiring the company to repay all or part of the funding it has received.

“I’m fed up, workers are fed up and Canadians are fed up. This is happening at a time when other automakers are doubling down on Canada and investing in their plant,” she said.

Joly sent the automaker a letter dated Nov. 12 that says Stellantis is in default of a 2022 federal funding agreement because it halted Jeep Compass production at the plant, failed or refused to identify a replacement vehicle, did not maintain any production at the facility, and closed the plant.

Stellantis has 30 days to demonstrate it will “correct these conditions,” Joly’s letter states, or face penalties, which could include terminating the funding deal and requiring the company to repay all or part of the funding it has received.

stories.title: Ontario fugitive arrested in Winnipeg hours after making most wanted list
stories.summary: An Ontario fugitive wanted in connection with two Toronto-area shootings was arrested in Winnipeg Thursday, less than six hours after being placed on Canada’s most wanted list.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
An Ontario fugitive wanted in connection with two Toronto-area shootings was arrested in Winnipeg Thursday, less than six hours after being placed on Canada’s most wanted list.

Filmon Fesshaghirgis, 28, of London, Ont., was ranked No. 14 when the updated list was unveiled at 10:30 a.m. Police arrested him at approximately 4:10 p.m.

Fesshaghirgis was wanted on Canada-wide warrants for two shootings that happened at the start of the decade.

The first occurred on Nov. 12, 2020. At roughly 6:30 p.m. that day, York Regional Police officers were called to a shooting at a business on Steeles Avenue West in Vaughan. One person was taken to hospital.

At about 12:30 p.m. Jan. 18, 2021, Ontario Provincial Police responded to reports of a shooting at a house in Bolton.

Two people were hurt, including the victim from the incident in Vaughan. The second victim, Bolton resident Giovanni Costa, 65, died at the scene.

Fesshaghirgis faces one count of first-degree murder, two counts of attempted murder and one count of conspiracy to commit murder. The OPP said it’s planning to bring Fesshaghirgis to the province.

Most of the fugitives placed on Bolo’s list are wanted for murder or attempted murder across the country. Bolo has published life-sized, AI-generated depictions of the 25 fugitives to show how they May appear in public. The allegations against them have not been proven in court.

At the top of this year’s list is Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, who is wanted by Winnipeg police for the September 2023 killing of 39-year-old Sukhdool Singh Gill.

A reward of up to $250,000 for information leading to Singh’s arrest in Canada or the United States is being offered by Bolo.

Singh is also on the Fbi’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, and he has been wanted for murder by Indian authorities since 2022.

“The harm we believed he has caused and will continue to cause if he’s not caught extends well beyond one community, one city, one country. This is one extremely dangerous individual,” Winnipeg police Deputy Chief Cam Mackid told reporters Thursday.

“We will be absolutely relentless when it comes to pursuing these types of investigations. We also believe public safety is a shared responsibility, and one has been answered by Canadians time and again through the Bolo Program. We’re now asking all Canadians to be on the lookout for Goldy Brar. He should be considered extremely violent, armed, and dangerous.”

Kyle Prouse , Cody Rudifo, Ayoub Mohamed and Sabrina Agusto-Ramirez round out Bolo’s top five.

Rewards of up to $100,000 and $50,000 are being offered for information leading to the arrests of Prouse and Rudifo, respectively. Toronto police say Prouse is wanted for attempted murder and Rudifo is wanted for murder.

Mohamed is being sought by Quebec provincial police for murder, with a reward of up to $50,000 available.

A $50,000 reward has been issued for Agusto-Ramirez, who is wanted by the U.S. Marshals for murder-related charges in connection with a 2023 homicide case in Fresno, Calif. Agusto-Ramirez is believed to be in the Greater Toronto Area.

Joseph Madore, Brayton Kennedy and Dylan Denis all have a $50,000 reward in place; Madore and Kennedy are wanted by Ontario Provincial Police for murder, while Denis is wanted by police in Montreal for murder.

The remaining entries do not currently have Bolo rewards attached.

The rewards expire on Nov. 2, 2027.

Anyone with information is asked to contact their local police service.

stories.title: Oil prices are finally decreasing. This expert explains why
stories.summary: As of Friday morning, the Canadian Automobile Association recorded the national average for gas prices at 144.4 cents per litre, almost 30 cents lower from late October.
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
Gas prices in Canada are finally falling.

As of Friday morning, the Canadian Automobile Association recorded the national average for gas prices at 144.4 cents per litre.

That’s almost 30 cents-per-litre lower since late October, when the average sat at 171.3 cents per litre, and a 46 cents-per-litre drop since the year’s highest price, recorded in May at 190.4 cents per litre.

“Oil prices have come down to their lowest level in about two months,” former Cibc World Markets chief economist Jeff Rubin told CTV’s Your Morning on Friday.

He attributed the drop to a significant decrease in global demand and supply diversification.

“On the supply side, they’re diverting oil flows from the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. “(And) higher oil prices raise supply, but they also kill demand and the world’s consuming about almost four million barrels a day less than it was before the war started because of the higher oil prices.”

Supply up, demand down

The war between the U.S., Iran and Israel, which began in February, has choked one of the world’s most important shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz , by damaging refineries, offshore oil platforms and processing facilities, stranding tankers and forcing suppliers to rethink routes, adding weeks to delivery time.

Approximately eight million barrels of oil are transported through the Hormuz strait, Rubin said. “But there are another five or six (million) that are getting through other routes.”

“Middle Eastern producers have been relatively successful at finding ways of getting their product to world markets, bypassing the straits.”

The U.S. has also increased its oil production to almost 14 million barrels a day , he added.

“Refineries are running at 96 per cent capacity,” he said. “So yes, inventories have increased.

Thursday’s meeting between the U.S., China and Russia, out of which the leaders of all three nations pledged to stabilize energy flows , could also have implications, he said.

“China’s got the most to gain from that because China’s the largest energy importer,” Rubin said. “(And) will the Trump administration put pressure on Zelenskyy not to target Russian diesel installations. These are all certainly factors that could affect the ultimate outcome.”

On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials confirmed strikes on two refineries in Russia’s Krasnodar region . Together the refineries process around 95 million barrels of oil a year and supply Russian forces in southern and eastern Ukraine.

Ukraine has consistently struck refineries in Russia, aiming to hurt its oil sector, a mainstay of the country’s economy.

stories.title: N.B. RCMP are investigating preterm fetus remains found in an airport bathroom
stories.summary: Police say they're investigating the circumstances surrounding the discovery of the remains and provided no further details.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
RCMP in New Brunswick are investigating after the remains of a preterm fetus were found in an airport.

Police say members of the Oromocto detachment responded to a report of human remains found in the Fredericton International Airport Wednesday morning.

Officers located the remains of what they described as a preterm fetus inside an airport bathroom.

Police say they’re investigating the circumstances surrounding the discovery of the remains and provided no further details.

No charges have been laid.

Police say a member of the New Brunswick coroner’s office attended the scene and is assisting with the ongoing investigation.

stories.title: Robots helping build houses, a bright side of price-drops and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Nov. 20
stories.summary: Plus, a closer look at mortgage rates in Canada
stories.author: Moira Wyton
stories.content:
This week: A company using AI and robots to help build more homes, and the bright side of lower prices for boomers. Plus, a growing family’s house hunt in B.C., and one property worth a look.

Would you live in a home robots helped build? A Toronto artificial intelligence startup is betting on yes. Promise Robotics Inc. has developed AI software that breaks up developers’ existing home designs into wall, floor and ceiling-sized pieces that robots produce in a factory, down to the Hvac and plumbing systems. Then the components get shipped to the site, where a crew hired by Promise actually puts them together as finished houses.

Pretty cool, huh? Residential developers, who are struggling to increase their productivity and find enough skilled workers, think so too. As Murad Hemmadi reports, Promise has built 200 homes to date, has a contract with one of Canada’s largest home builders, and just raised an additional $40-million to scale up . Part of what makes Promise so attractive to developers is that they aren’t the factory-made modular or shipping container homes some critics call bland and ugly. “They just look like houses,” Murad told me.

But humans aren’t going the way of the dinosaur just yet. “The trades are harder to automate, because most robots that aren’t fixed to a manufacturing line don’t have fine motor control skills,” Murad told me. “And where precisely you put a nail – not to mention what you avoid hitting along the way – still really matters.” Read Murad’s story for a glimpse of our homes’ potentially automated futures.

People thought they “were crazy” to live in a fifth-wheel RV with their newborn baby, but Rebecca Nestman says she and her husband Tyler “made it work.” It meant the family could stay together when Tyler’s job required him to travel in 2020, and when he changed jobs, they parked it at his parents’ home in Gibsons on B.C.’s Sunshine Coast.

After being outbid on an apartment they had liked in the town, the Nestmans turned to another unconventional idea: Tyler’s parents offered to build a two-bedroom carriage house on their property and charge below-market rent, which helped the couple save up and welcome their second son with a little more room. But earlier this year, the Nestmans found out they were pregnant again, and set out to find a home with more space to breathe before Rebecca’s December due date.

So with an $800,000 budget, thanks to their savings and a gift from Rebecca’s parents, what did they buy just a short ferry ride away from Vancouver? As Andrea Yu reports, the couple’s hunt took them from a centrally-located mobile home to a split-level with a basement suite. Read the story to see which home they chose and vote for the one you would have picked.

Rates shown are the lowest available for each term/type and category (insured vs. uninsured) as of market close on Thursday, Nov. 19 .

Is the recent decline in home values a good thing for everyone, even the boomers feeling the burn on their equity the most? Rob Carrick certainly thinks so. In fact, he argues in his latest column , “lower real estate prices are almost a relief.”

“Boomers who are rich in home equity give a little bit back as prices fall, and doors open for young buyers currently priced out,” Rob writes. And while many boomers who can afford to are helping their kids with down payments to get on the property ladder, he says lower home prices will reduce that pressure and leave more money in their pockets or retirement accounts.

So boomers today face a dilemma: “higher house prices for my retirement or declines to help my kids?” Rob writes. Even though “no one is expected to welcome the news that their home is worth less,” he argues the latter choice is just what this country needs. Read the full column – or send it to your boomer relatives.

Is there a movie set you wish you could live inside? For me, it’s any of the cozy and eclectic homes of Nora Ephron’s romantic comedies. Films are often where we discover our next favourite outfits, songs and on-screen crushes, but great cinema can also inspire our sense of design.

Nathalie Atkinson spoke to Canadian architects and interior designers about the movies that helped shape their perspectives on interiors , and you might be surprised about some of the films on the list. From the absolute intention in Ex Machina to Lovers Rock’s lesson in making space, here are seven movies to watch if you want to think about design in a new way.

34 Glenbrae Ave., Toronto – Full gallery here

Living on a busy street in Toronto sent one family on a search for a more peaceful piece of the city, but they didn’t have to go far. This traditional red-brick house in north Leaside made the short move from the Bayview and Eglinton area more than worth the hassle. The family-friendly area and excellent schools had already sold Monique Steger and her husband once, and they were thrilled to find a tranquil home that didn’t disrupt their older son’s elementary classes nearby.

The new-build was nearly done by the time Steger toured it in 2010, but the family of four moulded it into their very own homebase. The coffered-ceiling family room is where the family gravitates, and on the way there from the kitchen you’ll pass the second fridge they added to help make entertaining a little easier. That’s not to mention the large island and breakfast nook that make the kitchen the centre of the home, even before Steger added a custom pantry.

With four bedrooms upstairs – one even boasts a wall of built-in bookshelves surrounding a window - and two more plus a rec room downstairs, the interior is spacious, but the backyard set-up is what often drew a crowd. Next to the saltwater pool and waterfalls the family added in 2012, an outdoor kitchen with a TV and plenty of seating became the destination for every major sporting event and the two boys’ sports teams’ year-end celebrations.

What do you think is the asking price for the property?

a. $2,799,000 b. $2,999,000 c. $3,199,000 d. $3,399,000 c. The asking price is $3,199,000.

Pretty cool, huh? Residential developers, who are struggling to increase their productivity and find enough skilled workers, think so too. As Murad Hemmadi reports, Promise has built 200 homes to date, has a contract with one of Canada’s largest home builders, and just raised an additional $40-million to scale up . Part of what makes Promise so attractive to developers is that they aren’t the factory-made modular or shipping container homes some critics call bland and ugly. “They just look like houses,” Murad told me.

But humans aren’t going the way of the dinosaur just yet. “The trades are harder to automate, because most robots that aren’t fixed to a manufacturing line don’t have fine motor control skills,” Murad told me. “And where precisely you put a nail – not to mention what you avoid hitting along the way – still really matters.” Read Murad’s story for a glimpse of our homes’ potentially automated futures.

People thought they “were crazy” to live in a fifth-wheel RV with their newborn baby, but Rebecca Nestman says she and her husband Tyler “made it work.” It meant the family could stay together when Tyler’s job required him to travel in 2020, and when he changed jobs, they parked it at his parents’ home in Gibsons on B.C.’s Sunshine Coast.

After being outbid on an apartment they had liked in the town, the Nestmans turned to another unconventional idea: Tyler’s parents offered to build a two-bedroom carriage house on their property and charge below-market rent, which helped the couple save up and welcome their second son with a little more room. But earlier this year, the Nestmans found out they were pregnant again, and set out to find a home with more space to breathe before Rebecca’s December due date.

So with an $800,000 budget, thanks to their savings and a gift from Rebecca’s parents, what did they buy just a short ferry ride away from Vancouver? As Andrea Yu reports, the couple’s hunt took them from a centrally-located mobile home to a split-level with a basement suite. Read the story to see which home they chose and vote for the one you would have picked.

Is the recent decline in home values a good thing for everyone, even the boomers feeling the burn on their equity the most? Rob Carrick certainly thinks so. In fact, he argues in his latest column , “lower real estate prices are almost a relief.”

“Boomers who are rich in home equity give a little bit back as prices fall, and doors open for young buyers currently priced out,” Rob writes. And while many boomers who can afford to are helping their kids with down payments to get on the property ladder, he says lower home prices will reduce that pressure and leave more money in their pockets or retirement accounts.

So boomers today face a dilemma: “higher house prices for my retirement or declines to help my kids?” Rob writes. Even though “no one is expected to welcome the news that their home is worth less,” he argues the latter choice is just what this country needs. Read the full column – or send it to your boomer relatives.

Is there a movie set you wish you could live inside? For me, it’s any of the cozy and eclectic homes of Nora Ephron’s romantic comedies. Films are often where we discover our next favourite outfits, songs and on-screen crushes, but great cinema can also inspire our sense of design.

Nathalie Atkinson spoke to Canadian architects and interior designers about the movies that helped shape their perspectives on interiors , and you might be surprised about some of the films on the list. From the absolute intention in Ex Machina to Lovers Rock’s lesson in making space, here are seven movies to watch if you want to think about design in a new way.
34 Glenbrae Ave., Toronto – Full gallery here

Living on a busy street in Toronto sent one family on a search for a more peaceful piece of the city, but they didn’t have to go far. This traditional red-brick house in north Leaside made the short move from the Bayview and Eglinton area more than worth the hassle. The family-friendly area and excellent schools had already sold Monique Steger and her husband once, and they were thrilled to find a tranquil home that didn’t disrupt their older son’s elementary classes nearby.

The new-build was nearly done by the time Steger toured it in 2010, but the family of four moulded it into their very own homebase. The coffered-ceiling family room is where the family gravitates, and on the way there from the kitchen you’ll pass the second fridge they added to help make entertaining a little easier. That’s not to mention the large island and breakfast nook that make the kitchen the centre of the home, even before Steger added a custom pantry.

With four bedrooms upstairs – one even boasts a wall of built-in bookshelves surrounding a window - and two more plus a rec room downstairs, the interior is spacious, but the backyard set-up is what often drew a crowd. Next to the saltwater pool and waterfalls the family added in 2012, an outdoor kitchen with a TV and plenty of seating became the destination for every major sporting event and the two boys’ sports teams’ year-end celebrations.
What do you think is the asking price for the property?

stories.title: Man arrested hours after being placed on Canada’s most wanted list
stories.summary: Filmon Fesshaghirgis, originally from London, Ont., was wanted in connection with two shootings incidents in the Greater Toronto Area in 2020 and 2021
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police say they have arrested a man in a homicide investigation, only hours after he was placed at No. 14 on Canada’s most wanted list of fugitives.

Officers say they arrested Filmon Fesshaghirgis, 28, in Winnipeg on Thursday at 4:10 p.m., with help from the Winnipeg Police Service and the Manitoba RCMP, and are making arrangements for his return to Ontario.

They say they acted on information they received about the man, originally from London, Ont., who was wanted in connection with two shootings incidents in the Greater Toronto Area in 2020 and 2021.

In November 2020, York Regional Police responded to a shooting at a business in Vaughan, where one person was taken to the hospital.

In January 2021, Caledon police responded to reports of a shooting at a home in Bolton, where they found two people, including the victim from the Vaughan incident, with gunshot wounds. A 65-year-old old man from Bolton was found dead.

The accused was charged with first-degree murder, two counts of attempted murder and conspiracy to commit murder.

Police say the investigation remains ongoing and ask anyone with information to come forward.

stories.title: Tranquil setting and nearby school sold couple on Leaside home
stories.summary: The traditional red-brick house also features a saltwater pool and waterfalls in the backyard
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
34 Glenbrae Ave., Toronto

Asking Price: $3,199,000

Taxes: $15,046.96 (2026)

Lot Size: 31 by 133.5 feet

Agent: Patrick Rocca, Bosley Real Estate

The builder was putting the finishing touches on a new four-bedroom house in north Leaside when Monique Steger and her husband toured the property in 2010.

The couple and their two young sons were already living near Bayview Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East, but their home sat on a busy road.

The detached two-storey house on Glenbrae Avenue would provide a quieter setting without disrupting their seven-year-old son’s classes at a nearby elementary school and his two-year-old brother’s playdates with neighbourhood kids.

“It was the school and also the sense of community,” Ms. Steger says of the decision to move just up the street. “It’s a great neighbourhood to raise a family. It’s safe, and there are so many kids.”

The traditional red-brick house was nearing completion, but Ms. Steger still had the chance to choose the light fixtures and some of the paint colours.

“Most of the design decisions had been made,” she says.

At the front of the home, a foyer opens to the living and dining area with crown mouldings, panelled walls and a bay window overlooking the street.

The kitchen, with built-in appliances, a large island and a breakfast area, stands at the centre of the home.

The family room at the rear has a coffered ceiling, built-in cabinets and doors opening to a porch and stairs to the backyard.

“That’s where we spend the most time,” says Ms. Steger.

Over time, Ms. Steger brought in the developer’s designer to add customized elements, such as a pantry in the kitchen and a hutch and bar in the dining area.

Ms. Steger added a second fridge between the kitchen and family room to make entertaining easier during large family gatherings.

“I put all of my platters in there,” she says.

Upstairs, the primary suite has a walk-in closet and a large bathroom with a soaker tub, walk-in shower and double vanity.

One bedroom has a wall of built-in bookshelves surrounding a window seat overlooking the street.

“It’s a pretty magical little space,” says Ms. Steger.

There are two additional bedrooms on that floor.

On the lower level, the couple created a recreation room and turned a fifth bedroom into a home office with a desk for each family member.

An island in the centre serves as a gift wrapping station.

Ms. Steger says the neighbourhood has plenty of green space, with Serena Gundy Park a short walk away and Sunnybrook Park and Edwards Gardens nearby.

An automated cover slides across to secure the pool when it’s not in use.

There’s a pergola sheltering the al fresco dining table and an outdoor kitchen with bar seating and a television set.

Every major televised sporting event and playoff series seems to attract a crowd, says Ms. Steger.

“We would have the team over for a swim and a barbecue,” says Ms. Steger.

stories.title: New half duplex appealed to busy Vancouver buyers
stories.summary: Three bed, four bath in Fraser Street neighbourhood sold for $1,685,000
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
4161 Windsor St., No. 1, Vancouver

Asking price: $1,699,900 (September 2026)

Selling price: $1,685,000 (September 2026)

Days on the market: Four

Buyer’s agent: Bronwyn Bertles, Engel & Volkers Vancouver

The seller was a local developer who does duplexes on the east side of the city, said the buyer’s agent Bronwyn Bertles. Her buyers are busy professionals who didn’t have time to take on a renovation, so they decided to look for one of the many new duplexes that are on the market, said Ms. Bertles.

“There are a lot of options. You are seeing half duplexes all the way to Dunbar, and all over. What drew them to this one was the quality, and also it was a bit more unique. This one didn’t have a back alley, so the orientation was different.”

The back unit of the duplex sold a month previously for $1.75-million.

This newly-built three-level, half duplex sits on a standard 33-foot lot on a designated bike street in the Fraser Street neighbourhood, within walking distance to fine dining, bakeries, cafés and shops.

The contemporary design includes three bedrooms and four bathrooms over nearly 1,500 square feet, blonde oak floors, a patio on the ground floor and balconies on the other two levels.

There’s a vaulted ceiling on the top floor and an attached garage. Other features include air conditioning, a heat pump and a fenced yard.

Ms. Bertles said she is careful to include the GST in writing when making an offer on a newly built home. She has heard of several recent legal disputes over the tax, and whether it is part of the final sale price.

“My tip to buyers is that it doesn’t matter if the list price says it includes or doesn’t include the GST; make sure it’s clearly stated in the agreement that it’s included. Everyone needs to be on the same page.”

The sale completed at the end of October.

stories.title: What happens when a city museum’s funding is stuck in the past?
stories.summary: Museum of Vancouver is languishing at a time when we should be preserving our cultural and historical institutions
stories.author: Marsha Lederman
stories.content:
A city museum is a beautiful thing. Taken for granted, it can become something else.

News this week that Toronto is finally getting a city museum (or two) brought to mind the plight of the Museum of Vancouver. In the fall, MOV hosted a series of “Austerity Tours” so the public could go behind the curtain and see for themselves what happens when funding does not keep up with needs or expectations. Cracks begin to show.

On a tour, MOV CEO Ryan Hunt showed us some of those often-literal cracks, beginning with a ceiling light installation in the lobby, which is shared with the H.R. MacMillan Space Centre. When the building opened in 1968 – a Centennial project – the whole ceiling lit up. Now, most of the bulbs are burned out, including the spotlight in the middle, because of oil dripping over the years from the planetarium’s projector, Mr. Hunt said. The ceiling, stripped back over decades, has become a shell of its older self, he added. “And that is such a great metaphor for what austerity does to cultural institutions.”

We passed empty planters, a plastic tube connected to a drip-catching tray, seasonally replaced with a bucket. We stepped into a public washroom, which Mr. Hunt described, accurately, as having the ambiance of a middle-school bathroom. “It leaves people, visitors to Vancouver, with the feeling ‘Vancouver maybe isn’t doing so well,’” he said.

The museum recorded more than 60,000 visitors in 2025. What impression were they left with?

He took us to the large walk-in freezer, a necessity for any museum. Dating back to 1968, it’s the oldest continually operating freezer in Vancouver, Mr. Hunt told us, making it difficult to fix. Further, the freezer was installed next to the pump that controls the outdoor pond; once or twice a year, the pump backs up, flooding the entire hallway.

There is still lead paint on the ceiling of the collections room. Last year, the museum had to decline the offer of an Arthur Erickson-designed furniture set; there’s no room to store it.

How does a city museum get to this sad point? The MOV operates independently but receives about a quarter of its annual funding from the city. That’s down from 65 per cent of its funding in 1993. “That leaves an ever-widening gap that we have to fill through entrepreneurialism, creativity, begging sometimes,” said Mr. Hunt.

The point of the tours was to get the public engaged in arts and culture funding during the municipal election period (which also became the provincial election period).

Provincially, in 1993 the museum received $200,000 from what is now the BC Arts Council. Its operating funding from the Bcac in 2026 is $198,000. This isn’t just stagnation. With inflation, it’s regression.

In 2025, the museum recorded a net loss of $611,480.

This past summer was Mov’s worst in 20 years (excluding 2020), which Mr. Hunt connects to the Fifa World Cup coming to town. He says attendance began dropping off when the games started, and picked back up again after they ended.

Meanwhile, he notes, the projected governments’ cost for the games in Vancouver could be as high as $729-million . Mr. Hunt has done the math. “If you took the current estimated investment from all three levels of government in bringing the World Cup to Vancouver – just Vancouver, not Toronto – and then compared that to the amount of annual funding the BC Arts Council provides to every operating assistance client that’s a museum, gallery or cultural centre, the BC Arts Council could have doubled the amount they currently give for the next 429 years,” he said.

Still, the museum does what it can with its programming and curation. This week, it opened a new exhibition, “Taking Care: Disability Activism and Possible Futures.” It also continues the important work of repatriating Indigenous objects and remains.

At a time when Canadian sovereignty is top of mind – see the federal budget – the institutions that preserve and show off our culture and history should also be top of mind.

This week, after reading about the Toronto museums, I checked in with the MOV to see if they had made any headway since my September tour. My e-mail to their publicist received an autoreply. “The MOV is undergoing layoffs and the Marketing Department is no longer in operation.”

Over the past three weeks, the MOV has laid off about a quarter of its staff, with the final layoff made on Tuesday. It’s largely due to the things noted in the tour, said Mr. Hunt. But given Ottawa’s focus on culture and Vancouver’s new city council, which is perceived to be more arts-friendly, he’s somehow hopeful.

“Is it horrible here? Yes. But I am much more optimistic in the direction that we’re headed.”

This week, after reading about the Toronto museums, I checked in with the MOV to see if they had made any headway since my September tour. My e-mail to their publicist received an autoreply. “The MOV is undergoing layoffs and the Marketing Department is no longer in operation.”

Over the past three weeks, the MOV has laid off about a quarter of its staff, with the final layoff made on Tuesday. It’s largely due to the things noted in the tour, said Mr. Hunt. But given Ottawa’s focus on culture and Vancouver’s new city council, which is perceived to be more arts-friendly, he’s somehow hopeful.
“Is it horrible here? Yes. But I am much more optimistic in the direction that we’re headed.”

stories.title: Historic guns locked away as RCMP centre set to become next national museum
stories.summary: At the RCMP Heritage Centre in Regina, which is set to become Canada's next national museum, one display case is glaringly empty.
stories.author: Jeremy Simes
stories.content:
At the RCMP Heritage Centre in Regina, which is set to become Canada’s next national museum, one display case is glaringly empty.

The large wood and glass cabinet is supposed to show “Weapons of the Plains,” but the only things inside are wall labels and empty hooks.

Vintage RCMP carbines and revolvers used over 140 years ago are no longer on display. And gone are the antique rifles used by Prairie settlers and Indigenous people.

All other displays have had guns removed too.

The centre, known for its vintage memorabilia and tales of true crime, says the weapons have been locked away.

The federal government announced earlier this month that it plans to designate the centre a national museum. Ottawa’s budget says the centre is to receive $3 million in annual funding for national designation.

Sam Karikas, the centre’s CEO, said the guns were removed a year ago to comply with provincial firearms regulations. The RCMP owns the weapons and provided them on loan.

“In order to have them on display, we would need to alter the firearms, which the RCMP doesn’t want to do,” Karikas said in an email.

“We’re currently working on solutions and are hoping to have printed replicas introduced early in the new year.”

One firearm removed from the museum is the rifle of Sam Steele, a prominent Mountie who helped bring law to the West in the 1870s.

Also gone is the RCMP’s centennial rifle, made in 1973 to mark the force’s 100th anniversary.

A 1920s machine gun, gas guns from the 1960s and a harpoon gun used in a former northern detachment were placed in storage. Even a pistol from a modern-day duty belt was taken out of the museum.

Still on display are some swords, batons, homemade weapons used in the Regina riot of 1935, and a bow and arrow from 1876. There’s also memorabilia from Métis leader Louis Riel, including his knife, crucifix, Bible and revolver holster.

RCMP said their historical collections unit removed the guns to be in compliance with a decision made by both the Saskatchewan Firearms Office and federal firearms legislation.

“The firearms in the collection are stored in an RCMP secured vault for storage,” Mounties said in an emailed statement.

In response to questions to the firearms office, a spokesperson from Premier Scott Moe’s office said Saskatchewan’s regulations align with Ottawa’s and don’t impose additional requirements.

“It is more likely that the RCMP Heritage Centre’s issue arises from requirements or standards established by the Museum Association of Saskatchewan, rather than from any provincial government body, provincial legislation or regulations,” the spokesperson said in an email.

Emma Morris, executive director of the museum association, said it doesn’t regulate firearms but provides recommendations.

Federal regulations state museums with guns on display must have a valid firearms business licence and all staff must have a valid possession and acquisition licence.

Regulations also require a gun on display to be secured by a metal bar and with a chain or metal cable that passes through the trigger guard. A firearm should also be rendered inoperable by a secure locking device.

Morris added that the regulations don’t say whether a firearm should be deactivated, which requires permanent alteration making it inoperable.

“We really don’t want somebody to steal a firearm and use it to hold up a gas station or a school and cause a very real threat in their community,” she said. “There is that liability risk.”

The association previously flagged a case where nine handguns were stolen from a Saskatchewan museum.

Morris said she has no details on when or where that theft happened, as it was before her time as executive director.

Other museums in the province currently display guns, including the Saskatoon Police Museum.

A spokesperson with the Saskatoon force said those firearms were rendered inoperable before being placed in locked cabinets.

Meanwhile, Karikas said she’s looking forward to the centre becoming a national museum. It would be the country’s 10th national museum and the second in Western Canada.

The federal funding would also help it enhance services, she said.

“We have a lot of room to grow in the stories that we’re telling, particularly around more of the complex nature of what happens at the time of colonialization,” Karikas said.

“We would not be at 160 years of Confederation were it not for the establishment of the North West Mounted Police. With that, of course, comes a whole lot of complexity and colonial stories of what that looks like.”

stories.title: Ontario Liberals to select third new leader since 2018
stories.summary: Ontario's Liberal Party will wrap up a long leadership race Saturday, and, they hope, an even longer stretch without a long-term leader.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario Liberals wrap up a long leadership race Saturday, and, they hope, an even longer stretch without a long-term leader, as the party gets set to name the person they have selected to shepherd them into the next election.

That general election May not come until 2030, which should provide a lot of time for the next leader of the third-place party to introduce themselves to Ontarians. The candidates are all relatively unknown, with polling suggesting the general public is not familiar with any of them.

There’s Lee Fairclough, currently in the Liberal caucus in the legislature and a former hospital executive; Navdeep Bains, a former federal cabinet minister and Rogers executive; Stephanie Bowman, a caucus member and former bank executive; and Dylan Marando, a former political staffer and strategist.

Voting concludes Friday under a ranked ballot system, and when the results are revealed Saturday at a downtown Toronto event, many expect it to come down to two people — though few are certain about who will prevail.

“I think ultimately it will come down to Lee and Nav,” said Blue Knox, a longtime Liberal strategist who is staying neutral in this contest.

“This is still a close race, and I don’t think there’s anybody in the party who is 100 per cent confident any one candidate is going to win, which is really exciting.”

Already, the next leader will start off on good footing, likely able to unite the party behind them, Knox suggested.

“The tone and tenor of this race has been much more amicable than the last leadership, which is very useful in several ways,” she said.

“After any leadership, looking back on them historically, no matter how contentious or non-contentious they were, at the end of the day, someone gets elected, and the Liberal team needs to come together, but that can be a lot tougher when the debate has been a little bit more tense.”

The 2023 leadership race that crowned Bonnie Crombie leader saw friction between her and runner-up Nate Erskine-Smith, who had signalled he wanted to run again this time but failed to win a local nomination race.

Crombie resigned after about two years in the top job, after a lukewarm show of support at an annual general meeting. The previous leader, Steven Del Duca, was also in the role for about two years, resigning after a disappointing showing in the 2022 provincial election.

Neither Crombie nor Del Duca had a seat in the legislature when they became leader, and neither managed to win one in an election.

The question of whether or not the next leader should have a seat has come up in this race, with the two current caucus members — Fairclough and Bowman — making the case that it matters a lot.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser, who is also remaining neutral in the race, said if the next leader doesn’t have a seat, they need to at least know how they will get there.

“You need to have a plan to get a seat,” Fraser said. “Doesn’t (mean) you have to have one right away, but you need to have a plan because the last two leaders didn’t really have a plan, and it didn’t work out so well.”

The most important jobs for the next Liberal leader are to travel the province and talk to Ontarians outside the legislature, Fraser said. It’s not enough to oppose Premier Doug Ford, the party has to develop policies that present a credible alternative, he said.

The party has been in relative political wilderness since 2018, when 15 years in power ended in the Liberals not just losing to Ford’s Progressive Conservatives, but losing official party status. They grew their ranks in the 2025 election to 14 members and regained that status, which affords them more resources and more speaking time in the legislature.

It’s a good start, but the path to becoming premier often takes more than one election cycle, Fraser cautioned. He worked for former premier Dalton McGuinty, who was elected premier seven years after winning the party leadership.

About 55,000 party members were eligible to vote, a number the party says is double their membership before the race. However, it still represents about half the size of the party membership before the previous leadership race in 2023.

content_blocks.text: Ontario Liberals wrap up a long leadership race Saturday, and, they hope, an even longer stretch without a long-term leader, as the party gets set to name the person they have selected to shepherd them into the next election.

That general election May not come until 2030, which should provide a lot of time for the next leader of the third-place party to introduce themselves to Ontarians. The candidates are all relatively unknown, with polling suggesting the general public is not familiar with any of them.

There’s Lee Fairclough, currently in the Liberal caucus in the legislature and a former hospital executive; Navdeep Bains, a former federal cabinet minister and Rogers executive; Stephanie Bowman, a caucus member and former bank executive; and Dylan Marando, a former political staffer and strategist.

Voting concludes Friday under a ranked ballot system, and when the results are revealed Saturday at a downtown Toronto event, many expect it to come down to two people — though few are certain about who will prevail.
“I think ultimately it will come down to Lee and Nav,” said Blue Knox, a longtime Liberal strategist who is staying neutral in this contest.
“This is still a close race, and I don’t think there’s anybody in the party who is 100 per cent confident any one candidate is going to win, which is really exciting.”
Already, the next leader will start off on good footing, likely able to unite the party behind them, Knox suggested.
“The tone and tenor of this race has been much more amicable than the last leadership, which is very useful in several ways,” she said.

“After any leadership, looking back on them historically, no matter how contentious or non-contentious they were, at the end of the day, someone gets elected, and the Liberal team needs to come together, but that can be a lot tougher when the debate has been a little bit more tense.”

The 2023 leadership race that crowned Bonnie Crombie leader saw friction between her and runner-up Nate Erskine-Smith, who had signalled he wanted to run again this time but failed to win a local nomination race.

Crombie resigned after about two years in the top job, after a lukewarm show of support at an annual general meeting. The previous leader, Steven Del Duca, was also in the role for about two years, resigning after a disappointing showing in the 2022 provincial election.
Neither Crombie nor Del Duca had a seat in the legislature when they became leader, and neither managed to win one in an election.
The question of whether or not the next leader should have a seat has come up in this race, with the two current caucus members — Fairclough and Bowman — making the case that it matters a lot.
Interim Liberal leader John Fraser, who is also remaining neutral in the race, said if the next leader doesn’t have a seat, they need to at least know how they will get there.

“You need to have a plan to get a seat,” Fraser said. “Doesn’t (mean) you have to have one right away, but you need to have a plan because the last two leaders didn’t really have a plan, and it didn’t work out so well.”

The most important jobs for the next Liberal leader are to travel the province and talk to Ontarians outside the legislature, Fraser said. It’s not enough to oppose Premier Doug Ford, the party has to develop policies that present a credible alternative, he said.

The party has been in relative political wilderness since 2018, when 15 years in power ended in the Liberals not just losing to Ford’s Progressive Conservatives, but losing official party status. stories.title: London man arrested hours after being placed on Canada's most wanted list
stories.summary: Ontario Provincial Police say they have arrested a man in a homicide investigation, only hours after he was placed at No. 14 on Canada's most wanted list of fugitives.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police say they have arrested a man in a homicide investigation, only hours after he was placed at No. 14 on Canada’s most wanted list of fugitives .

Officers say they arrested the 28-year-old man in Winnipeg on Thursday at 4:10 p.m., with help from the Winnipeg Police Service and the Manitoba RCMP, and are making arrangements for his return to Ontario.

stories.title: Dateline comes to Canada: Keith Morrison and Diana Swain on true crime and Primetime
stories.summary: As Dateline expands into Canada, its stars reflect on true crime’s appeal and the blurred line between journalism and entertainment
stories.author: J. Kelly Nestruck
stories.content:
No TV show has played a larger role in making true crime into a genuine pop-culture phenomenon as NBC’s Dateline .

But while two of the long-running investigative program’s most prominent correspondents are Canadian – Keith Morrison and Andrea Canning – the U.S. franchise is only getting an official Canadian spinoff this month.

Dateline Canada launches as a brand on Nov. 26 with a two-hour special on the 1990 disappearance of Elizabeth Bain (on Citytv and Citytv+, 8 p.m. ET/PT). It’s a pilot of sorts: If it performs well, Rogers Sports & Media may commission more.

To mark the extension of the brand, Morrison – a former CBC and CTV broadcaster who was once tipped to become Lloyd Robertson’s successor on the nightly news – has flown to Toronto from the U.S. to sit on the other side of an interview with The Globe and Mail in a Rogers studio.

It’s a titillating treat to hear the 79-year-old journalist and cultural icon from Lloydminster, Sask. – who once had a cameo on Seinfeld and was impersonated by Bill Hader on Saturday Night Live – talk about such banal matters as Toronto traffic and the shoelace-less sneakers he’s wearing.

He does so in the same soothing baritone that has tucked hundreds of millions of TV viewers into bed over the years with tales of grisly murder.

Morrison, however, shows some discomfort about the nickname he has earned through the show: The grandaddy of true crime.

“It’s awful,” he says of the moniker. Then, Morrison quickly softens his tone: “It’s not awful; I mean, it is what it is.”

Dateline Canada , which Morrison has no involvement with but only is in town to help promote, kicks off with a 36-year-old cold case that many Canadians will be familiar with.

Elizabeth Bain was a 22-year-old University of Toronto student when she disappeared in 1990; her car was recovered, her blood inside, near the Scarborough campus’s tennis courts, but her body has never been found.

Robert Baltovich, Bain’s boyfriend at the time, was wrongly convicted for her murder in 1992. His long ordeal to clear his name continued until 2008, when he was found not guilty on retrial.

The Bain case has never really been that far from the public eye – lurid interest in it only increased by the fact that serial killer Paul Bernardo was active as the “Scarborough Rapist” at time of her disappearance; his name often gets mentioned in connection to the case despite no evidence to connect him along with his own denial of any involvement.

Diana Swain, who had a 33-year career at CBC News leading investigative teams on shows such as The Investigators and The Fifth Estate, will be Dateline Canada ’s inaugural contributing correspondent on the Bain special, lending her own distinctive voice and respected on-screen presence to the story.

Arriving for a joint interview with Morrison a few minutes after him, Swain says the Dateline Canada team has not solved the Bain case – and did not set out expecting to do so. “What we do in a meaningful way is pull together all of the threads of this story that have existed over more than three decades,” she says. “But we will be adding more to what took place.”

Swain, who retired from the CBC in 2023, had just moved to a small mountain town in B.C. in April when she got a call from Rogers exploring her interest in getting back into the TV investigation business.

“Part of what persuaded me to continue the conversation was the fact that it’s Dateline ,” she says. “ Dateline has done what few programs have been able to do: you say the name of the show, and everyone knows what you’re talking about.”

While everyone does know Dateline , not everyone has purely positive feelings about it – or the true-crime genre it has come to exemplify, which to critics can seem a profit-oriented mix of journalism and entertainment built on sordid sensationalism.

When it was first launched in 1992, however, Dateline was just NBC’s latest attempt to create a newsmagazine to compete with CBS’s 60 Minutes or ABC’s 20/20.

Morrison joined its team of correspondents in 1995 – and recalls how the show slowly morphed toward crime. “I did everything from animal stories to medical stories to rescue stories to political stories,” he recalls. “But when we did crime, the audience immediately reacted to it.”

Even with the current explosion of true crime options on TV, not to mention in the podcast space, Dateline continues to dominate the genre. Its linear audience grew year-over-year last season to a total of 126.7 million total viewers in the U.S., according to industry website Deadline

On a recent day, the Dateline NBC podcast was the second most popular on Apple Podcasts and ninth most popular on Spotify in Canada. Citytv has simulcast new episodes of the Friday edition of Dateline since the fall of 2022 – and the proof that it does well for Rogers comes in the company’s licensing of the brand and production of this Dateline Canada special.

Claire Adams, director of Rogers Studios and an executive producer on Dateline Canada , says future specials – she doesn’t envisage a weekly series – will depend partly on the viewer response of this one, but also on whether there’s an ability to move stories forward.

While Dateline NBC mainly focuses on close-ended cases now, Adams wanted the Canadian expression of the show to advance a case.

But Dateline Canada arrives, too, at a moment when the franchise’s history of mashing up entertainment and investigation is under the microscope thanks to Lance Oppenheim’s film Primetime .

That big-screen drama revolves around the show’s old recurring sting segment targeting men seeking sexual encounters with teens online, which was hosted by Chris Hansen and evolved into the early 2000s reality show To Catch a Predator. The film has Oscar buzz around it, especially regarding Robert Pattinson’s dark and unhinged anti-hero portrayal of Hansen.

“Most of the people I work with have not seen it, which surprises me,” says Morrison, who has, indeed, gone to see it.

While reluctant to criticize a successful movie, Morrison says Pattinson’s portrayal of Hansen is not anything like the man he knew and worked with for many years. But he does not seem to necessarily disagree with the movie’s implied critique that the predator segments veered into vigilantism. “I would never have done one of those shows, and never did,” Morrison says.

“You know that was something they tried to do; at some point along the way, they recognized this was not something we should be doing, and they stopped.”

As for true crime in general, however, the genre’s reluctant granddaddy says that though he initially complained about having to veer into that territory to his Dateline bosses – he felt it was a bit “tabloid” – he’s come to believe in its capacity for storytelling. Crime stories allow him to practice in-depth reporting, branch out into issues connected to the justice system and explore human nature at its most fascinating.

True crime stories are not compelling for no reason – and Swain was pulled in to the Bain story by a sense of moral injustice. “I’ve said many times through this investigation: it’s not right that someone should just disappear, and we never get an answer to why,” she says. “Even though it has been 36 years, I think she deserves that.”

stories.title: Two young Ontario hockey players get 40 months behind bars for unwanted threesome
stories.summary: 'The sexual activity was, at times, rough and degrading,' said the judge
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
Two young hockey players who sexually assaulted a 17-year-old girl at the same time without her consent at a Brampton, Ont., party have each been sentenced to 40 months in prison.

The men, identified only by their initials in a decision from Ontario’s Superior Court of Justice, were both 18 at the time of the 2023 Halloween party at a Brampton home. The victim’s identity is also protected by a publication ban.

“This court is faced with the difficult task of sentencing two youthful offenders with otherwise excellent backgrounds to a period of imprisonment on account of their joint sexual violation of a young girl,” Justice J. Scott Cowan wrote in a recent decision

The court heard that, during the evening in question, the girl went to a bedroom with one of the men.

“Initially, she willingly engaged in consensual kissing with him,” said the decision. “When he sought to escalate the sexual activity, the complainant reluctantly acquiesced.”

The judge harboured “significant reservations as to the extent to which she was genuinely agreeable to the sexual activity that immediately followed.”

Oral and vaginal sex occurred, he said.

“However, I was not satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that any criminal offence arising from this initial encounter had been proven. The addition of vaginal intercourse was introduced by the complainant,” Cowan said in his Nov. 3 decision.

The man then telephoned his friend, stating: “it’s happening.”

The girl told police that when the second man showed up in the bedroom about three minutes later, one of the men said to his buddy, “I can’t believe this is happening” and then they did some sort of celebratory high five “dapping” each other.

The second man asked the girl to perform oral sex on him.

“She did so,” said the judge.

The psychological and emotional impact of the offence was apparent from her evidence

Notably, said the judge, around this time the second man asked the girl: “are you OK with this?”

While she didn’t give a verbal response, Cowan “was not satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the ensuing oral sex constituted a criminal assault.”

But “the criminal conduct crystallized shortly thereafter,” said the judge.

While the girl was performing oral sex on the second man, he told the first man on the scene to: “hit that from behind.”

The girl was never consulted about this proposed activity, Cowan said.

“I accepted her evidence that she did not want to participate in a threesome.

Notwithstanding her lack of consent, he immediately acted on the suggestion. At that point, the complainant was subjected to simultaneous oral and vaginal penetration by the two offenders.

“For several minutes, the offenders alternated positions and each penetrated her orally and vaginally without her consent,” said the judge.

“The sexual activity was, at times, rough and degrading. The complainant gagged and regurgitated to some extent during the encounter. This did not stop either offender from resuming the activity. She was digitally scratched inside her vagina and suffered a visible bruise to her face from aggressive oral sex.”

The encounter ended, said the judge, “when one of the offenders asked the complainant whether she could continue and she responded that she could not.”

After the threesome, while all three were “in various phases of undress, other partygoers entered the bedroom and directed gendered and sexualized insults toward the victim,” Cowan said. “The offenders did nothing to intervene.”

While their silence “was regrettable,” Cowan said he didn’t treat it as an aggravating factor.

“I do accept that this feature of the case made the experience for the victim extremely painful,” he said. “Victims unfortunately attach much self-blame in the hurt suffered, and this could only have exacerbated such shame.”

The girl promptly reported the joint sexual assault and sought medical attention, said the judge.

“The facial bruise she sustained was photographed. The psychological and emotional impact of the offence was apparent from her evidence.”

The girl told the court that “the impact of sexual assault is very overwhelming, chaotic and has become entangled into every aspect of my identity and life.”

She described “feelings of powerlessness, depression, difficulty showing affection and vulnerability, and worry that the hurt May never end.”

Neither man has a criminal record.

“Both enjoy support of their families, friends and potential work associates,” Cowan said.

Both men “are skilled hockey players,” said the judge, noting one of them “had designs on earning his living as an elite athlete. The offence and court process derailed those hopes.”

According to Cowan, “The rigours of high level sports and the discipline seen in both these men bodes well for their potential.”

The Crown argued both men should be sentenced to seven years in prison.

Defence lawyers sought “a sentence at the bottom of the penitentiary range, (which is two years in prison) citing their clients’ very young ages and otherwise good backgrounds.”

“I want to address the complainant directly at this point,” Cowan said. “I am sentencing these young men to a period of jail less than the Crown has asked for. This does not mean that I think you have suffered any less than (Crown Sydney Hopkins) has suggested. It does not mean that Ms. Hopkins has failed to persuade me that the effects of this offence on you are profound.”

Cowan stressed that “sentences imposed on youthful first offenders should emphasize rehabilitation and, where necessary, individual deterrence.”

The judge wished both men well in their future.

“To the complainant, thank you for putting your trust in the criminal justice system,” Cowan said.

The two men will be eligible for full parole after having served one-third of their sentence, and they will be eligible for day parole six months before then.

Chris Lambie is Atlantic bureau chief for National Post. He has worked for news organizations from Newfoundland to the Northwest Territories and is a three-time National Newspaper Award nominee, with a win for local reporting.

stories.title: Sunny, mild weather before rain moves in
stories.summary: Southwestern Ontario is in for a sunny and unusually mild Friday, with temperatures reaching 15 C before a wet and cooler start to next week, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Southwestern Ontario is in for a sunny and unusually mild Friday, with temperatures reaching 15 C before a wet and cooler start to next week, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Friday will bring a mix of sun and cloud, with light winds. Saturday is expected to be another beautiful day, with plenty of sunshine and a high of 15 C.

Cloud cover will increase Sunday afternoon and evening, bringing a 60 per cent chance of rain overnight.

Monday is expected to be a wet day, with rain in the forecast. Temperatures will drop below freezing Monday night, potentially bringing mixed precipitation.

A mix of sun and cloud is expected Tuesday and Wednesday, with the risk of lake-effect flurries early next week.
