stories.title: Forget power exports. Ontario and Quebec are running short of electricity
stories.summary: Premier Doug Ford’s promotion of a ‘sovereign energy system’ is wishful thinking
stories.author: Konrad Yakabuski
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford confessed to being “ stressed ” about delivering a few lines in French during a rare speech this week in Quebec.

Alas, despite massacring la langue de Molière before the Chamber of Commerce of Metropolitan Montreal, Mr. Ford got an enthusiastic ‘A’ for effort from the amused crowd of Quebec business leaders and politicians.

Amusement aside, the viral moment overshadowed the main message of Mr. Ford’s speech – that Canada’s two largest provinces should work together to create a “sovereign energy system” so that “we will never have to rely on anyone in the world except ourselves.”

If Mr. Ford is suddenly looking east it is in part because Ontario faces a growing electricity supply crunch. Unfortunately, Quebec has no power to spare.

Ontario’s Independent Electricity System Operator last month announced that it would import 600 megawatts (MW) of power this winter from U.S.-based Alpha Generation to ensure the province has sufficient supply to meet demand peaks.

For decades, though electricity moved smoothly across the Canada-U.S. border in both directions, Ontario and Quebec exported more power south during the summer than they ever imported north during the winter.

Not any more. Both Ontario and Quebec are running short of electricity. And neither is moving fast enough to fill what threatens to become a significant supply gap in the future. Until that changes, both provinces will rely increasingly on imported U.S. power.

That casts Mr. Ford’s threats of cutting off electricity exports amid the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war in an entirely different light. Any such move could come back to haunt Ontario if Washington responded in kind.

The Ieso stresses that Ontario is still a net exporter of electricity, selling seven times more power (measured in terawatt-hours) to neighbouring states and provinces in 2025 than it bought from them. But that is not the whole story. Ontario exports surplus power from its nuclear plants during off-peak nighttime hours, when prices are low. But it imports power to meet demand surges during the day, when spot prices soar.

Ontario’s looming daytime power shortage is not helped by the shutdown of the aged Pickering Nuclear Generating Station during a $26.8-billion refurbishment, and as units at the Darlington Nuclear Generating Station experience planned and unplanned outages that are adding billions of dollars to the $12.8-billion spent on their recent refurbishment.

Growing concerns about the reliability of Darlington’s newly refurbished reactors has raised questions about the Ford government’s decision to proceed with an even costlier refurbishment of the much older Pickering facility. But without Pickering’s 2,200 MW, Ontario would be facing an even larger supply crunch by the mid-2030s.

Ontario Power Generation’s Nov. 10 announcement of undetermined delays and cost overruns on the construction of the first of four small modular reactors (SMRs) at Darlington casts a cloud over that project, initially budgeted at $21-billion. Instead of the “first-mover advantage” Ontario hoped to gain by pioneering SMRs in North America, OPG now risks making potentially costly stumbles on an untested technology.

That is the main reason Hydro-Québec has taken a pass on building SMRs despite facing a supply crunch of its own. The Quebec government-owned utility projects it needs to add 12,000 MW of new capacity by 2041. But that timeline will be hard to meet as the recently elected Parti Québécois government seeks to “rework” a deal with Newfoundland and Labrador to jointly develop a new hydroelectric generating station at Gull Island.

Unfortunately, Hydro-Québec has no time to waste. Already, it has become a net importer of electricity, as low water levels in its reservoirs caused by four consecutive years of below-normal precipitation forces it to curtail exports. In fact, the utility spent $3.6-billion on power imports during the first nine months of 2026, while exporting $1.8-billion worth of electricity.

A large portion of those exports stemmed from two long-term contracts with customers in New England and New York that took effect this year, but which were negotiated several years ago when Hydro-Québec was sitting on huge power surpluses. The fixed-price contracts, which bring in far less revenue than spot-market sales, were a big mistake.

Hydro-Québec’s move to suspend power deliveries to New England during cold spells last winter has landed it in court, with its U.S. customers alleging breach of contract. But the Quebec utility has not ruled out similar action in the future.

“If Hydro-Québec were a car, it would be driving down a rocky road without a spare and the fuel tank nearly empty,” U.S. energy analyst Robert McCullough wrote in a recent report.

All that makes Mr. Ford’s call for a “sovereign energy system” sound like wishful thinking, in both official languages.

stories.title: Ontario Liberal Party to name new leader Saturday, the third since Doug Ford took office
stories.summary: Lee Fairclough could beat Navdeep Bains to take the helm of the third-place party
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
The Ontario Liberal Party will name its new leader – once again – on Saturday, as it looks to rebuild after three consecutive election losses with the goal of presenting a serious alternative to Premier Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives in the next election.

The best-known candidate in the race is former federal cabinet minister Navdeep Bains, who is facing a stiff challenge from first-term MPP Lee Fairclough, who represents Etobicoke-Lakeshore in west-end Toronto – not far from Mr. Ford’s home turf.

If Ms. Fairclough, a former hospital executive and national women’s rugby player, wins the leadership, it would be a significant upset for Mr. Bains. Once the federal industry minister in former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government, Mr. Bains left his high-profile position at Rogers Communications earlier this spring to return to politics.

The other contenders are Stephanie Bowman, a former finance executive and two-term MPP from Toronto, and Dylan Marando, a former senior adviser in federal and provincial Liberal governments.

The Ontario Liberals, currently in third place in the legislature, have struggled to regain prominence since losing government to Mr. Ford’s PCs in 2018. The new leader will be the party’s third since 2020. Interim Leader John Fraser has held the temporary job three times.

But there are signs of a resurgence for the former ruling party, which has seen its popularity rise in polls this year as Mr. Ford struggled with controversies such as the purchase and hasty resale of a $28.9-million private government jet. The government is also under pressure this fall as it grapples with the fallout from alleged abuse of the Ontario Student Assistance Program by private career colleges.

The debate over whether the new Liberal leader should have a seat in the legislature has also dominated the discussion, with Ms. Fairclough and Ms. Bowman, the only contenders currently in the legislature, arguing it is necessary to take on Mr. Ford immediately.

Previous Liberal leaders Steven Del Duca and Bonnie Crombie resigned their posts after the party lost the 2022 and 2025 provincial elections. Neither held a seat when they were named leader.

Liberal strategist Marcel Wieder, who has served as an adviser to Ms. Crombie, said this year’s leadership race comes at a critical time for the party.

“The government has a shelf life. And the Ford government has basically reached that shelf life,” said Mr. Wieder, president and chief advocate at public affairs firm Aurora Strategy Global, who is neutral in the Liberal leadership race.

“The Liberals have a very good shot at being the alternative to the Ford government, but they need a leader who’s going to be able to step up and demonstrate that. And that’s the challenge right now.”

Ms. Fairclough, who has visited all 124 ridings, has built momentum throughout the race, gaining volunteers and donors as well as high-profile endorsements, including from former premier Kathleen Wynne. Ms. Fairclough has pitched herself as the antidote to Mr. Ford: a serious leader, with substantive policy around health care and affordability.

But others in Mr. Bains’ orbit believe his higher profile and experience as a long-time political organizer in the Greater Toronto Area will benefit him in a race where a candidate’s ability to get out the vote will be crucial to electoral success.

Mr. Bains’ camp estimates that he has signed up about 80 per cent of the new members enrolled during the leadership race, who total less than half of the party’s 55,000 eligible voters.

Mr. Bains is also the top fundraiser, taking in about $900,000 during the course of the race, compared with Ms. Fairclough at $700,000, Ms. Bowman at nearly $600,000, and Mr. Marando at more than $200,000, according to the campaigns’ latest numbers.

The Ontario Liberals are using a new two-step voting system, mirroring that of the federal party, although the provincial party says it has made improvements since Mark Carney won the federal leadership in March 2025. The Liberal Party of Canada instituted a rigorous process during that race to stave off concerns about foreign interference , which led to a 38 per cent turnout and some reports from registered Liberals of difficulty verifying their identities.

In the provincial contest, the party is using the same Canada Post Identity+ phone app to verify members identities. Earlier this week, the party experienced a glitch with its in-person verification system that it said affected less than 20 per cent of members – but it said the problem was remedied in time to allow members to cast ballots.

Liberals vote using a ranked-ballot system, with all ridings weighted equally by points. If a contender does not get more than 50 per cent support on the first ballot, voters’ second or even third choices are distributed until a winner is named.

Liberal strategist Dan Moulton, a partner at public-affairs agency Crestview Strategy who donated to Mr. Bains’ campaign, said he believes the former federal minister has the most sophisticated organization of any candidate.

“Turning out new members and getting them to vote is what wins a leadership race like this,” said Mr. Moulton, who doesn’t have a formal role on the campaign.

All four candidates spent the past week reaching out to voters to ensure they mark their ballots.

Mr. Bains said he’s feeling positive heading into Saturday’s leadership announcement event, making upwards of 200 calls a day.

“The goal is always to win on the first ballot. I mean that’s how we started the campaign with that mindset, and that remains our focus,” he said in an interview.

Regardless of the outcome, he said he’s committed to running in the next provincial election.

For Ms. Fairclough, the focus has been on meeting as many supporters as possible and pushing her vision for a more serious government.

“I have asked to be first on the ballot, and if I am not first on your ballot, I would like to be second as well,” she said. “I do feel strong support.”

Ms. Bowman has told her supporters to vote with their hearts, but believes the next leader having a seat is crucial. “Being a third place party for the last eight years, and having tried a leader without a seat twice – you know, it is important for us to not make that mistake again.”

At 39, Mr. Marando has focused on generational change, and said his policy ideas have been cited by other candidates. “I’m in, potentially, the deluded stage of the campaign, because I’m convinced I’m going to win,” he said.

As for Mr. Ford, he told reporters this week he doesn’t have a preferred pick.

“All of them would be a disaster for this province.”

stories.title: How to make friends and beat loneliness, according to Star readers
stories.summary: We asked readers to share their best hacks to tackle loneliness. Here's what you said
stories.author: Paige Oldfield
stories.content:
Toronto residents are still struggling to make and keep close friends and build strong family ties — three years after the city was named the loneliest in Canada. That’s according to the Vital Signs 2026 report, which is based on responses from 3,377 people between March and May.

It also revealed that Torontonians are close to fewer people than they were eight years ago. The study says our closest circles shrank sharply by 2022 and have not grown back, with our wider circles of friends and acquaintances continuing to shrink.

And though some regions in Canada have adopted permanent daylight saving time, most of Ontario turned back the clocks earlier this month — starting up brighter mornings but shorter, colder days and less sunlight.

So when we asked readers to share their best hacks to tackle loneliness — whether it be an activity or a group — the comment section did not disappoint. Here’s what you said:

“The dog, he was passed on to us and is a huge joy. We now know our neighbours, walk together, chat, gossip and visit for coffee. One neighbour works in the far north, as soon as she’s back home sends a text to ask when will we have coffee or go to the local art gallery. We love to share lunch dates too. Our adorable old English is a professional therapy pup, my husband takes him to the local care home to bring joy to people who can’t have pets. Dogs are the best of us.” — Linda

“My husband and I joined a pickleball group 12 years ago and still play at 75 and 77. It keeps us active and we have formed a whole new friend group. Everyone plays with a constant smile on their face. It is our happy place.” — Judy

“Just get out and do stuff. When I retired, I started swimming every day (in Toronto, it’s free!). My only goal was to get moving for an hour every day, but I made a lot of friends just talking to people in the change rooms and the pool.” - Lerryn

“I joined an exercise class. I go a few times a week. It is a healthy activity, not expensive, and exchanging pleasantries with people you see regularly just naturally led to conversations and friendships.” - Jill

“Join a smaller club such as a hiking group to do what you already like with similar minded people. Or pick up a new hobby such as pickleball, knitting, language class to learn a new skill and meet people. Since retiring my friends group has increased significantly.” — Bernadette

“I joined a local Probus Canada Club to meet and interact with people. Probus clubs are for retired and near retired persons. They hold monthly meetings with various speakers, organize events including lunches, plays and day trips, and have sub-clubs of special interests such as book clubs, euchre playing, adult colouring clubs. Each club is autonomous and charges a yearly membership fee, many are below $100/yr.” — Renate

“My kids are grown and my husband passed away. I fill my social calendar with activities I enjoy. I’ve recently joined My Pop Choir. I enjoy singing even though it’s not a particular skill. This choir is my social and creative outlet.” — Sherry

“One solution to loneliness: join a choir. My non-audition community choir welcomes anyone who wants to sing. Over the years it has become a true community.” — Chris

“My friends started a Dungeons & Dragons campaign during COVID lockdown. Six years on, we still meet on Discord video chat, every Sunday afternoon. No travel time, no bar bill, come as you are. Our Dungeon Master, who is a graphic designer, has built a massive library of tabletop scenery, figures and props, most of it from dollar store toy sections. We’ve had a lot fun, laughs and simulated danger. It’s the highlight of everyone’s week.” — James

“Hobbies! I discovered social/folk dancing 15+ years ago, and most of my local-ish friends are in that community. I’m also part of a tight-knit online community that started during a larger writing challenge 21 years ago.” — Siri

“Volunteer! Great way to meet people and help others. Just Google ‘Volunteer opportunity near me.’” - Joanne

“Churches have groups for all ages and they do things outside of the church. I have played on a baseball team, gone to a Muskoka resort, volunteered to take children to the zoo. It is more than just a Sunday service, we are people that care about each other.” - Irene

What helps you whenever you feel alone? What activities or plans or routines do you use to fight loneliness? Let us know in the comments section below.

These comments have been edited for clarity and length .

stories.title: B.C. driver caught with open laptop on lap. Really? It’s time to increase these featherweight fines
stories.summary: Across Canada, distracted driving carries a fine of around $200 to almost $700, but imagine if the fine was $10,000
stories.author: Andrew Clark
stories.content:
When cellphones arrived in the 1990s, back in the age of baggy double-breasted suits and grunge rock, early adopters used them while driving. It seemed like that was the reason they existed, so you could “maximize” your time and make calls from your mobile office. They were rare and many drivers got a kick out of calling friends and asking, “Where do you think I’m calling from?” This attitude held steady when they went mainstream in the 2000s.

No one really worried about the dangers of distracted driving.

What’s our excuse now? No sentient being in this world (or worlds as yet unknown) thinks it’s okay to drive while distracted by an electronic device. The statistics leave no room for debate. In 2021, according to data from Transport Canada’s National Collision Database , distracted driving played a role in an estimated 22.5 per cent of fatal collisions and 25.5 per cent of serious injury collisions in 2021, an increase from 21.3 per cent of fatal collisions and 23.8 per cent of serious injury collisions in 2011. The Ontario Provincial Police reported that 82 deaths were caused by distracted driving in 2024, an increase of 43 per cent from 2023. A study sponsored by the Canadian Automobile Association found that while 94 per cent of drivers are worried about distracted driving, 54 per cent admit to doing it.

And yet, week after week we get reports of drivers being ticketed for the most egregious forms of distracted driving. Sometimes the transgressions go beyond the mere use of a smartphone. A driver in Ottawa was recently found asleep while driving a Tesla in rush hour traffic. It’s illegal and dangerous but you can at least see the possibility of some extenuating circumstances. The driver May have intended to remain awake while the Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” system was engaged but drifted off.

And then there is the case of the woman in West Kelowna, B.C., who was recently fined for driving with an open laptop on her lap. She was travelling along Highway 97 near Vernon. The Kelowna Laptop Wrangler was caught during a 2.5-hour blitz that “resulted in a total of 25 cell phone tickets and 10 tickets for seatbelt violations.”

“Driving is a complex task that requires your complete attention to deal with the unexpected,” Sergeant Michael McLaughlin with B.C. Highway Patrol said in a statement . He also said, in a masterwork of understatement, “Just because you’re comfortable behind the wheel, and you have something you ‘need’ to do, doesn’t mean the rules of the road don’t apply to you.”

What possible reason can there be to use your laptop while driving?

How can someone think that operating a laptop – perhaps watching a TV show or getting ahead on some admin work that needs doing – while driving a vehicle that weighs a couple metric tonnes and can go 180 kilometres an hour would be safe?

You can almost hear her engaging with the police officer who gave her the ticket.

“Was that wrong?” she May have said, echoing the words of George Costanza , when he was accused of making love to an office cleaner atop his work desk. “Should I not have done that?”

We don’t know the specifics of the Kelowna Laptop Wrangler. All we know is that a ticket was issued for “allegedly driving while using her laptop” and the B.C. Highway Patrol have photographs of the laptop perched on lap.

My concern is the lightweight nature of the fine. The Laptop Wrangler was fined $368 for the use of an electronic device while driving, contrary to section 214.2(1) of the BC Motor Vehicle Act.

Let’s imagine she’s guilty. You should suffer more than a $368 fine for knowingly putting people’s lives at risk. In British Columbia, a driver gets fined around $200 for having illegible plates and $261 for driving without a valid license. These are both bad but driving with a laptop is far more dangerous.

It is willful negligence.

There is no possible explanation other than, “I knew it was wrong and I didn’t care.” Maybe, if a person is suffering from a mental health issue that severs them from reality, that could explain it. Otherwise, it’s as premeditated as premeditated gets.

Think of the work involved. Let’s break it into hypothetical steps.

Get in vehicle and bring laptop

Turn on car

Adjust seat to allow room for laptop

Open and turn on laptop

Begin driving

Use laptop while driving

Think: “This is a good idea and completely acceptable driving behaviour”

Keep doing it

Get pulled over

Be surprised

Get $368 fine

The penalties for dangerous driving are a joke. Stunt driving penalties, for instance, are said to be among the most stringent. In Ontario, a driver can face $2,000 to $10,000 upon conviction and up to six months imprisonment. The only reason that seems high is that the rest of the penalties are featherweight.

B.C. is on the low end, but across Canada, distracted driving carries a fine of around $200 to almost $700 with Manitoba being the highest. Imagine if the fine for a first offence was $10,000. Even if the chances of being caught were low, a lot more drivers would think twice about picking up their phone or, for some, their laptop.

Higher fines and penalties won’t eliminate these unfortunate infractions but at least they’ll show that we, as a society, are serious about stopping them.

Otherwise, somewhere out on our streets and highways someone is turning on the ignition and firing up their laptop.

Let’s imagine she’s guilty. You should suffer more than a $368 fine for knowingly putting people’s lives at risk. In British Columbia, a driver gets fined around $200 for having illegible plates and $261 for driving without a valid license. These are both bad but driving with a laptop is far more dangerous.
It is willful negligence.

There is no possible explanation other than, “I knew it was wrong and I didn’t care.” Maybe, if a person is suffering from a mental health issue that severs them from reality, that could explain it. Otherwise, it’s as premeditated as premeditated gets.
Think of the work involved. Let’s break it into hypothetical steps.
Get in vehicle and bring laptop
Turn on car
Adjust seat to allow room for laptop
Open and turn on laptop
Begin driving
Use laptop while driving
Think: “This is a good idea and completely acceptable driving behaviour”
Keep doing it
Get pulled over
Be surprised
Get $368 fine

The penalties for dangerous driving are a joke. Stunt driving penalties, for instance, are said to be among the most stringent. In Ontario, a driver can face $2,000 to $10,000 upon conviction and up to six months imprisonment. The only reason that seems high is that the rest of the penalties are featherweight.

B.C. is on the low end, but across Canada, distracted driving carries a fine of around $200 to almost $700 with Manitoba being the highest. Imagine if the fine for a first offence was $10,000. Even if the chances of being caught were low, a lot more drivers would think twice about picking up their phone or, for some, their laptop.
Higher fines and penalties won’t eliminate these unfortunate infractions but at least they’ll show that we, as a society, are serious about stopping them.
Otherwise, somewhere out on our streets and highways someone is turning on the ignition and firing up their laptop.

content_blocks.text: When cellphones arrived in the 1990s, back in the age of baggy double-breasted suits and grunge rock, early adopters used them while driving. It seemed like that was the reason they existed, so you could “maximize” your time and make calls from your mobile office. They were rare and many drivers got a kick out of calling friends and asking, “Where do you think I’m calling from?” This attitude held steady when they went mainstream in the 2000s.

content_blocks.text: What’s our excuse now? No sentient being in this world (or worlds as yet unknown) thinks it’s okay to drive while distracted by an electronic device. The statistics leave no room for debate. In 2021, according to data from Transport Canada’s National Collision Database , distracted driving played a role in an estimated 22.5 per cent of fatal collisions and 25.5 per cent of serious injury collisions in 2021, an increase from 21.3 per cent of fatal collisions and 23.8 per cent of serious injury collisions in 2011. The Ontario Provincial Police reported that 82 deaths were caused by distracted driving in 2024, an increase of 43 per cent from 2023. A study sponsored by the Canadian Automobile Association found that while 94 per cent of drivers are worried about distracted driving, 54 per cent admit to doing it.

stories.title: Why this money manager is buying quant and dividend growth funds
stories.summary: Linda Shick at Raymond James is also looking for ‘rock solid’ fixed-income exposure
stories.author: Brenda Bouw
stories.content:
Although some money managers are turning to private markets to diversify their clients’ portfolios, Linda Shick is avoiding asset classes she believes are overly complex.

“Simple works better, particularly when you’re managing a discretionary book,” says Ms. Shick, senior portfolio manager and senior wealth advisor with Family Wealth Counsel Advisory Group at Raymond James Ltd. in Toronto.

“While we continue to evaluate many types of private investments offered through various funds and platforms, we have yet to invest in any type of direct private alternative asset fund because of liquidity constraints and possible gating of investments,” says Ms. Shick, who manages more than $310-million in assets for discretionary and non-discretionary clients with her business partner, David Angas.

Instead, Ms. Shick invests in a mix of publicly traded stocks, bonds, mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), some of which provide exposure to private investments, such as Brookfield Corp. BN-T .

Her balanced portfolio, which is about 70 per cent equities, 27 per cent fixed income and 3 per cent cash, has seen a return of 12 per cent over the past 12 months. Its three- and five-year annualized returns are 16 per cent and 7 per cent, respectively. The performance is based on total returns, net of fees, as of Oct. 30.

The Globe spoke with Ms. Shick recently about what she’s been buying and selling:

What have you been buying recently?

Mackenzie GQE Global Equity Fund ( MFC099 ), a quantitative global equity mutual fund benchmarked against the Msci World Index, is a fund we started buying in May.

We like that it’s actively managed, given how volatile markets are these days. It’s a factor-based fund, which rebalances twice daily. It factors in fundamentals such as quality, momentum and value. It has a manager overlay rather than being computer-driven. [The fund has outperformed the Msci World Index over the past year; it’s up 16 per cent versus 11.7 per cent for the benchmark, as of Oct. 30.]

RBC Target 2030 Canadian Corporate Bond Index ETF ( RQS-T ) is a fixed-income ETF that we started buying in early October. [It tracks the Ftse Canada 2030 Maturity Corporate Bond Index]. One of our other bond funds came due and we wanted to continue our strategy of laddering bonds to take advantage of different rates and secure the portfolio.

We like these ETFs because, in a discretionary book, it’s hard to trade individual bonds as money’s coming in and out of client portfolios all the time.

This type of ETF includes a diversification of high-quality bonds that all come due in a given year, which is 2030 in this case. And, unlike a bond fund that doesn’t have a maturity date and can be quite negative – which is what’s happening now with rates going up a little bit – we want our bond part of the portfolio to be safer.

These securities will trade with the markets, but if you hold them to maturity, you’re basically getting the yield you bought it at. We want our fixed income to be rock solid and take our risk on the equity side.

CI Canada Quality Dividend Growth Index ETF ( Dgrc-T ), is an ETF we’ve held for about 18 months and added to most recently in April. [It tracks the WisdomTree Canada Quality Dividend Growth Index].

When we first bought it, it was for its exposure to the oil and gas sector. It recently added more bank exposure. We own dividend stocks, but this is a higher-quality Canadian dividend-grower stock ETF. It doesn’t necessarily have high-yield stocks, but more securities that are growing their dividends, which means they’re more cash-accretive.

Name a security you sold recently.

We trimmed about a third of our holdings in Capital Group Global Equity Fund ( CIF823.CF ) in May. We’ve held it for several years and still hold it, but wanted to reduce our exposure, especially after huge gains in sectors such as technology. It was the largest position, by asset allocation, in the global part of our portfolio. We wanted to add a quant fund, so we bought Mackenzie GQE Global Equity Fund.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

stories.title: British Columbia's premier-designate Lorne Doerkson, cabinet to be sworn in today
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia's first Conservative government in almost a century will take the reins of power when Lorne Doerkson becomes premier and unveils his first cabinet.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - British Columbia has a new Conservative government after almost a century, along with a premier and a novice cabinet that now needs to fulfil a long list of promises made by Lorne Doerkson during the election campaign.

From reviving the economy to solving health-care struggles and changing its working relationship with First Nations, Doerkson said he is committed to leading a unified government to carry out those promises.

“I know the task before us is gargantuan, but we are absolutely committed,” Doerkson said during a news conference after the premier and cabinet were sworn in on Friday.

He told his new cabinet and others at Government House in Victoria after the oaths of office were administered that government has “a responsibility to the people of British Columbia and a desire to leave this province better than we found it. We should never lose sight of that common purpose.”

Some of the high-profile ministers given portfolios include Claire Rattée, who becomes the minister of social development and the deputy premier.

Doerkson said he chose Rattée as his deputy because she is an inspiring woman.

“She’s an amazing human being, and she has certainly lived a full life,” Doerkson said.

Rattée experienced homelessness and addiction before undergoing treatment and entering public life.

She received a standing ovation during the swearing-in ceremony when her name was called Friday, which she said was moving and humbling.

“I have tried really hard over the last few years to do my job well and represent my constituents, and I appreciate the recognition of it,” she said.

“But I certainly wouldn’t be here today without the premier and I’m very grateful for his friendship.”

Peter Milobar was appointed to finance, Caroline Elliott becomes attorney general, Ryan Peterson is the health minister and Ian Paton assumes the Agriculture Ministry.

Milobar, Rattée and Paton are incumbent members of the legislature and had critic portfolios, but Elliott and Peterson are newly elected.

Conservatives have promised an independent review of the provincial books and Milobar said Friday that additional details will come next week.

“It’s meant to be an independent, full-encompassing review of where exactly we are fiscally in the province, so we have a good understanding of … the mess we need to clean up,” he said.

The most current figures forecast a deficit of almost $14 billion under the former NDP government.

Elliott, the new attorney general, came in second behind Kerry-Lynne Findlay in the party’s leadership race in May, but Findlay then resigned amid a fractured caucus a few days before the snap election was called. Elliott has a PhD in political science and taught at Simon Fraser University.

She will have responsibility over several major court cases involving the provincial government, including the Cowichan Tribes land decision, and the lawsuit against OpenAI over the Tumbler Ridge shooting.

Doerkson said his government will be focused on learning how it can better respond to situations related to artificial intelligence, adding that he recently spoke to Tumbler Ridge Mayor Darryl Krakowka and that the community is still hurting a great deal after eight people were killed in February.

Doerkson said he chose Peterson to handle the Health Ministry because it needs somebody with a business background.

Peterson co-founded Finger Food Studios, a technology company that was named B.C. Exporter of the Year in 2017.

“This is a massive ministry with $40 billion of expense, and I’m convinced that Ryan’s the fellow for the job,” Doerkson said. “He has got quite a large business history, and he’s very well liked throughout the Lower Mainland, and he’s got great connections throughout the province.”

Doerkson’s cabinet is smaller than the former NDP government’s at 18 ministries, but there are also six ministers of state, covering issues such as labour, infrastructure and red-tape reduction.

The premier also appointed a dozen parliamentary secretaries to oversee issues such as seniors, sport and culture, tourism and TransLink.

Doerkson said his new cabinet will focus on making B.C. more affordable through reducing costs and tax relief, restoring investor confidence, protecting universal health care, making the province safer by strengthening policing and the justice system, while also protecting freedoms and B.C.‘s environment and advancing reconciliation with First Nations.

He said he does not take being sworn in as the province’s 38th premier lightly.

“I know that the trust that’s been placed in myself and certainly all of our members is incredible and I’m absolutely committed to it and we are going to work very, very hard to obviously keep the promises that I’ve made and the promises that our platform has made as well.”

His first order of business is a cabinet meeting next week.

Key items on the agenda include the future of sexual orientation and gender identity programming in schools, which the government plans to repeal.

“Of course, our economy will be discussed in many ways,” he said.

While government won’t hold a fall session, tools other than legislation are available.

“Of course, we are working right now on orders-in-council that we May be able to navigate at that meeting,” he said.

Doerkson took over the leadership job just days before the election was called in September and pulled the fractured party and its members back together, leading it on the path to election victory.

Friday’s ceremony in Victoria came just under two months after former New Democrat premier David Eby called the snap election that diminished his party to 27 seats.

The Conservatives gained government with a confirmed 63 seats and two judicial recounts are underway.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Who are the four candidates vying to lead the Ontario Liberals?
stories.summary: Toronto - Members of the Ontario Liberal party will learn Saturday who their next leader will be, after months of campaigning and weeks of voting. They have four contenders to choose from on their ranked ballots. Here are some facts about Lee Fairclough, Navdeep Bains, Stephanie Bowman and Dylan Marando.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Members of the Ontario Liberal party will learn Saturday who their next leader will be, after months of campaigning and weeks of voting. They have four contenders to choose from on their ranked ballots. Here are some facts about Lee Fairclough, Navdeep Bains, Stephanie Bowman and Dylan Marando.

Lee Fairclough

Political experience: Beat a Progressive Conservative incumbent in the 2025 election to win a seat in the Ontario legislature representing Etobicoke-Lakeshore.

Career experience: Began her career as a radiation therapist at Princess Margaret hospital before moving into health-care management, ultimately serving as president of St. Mary’s General Hospital.

Personal: Represented Team Canada on the national women’s rugby team, and is the mom of two teenage boys.

Quote: “I think that this race is about bringing the change for Ontario that people are looking for, and that means serious government, and it means rebuilding our party from the grassroots up, so that we can be ready to take on the Conservatives and unify and direct all our energy at doing just that.”

Navdeep Bains

Political experience: Represented Mississauga ridings as a Liberal MP for 13 years, and served as federal minister of innovation, science and industry.

Career experience: Before entering politics he was a senior financial analyst at Ford Motor Company, and after leaving Parliament in 2021, he worked as an executive at CIBC and later at Rogers Communications.

Personal: Father to two daughters.

Quote: “The biggest misconception is that people believe I’m a front-runner. I’ve learned a long time ago not to take anything for granted and work hard.”

Stephanie Bowman

Political experience: Elected to the Ontario legislature in 2022 in Don Valley West.

Career experience: Accountant who had a long finance career before politics, including as a vice-president at CIBC and Scotiabank, and a board member of the Bank of Canada.

Personal: Mom of two.

Quote: “It’s all about the economy. People are worried. They’re facing a cost-of-living crisis, a housing-affordability crisis, and we need to build a strong economy with heart so we can pay for the public services we all rely on.”

Dylan Marando

Political experience: Worked as a senior adviser to former premier Dalton McGuinty and later worked as a policy adviser to former prime minister Justin Trudeau.

Career experience: Worked in strategy and government affairs since leaving the Prime Minister’s Office in 2023.

Personal: The youngest in the race at 38 years old.

Quote: “Our job is not to oppose. Our job is to propose. We need to become an alternative to this government. We need to show that we are ready to govern, that we have a team that knows how to govern.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

stories.title: London drivers get ready to put winter tires on cars, but say it isn’t always a smooth ride
stories.summary: As November pushes closer to December and the temperature continues to drop, many London drivers are either ge...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
As November pushes closer to December and the temperature continues to drop, many London drivers are either getting ready to or already have put winter tires on their vehicles. In some cases though, the choice of whether or not to put them on can cause problems with either decision.

Around Fanshawe college, many people who have their own cars have been faced with that decision already. Business marketing professor Rayna Elabed said that even though her brother isn’t a mechanic, she hasn’t put winter tires on her vehicle yet.

“I probably should book an appointment, but there’s no snow yet,” Elabed said.

Elabed wasn’t the only one who hadn’t installed winter tires yet, though some others had different reasons than her. Project management and business analysis professor Nessen Ramsamy said he was not going to install winter tires on his car, citing his car’s four-wheel-drive capability and his current all-season tires as to why. Pre-media student Jay O’Donnell was also confident in his all-season tires.

“As long as they don’t blow up, I think I’ll be good,” O’Donnell said.

There were many other staff and students who had already gotten winter tires on already. First-year general arts & sciences student Emelyn Fletcher said her father and cousin had put them on her vehicle.

“The hardest part was probably just carrying them,” Fletcher said.

For others, there were more difficulties when it came to putting on winter tires. Ramsamy said that with a previous car he’d had, he’d often found that tire and auto shops would overbook appointments. Elabed said that the need for maintenance such as an alignment on winter tires as well as the price of a set factored into her decision.

“It’s almost a luxury to be able to have two sets of tires,” she said.

O’Donnell also said he believed “the whole thing sounds … like a handful.”

Even so, nearly every person interviewed said they feel it’s important for people to put winter tires on vehicles. Elabed said she does so for insurance purposes, a reason echoed by acrylic art professor Elizabeth Bishop. Most others, meanwhile cited safety as a main reason.

“I live in the country, so sliding off of dirt roads into ditches is very popular,” said 9-1-1 and public safeties student Renee Grahamgoggin. “I kinda like to have a safer option so I don’t end up in a ditch.”

Most of the beliefs and concerns that Fanshawe staff and students had were things that Hanford’s Tire and Service owner Jeremy Hanford is familiar with. At his business, he said that he and his employees install 40 sets of winter tires per day, even after the warm weather in October having slowed business somewhat.

Hanford also said that if it were to start snowing in the near future, “our calls spike, our email requests spike massively,” for people wanting to put on winter tires.

Even with the weather, Hanford said that Londoners should take into account how much they themselves drive and when the temperature starts dropping significantly at night.

“Once that happens, then you’re usually pretty good to put your snow tires on,” he said.

Tire logos on the storefront of Hanford’s Tire and Auto in London. Many of these brands offer rebates for people buying a set of winter tires. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

Hanford also addressed the issue raised by some Fanshawe staff and students of the price of winter tires. He said that problems with booking appointments are usually solved by their customers planning ahead. He also added that even though the price of tires has increased in recent years, some larger tire brands such as Firestone will offer rebates of between $50 and $150 on sets of winter tires.

“We’ve also found that people are going with all-weather tires,” Hanford said. “And that still gives you your insurance discount because they have the mountain and snowflake on them so they’re winter approved.”

Ultimately, Hanford said he believes it’s important to get winter tires on before it starts to snow, and that putting them on is safer because they provide more traction in cold weather when roads get slippery.

“The least expensive snow tire is still gonna be way better than one of the best all-seasons [tires],” he said.

stories.title: Ontario Wsib rules cut off benefits for older injured workers as more people work past 65
stories.summary: Legal team launches a campaign calling for Ontario to end age-based benefit cutoffs for older workers covered by Wsib.
stories.author: Ghada Alsharif
stories.content:
Brian Ellacott had no plans to retire. He loved his job and spent more than four decades working as a mason, helping build infrastructure projects across Ontario.

“I wanted to work as long as I possibly could,” the 69-year-old said.

But in July 2021, at age 63, he stepped on an overhanging scaffold plank and fell two and a half metres to the ground, injuring both legs.

“It’s like somebody took a gun to the bottom of my foot and shot it off and shattered everything,” said Ellacott, who can’t work. “My left leg was totally destroyed and my right leg now has a titanium heel in it.”

In 2023, two years after the fall, Ontario’s Workplace Safety and Insurance Board (Wsib) ended Ellacott’s loss-of-earnings benefits under a rule that limits payments for workers injured at age 63 or older to two years.

Ellacott’s case is among a growing number that prompted lawyer Tebasum Durrani and paralegal Chris Grawey — both with the Injured Workers Community Legal Clinic — to launch Rights Don’t Retire , a campaign calling for Ontario to end age-based benefit cutoffs for older workers covered by the Wsib.

The campaign proposes that workers injured before age 65 would continue receiving loss-of-earnings benefits until age 70 and that those injured at 65 or older would receive benefits for five years after the date of injury or recurrence. And if Wsib determines that a worker would have continued working beyond those timelines, benefits would continue until their expected retirement date.

The policy’s restrictive requirements are discouraging workers from filing claims in the first place, experts say.

Under the decades-old rules , loss-of-earnings benefits generally end at age 65. Workers injured at 63 or older, like Ellacott, can receive them for two years at most. The cutoff dates back to the era of mandatory retirement, which Ontario abolished in 2006.

But after the pandemic and amid the rising cost of living, Durrani and Grawey saw a surge in older injured workers contacting them for help after losing benefits because of their age.

“More and more people are working longer,” Durrani said. “The law as it stands is not keeping up with how people live and work today. That is problematic and has significant consequences for older injured workers.”

Canadians are retiring later than they did decades ago. The average retirement age hit a record high of 65.4 years in 2025, up from 61.6 two decades ago, according to Statistics Canada data. One in five seniors age 65 to 74 worked in 2022 (full time or part time), almost half of them by necessity.

Grawey and Durrani gathered Wsib data through freedom-of-information requests that showed a sharp increase in workplace injury claims among older workers. Wsib claims from workers 63 and older rose 279 per cent between 1994 and 2024, reaching nearly 17,000, according to the data.

“The legislation discriminates against older injured workers and is based on outdated assumptions about people’s working lives,” Grawey said. “The Workplace Safety Insurance Act should be amended to reflect the current reality.”

In an emailed statement, the Wsib said “rules regarding entitlement to benefits related to a person’s age are set out in the Workplace Safety and Insurance Act . Any changes would require legislation.”

Ellacott said he had hoped he would at least get support while recovering from his injuries, but he has been without employment income since he was cut off.

“I’m not asking for money for the rest of my life, I’m asking for benefits to continue while I’m hurt — that just seems normal,” said Ellacott, who has undergone four surgeries. “Age shouldn’t be a determining factor when you’ve got three more surgeries to go because of a work injury.”

Tebasum Durrani, left, a lawyer, and Chris Grawey, a paralegal, of the Injured Workers Community Legal Clinic in Toronto’s east end. They’ve launched a campaign calling for an end to age-based benefit cutoffs for older workers covered by Ontario’s Wsib.

Durrani says she can feel the anxiety and uncertainty on calls from older injured workers whose loss-of-earnings benefits are set to end when they turn 65.

Like Ellacott, many tell her that if not for their work-related injuries or illnesses, they would have kept working, either because they wanted to or needed the income due to high cost of living.

Some consider selling their homes or downsizing, she said. Others worry about how they will care for a spouse with an illness or disability once they lose access to workplace benefits.

“These are potentially life-altering decisions they’re making all the while dealing with their own injuries,” Durrani said. “I feel very inadequate because I don’t have a sure answer to offer them.”

As Canada moves to fast-track mineral extraction projects across the country, observers warn the push is outpacing worker protections.

In April, the government introduced Bill 105, which, if passed, would allow injured workers to continue receiving loss-of-earnings benefits past 65 if they can demonstrate they would have kept working. While Durrani and Grawey and other advocates see the bill as a step forward, they say it falls short by placing the burden on injured workers to prove they would have remained in the workforce.

Ontario’s approach to injured workers over 65 is among the strictest in Canada, Durrani and Grawey say.

Provinces such as British Columbia and Alberta have more flexible systems that allow workers to provide evidence they intended to keep working beyond 65, an approach that takes individual circumstances into account rather than applying a blanket age cutoff, said Grawey.

So far, the Rights Don’t Retire campaign has been endorsed by the Ontario Federation of Labour and has united a broad coalition of injured workers groups and labour organizations in Ontario to advocate for a solution that incorporates aspects from other provinces’ laws, along with data from Statistics Canada and the Wsib.

The campaign has helped bring the issue to the attention of politicians, including through a meeting with Ontario Liberal interim leader John Fraser, Durrani said. It has also attracted support from unions representing thousands of workers.

In November 2025, the Injured Workers Community Legal Clinic organized a lobby day at Queen’s Park that brought together more than 50 people, including MPPs, injured workers, advocates and union representatives.

Grawey and Durrani said the campaign has prompted more workers to contact the clinic after reading their articles or hearing about the initiative through union and community referrals.

According to the legal experts, the campaign’s approach helps to recognize two realities: First, more people are working later in life, by choice or for financial security. Second, workers are individuals, and their employment and retirement plans are not uniform.

“The idea that people automatically retire at a particular age is so out of touch with what people are actually dealing with,” Durrani said.

“It sends the message that the losses of older injured workers are somehow less real or less worthy of protection.”

stories.title: Final paving approaches for Wellington Gateway Phase 4
stories.summary: Final paving on Wellington Road, between Harlech Gate and the Wellington Commons entrance, is expected to begin Monday, November 23.
stories.content:
Final paving on Wellington Road, between Harlech Gate and the Wellington Commons entrance, is expected to begin Monday, November 23.

This marks one of the final stages of construction for Wellington Gateway Phase 4, and drivers will see a significant improvement to the roadway once paving is complete.

Nearby Wellington Gateway Phase 3, between Wilkins Street and Harlech Gate, is now complete. Remaining work on Phase 4, including transit shelter installation, permanent traffic signals, landscaping, and other finishing touches, will take place in 2027.

Paving is expected to take place over four days, from November 23 to 26. Crews will work along Wellington Road during this period, with work taking place during daytime hours.

The schedule May change depending on weather and construction conditions.

Traffic will be maintained during the paving operation, but drivers should expect delays and temporary traffic disruptions while paving takes place.

Drivers travelling through the area are encouraged to allow extra time or consider alternate routes where possible.

Local businesses and shopping centres, including White Oaks Mall and Wellington Commons, will remain open during construction.

Access to business entrances, parking lots and driveways will be maintained throughout the work where possible. However, short-term interruptions May occur as paving equipment moves across individual driveways and plaza entrances.

Construction crews will work to maintain and restore access as paving progresses through the area.

Pedestrian access to nearby businesses and shopping areas will be maintained during construction. Temporary adjustments May be required as crews move through the work area.

Please follow posted signs and use designated pedestrian routes.

LTC buses will detour around the work area. Visit the London Transit Commission website for the latest bus schedules and detour information.

Following paving, crews will return in 2027 to complete the remaining work, including transit shelter installation, permanent traffic signals, landscaping, and other finishing touches. This work is expected to require little traffic disruption.

For more information and updates on Wellington Gateway, visit the Wellington Gateway project webpage

To learn more about construction projects across London, visit the Renew London map .

stories.title: Two men convicted in the murder of a Canadian animation pioneer to be sentenced in Dominica
stories.summary: Americans Jonathan Lehrer, 60 and Robert Snyder Jr., 66, were both found guilty of murder by a jury in the High Court of Justice in Roseau, the capital city of
stories.author: Jason Miller
stories.content:
The prosecutor in the case of two American men convicted for the 2023 murder of Canadian entrepreneur Daniel Langlois and his partner Dominique Marchand is asking the courts in the Caribbean island nation of Dominica to sentence both offenders to life in prison.

The prosecution’s request that both men spend the remainder of their “whole life,” in prison comes after the Crown opted not to seek the death penalty due to a special agreement it made with the French government in order to get access to Norville Williams, a key witness in the prosecution’s case, special prosecutor Keith Scotland told the Star.

“Although the state is not asking for the death sentence to be applied it submits that this matter is appropriate for a whole life sentence,” Scotland wrote in his sentencing submissions obtained by the Star in advance of Monday’s sentencing.

American entrepreneur Jonathan Lehrer, 60 and fellow American Robert Snyder Jr., 66, were both found guilty of murder by a jury in the High Court of Justice in Roseau, the capital city of Dominica, in July. Both men are to be sentenced Monday.

Court documents revealed that both victims were known for their charitable work in their adopted home and just a month before their murder Langlois had received a meritorious service award from the president of Dominica for his contributions to business, sustainable development, research and hospitality.

Robert Snyder and Jonathan Lehrer have been convicted of murder in the December 2023 killings of Canadian businessman Daniel Langlois, 66, and his partner Dominique Marchand, 58, who are pictured.

A statement from the families of the victims says they are relieved by the guilty verdict and “given the needs of the investigation, the ashes have just been repatriated to Canada, which prevented the families from organizing the funerals.”

The families expressed thanks to those who “showed their support throughout this heartbreaking tragedy.”

“It is still very difficult for me to believe that my son is gone, but the fact that the criminals were found guilty and that the ashes have just been repatriated, will finally allow me to bury my son with dignity,” Langlois’ mother said in the statement released Friday.

Scotland argued the “callousness” of the offenders makes it the “worst of the worst,” and that it was particularly aggravating that the men ambushed two victims, shot and burned them before attempting to conceal the bodies.

“It was planned and cold-blooded,” Scotland told the Star.

Lawyer for the convicted men Ravi Rajcoomar said Dominican law doesn’t provide the defence any wiggle room to challenge the sentence in a murder with those aggravating features. His clients have appealed the conviction.

“Because two persons were killed violently and there was an attempt to conceal the body, under Dominican law, you can only have a whole life sentence,” Rajcoomar said. “The law doesn’t allow us to do anything else. Whether or not that is constitutional is another issue.”

He added, “my clients maintain their innocence.”

Rajcoomar argued that “detaining someone with no chance of ever regaining freedom is also incompatible with human dignity.”

Langlois, a Canadian computer animation pioneer, and Marchand were found dead in a burnt-out SUV not far from the off-grid mountaintop resort they owned on the island on Dec. 1, 2023. Four days later Lehrer and Snyder Jr., who was purportedly working for Lehrer as a mechanic were arrested.

The state’s case was premised on the allegation that it was a “contract killing,” and that Lehrer hired Snyder to kill them, according to court filings.

Snyder was said to be a hit man who, armed with a licensed firearm belonging to Lehrer, who shot Langlois and Marchand as they returned to their home.

The police discovered five spent casings that were linked to Lehrer’s licensed firearm. They also obtained bullet fragments which were linked as having been fired from a barrel owned by Lehrer, and which fitted his licensed firearm. Snyder had burns along his right leg the state argued to the jury were due to the fire, court documents show.

“The state’s case therefore was that this was a premeditated contract killing,” Rajcoomar wrote, adding that the prosecutor argued that Lehrer had procured Snyder “as a hit man and then assisted Snyder to incinerate the evidence.”

Langlois and Marchand built a 285-acre, 14-suite eco-resort that opened in 2022; Lehrer oversaw Bois Cotlette Estate, a historic cocoa plantation next door.

Prior to the killings, Langlois and Lehrer had been locked in a protracted legal battle over the use of a road, known as the Morne Rouge Public Road, that connects their properties, according to court records.

The road crossed through the Lehrer estate, sparking the conflict.

Evidence called at trial proved that Langlois, 66, and Marchand, 58, were ambushed on a remote trail near Soufriere, a village in the southern part of the island, as they returned to their upscale resort.

The prosecutor’s sentencing filings indicate that the couple would often use the road through Bois Cotlette to get to Soufriere for their meals and “on numerous occasions they encountered confrontations with Jonathan, his wife Victoria,” and their employees, including Norville Williams, who “repeatedly engaged in verbal abuse and threats.”

The couple was making that routine return trip in their Nissan X-Trail on Nov. 30, 2023, when they were attacked and shot by Snyder, the court heard. The accused then transported the victims to an isolated road about two kilometres from the ambush site. The vehicle was riddled with bullets before it was set on fire with Langlois and Marchand inside.

“They were burnt beyond recognition,” Scotland said.

Scotland said Williams was in France at the time of the trial and in exchange for the co-operation of the French government to facilitate his testimony, the prosecutor agreed that it wouldn’t seek the death penalty for the accused.

“He was a main witness for the state,” Scotland said. Although Williams did not see the shooting, he heard the shooting and heard Marchand cry out, “oh my God, oh my God.”

The court also heard evidence from a German hiker, who testified to hearing the shots and identified one of the accused leaving the scene where the car was burned.

The guilty verdict was returned on July 28 after two hours of deliberation by the jury. The murder trial ran for four weeks and featured more than 40 witnesses.

Langlois made his fortune in the 1990s selling his Montreal-based company, Softimage, which produced software used in Hollywood blockbusters such as “Jurassic Park,” the “Harry Potter” franchise and “Titanic.” He and Marchand moved to Dominica in 1997.

The maximum penalty for murder in Dominica is the death penalty, Scotland said, adding that while the island nation maintains capital punishment within its criminal code, executions have not been used for the past four decades.

“Because two persons were killed violently and there was an attempt to conceal the body, under Dominican law, you can only have a whole life sentence,” Rajcoomar said. “The law doesn’t allow us to do anything else. Whether or not that is constitutional is another issue.”
He added, “my clients maintain their innocence.”
Rajcoomar argued that “detaining someone with no chance of ever regaining freedom is also incompatible with human dignity.”

Langlois, a Canadian computer animation pioneer, and Marchand were found dead in a burnt-out SUV not far from the off-grid mountaintop resort they owned on the island on Dec. 1, 2023. Four days later Lehrer and Snyder Jr., who was purportedly working for Lehrer as a mechanic were arrested.
The state’s case was premised on the allegation that it was a “contract killing,” and that Lehrer hired Snyder to kill them, according to court filings.
Snyder was said to be a hit man who, armed with a licensed firearm belonging to Lehrer, who shot Langlois and Marchand as they returned to their home.

The police discovered five spent casings that were linked to Lehrer’s licensed firearm. They also obtained bullet fragments which were linked as having been fired from a barrel owned by Lehrer, and which fitted his licensed firearm. Snyder had burns along his right leg the state argued to the jury were due to the fire, court documents show.

“The state’s case therefore was that this was a premeditated contract killing,” Rajcoomar wrote, adding that the prosecutor argued that Lehrer had procured Snyder “as a hit man and then assisted Snyder to incinerate the evidence.”
Langlois and Marchand built a 285-acre, 14-suite eco-resort that opened in 2022; Lehrer oversaw Bois Cotlette Estate, a historic cocoa plantation next door.

Prior to the killings, Langlois and Lehrer had been locked in a protracted legal battle over the use of a road, known as the Morne Rouge Public Road, that connects their properties, according to court records.
The road crossed through the Lehrer estate, sparking the conflict.

Evidence called at trial proved that Langlois, 66, and Marchand, 58, were ambushed on a remote trail near Soufriere, a village in the southern part of the island, as they returned to their upscale resort.

The prosecutor’s sentencing filings indicate that the couple would often use the road through Bois Cotlette to get to Soufriere for their meals and “on numerous occasions they encountered confrontations with Jonathan, his wife Victoria,” and their employees, including Norville Williams, who “repeatedly engaged in verbal abuse and threats.”

The couple was making that routine return trip in their Nissan X-Trail on Nov. 30, 2023, when they were attacked and shot by Snyder, the court heard. The accused then transported the victims to an isolated road about two kilometres from the ambush site. The vehicle was riddled with bullets before it was set on fire with Langlois and Marchand inside.
“They were burnt beyond recognition,” Scotland said.

Scotland said Williams was in France at the time of the trial and in exchange for the co-operation of the French government to facilitate his testimony, the prosecutor agreed that it wouldn’t seek the death penalty for the accused.
“He was a main witness for the state,” Scotland said. Although Williams did not see the shooting, he heard the shooting and heard Marchand cry out, “oh my God, oh my God.”
The court also heard evidence from a German hiker, who testified to hearing the shots and identified one of the accused leaving the scene where the car was burned.
The guilty verdict was returned on July 28 after two hours of deliberation by the jury. The murder trial ran for four weeks and featured more than 40 witnesses.

Langlois made his fortune in the 1990s selling his Montreal-based company, Softimage, which produced software used in Hollywood blockbusters such as “Jurassic Park,” the “Harry Potter” franchise and “Titanic.” He and Marchand moved to Dominica in 1997.

The maximum penalty for murder in Dominica is the death penalty, Scotland said, adding that while the island nation maintains capital punishment within its criminal code, executions have not been used for the past four decades.

stories.summary: Toronto - Education workers represented by the Canadian Union of Public Employees in Ontario have voted in favour of a strike mandate.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Education workers represented by the Canadian Union of Public Employees in Ontario have voted in favour of a strike mandate.

The Ontario School Board Council of Unions says voting members were more than 94 per cent in favour.

A 30th Nova Scotia long term care home will be joining the ongoing strike that began 11 days ago. A Canadian Union of Public Employees (Cupe) flag during an education support workers rally outside of the Saskatchewan Legislative Building in Regina, Tuesday, Nov. 25, 2025.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada’s most wanted list gets an AI-powered makeover
stories.summary: Canada’s 25 most wanted fugitives showed up at the Toronto Police College on Thursday morning as life-sized, AI-generated videos projected onto a big screen.
stories.author: Heather Wright
stories.content:
Canada’s 25 most wanted fugitives showed up at the Toronto Police College on Thursday morning as life-sized, AI-generated videos projected onto a big screen.

“With the help of AI we bring our top 25 fugitives into this room… moving as they might if you saw them on the street, at the supermarket, at the airport or anywhere else,” said Max Langlois, executive director of the Bolo Program.

“If it feels uncomfortable that’s the point.”

Police services from across Canada and the United States joined Bolo, short for “be on the lookout,” to unveil the new list and renew their pleas for the public’s help. The program has been running since 2018 and is funded by a private foundation.

Both police and Bolo say the program works, and many featured fugitives do get caught. But Bolo does not receive tips and it remains difficult to gauge how many arrests can be attributed to the campaign. Still, police believe the nationwide awareness it brings plays a role in their ability to apprehend fugitives.

“The Bolo program has shown time and time again what happens when police and the public work together,” said Myron Demkiw, Toronto’s police chief.

“Since 2018, 19 of the 28 Toronto cases featured by Bolo have ended in arrest. Including the case that held last year’s number one spot,” he said.

That case was Bryan Fuentes Gramajo who topped the 2025 list after a fatal shooting outside Yorkdale Shopping Centre in downtown Toronto. Bolo’s website lists him as arrested on March 5, 2026.

When last year’s list came out in October 2025, Bolo said 42 of the 78 suspects it had featured since 2018 had been located, or roughly 54 per cent. It appears as though only six names from last year’s list carried over to this year: Dylan Denis, Tamah McLean, Dellano Robertson-Berry, Gurkirat Singh, Yusuf Ali and Tommy Bernier-Thibault. Several others are now marked as arrested on Bolo’s site.

At Thursday’s news conference a statement from the security guard allegedly shot by Kyle Prouse, this year’s second most wanted fugitive, was read. The man, whose identity remains anonymous, thanked police and the Bolo program while delivering a message directly to Prouse.

“For the past seven months, you have had a police service looking for you. Now you have the Bolo program that means you have the whole country on the look out for you,” he said. “Wherever you go, wherever you sleep, wherever you hide... it’s only a matter of time. Someone will spot you. Someone will turn in that tip. Someone will turn against you.”

Most of the names on the Bolo list are wanted for violent crimes ranging from murder to assault to weapons offences. Police services are already actively looking for them but experts say the increase in awareness does help.

“It doesn’t change the police direction,” said Chris Lewis, former OPP commissioner and public safety analyst for CTV News. “They continue investigating and tracking down leads. But it offers potentially more communication across the country to make someone aware of it... or reminds people who might be aware of it but who have been reluctant to come forward,” he said.

Police say many of the 25 are considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached. Rather tips should be made directly to police departments, many of which have confidential tip lines.

Police also warned that anyone knowingly helping one of the fugitives could be arrested and charged.

The full list, with the AI-generated videos, is posted at boloprogram.org .

Now you have the Bolo program that means you have the whole country on the look out for you,” he said. “Wherever you go, wherever you sleep, wherever you hide... it’s only a matter of time. Someone will spot you. Someone will turn in that tip. Someone will turn against you.”

Most of the names on the Bolo list are wanted for violent crimes ranging from murder to assault to weapons offences. Police services are already actively looking for them but experts say the increase in awareness does help.

“It doesn’t change the police direction,” said Chris Lewis, former OPP commissioner and public safety analyst for CTV News. “They continue investigating and tracking down leads. Police say many of the 25 are considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached. Rather tips should be made directly to police departments, many of which have confidential tip lines.
Police also warned that anyone knowingly helping one of the fugitives could be arrested and charged.

stories.title: Tumbler Ridge shooter used ChatGPT to help alter guns, report alleges
stories.summary: OpenAI’s chatbot allegedly provided advice on making illegal 3D-printed weapon parts and engaged in detailed violent fantasies about mass shootings
stories.author: Jesse Winter, Mike Hager
stories.content:
OpenAI’s chatbot helped the Tumbler Ridge shooter by providing advice on making illegal 3D-printed weapon parts and engaged in detailed violent fantasies about mass shootings, alleges a new report from a U.S. non-profit media outlet .

Journalist Mark Follman said his reporting was based on copies of the Tumbler Ridge shooter’s ChatGPT conversation history and sources with direct knowledge of the matter.

ChatGPT helped the shooter design a 3D-printed foregrip for one of her weapons, and May have helped design a device that can allow a semi-automatic rifle to operate in a fully automatic capacity, the Mother Jones article alleges. It also said the shooter received help from the chatbot when she asked about fixing a spring inside a 3D-printed high-capacity magazine capable of holding 35 rounds of ammunition.

The new reporting underlines concerns about the shooter’s use of OpenAI’s technology in the lead-up to February’s deadly mass shooting in British Columbia. At least 37 lawsuits have been filed against OpenAI in California in connection with the incident, after it was revealed that months before the shooting the company had flagged, but not reported to authorities, worrying interactions between the shooter and ChatGPT. The chat logs Mr. Follman said his reporting is based on are expected to be central to those lawsuits.

On Feb. 10, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight people and injured dozens of others in the northern B.C. community before killing herself. Before entering the town’s school, she killed her mother and 11-year-old half-brother in their family home. The Globe and Mail has previously reported that friends of the family and a relative said Ms. Van Rootselaar had a history of mental illness, including stints being held involuntarily in hospital.

Mother Jones’s reporting alleges that ChatGPT provided Ms. Van Rootselaar with vivid, violent fantasies about mass shootings, including descriptions torturing wounded victims. The news outlet has previously reported on the Tumbler Ridge shooting based on chat logs it obtained.

Lawyers have previously told The Globe they expect OpenAI to argue to keep Ms. Van Rootselaar’s ChatGPT history out of the public eye, especially as the company readies for an initial public offering that could see it valued at $1-trillion.

A spokesman for OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. In April, CEO Sam Altman formally apologized for his company’s role in the mass shooting, saying he was deeply sorry that OpenAI did not alert law enforcement to Ms. Van Rootselaar’s account.

B.C. politician Niki Sharma, who will be replaced Friday as Attorney-General after the New Democrats lost last month’s provincial election, said the latest details of the chat logs are “really disturbing.”

“It’s more horrifying every time.”

Ms. Sharma said the alleged snippets of these logs that have been leaked to the media shed light on how disturbing the chatbot’s interactions with the Tumbler Ridge shooter are alleged to have become, but also point to concerns about how seriously public safety is treated inside OpenAI.

“What is the actual corporate culture and responsibility within [OpenAI] that so many people quit or feel compelled to leak stuff ... that so much that alarms them is going on inside the corporation,” said Ms. Sharma, who launched the province’s own lawsuit against OpenAI.

“This is one of the most powerful companies in the world, driving this technology that is going to affect all of our lives. And we have signs of the internal workings that are just not very good,” Ms. Sharma said. “So it should scare people.”

Ms. Sharma reiterated her call for strong regulation of the AI industry, and better guardrails to protect Canadians.

Separately, the FBI arrested Washington resident James Cody Bryant, 30, of Bellingham, Wash., in October for allegedly helping Ms. Van Rootselaar while she was contemplating her mass shooting.

Ms. Bryant (who authorities said uses she/her pronouns) faces charges of aiding Ms. Van Rootselaar, including providing money and advice while planning the attack.

About six months before the attack, “Van Rootselaar told Bryant that she had stolen guns and ammunition from her family’s gun safe and was hiding them in her room in preparation for a mass shooting,” according to the court documents in Ms. Bryant’s case, which is expected to go to trial in December 2027.

“Van Rootselaar also said she convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf.”

According to Ms. Bryant, Ms. Van Rootselaar was “fixated on mass shootings and watched livestreamed recordings of past shootings to learn from them,” the document said. It said she asked Ms. Bryant to livestream her planned attack and Ms. Bryant agreed.

The two discussed possible locations, with the shooter wanting one that would “lead to the largest number of victims.” Ms. Bryant said it would be a “bad idea to attack a school because there would be too many young victims” and suggested instead a grocery store or church, court documents say.

Canada’s Minister Responsible for Artificial Intelligence, Evan Solomon, said in a statement that the new details in Mr. Follman’s reporting are “deeply disturbing.”

“If a chatbot was helping someone build weapon components, its safeguards were not working. AI companies must not let their products be used this way, and they must be held accountable when it happens,” the statement said.

His office did not make anyone available for an interview.

With reports from Justine Hunter and Andrea Woo
