content_blocks.text: Desjardins’ Jerome Dubreuil said it is “natural for BCE to kick the tires” on Telus, especially given the longstanding wireless network sharing agreement between those two companies.
“BCE and (Telus) were the two historical phone monopolies and their fixed networks are therefore very complementary,” he said in a note, adding their networks are “fitting together like a glove.”
“However, the fit is less compelling from a regulatory standpoint, as securing Competition Bureau approval for a combination of two Big Three members would likely be a long shot.”

Dubreuil said that without further moves to resolve that concern, a combined Bell-Telus company would control 55 per cent of Canada’s wireless market, compared with a Quebecor-Telus merger that would account for 40 per cent. He said a Bell-Telus merger would create “significant synergies,” but that entering the process after Quebecor would likely require BCE to put forward a more compelling offer.

He said Bell throwing its hat into the ring could spark a bidding war with Quebecor that leads to it sweetening its original offer. Alternatively, Quebecor could end up serving as a “remedy partner” to a Bell-Telus acquisition, he said, buying up assets divested by the pair in order to appease regulators’ competition concerns.
“If Quebecor thinks it can close this, Bell’s chances should be similar,” said Scotiabank analyst Maher Yaghi in a note earlier this week.

“Quebecor’s move May even push Bell to present a competing bid from which Quebecor could benefit when it comes to proposed remedies to get it through to the finish line. Bell could also force Quebecor to overpay, or table its own offer and make it stronger by stating upfront which remedies it would accept.”

Quebecor made a non-binding proposal to Telus on June 26 to serve as the basis for negotiations and then submitted an “enhanced proposal” on Nov. 9. Telus president and CEO Victor Dodig said in an interview that the proposal undervalues his company, and that he has concerns around how the offer, if accepted, would satisfy regulators.

A potential transaction would likely lead to reviews by the Competition Bureau, the Crtc and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has said the government “will not predetermine the outcomes.” On Wednesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said more competition, lower prices and better service would be key to any decision.

The prime minister declined to comment directly on Quebecor’s proposal, but said that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly situation can lead to more competition with fewer players, though he didn’t elaborate further.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Rogers takeover of Shaw approved by Ottawa: Minister Champagne'

content_blocks.text: In an interview on Monday, Quebecor president and CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau pitched the merger as a way to save cash by combining networks, spectrum and operations, which would boost investment capacity. He said a stronger company would be better positioned to protect “sovereignty” in the Canadian telecom sector as foreign competitors like Elon Musk’s Starlink gain market share.

“The interest successively shown by Quebecor and then Bell in Telus points to the same reality: Canada’s telecommunications sector must be strengthened, particularly in the face of new American technology and satellite players,” said Quebecor’s statement on Thursday.
“Canada needs strong companies that can invest at scale while remaining under Canadian control.”

Péladeau has touted Quebecor as a fourth national carrier since his company acquired Freedom Mobile in 2023, as part of a deal associated with the larger takeover of Shaw by Rogers Communications Inc.
Péladeau and Dodig are slated to meet Monday to discuss next steps.

stories.title: Students count down the days until winter break
stories.summary: As the fall semester winds down, Fanshawe students are looking forward to taking a break from schoolwork, spen...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
As the fall semester winds down, Fanshawe students are looking forward to taking a break from schoolwork, spending time with family and friends, and recharging before the start of the new semester.

For some students, winter break is a chance to catch up on things they haven’t had the time for during the semester. Others are looking forward to working on personal projects and getting ready for the next term.

Saear Palmer, graphic design, year 1. (Torey Joseph Legarrie)

Fanshawe student Sarea Palmer said she likes how exams are right before the winter break.

“Then we can at least get the bulk of the stuff out of the way, and the winter break can be used to actually relax and just kind of chill.”

Palmer said a break will provide some much-needed time to relax after a busy semester.

“Between Christmas and New Year’s, just kind of settling down, finally getting to relax for once and just kind of spend time with friends and family.”

Exams will be start on December 14 and the winter break will be from December 22 until Jan 4.

Fanshawe student Irelynn Donerty said she thinks the winter break comes at the right time.

“I think it comes just when things start getting too stressful. Its a nice little break.”

Irelynn Doherty, film production, year 1. (Torey Joseph Legarrie)

She said that she think the break provide is a good amount of time for a break.

“I think it depends on the program and how stressful the year was, but I think that its a decent amount of time to recharge.”

Donerty has a different perspective if exams should be before or after the winter break.

“I feel like after would be a better choice.”

She said the semester has been busy but rewarding, particularly while studying film production.

“I have a lot of work, and its a little stressful, but I get to do what I love, which is film production.”

stories.title: Experts cite child suicide, trafficking as they urge MPs to pass digital safety bill
stories.summary: Ottawa — A pediatrician who is urging the Liberal government to quickly pass its digital safety bill says social media and AI chatbots amount to a massive, unregulated experiment on children’s brains.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A pediatrician who is urging the Liberal government to quickly pass its digital safety bill says social media and AI chatbots amount to a massive experiment on children’s brains.

“The unfettered, unchecked introduction of social media and AI chatbots into the lives of children, with no enforced safety standards and no meaningful platform accountability, is, in effect, the largest fully unregulated clinical trial manipulating the human brain in the history of civilization,” said Charlotte Moore Hepburn of Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children.

Hepburn testified Thursday at the House of Commons heritage committee, which is studying the Liberal government’s digital safety bill. Once the committee hears from witnesses and makes amendments, the bill must make its way through the parliamentary process in both the House and Senate before it can become law.

Bill C-34 would impose a duty to act responsibly on the companies behind social media platforms and AI chatbots. It also would force social media platforms to block access for kids under 16, though platforms would be able to obtain an exemption if they put sufficient safeguards in place.

Hepburn said the digital space has caused the biggest disruption to the developing mind she has seen in her 20-year career

She gave composite examples of cases involving children — such as a 13-year old girl admitted to hospital after a deliberate, near-fatal overdose that followed relentless internet bullying.

“People with no names, no faces, no accountability for their speech told her that she was fat and that she was ugly, and that the world would be better off without her,” she said.

Social media also gives kids instructions on how to harm themselves, Hepburn added.

“Social media offers children the precise dose of Tylenol or Benadryl or iron that they should take if they want to successfully end their life,” she said. “AI chatbots even have offered detailed advice on how to swallow large amounts of pills at a single time.”

Hepburn told MPs her hospital has had to establish a dedicated clinic for the growing number of child victims of sexual trafficking.

Lianna McDonald, executive director of the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, said the number of luring reports sent to the centre’s tip line has shot up 300 per cent since 2020, and most of them involve online platforms.

She said she has been working to combat sexual violence and exploitation of children for 25 years and has “never seen it this bad.”

McDonald gave the example of a youth in Nova Scotia who was sexually extorted. Even though he told his parents, those behind the extortion attempt were relentless, McDonald said.

“In the morning, they found him. He’d taken his own life,” she said.

The ban on social media for kids under 16 has been a high-profile element of the proposed bill. Many details about how it would work are still undecided — including how user ages will be verified and which platforms, beyond the big social media sites, will be covered.

McDonald said while a minimum age for social media access wouldn’t be a panacea, it would be “a meaningful harm reduction measure.”

Conservative MP Andrew Lawton pressed Hepburn over her stance on the age restriction elements of the legislation. He pointed to a report issued by the institute where she works as medical director that said bans for children can be counterproductive.

Hepburn said the report looked at an age ban “in the absence of the constellation of other services as outlined in C-34,” which include a robust regulator, safety-by-design rules, and a regime that would allow children to rejoin platforms once they are safe.

She said she supports the age limits outlined in the bill.

“The strength we see of C-34 is the fact that it’s a full complement of measures,” Hepburn said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Man arrested over alleged racist threat to run over people in Toronto
stories.summary: A 55-year-old man is facing charges after allegedly threatening to drive into people in Toronto 'because of their perceived race,' Hamilton police say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A 55-year-old man is facing charges after allegedly threatening to drive into people in Toronto “because of their perceived race,” Hamilton police say.

Police said Thursday the man was arrested Monday after officers were notified of the incident.

Investigators said police got a report the man told his social worker he was heading to Canada’s largest city and intended to run over people because of their race.

Officers notified the Ontario Provincial Police and Toronto Police Service, and issued an alert for the vehicle.

“At approximately 4:26 p.m., Hamilton police officers located the vehicle on Eastport Drive beneath the Skyway Bridge and arrested the man for uttering threats to cause death — motivated by hate,” police said in a news release.

He remains in custody. His identity wasn’t released.

“Hamilton police take hate-motivated incidents seriously and remain committed to addressing hate, supporting those impacted, and working alongside community partners to foster a safe and inclusive city,” police said.

“Hamilton police encourage anyone who experiences or witnesses a hate-motivated crime or incident to report it. This includes incidents that May not meet the threshold of a criminal offence.”

stories.title: Getting older hasn’t stopped me from having an eccentric commute
stories.summary: Have you seen a guy in his late 60s riding an e-bike in minus 20 degrees, wearing a one-piece snowsuit? That’s me
stories.author: Ian Blumer
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

The way I see it, I didn’t choose eccentricity; eccentricity chose me.

I’ve led a traditional life. Grade school, high school, university, work, marriage, children, home in the suburbs; the whole nine yards.

As my wife and I reached our 60s, with our children (sort of) on their own, we looked around our now-unnecessarily large home, reflected on the collective and continuing toll of dealing with leaky roofs, wet basements, mice (and, yikes, worse), and decided that the time had come to go where so many have gone before. We needed to downsize.

We looked at condos in the suburb, but our kids berated us for acting like stodgy old farts and pressured us to move downtown. Like, right downtown. Beside City Hall, downtown. Where the action is.

Soon thereafter, we found ourselves living in a shoebox in the sky in the insanely busy, noisy, at-times dangerous, but always exciting heart of Toronto.

While my home had relocated, my workplace had not.

I work in the eastern suburbs of Toronto. And I quickly discovered that I could drive to or from my new downtown home to my office in 40 minutes. Well, I could do that if I was going to be driving at, say, 4 a.m. on a Sunday. But if I was trying to make this same drive during rush hour, it was taking me up to two hours. Forty minutes I could handle, even 60 minutes, but two hours? No way.

So I came up with a plan.

I was going to walk. Well, walk, train and e-bike. Every day, 30 C above or below. Sun-drenched days or cloudy skies. Pouring rain or, this being the Great White North, blinding snowstorms.

Would it save me time on my commute? Maybe not. But at least I could get some work done during my nearly hour-long train ride.

My kids thought I had gone off the deep end. “Dad, you’re a senior citizen. And you’re soft. No way you’re going to do that crazy commute. And e-biking? At your age. In the winter? No way. You’ll last a week.”

That was four years ago.

Every working day for the past four years, I’ve been walking from my home to the train station, taking the train from downtown to the suburbs, walking from the train station to a nearby storage locker and e-biking to my office.

Have you ever seen a guy in his late 60s riding an e-bike? More specifically, have you ever seen a guy in his late 60s riding an e-bike in January, in minus-20 C weather, in the snow, wearing a one-piece snowsuit made for Arctic oil rig workers, wearing a heated hat, a heated balaclava, a heated vest, heated gloves, ski goggles, a helmet with flashing lights and a yellow reflective vest?

No, I didn’t think so. Trust me, it is a memorable sight. All of which would be much more amusing if it wasn’t me being the memorable sight.

I suspect I am also the only person around who parks his bike on a Ford F-150 bed mat in his office to catch the melting snow, slush and sleet that accumulate on my daily ride.

Truth be told, there have been a few hiccups along the way.

Like when people get irritated that I don’t have their Uber Eats food order. Or frustrated that I don’t know why the GO Train is late, and no, I’m sorry, I really don’t work for Metrolinx.

Or when I decided it would be more convenient to keep my bike at the train station, only to shortly thereafter learn that “unbreakable” locks are, well, not actually unbreakable.

Or when a cable came loose on my bike mid-commute and I suddenly came to a dead stop. Damn, stranded! Oh, wait, the bike has pedals! D’oh.

Or, worst of all, wiping out on an icy road and face-planting as people in their cars and trucks gawked (which I could live with), avoided hitting me (which I could definitely live with) and called out to see if I was okay (which, in my embarrassment, I could foolishly not live with).

Do I “like” my daily commute? Well, it’s not ideal. But would I give it up and go back to my daily sitting-in-traffic-for-an-eternity-slowly-going-out-of-my-mind former existence? No way.

So if some time you happen, ON a cold, snowy winter’s day, to come across an old guy on an e-bike, resembling nothing so much as a black bear wearing Christmas lights, don’t feel sorry for him. I May look bizarre, I May be doing something bizarre, but truth be told, I’m finding this new-found bit of eccentricity strangely liberating.

Ian Blumer lives in Toronto.

stories.title: ‘Difficult to predict’ timeline to end CAF ammunition shortage: official
stories.summary: Conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have led to global ammunition shortages that make procurement on the open market difficult, official says.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Canada’s defence department can’t say how long it will take to reverse a serious shortfall in the country’s stockpile of military ammunition.

For years, the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) have warned that they would run out of ammunition within days of a shooting war breaking out. But despite the Liberal government’s commitment of $9.2 billion to replenish the Caf’s strategic ammunition stockpile in 2024, the Department of National Defence’s top public servant can’t say how long it will take to re-supply.

The problem, according to DND Deputy Minister Christiane Fox, is twofold: wars in Ukraine and Iran contributing to a shortage of ammunition on the market, and significant timelines in building up Canada’s domestic industrial capacity — even with a recent influx of money from the federal government.

“We want to fill our gaps as quickly as we possibly can, but timelines are difficult to predict at this moment in time when you’ve got a Middle Eastern conflict where there’s been a lot of ammunition used in Iran, you’ve got a lot of Western countries providing ammunition to Ukraine,” Fox told a House of Commons committee Thursday.

“And we are looking at accelerating (domestic) production to be able to meet that global need.”

Fox and senior officials from the CAF testified Thursday that they were making progress on the file after Auditor General Karen Hogan’s office reported serious issues not only with the stockpiles, but how the federal government both procures and keeps track of ammunition.

Hogan’s office estimated it will take several years to bring the Caf’s ammunition stockpiles up to where they should be. In a report released last month, Hogan’s office also flagged a flawed inventory management system and problems with Dnd’s data analysis that made it difficult to say how much ammunition they actually have, or how much more they need.

Hogan’s report suggested the current pace for new ammunition contracts was insufficient to meet the Caf’s demand.

“National Defence lacked reliable inventory information, and a comprehensive assessment of its ammunition needs. We also found that significant gaps remained in its strategic stockpile,” Hogan told MPs Thursday.

“For more than 20 years, our financial audits have identified problems with National Defence’s inventory records, including those for ammunition.”

Asked why problems that have been repeatedly identified for more than two decades persist, Fox said “hard choices” have been made over the years about where the department spends scarce resources.

“Unfortunately ammunition data management systems were not necessarily funded or invested in over time,” Fox said.

Fox said the department is currently working on a single data management system that will give the department and the CAF a better understanding on both what it has and what it needs, and will boost Canada’s overall defence logistics.

The new system is expected to begin rolling out this month, and be fully implemented by March of 2027, Fox added.

stories.title: Court quashes B.C. mine's substantial start determination, orders consultation
stories.summary: Hazelton, British Columbia - A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has ordered that a decision to label a mine in northwestern B.C. as "substantially started" be sent back to the provincial government and that it must have "deep consultation" with the territory's First Nation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Hazelton, British Columbia - A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has ordered that a decision to label a mine in northwestern B.C. as “substantially started” be sent back to the provincial government, and that it must have “deep consultation” with a First Nation with territory in the area.

The province’s assessment officer ruled in 2024 that Seabridge Gold’s KSM Project, a proposed copper, gold and silver mine 65 kilometres northwest of Stewart, B.C., had substantially started, meaning it had made enough progress to retain its environmental approval.

'If you have enough money, you’re going to find someone to do whatever you want.' — Dr. Ian MacArthur, a plastic surgeon

Morrice became the Green Party's leader over the weekend, taking over from the party's sole MP and longtime leader Elizabeth May

NDP Leader Avi Lewis speaks during a press conference on Parliament Hill on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia)

November 19, 2026 at 1:29 p.m.

Ottawa — The newly elected leader of the Green Party has asked the New Democrats if they’d consider working together in a more formal way.

Mike Morrice released a letter he sent to NDP Leader Avi Lewis on Thursday. In it, Morrice said the two progressive federal parties “share much common cause.”

Morrice asked Lewis to begin a conversation “about what solidarity between our parties could look like, including the possibility of electoral co-operation until we win proportional representation in Canada.”

The letter said the Liberal and Conservative parties are looking more similar by the day and said “it’s past time for progressive parties to engage with each other in good faith to come up with solutions to take back power from the billionaire class and the political parties that prop them up.”

Lewis, who won the NDP leadership in late March, said at a press conference on Thursday that he has not received a letter from Morrice yet and that he’s looking forward to meeting the Green leader for the first time.

He would not comment on what he thinks about the idea of electoral co-operation.

Neither Lewis nor Morrice has a seat in Parliament.

Morrice was an MP from 2021 to 2025 but lost his seat in Kitchener Centre in the most recent election. Lewis has never run for federal office.

The Greens have long advocated for Canada to ditch the first-past-the-post electoral system and replace it with a form of proportional representation.

May has also previously floated the idea of working with other progressive parties, including, for example, by agreeing not to run candidates against one another in specific ridings during federal elections or agreeing not to attack one another.

Just before the 2025 federal election May said the Greens would work with the NDP, the Liberals or the Bloc Québécois “to consider how we might co-operate, even if only for one election cycle, to move Canadians closer to the fair, proportional system they consistently tell us they want.”

Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

stories.title: Quebec survey captures complexity of grief among people affected by suicide
stories.summary: A new Quebec survey has found that many respondents who lost a loved one to suicide can have conflicting responses to the tragedy.
stories.author: Katrine Desautels
stories.content:
A new Quebec survey has found that many respondents who lost a loved one to suicide can have conflicting responses to the tragedy.

The survey revealed 56 per cent of people who had someone close to them die by suicide had reported experiencing suicidal thoughts at some point in their lives and that 20 per cent of these respondents had experienced suicidal thoughts over the past year.

The survey also found that 56 per cent of respondents reported feeling satisfied with their lives today.

The numbers highlight the complexities of the grieving process for those who have lost a loved one to suicide, according to Cécile Bardon, psychology professor at l’Université du Québec à Montréal.

Bardon, the director of a research centre on suicide and end-of-life ethics, says the survey also shows how feelings of grief and of satisfaction are not mutually exclusive.

“You can go through something that is emotionally profound and deeply troubling, yet still be able to experience good moments along the way,” Bardon said in an interview.

Three suicide prevention groups surveyed over 304 Quebecers who had someone close to them die by suicide between September and October 2026 as part of the study.

The report notes that its results are not representative of the general population of those bereaved by suicide but provides a first insight into their experiences and needs.

Grief stemming from a suicide is long-lasting, said Hugo Fournier, president and CEO of a Quebec suicide prevention association.

“It’s unique because those who are grieving can find a certain balance in their lives while still suffering. They May experience distress and despair and, at the same time, feel satisfied with certain aspects of their lives,” he said.

Some people express guilt over feeling fulfilled in certain aspects of their lives — at work or socially — while still bearing the burden of grief over a loved one who died by suicide, Fournier adds.

According to the researchers, grief related to suicide often brings about regret, difficulty understanding what led to the act, and even anger toward the person who died.

“It’s very difficult to reconcile that anger with the sorrow we feel and the guilt we experience. It results in a grieving process that can be very, very complex,” Bardon explained.

She added that a “core group of people” will experience traumatic grief, meaning they are severely impacted by the event.

According to the study, an average of about 80 people are affected by each suicide. These include the person’s loved ones — family and friends — but also co-workers, classmates, and perhaps teammates on a sports team or in a theatre troupe.

First responders, such as police officers, paramedics, or medical staff, May be confronted with several suicides in a year. They are exposed not only to death but also to the distress of the bereaved.

“Their coping mechanisms must also be supported so that they can continue to fulfil their role as a conduit for consistent and effective information to those who are grieving,” said Bardon.

“A first responder who is deeply affected and shaken by what they’re experiencing May become someone who clings rigidly to procedures, withdraws into themselves, and fails to show empathy toward the family,” she added.

In fact, the survey highlights a need for faster access to support and resources following the death.

The report shows that 43 per cent of participants received support services they considered acceptable within the month following the death, but 46 per cent would have liked to receive them more quickly. Another 14 per cent reported not receiving services they considered acceptable.

Fournier believes that at the critical moment when the event occurs, front line responders do act quickly and suicide prevention centres typically offer support.

However, followup care needs to be improved, said Bardon.

While the bereaved are often well-surrounded very soon after the death, “it’s when everyone goes back to their normal lives that they find themselves all alone,” she noted.

Among the resources used, support groups are the most highly valued. Online discussion forums are also becoming increasingly popular, said Fournier.

Some rather unexpected sources of comfort were also mentioned in the survey, such as the coroner, who often speaks with the family to prepare a report. The exchange of information between the coroner and the bereaved can potentially have a positive effect and shed light on the circumstances around the death, said Bardon.

Fournier hopes that the survey will help those who have lost a loved one by suicide feel less alone and relieve their feelings of guilt, especially on international suicide bereavement day, which takes place Nov. 21.

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24/7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

stories.title: Regulatory harmonization not a goal of associate membership for Canada: EU ambassador
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canada and the European Union aren't looking at sweeping regulatory harmonization as they work to establish closer ties, says the EU's ambassador to Canada.
stories.author: David Baxter The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Canada and the European Union aren’t looking at sweeping regulatory harmonization as they work to establish closer ties, the EU’s ambassador to Canada said Thursday.

Geneviève Tuts told the Senate foreign affairs and international trade committee that the goal is to share legislative proposals and make some regulations in both jurisdictions more similar while maintaining sovereignty on both sides of the Atlantic.

“What we are trying to achieve is not harmonization, is not regulatory alignment between our legislative framework and the Canadian one,” Tuts told the committee.

“What we’re trying to achieve is to be as close as possible, to share maybe some legislative proposals, the share best practices as well, and to try to align but not to have equivalent regulation.”

During a summit in Montreal in October, Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission leaders signed an agreement to work toward making Canada the first associate member of the European Union next year.

Senators pressed Tuts to explain why nine European nations still have not ratified the decade-old Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement with Canada, better known as Ceta.

Conservative Senator Michael MacDonald noted Poland is among those who haven’t ratified it and France voted against doing so.

“I believe that if Canada wants go forward with the EU, these important states have to sign on and fully participate,” MacDonald said.

“When you’re dealing with the EU, it’s like herding cats. There’s 27 members and it seems like any one of them at any time could throw a monkey wrench into it and shut everything down.”

Tuts said the European Commission is working to get all member nations to ratify the trade deal and noted “movement” in countries like Ireland and Belgium.

“I can assure you there are efforts made at every level, at the commission level as well, to find solutions to help these member states to finally ratify Ceta,” Tuts responded.

“There are some movements as well in some member states. We see some new development in Ireland, in Belgium. So there May be others able to ratify, probably in 2027.”

Cyprus President Nikos Christodoulides also told Carney at a meeting in Ireland on Nov. 12 that his country was on its way to ratifying Ceta.

The ambassador said Canada’s supply management system for dairy has come up in trade discussions but both sides are looking for mutually beneficial solutions.

Independent Senator Peter Boehm, who chairs the committee, asked Tuts if she has anymore insight on what “associate membership” means as there currently is no formal definition despite the term being used by both Canadian and European leaders.

Tuts said it caught many EU member states by surprise when European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen used that term in a speech to European Parliament in September, and said there is concrete work between both sides to figure out exactly what the term means.

“You have to trust the ambition and the willingness and the creativity of our leaders, but also all the people who are working on it,” Tuts said.

Both Canada and Europe are looking to conclude the talks for associate membership, which would include defining it, by the next EU-Canada summit in June 2027.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Alouettes place eight players on All-CFL team
stories.summary: Montreal Alouettes quarterback Davis Alexander and receivers Tyson Philpot and Tyler Snead earned All-CFL all-star honours Thursday.
stories.author: n The Canadian Pressn
stories.content:
Toronto – Montreal Alouettes quarterback Davis Alexander and receivers Tyson Philpot and Tyler Snead earned All-CFL all-star honours Thursday.

Alexander captured the George Reed Most Outstanding Player award after guiding Montreal to a CFL-best 14-4 regular-season record. Philpot earned top Canadian honours after leading the CFL in catches (124) and yards (1,809) — setting single-season marks for a Canadian.

Snead was second overall in receiving yards (1,474) and finished tied with Philpot for most TD grabs (13 apiece). Alexander and Philpot earned their first All-CFL selections, while Snead was honoured for the second straight year.

But Montreal’s solid regular season ended with a 37-30 Grey Cup loss to the Edmonton Elks on Sunday.

Voting was conducted by the Football Reporters of Canada, CFL head coaches and fans.

Montreal placed eight players on the squad, one more than Edmonton. Winnipeg (five), Toronto (three), Saskatchewan, Calgary and B.C. (all two) rounded out the selections.

CFL rushing leader Brady Oliveira of the Winnipeg Blue Bombers (1,493 yards) secured the running back spot for his third all-time selection. Edmonton’s Skyler Griffith earned his first at fullback/tight end.

Joining Philpot and Snead at receiver are Saskatchewan’s KeeSean Johnson and Edmonton’s Austin Mack (both second selections), as well as Toronto’s Damonte Coxie (first).

Saskatchewan centre Logan Ferland (third selection) anchors the offensive line. Montreal’s Pier-Olivier Lestage and Calgary’s Christy Nkanu were first-time selections at guard, while Alouette Nick Callender and Winnipeg’s Jarell Broxton — the CFL’s top offensive lineman — are the tackles.

Calgary’s Clarence Hicks and Edmonton’s Malik Carney are the defensive ends, flanking Toronto’s Ralph Holley and Winnipeg’s Jake Ceresna.

The middle linebacker is B.C.’s Darnell Sankey, the CFL’s top defensive player this season. The others are Montreal’s Tyrice Beverette and Toronto’s Adarius Pickett.

Ceresna and Beverette were named to the team for the third time.

Edmonton’s Tyrell Ford and Montreal’s Lorenzo Burns are the cornerbacks, while Kordell Jackson of the Elks and Winnipeg’s Evan Holm are the halfbacks.

B.C.’s Jackson Findlay earned the safety spot.

Edmonton’s Vincent Blanchard and Jake Julien secured the kicker and punter spots, respectively. Winnipeg kick returner Trey Vaval, the first player to win the CFL’s top special-teams award in consecutive seasons, earned his second straight All-CFL selection.

Montreal’s Louis-Phillipe Bourassa is the long snapper.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Chinese man flees Canada after threatening to ‘kill’ protesters outside consulate: Toronto police
stories.summary: Rui Chen, 41, is accused of assault, mischief and uttering threats against demonstrators outside China's consulate-general
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
An arrest warrant has been issued for a Chinese man who police said immediately fled Canada after allegedly threatening to shoot a woman protesting outside the Consulate-General of the People’s Republic of China in Toronto, an incident captured on video and shared on social media.

Officers were called to a reported assault outside the building on St. George Street just after 9 a.m. on Sept. 22, Toronto Police Service said in a news release.

It’s alleged the man, identified as 41-year-old Rui Chen of China, approached the Falun Dafa demonstrators, damaged their signs and banners, assaulted one of them and uttered death threats before fleeing.

Joel Chipkar, spokesperson for the Falun Dafa Association of Canada (Fdac), identified the alleged victims as Na Li and Ling Huan Geng, both of whom are practitioners of the spiritual movement rooted in kindness, compassion, and traditional values, which was founded in the early 1990s and has faced more than 27 years of persecution from China’s communist government.

The video, shot by Geng with English subtitles confirmed by police and the Fdac, shows Na confronting Chen as he tears down more of their banners on the sidewalk outside the consulate.

Is Canada becoming China? This happened in front of Chinese Consulate in Toronto around 9:20am Sep 22, 2027. Interestingly the man asked to take a video of his activity. pic.twitter.com/5k9DwxZDm6 — What is on Toronto (@WhatisonToronto) September 22, 2026

“This is Canada,” she tells him.

“Do you want to hit me,” asks Chen, who police said was wearing a “Li-Ning branded wind jacket with its logo on the front right chest and a red Chinese national flag embroidered” on the left.

“I hit you? Did I hit you,” she responds, prompting Chen to reply: “Let her hit me.”

He then grabs a banner staked into the ground and starts tugging at it as Na twice tells Geng to call 911. Chen encourages them to do so.

“Help me make a video,” Chen says to another person off camera as he struggles to destroy their signage, dropping a “f—k” at one point.

“I’m telling you, this is an illegal thing, don’t you know,” he says as Na approaches.

“It is an illegal thing or not, let the police judge,” she responds.

Chen then claims Na is touching him again and says he doesn’t care that it’s their property, “just remove it.”

“This is the Chinese consulate, don’t you know? Don’t you know what kind of place this is? This is Chinese soil, don’t you know,” he yells in Na’s face. “You’re breaking the anti-secession law.”

Rui Chen, 41, is described as five-foot-seven with a medium build, short black hair and prescription eyeglasses. He was last seen wearing a black Li-Ning branded wind jacket with its logo on the front right chest and a red Chinese national flag embroidered on the front left chest. Screenshot / Toronto Police Service

China’s anti-secession law, enacted in 2005, is aimed at opposing Taiwan’s independence and promoting unification under the “One China” principle.

“I can shoot you in China,” he continues.

As Na continues to interfere with him, Chen says, “I will kill you.”

“Do you believe I will kill you,” he asks her, again claiming the sidewalk as Chinese territory and continuing his efforts to dismantle their signage. Na, in the background, is on the phone with 911, telling the dispatcher Chen is destroying their property.

“You are the ones who are destroying,” Chen says as another man steps into frame, recording the incident on his phone.

Chipkar believes that person “was an accomplice” and likely an employee at the consulate, though no one has been able to identify him and he’s not being sought by police.

Chen then successfully dismantles one sign and starts to walk away as Na jogs up behind him to try to grab it, resulting in him spinning on her and warning her not to hit him.

“I hit you? You’re damaging my stuff,” she replies, after which the two exchange shoves and tussle briefly.

After their struggle, Chen pulls down another banner and accuses the women of being “up to shady crap here” before appearing to try to kick Geng. Geng told the Falun Dafa Infocenter she moved out of the way.

Chipkar, who arrived on the scene within an hour, said another man riding his bike stopped to assist the women and Chen, still holding one of the banners, called an Uber and left.

Witnesses on the scene recorded the car’s license plate, Chipkar explained, which Toronto police used to confirm with the Canada Border Services Agency that Chen had flown back to China that same afternoon.

Should he return to Canada, he will face charges of mischief under $5,000, assault and uttering threats.

It’s not clear if the accused is affiliated with the consulate or the Chinese government. National Post has contacted the Chinese Embassy in Canada for more information.

Na, according to the Infocenter, suffered a small cut to her chin during the incident.

Chipkar said both women fled China for fear of persecution as Falun Gong followers — Na more than a decade ago and Geng only recently as a refugee claimant. Both have family members who have been imprisoned for their opposition to communist rule.

“So they come to Canada, and all of a sudden, you know, they’re attacked just like they would be in China, right here on a Canadian sidewalk, where the assailant is screaming at them, telling them that he could kill them, kicking them, pushing them, and tearing down their banners, and also claiming that this sidewalk is Chinese territory,” Chipkar lamented.

While this incident was particularly alarming due to its aggressive and violent nature, Chipkar said instances of alleged transnational repression by the Chinese Communist Party are nothing new in Canada.

The Fdac has documented more than 100 incidents of surveillance, intimidation, threats and other tactics carried out in the regime’s name.

Earlier this year, all six Toronto shows by a performing arts company founded by adherents to the movement were cancelled due to “non-credible” bomb threats at the venue.

Shen Yun organizer says non-credible threats that cancelled its Toronto shows are part of a broader CCP-linked intimidation campaign. Shen Yun Performing Arts

In May, Global News reported that Chinese consular officials met with a city employee responsible for the Vancouver theatre where the group was scheduled to perform, with a source alleging the diplomat wanted the show cancelled.

Meanwhile, a report from international human rights group Safeguard Defenders this year identified 18 Chinese overseas associations participating as police monitoring stations in Canada. The report also cited additional research by an American think tank which uncovered 575 organizations linked to China’s United Front Workers Department in Canada, per CTV.

All this comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in China this week to meet with President Xi Jinping, explores deeper trade integration between the nations.

“And no matter how much trade is on the table, Carney must stand up to protect Canadians and Canada. I mean, otherwise, we lose our country,” said Chipkar.

Kenn Oliver is a web editor and writer for National Post. He is a career journalist of more than 20 years, the bulk of which was spent as a sports writer, business reporter and web editor for the Telegram in St. John's, N.L.

koliver@postmedia.com

“You are the ones who are destroying,” Chen says as another man steps into frame, recording the incident on his phone.
Chipkar believes that person “was an accomplice” and likely an employee at the consulate, though no one has been able to identify him and he’s not being sought by police.
Chen then successfully dismantles one sign and starts to walk away as Na jogs up behind him to try to grab it, resulting in him spinning on her and warning her not to hit him.
“I hit you? You’re damaging my stuff,” she replies, after which the two exchange shoves and tussle briefly.
Editor’s Picks

After their struggle, Chen pulls down another banner and accuses the women of being “up to shady crap here” before appearing to try to kick Geng. Geng told the Falun Dafa Infocenter she moved out of the way.
Chipkar, who arrived on the scene within an hour, said another man riding his bike stopped to assist the women and Chen, still holding one of the banners, called an Uber and left.

Witnesses on the scene recorded the car’s license plate, Chipkar explained, which Toronto police used to confirm with the Canada Border Services Agency that Chen had flown back to China that same afternoon.
Should he return to Canada, he will face charges of mischief under $5,000, assault and uttering threats.
It’s not clear if the accused is affiliated with the consulate or the Chinese government. National Post has contacted the Chinese Embassy in Canada for more information.
Na, according to the Infocenter, suffered a small cut to her chin during the incident.

Chipkar said both women fled China for fear of persecution as Falun Gong followers — Na more than a decade ago and Geng only recently as a refugee claimant. Both have family members who have been imprisoned for their opposition to communist rule.

“So they come to Canada, and all of a sudden, you know, they’re attacked just like they would be in China, right here on a Canadian sidewalk, where the assailant is screaming at them, telling them that he could kill them, kicking them, pushing them, and tearing down their banners, and also claiming that this sidewalk is Chinese territory,” Chipkar lamented.

While this incident was particularly alarming due to its aggressive and violent nature, Chipkar said instances of alleged transnational repression by the Chinese Communist Party are nothing new in Canada.
The Fdac has documented more than 100 incidents of surveillance, intimidation, threats and other tactics carried out in the regime’s name.
Earlier this year, all six Toronto shows by a performing arts company founded by adherents to the movement were cancelled due to “non-credible” bomb threats at the venue.
Shen Yun organizer says non-credible threats that cancelled its Toronto shows are part of a broader CCP-linked intimidation campaign. Shen Yun Performing Arts

In May, Global News reported that Chinese consular officials met with a city employee responsible for the Vancouver theatre where the group was scheduled to perform, with a source alleging the diplomat wanted the show cancelled.

Meanwhile, a report from international human rights group Safeguard Defenders this year identified 18 Chinese overseas associations participating as police monitoring stations in Canada. The report also cited additional research by an American think tank which uncovered 575 organizations linked to China’s United Front Workers Department in Canada, per CTV.
All this comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in China this week to meet with President Xi Jinping, explores deeper trade integration between the nations.
“And no matter how much trade is on the table, Carney must stand up to protect Canadians and Canada. I mean, otherwise, we lose our country,” said Chipkar.

Kenn Oliver is a web editor and writer for National Post. He is a career journalist of more than 20 years, the bulk of which was spent as a sports writer, business reporter and web editor for the Telegram in St. John's, N.L.

stories.title: London man charged after woman robbed, assaulted following exchange for sexual services
stories.summary: London police lay robbery, sex services charges against 22-year-old man
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A London man has been charged after a woman was allegedly assaulted and robbed following an exchange for sexual services, police say.

The investigation began on Oct. 19 after London police received information about an incident that had reportedly occurred about a week earlier.

According to police, a woman arranged to meet a man at a residence in London’s Old East Village after communicating with him online. Investigators allege the man attended the residence and provided money in exchange for sexual services.

Police said that after the encounter, the man demanded the money back. When the woman refused, he allegedly attempted to take the money from her and assaulted her before fleeing the scene. The woman suffered minor injuries.

Members of the London Police Service Human Trafficking Unit identified a suspect through the investigation.

On Nov. 16, police arrested Sarkes Khawaja, 22, of London.

He has been charged with robbery and obtaining sexual services for consideration.

Police said investigators believe there May be additional victims and have released an image of the accused as part of the ongoing investigation. Anyone who May have had contact with him, or who has information related to the case, is asked to contact police.

Khawaja remains in custody and was expected to reappear in a London court on Nov. 19 in relation to the charges.

stories.title: Kelowna’s Apple Bowl expansion project moves forward despite parking concerns
stories.summary: Residents urged council to reject the development permit and parking variance, which reduces the required number of parking stalls by more than half.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Plans to expand Kelowna’s Apple Bowl stadium are moving forward following a public hearing Tuesday, despite concerns from nearby residents about parking and disruptions during major events.

The proposed expansion will increase spectator capacity to 5,000 seats, more than doubling the stadium’s current capacity.

But residents say the neighbourhood is already feeling the pressure.

“We experienced major disruptions during the CFL game this year,” one resident told council.

Others described problems during this summer’s Touchdown Kelowna events, including blocked driveways and spectators entering private properties.

“People couldn’t access their driveways,” another area resident said.

One speaker described what they say were serious intrusions into their neighbourhood.

“We had intoxicated people walking through our neighborhood, some of which were urinating in our backyards,’ said the resident. “These are serious intrusions into people’s homes.”

Residents urged council to reject the development permit and parking variance, which reduces the required number of parking stalls by more than half.

Coun. Les Bellamy was the only councillor to vote against the proposal, pointing to concerns about the city’s parking strategy.

“I do have concerns around the parking strategy and part of that was that we’re moving forward with this application without signed contracts for the parking program,” Bellamy said.

He also questioned how the stadium could accommodate a significant increase in spectators without adding parking on site.

“What we’re looking at right now is a 170 per cent increase to the seating capacity of the stadium with zero additional parking on site,” Bellamy said.

Bellamy said he supports revitalizing the Apple Bowl but believes agreements with third-party property owners for off-site parking should have been secured first.

“It’s a little bit of a chicken-and-egg scenario, so my question is, if those don’t come to fruition, what is the back-up plan?” he asked.

Kelowna Mayor Tom Dyas, however, is confident an adequate parking strategy can be developed, including arrangements with nearby businesses to use their parking lots during evenings and weekends.

“If they, those those individuals have the opportunity of looking at creating revenue from parking stalls that would be otherwise empty at that point in time, I believe those negotiations should end up to be pretty positive,” Dyas said.

The city says it May also consider residential parking permits to help ensure people living in the neighbourhood aren’t left competing with eventgoers for parking.

stories.title: Former colleges and universities minister refuses to answer Osap questions
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's former minister of colleges and universities, who presided over the file for three years until 2024, is refusing to answer questions about a growing Ontario Student Assistance Program scandal.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario’s former minister of colleges and universities, who presided over the file for three years until 2024, is refusing to answer questions about a growing Ontario Student Assistance Program scandal.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press shows massive growth in Osap usage at a relatively small number of career colleges over the past few years, and the government now says it suspects potential fraud and has referred the matter to the provincial police.

The current minister of colleges and universities, Nolan Quinn, has responded to dozens of questions about Osap in the legislature since it returned from a long break in late October, but former minister Jill Dunlop has not responded to multiple questions from the opposition or reporters about her role.

While she was minister, the province extended a pandemic-era policy of allowing online-only programs at career colleges to qualify for Osap funding — a policy Quinn is now reversing as he says those courses are where a lot of red flags arose.

Ford’s government initially reacted to Osap’s problems by slashing grants, which hurt blameless public institutions and their students.

Industry association Career Colleges Ontario says it started warning the government about rapid rises in Osap growth at certain schools in four different meetings with the government in 2023, which is when Dunlop was minister.

When asked by reporters Thursday after question period about those warnings, Dunlop only spoke to direct questions to Quinn instead.

“That really needs to be referred to the minister of colleges and universities,” she said while walking toward an elevator.

Dunlop would not stop to take questions. One staffer tried to shield the minister from being filmed.

Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser tried for several days this week to ask Dunlop questions in the legislature, but Quinn answered them.

“I called on the current minister to resign,” Fraser said Wednesday in the legislature.

“I think that the former minister holds as much responsibility as the current minister and that she should resign as well. It’s an absolute mess that they’ve made of thousands and thousands of people’s lives turned upside down.”

Quinn announced in early October that the preliminary findings of an ongoing Kpmg audit uncovered serious and widespread concerns about the integrity of Osap in the career college sector. As a result, he said, he was pausing Osap loan payments to all career college students until the audit is completed.

Some colleges have started laying off staff and have warned they May have to close, while some students are unable to pay for rent and groceries, let alone tuition, since they had been counting on their Osap approved loans for living expenses while they studied.

Fraser also noted that in 2022 Dunlop’s chief of staff left government and became CEO of Career Colleges Ontario, a role he left in early 2024, according to LinkedIn.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said it is unacceptable for Dunlop, who is the current minister of emergency preparedness and response, to try to dodge questions simply because she is in a new role.

“No minister should be absolved of what happened under their watch,” Stiles said. “She has to take responsibility as well as the minister of universities and colleges.”

Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said everyone in the Ford government, especially someone who was a minister of this file, needs to be held responsible for upending students’ lives due to the current Osap mess.

“I think this government doesn’t want to be held accountable,” he said.

Quinn earlier this year drastically reduced the amount of Osap grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive, while restricting career college students to Osap loans.

He cited “unsustainable” costs, but a freedom-of-information request by The Canadian Press showed that 95 per cent of the year-over-year growth in 2024-25 was due to career colleges.

A subsequent freedom-of-information request by The Canadian Press showed that most of that growth was concentrated among a small number of schools. Just seven career colleges accounted for about $385 million in Osap grants in 2024-25, the same amount that went to students at all of Ontario’s publicly funded colleges.

A lot of the Kpmg audit’s concerns have centred around asynchronous, online-only programs, Quinn has said.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the province temporarily extended Osap eligibility to students in online and/or asynchronous programs, then later made it permanent.

The government this week tabled legislation to again make online-only programs at private career colleges ineligible for Osap.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Weapons detection technology adds another layer of safety at London, Ont. hospitals
stories.summary: A weapons detection system at London Health Sciences Centre has screened more than 915,000 people and flagged 8,800 potential threat items since it was introduced last year.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A weapons detection system at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has screened more than 915,000 people and flagged 8,800 potential threat items since it was introduced last year.

The AI-powered, touchless technology was installed at University Hospital in London, Ont. in April 2025 and Victoria Hospital in May 2025 as part of LHSC’s efforts to strengthen security at its emergency departments.

Between April 2025 and September 2026, the system recorded 8,800 threat items, including approximately 4,200 knives or knife-like objects.

Other items detected include brass knuckles and pepper spray. The system scans people as they enter the emergency department, identifying objects that could pose a safety risk. When an item is flagged, security staff are alerted and can conduct additional screening.

LHSC says the initiative followed two high-profile incidents: a shooting outside Victoria Hospital’s emergency department in December 2024, which prompted a hospital-wide response, and a stabbing outside a Halifax hospital in January 2025.

Chris Askew, LHSC’s director of facilities management, says the system is helping change people’s behaviour and reduce the number of items being brought into the hospital.

“We saw average of 7.1 contraband items to the lowest average that we saw in September 2026 at 2.77 between our two sites,” Askew said.

“So the implementation has done its job in decreasing, and we continue to see that downward trend of items or people leaving them at home and changing their behaviours and what they bring to the hospital,” Askew said.

While LHSC says many of the items detected May not have been brought into the hospital with the intention of causing harm, officials say removing the potential risk is important.

Sarah Muto, LHSC’s interim vice-president of facilities and support services, says the system gives security staff an opportunity to speak with people carrying flagged items.

“Knives and items that are not contraband are taken away and potentially given back to the individuals when they’re finished their appointment or finishing visiting their loved one,” Muto said.

She says the goal is not to assume everyone carrying a flagged item intends to hurt someone, but to ensure potentially dangerous objects do not enter the hospital.

Muto says the technology is one part of a broader approach to workplace and patient safety that includes security cameras, panic buttons and de-escalation training for staff.

She describes the approach as a “Swiss cheese model,” with multiple layers of protection working together to reduce the chance of an incident.

“Our staff are very happy to see that we’re adding an additional layer of safety to protect them, the patients and the visitor,” she said.

Askew says there have been no situations involving detected items that have escalated to the point of requiring intervention. He adds that LHSC works closely with London police and has procedures in place should a more serious situation arise.

The hospital says the system also provides reassurance to patients and visitors that people entering the emergency department have been screened.

LHSC is reminding the public to leave knives and other potentially dangerous items at home when visiting the hospital to help maintain a safer environment for patients, visitors and staff.

stories.title: Cell service concerns span South Okanagan as locals call for action
stories.summary: Dropped calls spotty data are raising concerns about whether people can reach services when they need them most, concerns brought into sharper focus by the wildfires this summer
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
For residents across the South Okanagan and Similkameen, unreliable cellphone service is more than an inconvenience.

Dropped calls, dead zones and spotty data are raising concerns about whether people can reach emergency services when they need them most- concerns brought into sharper focus by the wildfires this summer, which highlighted just how important reliable cell service is during an emergency.

That concern is especially significant for Tim Roberts, a paramedic who works in the region and relies on reliable cellphone service while working or when trying to reach a loved one.

“Sometimes when I’m on an important call, we just lose contact with the people we’re speaking to,” Roberts said.

“And in my line of work, it’s important to have good, reliable communication sources for the work that we do.”

Roberts says the problem isn’t new, but he believes cellphone coverage has actually gotten worse as newer generations of technology have been introduced. He says areas that once had reliable service are now experiencing dropped calls and dead zones.

“It’s bad and it’s got worse,” Roberts said, pointing to the shift from 3G to 5G technology as one factor he believes has contributed to the problem.

The issue has become prominent enough in Penticton that city council asked staff to investigate residents’ complaints.

But the review does not provide a definitive answer about whether Penticton’s coverage is worse than other communities. The city did not conduct an in-depth comparison with other municipalities, meaning the extent of the problem remains unclear. The city hopes that asking the right questions and continuing to look into the issue can eventually bring the city and service providers together to get on the right track and tackle the problem once and for all.

For Roberts, the stakes are higher than simply having a dropped phone call.

“It’s a huge safety issue, especially of people travelling on the highways today,” he said.

That concern is particularly relevant in a region where people regularly travel long stretches between communities.

Roberts says reliable cellphone coverage has become essential for emergency communication, particularly during situations such as vehicle crashes or wildfires.

He points to the region’s past experience with emergency response as a reminder of how important communication can be.

Meanwhile, cellphone providers are making some upgrades.

Telus says it has been investing in new infrastructure across the region to improve coverage.

The company says it has built one new tower south of Summerland over the past two years.

Telus says its newest Penticton tower came online October 30, improving coverage and network performance in the city’s north end while expanding access to 5G+ service.

The company is also planning another tower in Penticton’s south end, with additional tower builds expected in the region in 2027.

Telus says it is also upgrading existing wireless sites each year to improve network performance and keep up with demand.

Bell did not provide information on what it plans to do to address the ongoing concerns. And with so many communities across the South Okanagan and Similkameen still reporting gaps in service, it appears there is still a long way to go before residents can feel confident in their cellphone coverage.

“You pay to have them work. Let’s make sure they work,” said Roberts

But while the coverage concerns remain, service providers say improvements are coming; now, residents are waiting to see when they’ll actually feel them.

stories.title: Widening Canadian, U.S. rates weighing on loonie
stories.summary: The Canadian dollar has been falling in recent weeks, now trading around 69.88 cents U.S. as of Thursday
stories.author: Daniel Johnson
stories.content:
Financial experts say a diverging interest rate path between Canada and the U.S. is weighing on the loonie, which has dipped below 70 cents US.

The Canadian dollar has been falling in recent weeks, closing at 69.85 cents US on Thursday.

“The essential driver of the Canadian dollar exchange rate has been that widening interest rate differential, the spread between short-term U.S. interest rates and short-term Canadian interest rates,” said Shaun Osborne, chief FX strategist at Scotiabank, in an interview.

“U.S. interest rates have moved up quite sharply. Canadian interest rates have moved up as well, but not quite as much.”

The Bank of Canada’s benchmark interest rate stands at 2.5 per cent, while in the U.S., the Federal Reserve’s target range is 3.75 per cent to four per cent.

Osborne said U.S. interest rates are expected to rise over the next few months.

Minutes released from the Fed’s October meeting suggest it’s likely the central bank will lift its key interest rate by a quarter point next month. Meanwhile, financial market odds of a Bank of Canada rate hike in December stood at roughly 65 per cent as of Thursday, according to Lseg Data & Analytics.

Osborne said the decline in the loonie’s relative value is also due to strength in the U.S. dollar, which has been pressuring a number of currencies.

“From our perspective, the Canadian dollar looks relatively cheap and we think it offers some value here,” he said.

“But against that you have this very strong underlying trend momentum in the U.S. dollar, with the focus on interest rates. It’s probably going to keep the U.S. dollar trading on the stronger side in the near term at least.”

Looking further ahead, Osborne said U.S. interest rates are likely to fall in late 2027 and into 2028, which should bring “some meaningful compression in that yield differential,” so there is a more positive longer-term outlook for the Canadian dollar.

Sadiq Adatia, chief investment officer of BMO Global Asset Management, said in an interview that trade uncertainty is also a big overhang on Canada’s currency.

“The question mark there still remains that we don’t have a deal yet and people are not likely to be investing significantly in Canada, which means they’re not buying Canadian dollars. That puts a little bit more of a cloud over the Canadian dollar,” he said.

Sal Guatieri, senior economist at BMO, said in a note Wednesday that the Canadian dollar was at its “lowest ebb against the big dollar since March 2025,” when the trade dispute with the U.S. began.

Adatia said the U.S. economy is also seeing greater strength with more money flowing into it compared with Canada.

Once Canada and the U.S. hash out a trade agreement, Adatia said the loonie could start to regain ground.

Adatia said currencies often trade above or below their fair value due partly to psychological considerations.

“Now that it’s broken through the 70 cent barrier, there probably is a threshold there that it’s heading lower from that standpoint. Normally, you don’t see it break through a barrier and then just come back again; it goes a little bit further down,” he said.

– With files from The Associated Press.

stories.title: Susan Knabe appointed dean of Western’s Faculty of Information and Media Studies
stories.summary: Susan Knabe has been appointed dean of Western University’s Faculty of Information and Media Studies bringing vast experience to the role.
stories.author: Keri Ferguson
stories.content:
Susan Knabe has been appointed dean of the Faculty of Information and Media Studies (Fims) for a term extending to July 2031.

Knabe has served as interim dean since July 2025. She said the role gave her a chance to think more deeply about the faculty’s future, sparking her decision to pursue the deanship.

“I’m a curious person. I’m excited by the possibilities for Fims and wanted to help actively plan how we can carry great projects forward,” Knabe said.

She previously served as Fims associate dean, undergraduate, for more than a decade. In that role, she led several key initiatives, including the development and launch of the Creative Arts and Production program, in collaboration with colleagues in the Faculty of Arts and Humanities and the Don Wright Faculty of Music.

Florentine Strzelczyk, Western’s provost and vice-president (academic), recognized Knabe’s institutional knowledge and cross-campus collaboration on numerous governance committees, working groups and as a founding member of Western’s equity, diversity and inclusion advisory council.

“Susan has contributed greatly to the continued growth and evolution of Fims, while enriching the Western community as a whole,” Strzelczyk said. “I am delighted Fims’ faculty, students and staff will continue to benefit from her knowledge, commitment and leadership.”

Knabe steps into her new role just ahead of the faculty’s 30th anniversary next year. She describes the technological change since Fims was founded in 1997 as “almost unfathomable.”

“We went from the ‘information superhighway’ to the dot-com bubble, Web 2.0, social media, and now we’re talking about generative AI,” she said.

As Knabe considers how the needs of the Faculty have changed over the past 30 years, she’s mindful of the common themes that still resonate.

“Our research and how we prepare our students to go forward is still anchored in the same pillars as in 1997, which is how technology, information and media shape individuals and societies,” she said.

That means asking hard questions, and Knabe said Fims is well positioned to do it. While some researchers are examining how technology can affect people’s lives in harmful ways that go unseen, others are exploring how it can advance social justice.

Knabe points to interdisciplinary projects, including one that examines AI systems designed to collect and analyze data about human emotions and whether they are accurate, ethical, useful or socially beneficial. Another uses ground-penetrating radar and geographic information systems to help locate unmarked graves in postwar El Salvador, providing evidence of state-sanctioned violence while preserving historical memory for marginalized communities.

“Our work includes being open to the possibilities of technology and underscoring the importance of information in our society right now,” Knabe said. “I’m happy to be in a position where I can help faculty think through opportunities to do so and take action.”

As Knabe reflects on her unique path to the dean’s office, she acknowledges the unexpected turns that led her from life sciences to Fims.

As an undergraduate, she pursued a double-honours degree in chemistry and biology, followed by three years of medical school at the University of Toronto.

Following the death of her brother in 1993, Knabe returned to university, this time at Trent, where she enrolled in a literary analysis class and a course on Shakespeare, drawn by her love for the playwright, cultivated during cherished childhood trips to the Stratford Festival.

“Science is fascinating, and I’m good at it, but that’s when I fell in love with critical theory,” Knabe said.

She went on to build her own degree in literature, gender and sexuality before completing her master’s at Trent and her PhD at Macquarie University in Australia.

Her graduate research focused on HIV/Aids, with her master’s thesis analyzing how Canadian medical literature presented HIV/Aids and queer identities during the first decade of the epidemic. Her PhD explored how cultural producers responded to the mass deaths of the HIV/Aids epidemic by drawing on the historical trauma of the Holocaust.

The work let Knabe carry her medical and scientific grounding into a critical-theory examination of gender, sexuality, race and class.

“I’m an interdisciplinary scholar, and I struggle against disciplinary boundaries,” she said. “So it makes perfect sense that I found my way to Fims.”

In her more than two decades at Western, some of Knabe’s most gratifying experiences have come from working with undergraduates as associate dean and with the graduate students she continues to supervise.

“It’s an amazing privilege to see a student you’ve worked with presenting a good defence. I get to watch them enter a conversation with experts who have read their work carefully, and observe as they ‘solo the plane,’” she said.

Knabe also sees students as the greatest resource to help Fims navigate the new realities of our rapidly changing world.

“We sometimes assume we know what matters to students, but I say it’s crucial to ask them,” said Knabe, who was instrumental in piloting a supported learning group model for first-year undergraduates. “My mantra in the classroom is to meet students where they’re at. To do that, you have to listen, and when you do, you learn a lot.”

stories.title: U.S. sanctions Canadian branch of Italian mafia, Australian biker gang
stories.summary: The United States on Thursday issued sanctions targeting the alleged Canadian branch of a major Italian mafia group and one of the oldest biker gangs in Australia, with both accused of running global drug trafficking operations.
stories.author: AFP Staff
stories.content:
Washington -- The United States on Thursday issued sanctions targeting the alleged Canadian branch of a major Italian mafia group and one of the oldest biker gangs in Australia, with both accused of running global drug trafficking operations.

In a statement, the U.S. Treasury said the sanctions targeted “a powerful transnational faction of the ‘Ndrangheta” mafia group in the Toronto area .

The faction is so powerful that “it dictates events in Italy from across the ocean, including the ‘Ndrangheta locale in Siderno, Calabria, where the organization originated,” the statement said.

The new sanctions target six individuals identified as key figures of the gang in the Toronto area, alongside three family members of one of the leaders.

Calabria is one of the poorest regions in Italy and the ‘Ndrangheta is the most powerful and richest Italian mafia, due to its strong grip on cocaine trafficking in Europe.

The ‘Ndrangheta is one of Italy’s three main organized crime groups, alongside Sicily’s Cosa Nostra and the Camorra, centered around the Naples area.

The ‘Ndrangheta’s Canadian branch is also accused of engaging in money laundering and extortion.

The Treasury said it was also targeting the Comanchero Motorcycle Club criminal gang, said to be based in Australia, New Zealand and Spain, but with branches in more than a dozen countries.

The U.S. government alleges that the gang has partnerships with South American drug cartels including the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (Cjng).

“The Comancheros facilitate shipments of cocaine from South America to North America, Europe, and Asia, working with the Sinaloa Cartel, Cjng, and Clan del Golfo,” the U.S. Treasury said.

It also accused the group of involvement in assassinations, arms trafficking and money laundering.

“The Sinaloa Cartel has been known to send ‘sleeper cells’ to Australia to facilitate local drug distribution and establish contacts with the Comancheros,” the U.S. Treasury said.

The new sanctions target an individual in Australia identified as the gang’s “world president” and a Spain-based “world commander.”

Three other individuals are also named in the new sanctions.

The Comancheros are best known for the so-called Milperra Massacre in 1984, when a fight with the rival Bandidos escalated into a gun battle that claimed seven lives.

stories.title: AI used to create virtual models of Canada’s 25 most wanted criminals
stories.summary: The national program encourages police and the public to help find fugitives
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Police agencies from across Canada have used artificial intelligence to create virtual models of the country’s 25 most wanted criminals moving as they would in real life.

The AI models of the fugitives appeared crossing hands and moving their heads, wearing casual shirts or hoodies and pants, ON a large screen at the Toronto police college while police announced the newest list in the Bolo Program.

The national program encourages police and the public to help find the fugitives.

Max Langlois, the program’s executive director, said it uses new ways every year to make sure people are on the lookout for the most wanted suspects on the list.

“This year with the help of AI, as you can see, we bring our top 25 fugitives into this room life-sized, moving as they might if you saw them on the street, at the supermarket, at the airport or anywhere else,” he said.

“If it feels uncomfortable, that’s the point.”

Satinderjeet Singh, who is also known as Goldy Brar, topped this year’s list. He is wanted by Winnipeg police on a Canada-wide warrant for what police say was an “execution-style murder” of 39-year-old Sukhdool Singh Gill on Sept. 20, 2023.

Winnipeg police deputy chief Cam Mackid said police are offering $250,000 for any information that leads to the arrest of 32-year-old Singh, who originally entered Canada on a student visa in 2017 and is now known to be a high-ranking member of the Lawrence Bishnoi Gang, which Canada designated a terrorist group.

“This is an India-based transnational organized crime syndicate,” Mackid said.

“(Singh) is currently wanted on charges of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder.”

Mackid said Singh has lived in California and various parts of Canada and he is now wanted in India, Canada and the United States.

“(He) has been wanted for some time by Indian authorities for a murder that occurred in that country in 2022,” Mackid said

“In July of this year, (he) was indicted by a U.S. federal grand jury in Los Angeles on numerous charges. And in September, he was added to the Fbi’s 10 most wanted list with a substantial reward.”

Kyle Douglas Prouse, who allegedly shot a security guard inside Fairview Mall in Toronto in April before fleeing the area, held the No. 2 spot on the list of Canada’s 25 most wanted suspects.

Police are offering a $100,000 reward for information leading to his arrest.

Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw said Prouse has ties to Toronto and Vancouver and is believed to be armed and dangerous.

Six of the top 25 most wanted fugitives have connections to Toronto, including Cody Rudifo, No. 3 on the list, who is wanted in the fatal shooting of 34-year-old Christopher Gordon last month in the Lawrence Heights area of the city, Demkiw said.

“The Bolo Program has shown time and time again what happens when police and the public work together,” Demkiw said.

“Since 2018, 19 of the 28 Toronto cases featured by Bolo have ended in an arrest, including the case that held last year’s No. 1 spot.”

“Bolo” is a common term used by police forces that stands for “be on the lookout.”
