'If you have enough money, you’re going to find someone to do whatever you want.' — Dr. Ian MacArthur, a plastic surgeon

Navigate

Francis Scarpaleggia, Speaker of the House of Commons speaks during the swearing-in of the new pages in the House of Commons on Sept. 20, 2026. (Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia)

Christopher Nardi,Sarah Ritchie

November 19, 2026 at 12:44 p.m.

Ottawa — The Speaker of the House of Commons has a message for professional regulatory bodies wanting to investigate an MP for comments made in Parliament: get lost.

In a first-of-its-kind decision issued Tuesday, Speaker Francis Scarpaleggia warned professional regulatory authorities against investigating a member of Parliament for comments under the auspices of parliamentary privilege.

“Members should not fear professional disciplinary measures will be imposed because of the ideas they express during parliamentary proceedings,” Scarpaleggia told the House.

“Members must have complete confidence that they enjoy freedom of speech in our work, and such investigations could have a chilling effect on members of professional bodies. I find that unacceptable.”

The decision also confirmed that an MP’s comments contained in a supplementary or dissenting opinion of a Commons committee report are also covered by parliamentary privilege, which gives legislators immunity for actions undertaken as part of their duties.

In an unusual twist, Scarpaleggia was ruling on concerns raised by Conservative MP Matt Strauss over a complaint to the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario levelled against MP Marcus Powlowski, a Liberal.

At issue were comments by Powlowski on medical assistance in dying, in a supplementary opinion added to a parliamentary committee’s study of Maid for mental illness.

The committee, which he co-chaired with Sen. Yonah Martin, recommended the government indefinitely exclude people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness from accessing Maid.

Powlowski’s written opinion included a section titled “Why do we try to prevent suicide?” drawing on his experience as an ER doctor to argue that society ought to have the power to intervene when a person is suicidal, including by institutionalizing a patient at risk of taking their own life.

In that section, he also wrote that “the option to end one’s life remains, irrespective of Maid, readily available in Canada,” and said there are “painless options readily available” such as narcotics like fentanyl, which he said are easily accessed.

That comment was the basis of a complaint filed with the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, according to a report last month by the Canadian Press. The complainant, Claire Brosseau, argued to the College that the statements “identify and normalize a lethal means, present a medically misleading account of opioid poisoning, and create a foreseeable risk of harm to vulnerable readers.”

Brosseau is also the lead plaintiff in a case before the Federal Court in which Dying With Dignity Canada is arguing that barring people with mental illness from accessing assisted dying violates their Charter rights.

Powlowski was given until Oct. 22 to respond to the complaint before an investigator would refer it to a review committee, according to the CP story.

The media report raised the hackles of fellow physician Strauss, who complained to the Speaker that the complaint and regulator’s investigation was an attack on Powlowski’s parliamentary privilege.

Strauss argued that the regulator’s investigation could set a “dangerous precedent” if it went unchallenged by Parliament.

“What good is the freedom of speech if it is only meant to protect the things that we can all agree on or, worse, that only those in positions of authority agree on?” he said.

“This is why I, a Conservative MP, am rising today on this question of privilege about something concerning a political opponent who sits on the Liberal benches.”

Strauss said in an interview that parliamentary privilege is an “absolutely sacrosanct constitutional principle in Canada,” and one that cannot be allowed to erode.

“Being a physician myself, I am aware of how much anxiety and stress this sort of college complaint can cause someone,” he said.

Strauss did have a conversation with Powlowski — his “favourite Liberal MP” — before raising the matter with the Speaker on Oct. 20.

The Speaker’s response, he said, was “even better than I hoped for.”

“We’re not going to have good public policy if you try to chill the speech of the people who are in the best possible place to speak openly and make decisions,” he said.

Powlowski did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Scarpaleggia said in his decision that he asked the House of Commons law clerk to write to the Ontario regulator expressing his concerns about the investigation.

But he stopped short of saying that the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario breached Powlowski’s privilege pending the outcome of the investigation.

Ultimately, Scarpaleggia will likely never have to rule on that.

In a statement to National Post, the college’s spokesperson Laura Zilke confirmed that the regulator was aware of the Speaker’s decision.

“I can confirm that Cpso is not currently investigating Dr. Marcus Powlowski in relation to this matter,” Zilke said.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government. Reach him on Signal: ChrisNardi.01 cnardi@postmedia.com

stories.title: Many bereaved by suicide feel satisfied with life, Quebec survey shows
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - A new Quebec survey has found that many respondents who lost a loved one to suicide can have conflicting responses to the tragedy.
stories.author: Katrine Desautels The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - A new Quebec survey has found that many respondents who lost a loved one to suicide can have conflicting responses to the tragedy.

The survey revealed 56 per cent of people who had someone close to them die by suicide had reported experiencing suicidal thoughts at some point in their lives and that 20 per cent of these respondents had experienced suicidal thoughts over the past year.

The survey also found that 56 per cent of respondents reported feeling satisfied with their lives today.

The numbers highlight the complexities of the grieving process for those who have lost a loved one to suicide, according to Cécile Bardon, psychology professor at l’Université du Québec à Montréal.

Bardon, the director of a research centre on suicide and end-of-life ethics, says the survey also shows how feelings of grief and of satisfaction are not mutually exclusive.

“You can go through something that is emotionally profound and deeply troubling, yet still be able to experience good moments along the way,” Bardon said in an interview.

Three suicide prevention groups surveyed over 304 Quebecers who had someone close to them die by suicide between September and October 2026 as part of the study.

The report notes that its results are not representative of the general population of those bereaved by suicide but provides a first insight into their experiences and needs.

Grief stemming from a suicide is long-lasting, said Hugo Fournier, president and CEO of a Quebec suicide prevention association.

“It’s unique because those who are grieving can find a certain balance in their lives while still suffering. They May experience distress and despair and, at the same time, feel satisfied with certain aspects of their lives,” he said.

Some people express guilt over feeling fulfilled in certain aspects of their lives — at work or socially — while still bearing the burden of grief over a loved one who died by suicide, Fournier adds.

According to the researchers, grief related to suicide often brings about regret, difficulty understanding what led to the act, and even anger toward the person who died.

“It’s very difficult to reconcile that anger with the sorrow we feel and the guilt we experience. It results in a grieving process that can be very, very complex,” Bardon explained.

She added that a “core group of people” will experience traumatic grief, meaning they are severely impacted by the event.

According to the study, an average of about 80 people are affected by each suicide. These include the person’s loved ones — family and friends — but also co-workers, classmates, and perhaps teammates on a sports team or in a theatre troupe.

First responders, such as police officers, paramedics, or medical staff, May be confronted with several suicides in a year. They are exposed not only to death but also to the distress of the bereaved.

“Their coping mechanisms must also be supported so that they can continue to fulfil their role as a conduit for consistent and effective information to those who are grieving,” said Bardon.

“A first responder who is deeply affected and shaken by what they’re experiencing May become someone who clings rigidly to procedures, withdraws into themselves, and fails to show empathy toward the family,” she added.

In fact, the survey highlights a need for faster access to support and resources following the death.

The report shows that 43 per cent of participants received support services they considered acceptable within the month following the death, but 46 per cent would have liked to receive them more quickly. Another 14 per cent reported not receiving services they considered acceptable.

Fournier believes that at the critical moment when the event occurs, front line responders do act quickly and suicide prevention centres typically offer support.

However, followup care needs to be improved, said Bardon.

While the bereaved are often well-surrounded very soon after the death, “it’s when everyone goes back to their normal lives that they find themselves all alone,” she noted.

Among the resources used, support groups are the most highly valued. Online discussion forums are also becoming increasingly popular, said Fournier.

Some rather unexpected sources of comfort were also mentioned in the survey, such as the coroner, who often speaks with the family to prepare a report. The exchange of information between the coroner and the bereaved can potentially have a positive effect and shed light on the circumstances around the death, said Bardon.

Fournier hopes that the survey will help those who have lost a loved one by suicide feel less alone and relieve their feelings of guilt, especially on international suicide bereavement day, which takes place Nov. 21.

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24-7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

In fact, the survey highlights a need for faster access to support and resources following the death.

The report shows that 43 per cent of participants received support services they considered acceptable within the month following the death, but 46 per cent would have liked to receive them more quickly. Another 14 per cent reported not receiving services they considered acceptable.
Fournier believes that at the critical moment when the event occurs, front line responders do act quickly and suicide prevention centres typically offer support.
However, followup care needs to be improved, said Bardon.
While the bereaved are often well-surrounded very soon after the death, “it’s when everyone goes back to their normal lives that they find themselves all alone,” she noted.
Among the resources used, support groups are the most highly valued. Online discussion forums are also becoming increasingly popular, said Fournier.

Some rather unexpected sources of comfort were also mentioned in the survey, such as the coroner, who often speaks with the family to prepare a report. The exchange of information between the coroner and the bereaved can potentially have a positive effect and shed light on the circumstances around the death, said Bardon.

Fournier hopes that the survey will help those who have lost a loved one by suicide feel less alone and relieve their feelings of guilt, especially on international suicide bereavement day, which takes place Nov. 21.

stories.title: London man added to list of Canada’s most wanted
stories.summary: OPP said Filmon Fesshaghirgis, 28, of London, was named No. 14 on the list. Police said he is known to frequent London and the Greater Toronto Area.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A London man wanted in connection with a homicide investigation in Bolton has been added to Canada’s 25 Most Wanted list.

OPP said Filmon Fesshaghirgis, 28, of London, was named No. 14 on the list. Police said he is known to frequent London and the Greater Toronto Area.

The case stems from a series of shootings that began on Nov. 12, 2020, when York Regional Police responded to a shooting at a business on Steeles Avenue West in Vaughan around 6:30 p.m. One person was taken to hospital.

More than two months later, ON Jan. 18, 2021, officers with the Caledon OPP responded to reports of a shooting at a residence in Bolton around 12:30 p.m. Two people suffered gunshot wounds, including the victim from the Vaughan shooting. Police said Giovanni Costa, 65, of Bolton, was found dead at the scene.

Police said five people have been arrested since the investigation began.

A Canada-wide warrant has been issued for Fesshaghirgis, who is wanted on charges of first-degree murder, two counts of attempted murder and conspiracy to commit murder.

Investigators are urging members of the public not to approach him and to contact police immediately if he is seen.

The Ontario government is offering a $50,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the person or persons responsible for Costa’s murder.

The investigation remains ongoing by the Caledon OPP crime unit under the direction of the OPP Criminal Investigation Branch, in conjunction with the Office of the Chief Coroner and the Ontario Forensic Pathology Service. OPP Forensic Identification Services has also assisted with the investigation.

Anyone with information about Fesshaghirgis’ whereabouts is asked to contact OPP at 1-888-310-1122.

stories.title: B.C. Environmental Assessment Office pauses review of Massey Tunnel project
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia's Environmental Assessment Office has paused its review of the Massey Tunnel replacement project at the request of the province, saying it "understands the rationale" related to the transition to a new government.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - British Columbia’s Environmental Assessment Office has paused its review of the Massey Tunnel replacement project at the request of the province, saying it “understands the rationale” related to the transition to a new government.

A letter posted to the project page on the office’s website shows the Transportation Ministry and the Transportation Investment Corporation asked for the pause given the interregnum period after the B.C. Conservatives toppled the NDP government in the Oct. 24 snap election.

stories.title: Alberta proposes provincial law giving it power to remove municipal bike lanes
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta's government is moving to give itself the power to rip up municipal bike lanes and curb future cycling infrastructure.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - The Alberta government moved Thursday to give itself the power to rip up municipal bike lanes and curb future cycling infrastructure.

Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen proposed legislation that, if passed, would prohibit any new bicycle lanes from taking away road space from vehicles, unless he approves them.

Dreeshen said the bill is in response to concern that some bike lanes reduce road capacity and parking, increase congestion and sometimes get in the way of emergency vehicles.

“This (means) working with both Edmonton and Calgary to identify where those bike lanes don’t make sense,” he said.

The bill dictates municipalities foot the cost for bike lane removals.

Dreeshen said the goal is to use traffic assessments to identify troublesome bike lanes. They could be removed when road maintenance is already scheduled, he said, so it’s cheaper.

When asked whether he believes the provincial government knows better than municipal governments on the issue, Dreeshen stressed that he wants to collaborate with them.

“We want to make sure the road networks in cities, in counties and towns work with our highway, with our provincial highway network.”

He added that the province’s two largest cities “have extensive budgets for bike lanes.”

Dreeshen said he supports cyclists being able to move around Calgary and Edmonton, “but it can’t cripple the road capacity in both those cities,” he said.

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas has spoken out against the province intervening, saying it should instead focus on more important issues.

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said Thursday the legislation will make roads less safe, force property tax increases and undermine the voices of Edmontonians.

“The legislation doesn’t say you must own a car, but that’s what it actually means,” he said.

“What’s the point of local governments, if (provincial politicians) want to have that level of attention paid to local roadways?”

Knack said professional engineers and experts led bike lane network building based on evidence and that removing lanes installed in the last decade could cost $150 million.

He said detailed traffic information was provided to Dreeshen.

And after meeting face to face with the government, Knack said, he thought they were aligned on safety and affordability priorities.

“Their words mean nothing to me anymore.”

If the legislation passes debate in the legislature, it’s expected to take effect in the spring.

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told reporters that the bill is another example of “unbelievable overreach” by the United Conservative Party government.

“This has nothing to do with bike lanes. They’re just trying to start up yet another front in their culture war garbage.”

Tyrel Brochu, with the advocacy group Paths for People, told reporters at the legislature that the government’s approach to traffic safety, including its previous move to reduce photo radar, has resulted in more serious and fatal collisions.

“Parents shouldn’t have to worry about their kids getting hit by a truck when they’re biking to school or the rec centre.”

Brochu said you don’t need to ride a bike to know that spending tens of millions of dollars to tear out concrete is fiscally reckless.

Heather Young-Leslie, with the Bikeology Guild of Canada, said being able to safely use a bike is about personal choice.

“People who say cyclists should only be on the side streets aren’t understanding what it means to actually use a bicycle as a main form of transportation – which we’re not expecting everyone to do,” she said.

Alberta’s legislation comes after a years-long battle over bike lanes in Ontario.

Premier Doug Ford’s government targeted some bike lanes in Toronto for removal, arguing they were creating traffic congestion.

The plan was blocked by a lower court judge who found it to be an unconstitutional risk to cyclist safety.

That decision was overturned by the Ontario Court of Appeal in August. In a strongly worded ruling, it said the lower court had effectively created a right to bike lanes where none existed.

Protests last month while crews were working to remove a lane on one of the city’s busiest routes led to the arrests of four people.

At the time, Dreeshen called the Ontario Appeal Court’s ruling a “win for common sense.”

Cycling advocacy groups in Ontario have asked the Supreme Court of Canada to weigh in. The province has said removals and the restoration of vehicle lanes along Bloor Street West was already completed.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

— With files from Jack Farrell

stories.title: Al models used to announce new list of 25 most wanted fugitives in Canada
stories.summary: Police agencies from across Canada are using artificial intelligence to create virtual models of the country's 25 most wanted criminals moving as they would in real life.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Police agencies from across Canada have used artificial intelligence to create virtual models of the country’s 25 most wanted criminals moving as they would in real life.

The AI models of the fugitives appeared crossing hands and moving their heads, wearing casual shirts or hoodies and pants, ON a large screen at the Toronto police college while police announced the newest list in the Bolo Program.

The national program encourages police and the public to help find the fugitives.

Max Langlois, the program’s executive director, said it uses new ways every year to make sure people are on the lookout for the most wanted suspects on the list.

“This year with the help of AI, as you can see, we bring our top 25 fugitives into this room life-sized, moving as they might if you saw them on the street, at the supermarket, at the airport or anywhere else,” he said.

“If it feels uncomfortable, that’s the point.”

Satinderjeet Singh, who is also known as Goldy Brar, topped this year’s list. He is wanted by Winnipeg police on a Canada-wide warrant for what police say was an “execution-style murder” of 39-year-old Sukhdool Singh Gill on Sept. 20, 2023.

Winnipeg police deputy chief Cam Mackid said police are offering $250,000 for any information that leads to the arrest of 32-year-old Singh, who originally entered Canada on a student visa in 2017 and is now known to be a high-ranking member of the Lawrence Bishnoi Gang, which Canada designated a terrorist group.

“This is an India-based transnational organized crime syndicate,” Mackid said.

”(Singh) is currently wanted on charges of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder.”

Mackid said Singh has lived in California and various parts of Canada and he is now wanted in India, Canada and the United States.

”(He) has been wanted for some time by Indian authorities for a murder that occurred in that country in 2022,” Mackid said

“In July of this year, (he) was indicted by a U.S. federal grand jury in Los Angeles on numerous charges. And in September, he was added to the Fbi’s 10 most wanted list with a substantial reward.”

Kyle Douglas Prouse, who allegedly shot a security guard inside Fairview Mall in Toronto in April before fleeing the area, held the No. 2 spot on the list of Canada’s 25 most wanted suspects.

Police are offering a $100,000 reward for information leading to his arrest.

Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw said Prouse has ties to Toronto and Vancouver and is believed to be armed and dangerous.

Six of the top 25 most wanted fugitives have connections to Toronto, including Cody Rudifo, No. 3 on the list, who is wanted in the fatal shooting of 34-year-old Christopher Gordon last month in the Lawrence Heights area of the city, Demkiw said.

“The Bolo Program has shown time and time again what happens when police and the public work together,” Demkiw said.

“Since 2018, 19 of the 28 Toronto cases featured by Bolo have ended in an arrest, including the case that held last year’s No. 1 spot.”

“Bolo” is a common term used by police forces that stands for “be on the lookout.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Forensic pathologist 'shocked' Francique survived as long as he did after gunshot
stories.summary: A forensic pathologist is telling a coroner's inquest he's "shocked" a man who was shot in the head by police survived as long as he did given the severity of the injury.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A coroner’s inquest into the death of a Black man shot in the head by police heard from the supervisory officer on scene that day that his team would not have done anything differently as they were on-site to complete what they believed would be a routine arrest.

Jamal Francique, 28, was shot during an attempted arrest at a Mississauga, Ont., townhouse complex on the evening of Jan. 7, 2020.

Francique’s car then smashed into the pillar of a nearby garage, the inquest heard.

He did not receive medical care until after a Peel regional police tactical unit arrived at the scene roughly 20 minutes later and removed him from the car, the inquest has heard.

The inquest heard from Det. Jason Sweeting, the supervisory officer of the investigation into Francique, who said the arrest didn’t happen the way they expected.

“I wish this never would have occurred the way it did, but having hindsight, I can see how it turned out,” he said.

Officers advised the ambulance to “stand by” since police had not cleared Francique’s vehicle for them to approach, the inquest heard.

Sweeting said the ambulance could have been near the scene at the time and dispatchers were asking if it was safe to approach. While he did have concerns for Francique’s well-being in the vehicle, Sweeting said he also took into consideration his own safety as well as that of the other officers.

Police had been surveilling Francique for days as they investigated a tip that he was trafficking drugs and had a gun, according to an agreed narrative presented at the inquest. They couldn’t find evidence to corroborate the allegations but determined he could be arrested for an alleged violation of his bail conditions, the inquest heard.

“We hadn’t confirmed anything, that he was in the possession of a firearm,” Sweeting said. “We had taken precautions to make the arrest in an open environment where we had maximum control over the environment. We had taken steps to stop any pursuit if it had occurred.”

This included a tire-deflation device on the front tire on the passenger side and a vehicle that was supposed to block Francique’s car if he got inside before an arrest was made, the inquest heard.

A team of plainclothes officers in unmarked vehicles set up at the townhouse complex where he lived with his mother and stepfather, waiting for Francique to leave the home, jurors heard.

He eventually emerged and headed to his car, but the officer who was meant to block the vehicle’s path was late, they heard. Officers in unmarked cars and on foot rushed to contain his car, and one of the officers on foot fired four gunshots, they heard.

Sweeting said Francique moved to his vehicle quicker than officers anticipated, which “threw a bit of a wrench into the plan.”

When asked why the arrest was not made at the home, Sweeting said there were safety concerns for officers and the residents of the home to take into consideration.

“It just felt like a safer plan to have him on his own in an open area than an enclosed area with other family members and other potential things going wrong,” he said.

Sweeting did not consider their plan to be “high-risk” until after Francique got into the vehicle, the inquest heard.

Sweeting said they could have enlisted the support of a tactical unit, who are called in high-risk situations, but he did not think they had to since it was supposed to be a routine arrest.

“At the moment that this interaction became high-risk, it would have been when he entered his vehicle and began to put it into motion,” he said, which placed officers at risk, the inquest heard.

A forensic pathologist told the inquest earlier that he was “shocked” Francique survived as long as he did given the severity of the injury.

Dr. Ashwyn Rajagopalan, who performed an autopsy on Francique in 2020, testified the cause of death was determined to be a gunshot wound to the head.

The inquest has heard Francique’s car crashed into a garage moments after the shooting, but Rajagopalan said the collision didn’t contribute to the head injury or death.

Francique was declared brain dead once he arrived in hospital and somatic death — when his heart stopped beating — occurred days later, the forensic pathologist said.

Asked by inquest counsel whether Francique would have “retained the capacity for purposeful movement or communication” after sustaining such an injury, Rajagopalan said it’s difficult to be certain.

“I do not think he would have been vocal or conscious at all, or if he was vocal or conscious, it would have been a matter of seconds if anything else,” he said.

“I’m frankly shocked that he survived as long he did given the severity of his brain injury.”

Rajagopalan said he was told before the autopsy that there had been a 15-minute delay in delivering medical aid, but said under cross-examination that knowing it took longer would not have significantly affected his findings.

“I would not have expected this to be a survivable brain injury … the fact that his heart was still beating 26 minutes after this injury is surprising to me,” he said.

Sabrina Shillingford, who represents Francique’s father, asked whether Francique’s chances of survival would have increased had he received immediate emergency care.

The forensic pathologist said he didn’t think it would have made a difference, but noted a neurosurgeon May offer a different or more detailed opinion.

“There’s a lot of bleeding inside the interventricular space of the brain, so blood is pouring into the brain,” he said.

“For this to be a survivable injury with meaningful recovery of function, even if it had occurred on an operating room table, I would not expect a good neurological outcome.”

Jurors in coroner’s inquests do not assign legal responsibility but May make recommendations meant to prevent similar deaths in the future.

Some of the topics expected to be explored at the inquest include Peel regional police procedures and training, including on use of force when a vehicle is involved, oversight of preplanned arrests, medical care for suspects who are incapacitated and anti-Black racism.

“There’s a lot of bleeding inside the interventricular space of the brain, so blood is pouring into the brain,” he said.

Jurors in coroner’s inquests do not assign legal responsibility but May make recommendations meant to prevent similar deaths in the future.

stories.title: Report into deadly Manitoba plane crash raises concerns about weight balance, fuel
stories.summary: The report says the weight balance could have made the plane more sensitive to fly, and significantly harder to recover from a stall.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An investigation into an airplane crash that killed four in northern Manitoba last year has raised concerns about weight balance and fuel storage on a flight that almost didn’t happen.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada report into the Sept. 13, 2025, accident says the pilot made two attempts to take off in the De Havilland Canada Beaver float plane that day, but was told to turn back to the dock both times by a passenger who had anxiety about flying.

The report says the planned flight for a hunting trip was called off for the day, only to have the passengers from St. Theresa Point First Nation call back hours later saying they wanted to try again.

It says the skies were clear and weather fine and there was no indication of fatigue or medical issues with the 20-year-old pilot, who survived after the plane plummeted into the forest and burst into flames.

In determining what May have contributed to the crash, the report notes that the plane’s centre of gravity May have been further back than it was supposed to be.

The report says the weight balance could have made the plane more sensitive to fly, and significantly harder to recover from a stall.

The report also notes that while it wasn’t against the rules, hauling two jerrycans in the cabin of the aircraft could have significantly increased the size and intensity of the fire after the crash.

stories.title: Activists call for ban on keeping elephants, great apes in captivity
stories.summary: Ottawa - Activists are calling on the federal government to take up a defunct bill that would phase out elephant and great ape captivity in Canada.
stories.author: Alyssa Wheeler The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The federal Liberals have not decided if they will reintroduce a bill that would phase out elephant and great ape captivity in Canada, despite pressure from animal rights activists to do so.

Bill S-15 was introduced in the Senate in 2023, and had the backing of world renowned primatologist and conservationist Jane Goodall. An earlier version of the bill carried her name.

It proposed fines of up to $200,000 for breeding elephants or great apes and for using them for entertainment purposes, and would have banned imports and exports of the animals without ministerial approval.

The legislation’s public profile exploded earlier this month when the American pop star Cher said it broke her heart to see Goodall’s legacy “gathering dust” and called for the bill’s return.

“By protecting elephants & great apes, Canada can set a precedent for other nations to follow,” Cher wrote on X on Nov. 14. “Please DO NOT let this bill fade to nothing.”

The Liberals did not campaign on restoring the bill in 2025, though former MP Nathaniel Erskine-Smith said during a debate in that campaign that the government would reintroduce it if the Liberals won the election.

Melissa Matlow, a campaign director at World Animal Protection, said Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin told her she had plans to act on S-15 earlier this year.

“When I met with the minister of environment this past summer, she assured me it was still on her agenda. It was just a little lower down the list,” she said.

“So I remain cautiously optimistic, but I know how quickly priorities can fall off someone’s list.”

But Dabrusin would not commit to bringing the bill back when asked Wednesday about Cher’s comments.

“I personally care about animal welfare a lot and I’m always excited when other people are standing up on animal welfare issues,” Dabrusin said Wednesday on Parliament Hill.

“We’ve done a lot on animal welfare over the last decade, including ending the captivity of whales and dolphins. It’s a good time for us to think about what the next steps will be.”

Her spokesperson on Thursday said “no further decision has been made regarding the future of this bill.”

The late Sen. Murray Sinclair introduced a bill to ban elephant captivity in 2020 as the Jane Goodall Act but it did not pass before the 2021 election.

Sen. Marty Klyne revived the bill in 2023. It had passed the Senate but had not yet been debated in the House of Commons when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025.

Klyne said bringing it back would make Canada a world leader in elephant and great ape protections.

“In addition to an election promise, it would honour the legislative legacies of the late Dr. Jane Goodall and the late Honourable Murray Sinclair, whose efforts were inspired by science and Indigenous values of respect for nature. The time to act is now,” he wrote in a statement to The Canadian Press.

Dr. Mary Lee Jensvold, who spoke to the Senate in 2024 on behalf of the Fauna Foundation, said she was disappointed when the bill was dropped.

“It was such progressive legislation. And so often with animal things, when we get into difficult times, people are like, ‘We can’t worry about non-human animals,’” she said.

Dolf DeJong, chief executive officer of the Toronto Zoo, called the bill’s demise “tremendously disappointing.”

“Now it’s just back to doing the hard work and raising the profile and making sure people realize that, in some cases, Ontario in particular has some of the weakest wildlife regulations in the country of Canada,” he said.

Barry Kent MacKay, the honorary director of the Animal Alliance of Canada, said elephants and great apes have no place in captivity.

“I think we have to move forward and say, ‘There certain types of animals that just don’t fit in Canadian zoos, and these are two of them,’” he said.

Three facilities in Canada currently house elephants. Quebec’s Granby Zoo has three, Edmonton’s Valley Zoo in Alberta has one and the African Lion Safari in Ontario has 19.

Great apes are housed in four facilities in Canada: the Toronto Zoo, the Calgary Zoo, the Granby Zoo and the Fauna Foundation Sanctuary.

Edmonton’s Valley Zoo and the African Lion Safari have not responded to a request for comment from The Canadian Press.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray

stories.title: Liberals won’t commit to bringing back bill to ban elephants, great apes in captivity
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal Liberals have not decided if they will reintroduce a bill that would phase out elephant and great ape captivity in Canada, despite pressure from animal rights activists to do so.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal Liberals have not decided if they will reintroduce a bill that would phase out elephant and great ape captivity in Canada, despite pressure from animal rights activists to do so.

Bill S-15 was introduced in the Senate in 2023, and had the backing of world renowned primatologist and conservationist Jane Goodall. An earlier version of the bill carried her name.

It proposed fines of up to $200,000 for breeding elephants or great apes and for using them for entertainment purposes, and would have banned imports and exports of the animals without ministerial approval.

The legislation’s public profile exploded earlier this month when the American pop star Cher said it broke her heart to see Goodall’s legacy “gathering dust” and called for the bill’s return.

“By protecting elephants & great apes, Canada can set a precedent for other nations to follow,” Cher wrote on X on Nov. 14. “Please DO NOT let this bill fade to nothing.”

The Liberals did not campaign on restoring the bill in 2025, though former MP Nathaniel Erskine-Smith said during a debate in that campaign that the government would reintroduce it if the Liberals won the election.

Melissa Matlow, a campaign director at World Animal Protection, said Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin told her she had plans to act on S-15 earlier this year.

“When I met with the minister of environment this past summer, she assured me it was still on her agenda. It was just a little lower down the list,” she said.

“So I remain cautiously optimistic, but I know how quickly priorities can fall off someone’s list.”

But Dabrusin would not commit to bringing the bill back when asked Wednesday about Cher’s comments.

“I personally care about animal welfare a lot and I’m always excited when other people are standing up on animal welfare issues,” Dabrusin said Wednesday on Parliament Hill.

“We’ve done a lot on animal welfare over the last decade, including ending the captivity of whales and dolphins. It’s a good time for us to think about what the next steps will be.”

Her spokesperson on Thursday said “no further decision has been made regarding the future of this bill.”

The late Sen. Murray Sinclair introduced a bill to ban elephant captivity in 2020 as the Jane Goodall Act but it did not pass before the 2021 election.

Sen. Marty Klyne revived the bill in 2023. It had passed the Senate but had not yet been debated in the House of Commons when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025.

Klyne said bringing it back would make Canada a world leader in elephant and great ape protections.

“In addition to an election promise, it would honour the legislative legacies of the late Dr. Jane Goodall and the late Honourable Murray Sinclair, whose efforts were inspired by science and Indigenous values of respect for nature. The time to act is now,” he wrote in a statement to The Canadian Press.

Dr. Mary Lee Jensvold, who spoke to the Senate in 2024 on behalf of the Fauna Foundation, said she was disappointed when the bill was dropped.

“It was such progressive legislation. And so often with animal things, when we get into difficult times, people are like, ‘We can’t worry about non-human animals,'” she said.

Dolf DeJong, chief executive officer of the Toronto Zoo, called the bill’s demise “tremendously disappointing.”

“Now it’s just back to doing the hard work and raising the profile and making sure people realize that, in some cases, Ontario in particular has some of the weakest wildlife regulations in the country of Canada,” he said.

Barry Kent MacKay, the honorary director of the Animal Alliance of Canada, said elephants and great apes have no place in captivity.

“I think we have to move forward and say, ‘There certain types of animals that just don’t fit in Canadian zoos, and these are two of them,'” he said.

Three facilities in Canada currently house elephants. Quebec’s Granby Zoo has three, Edmonton’s Valley Zoo in Alberta has one and the African Lion Safari in Ontario has 19.

Great apes are housed in four facilities in Canada: the Toronto Zoo, the Calgary Zoo, the Granby Zoo and the Fauna Foundation Sanctuary.

Edmonton’s Valley Zoo and the African Lion Safari have not responded to a request for comment from The Canadian Press.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray

Alyssa Wheeler, The Canadian Press

November 19, 2026 at 12:01 p.m.

The new B.C. government intends to follow through on a campaign promise to “bring back singing O Canada at the beginning of the school day.”

Part of “getting back to basics in education…means fostering pride in our province and country by bringing back the singing of O Canada and proudly flying Canadian and British Columbia flags in our schools,” Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson told National Post in an email Wednesday.

It’s not that O Canada is never sung in B.C. schools. Under the B.C. School Act, schools must hold three assemblies a year and sing the national anthem on each occasion.

But the Doerkson government intends to make it a daily practice.

Meanwhile, the School Act regulations already mandates that the Canadian and B.C. flags are “displayed at each school while in session.”

Doerkson’s government will be focusing on higher academic standards, he says. And that means “restoring letter grades and ensuring parents have a clear understanding of their children’s progress … We’ll have more to say following this week’s swearing-in of cabinet.”

Sixty-four B.C. Conservative MLAs will be sworn in today. Doerkson and his cabinet will be sworn in on Friday, according to the Vancouver Sun.

Back in 2025, National Post reported on the return of O Canada to Nova Scotia classrooms after Halifax high school students sent a letter to the provincial department of education that it wasn’t happening in their school.

Looking to schools in other parts of the country, since 2009%20of,the%20Education%20Act%20is%20repealed.&text=29.1(1)Subject%20to%20any,the%20District%20Education%20Council%20concerned.&text=(b)%20the%20District%20Education%20Council,frequency%20appropriate%20in%20the%20circumstances.&text=(b)%20an%20independent%20pupil%20applies,force%20on%20July%201%2C%202009) New Brunswick has mandated that each school “principal shall ensure the broadcast of the national anthem within the school.”

Under Ontario’s Education Act, “every board shall ensure that opening or closing exercises are held in each school under the board’s jurisdiction.” Further, the “opening or closing exercises must include the singing of O Canada and May include the recitation of a pledge of citizenship.”

However, the Education Act’s regulations state that a pupil is not required to sing O Canada or recite a pledge of citizenship if the pupil is less than 18 years old and the pupil’s parent or guardian has applied to the principal to be exempted from doing so. Also, a pupil who is at least 18 years old can apply to be exempted.

In Manitoba, under the Education Administration Act, the beginning of every school day, is to begin with the principal of each school ensuring that “the first verse and chorus of O Canada are sung in the school and observed in a respectful manner.”

As previously reported by National Post, Saskatchewan, Yukon and the Northwest Territories leave it to local school boards or schools when the national anthem is played.

The federal government’s website says there is no hard-and-fast rule regarding when it is appropriate to sing O Canada at a public event.

Instead, it “is up to the organizers to determine if instrumental or sung versions of O Canada will be used, and whether these will occur at the beginning or at the end of the event.”

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

Part of “getting back to basics in education…means fostering pride in our province and country by bringing back the singing of O Canada and proudly flying Canadian and British Columbia flags in our schools,” Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson told National Post in an email Wednesday.
It’s not that O Canada is never sung in B.C. schools. Under the B.C. School Act, schools must hold three assemblies a year and sing the national anthem on each occasion.
But the Doerkson government intends to make it a daily practice.
Meanwhile, the School Act regulations already mandates that the Canadian and B.C. flags are “displayed at each school while in session.”

Doerkson’s government will be focusing on higher academic standards, he says. And that means “restoring letter grades and ensuring parents have a clear understanding of their children’s progress … We’ll have more to say following this week’s swearing-in of cabinet.”

Looking to schools in other parts of the country, since 2009%20of,the%20Education%20Act%20is%20repealed.&text=29.1(1)Subject%20to%20any,the%20District%20Education%20Council%20concerned.&text=(b)%20the%20District%20Education%20Council,frequency%20appropriate%20in%20the%20circumstances.&text=(b)%20an%20independent%20pupil%20applies,force%20on%20July%201%2C%202009) New Brunswick has mandated that each school “principal shall ensure the broadcast of the national anthem within the school.”

Under Ontario’s Education Act, “every board shall ensure that opening or closing exercises are held in each school under the board’s jurisdiction.” Further, the “opening or closing exercises must include the singing of O Canada and May include the recitation of a pledge of citizenship.”

However, the Education Act’s regulations state that a pupil is not required to sing O Canada or recite a pledge of citizenship if the pupil is less than 18 years old and the pupil’s parent or guardian has applied to the principal to be exempted from doing so. Also, a pupil who is at least 18 years old can apply to be exempted.

In Manitoba, under the Education Administration Act, the beginning of every school day, is to begin with the principal of each school ensuring that “the first verse and chorus of O Canada are sung in the school and observed in a respectful manner.”
As previously reported by National Post, Saskatchewan, Yukon and the Northwest Territories leave it to local school boards or schools when the national anthem is played.
The federal government’s website says there is no hard-and-fast rule regarding when it is appropriate to sing O Canada at a public event.
Instead, it “is up to the organizers to determine if instrumental or sung versions of O Canada will be used, and whether these will occur at the beginning or at the end of the event.”

stories.title: Canada’s efforts to fast-track development could launch a new Oka or Ipperwash crisis
stories.summary: By bulldozing First Nations consultations in the name of building faster, the Ontario and federal governments might actually be slowing things down
stories.author: Tanya Talaga
stories.content:
In this new era in Canadian politics, in which building the national economy apparently trumps environmental protections and Indigenous rights, a dangerous precedent has been set.

Laws are being introduced as “emergency” measures so they can be rammed through Canadian legislatures quickly without proper debate and consultation, upturning the democratic process.

The most recent incarnation of this tactic can be found in Ontario, where an omnibus piece of legislation called Bill 140, the Building Ontario Faster Act , promises to gut the remaining requirements around environmental assessments and public consultations before development occurs. Ontario says the bill is needed to cut red tape, transform environmental oversight and strengthen the province’s competitiveness.

What the bill also does is effectively scrap Ontario’s Environmental Bill of Rights, eliminating public notices and preventing appeals and concerns from being raised, says the Canadian Environmental Law Association. If Ontarians don’t know what’s happening behind closed doors, they can’t speak up. Public opposition averted the destruction of Ontario’s Greenbelt; it seems clear that Bill 140 is a reaction to that movement.

Yet, there was just a single day of committee hearings on the bill, which occurred on Tuesday; an NDP effort to add more time was denied by Progressive Conservative MPPs. This is not normal for a major piece of legislation. Now, Bill 140 looks set to move to third reading by month’s end, when it is expected to receive a rubber stamp from a PC majority government and then royal assent to become law.

The legislation follows in the footsteps of the province’s Bill 5, which creates special economic zones where consultation and environmental assessments are not needed. That bill is the little brother to the federal government’s Bill C-5, which allows for fast-tracked development of whatever Ottawa labels a major project, which can include pipelines and mines.

All of this is occurring so that governments can move quickly to replace the auto and manufacturing jobs lost due to U.S. President Donald Trump ’s wall of tariffs against Canada. Their answer seems to be to introduce bills that gut environmental protections and blatantly ignore Indigenous rights, specifically Section 35 concerning free, prior and informed consent, not to mention the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (Undrip), to which the federal government committed in 2021 to aligning Canadian laws. But apparently, it’s on trend now to turn against these commitments: British Columbia’s new Conservative government said it will repeal the province’s historic Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (Dripa) law as soon as it can. Consent is awful hard to achieve when there’s no real consultation.

On Tuesday, Grand Chief Joel Abram of the Association of Iroquois and Allied Indians spoke to the committee about the bill’s implications as the representative for the Chiefs of Ontario, which has called for Bill 140 to be withdrawn . Beyond the environmental concerns, he argued, the bill turns Ontario’s 133 First Nations into obstacles to be driven around rather than treaty partners who have a right to be heard and consulted. He was also frustrated by how the single day of hearings limited First Nations voices: “Each First Nation should have had their chance at the mic, to make their own presentation,” Mr. Abram said.

The Chiefs of Ontario say one of the bill’s sweeping changes would allow people who aren’t licensed archeologists to undertake archeological work so surveys can be done faster and shovels can get in the ground sooner, in the name of cutting through red tape.

But this “red tape” is actually an important barrier: it protects sacred Indigenous sites, burial grounds, ancestral remains and cultural heritage items at risk of irreversible damage. It should be done with care, by experts. “Once you break ground, you can’t go back and consult,” Mr. Abram said. “We have to think about the next seven generations, not just the next four quarters.”

He also issued a warning that Canada needs to hear: “You won’t speed things up with this bill, you’ll slow them down. First Nations will protect their rights.” Asked what that looks like, Mr. Abram referred to the Oka and Ipperwash crises, saying that these legislative changes could cause deep unrest and ignite movements.

Ramon Kataquapit and his cousin Jeronimo, who are members of Attawapiskat First Nation, echoed Mr. Abram in a separate press conference after being denied the chance to speak. “We will be present in every fashion possible,” Ramon said. “You’ll see us on the ground and in the courts.”

So the bill that’s moving quickly through the Ontario legislature, and is aimed at getting things done fast, could do exactly the opposite of what it’s meant to as it runs up against democratic protest. Is that seriously a risk that Canada wants to take?

stories.title: Green think-tank welcomes Alberta well cleanup plan, but says more needed
stories.summary: Calgary - An environmental think-tank is welcoming proposed Alberta legislation that would require oil and gas companies to pay upfront for the eventual cleanup of each well.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Alberta legislation that would require oil and gas companies to pay upfront for the eventual cleanup of each well seems positive on the surface, but much will depend on how it’s implemented and enforced, says a rancher and landowner advocate.

“It looks good on paper,” Bill Heidecker, president of the Alberta Surface Rights Federation, said Thursday. “We got lots of questions on how it will actually work.”

The legislation introduced as part of a broader bill Wednesday would require companies to make an initial payment of up to $50,000 followed by yearly incremental payments over a 10-year period, with the funds attached to each well regardless of any ownership changes.

The new rules are expected to apply to wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The backlog of thousands of wells that have yet to be properly closed remains an ongoing issue.

Heidecker has a cattle ranch near Coronation, Alta., in the eastern part of the province, and says there are a “couple dozen” wells on his land — some producing and some not. Dealing with the industry has been a “constant headache,” he said.

He wants assurances companies will be held to their obligations.

“There are a lot of laws and regulations on the books that haven’t been enforced to the degree they should have,” he said.

It’s also unclear what the rules are for energy infrastructure beyond wells, such as pipelines, he said. And he wants more detail on the formula to calculate the cost of well cleanup — is it based on today’s costs or future projected ones? What if there are multiple well bores stemming from one pad? — as well as how to prioritize which wells are cleaned up first.

“We’ve seen that in the existing cleanup, the companies tend to clean up the easy simple ones and they’re leaving the difficult expensive ones lower down on the list,” he said.

“So we welcome this, of course, but we’re reserving judgment until we see what actually happens.”

Heidecker’s group sent a letter to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith last week expressing “profound dissatisfaction” with her government’s handling of energy policy and landowner rights, listing off a litany of concerns around both current development and inactive infrastructure. It urged landowners to withhold consent for oil and gas development on their properties and not voluntarily sign new leases.

Heidecker said the call for resistance remains, despite the province taking a “step in the right direction” with the proposed upfront closure funding.

“There’s so many other things they need to address,” he said. Those matters include a lack of firm cleanup deadlines, unpaid municipal taxes and inadequate enforcement.

Meanwhile, an environmental think-tank offered qualified praise for the move.

The new rules would be “an important and positive step toward ensuring industry meets its legal responsibility to clean up after itself,” said Amanda Bryant, manager of the oil and gas program at the Pembina Institute.

But she said to be successful, the new rules should include minimum thresholds for how much financial security is set aside for cleanup.

“Additional action is needed to address existing inactive and orphan wells, such as implementing enforceable timelines for well closure, charging an inactive well fee, or increasing the orphan well levy charged to industry to reflect the scale of the cleanup work ahead,” Bryant said.

Wells are deemed orphans when there is no entity legally responsible for their cleanup, for instance when their owner goes bankrupt. Such wells become the responsibility of the non-profit Orphan Well Association, which is funded through an industry fee.

The Orphan Well Levy for the 2026-27 fiscal year is $154.56 million. The well association has pegged total cleanup costs of its inventory at $1.66 billion. Landowner advocates say the current levy isn’t high enough to address the scale of the backlog, and some have raised concern about the health and environmental effects of potential contamination from improperly managed wells.

Heidecker’s group is part of a lawsuit filed in September by landowners challenging what they call the Alberta Energy Regulator’s “chronic underfunding” of the Orphan Well Levy, the amount of which is determined by the Alberta government based on the regulator’s recommendation.

The latest monthly numbers from the Orphan Well Association say there are 7,328 wells waiting to be decommissioned, which involves permanently dismantling equipment so that the site is safe. Another 9,258 sites are in need of reclamation, which means restoring the land so it’s similar to its original state.

In the 2025-26 fiscal year, the combined cost of decommissioning and reclaiming a well was more than $56,000.

Brian Jean, Alberta’s energy and minerals minister, said the cost of putting funds into the new Resource Asset Closure Assurance and Stewardship Fund shouldn’t have a negative impact on industry. He figures the funds would amount to an initial one per cent of the cost of drilling the well, plus another one per cent from the incremental payments over the following decade.

He told reporters Thursday that as companies become more efficient and find ways to drive down the cost, “frankly, there are good opportunities to make money.” Under the legislation, companies would be able to unlock the funds — which would have accrued compound interest over the years — once reclamation is complete.

Jean said if companies don’t put down the deposit, they can’t get a licence to drill.

“It’s a cost of doing business,” he said.

“The truth is that it’s a very innovative approach. It’s a one-of-a-kind approach, the first in the world, and it’s going to work.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

“It looks good on paper,” Bill Heidecker, president of the Alberta Surface Rights Federation, said Thursday. “We got lots of questions on how it will actually work.”

The legislation introduced as part of a broader bill Wednesday would require companies to make an initial payment of up to $50,000 followed by yearly incremental payments over a 10-year period, with the funds attached to each well regardless of any ownership changes.
The new rules are expected to apply to wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The backlog of thousands of wells that have yet to be properly closed remains an ongoing issue.

Heidecker has a cattle ranch near Coronation, Alta., in the eastern part of the province, and says there are a “couple dozen” wells on his land — some producing and some not. Dealing with the industry has been a “constant headache,” he said.
He wants assurances companies will be held to their obligations.
“There are a lot of laws and regulations on the books that haven’t been enforced to the degree they should have,” he said.

It’s also unclear what the rules are for energy infrastructure beyond wells, such as pipelines, he said. And he wants more detail on the formula to calculate the cost of well cleanup — is it based on today’s costs or future projected ones? What if there are multiple well bores stemming from one pad? — as well as how to prioritize which wells are cleaned up first.
“We’ve seen that in the existing cleanup, the companies tend to clean up the easy simple ones and they’re leaving the difficult expensive ones lower down on the list,” he said.
“So we welcome this, of course, but we’re reserving judgment until we see what actually happens.”

Heidecker’s group sent a letter to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith last week expressing “profound dissatisfaction” with her government’s handling of energy policy and landowner rights, listing off a litany of concerns around both current development and inactive infrastructure. It urged landowners to withhold consent for oil and gas development on their properties and not voluntarily sign new leases.
Heidecker said the call for resistance remains, despite the province taking a “step in the right direction” with the proposed upfront closure funding.
“There’s so many other things they need to address,” he said. Those matters include a lack of firm cleanup deadlines, unpaid municipal taxes and inadequate enforcement.
Meanwhile, an environmental think-tank offered qualified praise for the move.

The new rules would be “an important and positive step toward ensuring industry meets its legal responsibility to clean up after itself,” said Amanda Bryant, manager of the oil and gas program at the Pembina Institute.
But she said to be successful, the new rules should include minimum thresholds for how much financial security is set aside for cleanup.

“Additional action is needed to address existing inactive and orphan wells, such as implementing enforceable timelines for well closure, charging an inactive well fee, or increasing the orphan well levy charged to industry to reflect the scale of the cleanup work ahead,” Bryant said.

Wells are deemed orphans when there is no entity legally responsible for their cleanup, for instance when their owner goes bankrupt. Such wells become the responsibility of the non-profit Orphan Well Association, which is funded through an industry fee.

The Orphan Well Levy for the 2026-27 fiscal year is $154.56 million. The well association has pegged total cleanup costs of its inventory at $1.66 billion. Landowner advocates say the current levy isn’t high enough to address the scale of the backlog, and some have raised concern about the health and environmental effects of potential contamination from improperly managed wells.

Heidecker’s group is part of a lawsuit filed in September by landowners challenging what they call the Alberta Energy Regulator’s “chronic underfunding” of the Orphan Well Levy, the amount of which is determined by the Alberta government based on the regulator’s recommendation.

The latest monthly numbers from the Orphan Well Association say there are 7,328 wells waiting to be decommissioned, which involves permanently dismantling equipment so that the site is safe. Another 9,258 sites are in need of reclamation, which means restoring the land so it’s similar to its original state.
In the 2025-26 fiscal year, the combined cost of decommissioning and reclaiming a well was more than $56,000.

Brian Jean, Alberta’s energy and minerals minister, said the cost of putting funds into the new Resource Asset Closure Assurance and Stewardship Fund shouldn’t have a negative impact on industry. He figures the funds would amount to an initial one per cent of the cost of drilling the well, plus another one per cent from the incremental payments over the following decade.

He told reporters Thursday that as companies become more efficient and find ways to drive down the cost, “frankly, there are good opportunities to make money.” Under the legislation, companies would be able to unlock the funds — which would have accrued compound interest over the years — once reclamation is complete.
Jean said if companies don’t put down the deposit, they can’t get a licence to drill.
“It’s a cost of doing business,” he said.
“The truth is that it’s a very innovative approach. It’s a one-of-a-kind approach, the first in the world, and it’s going to work.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Poilievre brushes off questions about staff departures from his office
stories.summary: Saint-Hyacinthe - Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre brushed off questions today about the departure of five staffers from his office.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Saint-Hyacinthe - Pierre Poilievre brushed off a suggestion his leadership of the federal Conservative party needs rebranding Thursday following the departure of five staffers from his office.

Speaking at a news conference in Saint-Hyacinthe, Que., Poilievre said staff turnover is normal and noted some of the employees have worked in his office for several years. He also said one of the departing staffers is expecting a baby soon and is leaving to be closer to family.

stories.title: New Brunswick announces new rules for data centre projects
stories.summary: Fredericton - The New Brunswick government is introducing new rules data centre proponents must follow to set up shop in the province.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Fredericton - New Brunswick and Alberta both laid out ground rules for data centre projects this week, and one artificial intelligence expert says that’s just the kind of regulatory certainty the sector is looking for.

“It makes it more attractive for a proponent to invest in a project in your province because you’ve removed the regulatory risk,” Mark Daley, the chief AI officer at Western University in London, Ont., said in an interview Thursday.

“If you’re going to build a data centre in a province that doesn’t have a data centre strategy and doesn’t have clear regulations around data centres, you take the risk that that could change halfway through your project.”

On Thursday the New Brunswick government released its data centre development policy, saying projects that don’t follow the new rules will be rejected.

The province is planning legislative amendments that will give it the power to review and approve electricity supply arrangements for data centres with a focus on protecting existing ratepayers.

It says data centre developments will have to provide a “net benefit” to utilities such as Crown-owned NB Power, which confirmed last month that it had 10 data centre applications that would need up to 900 megawatts of power combined.

Energy Minister René Legacy told reporters Thursday that data centre proponents are currently applying directly to NB Power, which doesn’t have any criteria to assess a project’s benefits to the province. He said the utility looks only at the project’s power demand and negotiates a contract.

Now the province will look at project benefits before the application comes to the utility.

“Once we feel there’s potentially some net benefit, then we will introduce it to NB Power to see if there’s a potential deal to be made that doesn’t risk our electricity grid or our rates, or our customer (reliability),” said Legacy.

The new policy requires data centre developers to consult with First Nations and to formalize any commitments they make in binding agreements.

Data centres will have to minimize their impacts on the environment, demonstrate the economic benefits they will create and prove that they are technically and financially sound.

It also proposes legislative changes that would give local governments the power to negotiate community benefit agreements for things such as amenities, local hiring and in-kind benefits.

Large data centre projects will need to register for an environmental impact assessment to move forward. The new rules apply to all data centres proposals, including those already under consideration.

“This policy will ensure that data centre projects meeting our strict criteria can move forward while ensuring that those that do not meet these criteria will never be developed in New Brunswick,” Post-Secondary Education and Training Minister Jean-Claude D’Amours said Thursday.

The announcement came the day after Alberta Technology Minister Nate Glubish announced proposed legislation that would limit large data centre developments near homes and farmland.

The proposed rules would also allow Alberta to set future standards and limits on data centre water use, with details to be finalized later through regulation.

The government said it’s aiming for “close to zero” water use. Glubish said the new standard would be strict and effectively prohibit data centres from using evaporative cooling methods.

The rules will not apply to projects that have already secured development permits, such as tech giant Meta’s $13-billion AI data centre campus north of Edmonton which is already under construction.

Not every province plans to bring in new rules. For example, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston has said the province’s existing industrial approval process is sufficient and the government won’t require the same environmental assessments for data centres that it needs for developments such as mines, quarries and energy generation projects.

Houston said projects such as the $10-billion data centre EverWind Fuels is proposing in Point Tupper, N.S., must also follow the federal government’s development principles for the sector.

“We’re letting the process unfold from company town halls to government information sessions, to answering Nova Scotian’s questions that get sent to MLAs (and) ministers. If there’s a gap that we need to fill, we will do so,” said Houston’s spokesperson, William Burns, in an email on Thursday.

Burns also said that the government acknowledges that binding documents and principles give companies more investment certainty

U.S. AI giant Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for the proposed $10-billion, 95-megawatt project. The firm, which went public with the largest initial stock offering in Wall Street history on Thursday, has said the Nova Scotia facility, set to open by the end of next year, would be its first data centre in Canada.

Daley said it’s clear Alberta and New Brunswick are building on the federal government’s data centre strategy, which he said was really advice on best practices for provinces and municipalities on how to regulate their jurisdictions.

“Alberta and New Brunswick have picked that advice up and turned it into something with regulatory teeth,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

— By Devin Stevens in Halifax.

stories.title: Driver dies in single-vehicle rollover in Woodstock
stories.summary: Emergency crews located the vehicle’s sole occupant, an 87-year-old driver, who was transported to hospital and later pronounced dead.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
An 87-year-old driver has died following a single-vehicle collision in Woodstock.

Police said members of the Woodstock Police Service, along with Woodstock Fire Services and Oxford County Paramedic Services, responded to the area of Parkinson Road and Towerline Road at about 3 p.m. on Tuesday after receiving reports of a collision.

Emergency crews located the vehicle’s sole occupant, an 87-year-old driver, who was transported to hospital and later pronounced dead.

According to Woodstock police, officers, including an accident reconstruction officer and an identification officer, assisted with the investigation. Police spoke with witnesses and determined the vehicle left the roadway and rolled.

The collision remains under investigation. Police said no other vehicles were involved and no additional injuries were reported.

Anyone with video footage from the area at the time of the collision is asked to contact the Woodstock Police Service at 519-537-2323.

stories.title: LeBlanc to chair first meeting of Canada-U.S. advisory committee since midterms
stories.summary: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc is set to hold the first meeting of an advisory committee on bilateral economic relations since the midterm elections that delivered a sharp rebuke of the Trump administration. LeBlanc’s office confirmed the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations will hold a virtual meeting today. Canadian Ambassador…
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Members of an advisory committee on economic relations with the U.S. heard Thursday that Ottawa is more optimistic now about the odds of an interim deal with the Trump administration — but challenging negotiations are expected to continue.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc delivered the update on trade talks to a meeting of the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations in Ottawa. It was the first such meeting since midterm elections in the U.S. delivered a sharp rebuke of the Trump administration.

“It’s clear that the counterparty is still the administration and until the Congress takes hold, the political dynamic hasn’t changed,” Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association and a member of the advisory committee, said in a text message.

The virtual committee meeting also included Ambassador to the United States Mark Wiseman and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette.

The committee discussed “the evolving Canada-U.S. trade relationship and Canada’s approach to advancing its economic interests,” according to a readout from Global Affairs Canada.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada rapidly escalated after negotiations broke down in August. Ottawa and Washington accused each other of putting eleventh-hour demands on the table.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said at the time that Trump’s team wanted to restrict Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries, endanger Canada’s protections for language and culture, and maintain hefty tariffs on some automobiles.

In response, Trump hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs and banned imports of others. He threatened to further increase duties in January if no deal is made by then.

The president also signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The Trump administration’s tone on Canada softened somewhat after midterm election exit polling indicated that the president’s trade war and his sweeping tariff agenda were unpopular with American voters.

“I remain optimistic that the conditions are present to do better than we did when we broke from the table in August,” Volpe said. “The negotiating team is making a fulsome effort to properly understand the implications otherwise.”

A source on the committee — who is not authorized to speak publicly — said that while there is a chance that an interim deal can be struck in the “lame duck” period between the midterms and the arrival of the new Democrat-controlled Congress in January, the midterm results won’t solve all of the problems in the bilateral relationship.

Democrats have indicated that ending the trade war with Canada will be among their top priorities in January — but they could struggle to achieve the supermajority they need to override the president’s veto.

Democrats likely will only tackle one of Trump’s tariff tools — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — while leaving in place other duties still hammering parts of the Canadian economy.

Volpe said “there is some concern” that Canada’s moves to normalize trade with China — particularly in sectors that have been targeted by Trump’s national security tariffs — could undermine progress toward a deal.

White House trade adviser Peter Navarro has repeatedly criticized Carney’s trade strategy. In a video posted on social media Thursday, Navarro said Ottawa is misreading its position and compared it to “a high school team taking on the New York Knicks.”

“They are living in the past if they think Donald John Trump is going to let them continue to push us around,” Navarro said. “They can cry all they want about America being a bully and this and that … Those are arrogant people.”

Carney and Trump met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific economic summit in Shenzhen, China, ON Wednesday. Both leaders also met separately with Chinese President Xi Jinping; on Thursday Trump held a rare three-way meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Following Carney’s meeting with Trump, the prime minister said a “very good trade arrangement” with the United States is possible but Canada won’t just sit around and wait.

During a meeting Tuesday of the House of Commons international trade committee in Ottawa, LeBlanc and Charette cautioned MPs that there is no guarantee Canada can restore the terms of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, better known as Cusma.

Charette said Canada has to prepare for a world where a tariff-free arrangement May no longer be possible.

The objective is to “get to the lowest rate of tariff on the narrowest basket of goods with the most preferential access for Canadian businesses and Canadian workers,” Charette said.

The Trump administration chose not to renew Cusma in July. The decision triggered a rolling annual review for up to a decade, at which point the agreement will expire if the three countries cannot agree on an extension.

Thursday’s readout said committee members “brought forward insights from their respective sectors and regions, highlighting the challenges businesses and workers continue to face because of U.S. trade measures.”

“The discussion also addressed the implementation of federal measures to support Canadian businesses and workers affected by U.S. tariffs, including the effectiveness of existing supports and opportunities to better respond to the needs of affected businesses,” it said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

— By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Liberal Maid committee chair wants separate votes for mental illness, diseases
stories.summary: Ottawa — A Liberal MP who chaired a committee on medical assistance in dying says he agrees with calls from Conservative MPs for the government to split its Maid legislation to allow for separate votes on mental illness and degenerative diseases.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A Liberal MP who chaired a committee on medical assistance in dying says he agrees with Conservative MPs who want the government to split its Maid legislation to allow for separate votes on mental illness and degenerative diseases.

The bill would amend the Criminal Code to allow people to make advance requests to access Maid. It also would prevent a scheduled expansion of Maid access to those suffering solely from a mental illness.

Members of Parliament voted 225 to 89 to send the bill to the House of Commons justice and human rights committee for study. Nearly 40 Conservative MPs voted yes, despite some raising concerns about the legislation.

The Liberal government limited debate Monday on Bill C-41, which was introduced in the House late last month. MPs adopted a motion by Justice Minister Sean Fraser to limit debate at second reading to one more day, despite calls from the Opposition for more time to study the bill.
