stories.title: LHSC names new board as hospital works toward end of provincial supervision
stories.summary: London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has appointed eight new volunteer board members and five community representatives, marking a significant step toward restoring local governance nearly two years after the province took control of the hospital.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has appointed eight new volunteer board members and five community representatives, marking a significant step toward restoring local governance nearly two years after the province took control of the hospital.

The renewed board will work alongside provincial Supervisor David Musyj until supervision ends, at which point it will assume full authority over the organization.

Ron Sapsford, a former Ontario deputy minister of health and long-term care and former CEO of the Ontario Medical Association, has been named board chair.

“It’s an important hospital, not only for London, but for southwestern Ontario. So I think it’s important to get the board back in operation. That to me is the crucial part,” Sapsford said.

The other board members are Scott Courtice, Cedric Gomes, Christi-Ann Poulette, Michael G. Power, David Smith, Melanie Stanley and Lori Van Opstal.

Five community members will also serve on board committees: Catherine Osborne, Leo Plue, Mike Tidy, Nick Vander Gulik and Lloy Wylie.

The appointments follow a recruitment process that attracted more than 90 applicants.

The move comes after a turbulent period for LHSC. In 2024, the province placed the hospital under supervision following serious concerns about governance, financial oversight and organizational leadership.

A provincial review identified significant governance failures, while subsequent investigations uncovered allegations of fraud involving former executives and contractors. The allegations have not been proven in court.

Musyj says the hospital has spent the past two years making structural changes to strengthen accountability and oversight.

Those changes include consolidating management positions, introducing 360-degree performance reviews, tightening spending controls, expanding internal audits and strengthening whistleblower protections.

The hospital has also refreshed its bylaws, policies and procedures and introduced additional oversight of budgeting, staffing decisions, quality indicators and patient safety.

“We’re in a good spot moving forward,” Musyj said, adding that the individuals involved in the alleged misconduct are no longer with the organization.

The renewed board will operate through four standing committees: finance and audit, quality and safety, human resources, and research.

Despite the appointments, Musyj says provincial supervision will not end immediately.

“You don’t want to do this again, right? So you don’t want to stay too long, but you don’t want to leave too early,” Musyj said.

Meanwhile, legal proceedings related to the alleged fraud remain ongoing. Musyj said the civil lawsuits are in the discovery phase, which involves exchanging documents and sworn evidence, as well as examinations for discovery.

He also confirmed the hospital is co-operating with a police investigation and responding to requests for information.

Musyj said further developments involving the civil proceedings are expected to be announced.

The renewed board’s first public meeting is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027. LHSC says meetings will be open to the public and livestreamed as part of its commitment to transparency and community engagement.

The hospital says the goal is to eventually return to local governance with stronger oversight and accountability measures in place.
paragraphs: London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has appointed eight new volunteer board members and five community representatives, marking a significant step toward restoring local governance nearly two years after the province took control of the hospital.
The renewed board will work alongside provincial Supervisor David Musyj until supervision ends, at which point it will assume full authority over the organization.
Ron Sapsford, a former Ontario deputy minister of health and long-term care and former CEO of the Ontario Medical Association, has been named board chair.
“It’s an important hospital, not only for London, but for southwestern Ontario. So I think it’s important to get the board back in operation. That to me is the crucial part,” Sapsford said.
The other board members are Scott Courtice, Cedric Gomes, Christi-Ann Poulette, Michael G. Power, David Smith, Melanie Stanley and Lori Van Opstal.
Five community members will also serve on board committees: Catherine Osborne, Leo Plue, Mike Tidy, Nick Vander Gulik and Lloy Wylie.
The appointments follow a recruitment process that attracted more than 90 applicants.

The move comes after a turbulent period for LHSC. In 2024, the province placed the hospital under supervision following serious concerns about governance, financial oversight and organizational leadership.

A provincial review identified significant governance failures, while subsequent investigations uncovered allegations of fraud involving former executives and contractors. The allegations have not been proven in court.
Musyj says the hospital has spent the past two years making structural changes to strengthen accountability and oversight.

Those changes include consolidating management positions, introducing 360-degree performance reviews, tightening spending controls, expanding internal audits and strengthening whistleblower protections.
The hospital has also refreshed its bylaws, policies and procedures and introduced additional oversight of budgeting, staffing decisions, quality indicators and patient safety.
“We’re in a good spot moving forward,” Musyj said, adding that the individuals involved in the alleged misconduct are no longer with the organization.
The renewed board will operate through four standing committees: finance and audit, quality and safety, human resources, and research.
Despite the appointments, Musyj says provincial supervision will not end immediately.
“You don’t want to do this again, right? So you don’t want to stay too long, but you don’t want to leave too early,” Musyj said.

Meanwhile, legal proceedings related to the alleged fraud remain ongoing. Musyj said the civil lawsuits are in the discovery phase, which involves exchanging documents and sworn evidence, as well as examinations for discovery.
He also confirmed the hospital is co-operating with a police investigation and responding to requests for information.
Musyj said further developments involving the civil proceedings are expected to be announced.

The renewed board’s first public meeting is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027. LHSC says meetings will be open to the public and livestreamed as part of its commitment to transparency and community engagement.
The hospital says the goal is to eventually return to local governance with stronger oversight and accountability measures in place.

stories.title: Lack of lawful access regime tied to ‘exponential growth’ of online child abuse material: police
stories.summary: They argued that police are feeling increasingly powerless to deal with online crimes with powers designed in the pre-Internet era
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
'If you have enough money, you’re going to find someone to do whatever you want.' — Dr. Ian MacArthur, a plastic surgeon

They argued that police are feeling increasingly powerless to deal with online crimes with powers designed in the pre-Internet era

Tom Stamatakis, president of the Ottawa-based Canadian Police Association. (Ashley Fraser / Postmedia)

November 18, 2026 at 5:53 p.m.

Ottawa — “Continuous kicking of the can” on lawful access reform like Bill C-22 has contributed to the “exponential growth” of online child abuse material, the head of a group of detectives focused on online child exploitation told senators.

On Wednesday, child protection agencies and law enforcement representatives made a passionate plea to senators on the national defence committee to quickly pass the Liberals’ controversial lawful access Bill C-22.

Every day that law enforcement don’t have access to a new lawful access regime fit for the digital age is another day where police struggle to tackle heinous online crime, particularly child sexual abuse material, they argued.

“To be blunt, our society is losing the effort to combat the exploitation of children over the internet,” said Andrew Ullock, chair of the Ontario Child Sexual Exploitation Investigators Association and a longtime detective with Peel Regional Police.

Ullock, as well as the heads of the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, the Canadian Police Association and the National Police Federation, pleaded with senators to pass Bill C-22 as quickly as possible and dismissed calls for further tightening of the contested bill.

They argued that police are feeling increasingly powerless to deal with online crimes with powers designed in the pre-Internet era. They said that they are required to get court warrants to obtain the most basic information about online activity without knowing if a company even holds the data they seek.

“In practical terms, (Bill C-22) would help police avoid wasting valuable time by seeking judicial orders from the wrong service provider, obtain basic subscriber information based on reasonable suspicion, and address lengthy delays when critical evidence is held outside of Canada and at risk of disappearing,” said Tom Stamatakis, the president of the Canadian Police Association union.

Lawful access is one of the most intrusive powers afforded to police and intelligence agencies. Creating such a regime for the digital age in Canada has been the subject of fierce debate for decades.

Bill C-22 proposes a new lawful access regime which would make it easier for police and intelligence agencies to intercept private communications or personal data as part of their investigations.

It creates new and faster legal tools for authorities to find out if a person is a client of a specific organization and then obtain some of their subscriber information with a warrant.

It also proposes new obligations to electronic service providers to organize and retain various types of client data in a way that makes it obtainable by law enforcement or Csis with a warrant.

That means that if passed, the bill would compel electronic service providers to store and make information like device locations or cameras available to police or Csis with the requisite warrant. That could be used to track a person’s live location in case they pose a threat to national security or are considered to be in danger, the government has said.

It also controversially allows the minister to issue a secret order compelling any electronic service provider to create such a capacity and retain users’ metadata for up to six months.

Some critics and privacy advocates told the committee that the metadata retention requirement is either too broad, too long, or both.

But police and child protection agencies dismissed those fears Wednesday, arguing that the bill shouldn’t only target specific metadata to be retained because police don’t know what information they will seek before an investigation is underway.

They also objected to suggestions the retention be reduced from six months to 30 days.

“If they only kept the metadata for 30 days, that would be useless to us,” Ullock added.

The bill has been applauded by police forces as a long-overdue fix to growing obstacles to investigations, but panned by civil liberties advocates and tech companies as an attack on privacy and encryption.

In an interview with National Post last week, a senior Meta executive said all options are on the table — including pulling uber-popular messaging app WhatsApp from Canada — if the government uses any proposed powers in its lawful access bill to undermine the company’s encryption.

But on Wednesday, many witnesses pooh-poohed Meta and other tech companies’ threats to leave the country over C-22.

“It’s a big bluff. I think everyone in this room knows that WhatsApp is not going to disappear from Canada if this legislation passed as is. It’s all a big gambit, that’s all it is,” said Lloyd Richardson, the director of technology at the Canadian Centre for Child Protection.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government. Reach him on Signal: ChrisNardi.01

stories.title: Ford admits his French needs work after shaky Montreal speech
stories.summary: Critics of the Ford government told reporters they didn’t find it funny that the premier of Canada’s largest province is unable to speak French, an official language.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
It’s all French to Premier Doug Ford, who is sheepishly hoping the public will excuse his shaky attempt to speak en français, after a video of him addressing a Montreal crowd went viral.

“It’s a little rougher than I thought,” Ford told reporters Tuesday.

“I was as nervous as anything, practising four lines, but it was a very warm welcome in Quebec,” he said.

The premier was in Montreal on Tuesday to promote stronger trade ties between the province and Quebec in the face of the trade war with the United States.

But it was his French during his address to the Chamber of Commerce of Metropolitan Montreal that drew the most attention.

“Oh, I’m really messing this one up,” Ford told the Chamber after stumbling through some French lines. Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Oh, I'm really messing this one up," Ford told the Chamber after stumbling through some French lines.

Critics of the Ford government told reporters they didn’t find it funny that the premier of Canada’s largest province is unable to speak French, an official language.

“It’s actually not something to laugh about,” said Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser.

Fraser, who also admitted that he too is not entirely fluent in French, said that at least he takes his weekly lessons seriously. ‘It’s important as a legislator to be able to do it,’ he said.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the “very significant” Francophone community in Ontario should expect their premier to know “basic phrases”.

“I wish he would practice a little more. I didn’t think it was particularly funny; I just thought it was kind of embarrassing,” she said.

stories.title: The seizures of more than 120 dogs renew calls for tougher breeder rules on P.E.I.
stories.summary: More than 120 dogs have been seized during two major operations on P.E.I. this year, renewing calls for tougher provincial oversight of animal breeding.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown - More than 120 dogs have been seized during two major operations on P.E.I. this year, renewing calls for tougher provincial oversight of animal breeding.

The P.E.I. Humane Society is still caring for 84 dogs seized earlier this month, after another 43 were taken into custody in February. Neither case has been confirmed to involve breeders, and the latest investigation remains ongoing.

“It was really, really challenging to see that many animals coming in, in need (of medical care) all at one time,” said Ashley Travis, the Humane Society’s development and communications co-ordinator.

Advocates call for stricter measures

P.E.I. has standards of care for kennels, but no mandatory licensing system specifically for breeders.

Non-profit organization P.E.I. Cares, is behind a petition signed by nearly 2,000 people calling for licensing, routine inspections and record-keeping requirements, among other measures. It was presented to the provincial legislature Friday.

Karla Shalley, the organization’s president, said the Island’s Animal Welfare Act was fairly progressive when it came into force in 2017, but her group believes it remains inadequate.

“We see neglect and situations like this on a very small scale,” she said, adding that people contact the organization with concerns almost daily.

In a statement to CTV News, the Department of Agriculture said the existing law already requires breeders to meet national standards for animal health, housing and welfare. It said complaints are investigated and the province is always reviewing its legislation for possible improvements.

Elsewhere in Atlantic Canada, New Brunswick requires those breeding dogs for sale, to obtain a licence following an inspection.

In Nova Scotia , a veterinary health certificate is required when a cat or dog is sold.

“I think there’s room to talk to some other provinces about what they’re doing and how they’re strengthening their laws,” Travis said.

For now, the fate of the latest group of dogs remains uncertain as the legal process continues. The Humane Society is asking for donations to help cover their medical care and other ongoing needs.

stories.title: A ‘long road’ lies ahead for Regina boy, 4, after alleged medical malpractice
stories.summary: The family of a Regina boy, 4, who needs a small intestine transplant alleges that it is the result of medical malpractice stemming from his appendicitis treatment in September.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The family of a young boy in need of an organ transplant alleges he was subject to medical malpractice, which required him to undergo multiple surgeries in two weeks’ time.

Four-year-old Sheldon One Bear Rosebluff needs a small intestine transplant after his family says he fell ill in October due to a complication from surgery to treat his appendicitis, which he had received a month earlier.

In October, a surgeon in Regina, where the family lives, told his caregiver and aunt, Kristin Lerat, that Rosebluff needed surgery to address a blockage in his bowel, she said. The procedure was performed five hours later.

“(The surgeon was) not communicating with me, or my partner, (about) what had happened in surgery,” Lerat said at a news conference in Saskatoon Wednesday.

She said she had had care of the boy for three years and her rights to make his medical decisions were revoked and granted to doctors in Regina when his condition became critical.

Rosebluff received four surgeries in two weeks, according to the family’s spokesperson.

“He was dying in Regina. They airlifted us by ambulance to Saskatoon,” Lerat said, adding that he remains in the Jim Pattison Children’s Hospital. “The surgeon here didn’t want to do surgery on him unless it was life and death. So, the next day it was life and death. And they did surgery on him.”

That surgery revealed that the main blood supply to his small intestine was cut off – effectively killing the organ, Lerat said.

“In the last surgery, he was critical the whole time but became very, very critical. His body just couldn’t handle that many surgeries. He is still in critical condition with breathing support,” she added.

“This is going to be a long, long road. For him to be on the transplant list, to be fed by the tube – he cannot eat – he has to be fed by a tube until he gets the surgery and this transplant. But we’re not there yet, there’s steps to take.”

One of those steps will take the family to Edmonton, where Rosebluff will be assessed and put on the transplant list, Lerat said.

They will then return to Saskatoon, where the four-year-old will await a transplant in hospital. Lerat said she, the rest of the boy’s family and his entire support system will stand beside him as his treatment continues.

“We will be One Bear’s voice. And he will be heard. He will not fall through the cracks, and the red tape will be (removed),” she said.

The alleged malpractice that occurred in Regina is being investigated by the First Nations Health Ombudsperson Office (Fnhoo) and Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA).

Dianne Lafond, a health ombudsperson with the Fnhoo, told reporters she could not comment on the active probe until it is completed.

The organizations will determine what happened, how it was allowed to happen, and how the system can be improved, she said.

“You put yourself in (Rosebluff’s family’s) shoes in those situations and it’s not a good place to be. You feel helpless, frustrated, defeated. A lot of these symptoms that First Nations people have been feeling in so many systems for so long,” Lafond said.

In an emailed statement to Global News, the chief medical officer of SHA, Dr. Rashaad Hansia, extended his sincere concern and support to Rosebluff and his family, but said he could not comment on their specific case – citing privacy concerns.

“The SHA is committed to providing the child with high-quality, compassionate care and to working collaboratively with the family and partners involved in the child’s care. Social Work supports are in place to assist in liaising with the family and coordinating with partner agencies, and we are (committed) to ensuring these interactions and supports are provided in a culturally respectful way,” Hansia wrote.

“Patient safety and the delivery of high-quality, patient-centred care remain top priorities for the SHA, and we take patient safety concerns very seriously. Anytime there is a concern about patient care or outcomes, the SHA conducts a thorough review to understand what might have occurred. We can confirm that a review is currently underway.”

Chief of Cowessess First Nation Erica Beaudin told reporters she has spoken with government representatives and Premier Scott Moe about Rosebluff’s medical care.

“They have given me the assurance that they will do what they need to do to keep little One Bear at the forefront and the priority,” she said.

The Cowessess chief called on the relevant Saskatchewan government departments, including the Ministries of Health and Social Services, to partner with the First Nation. Together, Beaudin said they can work to ensure the boy’s life is prioritized, and his family has the support they need.

“We are not here to denounce a health care system or the people in it per se. But what we’re talking about is how we must recognize when we must do better,” she said.

The Saskatchewan government ministries were asked for comment. None was received before publication.

“Next week, the week after that, there could be another little One Bear,” Beaudin said.

“Any race, any creed. They are all our children.”

stories.title: Quebec environmental group takes province to court over delayed climate target
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - A Quebec environmental law group and eight citizens are taking the provincial government to court, challenging its decision to delay a greenhouse gas emissions reduction target by five years.
stories.author: Stéphane Blais The Canadian Press
stories.content:
QUÉBEC - A Quebec environmental law group and eight citizens are taking the provincial government to court, challenging its decision to delay a greenhouse gas emissions reduction target by five years.

The Centre québécois du droit de l’environnement announced Wednesday that it had filed an application for judicial review in Quebec Superior Court seeking to overturn a decision that pushed back the deadline for reducing emissions by 37.5 per cent below 1990 levels from 2030 to 2035. The applicants argue the move violates environmental law and their fundamental rights.

The legal action is challenging an order-in-council adopted in January under the previous Coalition Avenir Québec government. It asks the court to declare the decision invalid and require the government to reconsider its climate target in accordance with its legal and constitutional obligations.

The applicants also describe their legal action on provincial climate change mitigation goals as the first of its kind against the Quebec government.

“We believe Quebec cannot backtrack and that the order-in-council adopted under the previous government does not comply with the law and infringes on Quebecers’ fundamental rights,” executive director Geneviève Paul told a news conference at the provincial legislature.

“The new government inherited this setback, but it also inherited the opportunity to correct the situation.”

The office of Quebec’s new Environment Minister Jean Pellerin, who is attending the United Nations COP31 climate conference in Turkey, said in a statement that his department would carefully review the legal filing.

“This lawsuit concerns an action taken by the previous government,” the statement said.

The applicants argue the decision violates Quebec’s Environment Quality Act, is inconsistent with the province’s commitments under the Paris climate agreement and infringes on rights protected by the Canadian and Quebec charters.

Under Quebec’s environmental law, the government must consider scientific knowledge; the economic, social and environmental consequences of climate change; and its international commitments when setting emissions targets.

The applicants argue the delay also runs counter to the Paris Agreement’s principle of progression, which calls for increasingly ambitious climate commitments over time. Quebec declared itself bound by the agreement in 2016 within areas of provincial jurisdiction.

In January, then-environment minister Bernard Drainville announced the decision to delay the climate target despite opposition from the province’s advisory committee on climate change, a body established to advise the government.

Drainville cited economic uncertainty and U.S. tariffs, noting that several economic partners, including the United States, Ontario and British Columbia, had scaled back their climate commitments.

But the environmental law group argues those economic justifications were not supported by evidence and failed to adequately consider the growing costs of climate inaction.

The group’s lawyers also argue that delaying emissions reductions increases risks to people’s lives and safety, violating fundamental rights protected under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Quebec’s Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms.

The eight individual applicants come from different regions of Quebec and include students, an agricultural entrepreneur, a social worker and a retired municipal manager.

“The science hasn’t changed, so why should our targets change?” said 16-year-old Flavie Léveillé, a high school student from Longueuil, a Montreal suburb, at Wednesday’s news conference.

“We’re never certain we’ll meet our targets, but without ambitious, science-based goals, progress becomes even less likely.”

In a statement accompanying the lawsuit, Léveillé said she worries about the world future generations will inherit. “I would like to have children one day, but I can’t have a clear conscience if I do nothing to ensure they have a future,” she said.

Sylvie Beauregard, a retired municipal manager from Bedford, a town southeast of Montreal near the U.S. border, said climate change is already affecting her daily life.

The mother of three and grandmother of eight pointed to droughts driving up grocery prices, wildfires affecting her grandson who has asthma, the spread of ticks that carry Lyme disease and frequent hailstorms threatening vineyards in her region.

“We can no longer put off the fight against climate change, because our children and my grandchildren will pay the price,” Beauregard said. “My generation has degraded the environment. We have a duty to repair the damage.”

The lawsuit comes as Quebec’s new Parti Québécois government has outlined its own climate ambitions without specifying an emissions reduction target for 2030.

During the provincial election campaign, the sovereigntist party pledged to establish interim targets for 2030, 2035, 2040 and 2045 as part of a plan to reach carbon neutrality by 2050.

The party has committed to reducing emissions by 42.5 per cent below 1990 levels by 2034.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Air Force major charged with negligent performance, abuse of subordinates
stories.summary: Maj. Peter Headley has been charged with four military service offences related to his time as commander of Air Task Force Prestwick in the United Kingdom.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Maj. Peter Headley has been charged with four military service offences related to his time as commander of Air Task Force Prestwick in the United Kingdom.

A statement from the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal says Headley has been charged with two counts of negligent performance of military duty, one count of abuse of subordinates and one count of conduct to the prejudice of good order and discipline.

The negligence and prejudice charges could result in dismissal with disgrace, while an abuse charge can result in a short prison term.

The provost marshal’s statement says the investigation was launched in July and Headley has returned to Canada and remains employed by the Royal Canadian Air Force.

If the charges result in prosecution, they will be heard by the military justice system, says the statement.

As with non-military criminal matters, the accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

stories.title: Women's group says MPs gutted protections for women in Divorce Act bill
stories.summary: Ottawa - A women’s group says a House of Commons committee has dropped protections for women and children from a private member’s bill to update the Divorce Act.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - A women’s advocacy group says a House of Commons committee has stripped a private member’s bill of key measures that were designed to protect women and children experiencing family violence.

But the MP sponsoring the legislation says the justice minister is committed to further studying the issue.

The National Association of Women and the Law said the House justice committee dropped clauses in the bill that were focused on parental alienation claims.

Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner introduced Bill C-223 to amend the Divorce Act to curb parental alienation claims, among other changes.

She said in an interview Wednesday that Justice Minister Sean Fraser “has personally committed to me to studying this issue in further detail.”

“He has told me that he completely agrees that there are problems that he wants to address and that the Justice Department is excited to get working on analyzing the family law system and how these … concepts are being misused.”

Suzanne Zaccour, the National Association of Women and the Law’s director of legal affairs, said in a press release the organization is “deeply disappointed that the government and committee members chose not to protect women and children from harmful allegations of parental alienation.”

“Too often, protective mothers are punished for disclosing abuse and cut off from their children’s lives, for months or sometimes years, based on the assumption that the child’s fear of the father is due to the mother’s brainwashing. This bill was a chance to end that injustice, and the committee let it go.”

An earlier report from the organization that looked into the deaths of eight children said the concept of parental alienation is frequently invoked in courts, and is used to cast doubt on allegations of domestic violence.

Zaccour said in the release the committee didn’t invite survivors to testify. She also said the committee could have proposed amendments instead of just removing the clauses.

But Hepfner said the legislation still includes some wins, including removing the “friendly parent” rule.

“Even if a mother is afraid that her child is in physical danger with the other parent, she’s expected to support the relationship with the child and the other parent,” Hepfner said.

Hepfner said that “although we didn’t get everything we wanted out of the bill, I think there’s some really big wins here.”

Zaccour said removing the “friendly parent” rule would meaningfully improve the safety of children in divorce cases.

“This provision, which requires courts to evaluate parents’ willingness to support the child’s relationship with the other parent, presents a Catch-22 for mothers who are victims of violence: if they say the father is dangerous, they are blamed for not being supportive of the father-child relationship; if they say they support that relationship, their safety concerns become less credible,” Zaccour said.

While the House committee has now completed its process of amending the bill, it must still pass through the rest of the legislative process, including the Senate, before it becomes law.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Key Crown witness wraps up testimony at trial of man charged with setting best friend on fire
stories.summary: Robert Beasley started his lengthy testimony on Monday giving startling evidence about hearing the accused say he wanted get to 29-year-old Jonathan Graham and that he was going to die.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Robert Beasley started his lengthy testimony on Monday giving startling evidence about hearing the accused say he wanted get to 29-year-old Jonathan Graham and that he was going to die.

Beasley said the comments were made by an angry Bradley Joudrey after he got into a fight with the victim on July 12, 2022.

The court has heard a short while after the confrontation, Graham would be doused with gasoline and set on fire.

During cross-examination from defence lawyer Alexandra Mamo, Beasley was asked if the accused intended to set the victim’s White Jeep on fire and Beasley responded, “It’s possible.”

Beasley who was with both men that night gave his testimony with frequent breaks because he felt ill during the proceedings.

It’s the Crown’s theory that both the victim and the accused met after the fight, at a convenience store parking lot at Admiral Drive and Trafalgar Street in east London.

In its opening address the Crown also said that the accused filled up a Pepsi bottle with gasoline before meeting up with the victim.

Graham would die in hospital after suffering thermal injuries.

Joudrey would be charged with first degree murder and has plead not guilty.

The Crown’s case resumes.

stories.title: Health Canada approves new Eli Lilly GLP-1 pill for weight loss
stories.summary: Eli Lilly's Foundayo is also approved to help treat Type 2 diabetes.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland
stories.content:
Health Canada has authorized a new GLP-1 medication for weight loss that is a pill taken every day, rather than weekly injections.

Eli Lilly’s Foundayo is approved for adults with obesity as well as those who are overweight and have at least one related medical problem, such as high blood pressure or sleep apnea.

In addition to promoting and maintaining weight loss, the pill is also approved to help treat Type 2 diabetes.

Eli Lilly also makes the injectable drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound, which contain the active ingredient tirzepatide. Tirzepatide acts on two receptors associated with insulin production and hunger: GLP-1 and GIP.

Competitor Novo Nordisk manufactures injectables Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain the active ingredient semaglutide. Semaglutide acts on GLP-1 receptors. Several other companies make generic semaglutide sold in Canada.

The class of drugs known as GLP-1s have revolutionized weight-loss treatment and experts say some patients May prefer to take a pill rather than an injection.

There is another GLP-1 pill — Novo Nordisk’s Rybelsus — already on the market in Canada, but it is only approved for Type 2 diabetes management and not for weight loss.

The active ingredient in Foundayo is orforglipron, a non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist.

Because it’s a smaller molecule than peptides semaglutide and tirzepatide, orforglipron can be taken orally and absorbed without being broken down by the digestive system, said Dr. Ehud Ur, an endocrinologist in Vancouver who is not associated with either Eli Lilly or Novo Nordisk.

“It seems to be just as good as if not better” for weight loss as semaglutide and tirzepatide, he said.

The most common side effects of GLP-1 medications — both injectable and oral — include gastrointestinal issues, such as nausea or vomiting.

Ur said whether he would prescribe Foundayo depends on the patient, partly because he is still waiting for clinical trial results on whether or not orforglipron has a cardiovascular benefit like semaglutide and tirzepatide do.

Foundayo received Health Canada authorization on Nov. 13. Eli Lilly spokesperson Ethan Pigott said the company expects the pills to be available in pharmacies in January.

There May soon be a second GLP-1 weight-loss pill option in Canada: competitor Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill, which is still awaiting Health Canada approval.

Both Foundayo and the Wegovy pill are approved and available in the U.S.

Even though Wegovy is made of the large peptide molecule semaglutide, Novo Nordisk is able to manufacture it in pill form by adding an ingredient called salcaprozate sodium to protect it from being broken down by digestive enzymes.

Once the pill is swallowed, salcaprozate sodium, or Snac, temporarily makes the area around it less acidic and helps it pass through the stomach lining into the bloodstream, Novo Nordisk spokesperson Kate Hanna said in an email on Wednesday.

Even though Wegovy is made of the large peptide molecule semaglutide, Novo Nordisk is able to manufacture it in pill form by adding an ingredient called salcaprozate sodium to protect it from being broken down by digestive enzymes.

Once the pill is swallowed, salcaprozate sodium, or Snac, temporarily makes the area around it less acidic and helps it pass through the stomach lining into the bloodstream, Novo Nordisk spokesperson Kate Hanna said in an email on Wednesday.

stories.title: Man who viciously stabbed former roommate designated a dangerous offender
stories.summary: It was a vicious machete attack and beating that lead to the death of Kenneth Wallis, 56, just days before Christmas in December 2021.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
It was a vicious machete attack and beating that lead to the death of Kenneth Wallis, 56, just days before Christmas in December 2021.

Robert Charnock, 43, who lived at the same rooming house on Wharncliffe Road South would be convicted of manslaughter in summer 2024 after going on trial for second degree murder.

After a dangerous offender hearing got underway in September, both the Crown and the defence gave a joint sentencing submission to Justice Helen Rady last week.

They requested that Charnock be deemed a dangerous offender but also requested a 10 year sentence for the manslaughter conviction followed by a 10 year long term offender supervision order.

On Wednesday morning, Justice Rady agreed with both sides when handing down her decision.

The decision is unlike other dangerous offender designations where an indeterminate sentence is handed down to the offender.

During the trial there was evidence that Wallis had received more than 20 stab wounds during the attack.

The court heard that Charnock has dealt with mental health issues for most of his adult life and he will carry the dangerous offender designation for life.

When Wallis’ daughter Ashley Johnston addressed the court with her victim impact statement she spoke about the constant fear that she carries with her.

“This experience has affected my sense of security and safety,” said Johnston. “I should not have to live with fear because of what happened to my father.”

stories.title: Ex-RBC employee who viewed Carney’s bank data could face jail time
stories.summary: Ibrahim El-Hakim pleaded guilty in August to fraud over $5,000, unauthorized use of a computer and identity theft
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Crown says a former bank employee who admitted to opening fraudulent accounts and viewing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s personal information should be sentenced to two years behind bars.

Ibrahim El-Hakim, who worked at a Royal Bank of Canada branch in downtown Ottawa, pleaded guilty in August to fraud over $5,000, unauthorized use of a computer and identity theft.

A sentencing hearing for El-Hakim, 24, took place in an Ontario court Wednesday.

The Ottawa-born man was not at the hearing. It’s the second consecutive court date he has missed.

Justice Norm Boxall told the court the Canada Border Services Agency notified the RCMP in late September that El-Hakim had left Montreal for Doha, Qatar, earlier in the month.

His baggage was checked through to Lebanon and no return flight was booked, Boxall said.

Police were unable to locate El-Hakim, the judge said.

“The only reasonable inference on the evidence or information before me in this case is that Mr. El-Hakim deliberately left Canada to thwart the sentencing process,” Boxall said.

The judge added the sentencing needs to be conducted in a timely manner.

“The administration of justice would be undermined if the sentencing was postponed to when he returns to Canada, if he ever does,” he said.

The RCMP began an investigation last year following a complaint from RBC.

An agreed statement of facts in the case says El-Hakim was recruited by someone he believed “to be associated with organized crime.”

The agreed statement says El-Hakim opened at least 43 fraudulent accounts at the bank between November 2023 and June 2025.

El-Hakim received at least $5,000 in compensation – $500 for each account, issued in the form of an e-transfer deposited into one of his accounts at other banks, the statement says.

On June 17, 2025, El-Hakim accessed the customer banking profiles of Carney, Justin Trudeau and another individual, the statement adds. The Trudeau account he accessed “was determined not to belong to the former prime minister.”

While accessing these profiles, El-Hakim was observed consulting a smart watch, the statement says. On surveillance video, he was seen at one point taking a cellphone out of his pocket, using it and alternating his gaze between the phone and the computer screen of his bank workstation.

The Mounties have said the investigation did not lead them to believe there was any threat to Carney’s safety or to national security.

The Crown is seeking a sentence of 24 months in custody, followed by 24 months of probation with a variety of conditions.

Crown attorney Lindsay Little told the court Wednesday that El Hakim’s actions amounted to months of “sustained, dishonest conduct. This was not an isolated incident.”

Little highlighted the fact that El-Hakim queried Carney’s data and apparently tried to access Trudeau’s banking details.

“Public confidence is eroded by a case like this,” she said.

“Privacy is a right that applies to everyone, regardless of their status. Elected officials do not lose their financial privacy because they have chosen to dedicate their lives to politics or to the public sphere more generally.”

Ron Guertin, a lawyer who once represented El-Hakim, asked last month to be removed from the case because his client had left Ottawa.

Lawyer Paul Lewandowski has been appointed as amicus, or friend of the court, to assist with sentencing.

He said Wednesday in court that El-Hakim should receive a suspended sentence, meaning no jail time with a period of probation.

In the alternative, he said, a “short, sharp” jail term of 30 to 90 days would be appropriate.

Such a sentence would deter other bank employees from this kind of activity, given that “the spectre of a jail term is looming,” Lewandowski said.

Boxall said he plans to sentence El-Hakim next month.

stories.title: Ford puts onus on Ottawa ahead of Stellantis Brampton plant talks
stories.summary: The Ford government is pointing to Ottawa to do the heavy lifting on Stellantis, despite Joly urging that they need to be on the same page.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Federal Industry Minister Melanie Joly says the Ford government and Unifor need to “play their part” in the effort to keep the Brampton assembly plant in operation, as politicians and the union prepare to meet with the global CEO of Stellantis on Friday.

Yet the Ontario government is pointing to Ottawa to do the heavy lifting at the second high-stakes meeting with Stellantis in the last week, despite Joly urging that the provincial and federal governments need to be on the same page.

Those tensions cast doubt on government co-operation ahead of the meeting with the automaker. While Premier Doug Ford faces mounting pressure to protect Ontario workers, his government is also pushing back against federal emissions rules it says burden the company.

Ford said Tuesday that stepping in or cancelling Stellantis’ sale to Canadian defence manufacturer Roshel will “be up to the federal government.”

“(Ottawa) gave them money. We never gave them any money. So we’ll have to see how that discussion goes,” Ford told reporters Wednesday.

“We’re going to meet with (Stellantis) and see where they stand. Our goal is always to make sure that we bring back the jobs to the Brampton facility,” he said.

Ford is also calling on the federal government to reduce emissions regulations on firms like Stellantis, previously stating the company spends “about $340 million” in emissions taxes.

Vic Fedeli, Ontario’s economic development minister, said he will attend the meeting alongside Ford and added that “we’re hopeful and confident that we have a good meeting.”

Joly told reporters Wednesday morning that the Ford government and the union need to step up at the upcoming meeting, alongside Ottawa.

“We need to work as one because this is something that is important. Two thousand jobs are at stake,” she said.

For more than a week, Stellantis has faced major political backlash after it announced the sale of its idled Brampton plant last week to Roshel.

The sale was condemned by the union representing more than 9,000 of Stellantis’ workers who fear the Roshel takeover will mean the 2,000 employees who were laid off from the Brampton plant in 2023 will not be called back.

While Prime Minister Mark Carney initially derided the sale, calling it a “betrayal,” he has since admitted his government was aware of some elements of the sale before it was finalized. He has since called the sale a “partial solution.”

Joly said last week that Stellantis must repay “hundreds of millions of dollars” to Ottawa after it failed to restore jobs at the Brampton plant.

She sent the automaker a letter dated Nov. 12 that said Stellantis is in default of a 2022 federal funding agreement because it halted Jeep Compass production at the plant, failed or refused to identify a replacement vehicle, did not maintain any production at the facility and closed the plant.

In 2022, the federal government committed up to $529 million to help Stellantis retool its Brampton and Windsor facilities to produce electrified vehicles, while the Ontario government committed $513 million in provincial support.

Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser said Ford is shirking his responsibilities by relying on Ottawa to handle the Stellantis fallout.

“(The Ford government) has all the tools. It’s their responsibility,” he said.

'If you have enough money, you’re going to find someone to do whatever you want.' — Dr. Ian MacArthur, a plastic surgeon

Thirty-seven Conservatives voted with the Liberals, the Bloc Québécois, the NDP and the Greens to pass the bill at second reading

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre speaks during question period in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa Nov. 16, 2026. (Blair Gable / Postmedia)

November 18, 2026 at 4:02 p.m.

Ottawa — Dozens of Conservative MPs voted in favour of the Liberal government’s proposed changes to medical assistance in dying on Tuesday, though some of them say their votes May change as the bill comes to a third and final reading in the House of Commons.

The bill, known as the medical assistance in dying safeguards act, makes a number of changes to Canada’s existing Maid framework.

The first part is similar to a Conservative private member’s bill that was defeated earlier this fall, and proposes to indefinitely exclude mental illness from being considered as part of Maid eligibility. Under current law, people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness would become eligible for Maid in March.

The Conservative caucus has expressed support for that provision, and Conservative members of a special parliamentary committee helped write a report in the spring that recommended against allowing Maid for mental illness.

However, the second part of the bill has less clear-cut support on the Tory benches. The legislation also decriminalizes the use of advance requests for assisted dying.

That will allow people who’ve been diagnosed with a condition that will cause them to lose the capacity to consent to outline the conditions under which they would like to die with medical assistance.

Among them was Ontario MP Ben Lobb, who said it’s necessary to exclude people with mental illness from Maid and he’s taking a wait-and-see approach on advance requests. If there isn’t more clarity on that part of the bill after a committee study, he said he plans to vote against it at third reading.

Lobb also said he wasn’t concerned about a caucus split on the issue.

“We have a long history of being able to vote your conscience on topics such as this, and there’s different ways to come at it,” he said.

Lobb echoed what Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has said about the bill, calling for the government to split it in two parts to allow further study of advance requests.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser has said that’s not going to happen.

The MPs who voted for the bill faced blowback online on Wednesday, while others who voted against it — including Shuv Majumdar, Jeremy Patzer and Marc Dalton — took to posting on social media to highlight their vote.

The yea votes also included eight of the party’s 10 Quebec MPs (the remaining two were paired votes, meant to offset a Liberal MP who is away from the House during a vote).

That province effectively legalized advance requests two years ago, when it brought into place a legal framework and directed provincial prosecutors not to bring charges against health-care workers who carry out such requests. More than 2,000 people have filed a request so far.

At a press conference about the bill earlier this month, Quebec MP Dominique Vien argued for splitting the bill and said MPs should be able to make a personal decision about the law according to their conscience.

Saskatchewan MP Corey Tochor, who also voted in favour, didn’t clarify on Wednesday whether he supports advance requests. He told reporters he thinks “it’s horrendous what we’re doing with Maid in Canada today.”

“I believe the expansion of Maid is wrong for our society,” Tochor said.

Saskatchewan is the only other province that has so far said it plans to create a legal framework to permit Maid by advance request. Fraser’s bill requires the provinces to create safeguards around the handling of those requests, and allows provinces to opt out by not creating that framework.

Alberta’s government already passed legislation to bar advance requests and Maid for people with mental illness.

Several Alberta MPs voted in favour of the Liberal bill at second reading, including Laila Goodridge, Pat Kelly, Tom Kmiec, Mike Lake, David McKenzie and Greg McLean.

The bill is now headed to a House of Commons committee for study. The government limited the amount of debate on the bill at second reading in order to speed its passage.

Fraser said it must be in place before March 17 to avoid a scenario where Maid for mental illness becomes legal while Parliament is still debating the change.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

stories.title: Alberta government to require cleanup funds to be set aside for each new well drilled
stories.summary: Calgary - The Alberta government has introduced legislation that would require oil and gas companies to set aside funds for the future cleanup of every new well drilled.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - The Alberta government has introduced legislation that would require oil and gas companies to set aside funds for the future cleanup of every new well drilled.

If passed, the bill would create the Resource Asset Closure Assurance and Stewardship Fund. Money would follow each well through its life cycle, even if ownership changes hands.

Companies would be required to make an initial payment of up to $50,000 followed by equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The new rules are expected to apply to wells drilled after April 1, 2027.

Between the payments and compound interest that accrues over time, there should be enough money available to fund the eventual cleanup of a typical well, Brian Jean, minister of energy and minerals, told a news conference Wednesday.

“We are making sure that when these wells are drilled, we have something set aside for them to be cleaned up so that the taxpayers are not on the hook.”

Managing the backlog of old oil and gas wells that have no one legally responsible for them, due to bankruptcy and other factors, has been a long-running issue in Alberta. Farmers have raised concern about contamination from inactive wells on their land.

Cleanup of such sites is managed through the non-profit Orphan Well Association and is funded through an industry fee, the amount of which the Alberta Energy Regulator recommends to the Alberta government every year. That fee would continue to exist.

The Orphan Well Levy for the 2026-27 fiscal year is $154.56 million, up from $144.45 million the previous year, though the well association has pegged total cleanup costs of its inventory at $1.66 billion.

The latest monthly numbers from the Orphan Well Association say there are 7,328 wells are waiting to be decommissioned, which involves permanently dismantling equipment so that the site is safe. Another 9,258 sites are in need of reclamation, which means restoring the land so it’s similar to its original state.

In the 2025-26 fiscal year, the average cost of decommissioning a well was $28,800 and for reclaiming a site, it was $27,700.

Under the new rules — proposed as part of a broader bill that also includes new restrictions for data centres, greater illegal dumping fines and other matters — a company would be eligible to receive the funds that were set aside once reclamation is complete. If the well becomes orphaned, the funding would be transferred to the Orphan Well Association.

“We’re making good on a promise that we made to Albertans to stop the flow of unfunded wells to the Orphan Well Association,” Jean said.

“After these changes are put into effect, no new oil and gas well will end up at the OWA without industry-paid-for closure funding.”

Terry Schmidtke, who chairs the Alberta Small Producers Group, said the changes will give junior oil and gas companies greater confidence to buy and sell producing wells that are drilled after the rules take effect.

“By ensuring cleanup funding stays with each well when ownership changes, smaller producers can continue to invest and grow while meeting their long-term cleanup obligations and keeping Albertans employed in the industry right across the province,” Schmidtke said in the province’s news release.

Farmers have long demanded greater assurances that oil and gas sites on their land will be properly cleaned up, Peter Dobbie, a property rights advocate, said in the provincial release.

“These changes should ensure that any new wells drilled will be cleaned up and returned to full agricultural use when they stop producing.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: On his new album, saxophonist Joshua Redman channels the spirit of Sonny Rollins
stories.summary: After the jazz icon died earlier this year, Redman put together a tribute album
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
After jazz giant Sonny Rollins died earlier this year at 95, fellow jazz saxophonist Joshua Redman organized a tribute album. If Ever You Would Leave Us (we play for Rollins) is out on Friday. In advance of his concert at Toronto’s George Weston Recital Hall at the Meridian Arts Centre, Redman spoke to The Globe and Mail from his home in Berkeley, Calif.

Were you raised on Sonny Rollins’ music?

No, not in the way I was raised on John Coltrane’s music or on the music of my father [saxophonist Dewey Redman]. I discovered Sonny Rollins around the time I began playing saxophone, which was 10 or 11. I was trying to figure out what the language was all about and what improvisation was all about.

Was there a eureka moment when you arrived at Sonny’s music?

He opened the door. He made me grasp the power and the potential of improvisation. His was unscripted music on the edge, just raw and uninhibited, with an immediacy. But it also could have a narrative arc.

Yes. You never felt Sonny was playing isolated phrases.

Sonny played the sax solo on the Rolling Stones song Waiting on a Friend . You got to step into Sonny’s shoes at a Rolling Stones concert in St. Louis in 1997.

I was doing a week in L.A., at the Catalina Jazz Club. I got a call a day or two in advance to play Waiting on a Friend with the Rolling Stones. I was a big Stones fan too. I remember when that song came out, ON the album Tattoo You , in 1981. I was in high school.

The Stones asked him to play on their 1981 tour, but he said no.

I had read that in his biography. For the St. Louis show in ’97, what I was told was that Sonny Rollins can’t come. We had to really scramble to find someone to fill in for me in L.A. I was playing with Christian McBride and Brian Blade, and Branford Marsalis agreed to sub for me at the Catalina. He was no longer in the Tonight Show Band, but he was still in L.A.

So, you get to play with the Stones, second chair to Sonny Rollins in a way.

I don’t even feel I belong in the same room as Sonny Rollins. But it was an incredible honour. Just a blast to be able to play with the Rolling Stones. They were complete gentlemen.

When asked about Sonny in the past, you’ve talked about tapping into his spirit. Is that what you were attempting to do on this tribute album?

I feel like, ON a fundamental level, I wish I could sound like John Coltrane or Sonny Rollins. But I can’t. I can only sound like myself. Of course, I’ve taken language from them. I’ve studied all the great sax players, and Sonny is the greatest. There are ideas and phrases and approaches to the instrument and uses of the language that come from Sonny Rollins.

Is there ever a “what would Sonny do here” moment when you’re playing?

I try to play what I feel in the moment as honestly as I can in the spirit of the moment of what the other musicians are playing, and what I’m feeling from the audience and what’s inside of me in that moment. If you’re truly committed to the essence of improvisation, you can’t help but play yourself.

Putting this album together after Sonny died, do you see it as a responsibility?

I don’t. I wanted to celebrate Sonny out a sense of love for him and his music and everything he meant to me and the world of jazz – the world of music. I put together the album, but it’s really a collective effort. Sonny is like a father or a grandfather or a godfather to all of us on the album, as he was to everybody who came after him.

There’s a reason the word “colossus” is associated with Sonny.

paragraphs: After jazz giant Sonny Rollins died earlier this year at 95, fellow jazz saxophonist Joshua Redman organized a tribute album. If Ever You Would Leave Us (we play for Rollins) is out on Friday. In advance of his concert at Toronto’s George Weston Recital Hall at the Meridian Arts Centre, Redman spoke to The Globe and Mail from his home in Berkeley, Calif.
Were you raised on Sonny Rollins’ music?

No, not in the way I was raised on John Coltrane’s music or on the music of my father [saxophonist Dewey Redman]. I discovered Sonny Rollins around the time I began playing saxophone, which was 10 or 11. I was trying to figure out what the language was all about and what improvisation was all about.
Was there a eureka moment when you arrived at Sonny’s music?

He opened the door. He made me grasp the power and the potential of improvisation. His was unscripted music on the edge, just raw and uninhibited, with an immediacy. But it also could have a narrative arc.
Yes. You never felt Sonny was playing isolated phrases.
Sonny played the sax solo on the Rolling Stones song Waiting on a Friend . You got to step into Sonny’s shoes at a Rolling Stones concert in St. Louis in 1997.

I was doing a week in L.A., at the Catalina Jazz Club. I got a call a day or two in advance to play Waiting on a Friend with the Rolling Stones. I was a big Stones fan too. I remember when that song came out, ON the album Tattoo You , in 1981. I was in high school.
The Stones asked him to play on their 1981 tour, but he said no.

I had read that in his biography. For the St. Louis show in ’97, what I was told was that Sonny Rollins can’t come. We had to really scramble to find someone to fill in for me in L.A. I was playing with Christian McBride and Brian Blade, and Branford Marsalis agreed to sub for me at the Catalina. He was no longer in the Tonight Show Band, but he was still in L.A.
So, you get to play with the Stones, second chair to Sonny Rollins in a way.
I don’t even feel I belong in the same room as Sonny Rollins. But it was an incredible honour. Just a blast to be able to play with the Rolling Stones. They were complete gentlemen.
When asked about Sonny in the past, you’ve talked about tapping into his spirit. Is that what you were attempting to do on this tribute album?

I feel like, ON a fundamental level, I wish I could sound like John Coltrane or Sonny Rollins. But I can’t. I can only sound like myself. Of course, I’ve taken language from them. I’ve studied all the great sax players, and Sonny is the greatest. There are ideas and phrases and approaches to the instrument and uses of the language that come from Sonny Rollins.
Is there ever a “what would Sonny do here” moment when you’re playing?

I try to play what I feel in the moment as honestly as I can in the spirit of the moment of what the other musicians are playing, and what I’m feeling from the audience and what’s inside of me in that moment. If you’re truly committed to the essence of improvisation, you can’t help but play yourself.
Putting this album together after Sonny died, do you see it as a responsibility?

I don’t. I wanted to celebrate Sonny out a sense of love for him and his music and everything he meant to me and the world of jazz – the world of music. I put together the album, but it’s really a collective effort. Sonny is like a father or a grandfather or a godfather to all of us on the album, as he was to everybody who came after him.
There’s a reason the word “colossus” is associated with Sonny.

Right. So, what special permission or responsibility do we have to honour him? I see it more as debt of gratitude. The responsibility is to try in my own way as best I can, and I will always fail, to live up to his musical ideals.

stories.title: Alberta government proposes data centre buffer zone for homes, some farm land
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta's government is looking to set some new rules around major data centres and where they can be built.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson and Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Alberta’s government is looking to set new rules around major artificial intelligence data centres and where they can be built.

Legislation proposed Wednesday by Technology Minister Nate Glubish would, if passed, impose a 600-metre buffer zone from homes, high quality farm areas and irrigated land to data centres that are 10 megawatts or larger.

Glubish said the setback balances responsible development with protecting homeowners and communities.

He added that size of the buffer zone is equivalent to about six hockey arenas.

“It’s a significant distance,” he said.

The government said the rules won’t apply to projects that have already secured development permits and are well underway.

That includes tech giant Meta’s $13-billion AI data centre campus north of Edmonton, which has begun construction.

That project as planned would need one gigawatt of electricity, which is to be eventually provided by an adjacent $4.6-billion natural gas-fed power plant. Before the connected Greenlight Electricity Centre starts up in the second half of 2030 to power it, Meta has the rights to connect to Alberta’s power grid.

Earlier this year, a proposed project near the agricultural town of Olds, Alta., was scuttled after public outcry. The Alberta Utilities Commission denied the project’s application for a natural gas plant, citing its proximity to the town.

Glubish was also met with anger and concerns about data centres — particularly over pollution, power bills and water use — from hundreds of Albertans at a series of town halls over the summer.

Attendees expressed little trust in the government to regulate an industry poised to invest billions of dollars in the province to feed a growing global computing demand.

Glubish said Wednesday the bill shows the government listened to the feedback and that the new rules would protect communities.

He said it doesn’t mean that the government is backing down from its goal of positioning the province as an ideal place for industry investment.

Albertans should start seeing proposals for data centres in regions that are far from where the majority of people live, Glubish added.

“I think that’s going to calm a lot of folks, reassure a lot of folks.”

Glubish said he doesn’t regret not having stricter rules in place before the government launched its data centre attraction strategy in late 2024, when proposals began flooding in.

“Our systems are already working and protecting against irresponsible sites from being developed,” he said, adding a number of projects currently in the regulatory queue would likely have been rejected anyway.

The bill would also allow the government to set future standards and limits on data centre water use, with details to be finalized later through regulation.

The government said it’s aiming for “close to zero” water use.

Glubish said the new standard would be strict and effectively prohibit data centres from using evaporative cooling methods.

The province’s effort to recruit data centres included offering what it calls a concierge service to support proponents through the regulatory approval process. More than 70 proponents are working with the help of the concierge team.

Glubish said he recognizes that many Albertans didn’t trust that they were being protected.

“If that’s the case, then let me work hard on demonstrating to you that we’ve heard you, we’ve listened to you, and we care about the same things you care about,” he said.

Glubish said he believes the bill would give Alberta the strongest regulations for data centres in North America.

The Opposition NDP has called for a pause on data centre projects until better standards are developed.

NDP technology critic Nathan Ip said he’s baffled that the government is coming up with guidelines two years after releasing its strategy for the sector.

He said the bill lacks clear standards, including on water usage, and it doesn’t address Albertans’ concerns.

“I don’t think this bill does much of anything, other than a little bit of window dressing,” he said.

Beyond the new setback rule and promises of future water standards, the bill would also designate the Alberta Utilities Commission, the provincial utility regulator, to oversee all data centre projects over 10 megawatts.

Glubish said that means the commission would be the “primary vehicle” for public engagement on future projects. It would also be able to enforce noise and light pollution rules.

Data centres under 10 megawatts would continue to be managed by municipalities.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Banking outages are ‘a matter of when, not if.’ Do you know what to do?
stories.summary: As outages become more common, experts stress the importance of consumers and businesses having backup plans — especially when it comes to banking and finances.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Tech outages caused by glitches and cyberattacks are becoming more common, with a handful of major events occurring in the past week, and experts say those recent cases show the importance of consumers and businesses having backup plans — especially when it comes to finances.

Even if an outage is rare for a particular company or agency, the increasing frequency of these events can have major impacts for the consumers and businesses that rely on the services they provide.

“Let’s face it, our lives have become digital. We rely on these services to operate, and in some cases, we May not have contingency plans,” says Ritesh Kotak, a cybersecurity and technology analyst.

“It has a profound impact on just about every element of our lives. Just think about all the interconnected devices, all the apps and all the systems we use on a daily basis. When they get turned off, there’s a significant price to pay.”

Earlier this week, thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.

This came just days after a string of other outages in the past week.

On Monday, a suspected cyberattack using malicious code hit nearly 200 major websites , including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Ikea and Hsbc. The NSA also experienced an outage on Tuesday, but there have been no indications that this was related.

Last week, a global Microsoft software glitch made email services like Outlook unavailable for millions of people, which brought much of the economy to a standstill because of businesses’ reliance on it for communications. There was also an FAA ground stop last week , which brought most U.S. air travel to a halt for several hours and delayed flights in Canada and beyond.

Even a brief outage can have a major impact on consumers and businesses, especially when it involves banking and payments systems, which is why it’s key not to take these systems for granted.

“We are relying more on these services than we have traditionally, and we’re not allowing ourselves the luxury of having backups or workarounds or alternatives,” says technology analyst Carmi Levy.

“We need to ask ourselves, what do I do when these systems that I rely on inevitably go dark? Because they will — it’s a matter of when, not if.”

The majority of the economy runs on the digital exchange of money, rather than cash, paper cheques or money orders. Although this is still commonplace for many businesses, there is a push towards more digital payments and financial transactions, including paying for a coffee or processing a down payment on a home.

In Canada, Payments Canada is slowly rolling out its new sovereign payments platform known as RTR, or Real-Time Rail, which financial institutions are preparing to use as the main digital infrastructure to allow money to move faster and more reliably.

Although banks and financial institutions spend billions on cybersecurity and tech resilience, they May be more vulnerable than they realize.

“The financial services industry is particularly vulnerable to these kinds of outages because of the level of integration between different players. So banks, payment processors, other sort of network functions that we would never even see but are critical to ensuring that payments can happen. If one company has a problem, it ripples out across the entire industry,” says Levy.

“Next thing you know, dozens of companies with millions of customers are affected, and we kind of saw that with the JPMorgan Chase outage was that it rippled far and wide across the entire American financial system.”

He added: “When we talk about a bank outage, if your money is stuck within an account that is only accessible through an app, through a website, through a browser, you’re out of luck — there is no way to access it.”

Tech outages are inevitable, which means there is almost no way to realistically participate in modern digital society without assuming some issues will occur.

However, diversifying or expanding one’s financial arsenal allows for alternatives should one system go down.

“It’s important that we think about contingency plans such as having cash, knowing our account numbers, setting up auto payment where possible, maybe having multiple bank accounts so if there’s a glitch in one, at least you can still continue to access funds and be able to transact,” says Kotak.

“Our financial institutions are very strong. Are there gonna be glitches? Are there going to be outages? Absolutely, especially in the world that we’re living in. But if we spread our risk and not put all our eggs in one basket, we’ll be able weather the storm.”

Businesses also need to be prepared, because digital points of sale can also be impacted by outages. Those that decide not to keep cash on site or having other alternatives available May be risking a loss of revenue should those primary systems go down.

“Businesses need to recognize that they will lose significant revenue if they cannot process payments when their systems are unavailable, so they should think twice about cancelling cash as a viable method of payment,” says Levy.

Levy also suggests even if a bank account or credit card has a digital payment method available, like with a smartphone, keeping physical cards is another “low-tech alternative” like with cash.

“We should all be paying more attention to those alternative low tech cash-based methods and make sure that they’re working, they’re functional and everyone is familiar with them before a major outage happens that requires us to go there.”

Global News sent a request for comment on Wednesday to the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, which acknowledged the request, but did not provide a response by publication.

stories.title: Old Navy and Gap face probe over ‘deceptive’ marketing claims in Canada
stories.summary: The Competition Bureau said it is beginning an investigating into 'potentially false or misleading claims made by Old Navy and Gap.'
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The Competition Bureau is launching an investigation into Old Navy and Gap over allegations that the retail giants have made “fake or misleading claims” in their marketing campaigns.

The Competition Bureau said it has obtained a court order to “gather information and advance an ongoing investigation into potentially false or misleading claims made by Old Navy and Gap.”

The probe aims to determine whether Old Navy and Gap violated the deceptive marketing provisions of the Competition Act, however the Competition Bureau added that there was no evidence of wrongdoing from either brand at this time.

“The Bureau’s investigation includes an examination of whether regular prices are genuine when products are advertised as being on sale,” the Competition Bureau said in a statement.

The Competition Bureau said it is examining:

urgency cues, such as limited time offers, countdown timers or clocks.

messages suggesting products were in short supply, such as ”Selling Fast” or ”Only a Few Left’.’

popularity representations indicating consumer interest, such as the number of people viewing or purchasing a product.

claims about past prices or discounts, such as ”Price Drop” or ”Best Deal in 30 days”.

Both companies will be required to produce records and written information as part of the investigation, the Competition Bureau said.

stories.title: Health care professional orders urge Quebec to rethink services for unhoused people
stories.summary: Montreal - Four professional health orders are urging Quebec to adapt services to meet the needs of those experiencing homelessness.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The presidents of associations representing doctors, nurses, pharmacists, social workers and therapists published an open letter about the topic on Wednesday.

The professional orders say they visited Montreal’s largest homeless encampment and were appalled by the living conditions of residents and their difficulties in accessing care and services.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

They add that Quebec must strengthen its social safety net and loosen the administrative burdens that allow vulnerable people to fall through the cracks.

The encampment, which spans over two kilometres in the city’s east end, counts about 200 tents.

It became a flashpoint in the Quebec election campaign this fall, as the encampment is in Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s riding.

After police said a baby was found at the encampment, the Parti Québécois leader promised to make homelessness a top priority.

Following their visit of the encampment, the four presidents also met with those running a community organization nearby.

In their letter, they say they commend the work of community organizations who “are literally carrying the crisis on their shoulders.”

The health professionals acknowledge that homelessness is a complex issue that requires complex solutions.

“Individually, we do not have the necessary solutions to address these issues. Only together can we implement changes that will allow us to meet people’s needs first, and less those of the system,” they wrote.

The health professionals confirmed they will participate in the summit on homelessness promised by St-Pierre Plamondon’s government scheduled for winter 2027.

“We are already gathering to reflect and offer concrete proposals to simplify the work of health and social services professionals,” the letter says.

“The time is no longer for awareness, but for action,” they add. “Simply following the status quo is, in our eyes, inconceivable.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

The Canadian Press
