stories.title: Driver ticketed after transport truck gets stuck under Fredericton bridge
stories.summary: The driver of a transport truck was ticketed Wednesday after the vehicle became lodged under a walking bridge in Fredericton.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
The driver of a transport truck was ticketed Wednesday after the vehicle became lodged under a pedestrian bridge in Fredericton.

Fredericton Police Force says the semi-truck got stuck under the Bill Thorpe Walking Bridge on Waterloo Row at around 9 a.m.

Yellow signs on the overpass indicate the clearance height is 3.5 metres. Instances of trucks striking the bridge or becoming stuck have occurred in the past.

To remove the truck, police say they typically need to use heavy equipment, unload the cargo and possibly deflate the tires.

The truck was safely removed by 1:45 p.m. and the driver was issued a ticket, according to a police spokesperson.

Meanwhile, there is no visible damage to the bridge but police say the city will need to conduct an inspection as a precautionary measure.

stories.title: Porter Airlines already hinting at expansion as first flight from YXU departs London
stories.summary: Porter Airlines has launched its first flights from London, Ont., promising more if the region supports its international and domestic destinations.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Porter Airlines has launched its first flights from London, Ont., promising more if the region supports its international and domestic destinations.

On Wednesday morning, passengers boarded a 132-seat jet bound for Ft. Lauderdale, Florida.

Its flight marks the end of a long campaign by London International Airport (YXU) officials - and passengers alike - to get Porter service to London.

Gino Battel and Abigail Ferber were thrilled they did not have to travel to Toronto to catch a plane to the heat.

“This is the best thing that has happened. It’s great. Took us 20 minutes to get here this morning,” said an excited Battel.

Joe Da Costa and his wife Mira paid about $700 for tickets - which the couple said is far less than paying for hotels and gas if they drove south.

“We got a place down there. So usually, we drive. But this year we decided to just fly in. Really, it’s more convenient,” said Joe.

“And it’s easy!” added Mira.

And that advantage is exactly what Porter hopes to build on, according to Edmond Eldebs, senior vice-president and chief commercial officer.

“There’s a 2-million-person catchment area around London, and the London airport is the most convenient option for them,” said Eldebs.

Orlando, Jamaica, and Mexico flights begin over the next month, with domestic flights in the spring of 2027 to Halifax, Montreal, Ottawa, Edmonton, and Vancouver.

If the routes attract a steady stream of business and recreational travellers, Eldebs said Porter is eyeing expansion, “This is just the beginning for Porter. And I think you’ll see us add more flights and more frequencies over time.”

YXU CEO Scott McFadzean expects more flights will generate competition, leading to more revenue for the airport.

“That means terminal expansions, parking expansions and more amenities. You know, I’d like to see a hotel here at some point, to take advantage of those early morning flights with people coming from all over the region,” he said.

stories.title: Competition Bureau investigating ‘potentially false or misleading claims’ made by Old Navy and Gap
stories.summary: The Competition Bureau says it has obtained a court order to advance an ongoing investigation into Old Navy and Gap.
stories.author: Kayla Thompson
stories.content:
The Competition Bureau says it has obtained a court order to advance an ongoing investigation into Old Navy and Gap.

The independent law enforcement agency said on Wednesday that the investigation involves “potentially false or misleading claims” made by the clothing brands, each operated by Gap Inc.

“The Bureau is seeking to determine whether specific marketing practices used by Old Navy and Gap raise concerns under the deceptive marketing provisions of the Competition Act . There has been no finding of wrongdoing at this time,” the Competition Bureau said in a news release .

The agency says its investigation will examine whether regular prices are genuine when products are advertised as being “on sale,” as well as urgency cues such as limited-time offers and countdown timers.

The investigation will also examine promotional messages such as “Selling Fast” or “Only a Few Left,” which suggest products are in short supply.

According to the news release, Old Navy and Gap will be required to produce records and written information relevant to the Bureau’s investigation.

News about the investigation comes just a week ahead of Black Friday, ON Nov. 27, when brands frequently advertise price drops and their largest annual discounts.

The agency says it is committed to protecting “consumers from deceptive marketing practices in the digital economy,” and says it saw an increase in complaints about “inflated regular prices” in 2025.

In the same year, the agency published a warning to businesses reminding them that it’s illegal to advertise fake discounts by promoting a made-up “regular price.”

stories.title: Crown seeks jail for ex-bank worker who opened fraudulent accounts, viewed PM’s data
stories.summary: The Crown says a former bank employee who admitted to opening fraudulent accounts and viewing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s information should receive jail time.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Crown says a former bank employee who admitted to opening fraudulent accounts and viewing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s information should receive jail time.

Ibrahim El-Hakim pleaded guilty in August to fraud over $5,000, unauthorized use of a computer and identity theft.

A sentencing hearing for El-Hakim, who worked at a Royal Bank of Canada branch in Ottawa, took place in an Ontario court today.

El-Hakim was not at the hearing and Justice Norm Boxall said his location is unknown.

An agreed statement of facts in the case says El-Hakim was recruited by someone he believed “to be associated with organized crime.”

The agreed statement says El-Hakim opened at least 43 fraudulent accounts at the bank between November 2023 and June 2025.

stories.title: Seventeen injured as intense fire destroys building in Glace Bay, N.S.
stories.summary: Sixteen fire departments battled flames that engulfed the building for hours, finally extinguishing the blaze around noon
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An explosion in the Cape Breton community of Glace Bay ignited an intense fire Wednesday that injured 17 people and reduced a three-storey building to smouldering rubble.

Later that afternoon, fire officials had yet to determine if anyone who was living in the building was still unaccounted for, a spokesperson for the Cape Breton region said in an interview.

Christina Lamey said there were reports of an explosion around 6 a.m. on Commercial Street before the fire tore through the downtown building, which eventually collapsed.

She said 14 people were taken to hospital with minor injuries.

Cecil Clarke, mayor of the Cape Breton Regional Municipality, said the explosion and fire destroyed a pizza shop on the ground floor of the building, which had apartments in the two storeys above it. The blast also shattered windows in nearby buildings.

Photos and videos posted to social media show a plume of black smoke billowing over Glace Bay’s main strip while huge orange flames shoot up from the fast-burning building.

Lamey said 16 fire departments battled flames that engulfed the building for hours, finally extinguishing the blaze around noon.

“The long-serving fire chief of Glace Bay remarked that it was the biggest response that he had seen in his career,” said Lamey.

The mayor said emergency crews responded quickly.

“They all worked remarkably well together and were able to get this under control much sooner and contain it so it wasn’t much worse,” Clarke said in an interview.

The gutted building is next to the historic Savoy Theatre, a community landmark that is almost 100 years old.

Management at the theatre issued a statement saying damage to the building will be repaired.

Clarke said the theatre was saved by winds that carried the flames away from the building.

The cause of the explosion is under investigation.

Kim Masland, Nova Scotia’s emergency management minister, said her thoughts were with everyone affected by the fire.

“My heart goes out to those who have been injured,” she said in a statement “I’m deeply grateful to the firefighters, police officers, paramedics … and all of the emergency personnel who are working tirelessly at the scene.”

stories.title: Forest City Sports is keeping local sports coverage alive in London Ontario
stories.summary: A new Blackburn media platform is putting a new spotlight on all levels of London sports and athletes. Launche...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
A new Blackburn media platform is putting a new spotlight on all levels of London sports and athletes.

Mike Stubbs at office. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

Launched last month and headed by a man known as ‘the voice of the London Knights,’ Forest City Sports aims to enhance sports coverage that has been more difficult with a decline in local news coverage.

The platform joins another recent startup, London Ontario Sports, which is also showcasing local sports.

“The area used to have more reporters and flexibility to report on local sports stories. We are trying to put more (local sports) back in,” said Mike Stubbs, the longtime sports and news journalist who is leading Forest City Sports coverage.

From its October debut Instagram post on the London West Lady Tin Caps all-girls baseball team to this week’s coverage of the London Knights, Western Mustangs and the citywide high school football champs, the platform has something for all sports fans.

“I don’t know if I’ve had this much fun ever at work. It is just fun to go and cover sports, and it’s something that I’ve always loved doing.”

London Knights player Interview. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

On any given day, you might catch Stubbs interviewing high school athletes on the sidelines, shooting videos of Knights pre-game speeches or talking to Fanshawe and Western players and coaches.

Stubbs finds his stories by going to local events and games around the city. His long standing relationships with London organizations help give Forest City Sports the connections to get to the stories.

Recent stories highlight the London Knights, the Western Mustangs, the Fanshawe College Falcons and even high school sports.

Local media’s ability to cover sports has been challenged with staffing changes, Stubs said. A decade ago, it would be common to see at least five or six reporters and photographers at local sporting events, but these days there May only be one or two.

The city does still have solid Ontario Hockey League coverage, with journalists like Ryan Pyette from the London Free Press and Brent Lale from CTV following closely.

Since its launch, Forest City Sports has a modest following of just under 400 on Instagram and 500 on Facebook.

“The goal is designed to put more stories in the hands and eyes of people who want to read them” Stubbs said.

As Forest City Sports gains more popularity throughout London, its impact on the local sports community will continue to grow, giving local teams and athletes a voice.

stories.title: Health Canada approves Eli Lilly’s GLP-1 pill for weight loss
stories.summary: Health Canada has authorized a new GLP-1 medication for weight loss that is a pill taken every day, rather than weekly injections.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Health Canada has authorized a new GLP-1 medication for weight loss that is a pill taken every day, rather than weekly injections.

Eli Lilly’s Foundayo is approved for adults with obesity as well as those who are overweight and have at least one related medical problem, such as high blood pressure or sleep apnea.

In addition to promoting and maintaining weight loss, the pill is also approved to help treat Type 2 diabetes.

Eli Lilly also makes the injectable drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound, which contain the active ingredient tirzepatide. Tirzepatide acts on two receptors associated with insulin production and hunger: GLP-1 and GIP.

Competitor Novo Nordisk manufactures injectables Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain the active ingredient semaglutide. Semaglutide acts on GLP-1 receptors. Several other companies make generic semaglutide sold in Canada.

The class of drugs known as GLP-1s have revolutionized weight-loss treatment and experts say some patients May prefer to take a pill rather than an injection.

There is another GLP-1 pill — Novo Nordisk’s Rybelsus — already on the market in Canada, but it is only approved for Type 2 diabetes management and not for weight loss.

The active ingredient in Foundayo is orforglipron, a non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist.

Because it’s a smaller molecule than peptides semaglutide and tirzepatide, orforglipron can be taken orally and absorbed without being broken down by the digestive system, said Dr. Ehud Ur, an endocrinologist in Vancouver who is not associated with either Eli Lilly or Novo Nordisk.

“It seems to be just as good as if not better” for weight loss as semaglutide and tirzepatide, he said.

The most common side effects of GLP-1 medications — both injectable and oral — include gastrointestinal issues, such as nausea or vomiting.

Ur said whether he would prescribe Foundayo depends on the patient, partly because he is still waiting for clinical trial results on whether or not orforglipron has a cardiovascular benefit like semaglutide and tirzepatide do.

Foundayo received Health Canada authorization on Nov. 13. Eli Lilly spokesperson Ethan Pigott said the company expects the pills to be available in pharmacies in January.

There May soon be a second GLP-1 weight-loss pill option in Canada: competitor Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill, which is still awaiting Health Canada approval.

Both Foundayo and the Wegovy pill are approved and available in the U.S.

Even though Wegovy is made of the large peptide molecule semaglutide, Novo Nordisk is able to manufacture it in pill form by adding an ingredient called salcaprozate sodium to protect it from being broken down by digestive enzymes.

Once the pill is swallowed, salcaprozate sodium, or Snac, temporarily makes the area around it less acidic and helps it pass through the stomach lining into the bloodstream, Novo Nordisk spokesperson Kate Hanna said in an email on Wednesday.

stories.title: Watchdog investigating if Gap, Old Navy ‘best deal in 30 days’ claims hold up
stories.summary: Canada's competition watchdog says it's obtained a court order to help it advance an ongoing investigation into whether Old Navy and Gap have made misleading price claims in their marketing.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canada’s competition watchdog says it’s obtained a court order to help it advance an ongoing investigation into whether Old Navy and Gap have made misleading price claims in their marketing.

The Competition Bureau says information it will receive through the court order will help it determine whether the retailers are supplying customers with genuine regular prices when advertising items as on sale.

The bureau says it is also looking at urgency cues the retailers use, such as countdown timers or clocks, as well as messaging suggesting products are selling fast or advertising that there are only a few left.

It will also examine the accuracy of claims the companies make around how many people have viewed products or purchased them and investigate whether the company is being honest when it says the prices of some items have dropped or are the “best deal in 30 days.”

The bureau stressed its ongoing investigation has yet to find any instances of wrongdoing.

Gap and Old Navy share a parent company, Gap Inc., which says it’s co-operating with the bureau.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

Carney wouldn’t go as far as to say he now enjoys a 'bromance' with St-Pierre Plamondon but said they have a professional working relationship.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon share a laugh after a meeting in Phnom Penh,Cambodia, ON Nov. 15, 2026. (Facebook)

Catherine Lévesque

November 18, 2026 at 2:44 p.m.

Ottawa — Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is taking more of the blame for the rocky start to his relationship with the federal government, according to new polling data.

A Synopsis poll conducted for La Presse shows that 40 per cent of Quebecers consider St-Pierre Plamondon responsible for the tensions between Quebec and Ottawa in the past month, whereas half of them — 21 per cent — blame Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Twenty-four per cent of respondents believe both politicians are equally at fault.

St-Pierre Plamondon’s short tenure as premier has been marked by some friction with the federal government, starting with his decision not to attend a historic meeting in late October reuniting Carney, most premiers and First Nations leaders in Ottawa.

A few days later, St-Pierre Plamondon refused to attend the Canada-European Union Summit held in Montreal because he was not authorized to offer public remarks.

Both leaders then publicly sparred on the location of their first in-person meeting, with Carney offering to meet St-Pierre Plamondon in the Ottawa-Gatineau region or Montreal, while the Quebec premier insisted they meet in Quebec City instead.

They finally opted to meet at the Francophonie Summit in Cambodia over the weekend, where both men seemed to smooth things over.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he left the meeting feeling like they had a “very constructive” exchange on issues and that they were even able to crack a few jokes.

“Listen, ON a personal level, it was a very pleasant and very funny encounter. So, we share a sense of humour,” he told reporters afterwards.

St-Pierre Plamondon said him and Carney also exchanged phone numbers to prevent further miscommunication.

That was the case when they traded barbs last week when it was suggested that the Quebec government was trying to negotiate directly with newly elected U.S. officials.

Carney insisted Canada should have “a single negotiator” in the federal government which led St-Pierre Plamondon to tell the prime minister he is not his “boss.”

As it turns out, the letters sent by St-Pierre Plamondon to U.S. governors and senators after the midterms were essentially congratulating them, which is standard practice.

The Quebec premier expressed hope after his meeting with Carney in Cambodia that their teams would be able to better collaborate moving forward.

“We cannot agree on everything in politics, but when there is an effort on both sides to act in good faith, it becomes possible to open up channels of communication,” he said.

“Therefore, I believe that following this meeting, there will be significantly improved collaboration — not only on this particular issue, but on others as well,” he added.

“We had detailed, professional discussions covering all topics for a first meeting, and we will continue in a friendly and professional manner,” he said.

Carney then jokingly rejected the notion of romance, saying “I have a wife!”

The new numbers from Synopsis also show that Quebecers prefer Carney to St-Pierre Plamondon in general, but that there is also some crossover between the two.

Sixty-one per cent of Quebecers said they have a positive opinion of Carney, while the number is at 39 per cent for St-Pierre Plamondon. Of those numbers, Synopsis found 20 per cent of respondents hold both politicians in a favourable light.

That would suggest that any further dispute with Ottawa would probably hurt the Quebec premier more than it would affect the highly popular prime minister.

Carney’s Quebec lieutenant, Joël Lightbound, said the approach of the federal government would remain unchanged in dealing with the province.

“We are committed to maintaining a spirit of collaboration with Quebec, and I sense no appetite among the public for jurisdictional squabbles,” he said.

At the provincial level, the Synopsis poll also revealed some warning signs for St-Pierre Plamondon early in his tenure as the Parti Québécois is now shoulder-to-shoulder with the Quebec Liberals with each enjoying 31 per cent of popular support.

Even though it is an increase of three points for the PQ since the Oct. 5 election, the Liberals led by Charles Milliard enjoyed a leap of seven points in popular support.

The Quebec Conservative Party saw their support soften slightly with now 19 per cent in the polls while Québec solidaire sits at 12 per cent.

Meanwhile, the Coalition Avenir Québec, which was wiped off the electoral map last month, continues its plunge in the polls with only five per cent support.

The online poll of 1,000 Quebec adults was conducted Nov. 13-16.

Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

As it turns out, the letters sent by St-Pierre Plamondon to U.S. governors and senators after the midterms were essentially congratulating them, which is standard practice.
The Quebec premier expressed hope after his meeting with Carney in Cambodia that their teams would be able to better collaborate moving forward.
“We cannot agree on everything in politics, but when there is an effort on both sides to act in good faith, it becomes possible to open up channels of communication,” he said.
“Therefore, I believe that following this meeting, there will be significantly improved collaboration — not only on this particular issue, but on others as well,” he added.
“We had detailed, professional discussions covering all topics for a first meeting, and we will continue in a friendly and professional manner,” he said.
Carney then jokingly rejected the notion of romance, saying “I have a wife!”
The new numbers from Synopsis also show that Quebecers prefer Carney to St-Pierre Plamondon in general, but that there is also some crossover between the two.

Sixty-one per cent of Quebecers said they have a positive opinion of Carney, while the number is at 39 per cent for St-Pierre Plamondon. Of those numbers, Synopsis found 20 per cent of respondents hold both politicians in a favourable light.
That would suggest that any further dispute with Ottawa would probably hurt the Quebec premier more than it would affect the highly popular prime minister.
Carney’s Quebec lieutenant, Joël Lightbound, said the approach of the federal government would remain unchanged in dealing with the province.
“We are committed to maintaining a spirit of collaboration with Quebec, and I sense no appetite among the public for jurisdictional squabbles,” he said.

At the provincial level, the Synopsis poll also revealed some warning signs for St-Pierre Plamondon early in his tenure as the Parti Québécois is now shoulder-to-shoulder with the Quebec Liberals with each enjoying 31 per cent of popular support.
Even though it is an increase of three points for the PQ since the Oct. 5 election, the Liberals led by Charles Milliard enjoyed a leap of seven points in popular support.
The Quebec Conservative Party saw their support soften slightly with now 19 per cent in the polls while Québec solidaire sits at 12 per cent.
Meanwhile, the Coalition Avenir Québec, which was wiped off the electoral map last month, continues its plunge in the polls with only five per cent support.
The online poll of 1,000 Quebec adults was conducted Nov. 13-16.
Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

stories.title: Military suspends most cadet activities amid cost cuts; weekly training to continue
stories.summary: The Canadian Armed Forces is suspending most cadet activities across the country until next spring as military officials move to curtail spending.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Canadian Armed Forces is suspending most cadet activities across the country until next spring as military officials move to curtail spending.

Internal emails obtained by The Canadian Press said cadet units have been ordered to suspend or cancel weekend training, competitions and other activities until the end of March, citing “the current fiscal environment.”

The emails sent Monday said regular weekly training sessions, known as parade nights, can continue at cadet corps and squadrons.

In Ontario, restrictions on cadet activities took effect immediately, while similar measures take effect Nov. 21 in British Columbia.

In a statement Wednesday, a National Defence spokesperson confirmed the Cadets and Junior Canadian Rangers Group is reviewing its spending plans nationally and that changes to some planned activities will be necessary across the country.

“It is still too early to determine the full extent of any changes or their impacts,” Lt.-Cmdr. Tony Wright said in an email.

He said the focus is on “reducing costs that do not directly support core activities and program delivery.”

Wright said the program’s budget increased to about $265 million in the current fiscal year, which includes an added $27 million announced earlier this year.

He said the program has also seen increased interest and participation, which is requiring a review of how funds are distributed.

Meanwhile, internal emails sent to cadet staff in Ontario and British Columbia said the restrictions are part of an ongoing spending review.

“Over the past several days, regional staff have reviewed planned activities and identified opportunities to absorb financial pressures while protecting the training that matters most to our cadets: weekly Corps and Squadron parade night training,” said an email sent on behalf of Lt.-Col. Raphael MacKenzie, commanding officer of Ontario’s Regional Cadet Support Unit Central.

“As a result of that review, a number of regional and area-level activities, training opportunities, and support functions will be deferred, paused, or cancelled for the remainder of the fiscal year.”

The sweeping mid-year cuts to cadet programs could affect thousands of young Canadians.

The cadet program had more than 61,000 participants in the last fiscal year, according to the Department of National Defence’s 2025-26 departmental results report.

The program offers military-supported training in leadership, citizenship and outdoor activities to youth aged 12 to 18, with sea, army and air cadet units organized into five regions across Canada: Atlantic, Eastern, Central, Northwest and Pacific.

E. Patrick Shea, a former Cadet Instructor Cadre officer who taught young Canadians to fly gliders, said cancelling weekend exercises, competitions and regional training could discourage young people from staying in the program.

“I don’t know if the kids will necessarily be interested in doing all the hard work without the reward,” said Shea, who now works as a lawyer in Toronto.

He warned the cuts could widen disparities between cadet units in wealthier and lower-income communities, particularly if units are allowed to continue some local activities using money collected through fundraising.

“It shouldn’t matter whether you come from the poorest community in the country or the richest,” he said. “The program and all its training and opportunities should be available to you.”

The cadet program counts astronauts Chris Hadfield, Marc Garneau and Jeremy Hansen among its former members.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Charges laid in London weapons investigation
stories.summary: The London Police Service has laid charges in a weapons investigation in the city on Tuesday.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The London Police Service has laid charges in a weapons investigation in the city on Tuesday.

Around 11:45 a.m., police said a man was headed north on Lyle Street near King Street, when he heard a loud noise from the hood of his vehicle. The man looked to a nearby apartment building and saw a man on a balcony holding what looked like a gun.

Officers were called to the residence in the 400 block of Lyle. The LPS said the suspect was found and a replica gun was seized. Damage was consistent with being hit by a pellet on the vehicle.

Police added the suspect reportedly shot the gun several more time in the area. No injuries were reported.

A 57-year-old London man has been charged with pointing a firearm and mischief under $5,000.

stories.title: Investigation into Old Navy and Gap marketing practices advances: Competition Bureau
stories.summary: The Competition Bureau says it has obtained a court order to advance an ongoing investigation into Old Navy and Gap.
stories.author: Kayla Thompson
stories.content:
The Competition Bureau says it has obtained a court order to advance an ongoing investigation into Old Navy and Gap.

The independent law enforcement agency said on Wednesday that the investigation involves “potentially false or misleading claims” made by the clothing brands, each operated by Gap Inc.

“The Bureau is seeking to determine whether specific marketing practices used by Old Navy and Gap raise concerns under the deceptive marketing provisions of the Competition Act . There has been no finding of wrongdoing at this time,” the Competition Bureau said in a news release.

This is a breaking news story. More details to follow…

stories.title: EverWind says Cape Breton AI data centre project on track despite concerns
stories.summary: A representative of EverWind, the company behind a massive data centre project in Cape Breton, says everything is moving ahead as planned.
stories.author: Mitchell Bailey, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
A representative of EverWind , the company behind a massive data centre project in Cape Breton, says everything is moving ahead as planned.

EverWind has committed $10 billion in private investment for the project at its existing Point Tupper site near Port Hawkesbury, N.S., and AI development company Anthropic has signed a long-term lease to use it.

Last week, EverWind signed two agreements with Nova Scotia Power.

Brendan Chard, EverWind’s vice-president of power, says steps are being taken to connect its planned AI data centre to the utility’s electrical grid.

“We have a separate agreement with Nova Scotia Power that covers some of those terms, including covering all of our incremental costs of service to ensure that none of the costs incurred to serve electricity to our facility will be borne by other customers,” said Chard.

The electric service contract covers the project’s first 95-megawatt phase and outlines that electricity will be provided on an “interruptible basis,” meaning EverWind can be cut off from the grid whenever it’s under pressure.

“We’re prepared to cut service with 10 minutes’ notice from the grid operator if required at any point in time,” said Chard.

In the event that happens, Chard says the facility will be powered by batteries or a backup diesel generator.

He says the company ultimately plans for the facility to be largely powered by its proposed wind projects, but notes those first turbines won’t be operational until 2028.

This means the centre will be relying on Nova Scotia Power’s grid for its first year.

“We’re working through getting all of our permits in place so that we can move construction forward as quickly as possible and maintain our timelines to being online in 2027,” he said.

Protests against the project have taken place across the province since it was announced a month ago .

Nick Tsergas, a science and tech journalist who founded StopTheDataCentre.CA, says he began his advocacy work when a mega data centre was proposed near his home in Hamilton, Ont.

“I’ve just been living and breathing this issue, digging into it as much as I can, and noticing a lot of patterns in these data centre conversations as they pop up, mushroom up around the country,” he said.

He says AI data centres use significantly more power than traditional data centres, which were historically used for bank transactions or website hosting.

“They use 10 times the power, let’s say, 10 to 20 times the power that a traditional data centre of the same size would use,” said Tsergas.

“And when more power is used, more heat is also produced. So you need to come up with some very creative ways to cool the data centre so that the graphics cards basically don’t melt.”

EverWind’s plan for Point Tupper indicates it will use a closed-loop cooling system where a water–glycol mixture circulates through a sealed loop rather than being routinely discharged.

“Heat will be removed primarily using air, with water-assisted cooling used during the hottest weather,” EverWind said in a release.

“Nova Scotia’s cooler climate reduces cooling-water requirements for much of the year.”

But Tsergas points out the “full picture” of closed water-cooling systems and how much water this requires.

“Many of the data centres being proposed across Canada, the designs include either natural gas generating infrastructure or even backup diesel generators bundled into the data centre,” he said.

“Those things need water to cool them as well. So if you’re using more electricity to power the closed-loop cooling system, more and more of that water is going to be needed to cool the gas turbines attached to the data centre. “

EverWind will pay an interim large industrial tariff to access Nova Scotia’s power grid until a new fee is developed.

Nova Scotia Power said in a statement that the new fee is necessary because existing tariff structures were not designed for a customer of this scale.

“Our approach to data centres is consistent with what is becoming common across North America: ensuring existing customers do not bear the costs of serving new developments,” the statement said.

EverWind says the data centre’s second phase, which could see the project expand to 420 megawatts, should be complete sometime in 2028 and is subject to approvals and conditions.

stories.title: Petition to remove U.S. Ambassador Hoekstra gets nearly 300,000 signatures
stories.summary: Petition accuses Pete Hoekstra of making public statements that have undermined Canadian and U.S. relations
stories.author: Alyssa Wheeler
stories.content:
More than 285,000 people have signed a petition calling on the federal government to remove U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra from Canada.

The petition accuses Hoekstra of making public statements that have undermined Canadian and U.S. relations and says he described the 2025 Canadian federal election campaign as “anti-American.”

Months after that federal election, Hoekstra said he was frustrated by the “elbows up” rhetoric used during the campaign.

The petition says Hoekstra accused Canada of interfering in U.S. domestic politics while making repeated statements on Canadian politics “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol.”

Hoekstra said during an interview on The Really Big Show podcast in October that political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

The petition is now closed to new signatures. Most of those who signed live in Ontario or British Columbia.

Now that the petition has received more than the mandatory 500 signatures it needed to proceed, former Green Party leader Elizabeth May can present it to the House of Commons.

Speaking to The Canadian Press, May said she regularly brings forward petitions from her constituents.

Once the petition is presented to the House, the government has 45 calendar days to respond.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa told The Canadian Press that the embassy is aware of the petition and declined to comment further.
paragraphs: More than 285,000 people have signed a petition calling on the federal government to remove U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra from Canada.
The petition accuses Hoekstra of making public statements that have undermined Canadian and U.S. relations and says he described the 2025 Canadian federal election campaign as “anti-American.”
Months after that federal election, Hoekstra said he was frustrated by the “elbows up” rhetoric used during the campaign.
The petition says Hoekstra accused Canada of interfering in U.S. domestic politics while making repeated statements on Canadian politics “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol.”
Hoekstra said during an interview on The Really Big Show podcast in October that political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.
The petition is now closed to new signatures. Most of those who signed live in Ontario or British Columbia.
Now that the petition has received more than the mandatory 500 signatures it needed to proceed, former Green Party leader Elizabeth May can present it to the House of Commons.
Speaking to The Canadian Press, May said she regularly brings forward petitions from her constituents.
Once the petition is presented to the House, the government has 45 calendar days to respond.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa told The Canadian Press that the embassy is aware of the petition and declined to comment further.

November 18, 2026 at 2:12 p.m.

The organizer of a Krampus-themed float that has been banned from the Santa Claus parade in Strathroy, Ont., says she’ll still participate from the sidelines of Saturday’s event.

“We didn’t end up putting the float together,” Tanya Griffin told National Post. “But we are going to have (Krampus) here on Saturday. He will be at the shop. My tattoo shop is right on the route of the parade, so people can stop in, get their coal and their picture with Krampus if they want.”

Griffin is the owner of Coven House in Strathroy, a municipality of about 24,000 people near London, Ont. Last year she participated in the community’s annual Santa Claus parade with a float featuring Krampus, a horned figure from Alpine folklore, said to accompany Saint Nicholas on the night of Dec. 5, which is called Krampusnacht or “Krampus Night.”

Think of him as the anti-Santa. Whereas Saint Nicholas rewards good children with gifts, Krampus punishes the naughty by striking them with birch rods and handing out coal.

Griffin’s float was part of the parade last year, put on by the Lions Club. It won a prize for its costumes. It was initially approved for this year’s event as well.

“And then this past Thursday … I guess the Lions Club had received some complaints that we weren’t family-friendly. So then they came and told us that we were out,” she said. “They did give us a chance to prove that our float was not terrifying, and so we did that, and then they still came back with a no.”

She said she had multiple volunteers including children who were planning to participate.

“We had about eight children who were going to help hand out candy canes and temporary tattoos, and they don’t get to be a part of the float any more,” she said. “So they’re going to come hand out candy canes and temporary tattoos at my shop on Saturday instead.”

Griffin shared a letter with the National Post, sent to the Town Council and Mayor last year and signed by The Congregation of Calvary Pentecostal Church of Strathroy.

“Allowing the inclusion of satanic influences into what should have been a Christ-centred, Santa Claus Parade has caused great displeasure,” the letter said, adding: “The Municipality of Strathroy-Caradoc must be aware of the damage these demonic forces would have on the young children of our town.”

The letter also takes issue with the float’s second-place prize in the costume category, saying it added “further insult.” National Post has reached out to the church and the Lions Club for comment.

Griffin said she joined the parade last year because “we just wanted something different … because there was going to be a Jack Skellington and a Grinch, and we thought, let’s introduce a new character.”

She added: “There’s a bigger picture than the float here, which I think a lot of people are missing. Is that the Lions Club — I mean, I know they have the right to choose what goes in the float, but to exclude an entire culture becomes a problem.”

She pointed out that Krampus is a staple of Germanic folklore. “So we’re getting a ton of people from from Germany, even Dutch people, just furious that their culture has been excluded. They were excited to see it in the parade last year, and the fact that it’s just gone and missing now this year? There’s a bit of a backlash.

I mean, it sucks. Is like I said, the the whole bigger picture thing. Like, who’s like who’s next out? Like, who’s going to complain about who next, and then who has the right to say in in such like a a big community. I mean, we’re not a huge community, but we’re diverse. That that Germanic folklore is just not acceptable at the Christmas time. It’s ridiculous because a lot of people grew up with this this lore, right? So

Some adults have commented that Krampus is no longer a tradition but has become a mere spectacle. Did you know that Krampus is not just a tradition and a spectacle for adults? In fact, Krampus’s main audience is children and teenagers. As long as children and teenagers still enjoy Krampus, our Krampus tradition will never die out.

November 18, 2026 at 2:12 p.m.

The Toronto Police Service announced Wednesday that they have made 21 arrests and laid 112 charges following a long-running investigation into the city’s towing industry, dubbed Project Swords.

They have also cancelled a contract with Williams Towing, one of four contracts to tow vehicles that are illegally parked or abandoned. The other three are “picking up the slack” for now, police said.

Police noted that, beginning in early 2023, the Greater Toronto Area saw a sharp increase in violence linked to individuals and groups vying for control of the towing industry.

“That violence included homicides, shootings, arsons, intimidation and extortion,” they said in a press release. “It culminated in a number of high-profile incidents, including the March 2025 mass shooting at a pub in Scarborough that left a dozen people injured.”

Project Swords was launched in September 2025 following the completion of Project Yankee, which focused on a criminal faction within the towing industry known as The Union. Project Swords targeted a rival organization that police allege was led by Manoharan (Mano) Subramaniam.

Subramaniam, 43, of Whitby, was among the arrests and has been charged with several offences including two counts of conspiracy to commit murder, assault and threatening bodily harm.

Police allege that Subramaniam directed a conspiracy to murder two individuals connected to the towing industry. They also said that even though Williams Towing and another company, Bob’s Towing, were registered to others, “Mr. Subramaniam exercised control over aspects of those operations” and that he “was the de facto leader of the organization despite not being listed on any paperwork.”

Others have been arrested and charged, in one case with 24 separate offences. Police also seized multiple firearms, 84 rounds of ammunition and 250 grams of cocaine. They also made six arrests connected to an organized auto theft operation; two in connection with an arson investigation; and three connected to fraudulent physiotherapy clinics.

One correctional employee was also charged with breach of trust. Steve Matthews of the Integrated Gun and Gang Task Force said that individual worked at the Toronto East Detention Centre and was “looking to assist Mr. Subramaniam while he was in custody.” He added: “At no point was (Subramaniam) ever at the East Detention Centre, so there wasn’t an actual impact.”

Police said that, in 2024, 62 shooting and firearm discharge incidents were linked to tow truck-related disputes, accounting for almost 13 per cent of all such incidents in Toronto.

They said that number dropped to 18 last year, representing seven per cent of the total, and has fallen to just five incidents this year to date, or about two per cent of cases.

“It’s a very small percentage of tow operators that are actually part of the criminal underworld,” Chief Superintendent Joe Matthews of Detective Operations said. He predicted the arrest of Subramaniam “will be a significant impact to the violence, arsons and all of the criminal activity.”

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: Where does politics fit in sports
stories.summary: As Canada prepares for the 2026-2027 World Junior Hockey Tournament, its decision to keep Russia out of the to...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
As Canada prepares for the 2026-2027 World Junior Hockey Tournament, its decision to keep Russia out of the tournament has sparked controversy among political watchers and sports fans alike.

The decision punishes athletes for their country’s political actions, said Sharmistha Nag a Canadian political expert.

“The ban was purely a political reason,” said Nag, a political science professor at Fanshawe College. “The Canadian government is showing their disapproval. I t’s one way a country imposes pressure and shows disapproval of any policy the other country takes.”

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney Speaking (Harun Ozalp/Anadolu/Getty Images)

The initial ban on Russia took place in Feb. 2022 after their invasion on Ukraine. The court of arbitration for sport voted unanimously against the ban this year, ordering Russia’s reinstatement to five international championships.

This year, Prime Minister Mark Carney has been closely involved with this case and has made his ruling on the World Juniors.

“While Russia and Belorussia are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine, as long as that’s going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” said Carney.

Since Canada made it’s decision, hockey fans have been speaking out. Many online forums sections are filled with commenters saying the players should be allowed to play.

“Banning young athletes from a tournament for something they can’t control,” wrote one commenter on a TSN Instagram post.

“Athletes are missing out on big opportunities due to something they can’t control. I feel like people need to separate the athlete from a country’s leader when it comes to politics.”

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the decision “Unacceptable” and “unlawful,” saying it violated both the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling and an agreement under which the Iihf committed to implementing it immediately.

Edmonton and Red Deer will host the round robin games for these tournaments starting on Dec. 26.

“While Russia and Belorussia are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine, as long as that’s going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” said Carney.
Since Canada made it’s decision, hockey fans have been speaking out. Many online forums sections are filled with commenters saying the players should be allowed to play.
“Banning young athletes from a tournament for something they can’t control,” wrote one commenter on a TSN Instagram post.
“Athletes are missing out on big opportunities due to something they can’t control. I feel like people need to separate the athlete from a country’s leader when it comes to politics.”

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the decision “Unacceptable” and “unlawful,” saying it violated both the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling and an agreement under which the Iihf committed to implementing it immediately.
Edmonton and Red Deer will host the round robin games for these tournaments starting on Dec. 26.

stories.summary: The London Police are searching for a Thamesford man who is accused of being involved in a case of human trafficking.
stories.author: Kyle Freel
stories.content:
News Home

Wednesday, 18 November 2026 at 14:05

By Kyle Freel X @KFreelHeartFM

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

The London Police are searching for a Thamesford man who is accused of being involved in a case of human trafficking.

LONDON - A Thamesford man is wanted in a London Human Trafficking investigation.

London Police responded to a hotel on Saturday at 2 a.m. to check on the welfare of a woman. Through the investigation, police learned the two suspects were trying to exploit the victim in the sex trade to financially benefit. 57-year-old David Janssens of Thamesford and a 45-year-old St. Thomas man are each facing 7 charges.

The charges include one count each of Robbery; Forcible confinement; Assault; Assault with a weapon; Possession of property obtained by crime under $5,000; Obtain sexual services for consideration; and Procuring.

The St. Thomas man is also facing an 8th charge, which is one count of Pointing a firearm. He remains in custody and is set to appear in a London Courtroom tomorrow. Janssens is not in custody at this time and is being charged by way of an arrest warrant.

Anyone with information that could help with the investigation is being asked to contact the London Police.

stories.title: Canada to review where Chinese EVs are allowed to drive: transport minister
stories.summary: Concerns over Chinese cars ability to collect sensitive information have been routinely highlighted by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who often refers to them as 'spy cars.'
stories.author: Mackenzie Gray
stories.content:
Amid a push from the Canadian government to allow more Chinese electric vehicles into Canada, Transport Minister Steve MacKinnon says the government will review where those cars will be allowed to drive, which comes amid growing concerns about national security risks.

When asked by Global News if the Canadian government would limit Chinese EV’s access to Canadian military and government facilities, Transport Minister Steve MacKinnon said “that will be part of a more cross-governmental review of that matter that would involve Public Safety and other departments.”

When pressed as to why the Canadian government would allow cars into Canada that could potentially require restrictions on where they could go , MacKinnon said the government is “always on the lookout for risks” that connected vehicles bring.

Concerns over Chinese cars ability to collect sensitive information have been routinely highlighted by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who often refers to them as “spy cars.”

Germany recently announced a ban on some Chinese vehicles in secure military and government locations, according to German publication Der Spiegel, over concerns that the cars built-in sensors and cameras could record sensitive data and forward it to Chinese security authorities.

The U.K., Poland and Czechia also have full or partial bans on Chinese vehicles on military bases, with Poland telling military members not to connect their work phones to the systems of those cars.

The United States has banned Chinese auto giant BYD from having their cars at one of their biggest overseas military bases in Okinawa, Japan.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has said multiple times that Canadians attempting to drive a Chinese car into the U.S. would be blocked at the border.

In January, Prime Minister Mark Carney reduced Canada’s 100 per cent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 per cent, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time.

MacKinnon said Transport Canada is still in the middle of the process of certifying some Chinese auto companies for being able to sell their cars into Canada.

Chinese brands BYD and Chery have both expressed public interest in selling cars into the Canadian market, with International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu visiting a Chery manufacturing facility in China earlier in November.

stories.title: China’s growth a model for Canada, Carney says
stories.summary: Carney said the development of the city of Shenzhen — from a fishing village to a high-tech mega city — shows what can be achieved by cutting red tape.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canadians should learn from China’s breakneck economic growth, even as he insists Ottawa maintains guardrails on expanding trade with Beijing to limit interference and U.S. blowback.

“We try to be clear with them. There are opportunities to unleash investment, and there are not in other parts of our economy,” Carney said in French at a news conference in Shenzhen, China on Wednesday.

Carney, who is attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, also said the development of the city of Shenzhen — from a fishing village to a high-tech mega city — shows what can be achieved by cutting red tape.

“This city won investment with faster approvals, lower taxes and simpler rules for trade,” he said. “The choices that built this city can lift this whole region.”

The prime minister’s visit started with an announcement that Canada would drop certain restrictions on imports of Chinese steel and aluminum in exchange for more market access for Canadian pork and other agricultural products.

The announcement also included news of a partnership on artificial intelligence — even though Carney previously said AI was among three sectors off-limits to Chinese investment in Canada, along with critical minerals and defence industries.

Carney said discussions with China have focused more on how to guard against economic and biosecurity risks.

“The absence of any global governance around AI is an enormous risk,” Carney said. “I took the opportunity in the discussions with President Xi yesterday to share our views on a model for how this governance can be developed.”

Carney said Canada would shape its trade based on shared interests, citing the example of the European Union having press freedoms other countries and regions lack.

“The calibration depends on the values that we share with countries,” he said in French.

He said more market access to China benefits various sectors in Canada, such as fishing and farming, “but relative to many other countries, our trade with China is quite modest and the breadth of it is quite modest.”

Carney said his government is pursuing a “gradual opening” of its relationship with China after the diplomatic crisis of 2018 and reports that Beijing has engaged in political interference in Canada — reports which Beijing has denied.

“We’ve pursued a stabilization of the relationship first and a gradual opening of the relationship,” the prime minister said.

Carney’s recent agreements with China on trade have infuriated some of the people close to U.S. President Donald Trump.

Peter Navarro, the president’s trade adviser, has said it was “offensive in the extreme” for Carney to be “threatening to play China off the U.S.”

The prime minister said Canadian trade with China does not involve cutting-edge technology, as does American trade with Beijing.

Earlier Wednesday, Carney said Ottawa was trying to expedite major projects while working with countries such as China to limit its dependence on countries like the United States.

“I’ll be clear, these partnerships remain vital, but Canada is also a Pacific nation,” he told a gathering of CEOs at the Apec summit.

“The next chapter of Canada’s transformation will be written with partners in this region.”

stories.title: Talks with Meta ‘confidential’ following reports of possible deal, Miller says
stories.summary: Culture Minister Marc Miller says he won’t talk about any discussions the government has had with Meta about restoring news content to the company's platforms in Canada.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Culture Minister Marc Miller says he won’t talk about any discussions the government has had with Meta about restoring news content to the company’s platforms in Canada.

A day after Politico reported the company and the government were close to a deal before trade talks with the United States collapsed in August, Miller said Wednesday the discussions with Meta are confidential.

Citing an unnamed official, Politico said Meta put forward a proposal to stop blocking news content in Canada, pursue commercial deals with publishers and fund two positions at the Canadian Journalism Collective.

In exchange, Politico said, the deal would have given Meta an exemption under the Online News Act, which requires Meta and Google to compensate news publishers for the use of their content.

Politico reported the proposal was part of the wider U.S.-Canada trade negotiations that Canada shut down in August after accusing the White House of demanding last minute changes that threatened Canada’s sovereignty.

After the Online News Act became law in 2023, Meta blocked news content in Canada while Google received an exemption after agreeing to pay $100 million to Canadian news outlets.

stories.title: Schulich Medicine & Dentistry researchers identify pathway to reversing liver fibrosis
stories.summary: Study shows how specialized immune cells contribute to liver scarring, pointing to new possibilities for early treatment
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
A new study by Western University researchers has identified a potential pathway to reversing liver fibrosis, a condition that can progress to life-threatening liver disease.

Published in Sciences Advances, the findings demonstrate how specialized immune cells, known as mucosa-associated invariant T cells (Mait cells), contribute to liver scarring – and how targeting them could help mitigate or reverse the damage.

“Traditionally, Mait cells have been studied primarily for their ability to fight infections, but much less was known about their roles in tissue injury, repair and scarring,” said Nicole Ilayda Wang, a PhD candidate in microbiology and immunology at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry. “Our findings reveal a previously underappreciated role for these cells in chronic liver disease and fibrosis development.”

Liver fibrosis develops when ongoing damage leads to a buildup of scar tissue. In the liver, too much scar tissue can disrupt blood flow and impair liver function.

### “Tissue fibrosis, including liver fibrosis, can result from exposure to chemicals or toxins, viral infections such as COVID, metabolic stress, and autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. It affects millions of people worldwide.” – Mansour Haeryfar, Schulich Medicine & Dentistry professor of immunology

Liver fibrosis can progress to cirrhosis, or severe liver scarring, a life-threatening condition. According to the Government of Canada, liver disease and cirrhosis ranked among the 10 leading causes of death in Canada in 2024.

“There is an unmet need for early interventions to reverse fibrogenic processes before it is too late,” said Haeryfar.

Using preclinical mouse models and data from patients with fibrosis, Wang and Haeryfar investigated the role of Mait cells in liver scarring.

They discovered an interaction between Mait cells and regulatory T cells, immune cells that normally help keep inflammation under control.

Their findings showed that Mait cells worsen fibrosis by inhibiting regulatory T cells.

“Mait cells are best known for their antimicrobial properties. However, we found them to be pathogenic in this context,” said Haeryfar. “Mechanistically, they reduce regulatory T lymphocyte numbers in the liver, worsening fibrosis.”

In addition to being the first to explain the exact role that Mait cells play in fibrogenic processes, the study also shows that targeting Mait cells therapeutically by inhibiting their activity can reduce liver fibrosis when intervention occurs in the earliest stages of the disease.

“Our findings suggest that timing is critical, as targeting these cells early in the course of disease development May be particularly important for achieving therapeutic benefits,” said Wang.

A better understanding of Mait cells could also help researchers develop treatments for other diseases, including cancer, where these immune cells play different roles.

“There is growing interest in treatments that use the immune system to fight disease. In cancer, for example, the goal is to help immune cells attack tumours,” said Wang.

stories.title: Military suspends most cadet activities as officials move to cut spending
stories.summary: Regular weekly training sessions, known as parade nights, will continue at cadet corps and squadrons
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
The Canadian Armed Forces is suspending most cadet activities across the country until next spring as military officials move to curtail spending.

Internal emails obtained by The Canadian Press said cadet units have been ordered to suspend or cancel weekend training, competitions and other activities until the end of March, citing “the current fiscal environment.”

The emails sent Monday said regular weekly training sessions, known as parade nights, can continue at cadet corps and squadrons.

In Ontario, restrictions on cadet activities took effect immediately, while similar measures take effect Nov. 21 in British Columbia.

In a statement Wednesday, a National Defence spokesperson confirmed the Cadets and Junior Canadian Rangers Group is reviewing its spending plans nationally and that changes to some planned activities will be necessary across the country.

“It is still too early to determine the full extent of any changes or their impacts,” Lt.-Cmdr. Tony Wright said in an email.

He said the focus is on “reducing costs that do not directly support core activities and program delivery.”

Wright said the program’s budget increased to about $265 million in the current fiscal year, which includes an added $27 million announced earlier this year.

He said the program has also seen increased interest and participation, which is requiring a review of how funds are distributed.

Meanwhile, internal emails sent to cadet staff in Ontario and British Columbia said the restrictions are part of an ongoing spending review.

The sweeping mid-year cuts to cadet programs could affect thousands of young Canadians.

The cadet program had more than 61,000 participants in the last fiscal year, according to the Department of National Defence’s 2025-26 departmental results report.

He warned the cuts could widen disparities between cadet units in wealthier and lower-income communities, particularly if units are allowed to continue some local activities using money collected through fundraising.

“It shouldn’t matter whether you come from the poorest community in the country or the richest,” he said. “The program and all its training and opportunities should be available to you.”

stories.title: Inquest into Jamal Francique's death shown videos from after shooting
stories.summary: The inquest into the death of a Black man shot by police in early 2020 is watching videos showing the officers around his wrecked car after the shooting.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A police officer who helped pull a critically injured Black man from a wrecked car after a police shooting nearly seven years ago faced questions Wednesday about the time it took to call for medical treatment.

Const. Marc Charlebois, then a member of Peel regional police’s tactical unit, arrived at the Mississauga, Ont., townhouse complex about 20 minutes after the shooting, he told a coroner’s inquest into the death of Jamal Francique.

Charlebois heard an officer had shot at a car during an attempted arrest, and that nobody could see inside the vehicle because it was dark outside and the car’s windows were tinted, he said.

The constable told the inquest earlier this week that he knew after he broke the car’s rear passenger window that there had been a “traumatic incident” requiring intervention. He saw blood and could hear Francique’s agonal breathing, a type of laboured breath that indicates serious medical distress, he said.

Charlebois also wrote in his notes that he saw signs of trauma to the right side of Francique’s head at that time, the inquest heard.

After watching videos from the scene on Wednesday, however, Charlebois said he now believed he did not realize Francique had suffered a traumatic injury until he broke a second window, the one on the rear driver’s side. He made the inference based on his body language in the footage, he said.

Several lawyers pushed back during cross-examination, arguing Charlebois would have known Francique was in grave condition based on his breathing alone. The officer told Ontario’s police watchdog that he could immediately hear Francique was in respiratory distress after breaking the first window but wasn’t sure if the man was faking it, they noted.

Karifa Magassouba, a lawyer for the Black Action Defence Committee, argued Charlebois had other information that suggested it was a medical emergency, including the damage to the car and the knowledge that an officer had shot at the vehicle.

“You knew that for 20 minutes, he’s received no care,” Magassouba said.

“Yes,” Charlebois replied.

“And you understand that he is on his last breath of life,” the lawyer continued.

“Yes,” the officer said.

“So you had more to go on than just agonal breathing, would you agree with me?”

The officer also faced multiple questions on unconscious anti-Black bias, which he said played no role in his beliefs and actions that day.

Charlebois recalled receiving training on anti-Black bias around 2013, but couldn’t give specifics on the training, such as any stereotypes mentioned. He rejected the suggestion that he had not retained much of the training.

Several videos showing the officers around Francique’s car were played at the inquest Wednesday.

In one of the videos, an officer can be seen making a kicking motion near Francique as the critically injured man lays on the ground after being removed from the car. It’s not clear whether the officer’s foot connected with anything as the end of the motion is blocked from view by another officer’s body.

Charlebois testified Monday that an officer at one point kicked rubble to make space for a stretcher.

A lawyer representing Francique’s mother later suggested the officer was kicking Francique, which Charlebois said was “completely untrue.”

The inquest did not sit Tuesday as the presiding officer considered the submission of new videos not previously provided to the inquest.

Francique, 28, was shot during an attempted arrest in Mississauga, Ont., ON the evening of Jan. 7, 2020. He died in hospital days later.

A group of plainclothes officers in unmarked cars staged an operation to arrest Francique for allegedly violating one of the conditions of his bail, the inquest heard.

Police had been surveilling him for days after receiving a tip that he had a gun and was dealing drugs, but had not been able to corroborate that information, the inquest heard.

Francique left his home and headed to his car around 7:44 p.m., but the officer who was meant to block his car was late, jurors heard.

As officers moved to contain his car on foot and in unmarked vehicles, one of the officers on foot fired four shots at Francique’s car, they heard. One of the bullets hit Francique in the head.

His car plowed into the pillar of a nearby garage, the inquest heard. Photos of the scene show bricks and debris in the area.

Francique did not receive medical care until after the tactical unit arrived at the scene around 8:05 p.m., the inquest heard.

Someone called for a medic after Charlebois opened the front driver’s side door, and the officer reached for what he thought was the seatbelt, he testified. It turned out to be a satchel, and its weight led Charlebois to believe there was a gun inside, he said. He called out “gun” and handed the bag over to a colleague, he said.

Charlebois and another officer then took Francique out of the car and placed him on the ground, he said. Francique was later placed on a stretcher and into an ambulance. After that, Charlebois checked the bag and found a gun, he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Montreal metro station vandalized; group claims responsibility
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - Montreal's public transit agency says a group of masked individuals vandalized its Université-de-Montréal metro station.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The agency says the group damaged fare collection equipment, turnstiles, and a staff booth at the Blue Line station around 5:15 a.m.

The transit agency says the vandalism lasted less than two minutes.

Montreal police say the individuals allegedly used various objects and tools to damage station equipment and walls, and no arrests have been made.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

A group calling itself the Conseil pour le maintien des hostilités emailed news media outlets on Wednesday claiming it was responsible for the vandalism.

The email says the group is pursuing student protests from the previous week about the cost of living and is calling for free public transit.

The transit authority denounced the vandalism and says the station remains open to passengers.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Conservative legislators will be sworn in Thursday as Doerkson prepares to take power
stories.summary: Victoria - Sixty four B.C. Conservative legislators will be sworn in Thursday in two groups as premier-designate Lorne Doerkson gets ready to take the reins of power on Friday.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - Sixty four B.C. Conservative legislators will be sworn in Thursday in two groups as premier-designate Lorne Doerkson gets ready to take the reins of power on Friday.

The Office of the Clerk says the ceremony for the first batch of Conservative legislators, including Doerkson himself, will start at 3:30 p.m. in the legislature’s chamber, followed by the second group at 6 p.m.

stories.title: Metro says it converted 10 stores to Food Basics, with 9 more to come
stories.summary: In August, the company said it would convert 10 Metro stores in Ontario into Food Basics, to 'address our customers’ ongoing search for value.'
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Grocery retail giant Metro has already converted 10 of its outlets to Food Basics , with more conversions on the way, an executive told investors in an earnings call Wednesday.

In August, the company said it would convert 10 Metro stores in Ontario into Food Basics, to “address our customers’ ongoing search for value and to strengthen our competitive position in targeted markets.”

On Thursday, a Metro executive said nine more stores will be converted in the new year.

“We completed the first of 10 planned Metro to Food Basics conversions in the fourth quarter, with the remaining nine planned during fiscal 2027,” Metro CFO and executive vice president Nicolas Amyot told investors.

In addition to the conversions, Metro is also betting big on discount stores.

“We are also planning the opening of seven new discount stores this coming year, bringing the total to an expected 16 additional stores to our discount network by year-end,” Amyot said.

The shift is happening because Metro consumers “remain under pressure and highly focused on value,” Metro CEO Marc Giroux said.

“Consumers are increasingly focused on value, and discount continues to be an important part of how we respond to that need,” he said.

The move is “not a big surprise,” said retail analyst Bruce Winder.

“We’ve seen a massive trend within grocery, not just in Canada but in North America, where shoppers are migrating toward hard discount,” he said.

While Metro’s decision is a “smart” one, they might be a little late to the party, Winder said.

Many of its competitors, such as Loblaw, are already “significantly expanding” their discount offerings.

“Loblaw probably has a two-to-three-year head start on them. They kind of read the tea leaves a few years ago and aggressively started allocating capital toward these stores,” he said.

This change has meant that grocery stores have started to look significantly scaled down.

“They’re looking to strip all the amenities out, like butchers and bakers and things of that nature, and try to get by with as little as possible,” he said.

Cheap fresh produce is an especially competitive category, he said, with growing regions around the world coming under climate stress and high diesel costs increasing food prices.

The rise of discount grocery stores has meant a “K-shaped” grocery market in Canada, Winder said, referring to a term economists use to denote an uneven economic recovery.

“It doesn’t mean that full line grocery is going away. It’s actually doing well, but that’s part of the K-shaped economy,” he said.

A six-month-long labour strike at Metro’s Laval, Que., fresh produce distribution centre dented the grocery retailer’s fourth-quarter results, as many consumers opted to shop elsewhere.

“Our contingency plan ensured continuity, but certainly affected the business,” Giroux said.

“It created a lot of turbulence and affected freshness, assortment and store, and our ability to compete.”

Workers returned to work on Sept. 27, the first day of Metro’s fiscal 2027.

The strike cost the grocer an estimated $42 million in incremental direct expenses in the fourth quarter, Metro said in a release on Wednesday. It estimates a $132-million hit in fiscal 2026 due to the strike.

“The strike is now over, and the team are now focused on rebuilding our sales,” said the CEO, who also took the helm on Sept. 27.

Giroux said the Laval distribution centre is “back in shape,” while a multi-week plan remains underway for a gradual recovery for stores.

Metro reported it earned $201.9 million or 97 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 26. The result was lower, compared with a profit of $217 million or $1.00 per diluted share in the same quarter last year.

On an adjusted basis, Metro earned 97 cents per diluted share compared with an adjusted profit of $1.13 per diluted share a year ago.

Sales for the quarter totalled $5.18 billion, up from $5.11 billion in the same quarter last year.

Its food same-store sales fell 1.9 per cent.

Bringing back consumers and driving up sales are the “immediate priority,” Giroux said.

stories.title: Quebec Bar Association wants new hotline, tax credit to improve access to justice
stories.summary: The professional order of lawyers in Quebec is proposing a new hotline as part of a range of measures to make legal services more accessible to members of the public.
stories.author: Patrice Bergeron
stories.content:
The professional order of lawyers in Quebec is proposing a new provincial telephone hotline as part of a range of measures to make legal services more accessible to members of the public.

The Barreau du Québec is calling on the province’s new justice minister, Marie-Claude Sarrazin, to take action on its recommendations released in a new report.

The bar association says the hotline could be similar to the province’s 811 service for health care information.

It is also proposing the government introduce a new refundable tax credit for family law fees.

The association says the new measures are needed as the justice system becomes increasingly expensive and difficult to navigate.

The report does not estimate the cost of its proposals, but Marcel-Olivier Nadeau, the elected leader of the order, says failing to act would also come at a price.

“There is also a cost to doing nothing, a cost when people give up on the justice system, a cost in psychological distress,” he said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

The report follows a provincewide consultation tour conducted by the Barreau last spring and calls for “putting people back at the heart of the justice system.”

About a dozen forums were held across 11 regions of Quebec, bringing together 450 members of the legal profession, the judiciary and organizations involved in the administration of justice.

Another 45 people who had firsthand experience with the justice system also took part in the forums.

One of the 45 was a man who represented himself in the Court of Québec in a dispute over a hidden defect in a property. He said he felt he had not been taken seriously by a lawyer.

The Canadian Press agreed not to identify the man because he did not want to be publicly associated with having been involved in legal proceedings.

He described the justice system as one that “doesn’t fix anything.” He described the process as “very intimidating,” with language that was “difficult to understand” and made people “feel like idiots.”

Nadeau acknowledged that more needs to be done to provide people with support throughout legal proceedings, adding that people often “feel lost, alone and powerless.”

He said the consultations conducted last spring were intended, in part, to “put a human face to the data and findings.”

Nadeau said lawyers need to be able to discuss their fees “frankly” with clients, calling for greater transparency and predictability in legal costs.

He also urged the province to simplify civil and family law procedures to reduce unnecessary procedural steps that drive up legal expenses.

Nadeau said he is optimistic that Sarrazin will be receptive to the recommendations.

“She knows that the justice system needs some love and needs to be more humane,” he said.
