stories.title: The Pigeon King offers a glimmer of hope even as it highlights the world’s evaporating morality
stories.summary: The new Canadian documentary from director/producer Geoff Morrison explores the same quandaries as the Elizabeth Holmes film
stories.author: Johanna Schneller
stories.content:
The unnerving blue-eyed stare. The insisting that you’re innocent, all evidence be damned. Our inability to discern whether you’re consciously conning us, or completely delusional. The commingling of interviews and actor reenactments. And of course, pigeons.

Yes, pigeons, barnfuls of them, flapping across Canada and the U.S. Because I’m not talking about You Can See Everything , the Elizabeth Holmes documentary the world is currently obsessed with parsing. I’m talking about The Pigeon King , a new Canadian documentary from director/producer Geoff Morrison. It explores the same quandaries and asks the same questions as the Holmes film, but in a fleet 44 minutes rather than three hours. (It premieres Nov. 18 on The Passionate Eye on CBC, CBC Gem and the CBC Docs YouTube channel.)

You May remember news reports about Pigeon King International, one of those curiosities that made international headlines: From 2001 to 2008, Ontario farmer Arlan Galbraith – positioning himself as a saviour of struggling family farms – sold tens of thousands of pigeon breeding pairs to farmers across North America, and signed 10-year contracts adding up to hundreds of millions of dollars promising to buy back the offspring. He assured the breeders, many of them Mennonite, Amish and Hutterite, that the birds would be sold to wealthy pigeon racers, often flashing a photo of himself with Mike Tyson, a renowned pigeon fancier.

Instead, Galbraith simply passed the birds along to new breeders – a classic Ponzi scheme that collapsed in horrific fashion in 2008 when Pigeon King International filed for bankruptcy, farmers lost their life savings and 175,000 birds had to be slaughtered. Arrested for fraud, Galbraith defended himself in his 2013 trial in Kitchener; though sentenced to seven years, he served less than two.

In the documentary, Mark McKinney ( Kids in the Hall , Superstore ) and Kathleen Munroe ( Law & Order Toronto: Criminal Intent ), respectively, play Galbraith and his prosecuting attorney, Lynn Robinson, in court re-enactments. All dialogue is from the actual transcripts, and some of the lines are doozies, especially the one where Galbraith asks a former employee, “Were you recruited by the Amish mafia to destroy Pigeon King?”

They shot their scenes in one day, in what McKinney calls “Guinness Book record-breaking long takes,” on the same kind of pan-tilt zoom cameras courtrooms use. Galbraith himself appears, too, in a sit-down interview – the first time he’s publicly told his side of the story. But just like Holmes, Galbraith remains remorseless, either pretending not to understand, or refusing to let himself understand, that he did anything wrong.

“It’s a drama you can play with your comedy antennae up as well,” McKinney said last week in a joint video interview with Munroe and Morrison. “I think Galbraith’s internal architecture is different from most people’s. He believes his own lies, but then there are moments when his awareness breaks through. He doesn’t look like a mustache-twirling villain. He’s more bewildered – ‘Why aren’t you seeing this the way I want you to? Why are you looking at me like that?’”

“The difference between the court transcript and a parody of the court transcript is nothing,” Munroe says. “We’re in this ‘What is truth?’ era. Are people lying or misinformed? What is their motivation? Is Galbraith complicit in his own diabolical scheme, or sincerely trying to succeed in a business venture? I like asking those questions, because I don’t like to write people off, even if they don’t make sense to me on the surface. I like to investigate the person behind the behaviour we don’t understand.”

As the courtroom scenes play out, it becomes obvious that Galbraith, defending himself, is in over his head, and that Robinson is willing her eyes not to roll. “Shooting it, I was remembering when Hillary Clinton did that little shoulder wiggle in a debate against Donald Trump, so happy that Trump was tanking himself,” Munroe recalls. “I didn’t want Robinson to be smug, but you can see her containing her satisfaction as things are sliding off the rails. Geoff does a great job with the tone, treading the line between what could be funny and having pathos and compassion for everyone, including Galbraith.”

“I think Galbraith went into it thinking he just has to make lawyer noises and everything will be okay,” McKinney says. “Then he starts this symphonic descant into, ‘Oh, no.’”

“Mark, the heaviness in your hands as it goes on is amazing,” Munroe says.

“Listening to the court audio recording, you can hear the change in timbre in Galbraith’s voice,” Morrison adds. “There’s a moment after he’s convicted where he doesn’t understand he’s going into custody, where he asks, ‘What’s going to happen to my car?’ It’s so human.”

Morrison had done a shorter version of the Pigeon King story on the CBC Gem series Farm Crime , which he produces, focused on the journalists at Better Farming magazine who first investigated Galbraith back in 2007. But he always felt there was more to explore. “A lot of agricultural crime is not taken seriously,” he says. “The maple syrup heist story” – $18-million in syrup stolen from a Quebec warehouse in 2011 and 2012 – “was a big joke to people.”

So when Galbraith agreed to be interviewed, Morrison saw a chance to revisit the story, to both “honour the people who’d had terrible experiences,” and to delve into the “mixed or questionable motives of the person behind it. We’re inundated with people trying to scam us every time the phone rings. Is it even a real person? I saw that this could become a timely character study. Maybe Galbraith did just lose his way and was trying to stay above water.” Although the last shot of the film, lingering on Galbraith’s puzzled expression, suggests that his idea of truth is more flexible than most people’s.

“The scam artist is no longer an outlier – he’s the guy in the White House,” McKinney says. “We’re all trying to come to grips with this evaporating morality, the struggle to hold onto the values and principles we once expected the world to adhere to.”

Still, Munroe sees a glimmer of hope. A number of Galbraith’s victims appear in The Pigeon King , as well as former employees. “As heartbreaking as their stories are,” Munroe says, “they are earnest, sincere, genuine people. They are still shocked by dishonesty, and that’s heartening.”

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story included a photo caption that incorrectly identified actor Kathleen Munroe. This version has been corrected.

stories.title: Carney meets Trump in China, discusses ‘complex’ trade deal
stories.summary: The two spoke shortly after a news conference, where Carney said he doesn't believe Trump is uncomfortable with Canada furthering its trade relationship with China.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has met with U.S. President Donald Trump in China.

Carney’s office says the two leaders had a conversation that lasted just under 20 minutes, and that it included U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

The meeting also included Trump’s chief of staff Stephen Miller and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as well as Carney’s chief of staff Marc-André Blanchard and Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand.

The two spoke shortly after a news conference, where Carney said he doesn’t believe Trump is uncomfortable with Canada furthering its trade relationship with China.

Both leaders are attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the China’s tech hub, Shenzhen, where Canada and China agreed this week to drop trade restrictions on things like Canadian pork and Chinese steel.

Carney says it’s been easier for Ottawa to secure new trade arrangements with China because Canada’s trade relations south of the border are “much more complex.”

stories.title: Distribution centre strike dragged on Metro’s sales in fourth quarter
stories.summary: Retailer working to win back customers in Quebec after prolonged labour disruption
stories.author: Susan Krashinsky Robertson
stories.content:
Metro Inc. MRU-T is trying to win back shoppers after a prolonged strike at its produce distribution centre in Montreal led to fewer products available at its stores and drove customers to visit grocery competitors.

The strike, which dragged on for roughly six months and ended on Sept. 24, led to sales declines at Metro’s grocery stores, and resulted in lost profits and direct costs of $31-million after tax in the fourth quarter, the company reported on Wednesday. That was on top of $66-millon in costs and lost profits in the third quarter.

“As you can imagine, during the strike we couldn’t compete as we usually do. We had a bit of our hands tied behind our back,” president and chief executive Marc Giroux said during a conference call Wednesday to discuss the quarterly results, adding that the company lost some market share as a result.

“The focus now is rebuilding customer traffic, and rebuilding confidence in customers around our produce department and our business.”

Former chief operating officer Mr. Giroux took over the top job just as the strike was ending, after the retirement of Eric La Flèche, who was CEO for 18 years and remains chair of the company’s board of directors.

The labour dispute depleted the fruits and vegetables on store shelves in Quebec, requiring contingency plans that included shipping in some products from its Ontario distribution centre – a strategy that also created some turbulence for Metro’s Ontario stores, Mr. Giroux added.

The Montreal-based retailer reported sales of $5.18-billion in the quarter ended Sept. 26, 1.4 per cent higher compared with the same period last year. That modest increase was driven by new store openings.

But the impact of the strike was visible in same-store sales, an important metric that excludes the impact of store openings and closures on sales growth. Same-store sales at the company’s grocery stores declined by 1.9 per cent in the quarter.

Comparable sales are still negative in the first quarter, which is currently under way. The distribution centre returned to full operations two to three weeks ago, and stores now have a full assortment of products, Mr. Giroux said.

The company will use its loyalty program, personalized offers for customers, and promotions to win customers back, he added.

The disruption occurred at a time when competitive pressure has been ramping up in the grocery industry, as major retailers such as Loblaw Cos. Ltd. L-T , Costco Canada and Sobeys parent Empire Co. Ltd. EMP-A-T are building more stores – particularly under their discount banners.

A number of factors, including stubborn inflation, the effect of tariffs and high gas prices tied to the war in the Middle East, have squeezed Canadians’ budgets.

The trends are affecting retailers beyond the grocery sector as well: Last week, Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd. CTC-A-T CEO Greg Hicks warned that “the consumer psyche is still on high alert” ahead of the all-important holiday shopping season, and people are cutting back on expenses.

Like other grocers, Metro has been expanding its discount banners, converting one Ontario Metro location to Food Basics in the fourth quarter. The company is planning nine more conversions and seven newly built discount stores this year. Sales at discount locations are growing more than at conventional grocery stores.

“Consumers certainly – with fuel costs increasing and pressure on the cost of living – consumers are continuing to be value-centric,” Mr. Giroux said, adding that consumer demand is softening and “tonnage,” or the volume of products sold, has declined across the industry.

Metro has been seeing sales growth in its pharmacy business, which includes the Jean Coutu chain. Same-store sales increased by 5.5 per cent at the drugstores in the fourth quarter, led by higher prescription sales as well as front-of-store purchases.

The company’s fourth-quarter net earnings fell to $201.9-million or 97 cents in diluted net earnings per share, compared with $217.-million or $1 per share in the same period last year. That fell below analysts’ expectations of $204.9-million in net earnings, according to consensus estimates compiled by S&P Capital IQ.

The net earnings numbers were affected by the sale of Première Moisson Group Inc.’s commercial bakery manufacturing operations, which was announced in July. In addition, earnings in the same period last year included a writedown and costs related to a mechanical issue that shut down the company’s frozen-food distribution centre for nearly two months.

Excluding these items, adjusted net earnings fell by 18 per cent year-over-year, to $201.8-million or 97 cents per diluted share, compared with $246-million or $1.13 per share in the quarter last year.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this story incorrectly said Metro had converted 10 Ontario stores into Food Basics. This version has been corrected.

stories.title: Researchers on B.C. coast use drones to collect whale snot for genome sequencing
stories.summary: Eadin O’Mahony, lead researcher in the study published in the scientific journal Molecular Ecology Resources this week, said her team spent 2022 and 2023 collecting the samples.
stories.author: Brieanna Charlebois
stories.content:
Researchers studying humpback whales off the coast of British Columbia used drones to collect “whale snot,” allowing scientists to conduct a complete genome sequencing without darts, biopsies or approaching closely with a boat.

Eadin O’Mahony, lead researcher in the study published in the scientific journal Molecular Ecology Resources this week, said her team spent 2022 and 2023 collecting the samples.

“It was (about) getting the whole genome, but it was getting a whole genome in a non-invasive way,” she said of the project.

Genomic data is an important tool for conservation, she said, letting researchers measure population health, including genetic diversity and inbreeding, and helping them identify individuals and estimate population size.

“To have an understanding of the genetic resilience of a population of animals is really important for their long-term protection, their conservation,” O’Mahony said in an interview from Cork, Ireland.

To collect the DNA, she would pilot a drone from a small vessel or from land at the Fin Island Research Station in a remote location on B.C.’s northern coast.

Humpback whales forage in the region in the summer before migrating to Hawaii to breed in the winter, she said.

The drone flights were conducted under a Fisheries and Oceans Canada research permit.

O’Mahony said she would be watching through the video feed to ensure the animal was not visually showing any signs of distress as she approached. If any were detected, they would terminate the flight, she said, adding this happened “very rarely.”

The drone carried a sterile petri dish and would hover over the whale, waiting for it to take the typical five to six breaths per surfacing.

“I’m trying to pre-empt the whale’s behaviour somewhat positioning the drone just behind the blowhole so that when she comes up to take that exhale, I’m ready to just fly through the breath covering the petri dishes in these little ‘mucusy’ droplets that’s what is effectively snot,” O’Mahony said.

The drone would then capture a photo of the animal’s tail fluke as it dove below the water’s surface.

She said the tail fluke is similar to a “human fingerprint,” allowing scientists to easily identify each animal.

A second photographer would use a zoom camera to help ensure a “fluke ID photograph” is captured during each collection.

“The actual sampling event is very quick,” she said, noting each flight only takes a couple of minutes.

“The scientific study, ON the other hand — science is a slow game,” she said.

They collected 58 blow samples from a total of 26 humpbacks. The study said about 84 per cent of the DNA in the blow came from the whale itself.

Repeat samples from the same whales, collected in different encounters and across the two years, gave matching genomes. Blow genomes also matched previously collected biopsy genomes from the same animals, the study said.

Researchers, alongside collaborators from the Globe Institute at the University of Copenhagen, the North Coast Cetacean Society and Fisheries and Oceans Canada, also discovered genetic diversity estimated from blow samples was very similar to those of traditional biopsies.

The customary way of obtaining a genetic sample is from a biopsy, which requires getting a boat very close to the animal to dart it to obtain pieces of the whale’s blubber and skin.

The research also determined the population studied shows little evidence of recent inbreeding.

O’Mahony said the humpback whale population declined about 20 per cent between 2012 and 2021, which she called “quite significant and quite worrying.”

“Genetic understanding helps us make management plans for our conservation agencies, to make management plans that are sustainable and protect these animals going forward,” she said.

O’Mahony noted humpbacks were long subjects of commercial hunts, which “brought their numbers to the brink of extinction.”

She said there has been local recovery along B.C.’s coast, but there are conservation concerns over more expanded vessel traffic from tankers in the region, which increases the chances of fatal ship strikes.

“Getting that baseline information on what their genetic health looks like is really important in that context,” O’Mahony said.

She said there are scenarios where biopsy sampling is not possible, so this provides a non-invasive alternative.

“It’s not so much that the blow sampling will once and for all replace biopsy sampling, but there are a number of places where the blow sampling has its place,” she said.

“It just opens the door to more scenarios in which we might need to get the genetic material, but we haven’t been able to get it to such quality up until this point.”

She said she thinks blow sampling data is “only going to get better from here.”

“This is not the end of the road,” she said.

“It’s just going to open the door to increasingly non-invasive methods of research for conservation genomics.”

“I’m trying to pre-empt the whale’s behaviour somewhat positioning the drone just behind the blowhole so that when she comes up to take that exhale, I’m ready to just fly through the breath covering the petri dishes in these little ‘mucusy’ droplets that’s what is effectively snot,” O’Mahony said.
The drone would then capture a photo of the animal’s tail fluke as it dove below the water’s surface.
She said the tail fluke is similar to a “human fingerprint,” allowing scientists to easily identify each animal.
A second photographer would use a zoom camera to help ensure a “fluke ID photograph” is captured during each collection.
“The actual sampling event is very quick,” she said, noting each flight only takes a couple of minutes.
“The scientific study, ON the other hand — science is a slow game,” she said.
They collected 58 blow samples from a total of 26 humpbacks. The study said about 84 per cent of the DNA in the blow came from the whale itself.

Repeat samples from the same whales, collected in different encounters and across the two years, gave matching genomes. Blow genomes also matched previously collected biopsy genomes from the same animals, the study said.

Researchers, alongside collaborators from the Globe Institute at the University of Copenhagen, the North Coast Cetacean Society and Fisheries and Oceans Canada, also discovered genetic diversity estimated from blow samples was very similar to those of traditional biopsies.
The customary way of obtaining a genetic sample is from a biopsy, which requires getting a boat very close to the animal to dart it to obtain pieces of the whale’s blubber and skin.
The research also determined the population studied shows little evidence of recent inbreeding.
O’Mahony said the humpback whale population declined about 20 per cent between 2012 and 2021, which she called “quite significant and quite worrying.”
“Genetic understanding helps us make management plans for our conservation agencies, to make management plans that are sustainable and protect these animals going forward,” she said.
O’Mahony noted humpbacks were long subjects of commercial hunts, which “brought their numbers to the brink of extinction.”

She said there has been local recovery along B.C.’s coast, but there are conservation concerns over more expanded vessel traffic from tankers in the region, which increases the chances of fatal ship strikes.
“Getting that baseline information on what their genetic health looks like is really important in that context,” O’Mahony said.
She said there are scenarios where biopsy sampling is not possible, so this provides a non-invasive alternative.
“It’s not so much that the blow sampling will once and for all replace biopsy sampling, but there are a number of places where the blow sampling has its place,” she said.
“It just opens the door to more scenarios in which we might need to get the genetic material, but we haven’t been able to get it to such quality up until this point.”
She said she thinks blow sampling data is “only going to get better from here.”
“This is not the end of the road,” she said.
“It’s just going to open the door to increasingly non-invasive methods of research for conservation genomics.”

stories.title: Hamilton-area realtors say local housing market is gridlocked
stories.summary: Wary buyers in all price brackets are constraining movement in the city and the surrounding suburbs
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
On the tree-lined streets of Hamilton’s Westdale neighbourhood, homes for sale typically don’t linger for long.

The affluent enclave of Tudor and Georgian-style houses close to McMaster University often draws doctors who need proximity to the leading-edge medical centre and professors who teach on campus.

Recently, however, sales have softened as the weakness in most parts of the southern Ontario real estate market permeates that pocket and other sought-after areas as well, say Vivian Debruyn-Smith and Mark Debruyn-Smith of Royal LePage State Realty.

Wary buyers in all price brackets are constraining movement in the city of Hamilton and the surrounding suburbs, including Burlington, Ancaster and Dundas, they say.

“Everything is stalled,” says Mr. Debruyn-Smith. “It’s gridlock.”

The veteran agents have seen strong downturns and wild upswings during more than 35 years of selling real estate in the Hamilton area. The current slump, which has lasted nearly two years, is more confounding than most.

Sales in October in the Hamilton-Burlington area rose 7.1 per cent in October from September on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association (Crea), but activity dipped 1.8 per cent compared with the same month last year.

New listings rose 6 per cent last month from September’s level. Compared with October 2025, new listings fell 9.3 per cent.

The average sale price dropped 4.4 per cent in October from the same month last year to stand at $807,341.

On a national basis, sales in October were flat compared with September. Sales fell 10.6 per cent last month compared with the same period in 2025.

The national average price slipped 1.6 per cent in October from October of last year to stand at $678,584.

Overall, the country’s housing market is in balanced territory, according to Crea.

Data from Statistics Canada shows the annual rate of inflation held steady in October at 3.1 per cent.

Royal Bank of Canada economist Abbey Xu says the report shows energy prices are the reason inflation remains elevated while underlying price pressures stayed relatively contained.

The numbers leave the Bank of Canada facing a finely balanced decision in December, Ms. Xu says.

She expects policy-makers to raise the benchmark interest rate by one quarter of a percentage point in December, though downside economic surprises could bring a pause, she adds.

The central bank raised its key rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent on Oct. 28.

Potential buyers and sellers in Hamilton seem more concerned about the health of the overall economy than the Bank of Canada’s moves, say the Debruyn-Smiths.

Typically a sluggish market attracts aspiring move-up buyers because high-end properties have more significant price reductions than starter homes, which draw a larger buyer pool.

But the trade war with the United States, economic uncertainty and geopolitical tensions have rattled consumers, the Debruyn-Smiths say.

Ms. Debruyn-Smith points to a five-bedroom detached house which the couple listed in mid-September with an asking price of $1,499,900.

In a faster-paced market, the home on a ravine lot at 18 Forsyth Ave. N. would sell quickly because turnover in the area is so low.

This fall, buyers who would like to trade up to a property in Westdale and other sought-after areas May wonder how feasible it is to sell their existing house, Ms. Debruyn-Smith points out.

Deals conditional on “sale of purchaser’s property” are increasingly common, she says. In that case, a clause allows buyers to back out if they are unable to sell their current property before closing on the new one.

At the same time, lenders have become ultraconservative – requiring larger down payments and delving into financial records – even when the buyer has a secure job with Hamilton Health Sciences or St. Joseph’s Healthcare.

“The banks are giving these very specialized medical professionals a hard time,” she says. “It is another wrinkle added to all the other ones.”

Today the health care sector is the city’s largest employer.

While the former steel juggernauts Stelco and Dofasco once employed tens of thousands, the industry’s work force has continued to dwindle as operations have been idled.

As a result, the U.S. tariffs on the steel and manufacturing industries are worrisome, Mr. Debruyn-Smith says, but job losses have not led to a large swell in listings.

The consumers he has been speaking with are feeling cautious.

“I’m going to put everything off – I don’t want to assume any more risk right now,” is the attitude of move-up buyers today, he says.

First-time buyers are hesitating because the cost of living is so high and houses still seem out of reach for many, he says.

In previous decades, even people with modest incomes would buy a small fixer-upper on the Mountain, which is the local name for the Niagara Escarpment.

The seller of that house could then buy a newly-built house in one of the suburban neighbourhoods spreading beyond Rymal Road.

“You would get that knock-on effect,” he says.

This fall, many would-be buyers feel no sense of urgency.

“They say, ‘What’s my hurry? I’m going to take my time. I’m going to overanalyze,’” he says.

In Burlington, the Debruyn-Smiths have a two-bedroom condo unit listed for sale with an asking price of $648,888.

Condo inventory is high in the upscale suburb, they say, and prices have dropped significantly.

When a seller or their family member makes a massive adjustment, that sets a new benchmark for the complex.

“That’s really accelerating the downward slide,” says Mr. Debruyn-Smith.

In Ancaster, many neighbourhoods that have risen on former farmland have seen steep price reductions, Ms. Debruyn-Smith says.

“You’re looking at houses that are somewhat cookie-cutter,” she says of the newer developments. “They are really struggling because it’s hard to distinguish yourself. There’s a lot of competition.”

Historic Dundas, below the escarpment, offers a different housing landscape: Grand Victorian-era houses near the town centre will sell if they are priced well, she says.

“They don’t come up very often and there’s a lot of demand when they do.”

Looking ahead, the Debruyn-Smiths say they are hearing from potential sellers who are optimistic that the spring of 2027 will bring some brio back to the market.

Mr. Debruyn-Smith also believes the consumers on the sidelines will unleash pent-up demand at some point, but the timing for the next rush is hard to predict.

“How long can they live in their parents’ basements?”

stories.title: Two parking spots, amenities help in over-asking sale of condo
stories.summary: Unit has full-height windows in principal rooms, sliding doors to a balcony from the kitchen and second bedroom
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
99 Foxbar Rd., No. 2010, Toronto

Asking price: $1,595,000 (September 2026)

Selling price: $1.65-million (September 2026)

Previous selling price: $956,725 (August 2022)

Taxes: $7,281 (2026)

Days on the market: Five

Listing agents: Carol Lome and Brayden Irwin, Johnston and Daniel

This two-bedroom, corner unit has 1,156 square feet of living space with unobstructed views south and two parking spots in a roughly five-year-old building off St. Clair Avenue. Agent Brayden Irwin advised the owner to keep their price under $1.6-million, even though a similar unit with one-car parking traded for $1.65-million last summer.

“The nice thing about this particular condo was it had two parking spots and most only have one,” Mr. Irwin said.

“We wanted to be cautious not to overprice it because, whether it’s a condo or a house, in this market, if it’s priced too high, it’ll sit.”

The tactic paid off within days. The sellers received two bids, and one rose to $1.65-million.

“The market has softened from the peak, but there are a lot of people active and ready to buy,” Mr. Irwin said.

“We ended up getting two parties that made an offer on it, and it sold over the asking price, at the price of the previous sale.”

This unit has full-height windows in the principal rooms, and sliding doors to a balcony from the kitchen and second bedroom.

The primary bedroom has a Juliet balcony, a walk-in closet and a bathroom with heated floors.

There is another full bathroom and laundry machines.

The unit has two storage lockers. Monthly fees of $1,555 cover water and use of a 20,000-square-foot clubhouse at Imperial Plaza, a conversion project in the former Imperial Oil headquarters next door.

“It has an unobstructed view of the city skyline to the south,” Mr. Irwin said.

“This is in one of the newer buildings in the neighbourhood.

“The amenities are also unique. In what was the bomb shelter-type area built under the Imperial Oil building, they turned into a sports complex.”

stories.title: Crumbling 1879 row houses restored for social service use
stories.summary: Dixon Hall’s residential project houses some of the community’s most vulnerable members while also restoring heritage, reusing existing buildings
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
In architecture, the axiom goes something like this: adaptive reuse of a heritage building is a good thing, but it is also expensive. Therefore, with housing or commercial developments, this adds a luxury piece to the project, and unit prices (or lease rates) must reflect that with a monetary bump up.

Which also means heritage and affordable housing are like oil and water: they don’t mix.

Way back in the early 1990s, Margie Zeidler, architect and eldest child of Ontario Place and Eaton Centre architect Eberhard Zeidler, showed that wasn’t true with 401 Richmond, the now-beloved arts-and-culture hub that turned an 1899 tin factory into something magical – but not necessarily beautiful – thanks, in part, to the teachings of urbanist and author Jane Jacobs.

“I always thought architecture was about beautifying the city, and that all those old, ugly buildings need to be beautified and made more attractive,” she told me recently, “and then I suddenly understood their usefulness and fell in love.”

Now, social-service provider Dixon Hall has doubled down in Cabbagetown with a residential project that houses some of the community’s most vulnerable members while also restoring heritage and reusing existing buildings. And they’ve won a few awards for their efforts.

“We could have built something institutional and square, and everybody has the same room,” says Dixon Hall chief executive officer Janet Lambert. “Instead, everybody here has their own unique room; they’re all New York-style microlofts.” Some units, she explains, May have less square footage but sport a big bay window, while others are larger but offer a quirky floor plan. Regardless, it’s “just so beautiful to have people feel that they’re part of a heritage building; it makes it easier for them to be part of the community.”

And while the 1879 Second Empire-style row houses that span from 502 to 508 Parliament St. (J. Bowden, builder) weren’t fully designated as heritage by the City of Toronto, they had been listed in 1975. The city worked with Dixon Hall and ERA Architects to save as much as possible, especially on the exterior, since there weren’t many Victorian details left on the inside.

“They had been pretty heavily modified and renovated over time, so the building got a full gut,” says Era’s Shelley Ludman. “In 502, we were able to retain the original stairs.”

“We kept all the rough framing and repaired it,” adds Era’s Diana Roldan, “this is what full retention, full conservation really looks like. … This project shows the quantity and the gravity and the extent of the collaboration that’s needed between the owner, the architect, the contractors were very collaborative, and even with [Dixon Hall] staff too, they were helping us troubleshoot and interpret regulations to make this happen.”

Of course, for the person who has just exchanged a tent and camp-stove in a ravine for a climate-controlled unit with a lock on the door, minifridge, microwave, proper bed, storage and access to a communal kitchen (each townhouse has a full kitchen and dining area that faces the bay window on the ground floor), the layers of financing or bureaucracy required to turn these vacant, faded Victorian treasures into supportive housing are just abstract concepts … if considered at all.

“What we’ve been told by Reconnect [Health Services, who] provide the wraparound supports for people who come in,” says Ms. Lambert, “is they come in from an encampment, let’s say, and sleep for three weeks, just sleep, because they’ve just been in such cortisol-level, high mental, physical, emotional stress from being homeless.”

Viewed from the sidewalk, it’s easy to see dignity restored to the once lime-green-and-purple façade (the complex had been vacant for a few years before Dixon Hall purchased it from the city), but it’s more complex to understand what it takes to restore the dignity inside the 31 souls behind those walls. And if 31 seems a high number, it’s worth noting that unlike the typical Toronto 1,100 to 1,500 square-foot row house floorplate, these Victorians were abnormally large at 2,500 sq. ft. That also means these hotel-sized rooms are large enough to have a guest, a private meal, rediscover a hobby, or watch television.

When No. 502 wraps construction, Dixon Hall will add 11 more residences – these with full kitchens – to the already bustling street. And, says Dixon Hall director of real estate and property management Fahim Karmali, other projects have added even more, such as 41 Rose Ave., a stone’s throw away, and they’ve set their sights on the row houses at 265 to 277 Wellesley St. E., which are still up for grabs. These opportunities, says Mr. Karmali, are the result of Toronto Community Housing divesting itself, in 2019, of its “scattered houses portfolio,” which, at the time, asked for RFPs (request for proposal) on 623 houses which, collectively, contained 730 units.

While Dixon Hall admits heritage structures add another layer of complexity to building affordable housing – there was an unanticipated 16-foot dig in the front yard of the Parliament houses to fix sanitary and storm water systems which added greatly to the timeline – they’re not sure why there is “a sense within the city about nervousness with heritage properties,” says Mr. Karmali.

“Now we’ve got a ton of experience and a ton of partnerships and relationships that we know we could do this in a much better way,” finishes Ms. Lambert.

Perhaps winning the city’s own Heritage Toronto Adaptive Reuse Award for 2026 and the Cabbagetown Preservation Association’s Peggy Kurtin Award (also for 2026) for Excellence in Restoration will convince the city that there’s a new axiom about heritage and affordable housing.

stories.title: Ontario condo boards get tougher in enforcing rules
stories.summary: A court ruling could make enforcing condo rules more costly and complicated for boards and owners alike
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
A dispute over tree pruning highlights that condominium corporations will struggle to enforce rules in Ontario now that courts have restricted the use of legal fees as de facto fines.

Condo law experts warn that with the loss of a simple and powerful system that reigned in Ontario for 18 years – which left owners with little recourse but to pay legal fees associated with conflicts over rules or maintenance – the litigation that could replace it May end up being more expensive in the long run.

“Disputes that used to be resolved in a few days at a cost of a few hundred dollars will now cost thousands and take months to resolve,” said Bradley Chaplick, partner with Levitt, Di Lella, Duggan, & Chaplick LLP, in an e-mailed statement.

Some recent disputes straddle the changes and demonstrate the confusion around the new legal landscape.

On Aug. 5, Karen Li – who co-owns a condo townhouse where her parents live in Unionville – received a legal letter from Fatema Tokhy, a lawyer with Rutherford Law & ADR, demanding they pay $1,785.40 before Aug. 20. The letter alleged they had ignored a June 6 cease and desist letter telling them not to trim branches or “mutilate the common elements tree” in the backyard of their condo townhouse.

The condo’s rules don’t allow owners to alter the landscaping, including trees, without the board of directors’ consent, and Ms. Li’s parents allegedly cut branches from the tree after the June 6 letter. “We will not tolerate any unit owner’s blatant disregard of YCC 268’s governing documents,” Ms. Tokhy wrote.

Up until this past August, the costs of sending a legal letter demanding an owner obey the condominium corporation’s rules could immediately be applied to a common expenses bill, and if the owners failed to pay, a lien could be issued on title to their home. In extreme cases, those unpaid legal fees could empower the condo corporation to force the sale of an owner’s home in order to collect the debt.

These fees were de facto fines for non-compliance. Fines are not permitted under Ontario condo law, and condo experts say there was a practice of sometimes abusive pricing in the assessing of the legal fees that brought the practice into disrepute.

“One or two people who have essentially ruined it for the profession,” said Audrey Loeb, a leading condo lawyer with Shibley Righton, who said the more outrageous fees were the fault of a small number of bad actors. “A couple of lawyers whose fees were so exorbitant and so absurd they’ve ruined it for everyone else.”

On Aug. 7, a few days after Ms. Li and her parents got their legal letter, Ontario Superior Court Justice Edward Iacobucci cracked down on excessive legal fees in Chiarelli v. Toronto Standard Condominium Corporation No. 2339, ruling that the Condominium Act requires lawyers and condos to come in front of a court to obtain a judgment that any legal fees charged for enforcement were reasonable: “The legal costs cannot be added to common expenses without a court order,” he wrote.

Whether a case such as Ms. Li’s would gain a court’s approval to collect legal fees would come down to a judge or adjudicator’s ruling on the facts in the case, according to Rod Escayola, partner with Stack Condo Law. “Ultimately, the question will be whether the matter is a compliance matter – seeking to force owner to comply with governing docs? If it’s pure compliance, they need an order.”

After getting the demand letter, Ms. Li asked for an itemization of the $1,784 fee and raised Chiarelli as an example of the changed legal landscape, but still offered some form of reimbursement over what she called a “misunderstanding.”

“In good faith, we are open to settling this matter and reimburse the condo corp,” she wrote.

But on Oct. 9, Ms. Tokhy wrote back to reiterate her demand for the full fee and warned that even though the corporation had not yet assessed any costs related to maintenance or repair of the allegedly damaged tree, it could do so.

“For example, as mentioned above, if YCC 268 decides to engage an arborist to assess the failing tree, this cost May constitute a proper chargeback and May be lienable if not paid within the stipulated deadline. While the legal costs alone May not be lienable at this time, it is still recoverable,” she wrote.

In an e-mail to The Globe and Mail, Ms. Tokhy said her second letter “was consistent with the recent changes in the law.”

Some firms recognize that the old ways are gone.

“The standard practice at my firm since Chiarelli is that we no longer include a demand for payment of legal costs in our rules enforcement demand letters to owners,” Mr. Chaplick said. “While we have adapted, there are some firms out there who appear to be of the view that demanding costs is a worthwhile strategy, even though they know that the demand is unenforceable.”

However, he warned that with recent changes at the Condominium Appeal Tribunal around the awarding of costs, the days of pricey legal letters could come to be seen as preferable to a flood of enforcement matters that could take weeks or months to battle over, and May end up being much more expensive for owners and condominium corporations alike.

stories.title: How an ancient Greek love story rekindled Colin McAdam’s love of writing
stories.summary: In his new novel, Daphnis and Chloe, McAdam drops a pastoral idyll into the contemporary Pacific Northwest
stories.author: Emily Donaldson
stories.content:
Two thousand years ago, the Greek writer Longus told the story of Daphnis and Chloe, abandoned children who grow up together as shepherds and fall innocently, if somewhat cluelessly, in love.

Colin McAdam’s novel Daphnis and Chloe takes that pastoral idyll and drops it into the contemporary Pacific Northwest, where the dangers awaiting its young lovers are considerably less quaint. Dark as the story becomes, McAdam still claws his way toward the original’s hopefulness. The Giller-nominated novel is McAdam’s fifth; his previous include the Giller-shortlisted Fall and A Beautiful Truth , winner of the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize. He holds a Cambridge PhD in classical translation.

McAdam spoke to The Globe and Mail from his home in Chelsea, Que.

Your academic specialty was 17th-century translations of Greek stories. Do you think of this book as an act of translation too – not from one language to another, but from one historical setting to another?

Absolutely. I never thought that my thesis would have any use. It’s a conversation stopper, that thesis.

Classics are always turned back to in times of tumult or uncertainty. I should contextualize that I picked up Daphnis and Chloe to write and express my love of writing. I had no program or intention about it at first. I’d been through this dark period of watching my previous book just disappear, and also the way people had lived through COVID-19. I wanted to find some healthy energy.

The original was a reaction to its time. It was probably written around the turn of the second century. Rome would have been peaking in terms of its bureaucracy and infrastructure and everything else. Longus deliberately looked back to this pastoral world, a simpler world.

I guess what I was trying to do was rekindle my own love of writing , having gone through this bullshit with the publishing industry. It’s a lonely business, and it doesn’t pay well. You get long enough down that road, and you think: Why am I doing this?

Writing the book pulled me out of this dark place. Every day I was writing was like lighting a candle. It was like a prayer; like worshipping creation.

You could have written this story without the scaffold of Longus’s story. What did working within it give you?

There was a practical thing that was very helpful, which was, like you said, Longus provided an infrastructure, a scaffold that I could just take cues from. Normally I’m stuck for plot. What am I going to write? There’s a character named Dorcon, so I’m going to take that name and make something up. It helped me not to get stuck.

That weightlessness was there from day one. I was just really eager to wake up and write. I write longhand, and I’d read to my wife at the end of every week. It was so fun.

You’ve made the character of Cupid an orderly in a nursing home. Tell me about that approach.

I don’t really know why I did that. In the original, [the human narrator] is looking at a fresco – I think it was – of the events that will unfold in the narrative. I thought it’d be good to do it with an extra remove of having Eros himself be the narrator and putting him in an old folks’ home. I find these places moving. People coming to the end of their lives and they’ve got such rich stories; their internal world is immensely inspiring. Having Eros as an orderly would be a way into that sort of psyche. He’s got omniscience. He moves around.

Why set the novel in the Pacific Northwest? Have you lived there?

I lived there for a year when my father-in-law was dying, about 15 years ago, ON Vancouver Island. It’s this impossibly beautiful, inspiring place. Nowhere else on earth have I found that combination of feeling relaxed but also really energized and inspired, moved by natural beauty. It’s a place of the heart. And because the original is set on an island, I thought, why not Vancouver Island?

The original is a pastoral romance. The tone is light. Your version goes to some extremely dark places, particularly in the story of Chloe, who gets sex trafficked.

Maybe that speaks to my habit of mind. Except I only want to go to dark places with a light place in mind.

Daphnis and Chloe is kind of the same thing. There are pirates in the original. My novel is set in a garage, so why not have bikers instead of pirates and why not have sex trafficking instead of abductions?

I don’t like doing things half-heartedly. If I’m going to write about this stuff, then I’ll go hard and go honestly and see where I can find the light ultimately. And it’s believable. These things are going on all around us, in cities everywhere.

What felt most important to preserve from the original?

Again, to find that light at the end, because it’s there in the original: this classic wedding, the foundlings rediscovering their parents. I worked on the epilogue for a long time. I wrote the thing in two months, but I spent two months later doing the epilogue over and over, trying to get the right tone, which was hard.

If I’m going to contemporize this thing, I want to do it as honestly as possible and with as much respect for these small events as I can find. When a daughter goes missing, what does that feel like? What is she going through? What heroism can I tease out of that realistically? That was my main challenge vis-a-vis the original: to ultimately find some kind of catharsis.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

That weightlessness was there from day one. I was just really eager to wake up and write. I write longhand, and I’d read to my wife at the end of every week. It was so fun.
You’ve made the character of Cupid an orderly in a nursing home. Tell me about that approach.

I don’t really know why I did that. In the original, [the human narrator] is looking at a fresco – I think it was – of the events that will unfold in the narrative. I thought it’d be good to do it with an extra remove of having Eros himself be the narrator and putting him in an old folks’ home. I find these places moving. People coming to the end of their lives and they’ve got such rich stories; their internal world is immensely inspiring. Having Eros as an orderly would be a way into that sort of psyche. He’s got omniscience. He moves around.
Why set the novel in the Pacific Northwest? Have you lived there?

I lived there for a year when my father-in-law was dying, about 15 years ago, ON Vancouver Island. It’s this impossibly beautiful, inspiring place. Nowhere else on earth have I found that combination of feeling relaxed but also really energized and inspired, moved by natural beauty. It’s a place of the heart. And because the original is set on an island, I thought, why not Vancouver Island?
The original is a pastoral romance. The tone is light. Your version goes to some extremely dark places, particularly in the story of Chloe, who gets sex trafficked.
Maybe that speaks to my habit of mind. Except I only want to go to dark places with a light place in mind.

Daphnis and Chloe is kind of the same thing. There are pirates in the original. My novel is set in a garage, so why not have bikers instead of pirates and why not have sex trafficking instead of abductions?

I don’t like doing things half-heartedly. If I’m going to write about this stuff, then I’ll go hard and go honestly and see where I can find the light ultimately. And it’s believable. These things are going on all around us, in cities everywhere.
What felt most important to preserve from the original?

Again, to find that light at the end, because it’s there in the original: this classic wedding, the foundlings rediscovering their parents. I worked on the epilogue for a long time. I wrote the thing in two months, but I spent two months later doing the epilogue over and over, trying to get the right tone, which was hard.

If I’m going to contemporize this thing, I want to do it as honestly as possible and with as much respect for these small events as I can find. When a daughter goes missing, what does that feel like? What is she going through? What heroism can I tease out of that realistically? That was my main challenge vis-a-vis the original: to ultimately find some kind of catharsis.

stories.title: Chow to lay out vision for new term as Toronto council holds first meeting
stories.summary: The election has also set the table for a shuffling of key committee roles, with the retirement of housing chair Gord Perks and the defeat of transit chair Jamaal Myers.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Mayor Olivia Chow is expected to lay out her vision for her second term as Toronto City Hall hosts its first meeting of the new council.

Chow is set to address the council Wednesday afternoon for the first time since winning her re-election bid.

Also at the meeting, the speaker’s chair is expected to be filled by a new face after council’s longtime rules enforcer Frances Nunziata, who held the post for 16 years, was defeated in last month’s election.

The election has also set the table for a shuffling of key committee roles, with the retirement of housing chair Gord Perks and the defeat of transit chair Jamaal Myers.

Chow will have seven new councillors to consider for high-profile roles, including former Liberal MPs Nate Erskine-Smith and Shaun Chen.

Chow will be expected to make good this term on a campaign platform headlined by promises to boost renter protections, cap transit fares, expand a school nutrition program and build more affordable housing.

stories.summary: The future of Canada’s auto-building sector remains the crux of concern, as the fallout of Stellantis’ Brampton, Ont., plant sale to Canadian defence contractor, Roshel plays out on both economic and political fronts. Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Dr. Peter Frise, emeritus professor of mechanical and automotive engineering at the University of Windsor, to dis…
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
The future of Canada’s auto-building sector remains the crux of concern, as the fallout of Stellantis’ Brampton, Ont., plant sale to Canadian defence contractor, Roshel plays out on both economic and political fronts.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Dr. Peter Frise, emeritus professor of mechanical and automotive engineering at the University of Windsor, to discuss the impact on thousands of workers, the future of companies that require subsidies to sustain itself, and whether Roshel’s productivity will fill the economic gap left behind.

stories.title: Lewis and Rahman confirmed as London’s deputy mayors despite questions over different term lengths
stories.summary: London’s newly elected city council began its term with a pledge to deliver results, before a debate over two deputy mayor positions almost derailed their mostly ceremonial inaugural meeting.
stories.content:
London’s newly elected city council began its term with a pledge to deliver results, before a debate over two deputy mayor positions almost derailed their mostly ceremonial inaugural meeting.

All 15 members of council were led into the RBC Place Convention Centre by the London Police Service piper and colour guard to take their oaths of office in front of more than 200 people.

Mayor Josh Morgan recognized four outgoing councillors and the efforts of unsuccessful candidates who raised different perspectives and ideas during last month’s election.

“Everybody who took the time to come out here tonight, who was unsuccessful in the election but shared your thoughts, your passion, and your ideas with Londoners, your voices also matter,” Morgan said during a brief speech. “I know this council will listen to the people who they defeated in this election as important voices in this community.”

He then spoke about the priorities for the new council that includes 10 returning councillors and four rookies.

“This term is about executing really well on behalf of Londoners,” the mayor said. “It’s about ensuring that we take all of the groundwork we laid (last term), and take it to the next level. We don’t measure success by announcements of projects, but we measure success by the differences it makes in the lives of people in this community.”

However, Morgan’s motion to split the deputy mayor role into two positions, one focused on intergovernmental relations/advocacy and the other on community priorities, prompted a number of questions from councillors.

Coun. Sam Trosow’s concern centred on why Coun. Shawn Lewis would serve a four-year term as deputy mayor with the intergovernmental relations/advocacy portfolio, but Coun. Corrine Rahman would be appointed for just two-years as deputy mayor of community priorities before council either renewed her appointment or selected a different councillor.

“I really do think we need to have some more discussion about why one [deputy mayor position] is two-years and one is four-years, because I have not heard a satisfactory explanation to that,” said Trosow.

Morgan responded to Trosow that they could revisit the issue at an upcoming committee meeting, noting that the mayor recommends the appointments but council confirms them.

“We could make the decisions tonight. You could adjust the time frames at a subsequent meeting of (the) standing committee and council,” Morgan explained.

Trosow remained dissatisfied.

“I’m going to let this go,” he said. “I’m just going to say I’m very unhappy with the fact that we do not get to discuss the question of a two-year term versus a four-year term, and I think that is a flaw that is going to come back and will have to be adjusted.”

A subsequent vote by council confirmed Lewis for four years and Rahman for two years.

Coun. Steve Lehman was appointed as the new budget chair.

After the meeting, Deputy Mayor Rahman said she was comfortable with the length of her appointment.

“I’m satisfied. I think that a two-year term is a good way to start, see what needs to maybe be adjusted and tweaked as we move forward,” Rahman told CTV News. “I’m a big believer in performance reviews, having been an HR [human resources] Professor, so I’m okay with that.”

Council gets to work Wednesday making appointments to standing committees and external agencies, boards and commissions.

stories.title: An exodus of innovators: Benchmark Canada
stories.summary: The loss of some of Canada's most economically important citizens has become a ‘feeder system’ to the U.S. innovation economy
stories.author: Jared Lindzon, National Post
stories.content:
Countries don’t typically get report cards, but there are hard facts that can be collated, assessed and compared. Enter Benchmark Canada, a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings togethermore than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance. This fall, the National Post is examining many of those findings.

Canada is struggling to retain its high-potential startups, with far-reaching implications for the broader economy.

A study conducted by Toronto-based venture capitalists Leaders Fund in 2025 found that only 32 per cent of Canadian-founded high-potential startups — or those that have raised at least $1 million from venture capitalists — were headquartered in Canada as of 2024. Meanwhile, 48 per cent relocated across the border, and another 20 per cent established a headquarters in the European Union.

Between 2015 and 2020, Canada retained between 60 and 75 per cent of its high-potential startups before experiencing successively larger exoduses with each passing year for the following five.

Gideon Hayden, the co-founder and managing partner of Leaders Fund, says it’s hard to know for sure what changed after 2020, but speculates that a combination of factors were at play.

“The pandemic, no doubt in my mind, had a huge impact, even just on the way we work,” he says, suggesting remote work made relocation easier. “We also lived through some of the most restrictive COVID policies in the world, and for anyone building a business, that posed a challenge.”

Hayden adds that Canada has historically retained its startup founders by offering a high quality of life, but by the early 2020s that advantage was slipping. “When those metrics started to trend in the wrong direction, that maybe made the decision easier for folks,” he says.

There are broader societal benefits to these innovation clusters that go beyond just firms' employment and tax dollars

The final nail in the coffin, however, was the Trudeau government’s planned increase to the inclusion rate for capital gains taxes in Budget 2024, effectively taking a bigger bite out of successful startup founders’ payday when they exit the business.

That might also help explain a recent modest reversal, which followed Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to cancel his predecessor’s planned changes to capital gains taxes. “There’s definitely a (different) vibe happening where we have a more serious person leading the country, and that capital gains hike was cancelled,” Hayden says.

After five consecutive years of declines, the latest Leaders Fund study (which will be published exclusively in Financial Post on Dec. 1) shows some signs of improvement. In 2025, 40 per cent of Canadian-founded, high-potential startups remained in the country, largely due to declines in European relocation. That marks the first year-over-year improvement since 2018, but the country’s startup retention rate remains well below former averages.

The recent reversal is welcome news for Canadians within and beyond the innovation ecosystem. That’s because startup founders are uniquely positioned to deliver economic prosperity in new and innovative ways.

“We don’t inherently care about the number of entrepreneurs that live in Canada. At the end of the day, we care about productivity growth, and we care about our standard of living. Full stop,” says Francis Fong, a managing director and senior economist at TD Bank. “There are broader societal benefits to these innovation clusters that go beyond just firms’ employment and tax dollars.”

In a recent report, Fong labelled this exodus “Canada’s Silent Brain Drain,” noting that Canada was barely noticing the loss of some of its most economically important citizens. In fact, the report went so far as to suggest that Canada was acting as a “feeder system” to the United States’ innovation economy.

“We create the feeder system by dedicating public tax dollars to research, but not to helping the individuals that develop products and services in actually bringing them to market,” he says. “We are basically helping other countries.”

It wasn’t always this way. Fong explains that in the decade prior to 2016, Canada saw some of the highest productivity and growth metrics in the G7, thanks in large part to a significant corporate tax advantage over the United States.

“The U.S. has made substantive efforts to improve the competitiveness of their own tax systems, and that tax advantage is now gone,” he says. “If you look at the general corporate income tax statutory rate from a combined federal-provincial versus federal-state level, we are now on par. So, if you’re going to pay a particular tax rate, why not do it in the U.S., where you can access deeper capital markets and a larger consumer market?”

Though it’s unlikely Canada will be able to offer its businesses a more generous tax rate than its southern neighbour, Fong says the country can do more to lower some of the regulatory barriers that hurt startups more than they benefit society.

“A regulation is designed to protect consumers, society, the environment, something — and it’s a difficult decision for the government to say, ‘we’re going to deprioritize this,’” he says. “That’s a hard conversation, but I think it’s one that we at least need to begin.”

In a follow-up survey with 24 Canadian founders who relocated to the United States, Leaders Fund found the most common motivation for moving was to access a larger consumer market. That was followed by access to venture capital funding, a culture of ambition and risk-taking, and then talent density. However, when asked what would lure them back, almost all cited a more favourable tax environment.

Hayden explains that policymakers and governments can’t make a startup successful on their own, but they can play a role in creating the conditions that enable them to win.

“What countries can do is try (to) make that environment more conducive and create less friction in building a company,” he says. “That can take the form of reducing capital gains to incentivize more entrepreneurs to build here, making the government procurement process way faster to meet the timelines of a startup, making it easier for companies to recruit international talent — these things make a difference.”

stories.title: Canada’s emergency alert system to be tested across the country on Wednesday
stories.summary: A test message and tone will be broadcast on television, radio and compatible wireless devices
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
Canadians across the country can expect to hear the shrill screeching sound of Canada’s emergency alerting system today.

Pelmorex, which operates the Alert Ready system, says a test message and tone will be broadcast on television, radio and compatible wireless devices.

It says test messages will be issued in every province and territory at specific times between morning and early afternoon.

The system is usually tested in May and November and is part of Canada’s effort to ensure it works and raises awareness.

There is no option to opt out of the test or actual emergency alerts.

The Alert Ready system issued 1,215 alerts in Canada as of Oct. 31, for emergencies including Amber Alerts, tornadoes and thunderstorms.

stories.title: ‘Totally unacceptable’: Surgical nurses describe moral distress of being forced to care for post-op patients in hallways
stories.summary: Hallway health care — normally associated with gridlocked ERs — is steadily creeping into other parts of the hospital
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
It used to be rare for a recuperating surgery patient to find themselves forced out of their hospital room and into a chaotic hallway to make space for someone else.

But amid a chronic shortage of hospital beds in Canada, desperate measures are becoming the norm.

Hallway health care — normally associated with gridlocked emergency rooms and “harrowing accounts” of people languishing for hours while waiting for care — is steadily creeping into other parts of the hospital, according to a new study based on the experiences of nurses.

Nurses working in nine Ontario inpatient surgical units shared their realities of caring for people with surgical wounds, drains and other complex post-op needs in cramped, noisy hallway spaces.

Nurses described unsafe nurse-to-patient ratios, scant to no privacy for patients, worries over increased risks for wound infections and moral distress and burnout over not being able to give patients the care they deserve while still being expected to “make it work.”

Making it work meant not having access to equipment normally found in patient rooms, such as suction and in-wall oxygen. It meant improvising with heavy portable oxygen tanks that require close monitoring to make sure they don’t run out. It meant struggling with the “moral weight” of changing wound dressings and inserting catheters in essentially “thoroughfares that are not designed for this provision of care,” said senior author Christine McPherson, an associate professor of nursing at the University of Ottawa.

Makeshift curtains or screens didn’t stop sensitive conversations from being overheard, or keep people from feeling exposed and vulnerable, she and her co-authors said.

“You May be talking about end-of-life care, you May be talking about very private personal information…. This is all going on in a hallway where there are people wandering around,” said McPherson, who oversaw the research.

It’s a hidden problem most people May not appreciate unless they’ve lived it themselves, she said. “It’s crept in, more and more.”

Some nurses recounted “incidents of harm and near misses,” including a patient who suffered a head injury and concussion after a painting fell off the hallway wall.

“One key source of relational strain came from having to deliver news that a patient would be moved into the hallway,” even though the decision was beyond the nurses’ control, the researchers wrote in the Canadian Journal of Nursing Research. The tension was made worse when outraged patients, or their families, refused to be moved.

“What message does it send to people? It sends the message, ‘We don’t really care, we’re just going to move you into the hallway,'” McPherson said.

“You’ve had your surgery; you’re at increased risk of post-surgical complications, but you’re going to be moved into the hallway now. It’s just totally unacceptable.”

Zoe Ruddy, a surgical nurse who led the research as part of her master’s thesis in nursing, has seen 20 to 30 hallway patients in any given month.

Some discharged themselves home.

“They don’t want to stay in the hallway,” she said. “It’s just too much, especially when you’re sick already and being moved out into the open.”

They don't want to stay in the hallway

Many are older and recovering from hip and knee replacements or major gastrointestinal surgery.

People can spend as little as a few hours in a hallway, to a week or longer, their entire stay. People can be moved into hallways as soon as they’re past the critical time needed to recover from the anesthesia and are mobile — meaning able to walk to the hallway bathroom.

The phenomenon is a Band-Aid solution to ER overcrowding, a post-COVID surge in surgeries and nursing shortages that limit the number of “staffed” beds, the researchers said.

Moving patients needing surgery out of emergency and into hallways upstairs improves “patient flow” by freeing up stretchers in swamped emergency rooms that have no empty beds for new arrivals.

Meanwhile, surgeries are increasing,up 10 per cent in 2025-2026 compared to 2019-2020, and even higher (22 per cent) among adults aged 65 and older, according to the Canadian Institute for Health Information.

“But just moving a person into a hallway or an ‘unconventional space’ is not creating capacity,” McPherson said. “It’s just loading (staff) up with extra patients and it puts patients at risk.

“It’s not a good story for people who are living those realities.”

From the nurses’ perspectives, “providing care to patients in the corridors of their units was demoralizing and misaligned with their professional values,” Ruddy and her co-authors wrote.

Not having the usual bedside whiteboards in patient rooms to update status and care plans didn’t help. “Sometimes doctors don’t know where the patient is at all,” another remarked.

“Although there was an implicit assumption that only patients who were medically stable would be put in hallways, most participants stated that there were no explicit guidelines and decisions were not always consistent or with clear reasoning,” the researchers said.

Bed managers “just show up and we say where is this patient going to go? Then it’s like, ‘Oh, I realize he’s going to the hallway,'” one nurse said.

Nurses said that, before the COVID pandemic, “placing patients in hallways rarely happened,” the researchers wrote.

“It was viewed as a last resort, occurring once or twice a year during periods of high demand (like a bad flu season) and, for some, not regarded as a viable option at all.”

“When I started nursing 11 years ago, there was no space for extra patients outside their rooms,” one nurse said. Hallway health care wasn’t even on the table, she said.

The study has limitations, including a small sample size — nine nurses — working in one province. However, the nurses were working across the province, in different-sized hospitals. And nurses often don’t like to speak out for fear about job security.

Their experiences also reflect the sheer scale of hallway medicine, the researchers said: According to Ontario health ministry data, roughly 1,435 admitted patients, ON average, per day, were receiving care in a hallway or other “unconventional space” in March 2024.

By January 2025, an average of 2,088 people per day were being cared for in unconventional spaces, the highest since officials began tracking the number in 2017, The Trilliumreported.

In a larger study on hallway medicine published earlier this year, researchers analyzed 913 hallway stays involving 824 patients on six general internal medicine wards in an Alberta hospital.

Patient complaints and survey responses “revealed a lack of empathy, privacy, space, confidentiality, access to basic needs, dissatisfaction with bed location and expressions of gratitude for care,” the researchers reported.

Sharon Kirkey is a national reporter with National Post focusing on health and science stories. She is also a three-time National Newspaper Awards nominee, with a win for beat reporting.

In a larger study on hallway medicine published earlier this year, researchers analyzed 913 hallway stays involving 824 patients on six general internal medicine wards in an Alberta hospital.

content_blocks.text: It used to be rare for a recuperating surgery patient to find themselves forced out of their hospital room and into a chaotic hallway to make space for someone else.
But amid a chronic shortage of hospital beds in Canada, desperate measures are becoming the norm.

Hallway health care — normally associated with gridlocked emergency rooms and “harrowing accounts” of people languishing for hours while waiting for care — is steadily creeping into other parts of the hospital, according to a new study based on the experiences of nurses.
Nurses working in nine Ontario inpatient surgical units shared their realities of caring for people with surgical wounds, drains and other complex post-op needs in cramped, noisy hallway spaces.

Nurses described unsafe nurse-to-patient ratios, scant to no privacy for patients, worries over increased risks for wound infections and moral distress and burnout over not being able to give patients the care they deserve while still being expected to “make it work.”

Making it work meant not having access to equipment normally found in patient rooms, such as suction and in-wall oxygen. It meant improvising with heavy portable oxygen tanks that require close monitoring to make sure they don’t run out. It meant struggling with the “moral weight” of changing wound dressings and inserting catheters in essentially “thoroughfares that are not designed for this provision of care,” said senior author Christine McPherson, an associate professor of nursing at the University of Ottawa.
Makeshift curtains or screens didn’t stop sensitive conversations from being overheard, or keep people from feeling exposed and vulnerable, she and her co-authors said.

“You May be talking about end-of-life care, you May be talking about very private personal information…. This is all going on in a hallway where there are people wandering around,” said McPherson, who oversaw the research.
It’s a hidden problem most people May not appreciate unless they’ve lived it themselves, she said. “It’s crept in, more and more.”
Some nurses recounted “incidents of harm and near misses,” including a patient who suffered a head injury and concussion after a painting fell off the hallway wall.

“One key source of relational strain came from having to deliver news that a patient would be moved into the hallway,” even though the decision was beyond the nurses’ control, the researchers wrote in the Canadian Journal of Nursing Research. The tension was made worse when outraged patients, or their families, refused to be moved.
“What message does it send to people? It sends the message, ‘We don’t really care, we’re just going to move you into the hallway,'” McPherson said.
“You’ve had your surgery; you’re at increased risk of post-surgical complications, but you’re going to be moved into the hallway now. It’s just totally unacceptable.”
Zoe Ruddy, a surgical nurse who led the research as part of her master’s thesis in nursing, has seen 20 to 30 hallway patients in any given month.
Some discharged themselves home.
“They don’t want to stay in the hallway,” she said. “It’s just too much, especially when you’re sick already and being moved out into the open.”
They don't want to stay in the hallway
Many are older and recovering from hip and knee replacements or major gastrointestinal surgery.

People can spend as little as a few hours in a hallway, to a week or longer, their entire stay. People can be moved into hallways as soon as they’re past the critical time needed to recover from the anesthesia and are mobile — meaning able to walk to the hallway bathroom.
The phenomenon is a Band-Aid solution to ER overcrowding, a post-COVID surge in surgeries and nursing shortages that limit the number of “staffed” beds, the researchers said.
Moving patients needing surgery out of emergency and into hallways upstairs improves “patient flow” by freeing up stretchers in swamped emergency rooms that have no empty beds for new arrivals.

Meanwhile, surgeries are increasing,up 10 per cent in 2025-2026 compared to 2019-2020, and even higher (22 per cent) among adults aged 65 and older, according to the Canadian Institute for Health Information.
“But just moving a person into a hallway or an ‘unconventional space’ is not creating capacity,” McPherson said. “It’s just loading (staff) up with extra patients and it puts patients at risk.
“It’s not a good story for people who are living those realities.”
From the nurses’ perspectives, “providing care to patients in the corridors of their units was demoralizing and misaligned with their professional values,” Ruddy and her co-authors wrote.
Not having the usual bedside whiteboards in patient rooms to update status and care plans didn’t help. “Sometimes doctors don’t know where the patient is at all,” another remarked.

“Although there was an implicit assumption that only patients who were medically stable would be put in hallways, most participants stated that there were no explicit guidelines and decisions were not always consistent or with clear reasoning,” the researchers said.
Bed managers “just show up and we say where is this patient going to go? Then it’s like, ‘Oh, I realize he’s going to the hallway,'” one nurse said.

Nurses said that, before the COVID pandemic, “placing patients in hallways rarely happened,” the researchers wrote.
“It was viewed as a last resort, occurring once or twice a year during periods of high demand (like a bad flu season) and, for some, not regarded as a viable option at all.”
“When I started nursing 11 years ago, there was no space for extra patients outside their rooms,” one nurse said. Hallway health care wasn’t even on the table, she said.

The study has limitations, including a small sample size — nine nurses — working in one province. However, the nurses were working across the province, in different-sized hospitals. And nurses often don’t like to speak out for fear about job security.

Their experiences also reflect the sheer scale of hallway medicine, the researchers said: According to Ontario health ministry data, roughly 1,435 admitted patients, ON average, per day, were receiving care in a hallway or other “unconventional space” in March 2024.

stories.title: Sunny stretch continues after another foggy start
stories.summary: Another foggy morning on tap for Londoners, but sunshine will break through again with the high today back in the double digits.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Another foggy morning on tap for Londoners, but sunshine will break through again with the high today back in the double digits.

“Beautiful conditions. Sunshine will carry us right through the afternoon. The high today, 12 degrees,” said CTV News London Meteorologist Julie Atchison.

And the nice weather doesn’t end today, Atchison says.

“Thursday, full sunshine. Friday, another full sunny day. This is an incredible stretch of weather for this time of year,” she explained. “We are under the influence of high pressure at the surface and in the upper atmosphere that promotes lots of stability and beautiful weather.”

The next opportunity for any rain in our region isn’t until Sunday.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast

Wednesday: Sunny. Wind becoming southwest 20 km/h in the morning. High 12. UV index 2 or low.

Wednesday night: Clear. Low plus 3.

Thursday: Sunny. High 13.

Friday: Sunny. High 14.

Saturday: Sunny. High 13.

Sunday: Cloudy with 40 per cent chance of showers. High 9.
