stories.title: Canadian judge on International Criminal Court speaks out against Trump attacks
stories.summary: U.S. says it wants to dismantle ICC ‘brick by brick’
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
On a hot summer night in 1998, Kimberly Prost was in Rome as part of Canada’s delegation at a United Nations diplomatic conference, where countries had gathered to create a global tribunal to bring people to justice for genocide and war crimes. Success was uncertain. The clock had ticked well past midnight when the large auditorium erupted in applause: A 120-7 vote established the International Criminal Court.

Two decades later, after a range of work in international justice, she felt a frisson of nerves at UN headquarters in New York before she was elected as a judge to the ICC in The Hague.

It was the culmination, and a new beginning, of a life’s work. Last year, it turned upside down.

Early in 2025, shortly after his second inauguration, President Donald Trump imposed sanctions on the court by executive order, alleging illegitimate investigations of Americans and Israelis. That August, the U.S. designated Judge Prost under the financial restrictions.

It catapulted her life into chaos. One company immediately cancelled a credit card. Amazon e-mailed to say her accounts had been closed. Her Alexa stopped speaking with her. Navigating the modern world now requires constant savvy and the occasional cajoling of hotel clerks, alongside a few debit cards and a ready stack of cash.

“The whole point is not woe is me,” Judge Prost said in a recent interview.

“It’s just such a shocking attack on the independence of the judiciary. We will never be intimidated. We’re not going to break.”

She and fellow ICC judges are speaking out to stand up for the institution they helped build, one under a sustained assault from the U.S. President, even as he is politically weakened after the Democrats’ demolition of Republicans in the midterm elections this month.

Mr. Trump’s administration has clearly stated its goal: to dismantle the ICC. The court came into official existence in 2002, but the U.S. has never been a state party to the Rome Statute that established the ICC, having first voted against it in 1998 under Bill Clinton alongside countries including China, Israel and Libya.

In October, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated the country’s goal of taking down the court “brick by brick” as he announced further sanctions that seek to paralyze the court’s operations.

Judge Prost is among more than a dozen judges and court officials under the U.S. sanctions. She and two other judges, as well as civil-society groups, are taking on the President and his administration in a U.S. federal trial court, arguing the sanctions are unlawful.

“This is the moment when this attack has to be countered, in my view,” said Judge Prost, a 68-year-old Winnipegger whose nine-year term on the court ends in March.

One message she is trying to broadcast is that the sanctions are binding only on U.S. companies: Non-U.S. companies need to be convinced that they don’t have to comply.

“They have to be aware that if they choose to comply voluntarily, they are complicit in threatening the International Criminal Court and the judges,” she said.

In early October, South African jurist Navi Pillay, an ICC judge in its formative years who previously battled apartheid, won the Nobel Peace Prize. The award was widely viewed as a response from the Norwegian Nobel Committee to Mr. Trump’s attacks on international courts and judges. Mr. Trump also covets the prize.

Hours later, Mr. Rubio escalated the U.S. pressure on the “rogue court.” He announced a widening of U.S. financial sanctions on the Icc’s operations, set for next spring and aimed at “crippling its ability” to conduct its work. The court’s banking, technology and insurance are all in peril.

The same day, foreign ministers of nine countries – Australia, Britain, Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, and the Netherlands – issued a statement of “continuing and unwavering” support for the ICC. “We regret and strongly disagree” with the sanctions, they said.

They also noted a key meeting starting Nov. 30: the 25 th session of the Assembly of States Parties to the ICC, a gathering relocated to The Hague from the UN in New York because of the sanctions.

In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada’s support for the ICC is “unequivocal” and that Ottawa would “provide support as needed” for Judge Prost.

In a mid-October statement, Global Affairs Canada cited “privacy considerations and ongoing legal proceedings” in response to questions from The Globe and Mail about supporting Judge Prost.

Judge Prost said there is work happening behind the scenes to try to mitigate the effects of the sanctions on her. Foreign Minister Anita Anand called her when the sanctions first hit her and again in October, when the U.S. threatened sanctions on court operations.

Federal government officials have helped in talks with industry and banks.

“They’re dealing with a very complicated situation,” Judge Prost said of Ottawa, as it takes on the capricious President amid a trade war and myriad other issues.

Allan Rock, Canada’s ambassador to the UN in the mid-2000s, remembered working with Judge Prost when he was federal justice minister in the mid-1990s. “We’re proud of her,” he said in an interview. “She’s a distinguished judge.”

Mr. Rock has spoken out about Canada doing more to “express disapproval of the vindictive, lawless and crude sanctions” but he also said the federal government faces exceptional circumstances in its relations with Mr. Trump.

“We’re dealing with a man who can lash back in a vindictive way,” Mr. Rock said. “It’s a fine balance. I’m reluctant to be critical. I hope we can find a way to express support for the various legal proceedings attacking the validity of the sanctions.”

At the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, the case filed by Judge Prost and two other ICC judges – Solomy Balungi Bossa of Uganda and Reine Alapini-Gansou of Benin – argues that Mr. Trump exceeded his authority and violated the U.S. Constitution in his imposition of sanctions that are “tantamount to the financial death penalty.”

In response, the U.S. government called on the court to dismiss the case and said Mr. Trump’s executive order is “squarely within the broad powers” Congress granted the President “to address foreign threats to national security.”

The U.S. has said it encircled Judge Prost with sanctions because she took actions to authorize the Icc’s investigation of U.S. personnel in Afghanistan. This relates to a broad early-stage case she was a part of in 2020. The next year, the ICC effectively shelved the potential U.S. aspect of that case.

Judge Prost’s career, after law school at the University of Manitoba, began as a federal prosecutor in the mid-1980s in Winnipeg before she joined a new war crimes group at the Justice Department in Ottawa. In Rome in 1998, she recalled the seeming unlikeliness of the proposed court being embraced by enough countries to make it a reality.

“No one in that room knew whether we were going to be successful,” she said.

Judge Prost is Canada’s second judge on the court, following Philippe Kirsch in the Icc’s early years.

What will happen with the sanctions after her term ends in March is unclear. Day-to-day life remains an obstacle course. She recalled checking in to a hotel in Ottawa, which required a credit card. She only has debit. The clerk insisted on a credit card. Judge Prost blurted out: “The President of the United States has sanctioned me, and I no longer have a credit card.” The stunned clerk was taken aback.

The clerk Googled her and spoke with her manager, and the judge was allowed to pay with debit.

“It’s such an absurd story,” Judge Prost said.

“You never really get used to it. You get more accustomed to it.”

stories.title: Omers teams up to bid on Toronto project to build underwater electricity transmission line
stories.summary: The pension plan and Transmission Developers Infrastructure are hoping to build the Third Line, from the Darlington nuclear plant to the Port Lands
stories.author: James Bradshaw
stories.content:
The Omers pension plan and Blackstone Inc.-owned Transmission Developers Infrastructure are preparing a joint bid to build and operate an underwater electricity connection linking Toronto to an expanded nuclear plant east of the city.

Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System and the Canadian arm of New York-based TDI plan to bid on the Toronto Third Line, a project the Ontario government approved in January to meet an anticipated surge in demand for electricity in Toronto and make its energy grid more reliable.

The bid also has backing from Kilmer Group, the investment firm owned by Canadian businessman Larry Tanenbaum, who was formerly a part-owner of the parent company of the Toronto Maple Leafs and Toronto Raptors.

The 65-kilometre Third Line would be Ontario’s first underwater transmission line. It would lay a high voltage direct current (Hvdc) cable along the bottom of Lake Ontario from the Darlington Nuclear Generating Station in Clarington to a terminal in Toronto’s Port Lands district.

Initial engineering estimates put the project’s cost at $1.5-billion, with a potential range of $750-million to $3-billion, and it should take seven to 10 years to complete. Ontario’s independent energy authority is expected to launch a competitive procurement process to collect bids in mid-2027.

“The Toronto Third Line represents an opportunity to invest in essential infrastructure designed to support Toronto’s growing electricity demand and long-term system reliability that will serve Ontario communities for generations while delivering long-term value for Omers members,” the pension plan’s global head of infrastructure, Michael Hill, said in a statement.

Omers is Canada’s seventh-largest pension plan, managing $152-billion for 665,000 public-service workers, including nurses, firefighters and police officers.

In April, chief executive officer Blake Hutcheson said Omers will add at least $10-billion in new domestic investments over five years − the first of several similar pledges by Canada’s major pension funds to invest more at home.

Pension fund CEOs have said the climate for investing in Canada is improving in step with a drive by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government to launch major projects across the country. But major funds have also faced pressure from politicians and business leaders to add to their domestic portfolios.

TDI is the developer behind the 545-kilometre Champlain Hudson Power Express, completed in June, which connects Quebec’s hydroelectricity system to New York City via North America’s longest underground transmission link.

The company, which is owned by Blackstone, an investment manager with US$1.4-trillion in assets, said in a news release that the converter station that will need to be built in the Port Lands presents similar construction and engineering challenges to the station in Queens that serves the Champlain transmission line.

“Our team brings recent, directly relevant experience to the challenges of building underwater transmission and connecting to a major urban centre,” TDI chairman Brian Kubeck said in a statement.

In Depth: Ontario spent nearly $13-billion and 20 years refurbishing the Darlington nuclear station. Why has it struggled?

St. John’s-based Fortis Inc. and British-based National Grid Ventures also plan to bid on the Third Line project.

The Third Line could prove to be a key piece of infrastructure in the province’s broader plans to expand its supply of nuclear energy.

A plan to build four small modular reactors (SMR) at Darlington, the site of larger reactors built in the 1980s and nineties, was one of the first projects referred to the Major Projects Office that Ottawa set up last year to shepherd initiatives deemed to be of national importance.

It could also be a test of Ottawa’s efforts to approve and build large-scale projects more quickly − and shake off a reputation for regulatory headaches and project delays that has made global investors wary about committing money to Canada.

Construction on the first Darlington SMR started last year, and the project is already facing delays and cost overruns after an engineering setback. But Energy Minister Tim Hodgson has brushed off the issues as “a reality in all first-of-a-kind projects.”

The US$6-billion Chpe linking Quebec to New York finished construction in four years, and TDI said in a statement that it delivered the project on time and on budget. But the transmission line took 16 years to complete from conception, in part because of permitting, consultation and regulatory issues.

At the Canada Investment Summit in September, Blackstone president and chief operating officer Jon Gray cited the timeline of the Chpe project as an example of how “well-intended” regulations can bog down projects. But he was one of several influential CEOs who signalled that Canada’s investment environment is starting to look more appealing.

Blackstone recently announced several deals in Canada, including a US$3.1-billion transaction with four major Canadian pension funds in early November to invest in LNG Canada’s liquefied natural gas business.

stories.title: Large majority ‘concerned’ about Carney’s hiked immigration targets: poll
stories.summary: For 2027, the government plans to allow up to 200,000 people who are already in Canada on a temporary basis to become permanent residents
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
For 2027, the government plans to allow up to 200,000 people who are already in Canada on a temporary basis to become permanent residents

stories.title: Canada's Alert Ready system to be tested across the country Wednesday
stories.summary: Canadians across the country can expect to hear the shrill screeching sound of Canada’s emergency alerting system today.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canadians across the country can expect to hear the shrill screeching sound of Canada’s emergency alerting system today.

Pelmorex, which operates the Alert Ready system, says a test message and tone will be broadcast on television, radio and compatible wireless devices.

It says test messages will be issued in every province and territory at specific times between morning and early afternoon.

The system is usually tested in May and November and is part of Canada’s effort to ensure it works and raises awareness.

There is no option to opt out of the test or actual emergency alerts.

The Alert Ready system issued 1,215 alerts in Canada as of Oct. 31, for emergencies including Amber Alerts, tornadoes and thunderstorms.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

Aaron Sousa, The Canadian Press

stories.title: What 'Godzilla El Niño' means for Toronto snowfall and the prospect of a white Christmas
stories.summary: El Niño is expected to delay winter for the city and much of the province, semi-retired Environment Canada climatologist David Phillips said.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
A “Godzilla El Niño” is expected to delay winter for Toronto and much of the province, semi-retired Environment Canada climatologist David Phillips said.

Popular ski resort Mount St. Louis Moonstone, however, said they’re not panicking yet.

El Niño is a natural phenomenon, not caused by people, “but the oceans have never been hotter than they are now,” Phillips said.

The waters in the equatorial Pacific Ocean, off the coast of Ecuador and Peru, May be thousands of miles away from Toronto, but have a “profound” effect on global weather patterns, said Phillips.

“What I think is interesting about this El Niño is that it’s supersized and the largest in terms of strength ever seen,” said Phillips.

To meet El Niño standards, the water off the coast of South America has to be about a half a degree warmer than normal for three months in a row, said Phillips, but forecasts suggest that the temperature will continue to rise into December.

“Four degrees is like a different world, it’s like a hot tub out there … by the time it ends, it’ll probably be 4.5 degrees warmer than normal,” said Phillips. “So that’s why calling it super El Niño or Godzilla El Niño, is not really an exaggeration because it’s a different category. It’s almost like a different world in terms of this one.”

Mount St. Louis Moonstone, a ski hill north of Barrie hasn’t opened yet, but general manager Robert Huter said it’s “business as usual” for now.

They’ve hired about 60 staff and are inspecting their lifts ahead of opening, he said.

“Nothing has changed other than we’re not wearing a jacket yet. It’s a little bit warmer out there, but we’re still preparing for ski season, it’s coming,” said Huter.

Last season, the slopes opened between the last week of November and Dec. 2, and Huter expects similar timing this year. A few winters ago, they didn’t open until Dec. 23, he added.

About 100 to 120 days of skiing are expected this winter.

“We can make large amounts of snow in shorter windows,” he said.

“We will have something for people to slide on sometime in December for sure,” said Huter of the ski hill that has 36 runs with the longest being a two-kilometre trail.

The El Niño doesn’t mean that Canada is going to have a winter without cold temperatures or snow, said Phillips. There could be more rain and temperatures might not be as frigid, he added.

“We’re gonna get through November without a flake of snow appearing. I mean the next week looks ideal. It’s sunny, it’s warm,” Phillips said. “People are still raking (leaves) because the leaves have stayed in the trees, there haven’t been any wind storms.”

For the ones who don’t like winter, this might be good news, but recreation tourists and ski buffs might be “sitting this one out,” he added.

stories.title: How an Alberta farm kid became a global opera star — and why he’s bringing his work back to Toronto
stories.summary: Pulitzer winner Royce Vavrek talks Atom Egoyan, his Metropolitan Opera debut and staging ‘Dog Days.’
stories.author: Glenn Sumi
stories.content:
When librettist Royce Vavrek was growing up on a grain farm near Grande Prairie, Alberta, he remembers getting up one winter morning at 6:30 a.m. to listen to the 1998 Oscar nominations.

Ever since reading a Cannes Festival review of Atom Egoyan’s “The Sweet Hereafter,” he’d been obsessed with the movie. He checked out Russell Banks’ novel from the library and waited until the VHS tape of the film made it to Blockbuster Video. And then came the Oscar announcements.

“A friend in town had cable and so I listened to her TV through my phone,” he said. “When Egoyan’s name was announced in two categories, I screamed. I realized that you could be a Canadian artist and have an international career. It just blew my mind.”

Now Vavrek himself is blowing minds as a Canadian artist with a thriving international career.

In 2017, “Angel’s Bone,” his opera with composer Dun Yu, won the Pulitzer Prize in Music. Last month, he stood onstage at New York’s Metropolitan Opera for the glittering, star-studded premiere of “Lincoln in the Bardo,” his new opera (based on George Saunders’ Booker-winning novel), with composer and frequent collaborator Missy Mazzoli.

Vavrek says pop music, film, visual arts and dance all inform his approach to writing opera.

The kicker? He’s now friends with Egoyan after consulting with him on an opera based on his 2008 film “Adoration.”

“He’s been integral to my life as an artist,” said Vavrek, ON a recent Zoom call. “Without Atom even knowing it, he gave me permission to do what I’m doing.”

This month, the Brooklyn-based Vavrek is back in Toronto, revisiting his breakthrough work, “Dog Days,” a darkly funny chamber opera (with a score by David T. Little) about a family struggling to survive in a post-apocalyptic world where a mysterious stranger dressed as a dog turns their lives upside down.

It’s a co-production between Against the Grain Theatre, where Vavrek is artistic director, and Tapestry Opera, two indie companies that punch way above their respective weight classes. (Tapestry’s Michael Hidetoshi Mori is directing this revival.)

“Back in 2012, when the opera premiered, it felt really gnarly — in a good way — to be wrestling with contemporary politics,” said Vavrek about the piece. Among other things, the opera deals with issues like food shortages and societal breakdown.

“It feels as vital today as it did back then,” he said. “David’s music is informed by musical theatre, heavy metal rock and pop. The musical language and text seem to be in direct dialogue with what we’re living through right now.”

Vavrek, along with his composer collaborators like Little, Mazzoli and Paola Prestini, has been championed as a rock star in the world of contemporary opera.

“Missy talks a lot about how she grew up on MTV music videos, David sang and danced in classic musicals like ‘Oklahoma’ when he was younger, and I trained in musical theatre and film,” said Vavrek.

“We come with musical theatre and pop music as connection points. Even though we work outside pop music, we don’t live in a bubble. We take inspiration from pop music, visual arts, film and dance. Opera is this magical place where all these can converge.”

Vavrek hopes to create more Canadian operas, including a possible adaptation of “Anne of Green Gables.”

Vavrek is especially excited about all the recent initiatives to make opera accessible and open to audiences of all ages and income brackets.

Two years ago, Mazzoli and Vavrek’s opera “The Listeners,” based on a Jordan Tannahill story (later developed into a novel), launched Opera Philadelphia’s groundbreaking “Pick Your Price” program, under which any seat in the house could be had for as little as $11.

In September, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced his “Opera for All” program, guaranteeing 70,000 free tickets for New York City residents during the 2026–27 season. Eligible residents must never have attended a performance at the Met and must not have purchased a ticket since 2019. The day before Vavrek and I talked, the Met’s Peter Gelb announced that “Lincoln in the Bardo” would be available to stream on YouTube for one day.

“There’s this perception that opera is very expensive, or exclusive, and also that the stories in opera don’t connect with people’s lives,” said Vavrek. “None of that is true now.”

The librettist, who admits one day he would like to work on a musical theatre project, has lots of exciting projects for 2029-30, but they’re still being finalized so he can’t discuss them.

This spring, he’s premiering “Red Fox,” his follow-up with Du Yun for the Dutch National Opera, which deals with dementia. A month later, he and composer Matthew Ricketts are premiering “The Cremation of Sam McGee,” a Canadian chamber opera based on a Robert W. Service poem set during the Yukon gold rush, at City Opera Vancouver.

A planned opera based on Thomas King’s book “Indians on Vacation” was paused after it was revealed that King had no Indigenous ancestry. But earlier this year, many of the artistic team — including Métis and French Canadian composer Ian Cusson — took part in “Stories Don’t Die,” a night of excerpts and personal reflections on belonging, identity and authenticity.

Vavrek is excited to create more Canadian operas, including one based on the beloved “Anne of Green Gables.”

“Composer Luna Pearl Woolf and I are wondering what it would mean to write the definite ‘Anne’ opera,” he said. “It’s the first story I ever read. My mom gave me the book, and I’ve always wondered what it would be like as an opera.”

stories.title: Carney says Canada’s growing trade ties with China are not a top concern for Trump
stories.summary: Shenzhen, China (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Wednesday said that Canada ’s growing trade relations with China are not a top priority for U.S. President Donald Trump, pointing out that Canada primarily exports commodities to China rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Shenzhen, China (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Wednesday said that Canada ’s growing trade relations with China are not a top priority for U.S. President Donald Trump , pointing out that Canada primarily exports commodities to China rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.

“In my conversation with the president, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen, ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”

Carney’s comments came amid criticism from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro over Canada’s willingness to pursue closer economic relations with Beijing, including potentially bringing Chinese automakers to Canada.

Canada and the U.S. have one of the world’s largest trading relationships, but Trump’s tariffs have strained ties and pushed Ottawa to seek other markets . After negotiations collapsed in August, Washington imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting retaliation from Ottawa.

Carney said he plans to meet with Trump later Wednesday, after the U.S. president arrives in Shenzhen, where they are expected to discuss bilateral trade.

“We have been making progress,” Carney said on getting a deal with the U.S. But a deal, he added, “that is in the interest of Canadians.”

Carney has said in recent days that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.

On Tuesday, ahead of the Apec summit, Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and both agreed on additional tariff cuts .

Under the agreement, China will provide additional tariff relief on Canadian exports worth around 400 million Canadian dollars ($280 million), including frozen pork cuts, fish and seafood.

In return, Canada will extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.

Carney said Canada’s trade relationship with China is fundamentally different from the much larger and more complex U.S.-China relationship.

“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said, also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semiconductors.”

Navarro criticized Carney on Monday after the Canadian leader suggested Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with Washington fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme,” Navarro wrote on X. “You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive.”

Associated Press writer Rob Gillies in Toronto contributed to this report.

E. Eduardo Castillo, The Associated Press

stories.title: Canada’s Whitney Peak calls ‘Hunger Games’ role ‘too big to wrap my head around’
stories.summary: Toronto — When Whitney Peak moved to the Vancouver area when she was about 10 years old, the first friend she made was obsessed with "The Hunger Games."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — When Whitney Peak moved to the Vancouver area when she was about 10 years old, the first friend she made was obsessed with “The Hunger Games.”

“We watched the movie and she kind of put me onto it, and that was sort of my introduction to the world,” Peak says.

Now, Peak is part of that world.

The 23-year-old Ugandan-Canadian actress stars as Lenore Dove in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” the latest instalment in the dystopian mega-franchise.

The film, based on the novel of the same name, is a prequel to the original “Hunger Games” series of three books and four movies.

It follows a teenage Haymitch (better known as Katniss’s boozehound mentor in the original series) when he is chosen as a tribute and thrust into the Hunger Games, a tournament where young people are forced to battle-to-the-death in front of TV cameras. Lenore Dove is Haymitch’s girlfriend back home in impoverished District 12 — his motivation for surviving the brutal battle.

Her hope for a different future is a spark that Katniss fans into flames later in Haymitch’s life, making Lenore Dove a pivotal figure in the broader story.

That — and the career boost likely to come from her part in the film — hasn’t quite sunk in for Peak.

The original series was a launch pad for stars including Jennifer Lawrence, Amandla Stenberg, Liam Hemsworth and Sam Claflin.

“It doesn’t compute really,” Peak says. “It’s obviously such a great experience to be a part of it now, but I don’t know, it’s just too big of an idea for me to really wrap my head around, but it’s really exciting.”

It’s partway through a jam-packed press day in Toronto and Peak is antsy, bouncing up and down on a couch beside the film’s director, Francis Lawrence.

Here, Lawrence cuts in.

“I think sometimes when people join (the franchise) … you’re in this weird little bubble when you make the movies, and sometimes it’s not until you’re in Times Square and you see a billboard for it (that) it starts to sink in.”

He says that moment came for him when he was walking through the Hunger Games exhibition that toured following the release of the final film in the original series, “The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2.”

The exhibition ended up in Las Vegas, where it remained open for seven years.

“You realize like the impact that the series has had on people that it’s deserving of a museum with pieces of sets and costumes and props and the music,” says Lawrence, who joined the franchise for its second instalment, “Catching Fire.”

Many of the characters from the original series also appear in this film — Haymitch, originally played by Woody Harrelson, is portrayed by Australian actor Joseph Zada in “Sunrise on the Reaping”; Elle Fanning reimagines the character of Effie Trinket, who was first played by Elizabeth Banks.

“You can never get rid of the fact that Stanley Tucci has done a Caesar before; Donald Sutherland has done (President) Snow before,” Lawrence says.

Ralph Fiennes takes on the role of Snow in this film, and Lawrence uses him as an example. He didn’t want Fiennes to “act like Donald Sutherland.”

“What we start to do is just break down who President Snow is. What does he believe in? … How does he use power? How intelligent is he? How sophisticated is he?” Lawrence says.

“You just start to talk about those elements specifically as opposed to looking at Donald’s performance and saying, how can we get as close as possible to Donald’s performance?”

Peak says she had similar conversations with Lawrence about Lenore Dove, but without the spectre of other actors’ performances hanging over her.

“I was more looking to the book to guide me whenever I was feeling lost,” she says. “We would have conversations about what we wanted the shape of Haymitch and Lenore Dove to be, and who she was outside of their relationship as well.”

With the film coming out in theatres Friday, Peak is excited to have those same talks with her loved ones.

“I’m looking forward to seeing my friends watch it, and we’re going to have these conversations. I’m curious to see what each one takes away from it, and what is the thing that they’re going talk to me about first in terms of the movie and what ideas really stuck with them.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

Nicole Thompson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Can advocates elected to Toronto council help fix housing and homelessness crisis?
stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto's newly elected council includes several prominent tenant and housing rights activists and advocates for the city's homeless population who say they will bring the kind of first-hand outreach experience to the table that council needs.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
flag wire: true flag sponsored: false article_type: pubinfo.section: cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star bHasMigratedAvatar : false firstAuthor.avatar :

By Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press

Toronto - Toronto’s newly elected council includes several prominent tenant and housing rights activists and advocates for the city’s homeless population who say they will bring the kind of first-hand outreach experience to the table that council needs.

While some observers aren’t sure that advocates-turned-councillors can significantly change the direction of Toronto’s housing and homelessness policies, the rookie members say they have the political will to use their advocacy expertise to help address the city’s affordability crisis.

Diana Chan McNally, a longtime outreach worker who is now representing Parkdale-High Park in the city’s west end, said while she has a list of other priorities, such as improving public transit and ensuring the waterfront remains accessible and environmentally sound in her ward, she is committed to do what she did as an advocate in her new municipal decision-making role.

“I worked for 12 years with people on the streets and you learn very quickly that (homelessness) has nothing to do with the individual and it has everything to do with things like affordability, access to health care,” she said.

“So, (I’m) very interested in continuing this work, very interested in making sure that we have a platform and pathway, essentially, for people to have their voice heard and also for policies to actually reflect their needs.”

The current term of the housing rights advisory committee, established by city council in 2023, is ending this month and McNally, who was a member of the committee, said she is hoping to bring it back.

“I think this is a great space in which we can continue to push forward, ensuring that people’s rights, for those who are out on the street who don’t own property, are actually taken care of,” she said.

Chiara Padovani, a tenants’ organizer, is another well-known activist who secured a victory after unseating longtime councillor Frances Nunziata in York South-Weston in last month’s municipal election. She said that she will also continue advocating for tenants.

Cristine de Clercy, a political scientist who teaches at Trent University, said it is easier for activists to criticize lawmakers and offer policy ideas as outsiders. Once they become part of the government, they need to learn to compromise and navigate internal dynamics to successfully work on their priorities, she said.

“The new councillors, it’s inevitably the case that because now they’re inside of machinery of government, they don’t have free rein to simply advocate willy-nilly for whatever policy,” she said.

McNally said she is aware that being a politician and being an advocate are two different roles and she needs to be pragmatic, but she is certain she won’t compromise her core progressive values, including housing rights.

“My goal is to make sure that, you know, people who used to be my colleagues are holding my feet to the fire, that the public is ensuring that I stay true to my own values,” she said.

Toronto’s homelessness and housing affordability crises have always been pressing issues at city hall in recent decades and they’ve escalated since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Officials at different levels of government have been discussing the problem, providing funding and taking actions, but critics have often said too little is done to help homeless people and struggling tenants in Canada’s largest city.

Padovani was among the advocates who helped tenants organize several rent strikes against what she called unfair landlords.

She said road safety and flood protection are two major issues in her ward that she will focus on, but she will also always fight for tenants’ rights.

“Tenant voices have been ignored by … so many in the city government,” she said. “And I’m really looking forward to making sure that if you’re a slumlord in my community, I’m going to be taking you to task and I’ll be holding you accountable.”

As a councillor, she said she will make sure the city enforces building standards more vigorously.

“What I want to do is start passing bylaws at the City of Toronto that puts the onus on the city to protect tenant rights and alleviate some of the pressure on tenants,” she said.

Padovani said she understands that residential tenancy rights are primarily governed by the province, but that doesn’t mean the city can’t do anything to protect renters against abusive landlords.

She praised Mayor Olivia Chow for leading the effort to pass the rental renovation licence bylaw, which makes renovictions — a tactic critics say is used by landlords to evade rent control and increase rent prices — more difficult.

Padovani said she will push council to pass a similar bylaw against rent increases above the provincial guideline, known as AGI, which have sparked several rent strikes in Toronto in recent years.

“I have a feeling this is going to be something that a lot of my colleagues are going to be interested in, in order to start to think creatively about how to make life more affordable for the half of the city that rent their home,” she said.

Nearly half of Toronto’s population rents their homes. That number is over 70 per cent in the densely populated Toronto Centre, according to Curran Stikuts, the ward’s new councillor who said the area is also home to many homeless shelters and overnight respite centres.

Stikuts, an advocate with more than 15 years of experience working with renters and marginalized communities in the area, including queer youth who are homeless, campaigned on housing affordability and was elected over incumbent Chris Moise.

Stikuts said fighting against renovictions and ensuring that buildings are kept up to standards and the city provides support for tenants are among the issues he wants to tackle on council. He said working with homeless people has taught him that “four walls and a roof” isn’t enough to solve the problem.

“It’s really, I think, about focusing on the ways in which we’re building not just the units and spaces, but the levels of supports and wraparound care that we need to make people stable and then get back on their feet,” he said.

Pointing to a report from the Financial Accountability Office of Ontario, Toronto said homelessness in Toronto has deceased by over eight per cent, while increasing by nearly 18 per cent provincewide, between 2022 and 2025.

Despite the progress, the city said it is still in a state of “homelessness emergency” caused by unaffordable housing, inadequate income support and unmet health needs.

The recently tabled federal budget includes nearly $30 billion toward the government’s goal to end homelessness across the country over the next decade, and Stikuts said while he was encouraged by the news, he would love to see some of that money flow to Toronto quicker to get “shovels in the ground.”

Greg Cook, an outreach team lead at Sanctuary Ministries of Toronto, said improving living conditions for homeless people hasn’t been a top priority for Chow during her first term.

“The city has said it’s a crisis, but they’re not treating it as such,” he said.

The mayor’s office, however, said she has been working hard to build more shelters and supportive housing, and invest in eviction prevention programs aimed at curbing homelessness.

It said the city has moved 15,000 people from shelters and encampments into permanent housing, including 4,700 people in 2025.

“Over the past two years, homelessness in Toronto declined, despite growing across the province. There is more work to do and the mayor has been committed to addressing it,” Chow’s spokesperson Braman Thillainathan wrote in a statement.

Cook said even though a progressive-leaning council has an opportunity to make some progress, they can’t do it alone.

“It will require a significant kind of community pressure, and I think there might be some councillors who are more willing to kind of stick their neck out and speak on behalf of people who are poor,” he said.

Asked if community advocates who are joining council for the first time could serve as allies for the homeless community in municipal government, Cook said: “I wouldn’t probably go that far. I think politicians are going to do what is going to keep them in power.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Carney says Canada's trade relations with U.S. 'much more complex' than with China
stories.summary: Shenzhen - Prime Minister Mark Carney says it's been easier for Ottawa to reach new trade arrangements with China than the United States because Canada's trade relations south of the border are "much more complex."
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Shenzhen - Prime Minister Mark Carney said a “very good trade arrangement” with the United States is possible but those talks are far more complex than the trade discussions Canada is having with China and other partners.

Canada won’t just sit around and wait for the U.S., he added.

“We would like to do the deal. But if the U.S. doesn’t want to do the deal, we’re busy,” Carney said, in an interview as part of the New York Times 2026 DealBook Summit.

He pointed to trade deals reached in recent days with the Association of Southeast Nations, or Asean, during a summit last weekend in the Philippines, as well as a deal with the Philippines itself. Canada is also expecting to sign a new trade deal with India in the next few months.

Carney was speaking remotely from Shenzhen, China, where he is attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, or Apec, and made the comment shortly after he met with U.S. President Donald Trump. He called that meeting a “nice discussion” but said a deal with the United States isn’t at the finish line.

“Look, it should have been done six months ago, but, we’re not going to sign something that doesn’t make sense for Canada,” Carney said.

On Tuesday in Shenzhen, Carney held a bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, his second such meeting in China this year, both of which resulted in a number of tariffs and other trade irritants being resolved, including those affecting Canadian canola, seafood and pork, and Chinese steel, aluminum and electric vehicles.

Carney has raised eyebrows in the United States for appearing to play the U.S. and China off each other, and criticism in Canada for suggesting China has been easier to work with. He continued that commentary in his DealBook interview Wednesday.

“I can report that the trade negotiations are going exceptionally well,” he said. “We reached an agreement, we reduced tariffs and over 90 per cent of trade irritants. And, of course, I’m speaking about our trade negotiations with China. They’re very professional. They moved forward in a very linear fashion. and it’s all very rational and moving forward.

“Now, if you’re asking about the United States, well, we continue to have a series of issues there. Look, there is a very, very good trade arrangement that is possible. We had an existing one under (the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement). There is one under the new trade policy that is possible, but we’re not yet there.”

The meeting with Trump was not on Carney’s public itinerary, but Carney’s office said the prime minister and president spoke for just under 20 minutes around dinnertime in Shenzhen.

“The leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create good jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty,” said a readout from Carney’s office.

“They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact.”

Carney’s office said the meeting included U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Trump’s chief of staff Stephen Miller and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Carney’s chief of staff Marc-André Blanchard and Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand were there on the Canadian side.

Anand told reporters in China that the meeting between Carney and Trump covered a number of topics on which the two sides are negotiating.

She said the relationship between Carney and Trump has been “continually present” through negotiations, describing it as productive and strong.

“This was their first in-person meeting for some time,” said Anand, adding the leaders speak on the phone regularly. “The fact that the conversation is continuous I think has been useful in order for our concerns to continue to be raised.”

Anand said there’s a transition happening in the United States following the U.S. midterm elections, calling it a “lame-duck Congress.”

“Canada is pursuing our own strategy,” she said. “That is to ensure we have multiple trading options. We are growing our relationships regardless of the results relating to the midterms and the electoral races that are to come.”

The diplomatic relationship between Canada and the U.S. has been rattled by Trump’s heavy tariffs and calls for Canada to become the 51st state. It became more tense when Carney’s government walked away from formal trade talks in August, and as Ottawa and Washington accused each other of pushing eleventh-hour changes.

In response to the collapse of trade talks, Washington imposed tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods. Ottawa then followed up with retaliatory tariffs on American products.

Shortly before the meeting, Carney told a news conference that he doesn’t believe Trump is uncomfortable with Canada expanding its trade relationship with China. He said Trump has sought to understand where Canada is going with its trade ties with China.

At that news conference Carney said it has been easier for Ottawa to secure new trade arrangements with China because Canada’s trade relations with the United States are “much more complex.”

“The United States fundamentally changed its trade objectives and we are focused on getting the right deal for Canadians,” he said.

He added that Canada is focused on exporting to China commodities such as iron and oil, rather than sensitive advanced technologies like superconductors.

Stephanie Kusie, the Conservative international trade critic, said Wednesday it’s “always concerning” to see the government engage with China, given its human rights record and previous tariffs on Canada.

She said it’s good that Canada is diversifying its trading relationships but she accused Carney of using that effort as a “distraction” from his failure to secure a deal with the United States.

Kusie said Canada has a “far more significant” relationship with the U.S. “through history and geography … and we should be leaning into that, not into a nation which does not promote democracy, human rights, the rule of law.”

Canada’s relationship with China is being rebuilt after it nearly disintegrated entirely over China’s arbitrary detention of two Canadians in retaliation for Canada arresting a Chinese telecom executive at the request of the United States. Canada’s accusations of Chinese interference in federal elections added to the diplomatic and trade tensions.

Carney began to restore the ties during a meeting with Xi at Apec in South Korea a year ago, and that continued at their meeting in Beijing in January.

He defended the move in the DealBook discussion on Wednesday, as part of Canada’s need to diversify its trade relationships so they are not so dependent on the United States, but also on any one partner at all.

“Deeper integration with one partner is a huge risk,” Carney said, referring to his economic diversification as “insurance.”

He said there are lessons from the recent experience with the United States — which he says fundamentally has changed its trade and foreign policies, including threats to annex Greenland and Canada. That lesson extends not just to trade but also to digital sovereignty, and Canada’s push to develop its own secure military communications, and not use Elon Musk’s Starlink. Ukraine has said restrictions imposed on Starlink there have impacted its ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.

“It would be simpler if we could just align just within the Western alliance that was there. And we could take first best technologies. But you know, you can’t go through Greenland. You can’t go through 51st state. You can’t go through Ukraine and Starlink and responsibly hold that assumption 100 per cent. And that is a very difficult and that’s a very difficult reality. But it is reality.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa, Aaron Sousa in Edmonton and The Associated Press

stories.title: Carney pitches proposed Pacific Link crude pipeline to business leaders at Asian summit
stories.summary: Prime Minister touts Canada as reliable energy and food source for Asian markets at Apec CEO summit
stories.author: Steven Chase
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney pitched an Asian business summit Wednesday on a proposed new oil pipeline in the West Coast that could feed growing Chinese demand for Canadian crude.

Mr. Carney promoted the Pacific Link pipeline project – which would move heavy crude oil from Alberta to a marine terminal in British Columbia – in his speech to business leaders at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO summit in Shenzhen, China. The event is running alongside the Apec leaders’ summit.

“We are advancing Pacific Link, a new pipeline to the Pacific that will carry an additional one million barrels a day to growing markets here in Asia, diversifying our trade and reinforcing Canada’s role as a reliable partner for energy for this region,” Mr. Carney said.

Crude oil exports to China hit $3.5-billion in the third quarter of 2026, up nearly 159 per cent over the same period a year earlier, according to the University of Alberta’s China Institute. Volumes of crude were up nearly double from the same 2025 period at about 327,000 barrels per day.

Much of this is due to the extra capacity provided by the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion – which flows oil from Edmonton to Burnaby, B.C. – that began operating in 2024.

Ottawa announced earlier this fall it would expedite the federal approval process for Pacific Link, a decision that is attracting legal challenges from numerous First Nations.

Mr. Carney’s decision to tout the proposed new oil pipeline at Apec suggests he is willing to spend political capital to see it built.

The Prime Minister pitched CEOs on how he’s clearing red tape from regulatory approvals for major resource and infrastructure projects in Canada.

The federal government, at the start of October, announced the national-interest designation for the Pacific Link pipeline. This plan provides Ottawa’s backing at the start of the process and will enable it to grant necessary and varied permits much more quickly than in the past. It also marked the first such move under the Building Canada Act, a centrepiece of Mr. Carney’s work to shift Canada’s economy away from the capricious whims of the U.S.

In his speech, the Prime Minister noted that for much of its history Canada looked to the U.S. and Europe for trading opportunities. But now, he said, it’s also looking to Asia.

He noted Canada’s recent transformation into an exporter of liquefied natural gas to Asia. “Two years ago, we had never shipped a major LNG cargo to Asia. Since LNG Canada’s first shipment in June 2025, we have now shipped more than 11 million tonnes,” Mr. Carney said.

“We will quadruple this by the end of the decade, and double it again in the next one.”

Mr. Carney noted that the port of Vancouver on the Pacific Ocean is already Canada’s largest port.

“Apec economies are already four of our five largest trading partners,” Mr. Carney said, referring to countries that are part of Apec.

“We are seizing more opportunities in this region. And we are just beginning to scratch the surface of our potential.”

He pitched Canada as a stable source of energy and food where the government is also slimming down regulatory approvals.

“That is what co-operation looks like in practice: less paperwork at the border, more reliable food on the shelves and the power to fuel tomorrow’s innovations,” he said.

With reports from David Ebner

Wednesday, November 18, 2026

On Friday, December 4, Londoners are invited to watch Victoria Park transform into a dazzling winter wonderland at the annual Lighting of the Lights. This year’s celebration will shine bright once again as more than 100,000 lights and festive displays illuminate the park with holiday magic.

The evening will kick off at 6 p.m. with live music, featuring Saveria, Eleanor Gebrou, Amanda Movio, and Immogen Wasse. Londoners can enjoy free hot chocolate, indulge in a variety of food truck offerings, capture a festive selfie at the 360° photo booth, and send their holiday wish list to the North Pole at Santa’s mailbox.

The highlight of the night is the magical moment when the park is illuminated with the ceremonial flip of the switch at approximately 6:50 p.m. This year, Mayor Josh Morgan will be joined by London-raised, Juno award-winning rapper Shad and Francesca Wright, Director of the Paul Seed Fund, to set the park aglow.

“The Lighting of the Lights is one of those special London traditions that everyone in our city looks forward to each holiday season,” said Mayor Josh Morgan. “Seeing Victoria Park come alive with thousands of lights, with people from across our city sharing the excitement, is our city at its best and brightest. I hope to see everyone for a great evening downtown enjoying the festivities and making memories together.”

The light displays bring the park to life, along with an array of festive favourites, including Santa and his reindeer, a Christmas train, and a cheerful snow family.

City Hall observation deck

The City Hall observation deck will open for public viewing of the Lighting of the Lights and the Winter Wonderland in Victoria Park during the following dates and times:

Friday, December 4 (Lighting of the Lights) from 5:30 to 9:00 p.m.

Saturday, December 5 and Sunday, December 6 from 5:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.

Thursday, December 10 to Sunday, December 13 from 5:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.

Thursday, December 17 to Sunday, December 20 from 5:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.

Thursday, December 24 (Christmas Eve) from 5:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.

Saturday, December 26 to Sunday, December 27 from 5:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.

Outdoor skating

The outdoor skating rink at Victoria Park will not be open for the Lighting of the Lights event. Weather permitting, the rink will open mid-December. More details about outdoor skating will be shared in the coming weeks.

Victoria Park washrooms

Starting December 4, access to the washrooms in Victoria Park will be available daily from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at the Kiwanis Memorial Bandshell throughout the holiday season. If the washrooms are locked during this time, contact a nearby security guard for assistance.

The holiday magic continues at Covent Garden Market

After the Lighting of the Lights, Londoners are encouraged to head over to Covent Garden Market for the official opening of the Holly Jolly Holiday Market.

Visitors can enjoy local artisans and food vendors, cozy fire pits, live music, and dazzling light displays around the beautiful Christmas tree in Rotary Square. Don’t miss the annual tree-lighting ceremony that takes place at 7:45 p.m.

Experience Downtown for the Holidays

The Lighting of the Lights kicks off a month-long celebration of music, shopping, dining and holiday cheer in the heart of London.

The City of London, Downtown London, Covent Garden Market, and Tourism London are excited to once again treat Londoners to a variety of festive experiences this holiday season.

There’s so much holiday fun to discover downtown with events like the Holly Jolly Market, Candy Cane Lane, the Santa Claus Parade, Downtown Holiday Trails and the holiday carousel. Don’t forget, Winter Wonderland in Victoria Park continues to light up into January 2027.

VisitDowntown for the Holidaysto learn more about upcoming holiday events.

Thank you to our sponsors

This year’s lighting display is made possible through the generous support of Downtown London, London Music Office, The Paul Seed Fund, Salvation Army, London Community Foundation, Canada Life, Architects Tillmann Ruth Robinson and our official energy sponsor, London Hydro.

Wednesday, November 18, 2026

On Friday, December 4, Londoners are invited to watch Victoria Park transform into a dazzling winter wonderland at the annual Lighting of the Lights. This year’s celebration will shine bright once again as more than 100,000 lights and festive displays illuminate the park with holiday magic.

The evening will kick off at 6 p.m. with live music, featuring Saveria, Eleanor Gebrou, Amanda Movio, and Immogen Wasse. Londoners can enjoy free hot chocolate, indulge in a variety of food truck offerings, capture a festive selfie at the 360° photo booth, and send their holiday wish list to the North Pole at Santa’s mailbox.

The highlight of the night is the magical moment when the park is illuminated with the ceremonial flip of the switch at approximately 6:50 p.m. This year, Mayor Josh Morgan will be joined by London-raised, Juno award-winning rapper Shad and Francesca Wright, Director of the Paul Seed Fund, to set the park aglow.

“The Lighting of the Lights is one of those special London traditions that everyone in our city looks forward to each holiday season,” said Mayor Josh Morgan. “Seeing Victoria Park come alive with thousands of lights, with people from across our city sharing the excitement, is our city at its best and brightest. I hope to see everyone for a great evening downtown enjoying the festivities and making memories together.”
The light displays bring the park to life, along with an array of festive favourites, including Santa and his reindeer, a Christmas train, and a cheerful snow family.
City Hall observation deck
The City Hall observation deck will open for public viewing of the Lighting of the Lights and the Winter Wonderland in Victoria Park during the following dates and times:
Friday, December 4 (Lighting of the Lights) from 5:30 to 9:00 p.m.
Saturday, December 5 and Sunday, December 6 from 5:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.
Thursday, December 10 to Sunday, December 13 from 5:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.
Thursday, December 17 to Sunday, December 20 from 5:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.
Thursday, December 24 (Christmas Eve) from 5:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.
Saturday, December 26 to Sunday, December 27 from 5:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.
Outdoor skating

The outdoor skating rink at Victoria Park will not be open for the Lighting of the Lights event. Weather permitting, the rink will open mid-December. More details about outdoor skating will be shared in the coming weeks.
Victoria Park washrooms

Starting December 4, access to the washrooms in Victoria Park will be available daily from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at the Kiwanis Memorial Bandshell throughout the holiday season. If the washrooms are locked during this time, contact a nearby security guard for assistance.
The holiday magic continues at Covent Garden Market
After the Lighting of the Lights, Londoners are encouraged to head over to Covent Garden Market for the official opening of the Holly Jolly Holiday Market.

Visitors can enjoy local artisans and food vendors, cozy fire pits, live music, and dazzling light displays around the beautiful Christmas tree in Rotary Square. Don’t miss the annual tree-lighting ceremony that takes place at 7:45 p.m.
Experience Downtown for the Holidays
The Lighting of the Lights kicks off a month-long celebration of music, shopping, dining and holiday cheer in the heart of London.
The City of London, Downtown London, Covent Garden Market, and Tourism London are excited to once again treat Londoners to a variety of festive experiences this holiday season.

There’s so much holiday fun to discover downtown with events like the Holly Jolly Market, Candy Cane Lane, the Santa Claus Parade, Downtown Holiday Trails and the holiday carousel. Don’t forget, Winter Wonderland in Victoria Park continues to light up into January 2027.
VisitDowntown for the Holidaysto learn more about upcoming holiday events.
Thank you to our sponsors

This year’s lighting display is made possible through the generous support of Downtown London, London Music Office, The Paul Seed Fund, Salvation Army, London Community Foundation, Canada Life, Architects Tillmann Ruth Robinson and our official energy sponsor, London Hydro.

stories.title: Human trafficking investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (November 18, 2026) – Two men are facing multiple charges after a woman was assaulted, threatened with a firearm and held against her will in a south-end hotel.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 18, 2026) – Two men are facing multiple charges after a woman was assaulted, threatened with a firearm and held against her will in a south-end hotel.

On Saturday, November 14, 2026, at approximately 1 a.m., a female attended a hotel to meet a man who had requested sexual services for money. When she arrived at the hotel room, she was assaulted and held against her will by two suspects. She was threatened with a firearm and a knife and prevented from leaving.

At approximately 2 a.m., the London Police Service (LPS) received a call to attend the hotel to check the welfare of the female.

Officers attended and located the victim and a suspect inside a hotel room. The suspect fled but was arrested a short distance away. Police reviewed security footage that showed the suspect toss a bag under a car as he fled. Police located the bag and found an imitation firearm.

Through the investigation, police learned the two suspects were trying to exploit the victim in the sex trade to financially benefit.

The investigation was reassigned to members of the LPS Human Trafficking Unit, who were able to identify a second suspect.

As a result of the investigation, Chad Kuzler, 45, of St. Thomas, and David H. Janssens, 57, of Thamesford, have been jointly charged with the following offences:

Robbery;

Forcible confinement;

Assault;

Assault with a weapon;

Possession of property obtained by crime under $5,000;

Obtain sexual services for consideration; and,

Procuring.

Chad Kuzler has been additionally charged with one count of pointing a firearm.

Chad Kuzler remains in custody and is expected to reappear in London court tomorrow in relation to the charges.

David H. Janssens’ whereabouts are unknown, and as a result, he is being charged by way of a warrant of arrest.

Investigators believe there May be additional victims and are releasing photographs of both accused as part of the ongoing investigation as well as assisting in locating and arresting Janssens.

The victim suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

Anyone who May have had contact with either accused, or who has information relevant to this investigation, is encouraged to contact police.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.'

Wednesday, November 18, 2026

The City of London is inviting property owners to apply for the 2027 Tree Canopy Conservation Program, which provides financial assistance to help care for and preserve mature trees on private property.

Mature trees play an important role in London's urban forest. They provide shade, support wildlife, improve air quality and help make neighbourhoods more livable. Protecting these trees and extending their lifespan is an important part of the City's efforts to grow and maintain a healthy urban forest.

“Protecting London's mature trees is just as important as planting new ones. These trees are a valuable part of our neighbourhoods, and caring for them helps ensure they can continue providing benefits for generations to come,” says Shawna Chambers, Director, Climate, Forestry and Waste Services. “As the 2026-2027 Forest Capital of Canada, we are committed to protecting, maintaining, and growing our urban forest.”

The City's Urban Forest Strategy sets a target of achieving 34 per cent tree canopy cover by 2065. Reaching this goal means not only planting new trees, but also protecting the mature trees that already contribute to London's tree canopy.

Eligible property owners can receive financial assistance for the care and management of qualifying mature trees. To be eligible, trees must be at least 50 centimetres in diameter, and all work must be undertaken in consultation with a qualified arborist to help ensure the health of the tree and the safety of the property.

Property owners do not need to live at the property to apply.

To learn more and apply, visit london.ca/tccp.

Wednesday, November 18, 2026

The City of London is inviting property owners to apply for the 2027 Tree Canopy Conservation Program, which provides financial assistance to help care for and preserve mature trees on private property.

Mature trees play an important role in London's urban forest. They provide shade, support wildlife, improve air quality and help make neighbourhoods more livable. Protecting these trees and extending their lifespan is an important part of the City's efforts to grow and maintain a healthy urban forest.

“Protecting London's mature trees is just as important as planting new ones. These trees are a valuable part of our neighbourhoods, and caring for them helps ensure they can continue providing benefits for generations to come,” says Shawna Chambers, Director, Climate, Forestry and Waste Services. “As the 2026-2027 Forest Capital of Canada, we are committed to protecting, maintaining, and growing our urban forest.”

The City's Urban Forest Strategy sets a target of achieving 34 per cent tree canopy cover by 2065. Reaching this goal means not only planting new trees, but also protecting the mature trees that already contribute to London's tree canopy.

Eligible property owners can receive financial assistance for the care and management of qualifying mature trees. To be eligible, trees must be at least 50 centimetres in diameter, and all work must be undertaken in consultation with a qualified arborist to help ensure the health of the tree and the safety of the property.
Property owners do not need to live at the property to apply.
To learn more and apply, visit london.ca/tccp.

stories.title: Traffic enforcement blitz
stories.summary: London, ON (November 18, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Road Safety Section (RSS) impounded seven vehicles and laid multiple charges in a traffic enforcement blitz in the south end of the city earlier this week.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 18, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Road Safety Section (RSS) impounded seven vehicles and laid multiple charges in a traffic enforcement blitz in the south end of the city earlier this week.

On Monday, November 16, 2026, Members of the LPS Road Safety Section conducted traffic enforcement along Colonel Talbot Road between Orr Road and the 401.

As a result of the enforcement, eight individuals were charged with a combined total of 15 Highway Traffic Act and vehicle-related offences, and two of the individuals were additionally charged with impaired driving-related charges. All eight vehicles were impounded and towed as part of the enforcement action.

The charges related to stunt driving, unsafe vehicle operation, various vehicle equipment offences, and impaired driving. Speeds ranged between 101km/hr to 121 km/hr in a posted 60 km/hr zone.

"Stunt driving and impaired driving puts everyone at risk, including drivers, pedestrians and anyone just trying to get home safely," said Sgt. Chis Andrews of the Road Safety Section. "Our message is simple: slow down, drive sober and look out for one another. Everyone deserves to arrive safely to their destination, and our officers are out there working to make that happen."

The London Police Service reminds all motorists that public roads and parking lots are not appropriate places for stunts, racing, or other dangerous driving activities. Drivers are responsible for ensuring they operate their vehicles safely, obey traffic laws, and consider the safety of everyone around them, including passengers, pedestrians, and other road users.

Members of the public are encouraged to report dangerous driving and suspicious vehicle activity when it is safe to do so. Even seemingly minor information can assist police in identifying offenders and enhancing road safety throughout the community.

The London Police Service will continue proactive traffic enforcement in areas where community members have raised concerns, working to keep roads safe for everyone who uses them.

stories.title: Project Search Info Night: Learn about the award winning work transition program for students with developmental disabilities
stories.summary: General News
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
General News

All Notices and Updates

Project SEARCH Info Night

November 26, 2026 | 6-7 p.m. TVDSB Education Centre Cafeteria (1250 Dundas St., London)

Join us on November 26 for the Project SEARCH Info Night! Learn more about Project SEARCH, a secondary school transition program for students with developmental disabilities entering their last year of secondary school in 2027-2028, hosted by St. Joseph's Health Care London and supported by March of Dimes Canada.

Project SEARCH is an international, award winning one-year school to work transition program for students with intellectual disabilities. TVDSB is proud to partner with March of Dimes Canada and St. Joseph’s Health Care London to provide this program for secondary students. The goal of the program is to gain the skills to pursue year-round employment, of 20 hours per week or more, at a competitive wage in a work setting that is inclusive of interest to the student. St. Joseph’s Health Care London has organized three dynamic 10-week internships for the students interns at Parkwood Institute in a variety of departments. The student interns involved in Project SEARCH glean real life experiences through this initiative.

Learn more about Project SEARCH

stories.title: London Health Sciences Centre introduces its renewed Board of Directors
stories.summary: November 18, 2026
stories.content:
Members of London Health Sciences Centre’s renewed Board of Directors. Back row, from left to right: Ron Sapsford, Lori Van Opstal, Nick Vander Gulik, Scott Courtice, Mike Tidy, Dr. David Steven, Michael G. Power, Christi-Ann Poulette. Front row, from left to right: Cedric Gomes, Lloy Wylie, Catherine Osborne, Melanie Stanley, David Smith, Deborah Wiseman, Leo Plue.

November 18, 2026

London, Ontario – London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) is pleased to introduce its renewed Board of Directors, who will assume full authority when Supervision comes to an end. This marks an important milestone in the organization’s ongoing renewal journey and the next phase of strengthened governance, oversight, and accountability at LHSC.

Following an extensive and community-focused recruitment process, LHSC has appointed eight volunteer members to its renewed Board of Directors. Together, they bring a range of skills, experiences, perspectives, and areas of expertise that will help support strong governance, accountability, stewardship, and organizational success. Five volunteer community members have also been appointed to serve on Board committees, bringing additional experience, expertise, and perspectives to support the Board in fulfilling its governance responsibilities. The appointed Board members and community members serving on Board committees are unpaid volunteers.

The appointments build on two years of significant work to strengthen LHSC's governance, leadership, oversight, and accountability structures. The incoming Board represents the next phase of that work and reflects the organization's continued commitment to transparency, meaningful community engagement, and long-term success in support of the patients and communities it serves.

"Over the past two years, we have focused on strengthening the foundations that support effective governance, accountability, and organizational performance," says David Musyj, Supervisor of LHSC. "The appointment of the renewed Board represents an important milestone in that journey. We were encouraged by the strong response from the community throughout the recruitment process and are confident the individuals selected bring the experience, expertise, and perspectives needed to help guide LHSC into the future."

Candidates were evaluated through a comprehensive process overseen by Musyj and Board Chair, Ron Sapsford, with support from health system leaders, governance experts, and patient partners. Candidates were considered based on factors that included governance and leadership experience, professional expertise, lived experience, community involvement, and the perspectives they would bring to the Board.

More than 90 people applied to serve on the Board, and both the number and calibre of the applicants were notable. Candidates brought strong governance and leadership experience, professional expertise, varied lived experiences, and deep ties to the communities LHSC serves. Beginning with future recruitment cycles, candidates will be required to serve on an LHSC Board committee before applying to join the Board. Committee service will give prospective directors firsthand experience with LHSC’s governance and the responsibilities of Board membership.

The renewed Board of Directors includes:

Ron Sapsford, Chair

Scott Courtice

Cedric Gomes

Christi-Ann Poulette

Michael G. Power

David Smith

Melanie Stanley

Lori Van Opstal

The five community members appointed to serve on Board committees are:

Catherine Osborne

Leo Plue

Mike Tidy

Nick Vander Gulik

Lloy Wylie

The Board also includes ex-officio, non-voting members who serve by virtue of the leadership positions they hold at LHSC. Through their respective roles, they bring organizational, clinical, and professional perspectives that help inform the Board’s work and support its governance responsibilities and decision-making.

The ex-officio members are:

Dr. Jennifer Mandzia, President of the Professional Staff Organization

Dr. David Steven, Interim Chair of the Medical Advisory Committee

Deborah Wiseman, Corporate Nursing Executive

The renewed Board of Directors will provide oversight, strategic direction, stewardship, and accountability at LHSC, while the hospital’s executive team will continue to be responsible for the organization’s day-to-day management. The Board will work alongside and be accountable to David Musyj as Supervisor until Supervision ends.

The Board’s orientation is well underway. Board and committee members have reviewed their governance responsibilities, and Board members have met with LHSC’s executive leaders and Medical Advisory Committee at an orientation session. Members have also completed their technology onboarding and will spend several days touring LHSC campuses and clinical programs. They have also been provided with readings and program videos to help them get to know LHSC before the first public Board meeting on January 7, 2027. Early Board work will include establishing its committees and guiding LHSC’s strategic planning.

"Strong governance plays an important role in supporting high-performing organizations," says Sapsford. "Our Board brings together individuals with a broad range of experience and expertise who share a commitment to accountability, stewardship, and the communities we serve. We look forward to building on the progress made over the past two years and helping ensure LHSC remains well positioned to deliver outstanding care, advance research and education, and meet the needs of patients and families across the region."

London Health Sciences Centre media contact: Jess Brady Communications Consultant 226-927-7486 London Health Sciences Centre media@lhsc.on.ca

The renewed Board of Directors will provide oversight, strategic direction, stewardship, and accountability at LHSC, while the hospital’s executive team will continue to be responsible for the organization’s day-to-day management. The Board will work alongside and be accountable to David Musyj as Supervisor until Supervision ends.

The Board’s orientation is well underway. Board and committee members have reviewed their governance responsibilities, and Board members have met with LHSC’s executive leaders and Medical Advisory Committee at an orientation session. Members have also completed their technology onboarding and will spend several days touring LHSC campuses and clinical programs. They have also been provided with readings and program videos to help them get to know LHSC before the first public Board meeting on January 7, 2027. Early Board work will include establishing its committees and guiding LHSC’s strategic planning.

"Strong governance plays an important role in supporting high-performing organizations," says Sapsford. "Our Board brings together individuals with a broad range of experience and expertise who share a commitment to accountability, stewardship, and the communities we serve. We look forward to building on the progress made over the past two years and helping ensure LHSC remains well positioned to deliver outstanding care, advance research and education, and meet the needs of patients and families across the region."

content_blocks.text: London, Ontario – London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) is pleased to introduce its renewed Board of Directors, who will assume full authority when Supervision comes to an end. content_blocks.html: London, Ontario – London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) is pleased to introduce its renewed Board of Directors, who will assume full authority when Supervision comes to an end. This marks an important milestone in the organization’s ongoing renewal journey and the next phase of strengthened governance, oversight, and accountability at LHSC.

content_blocks.text: Following an extensive and community-focused recruitment process, LHSC has appointed eight volunteer members to its renewed Board of Directors. Together, they bring a range of skills, experiences, perspectives, and areas of expertise that will help support strong governance, accountability, stewardship, and organizational success. Five volunteer community members have also been appointed to serve on Board committees, bringing additional experience, expertise, and perspectives to support the Board in fulfilling its governance responsibilities. The appointed Board members and community members serving on Board committees are unpaid volunteers.
