stories.title: Mistrial declared in trial of former Saskatoon massage therapist
stories.summary: The courtroom filed with gasps and tears after hearing the declaration of a mistrial completely halting the jury trial for former massage therapist, 70, Kenneth Braun.
stories.author: Grace Miller
stories.content:
A Saskatoon King’s Bench courtroom filled with gasps and tears Tuesday, as Justice Daryl Labach declared a mistrial in the sexual assault trial of former massage therapist Kenneth Braun.

Defence counsel applied for a mistrial over crown counsel overstepping in the questioning of Braun and potentially put forward inadmissible evidence in front of the jury.

Braun is still facing three charges of sexual assault and one count of sexual exploitation of a minor. How those charges will be dealt with following Labach’s decision is yet to be determined.

Part of the submission included putting forward the option to remove the jury, shifting to a judge alone trial. Crown prosecutor Lana Morelli declined the option and offered to instead give a direction to the jury to not take into consideration the evidence raised.

“It had started with the jury and should end with the jury,” said Morelli.

“We believe it took an extraordinary amount of courage for all of these complainants to come forward, to testify, and to give their stories of what happened. We support the justice system, which include these complainants that have waited several years if not longer to say their stories.”

Morelli also pointed to the difficulties of arguing this case in a singular trial with multiple proceedings and multiple complainants.

“The fact that we are where we are is not a result of forethought, it is not a result that the Crown was trying to put forward inadmissible evidence, it was simply an error,” said Morelli.

Morelli says how the trial will move forward will depend on whether or not the defence will elect for a jury trial, and what the Crown can do with the evidence already brought forward.

Defence lawyer Pfefferle was also remorseful for what this might mean for the victims of the case possibly having to testify again. He also addressed the complexity of the case.

“This was a big issue about perception and so for that reason it was a complicated response that the accused had to give in order to toe the line and as a result of that that’s really what put us in this in this situation. So, it’s an unfortunate result but one that we believed in and as I say for that reason, we’re glad that we’re granted it,” said Pfefferle.

Pfefferle also said there is a good chance the charges May be dropped completely.

“ We have a court system that is absolutely bursting at the seams with judges sitting on holidays, over weekends,” said Pfefferle. “ With the burden on the court system, one of the real concerns here is can we get to a trial fast enough to be reasonable and deal with the constitutional principle that an accused has a right to a trial within a reasonable period of time .”

Morelli disagrees, saying there are other options still available. Morelli says how the trial will move forward will depend on whether or not the defence will elect for a jury trial and what the Crown can do with the evidence has already been brought forward.

The case will go before pre-trial proceedings in the next few weeks.

stories.title: Nova Scotia hosting three virtual information sessions on AI data centres this week
stories.summary: The Nova Scotia government is hosting virtual information sessions this week to answer questions about AI data centres.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government is hosting virtual information sessions this week to answer questions about AI data centres.

The government made the announcement Tuesday morning, saying the first of three sessions would take place at 7 p.m. that same evening.

The sessions will be livestreamed on YouTube and Facebook.

A proposed $10-billion AI data centre in southern Cape Breton has been met with opposition from many residents and sparked protests across the province earlier this month.

Premier Tim Houston says the sessions will provide an opportunity for Nova Scotians to ask questions, and for experts to address misinformation about AI data centres.

Also on Tuesday, the government confirmed that it was randomly calling Nova Scotians to ask if they would like to pose a question during the live session.

The two other sessions have been scheduled for Wednesday night and Thursday afternoon.

stories.title: Cadet captain paralyzed from waist down after Hamilton attack
stories.summary: Police have said the Nov. 8 attack stemmed from a confrontation over the harassment of young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A cadet leader who underwent spinal surgery after a violent attack says he is currently paralyzed from the waist down and will require months of physical rehabilitation.

Capt. Kenneth Kunkel provided an update on his situation last week in a statement shared online by a Hamilton member of Parliament.

Kunkel says he is in continual pain and his doctors cannot give him a prognosis at this time, but he remains “hopeful and positive.”

He thanked those who have reached out to express support or donated to an online fundraiser set up for his family.

Police have said the Nov. 8 attack stemmed from a confrontation over the harassment of young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies.

They said two youths approached young air cadets who were selling poppies in front of a restaurant on Barton Street East and blew an air horn “directly into their ears.”

Investigators said a man who was supervising the cadets followed the youths into the restaurant to confront them, leading to a struggle.

They allege a woman jumped in to help the youths and assaulted the air cadet leader, who fell to the ground. One of the boys allegedly hit the man multiple times.

A 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman were charged with aggravated assault in the incident.

In his statement, Kunkel said he wanted to clarify some details of what happened that day.

He said he confronted a youth in the restaurant about assaulting one of the cadets and told him they needed to go to the front and call police. The youth “immediately tried to run away,” Kunkel said, adding he grabbed the youth’s backpack and started walking toward the front of the restaurant while asking staff to call police.

The youth started punching him, he said, and a woman intervened on the youth’s behalf. Kunkel said he told her the boy had assaulted a cadet and they needed to speak with police.

While his attention was on the woman, the boy grabbed the lanyard holding Kunkel’s car key and ripped it off his neck, he said. When Kunkel reached to grab it back, the woman “blindsided” him, slamming him into a concrete pillar, he said.

“My legs buckled beneath me and I collapsed,” he said. “While I was lying on the ground helpless, the young male proceeded to violently punch me directly in the face numerous times.”

Kunkel was taken to hospital and underwent surgery that night, he said.

A GoFundMe page set up on behalf of Kunkel and his family said he is the commanding officer of 826 Gryphon Squadron Royal Canadian Air Cadets, and has been with the cadets for 20 years.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

stories.title: Harris returns for another CFL season with Riders
stories.summary: The decision to return for a fifth season with the Saskatchewan Roughriders was a rather easy one for Trevor Harris.
stories.author: n The Canadian Pressn
stories.content:
Regina – The decision to return for a fifth season with the Saskatchewan Roughriders was a rather easy one for Trevor Harris.

The veteran quarterback signed a one-year extension with the CFL club Tuesday. It came just over two weeks after the Riders’ season ended with a 33-26 loss to the B.C. Lions in the West Division semifinal.

“That night I came home from the West semifinal was tough,” Harris told reporters during a Zoom call. “And then when you’re driving to the stadium, your emotions hit you, and I think anybody who was there (at Riders’ season-ending availability) knew I was pretty emotional during that presser.

“Talking to my wife on the way home, it was like, ‘Why are we even deciphering this for?’ You only get to do this one time in life, and once you’re done, it’s over. I still feel I’ve got a lot more to give and room to grow as a player, as a person and as a leader.”

Harris turns 41 next season. But the six-foot-three, 212-pound quarterback certainly didn’t show any signs of slowing down in 2026.

Harris led the CFL in pass attempts (615), completions (431) and yards (5,370) over 17 regular-season starts while completing 70.1 per cent of his passes. He also had 32 touchdowns with 15 interceptions and nine 300-yard games.

“There’s always things you’re going to want to work on, but as I run through it, I know I can still be a tier 1 quarterback,” Harris said. “I still have a hunger and drive to do this.

“It’s not like a deal where I feel like I’m hanging on … if I don’t feel like I can get better and I will be better, I wouldn’t be coming back. If I am not better next year, then I’m not a man of my word.”

Harris is just over a year removed from leading Saskatchewan to a 25-17 Grey Cup victory over the Montreal Alouettes and being named the game MVP. He completed 23-of-27 passes (a Grey Cup record 85.2 per cent completion percentage) for 302 yards.

The 2026 season started well enough for Saskatchewan, which sported an 8-4 record. However, the Riders suffered four consecutive losses before ending the regular campaign with two straight wins for a 10-8 record.

Saskatchewan finished tied for second in the West Division with B.C. But the Lions got the higher spot after winning the season series 2-1.

“We get to the point where we’re 8-4 after Labour Day and for whatever reason I just felt like we had a tough time getting going the rest of the year,” Harris said. ‘Sometimes it was offence, sometimes it was defence, sometimes it was special teams.

“Before I signed back, I had some long talks with (head coach Corey Mace) and (offensive co-ordinator Marc Mueller). We’ve been able to have some good conversations, deep conversations and even some difficult conversations about things we feel like we need to be better at and I couldn’t be more excited about the direction we’re headed in.”

It’s been a well-travelled CFL career for Harris, who had stops with Toronto (2012-15), Ottawa (2016-18), Edmonton (2019, 2021) and Montreal (’21-2022) before arriving in Saskatchewan. But this will be Harris’s fifth season with the Riders, marking the longest stay of his Canadian professional career.

“What a blessing it is that it be my longest tenure with a team,” Harris said. “I just feel like I’m a residential Saskie now and you guys are stuck with me because I’m a Roughrider for life.”

“Talking to my wife on the way home, it was like, ‘Why are we even deciphering this for?’ You only get to do this one time in life, and once you’re done, it’s over. I still feel I’ve got a lot more to give and room to grow as a player, as a person and as a leader.”
Harris turns 41 next season. But the six-foot-three, 212-pound quarterback certainly didn’t show any signs of slowing down in 2026.

Harris led the CFL in pass attempts (615), completions (431) and yards (5,370) over 17 regular-season starts while completing 70.1 per cent of his passes. He also had 32 touchdowns with 15 interceptions and nine 300-yard games.
“There’s always things you’re going to want to work on, but as I run through it, I know I can still be a tier 1 quarterback,” Harris said. “I still have a hunger and drive to do this.

“It’s not like a deal where I feel like I’m hanging on … if I don’t feel like I can get better and I will be better, I wouldn’t be coming back. If I am not better next year, then I’m not a man of my word.”

stories.title: American Buffalo review: Coal Mine Theatre show spotlights a forgotten generation of working-class men
stories.summary: Director Jordan Laffrenier directs a coarse yet sensitive production of David Mamet’s 1975 drama
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Title: American Buffalo

Written by: David Mamet

Directed by: Jordan Laffrenier

Actors: Ted Dykstra, Shawn Doyle, Mackenzie Wojcik

Company and venue: Coal Mine Theatre

City: Toronto

Year: Runs until Dec. 6

“Action counts,” warns Don, the owner of a rundown pawnshop near the top of David Mamet’s American Buffalo. “Talk” – though the merchant uses a cruder word – is just that. Talk.

It’s an apt prelude for what’s to come: What American Buffalo ’s disillusioned men say is often a mutation of what they mean, the truth of which only surfaces in flashes of high-stakes conflict. The moments that really matter in the lives of America’s forgotten working class are those when something happens – when the men work up enough outrage to act.

But Don’s advice also serves as a summation of why it might not matter to some audiences that Coal Mine Theatre’s production of Mamet’s 1975 classic is perceptively staged, persuasively acted and beautifully designed. Director Jordan Laffrenier encourages richly nuanced performances from his cast of three – Ted Dykstra, also the company’s artistic director, is particularly riveting as the slur-slinging Teach.

The choice to separate art from its artist and their actions is personal, and often fraught – whether audiences decide to do so on this occasion will ultimately be up to them. Mamet, a vocal supporter of Donald Trump and his rhetoric, has long been a controversial figure on the American theatre scene; in recent years, he’s made headlines for colourful media appearances on a number of political issues. (In a now-infamous Fox News interview in 2022, for instance, about Florida’s so-called “Don’t Say Gay” bill, he asserted that school teachers are “inclined” toward pedophilia.)

Even so, Mamet’s plays remain some of the most illuminating of the American dramatic canon. You don’t get The Sopranos , The Wire or even Gilmore Girls without his no-nonsense approach to dialogue to light the way. In Mamet’s work, audiences see and hear real people in all their coarseness – even, and perhaps especially, those they might disagree with.

So it goes in American Buffalo , written well before the Trump era but uncannily representative of the politician’s most fervent supporters in middle America. Laffrenier’s production, gritty and wrenching in its frank portrayal of a lost generation of working-class men, cuts to the bone.

When we meet Don (Shawn Doyle) and his gopher Bob (Mackenzie Wojcik), there’s a palpable paternal warmth to the pair. Bob struggles to process the world around him – even direct instructions seem to slip just beyond his reach – but despite himself, Don feels a fondness for the boy, and even insists on paying for his breakfast (if only to ensure he eats something).

In comes barrelling Teach, whose vocabulary features an outsized number of words that rhyme with “duck” (and, when speaking of women, those that sound like “front”). Where Don shows wisps of softness – in his mentorship of Bob, in his decision not to detonate a crooked poker game – Teach reveals a soul of concrete. He’ll do most anything to make a buck, and, more importantly, to keep his last shreds of pride and dignity intact. (Teach’s thick walrus mustache is just one of several insightful choices by costume designer Des’ree Gray.)

The events of the play soon unfold like a natural disaster, inevitable and devastating in their destruction. When Don sells a rare nickel for US$90, a plan soon forms to steal the coin back – it’s likely worth even more than what the customer paid for it. But Teach’s meddling leads to an evening of unspeakable physical violence, which, as staged by Laffrenier, suggests a future for Bob even bleaker than the life he lives now.

Set designer Ken MacKenzie places American Buffalo in an emporium of junky tchotchkes, from dull ice skates to a collection of Midwestern license plates. When items start to fly in Teach’s second-act hurricane of rage, it’s tough not to weep for Don – glass display cases are notoriously expensive, and while the items he sells might not be worth much, they won’t be easy to replace, either.

But then again, it’s tough not to weep for all the men in Mamet’s scorcher of a drama – even Teach, as much a product of his surroundings as of his own fractured moral compass. These men have been abandoned by society; whatever might have been left of the American Dream in the hazy days of their respective childhoods has since been smashed to smithereens.

The recognition of that faction of the U.S. is what won Trump two elections. For his many faults, Trump managed during his campaigns to appeal to the Dons, Bobs and Teaches of the rust belt, the men and women left uninspired by a country that seemed to leave them for dead in the late 20th century.

Laffrenier’s production offers an unconventional sort of empathy for the Americans who have found community in their shared vitriol for others – for the gaps between their action and their talk. We might not like these people, Laffrenier’s staging posits, but we ought to make an honest attempt at understanding them.

stories.title: London edition of Level Up! Career Fair hopes to attract young people to skilled trades
stories.summary: The skilled trades industry is upping its game when it comes to efforts to attract new talent. The Level Up! Skilled Trades Career Fair is in London, Ont. this week.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
The skilled trades industry is upping its game when it comes to efforts to attract new talent. The Level Up! Skilled Trades Career Fair is in London, Ont. this week at the J-AAR Expo Centre, providing the next generation of trades-workers an up-close and hands-on look at career prospects.

“I just love the trades,” said Emily Meersseman, a 17-year-old Grade 12 student at Holy Cross Secondary School in Strathroy. “My parents have been in it since they were in their 20s. I want to do heavy equipment. We’re here, supposed to be building a shed but our lumber hasn’t shown up yet so we’re just exploring the trade show right now.”

Emily was one of thousands of students from school boards in the area taking in day-one of the three-day event.

The London stop is one of 12 Career Fairs being held across the province. It features local trades representatives, career colleges, and apprenticeship programs, said Ashlee Sahota, a manager with the Ministry of Labour, Immigration and Skills Development.

“A lot of these jobs are very well paid, they’re skilled. And you can make a lot of money and get paid while you learn, as well. You don’t come out with debt, depending on what field you go into,” she explained.

William Le Marquand is with the Operating Engineers Training Institute of Ontario. He’s using simulators to show youngsters to operate an excavator or mobile crane.

“All your training’s paid for, and you get the best real-world experience,” he said of Oetio. “All of our instructors are actually from the field. They’ve got over 10 years working in different industries, and actually hands-on with the real equipment.”

According to Skilled Trades Ontario, there continues to be a labour shortage in skilled trades. And with coming retirements and outdated stigmas, that’s not going to change without events like Level Up! to expose the next generation to potential opportunities.

It requires shifting a mindset that’s been in place for far too many years, said teacher Chris McKay from Arthur Stringer Public School in London.

“For years we spent a lot of time pushing university and college, and that sort of thing. And not enough time helping kids explore all the options that are out there. So, it’s really important for them to see what’s out there and what they can try,” McKay said

Organizers of Level Up! are expecting 9,000 visitors to the career fair, which runs for three days through Nov. 19.

stories.title: What are Chinese ‘kit cars’ and why they’re worrying Canada’s auto industry
stories.summary: Canada’s auto manufacturing sector directly employs 125,000 people and is indirectly supported by 427,000 jobs, according to Statistics Canada.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
As Ottawa looks to intensify its trade relationship with Beijing after a meeting between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping , Canada’s auto industry is sounding the alarm over the question of whether those talks could open the door to Chinese “knock-down kits” or “kit cars,” warning of their impact on domestic jobs.

“We see no evidence in markets around the world that China will do anything but knock-down kits,” said Brian Kingston, president and CEO of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers’ Association President.

A “knock-down kit” or a “kit car” is part of China’s strategy to quickly boost its auto exports, whereby car parts are quickly and cheaply manufactured in China, packed in boxes and shipped only to be assembled overseas.

“It’s like those toy models that you build at home. It comes in a box, and all the parts are there and then you get to assemble it,” said McMaster University economist Colin Mang.

“The worry about the idea of the kit cars is that all the parts would be manufactured in China. They would then be shipped to North America and then they would just be assembled into cars,” he added.

While most kit cars still require assembly, it is a significantly scaled back operation compared to traditional vehicle manufacturing and has spurred concerns from representatives of the auto industry that the “kit car” model would employ fewer workers.

“There would be an assembly line that employs workers, but much of the auto sector in North America and in Canada and in Southern Ontario, is not assembly of cars, it’s the manufacturing of the parts,” Mang said.

Chinese manufacturers use “lower labor standards, weak environmental laws, coal-fired electricity” to undercut global competition, Kingston said, adding that allowing Chinese EVs into the market has already cost job losses in Europe.

“This will destroy Canada’s auto industry. It will destroy our manufacturing base if we open our market to China,” said Kingston, who represents the operations of Ford Motor Company, General Motors and Stellantis in Canada.

Canada’s auto sector directly employs 125,000 people and is indirectly supported by 427,000 jobs, according to Statistics Canada, and contributed $16.8 billion to Canada’s GDP in 2024.

When asked about concerns around kit cars, Carney said on Sunday that any manufacturing deal with China would have to involve “significant value added” in Canada.

Ottawa would not accept a deal where only the final stage of automobile assembly is done in Canada, Carney said in Cambodia .

However, some experts say there has been no evidence that China has set up substantial automobile local supply chains anywhere outside its own borders.

“There’s been no public evidence of a Chinese manufacturing plant being set up in another country and then localization happening. Local domestic parts are not being integrated at a reasonable scale into the Chinese company’s operations,” said Elizabeth Donkervoort, senior advisor for China programs at the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada.

“Canada really doesn’t have a model for how they’re going to enforce this,” she added.

Carney also stressed the importance of vehicles made in Canada using Canadian critical minerals. However, some experts say that can be hard to enforce.

“They have a holistic and an entire comprehensive ecosystem within China, where everything from the processing of the critical minerals that are used in developing the technologies to the hardware for EVs are processed in China,” Donkervoort said.

Thailand has been an example of a country that has tried and failed to get China to build local supply chains instead of using knock-down kits.

“Thailand has been trying to do that. But Chinese companies, from my understanding, have not reached the same level of localization as Japanese and South Korean automakers in Thailand,” Donkervoort said.

Europe, particularly Germany, is an example of “what not to do,” Kingston said.

“They’ve allowed the Chinese into the market. They’re on route to get 20 per cent market share. We’re seeing massive job loss across the European automotive sector, 104,000 jobs in the past two years. Germany (alone) has shed over 40,000 jobs in the past six months,” he said.

Setting up domestic supply chains would mean Chinese companies lose their price advantage, Kingston said.

“There is no world in which a Chinese company comes to Canada and builds a domestic supply chain,” he said.

In Cambodia, Carney said U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs against Canada’s auto sector and Canada’s growing closeness with Beijing on trade were “all connected.”

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed (with) full opportunity in an integrated North American market. That market has become less integrated because of U.S.,” Carney said.

After decades of ever-deepening supply chains between Canada and the U.S., a trade deal with Washington is still the best bet for Canada’s auto industry, Kingston said.

“Diversification is not an option for the auto industry,” Kingston said.

stories.title: Hamilton air cadet leader ‘paralyzed from the waist down’ grateful for outpouring of support: MP
stories.summary: Kunkel confirmed that he is 'paralyzed from the waste down and still in hospital'
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Captain Ken Kunkel, the Hamilton, Ont. air cadet commander left paralyzed from the waist down by a horrific attack while selling poppies, has shared his thanks to Canadians who have expressed support for him and his family, as well as the more than$312,000 in donations made to a GoFundMe page.

“I would like to … thank everyone from the bottom of my heart for the outpouring of love you have given me, my wife, son and daughter during this very difficult time for us,” Kunkel said over the phone to Hamilton East—Stoney Creek MP, Ned Kuruc, last week.

Kuruc shared Kunkel’s message in a statement posted on X last Friday. In it Kunkel said that the “generous donations” have meant a lot to his family as he continues to recover from the attack and they plan for “the expenses ahead of us.” He is self-employed and his condition has prevented him from operating his business.

Kunkel confirmed that he is “paralyzed from the waist,“ down and still in hospital, ON medication for “continuous pain.” His doctors have not been able to give him a long-term prognosis. He has been told that he will be spending months undergoing rehabilitation therapy.

Kunkel was supporting two air cadets selling poppies in advance of Remembrance Day, when two male youths allegedly blew an air horn in a cadet’s ears.

Kunkel followed the boys into a nearby restaurant to speak with them. The 59-year-old Kunkel was attacked by one of the boys, 12 years of age, as well as a 48-year old woman not related to the initial incident. They both left the restaurant afterwards but were arrested and charged late that day, say Hamilton police.

“She proceeded to assault the victim, causing him to fall to the ground. One of the male youths then struck the victim several times before leaving the restaurant,” said Hamilton Police in a statement. The assault caused “life-altering injuries,” requiring emergency spinal surgery, National Post previously reported.

In his statement, Kunkel provided more details about the incident.

He was supervising several sets of cadets, while wearing his full uniform. He was parked in his car where he could see all of the cadets, when he received a call from one of the cadets who told him that a male youth had allegedly blasted the horn into her ear and assaulted her, before running away.

He said he was able to identify the youth from the cadet’s description and followed him into a nearby restaurant, telling him they would have to go to the front to call the police. He grabbed the youth’s backpack, containing the horn, he says in the statement.

But then, he says, the youth “started throwing punches at me.” Kunkel tried to deflect the punches, while an adult woman confronted him, saying the youth “was just a kid” the statement reads.

While the woman was distracting him, the youth yanked his lanyard from his neck. It contained his car keys. And while informing the youth of this, Kunkel says he was “blindsided” by the woman as she “forcefully (slammed him) into a concrete pillar right beside (him).”

His “spine took all the impact directly” and he immediately lost the use of his legs.

While “lying on the ground helpless,” he says the youth punched him in the face several times. The youth and woman left the scene before the police arrived, but were later arrested and charged.

Kimberly Deitrich, is Ken Kunkel’s daughter, has posted photos of Hamilton General Hospital and spinal unit where Kunkel is being treated. (Photo credit: Kimberly Deitrich/Facebook)

Kuruc described the phone call with Kunkel as tearfully emotional “not from pain” but from “all the love he and his family are receiving from Canadians.”

The GoFundMe page continues to receive donations to support Kunkel and his family, as he recovers from the horrific attack.

After the attack, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said during a press conference that the two male youths deserved an “ass-whooping in the woodshed” for what they are alleged to have done. He also said their parents “should be ashamed that they’ve raised their kids to beat up cadets.”

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

But then, he says, the youth “started throwing punches at me.” Kunkel tried to deflect the punches, while an adult woman confronted him, saying the youth “was just a kid” the statement reads.

While the woman was distracting him, the youth yanked his lanyard from his neck. It contained his car keys. And while informing the youth of this, Kunkel says he was “blindsided” by the woman as she “forcefully (slammed him) into a concrete pillar right beside (him).”
His “spine took all the impact directly” and he immediately lost the use of his legs.
While “lying on the ground helpless,” he says the youth punched him in the face several times. The youth and woman left the scene before the police arrived, but were later arrested and charged.
Kimberly Deitrich, is Ken Kunkel’s daughter, has posted photos of Hamilton General Hospital and spinal unit where Kunkel is being treated. (Photo credit: Kimberly Deitrich/Facebook)
Kuruc described the phone call with Kunkel as tearfully emotional “not from pain” but from “all the love he and his family are receiving from Canadians.”
The GoFundMe page continues to receive donations to support Kunkel and his family, as he recovers from the horrific attack.

After the attack, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said during a press conference that the two male youths deserved an “ass-whooping in the woodshed” for what they are alleged to have done. He also said their parents “should be ashamed that they’ve raised their kids to beat up cadets.”

stories.title: Iihf website hit by cyberattack after Russia excluded from world juniors
stories.summary: The International Ice Hockey Federation says it was the target of a cyberattack Tuesday after a message supporting Russia briefly appeared on its website before the site went offline.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
The International Ice Hockey Federation says it was the target of a cyberattack Tuesday after a message supporting Russia briefly appeared on its website before the site went offline.

An image of Russian players appeared alongside a message accusing the federation of banning a team its opponents couldn’t beat.

“We strongly condemn these actions and are taking all necessary steps to investigate the source of the attack and restore our systems,” the Iihf said in a statement. “Our platforms will be back online as soon as we are confident they are secure.

“The Iihf remains committed to protecting the integrity of our organization and safeguarding our sport.”

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation said in a statement that it was aware of the attack, but denied involvement.

“The Rihf views such actions negatively and considers the use of unlawful methods to express a sporting or public stance to be unacceptable,” it said.

The incident follows the Iihf’s confirmation Sunday that Russia would not compete at next month’s world junior hockey championship in Alberta.

Courtney Greenberg

November 17, 2026 at 3:06 p.m.

Cars were backed up for hours in Winnipeg after gas prices fell to under a dollar on Monday at Domo gas station. The scene was described as “insane” by a local resident.

The station, just outside of the Leila-McPhillips Triangle neighbourhood in the northwest part of the city, was rammed with vehicles fighting for their chance to fill up at the pump along McPhillips Street.

On Tuesday, the national average in Canada for the price of gas was 145.8 cents per litre, according to CAA. The national average has not reached below a dollar in Canada since the COVID-19 pandemic.

“I haven’t seen anything like this in many, many years,” local residentJason Lepine told National Post. He was at Domo on Monday night. He waited about an hour and a half to fill up his truck.

Domo has a 4 cents off promotion on Mondays and Thursdays at specific locations, which it says is a way to “give all our guests a break at the pump.”

Because of that deal, Lepine ended up spending 93.3 cents per litre. It cost him around $56 for gas, after arriving with about a quarter tank still in his truck.

National Post reached out to Domo for more information about the significant price drop. On Monday, its gas was priced at 97.9 cents per litre, but went back to 113.9 on Tuesday morning, according to price tracking site Gas Buddy.

Cars lined up outside of the Domo gas station in Winnipeg after gas prices fell to under a dollar on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. Jason Lepine

“By the time I got in line, the vehicles just kept lining up more and more and was wrapped around in the Northgate mall parking lot and beyond,” said Lepine. “Then as I got to the pump, a big truck carrying gas had cut into the line up on the side I was on to fill the gas tanks below, which made the wait for others much longer.”

He said there was likely an average wait of up to two hours. He was surprised by how patient most people were. Security had to direct traffic in the mall’s parking lot because vehicles were blocking certain areas, he said.

Some drivers even showed up with trucks that had huge containers to fill with gas, which made the wait times even longer.

Domo has 90 gas stations located in Western Canada. The first was built in 1970.

Rather than an entire corner service station, Domo constructed small structures with only two pumps, which it says was “revolutionary” at the time. This meant cheaper rents and only one person required to man the pumps. It assured “the operating costs were extremely low” and those savings would be “passed on to Domo guests.”

“Though it is quite a different era today, these principles remain the company’s guiding principles,” it says online.

Meanwhile, two other gas stations on the same street also lowered their prices, said Lepine, adding to the “crazy” traffic in the area.

The price drop was a welcome relief for Winnipeg residents. In late September, CTV News reported that some were frustrated over gas prices that had increased by nearly 10 cents. CityNews reported on Monday that Winnipeg’s average gas prices — 138 cents per litre — were the lowest they had been since March.

Courtney Greenberg is a Toronto-based journalist covering breaking news, with a focus on antisemitism in Canada. In 2026, she was a Postmedia Fellow with the Investigative Journalism Bureau, where she worked on in-depth investigations into women’s health and the justice system.

MIDDLESEX COUNTY, ON –Middlesex County celebrated dedication, leadership, and commitment to strengthening local communities at this year’s Warden’s Banquet, held last Saturday at the Middlesex County Administration Offices. As part of the evening’s tradition, Warden Sue Clarke selected several honourees for the Warden’s Honour Roll for their outstanding community contributions.

This year’s Honour Roll inductees included:

Steve Liggett

Steve was recognized for his decades of dedication to studying and sharing local history. As a longtime member of the London and Middlesex Historical Society, including serving as President, and currently overseeing membership inquiries, his efforts have helped generations of residents and visitors better understand and appreciate the region's rich history.

Patrick and Stephanie Sanders

Patrick and Stephanie were honoured for their ongoing support of community initiatives throughout Adelaide Metcalfe and neighbouring municipalities.Their contributions have supported youth programming, scholarships, major community projects, and local events across Adelaide Metcalfe, Strathroy-Caradoc, and Brooke Alvinston. Recently, Patrick and Stephanie served as Chairs of the Canadian Plowing Championship, helping deliver a successful event that brought together participants and visitors from across the Country.

Adelaide Metcalfe Fire Department

The Adelaide-Metcalfe Fire Department was recognized for its service both on and off emergency calls. In addition to protecting residents through emergency response and fire prevention education, the department regularly supports community events and charitable initiatives. The Department’s commitment to mutual aid also ensures neighbouring municipalities can rely on their assistance when needed.

The Bolton Family

Richard and Louise Bolton and family were recognized for generations of volunteer service to the Adelaide-Metcalfe community. stories.title: St. Thomas mayor Jeff Kohler aiming for 3.5 per cent tax increase in first budget
stories.summary: Minutes after being sworn in, Jeff Kohler is aiming high in his first budget as St. Thomas’ mayor.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Minutes after being sworn in, Jeff Kohler is aiming high in his first budget as St. Thomas’ mayor.

“We campaigned on inflation or a little bit more, so I’d like to see us in at 3.5 per cent,” Kohler told CTV News.

“That’s going to be very difficult this this year, but we’re working towards that.”

“All throughout the campaign we stressed fiscal responsibility is going to be key,” said Kohler.

Just hours before being sworn in Kohler’s term got off to a booming start. The city has landed defence manufacturer IMT Precision, who will build a new plant at Yarmouth Yards.

A media release was sent out announcing a groundbreaking for a manufacturing facility.

“The event will mark an important milestone in expanding Canada’s defence manufacturing capacity and creating new opportunities in Southwestern Ontario,” the release said.

A year ago, St. Thomas had a 6.1 per cent Municipal property tax increase. Getting to 3.5 per cent could be tricky with the Police Services Board asking for a 10.4 per cent increase to their budget over a year ago.

“I met with the police chief [Mark Roskamp] and we had a great meeting,” said Kohler.

“They were able to soften it a little bit for us [down from 12 per cent in September] to help us move forward. All the departments are doing their best right now to bring the budget in line. I’m not going to lie; we’ve still got a lot of work to do to get there.”

On Tuesday morning, Kohler and the city announced he plans to keep the same directive as former mayor Joe Preston when it comes to strong mayor powers.

He announced he’ll allow council and administration to govern when it comes to governance and budget development.

stories.title: Ottawa spent some $3.45 million on legal fees in connection with Bill 21
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canada’s Justice Department spent approximately $3.45 million in connection with the legal challenge to Quebec’s state secularism law, commonly known as Bill 21.
stories.author: Émilie Bergeron The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Canada’s Justice Department spent approximately $3.45 million in connection with the legal challenge to Quebec’s state secularism law, commonly known as Bill 21.

Nov. 17, 2026

New subscriber benefit!

ajw[](https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/quebec/ottawa-spent-some-3-45-million-on-legal-fees-in-connection-with-bill-21/article_77e97367-e15f-53f1-9baf-3b7906acf987.html)

By Émilie Bergeron The Canadian Press

This estimate is included in a response provided by the federal government to a written question from Bloc Québécois MP Rhéal Fortin.

Fortin says in a press release that it’s shameful that Ottawa is spending Quebecers’ money to challenge a law passed in the provincial legislature.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Bill 21 bans certain government employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols, while requiring anyone providing or receiving a government service to have their face uncovered.

It’s being challenged before the Supreme Court of Canada, which will have to rule on whether the Quebec government’s use of the notwithstanding clause is valid.

The federal government is one of the intervenors who were heard by the country’s highest court, but is not among the plaintiffs in the case.

In its response tabled in Parliament, the Department of Justice specifies that the $3.45 million covers total legal costs, including real and “notional” amounts.

“The services referred to here are litigation services as well as litigation support services,” the statement reads. “The attorneys, notaries, and paralegals at the Ministry of Justice are salaried public servants, and therefore, no legal fees are payable for their services. A ‘notional amount,’ however, may be provided to account for the legal services they render.”

The law was adopted in 2019 under François Legault’s former CAQ government, who hoped to put an end to a long-running debate over so-called “reasonable accommodations” in Quebec.

In February 2024, the Court of Appeal upheld Bill 21 and affirmed that Quebec had the right to preemptively invoke the notwithstanding clause. The Court of Appeal, however, rendered inoperative the section of the law that required elected officials to perform their duties with their faces uncovered.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Liberals hope to take Bloc stronghold in byelection — but it won’t be easy
stories.summary: The Bloc is ready to defend its turf for the federal byelection taking place on Dec. 7.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
After three terms under the banner of the Coalition Avenir Québec, Chantal Soucy said she had made the decision to retire from politics early on in 2026.

That was until she got a call from Prime Minister Mark Carney’s chief of staff, Marc-André Blanchard, in June. Bloc Québécois MP Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay had just announced he would be resigning his seat to run provincially for the Parti Québécois.

Soucy was asked to consider running for the federal Liberals in Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton, a rural riding east of Montreal that she had been representing provincially for the last 12 years.

After a few conversations with Blanchard, Soucy was convinced to run for Carney. She told her constituents in early August she would not be seeking a fourth term for the CAQ, knowing that she would soon be knocking on their doors in a federal byelection.

Soucy said she considered her years of experience as an elected official as well as her knowledge of local issues in making her decision to run at the federal level.

“I am from Saint-Hyacinthe and I am well-versed in the files. Furthermore, having an MP who is part of the government — especially in the current economic climate, with our southern neighbors putting many of our businesses under pressure — is crucial.”

The region is considered the heart of agriculture and agro-food processing in Quebec, and many small and medium businesses rely on the United States as a primary market.

“So, I accepted, saying: ‘Listen, I will be fully operational from day one. I know the issues well — let’s bring Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton into power,’” Soucy said.

It has been 33 years since the riding has had an MP in government. The Bloc Québécois has been the party of choice for voters in the area since 1993, with a brief interlude between 2011 and 2019 when the riding was represented by the NDP.

The Bloc is ready to defend its turf for the federal byelection taking place on Dec. 7.

Caroline Émond, a former delegate general of Quebec in Brussels and former director general of the International Dairy Federation, is counting on her wealth of experience in international relations and the agro-food sector to keep the riding in the blue team.

“So far, what I’m hearing is that (voters) see that my background is fitting the need of the riding, and they actually see that I do have the experience that they need to be a strong voice in Ottawa,” she said.

“I know agriculture. I know supply management. I know Americans. I’ve worked with them. I’ve negotiated with them,” she added.

Émond is back to her political roots, as she has worked for the Bloc in Ottawa in the past. She is also familiar with Bloc Leader Yves-François Blanchet, having worked with him when he was a minister in Pauline Marois’ government and she was a diplomat.

The Bloc was just a natural fit for her. “I’m back home. This is my political family.”

Even though this is the first time Émond is putting her name forward for public office, she said the reaction from voters has been overwhelmingly positive. But she said she is not taking anything for granted and is working hard to keep this seat for the Bloc.

The party even held a special caucus meeting in Saint-Hyacinthe last week and unveiled a local platform adapted to the needs of the riding.

“The reality is that Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton is a riding that has been with the Bloc for a long time, and they are very satisfied with the Bloc and what the Bloc has offered to them in terms of service and representation,” she said.

However, Soucy claims voters in the riding are realizing that they might be better off with an MP in the governing party, where decisions are made.

“The Bloc Québécois, being in the opposition, is left standing in the hallway,” she said. “I, however, can be at the table where those decisions take place.”

The crushing weight of Carney’s popularity in Quebec has made it difficult for the separatist party to make strides in federal byelections in the past year.

The Liberals won Terrebonne and Chicoutimi—Le Fjord despite the Bloc showing better scores in those byelections than in the 2025 election.

Émond is not ready to say that the wind is turning against Carney, but she thinks the federal Liberals won’t be able to use the trade war with the U.S. to their advantage to scare voters into voting for them like they did back in August.

“The reality is that, in the byelection in Chicoutimi, the Liberals actually used the situation with the Americans as a scarecrow,” she said.

“This time, I don’t think they can do it. The situation is a bit different.”

What might be more of a challenge for both parties in the riding is to motivate people to go out and vote. Soucy admitted voters are confused that there are more elections because the Quebec provincial election just wrapped up over a month ago.

But Soucy said the government is not to blame for voters going back to the polls.

“After all, it was the Bloc MP that resigned and abandoned citizens by deciding to run in the provincial election — they are the ones who left an empty seat,” she said.

Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

stories.title: Iihf says it was the target of a cyberattack, takes website offline
stories.summary: The Iihf said it was investigating the source of the cyberattack and was working to restore its systems. Its platforms would be back online soon, it says.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
The International Ice Hockey Federation says it was the target of a cyberattack , with its website currently offline.

Prior to the website going down, an image of Russian players appeared alongside a message accusing the federation of banning a team its opponents couldn’t beat, according to the Associated Press.

In a statement on X, the Iihf didn’t comment on the message that was briefly on its website but said it condemned the attack and was taking necessary steps.

The cyberattack occurred two days after the Iihf announced Russia would not be permitted to play in next month’s World Juniors hockey championship in Alberta.

That decision came after the Prime Minister’s Office said players playing for Russia or Belarus would not be able to compete for their countries “so long as the unjustified war against Ukraine continues.”

Following that decision, the Russian hockey federation said it expressed its “strong protest” against the Iihf decision and called it “unlawful” and “unacceptable.”

Its president had previously threatened to seek compensation from Canada and push for relocation or cancellation of the tournament if Russia was barred.

— with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Warmer El Nino waters heating up B.C.'s coast, ocean researchers say
stories.summary: Victoria - Scientists with Ocean Networks Canada are seeing record-high water temperatures off British Columbia's coast, saying it points to the arrival of El Nino conditions.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Scientists with Ocean Networks Canada have observed record-high water temperatures off British Columbia’s coast this month, saying the uptick points to the arrival of an El Nino pattern on top of underlying climate change.

The University of Victoria initiative operates two sea-floor observatories with cables connecting several research sites, including one off the west coast of Vancouver Island that recorded a temperature of 8.21 C at a depth of 400 metres on Nov. 8.

The reading at the Barkley Canyon Upper Slope was 2.49 C higher than the long-term average at the site, where monitoring began in 2009, and it was 0.89 C warmer than the previous record set in 2019, the group said in a statement issued Tuesday.

El Nino is the result of a reversal or weakening of winds that normally push warm water to the Western Pacific near Australia and Asia, explained Jay Cullen, an oceanographer and the interim president of Ocean Networks Canada.

During an El Nino pattern, he said that warm water “sloshes back” east and spreads once it hits the west coast of North and South America.

“For us here in British Columbia, that warm water travels as a trapped wave along the coast,” Cullen said, noting it also alters atmospheric circulation, potentially resulting in more rain and less snow in coastal areas this winter.

El Nino is a natural cycle. But it’s playing out against a backdrop of long-term global heating that’s already putting ecosystems and organisms under stress, Cullen said.

The warmer water temperatures mean lower dissolved oxygen in areas that include salmon and herring fisheries along with habitat for iconic species, including endangered southern resident killer whales in the Salish Sea, he said.

There’s also economic activity in the region, such as the Port of Vancouver’s Roberts Bank facility, where Ottawa has backed a proposal for a major expansion.

“Increased shipping, increased economic development along our coast, that needs to go hand in hand with monitoring and environmental stewardship,” Cullen said.

He said the warmer temperatures deeper in the ocean are concerning because that’s where many organisms live or retreat to find cooler conditions.

“If that warming associated with El Nino is not just in the very surface, but down to significant depths … that, again, puts the ecosystem under stress.”

El Nino also brings higher water levels, raising the risk of coastal flooding.

“We’ve got about 15 centimetres (of) additional sea level increase,” Cullen said.

“With winter storms and king tides, the potential for coastal flooding is higher … on top of an already warmer and higher sea level than we’ve had historically.”

A graph shared by Cullen’s group showed the daily average temperature at the Barkley site climbing markedly starting in late October.

Cullen said it shows the pulse of warm water moving north from the equatorial Pacific is arriving off B.C.‘s coast, though calmer winds are also a factor, reducing the “upwelling” of cooler water to the surface from depths below.

“Just recently, those upwelling winds relaxed, and that helped to sort of make the arrival of that warm water a little bit more dramatic.”

The Clayoquot Slope, a deeper site more than 1,200 metres below the surface, has also been recording temperatures “significantly” above average, Cullen’s group said.

The Cascadia basin, the deepest in the cluster of sites off Vancouver Island at 2,650 metres, is the lone exception, where temperatures are within usual ranges.

The El Nino pattern will likely peak early next year and “relax” heading into the spring, Cullen said.

Ocean Networks Canada is working with the Fisheries Department to monitor the El Nino and its effects along B.C.‘s coast, he added.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

“For us here in British Columbia, that warm water travels as a trapped wave along the coast,” Cullen said, noting it also alters atmospheric circulation, potentially resulting in more rain and less snow in coastal areas this winter.
El Nino is a natural cycle. But it’s playing out against a backdrop of long-term global heating that’s already putting ecosystems and organisms under stress, Cullen said.

The warmer water temperatures mean lower dissolved oxygen in areas that include salmon and herring fisheries along with habitat for iconic species, including endangered southern resident killer whales in the Salish Sea, he said.
There’s also economic activity in the region, such as the Port of Vancouver’s Roberts Bank facility, where Ottawa has backed a proposal for a major expansion.
“Increased shipping, increased economic development along our coast, that needs to go hand in hand with monitoring and environmental stewardship,” Cullen said.
He said the warmer temperatures deeper in the ocean are concerning because that’s where many organisms live or retreat to find cooler conditions.
“If that warming associated with El Nino is not just in the very surface, but down to significant depths … that, again, puts the ecosystem under stress.”
El Nino also brings higher water levels, raising the risk of coastal flooding.
“We’ve got about 15 centimetres (of) additional sea level increase,” Cullen said.
“With winter storms and king tides, the potential for coastal flooding is higher … on top of an already warmer and higher sea level than we’ve had historically.”
A graph shared by Cullen’s group showed the daily average temperature at the Barkley site climbing markedly starting in late October.

Cullen said it shows the pulse of warm water moving north from the equatorial Pacific is arriving off B.C.‘s coast, though calmer winds are also a factor, reducing the “upwelling” of cooler water to the surface from depths below.
“Just recently, those upwelling winds relaxed, and that helped to sort of make the arrival of that warm water a little bit more dramatic.”
The Clayoquot Slope, a deeper site more than 1,200 metres below the surface, has also been recording temperatures “significantly” above average, Cullen’s group said.
The Cascadia basin, the deepest in the cluster of sites off Vancouver Island at 2,650 metres, is the lone exception, where temperatures are within usual ranges.
The El Nino pattern will likely peak early next year and “relax” heading into the spring, Cullen said.
Ocean Networks Canada is working with the Fisheries Department to monitor the El Nino and its effects along B.C.‘s coast, he added.

stories.title: Pepper spray and hurt officer at scene of man’s beating death: Vancouver constable
stories.summary: Vancouver - A Vancouver police officer who responded to a call for backup on the day Myles Gray was killed says he arrived at the scene and saw a colleague red in the face and barely conscious after being punched.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A Vancouver police officer who responded to a call for backup on the day Myles Gray was killed says he arrived at the scene and saw a colleague red in the face and barely conscious after being punched.

Const. Nick Thompson was testifying Tuesday about the fatal confrontation between police and Gray at a public hearing where the officer faces allegations of abuse of authority for his use of force, having kicked and hit Gray with a baton multiple times as officers tried to subdue him.

Thompson said he arrived at the scene in August 2015 along with Constable Joshua Wong with their lights and sirens on and immediately noticed the smell of pepper spray in the air.

There had been an audible “commotion” from the yard, and he said he heard “nonsensical yelling, but more of that primal yelling that we’d heard on the radio that was ongoing.”

He told the hearing, called by B.C.‘s Police Complaint Commissioner, that a “primal roar” came over the radio while they were on the way to help officers who had encountered Gray.

Three officers had been trying to subdue Gray underneath a large shrub, and he saw Const. Kory Folkestad wide-eyed and “barely” conscious as if “there was nobody home,” Thompson testified.

A police baton and a can of pepper spray were “scattered” on the grass of the yard, he said.

Thompson said he found out later that Gray had knocked Folkestad out and possibly tried to throw him off a retaining wall to the ground, and he worried about “grievous bodily harm or death” from Gray’s “assaultive” actions.

He said Const. Hardeep Sahota, who had first encountered Gray, “kept stressing to us like, ‘be careful. He had knocked out Const. Folkestad.”

Thompson testified that he’d been concerned upon arrival as he saw Gray trying to “overpower” the three officers, thrashing violently and displaying “brute strength.”

“His hips were bucking, he’s trying to, you know, resist with his arms, with all his might. His feet kept thrashing about and kicking and lurching. I recognize that the officers there had some control, but it wasn’t going to last very long,” Thompson said.

He described the officers struggling with Gray as the man was trying to stand up, and said Gray was throwing wild punches with a handcuff around one wrist, which could have been “devastating.”

“I kicked him as hard as I could. There was no change in behaviour,” Thompson said. “That was like, very unusual. I did not expect that as a response.”

Thompson said he had never dealt with a comparable situation to the altercation with Gray.

He said other situations in his policing career have always seen officers gain control of suspects, including one who had jumped off a 21st floor balcony and scaled a building like “Spider-Man,” who Thompson subdued with a beanbag shotgun.

He’s seen people with significant mental illness, agitated, experiencing mania or catatonia, where they could resolve the situation, Thompson testified.

Thompson said Gray “wasn’t responsive to pain” and demonstrated being “physically capable of causing a tremendous amount of destruction.”

The officer also told the hearing Tuesday that he didn’t give a statement on the day of the incident after someone from the police union told him to not take notes or write anything down until he had spoken to a lawyer.

“I can’t remember who it was, but more than one police officer kind of reaffirm that message from the union, ‘don’t take any handwritten notes,’” Thompson said.

Const. Beau Spencer also told the inquiry on Monday that he could not remember which union officials directed him not to take notes.

Thompson testified that he was told at a meeting at police headquarters the night of the death to make his statement by creating a document on his home computer, and it was submitted several months after the altercation.

He said he remembers “bawling” his eyes out on his drive home that night, and said he dissociated in the weeks afterwards and has little memory of the weeks that followed.

He said senior members of the police union told him to be “cognizant” that the Independent Investigations Office, which investigates police actions in such incidents, would try to access his medical records, and it “became very difficult for me to feel comfortable accessing mental health support at that time.”

“My mental health has struggled ever since,” he said.

He’s since been diagnosed with significant anxiety disorder, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder and he’s taken “substantial” time off work, but he’s been accommodated by the police department.

“It is very difficult to have to replay the worst day of my life in a public forum. I just I can’t escape it,” Thompson said.

“I would very much like to move forward, get some closure. I think we all would, but the reality is, is that we’ve been stuck.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026

stories.title: Kinew targets business expansion, affordability in last Throne Speech ahead of election call
stories.summary: Manitoba Premier’s latest pledges focus far more heavily on industry growth than his government has been previously known for
stories.author: Temur Durrani
stories.content:
Just months ahead of a provincial election year, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew is introducing a wide range of new measures focused on health care, affordability and business development in sectors such as mining.

In a Throne Speech delivered on Tuesday by Lieutenant-Governor Anita Neville, the provincial government outlined its legislative priorities leading up to the 2027 election and touted the achievements of the New Democrats since the party came into power a little more than three years ago.

Manitoba ’s general election must be held by next October, though Mr. Kinew hinted earlier this month that he May send voters to the polls in the spring instead of the fall. He has declined to confirm any election dates, however. When pressed on the matter, he has cheekily told reporters to decide on the timing of the vote.

“This will be our last Throne Speech before we ask you for a second mandate,” the Premier said, directly addressing Manitobans in a news conference on Tuesday. “We have come a long way together in just three years, but we know there is a lot more work to do.”

Mr. Kinew’s latest legislative pledges focus far more on industry expansion than his government has been known for in previous years. Analysts and business groups have noted that welfare spending and union-friendly policies have frequently overshadowed broader business-related programs from Mr. Kinew’s government, as he and other NDP premiers in the past have prioritized social measures instead.

While Tuesday’s speech highlighted some health care initiatives – such as opening emergency rooms, rebuilding hospital facilities and providing free vaccinations for shingles – accelerating the pace of economic output was a marquee part of Ms. Neville’s address.

Her delivery in English, French and Anishinaabemowin included promises to increase mineral production, expand mining-related facilities in the province and, as The Globe and Mail first reported on Tuesday, hire industry stalwart Stacy Kennedy to become Manitoba’s first chief mining officer .

Additionally, Manitoba will freeze increased payments on Crown land leases for a fourth consecutive year, which the province says will keep operating costs lower for producers such as those in the cattle and livestock market.

And Manitoba will match the federal government’s Productivity Mega Deduction on business taxes, allowing companies to write off the full cost of acquiring or building new assets in an effort to attract global investors.

“The economic horse pulls the social cart,” Mr. Kinew said, repeating a phrase that has become the hallmark of his government’s guiding political principles.

He said the NDP is often known federally and provincially for its “great ideas” on social programs. “I always say to that, ‘great, but how are we going to pay for that?’ And the way we’ll pay for that is by growing our economy,” Mr. Kinew added.

In announcing Ms. Kennedy’s appointment as chief mining officer, the Premier said he’s proud of Manitoba for being the first province to create such a position on the backdrop of heightened global trade tensions.

“Part of us making sure that we stay competitive and meet the needs of what our economy is going to require to hit the next level is creating this position,” he said.

Konrad Narth, interim leader of the Progressive Conservatives, said his provincial opposition party welcomes Ms. Kennedy’s hiring, but added that Manitoba needs to see “some real action” now.

“We’re rapidly falling down the list of locations for mining interests,” he told reporters on Tuesday at the legislative building.

Criticizing the Premier’s plans, he said he has observed Manitobans wondering aloud if life is better today than it was before Mr. Kinew’s election. “And we’re saying ‘no’ to that question,” Mr. Narth said.

Karen Rees, president of Toronto-based Prospectors and Developers Association of Canada, which represents the interests of the mineral-exploration industry, said her organization is encouraged by Manitoba’s new efforts.

“Greater regulatory certainty and more efficient permitting can help attract investment and move mineral projects forward, and industry experience and knowledge of the province’s mineral sector are important for the new chief mining officer,” Ms. Rees wrote in an e-mailed statement. “A strong mineral sector is vital to Canada’s economic prosperity.”

The Throne Speech also revealed that Manitoba is planning to try and improve affordability with a new tax reduction for families, as part of the next provincial budget. The NDP has not balanced any of its three budgets so far , but Mr. Kinew said his government is on track to meet fiscal equilibrium for 2027-28.

Although he did not divulge many details about the family tax changes on Tuesday, he said they will target middle-class residents. “The rich obviously have a lot of folks helping them, so we think it’s the middle class’ turn to get some help,” he said.

Manitoba is also aiming to ban the use of AI-generated images in real estate. “Because when you get taken for a ride and you rent a bunk apartment that you were misled on, you’re getting ripped off,” Mr. Kinew said.

He declined to confirm whether the ban would be enforced through a new law.

stories.title: ‘Many’ arrested in GTA auto theft network bust will ‘face immigration enforcement action’: Peel police
stories.summary: Peel Regional Police’s Project Cadette resulted the recovery of 96 vehicles and charges against 12 men, eight of whom are Nigerian nationals
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Peel Regional Police busted a transnational auto theft network recently, recovering almost 100 high-end vehicles valued at roughly $4.5 million and arresting 12 men, many of whom “will also face immigration enforcement action” in addition to a lengthy list of charges, deputy chief Nick Milinovich said Monday.

Police identified the arrested parties as Toronto residents Odewale Abraham, 57, Oluyemi Sodade, 51, Tosin Damilola Oyebade, 45, Oluwaseyi Olawale Bameke, 39, Olushola Oke, 42, Vaughan’s Gbolahan Qudus Babatunde, 29, Brampton’s Stanley Udeh, 46, and 58-year-old Kenneth Okafor of no fixed address. All eight have been identified as Nigerian nationals by the BBC and Nigerian news outlet The Cable.

The remaining four are Karamveer Singh, 26, of Brampton, Darryl Davance, 25, of Saint Jerome, Que., as well as Henrik Gancz, 57, and Jaspreet Singh, 25, both of no fixed address.

Canada’s Privacy Act precludes police and the Canada Border Services Agency from disclosing any details about the individuals charged in Project Cadetta, details of which were announced in a Monday press conference, but authorities made it clear they’re serious about removing criminal elements from Canada.

“We do always keep a close eye on what’s happening in the courts,” Cbsa director of intelligence and investigations Abeid Morgan said. “We’re looking for foreign nationals who’ve committed criminal activity and our goal is to remove those individuals from Canada.”

Milinovich spoke even more plainly, explaining Peel police want to see immigration enforcement result from information sharing with federal partners.

“Canada is a great country. We welcome people to be a part of it and to benefit while they’re here. But if you’re targeting our community, then we’re happy to share that information with the appropriate partners to make sure that (you) can no longer benefit from it and the appropriate immigration enforcement can occur,” he said.

The 12 people arrested in Peel Regional Police’s Project Cadetta. Peel Regional Police

Police allege the network was led by five key suspects — Udeh, Abraham, Oyebade, Sodade, and Bameke — who were “responsible for coordinating the theft, movement and export of stolen vehicles,” with the others acting in support.

While some accused face just a handful of charges, others have more than 30, with Abraham facing 48. All 12 men have a combined 231 charges, but police anticipate more could be filed as the investigation continues.

Meanwhile, Peel police have issued arrest warrants for two more men in connection with the investigation — a 16-year-old of no fixed address who can’t be named under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, and 32-year-old Steven Gyamfi, also of no fixed address.

The investigation began this March when Peel police identified a property on Cadetta Road in Brampton’s industrial area that was “linked to the storage, loading, and exportation of stolen vehicles,” explained Detective Sgt. Ian Harloff from the commercial auto crime bureau.

He said it quickly led police to uncover a “larger criminal network operating across Peel region and throughout the GTA” in which stolen vehicles were re-vinned, placed in shipping containers, and moved through a network of loading sites waiting to be shipped to West Africa through Canadian ports.

Re-vinning refers to changing a Vehicle Identification Number — a combination of numbers unique to a vehicle and used to identify it.

When they acted on search warrants this fall, police found “96 stolen luxury SUVs, pickup trucks, and other high-value vehicles” worth an estimated $4.5 million. Most of the seizures took place at the port in Montreal, with some in Halifax, according to Harloff.

The officials gathered for Monday’s press conference also heralded Project Cadetta as another victory against vehicle thefts in the Peel region.

Milinovich said since the peak in 2023, when Peel “was hit with a stolen car almost every single hour,” police efforts in conjunction with partners “speak for themselves.”

“We’ve been able to reduce the number of auto thefts occurring here in Peel by over 50 per cent,” he said, noting a further 11.6 per cent reduction year-to-date in 2026. “We are making a difference.”

Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown celebrated the multi-jurisdictional success and how X-ray scanners the federal government introduced to the GTA region in 2024 have played a vital role.

“We had pushed for scanners not only at the intermodal hubs, but at the Port of Montreal, and with this new technology, with additional staffing, you see the results of this work,” he said Monday.

Six of the 96 vehicles recovered in Project Cadetta. Peel Regional Police

While pleased with their latest win and hopeful it sends a message to others involved in such crimes, officials say the work is far from done.

“Despite the momentum, it should be clear that we are not taking our foot off the gas,” Milinovich said.

Nationally, vehicle theft has been on the decline for the past couple of years, the federal government and the insurance industry reported this fall. The National Action Plan on Combating Auto Theft has led to police-reported incidents dropping 33 per cent since being launched in 2024 and Équité Association’s midyear trend report showed a drop of 10 per cent nationally in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025.

The Insurance Bureau of Canada has also said theft claims fell 24 per cent year-over-year in 2025 and the total theft-related losses fell by almost $370 million last year.

But car theft for the purposes of transnational shipping and sale continues to occur.

Last week, police in Cape Breton arrested four people allegedly involved in “the possession, trafficking, dismantling and resale of more than $10M in stolen motor vehicles and related property across several Canadian provinces and with international connections.”

In August, the RCMP reported that its Project NoCargo, launched in June 2025 with the aim of tracking down suspicious vehicle exports, “led to the interception and recovery of 392 vehicles, with an estimated total value of $28 million in Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver.”

In April, four men were arrested and 10 vehicles were seized in a Montreal police operation involving an alleged stolen vehicle export network, CTV reported.

Kenn Oliver is a web editor and writer for National Post. He is a career journalist of more than 20 years, the bulk of which was spent as a sports writer, business reporter and web editor for the Telegram in St. John's, N.L.
