content_blocks.text: When Christian Sewing became the chief executive of Deutsche Bank in 2018, after a string of scandals had tainted the international bank’s reputation, he promised that the institution would be different: more stable and “a bit more boring.”
The bank has since spent years trying to convince the world that its era of scandals is over.

But a leak of more than 15 million internal files to investigative journalists severely tests that narrative, laying bare a bank that built an enormous compliance machinery to ensure it was following its regulatory and standards obligations but repeatedly struggled to make it work.

Emails from senior executives. Secret risk assessments. Suspicious-transaction reports. Private information about billionaires, oligarchs, politicians and royalty. Records involving Jeffrey Epstein, businessmen sanctioned over ties to Russia, and even Donald Trump. Previously undisclosed companies linked to authoritarian regimes.
Together, they add up to the largest cache of internal documents ever leaked to journalists from within a bank.

The files show Deutsche Bank repeatedly missed warning signs of possible money laundering and sanctions violations. It bent its own rules for powerful clients. It allowed business considerations to override its own compliance regime. Sometimes, the bank only discovered serious failures years after suspicious money had passed through its systems.
A person passes a logo of Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt, Germany. Thomas Lohnes/Getty Images

For months, more than 200 reporters from around the world examined the huge cache as part of an investigation called Inside Deutsche Bank. The records span some of the bank’s most sensitive functions and activities: anti-financial crime, sanctions monitoring, internal auditing and the units responsible for deciding whether risky clients stay or go.
The bank operates across roughly 55 countries directly, including Canada, and more than 140 countries are reached by its correspondent banking network.

The leak of the documents, provided via two whistleblowers, was shared with Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife. Barracuda Media, a non-profit vehicle, was established to analyze the data and share it with reporters from more than 50 global media outlets spanning 46 countries, including the Investigative Journalism Bureau in Canada.

The whistleblowers, whose identities are being protected, say they copied the files and removed them from the institution. Besides giving them to Joseph and Sharife, they also provided material to the U.S. Department of Justice, the U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, and the U.K.’s HM Revenue and Customs, their lawyer said. It is not known what action those agencies have taken.
It is evident that the whistleblowers wanted to expose Deutsche Bank’s relationships with both Russian oligarchs and Russian money.

“We are deeply committed to serving the public interest,” they said in a statement. They said the public has a right to know about the bank’s misconduct and its extensive banking of oligarchs. According to one of the whistleblowers, they believed the files contained potential criminal misconduct regarding business relationships with corrupt regimes.
The files also expose the intimate financial information of well-known or extremely powerful people.
Bank ‘regrets’ Epstein connection

Deutsche Bank accepted Epstein as a client in 2013, years after his conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor. The leak shows the bank later identified more than US$600 million in suspicious transactions involving him and his network — more than twice the amount previously publicly known.
The leak also holds extensive details on alleged Vladimir Putin-allied oligarchs such as Oleg Deripaska and Roman Abramovich.

Deutsche Bank’s clients included a company whose ultimate beneficial owner was a Saudi businessman named on the famous “Golden Chain” list of purported sponsors of al-Qaida, discovered in 2002 during an anti-terrorism raid in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And as a third-party correspondent bank, Deutsche Bank helped process payments linked to the late Rifaat al-Assad, Syria’s former vice-president known as the Butcher of Hama for his role in a bloody 1982 crackdown in the Syrian city.

In 2015, despite mounting adverse media reports and its own suspicious activity reports, or SARs, surrounding Jho Low, Deutsche Bank continued to process millions in transfers linked to the Malaysian financier.
Oleg Deripaska, left, and Roman Abramovich. Anastasia Barashkova/Pool/AFP via Getty Images; Ben Stansall/AFP via Getty Images

Low is a central figure in the 1MDB scandal in which more than US$4.5 billion was allegedly stolen from Malaysia’s state investment fund and laundered through global banks. Deutsche Bank’s Malaysian entity Deutsche Bank (Malaysia) Berhad is now being sued in a civil claim by 1MDB over its alleged role in moving part of these funds.

In a statement on 1MDB, Deutsche Bank said: “Deutsche Bank has not been subject to any regulatory penalty or sanction arising from 1MDB.” It said 1MDB had made “material misrepresentations and omissions to Deutsche Bank officials” in connection with 1MDB’s transactions with the Bank, and said the bank “has cooperated fully with regulatory and law enforcement authorities in relation to inquiries concerning 1MDB.”
It added: “Allegations made by 1MDB in Malaysian civil proceedings concern a different Deutsche Bank entity. We reject any attempt to conflate separate matters.”
On the al-Assad payments, Deutsche Bank said:

“This matter has been resolved in 2022, as publicly disclosed. In the investigation proceedings of the public prosecutor’s office in Frankfurt in connection with two suspicious activity reports (SAR) filed by Deutsche Bank in the correspondent banking business, the bank accepted a fine of € 7.01 million. The administrative penalty notice contains the allegations that the SARs were submitted too late because they should have been made in 2017 already. The bank cooperated in the proceedings.”

Deutsche Bank did not respond to questions about the individual on the Golden Chain list. The individual, who is identified in bank files only by his initials, was identified by reporters but did not respond to a request for comment.
Deripaska, who has previously rejected accusations of wrongdoing and rejected the oligarch label, did not respond to requests for comment.
A law firm representing Abramovich told reporters it is “not for our client to comment on Deutsche Bank’s internal processes and decisions.”

“To the extent those internal processes documented unfounded speculation concerning our client, he rejects that speculation,” they added. “He denies any allegation or suggestion of wrongdoing, including any allegation of criminal conduct, corruption or impropriety.”
Abramovich has also previously rejected being characterized as an oligarch.
Low could not be reached for comment, but has previously denied wrongdoing. The bank said: “We do not comment on potential, former or existing client relationships.”
Jeffrey Epstein. File

On Epstein, the bank said it “acknowledges its error of onboarding Epstein in 2013 and regrets our historical connection with him. We have cooperated with regulatory and law enforcement agencies and the U.S. Congress regarding their investigations and have been transparent in addressing these matters in parallel.”

Deutsche Bank said that numerous findings relayed to it by the project’s reporters are “based on a misleadingly incomplete selection of data or on a misinterpretation of information taken out of context …”

In response to the wide range of topics raised in the leak, Deutsche Bank said matters raised by reporters “date back many years, in some cases decades.” Where relevant, the bank said, these matters were reviewed at the time and were discussed with regulators and competent authorities as necessary.
“We are a different bank today,” the bank added. “Under Christian Sewing’s leadership, Deutsche Bank has gone through a fundamental transformation.”
The bank said it had invested seven billion euros in its financial and regulatory control environment between 2019 and 2025, supported by significant technology investments.

“These investments have been accompanied by a reinforced approach to identify and manage risks and a fundamental shift in culture. This work has supported the remediation of legacy issues and the completion of significant regulatory milestones.”

“Our progress has been recognized by the market, key regulators and supervisory authorities, as well as clients and other stakeholders. We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity.”
Internal probe flagged firms for money laundering, organized crime
The files hold the secrets a major global bank is meant to keep confidential. Now, those secrets are out.

Deutsche Bank has paid more than 20 billion euros in fines and settlements since the year 2000 over identified failures related to mortgage securities, interest-rate manipulation, Russian mirror trades, anti-money-laundering failures, and other misconduct.
Though the bank told reporters it is a “different bank today,” the leaked files show it has not become “boring” as Sewing promised when he took the helm.

In one case never before made public, the leak shows that in 2019 employees found what they believed to be a sprawling money laundering network that had moved hundreds of millions of euros, using the bank’s systems, through companies in Cyprus, Britain, Hong Kong and Ukraine.

The bank’s monitoring systems had detected pieces of the puzzle, but missed the big picture. It took roughly three years before one employee spotted the pattern, leading a manager to joke that the bank had found another “employee of the month.” The manager soon made a more important observation: “Our systems explicitly failed to detect it.”

In a response, the bank said it “takes its anti-financial crime and sanction-related obligations extremely seriously.” It said it “reviews potentially unusual activity, reports matters to the relevant authorities where required, and cooperates with lawful requests for information.”

In Colombia the bank’s own internal investigation, dubbed Project Cali, showed that in 2019 it had processed thousands of transactions for companies linked to the adult entertainment business. The money had been sent to women in Colombia through suspicious paths without the bank reporting most of the transactions to authorities.

The internal investigation flagged at least eight companies for “money laundering,” and another as “organised crime.” When the bank finally spotted the red flags it had missed across 2019, it filed 230 SARs and prohibited all payments from those companies. By that point, millions had already been transacted.
Pedestrians walk by an advertisement for Deutsche Bank AG outside a bank branch in central Berlin, Germany. Krisztian Bocsi/Bloomberg

In a response on Project Cali, Deutsche Bank said it was “a historical review that led to specific remediation measures and a broader reassessment of financial-crime risks across Deutsche Bank’s correspondent- banking portfolio.”

“Decisions on suspicious-activity reporting are governed by jurisdiction-specific legal and confidentiality requirements, and we therefore cannot comment on individual reports, transactions, entities or counterparties.”

Reporters also found that beginning in 2015 Deutsche Bank facilitated transactions worth hundreds of millions of dollars involving the Singapore-based commodities trader Xangbo group without spotting, or acting on, warning signs of suspicious activity.

These included transactions, made via Deutsche Bank’s Singapore branch, between Deutsche Bank’s Xangbo group clients and three companies accused of laundering alleged kickbacks for the Gupta brothers, Indian-born businessmen who have been accused in massive corruption and state capture in South Africa.

The Gupta-linked companies were allowed to move about US$675 million between December 2012 and January 2017 through the Xangbo network, continuing even as South Africa erupted in public protests over the scandal that implicated the brothers. Of these movements, 30 pairs of transactions totalling US$167 million were carried out across multiple accounts, often being done within a day.

It took an external whistleblower’s December 2019 allegations about unrelated, allegedly fraudulent activity in Singapore and elsewhere to finally nudge Deutsche Bank to further examine Xangbo’s transactions in more depth. Even then, records show the bank did not begin the process of exiting its relationship with Xangbo until 2021. Records further show the bank decided there were “no reasonable grounds” to file a report about a suite of convoluted transactions involving Xangbo.
The headquarters of Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt, Germany. Hannelore Foerster/Getty Images

In a response, Xangbo told reporters its accounts at the bank were not closed because of any dealings the group had with the Gupta-linked companies. “That is absolutely false,” a spokesperson said, adding that Deutsche Bank “continued to be our prime broker till 2022.”
The Guptas did not respond to a request for comment. They have previously said allegations against them are politically motivated.

In a response, Deutsche Bank said reporters’ findings on its dealings with Xangbo contained “several inaccuracies.” It said that, “consistent with its legal obligations,” it could not elaborate but “takes its financial crime risk obligations seriously.”
Meanwhile, reporters found that transactions involving suspected North Korean front companies went undetected even though some payment information contained the words “North Korea.”
“As a matter of policy, Deutsche Bank restricted dealing with North Korea and engaged with law enforcement and our regulators, as required,” the bank told reporters.
Client policies ‘breaking the back of our revenue’
Sometimes, reporters found, the problem wasn’t incompetence — it appeared to be the bank’s appetite for business.

In one leaked email, Sewing, who was then a member of the management board, complained that know-your-customer or KYC rules — the basic requirement that banks understand who their clients are, and where their money comes from — were affecting the bottom line. “ KYC bricht uns das revenue Genick,” he wrote. In English, “KYC is breaking the back of our revenue.”
In a response, the bank said it strongly rejects what it called “false insinuations” about Sewing’s “alleged attitude.”

It added: “Christian Sewing always emphasized that controls and risk management must be taken seriously and set as boundaries for the business. His focus on strong controls and risk management builds on a career during which he worked across all three lines of defense, spending the majority of the time in control functions.”
Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing. Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images

A recurring tension runs through the leak: People charged with controlling risk were repeatedly met with people paid to generate revenue. Amid this clash, powerful customers often had room to manoeuvre.

Take Timur Kulibayev, the billionaire son-in-law of Kazakhstan’s former president. Files show the bank acknowledging “historical concern as to the legitimacy of (Kulibayev’s) original source of wealth.”

In internal documents which identify Kulibayev as a bank “client” since as far back as 2006, it is also pointed out that in 2013, a risk analysis commissioned by the bank on Kulibayev had “highlighted a number of corruption allegations” stretching back to the early 2000s.

The bank’s anti-financial-crime department noted that he had not been convicted of corruption, and that one of his companies had provided evidence to show that criminal investigations into him in Europe had been dropped.

Yet after Kulibayev provided insufficient explanation for a January 2020 “inflow” of US$15 million into his account from a United Arab Emirates account, files show Deutsche Bank blocked the incoming funds.

Records indicate that weeks later, employees began the process of opening a Deutsche Bank account in Luxembourg under his wife’s name. Only months after that point did the bank discuss the possibility of ending the long relationship.

Kulibayev, via his law firm, denied any wrongdoing. The law firm said the bank had been made aware of his sources of income, which derived primarily from a joint ownership, with his wife, of the investment firm Almex and its shareholding in Halyk Bank of Kazakhstan.

A statement added: “Any suggestion therefore that Mr Kulibayev (or individuals working for him) concealed his source of wealth from Deutsche Bank, or knowingly provided false or misleading information about it, is categorically false.”
The Deutsche Bank logo is seen in front of its headquarters in Frankfurt, Germany. Florian Wiegand/Getty Images

The law firm said their client was unable to identify the US$15 million transaction in question from their own records, based on the information provided by reporters. It added that any suggestion Kulibayev had personally banked with Deutsche Bank in the mid-2000s was false, and he “did not open a personal account until many years later.” It said reporters were appearing to “conflate the distinct personal and corporate banking relationships maintained by Mr Kulibayev and his businesses.”
Deutsche Bank said it does “not comment on actual, potential or former client relationships.”

Elsewhere, the bank can be seen choosing not to conduct a formal sanctions-risk review for subsidiaries of Bombardier, the Canadian aerospace and defence company, despite internal references to Bombardier’s doing business in “special risk” countries. The justification given for the decision to instead perform an “informal” review included Deutsche Bank’s long relationship with the company. Bombardier revenues from these high-risk countries, it was pointed out, were low.
Bombardier did not respond to a request for comment.
The leak also exposes the flexibility of the bank’s hiring processes.

It recruited the children of influential politicians, executives and government officials, including applicants who failed aptitude tests or lacked qualifications. Alexey Storchak, the son of Russia’s deputy finance minister, was hired in 2010 and subsequently supplied colleagues with non-public information surrounding a bond issuance. As a result, files show Deutsche Bank itself subsequently investigated whether the bank itself should have ever possessed such information.

In 2019, the bank paid US$16.1 million in a settlement after the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigated its hiring program. An internal calculation contained in the leak found that the bank generated roughly US$190 million in revenues from transactions linked to the hiring of relatives of foreign government officials.
Storchak did not respond to a request for comment.
‘Good and bad oligarchs’
Russia, and the bank’s dealings with it, were among the whistleblowers’ primary concerns when contacting reporters with their information.

After Putin annexed Crimea in 2014, Western sanctions forced banks to decide which Russian clients were still palatable. “We started making lists,” a former Deutsche Bank insider told reporters. “Good and bad oligarchs.”

The leaked documents show the bank repeatedly facilitating sanctioned or politically exposed Russians, and remaining reluctant to fully abandon its long Russian entanglement. Documents show that by May 2020, with expansion of certain Russian business being planned by bank leaders, the move was described by one anti-financial-crime specialist as akin to throwing her team in front of a train.
Russia has continued to haunt the bank.

Early this year, German investigators searched Deutsche Bank’s Frankfurt headquarters. Police and Deutsche Bank have not confirmed who was being investigated but a source close to the case told IJB partner paper trail media the raid was conducted over concerns about money the bank had allegedly transferred for Abramovich just days before the Ukraine invasion. The figure involved was several billion euros, the source said.

In their response, the law firm for Abramovich said that it had been instructed to say German authorities had “confirmed to our client that he is not under investigation in connection with the search of Deutsche Bank’s premises by the German Federal Criminal Police Office in January 2026.”

“Neither the German authorities nor Deutsche Bank has referred to our client (whether directly or indirectly) in any public statement about the searches, or indicated that any allegation is being made against him.”

Through correspondent banking, the invisible plumbing of global finance, Deutsche Bank moves money for other banks, giving them access to euros, dollars and international markets. It is lucrative and exceptionally difficult to police, and the underlying customers May be several steps removed from Deutsche Bank itself. Criminals, sanctioned entities and shell companies can disappear inside millions of ostensibly legitimate transactions.
A woman walks past Deutsche Bank headquarters in Frankfurt in January 2026. Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images
Can a bank reliably identify money laundering, drug trafficking and human smuggling within such a system?

“No,” said Ulrich Göres, former head of Deutsche Bank’s anti-financial crime department. Why do banks do it? “For banking for high risk countries, and for high risk industries generally, higher fees can be charged.”

In one of its biggest scandals to date, Deutsche Bank was a major correspondent bank for Danske Bank’s Estonian branch. Roughly 200 billion euros flowed through Danske Bank’s Estonian branch between 2007 and 2015, much of it involving customers from Russia and other former Soviet states. Deutsche Bank helped process international payments for the branch as a correspondent bank.

While German authorities concluded there was no evidence of criminal misconduct on the part of the bank, they levied an administrative fine of 13.5 million euros against Deutsche Bank, in connection with the affair. Such penalties are a weak deterrent, Göres said, unless the penalty payments exceed the income generated previously.
In a response, Danske Bank said:

“The money laundering case was clearly very serious, and what happened during those years should never have happened. We expressed our regret at the time and have consistently done so since. The case was subject to extensive investigations by the bank and the relevant authorities, and in 2022, the matter was concluded through coordinated resolutions with the Danish and U.S. authorities. Since then, Danske Bank has implemented fundamental changes across the bank and invested significantly in systems, capabilities and controls aimed at preventing and detecting financial crime.
On correspondent banking, Deutsche Bank said:

“Over the past decade, Deutsche Bank has substantially reduced its risk profile in this business, including exiting high-risk clients and countries. At the same time the bank has materially strengthened its financial crime controls and expertise … to manage the inherently elevated financial-crime risk in correspondent banking through significant investments.”
Trump bank data allegedly leaked

When Trump won his first presidential term on Nov. 8, 2016, Deutsche Bank faced an almost unprecedented situation: the president-elect was also one of its most controversial borrowers. The bank created a special project around him, codenamed “Novus Ordo.” New Order.

Trump-related documents were secured. Access was restricted. Communications were encrypted. Personal contacts minimized. But there was a larger problem: Trump and his businesses still wanted things from Deutsche Bank, like changes to existing loans.

The relationship had already gone spectacularly wrong once. After Trump failed to repay a loan for his Chicago tower during the financial crisis, claiming he was not required to because the financial crisis was an unforeseen event, he sued Deutsche Bank for US$3 billion, essentially blaming it for a crisis that had damaged his business (the case was settled before trial). Deutsche Bank continued doing business with him.
Trump did not respond to requests for comment.

Reporters found that by 2017, with Trump well into his first term, a Deutsche Bank employee accidentally sent an outside party a link containing financial information for 1,586 customers. Three accounts allegedly belonged to the newly-inaugurated president; these were called “DT” and “DJT” internally.
Managers debated whether Trump had to be informed of the leak, but concluded he did not. One manager called it a “brilliant outcome.” Sewing approved the case’s handling with a simple, “Ok.”
Donald Trump on Nov. 20, 2016. Drew Angerer/Getty Images

The Inside Deutsche Bank leak comes at a particularly sensitive time for an institution already under heightened scrutiny. This year alone, its offices have been raided at least four times by authorities, and the bank has reportedly filed several self-disclosures with authorities.

Amid this mounting pressure, the leak offers an unprecedented glimpse into what has been going on behind closed doors. Trump. Epstein. Deripaska. Abramovich. Jho Low. The list of major names, and global corporations, in the leak is enormous.
The bank itself had anticipated the danger.

After a much smaller incident involving misdirected customer information in 2021, an employee warned that specialized law firms might see a potential business model in suing the bank over data breaches. Soon, the employee predicted, customers would be able to find standard legal claims online and copy them “1:1”.
The Inside Deutsche Bank leak is of an entirely different magnitude.

Again and again, the files show the same sequence: a warning appears, compliance teams raise concerns, executives debate risk, and the bank finds a reason to continue. Sometimes the client was an oligarch. Sometimes the business involved a sanctioned market or a lucrative energy project. Sometimes, the bank’s systems simply failed to notice what was happening at all.

With files from: Sophia Baumann (PTM), Maria Christoph (PTM), Eva Jung (Berlinske), Michael Lund (Berlinske), Maria Fernanda Cruz (Barracuda Media), Aidila Razak (Barracuda Media), Nikita Saxena (Confluence), Craig Bentley-McKune (Financial Mail), Vernon Wessels (Financial Mail), Cynthia O’Murchu (Financial Times), iStories, Hakan Tanriverdi (PTM), Lukas Kotkamp (Follow the Money), Naish Gawen (Data Desk), Maria Teresa Ronderos (Clip), Francisca Skoknic (Clip), Karina Shedrofsky (Darc), Vivian Yap (Malaysiakini), Nigel Aw (Malaysiakini), Aung Naing (Myanmar Now), Amy Doffegnies (Myanmar Now), Hala Nasreddine (Daraj). The Inside Deutsche Bank investigation was coordinated by Barracuda Media in South Africa, with technical support from theData and Research Center(Darc) in Germany.

stories.title: Ontario’s first small modular reactor will not meet $7.7-billion budget, 2030 target
stories.summary: Small modular reactors have been pitched as a way to avoid the cost overruns that have plagued new nuclear plants.
stories.author: Marco Chown Oved
stories.content:
The Ontario government’s plan to build the first small modular nuclear reactor (SMR) in the G7 has had its first setback.

Ontario Power Generation (OPG), the province’s publicly owned power utility, announced last week that the SMR being constructed at Darlington will be both late and over budget — though it didn’t say by how much.

In its quarterly report, OPG blamed the designer, GE Vernova Hitachi for the delay, saying the company’s “ongoing engineering” has had “impacts on construction execution and supply chain performance.”

OPG did not provide a new timetable for the first of four planned SMRs, which was originally scheduled for completion in 2028, before being pushed back to 2030. No new budget was provided, but OPG is “no longer expected to achieve” the original $7.7 billion target. (The four SMRs had an initial total budget of $21 billion .)

SMRs have been pitched as a way to avoid the construction delays and cost overruns that have plagued new nuclear plants across Europe and North America. Because they’re smaller, many of the components can be built in a factory off-site and trucked in. This will allow for a more streamlined and repeatable construction process, which, it was said, would reduce costs and make timelines more predictable.

A nuclear plant can provide the power of tens of thousands of renewables all at once — even when the wind isn’t blowing, and the sun isn’t

“The problem is not so much that it is over budget; after all, you can make any project stay within budget if you make the budget big enough,” said veteran energy strategist Ralph Torrie, research director at Corporate Knights. “The real concerns here are that the plant is so expensive in the first place, that it is the Ontario taxpayers that are holding the bag, that it takes too long to build, and that nuclear plants keep generating unexpected costs even after they are built.”

In a statement, GE Vernova Hitachi said the overruns were the result of “engineering, procurement and construction, as well as evolving market conditions, including inflation and geopolitical risks.”

“We remain focused on working collectively with OPG and our partners to address challenges, apply lessons learned and support successful delivery and operations for OPG, Ontario and beyond,” wrote spokesperson Jon Allen.

In an email, OPG spokesperson Neal Kelly said the utility is undertaking a comprehensive cost and schedule assessment, due mid-next year.

Canada needs to prioritize investing in wind, solar, and battery storage, in addition to its costly, slow-moving $100-billion nuclear power

Energy Minister Stephen Lecce said the SMR project has delivered “first mover-advantage” in the form of $362 million in contracts and 18,000 new jobs.

“We expect GE Vernova Hitachi and project partners to deliver on their commitments and maintain rigorous project oversight to ensure maximum value for the Canadian supply chain,” Lecce said.

Premier Doug Ford’s government has gone all in on nuclear power to meet growing demand for electricity to run data centres, EVs and heat pumps. In addition to reversing the previous Liberal government’s decision to shut down the Pickering nuclear plant, which is now undergoing a decade-long refurbishment at an estimated cost of $26.8 billion , Ford’s Progressive Conservatives have also decided Ontario would build the first SMRs in the Western world and announced plans for two new full-sized plants — including one in Wesleyville, which if built, would be the biggest nuclear plant in the world.

With more than $73 billion already budgeted for nuclear projects, not including the new full–sized builds that have not yet been approved, provincial taxpayers and ratepayers could be on the hook for $100 billion or more . Critics say the province could get power more quickly and cheaply by investing in renewables, like solar, wind and batteries (all of which the province is also procuring).

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, left, and Prime Minister Mark Carney are shown equipment at the Darlington Energy Complex during an Oct. 23, 2025, announcement.

“New small and large nuclear reactors are the highest cost and slowest options to meet our future electricity needs. It doesn’t make sense to build new nuclear reactors when solar and wind projects can be built in two years or less at one-third the cost,” said Jack Gibbons, chair of the Ontario Clean Air Alliance.

The province says the equivalent amount of power from renewables would take up too much space.

As the nuclear build-out accelerates, Queen’s Park has changed a rule that governed how power is paid for, the Star previously reported. In order to avoid the entire cost hitting power bills when the plants come online, electricity bills now include charges for nuclear power plants that aren’t yet in service . In light of the delay, however, OPG said it has asked to defer some SMR costs until its project assessment is complete.

The province has boasted of its nuclear expertise being able to bring refurbishments in on time and on budget , citing the recent return to service of the last unit at Darlington in February. But reporting in the Globe and Mail has revealed the plant had to take reactors back out of service within weeks, and has now scheduled billions of dollars of additional maintenance.

Ontario taxpayers are still paying off the original construction debt for the Darlington nuclear plant, which was completed in 1993. Until 2017, it was listed as a “debt retirement charge” on power bills, but it has now been rolled into general provincial public debt. As of last year, billions in debt had yet to be paid off.

This article was updated following publication to include a statement from GE Vernova Hitachi.

In light of the delay, however, OPG said it has asked to defer some SMR costs until its project assessment is complete.

The province has boasted of its nuclear expertise being able to bring refurbishments in on time and on budget , citing the recent return to service of the last unit at Darlington in February. But reporting in the Globe and Mail has revealed the plant had to take reactors back out of service within weeks, and has now scheduled billions of dollars of additional maintenance.

Ontario taxpayers are still paying off the original construction debt for the Darlington nuclear plant, which was completed in 1993. Until 2017, it was listed as a “debt retirement charge” on power bills, but it has now been rolled into general provincial public debt. As of last year, billions in debt had yet to be paid off.

stories.title: Could this tool help more emergency patients avoid unnecessary hospital stays?
stories.summary: For patients arriving in the emergency department with lower gastrointestinal bleeding, one of the most important decisions physicians face is whether they can safely recover at home or require…
stories.content:
Stories November 17, 2026

For patients arriving in the emergency department with lower gastrointestinal bleeding, one of the most important decisions physicians face is whether they can safely recover at home or require admission to hospital. A new study led by Dr. Michael Sey, an associate professor of medicine and epidemiology and biostatistics at Western University and a gastroenterologist and scientist at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute, suggests the Oakland Score could help make that decision with greater confidence.

In a study involving 344 patients across eight Canadian hospitals, the Oakland Score outperformed other commonly used bleeding risk tools and performed comparably to physician clinical judgment when identifying patients who could be safely discharged. It also resulted in the fewest instances where a patient who required further observation was instead discharged home. The findings could help lower-risk patients avoid unnecessary hospital admissions while ensuring higher-risk patients receive the care and monitoring they need.

Lower gastrointestinal bleeding is a common reason for emergency department visits. While most patients recover without intervention, a small percentage experience serious complications that can require procedures, hospitalization or, in some cases, become life-threatening. Determining who can be safely discharged and who should remain under observation can be challenging for clinicians.

“The challenge is identifying the small group of patients who May develop serious complications while avoiding unnecessary admissions for those who are likely to recover safely,” says Sey. “Our study shows that the Oakland Score can help support that decision by identifying patients at low risk of complications.”

The study also addressed a longstanding gap in previous research. Although the Oakland Score was designed to help identify patients who can safely go home, most previous studies examined only patients who were admitted to hospital because they were easier to follow and study. As a result, researchers and clinicians knew a great deal about how risk scores performed in these patients, but little about how they performed in patients who were discharged from emergency departments.

“We developed and validated tools to identify patients who could be discharged safely,” says Sey. “But most of the data came from hospital admissions. To truly know whether a score works, you have to study the patients who went home without an admission to hospital, the very patients the risk scores seek to identify.”

To address this question, researchers followed patients who presented to the emergency department with lower gastrointestinal bleeding between 2019 and 2024. The team tracked outcomes in both admitted and discharged patients, which allowed researchers to evaluate how well the Oakland Score performed in real-world emergency department settings. Researchers compared the Oakland Score with several established bleeding risk assessment tools and physician clinical judgment. They then assessed whether patients experienced adverse outcomes, such as readmission, the need for further medical intervention, or death.

The findings suggest the Oakland Score can help clinicians identify low-risk patients who May be safely managed at home while reducing the likelihood of discharging patients who require additional observation.

“Due to the need to consider issues beyond the bleeding event, such as social supports, co-existing medical conditions, and the availability of timely follow up, there is no single risk score that can replace clinical judgment,” says Sey. “But when used alongside clinical assessment, tools like the Oakland Score can give physicians greater confidence in their decisions and help ensure patients get the right level of care.”

stories.title: Celebrating the generosity behind student success
stories.summary: At Fanshawe's recent donor appreciation event, two speakers offered different but equally meaning
stories.content:
At Fanshawe's recent donor appreciation event, two speakers offered different but equally meaningful perspectives on the impact of giving. One, among the College's longstanding donors, reflected on a commitment to supporting education. The other, a multi-award-winning student, shared how donor support has helped shape her educational journey.

Ruth Gates-Jensen's connection to Fanshawe spans more than five decades. She joined the College in 1970 as a teacher at the St. Thomas/Elgin Regional Campus and went on to hold several roles during her 31-year career, retiring in 2001 as Vice President of Business Development.

Shortly before her retirement, Gates-Jensen established an academic award to support a female student pursuing a career in a field where women were traditionally underrepresented. Her commitment to the next generation of women in technology and the skilled trades has continued well beyond her time at the College.

Through additional gifts, including setting up a life insurance policy payable to Fanshawe and a recent donation of stocks, she has helped ensure the long-term sustainability of the awards. Today, two students receive $2,000 awards each academic year.

“The awards were set up to demonstrate a vote of confidence in women and thus assist the recipients as they prepare for their careers in these challenging employment areas, knowing that they are supported by Fanshawe College and its supporters,” said Gates-Jensen. “I encourage anyone here to support the College and know that it will be one of the best investments you can make today.”

For Holly Venter, a student entering her final year of Fanshawe's Building Renovation Technician program, donor support has meant much more than financial assistance.

She says each of the three awards she has received has helped build her confidence, recognize her accomplishments and encourage her to pursue new opportunities.

Venter explained to donors how the awards have helped her persevere through challenging coursework by holding herself accountable. “I never gave up because I had to prove that you made the right choice (in selecting me),” she said.

She explained how having people she had yet to meet “in my corner and always rooting for me” stayed with her throughout her studies, empowering her to take on new experiences like participating in a timber framing trip abroad where she discovered a new passion and formed friendships across borders.

Venter said her most recent award – for Best Overall Video Creator in the Duke of Edinburgh’s 2026 Award in Action Video Contest – “ignited a fire that has not and will not stop burning until I reach my goals because you have given me the confidence to know that I will reach them.”

content_blocks.text: At Fanshawe's recent donor appreciation event, two speakers offered different but equally meaningful perspectives on the impact of giving. One, among the College's longstanding donors, reflected on a commitment to supporting education. The other, a multi-award-winning student, shared how donor support has helped shape her educational journey.
content_blocks.html: At Fanshawe's recent donor appreciation event, two speakers offered different but equally meaningful perspectives on the impact of giving. One, among the College's longstanding donors, reflected on a commitment to supporting education. The other, a multi-award-winning student, shared how donor support has helped shape her educational journey.

content_blocks.text: Ruth Gates-Jensen's connection to Fanshawe spans more than five decades. She joined the College in 1970 as a teacher at the St. Thomas/Elgin Regional Campus and went on to hold several roles during her 31-year career, retiring in 2001 as Vice President of Business Development.
content_blocks.html: Ruth Gates-Jensen's connection to Fanshawe spans more than five decades. She joined the College in 1970 as a teacher at the St. Thomas/Elgin Regional Campus and went on to hold several roles during her 31-year career, retiring in 2001 as Vice President of Business Development.

content_blocks.text: Shortly before her retirement, Gates-Jensen established an academic award to support a female student pursuing a career in a field where women were traditionally underrepresented. Her commitment to the next generation of women in technology and the skilled trades has continued well beyond her time at the College.
content_blocks.html: Shortly before her retirement, Gates-Jensen established an academic award to support a female student pursuing a career in a field where women were traditionally underrepresented. Her commitment to the next generation of women in technology and the skilled trades has continued well beyond her time at the College.

content_blocks.text: Through additional gifts, including setting up a life insurance policy payable to Fanshawe and a recent donation of stocks, she has helped ensure the long-term sustainability of the awards. Today, two students receive $2,000 awards each academic year.
content_blocks.html: Through additional gifts, including setting up a life insurance policy payable to Fanshawe and a recent donation of stocks, she has helped ensure the long-term sustainability of the awards. Today, two students receive $2,000 awards each academic year.

content_blocks.text: “The awards were set up to demonstrate a vote of confidence in women and thus assist the recipients as they prepare for their careers in these challenging employment areas, knowing that they are supported by Fanshawe College and its supporters,” said Gates-Jensen. “I encourage anyone here to support the College and know that it will be one of the best investments you can make today.”

content_blocks.text: For Holly Venter, a student entering her final year of Fanshawe's Building Renovation Technician program, donor support has meant much more than financial assistance.

content_blocks.text: She says each of the three awards she has received has helped build her confidence, recognize her accomplishments and encourage her to pursue new opportunities.

content_blocks.text: Venter explained to donors how the awards have helped her persevere through challenging coursework by holding herself accountable. “I never gave up because I had to prove that you made the right choice (in selecting me),” she said.

content_blocks.text: She explained how having people she had yet to meet “in my corner and always rooting for me” stayed with her throughout her studies, empowering her to take on new experiences like participating in a timber framing trip abroad where she discovered a new passion and formed friendships across borders.

stories.title: Ontario public high school teachers vote 96 per cent in favour of strike mandate
stories.summary: "Members have sent the Ford government a clear message: We are united, we expect better," said the union president.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
Ontario’s public high school teachers have voted 96 per cent in favour of job action, the second education union to have wrapped up a strike vote in advance of talks resuming.

Education workers represented by the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation had strong but slightly less support, with 92 per cent approval among those who voted.

“Our members are telling us they want us to go to the table and get the supports our students absolutely need,” said president Martha Hradowy, who was at Queen’s Park on Tuesday. “We should not be going to the bargaining table just asking for the basics.”

On Monday, the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association released its strike-vote results, with 98 per cent in favour.

Both unions have stressed that the votes don’t necessarily mean teachers and school staff will strike, but do give negotiators a stronger mandate at the bargaining table.

Unions are legally required to take a number of steps before calling any job action, including bargaining in earnest.

Initial talks last June were stalled after the province tried to add items to central bargaining tables that the unions said best remain at local negotiations with individual boards. (A labour board ruling on that issue is expected in the coming days.)

In the last round of bargaining, under a different president, the secondary union was the first to agree to send salary and other items to arbitration rather than hammer out a deal with the province, a controversial call that did, however, avert any labour disruption in schools.

Education Minister Paul Calandra said the strong strike vote results don’t stress him out because they are in line with past votes.

The underlying message is “get to the table, negotiate a deal, be fair to us,” he told reporters. “And it’s the same message to the union: Get to the table, make sure you come out with a fair deal, but ultimately put student achievement at the top of the agenda, and that’s what we’re going to do.”

But NDP Leader Marit Stiles disagreed, saying the results show “very clearly … that this minister has failed. Our kids are struggling. Our education workers are burning out.”

Hradowy expressed frustration that the government wouldn’t consent to bargaining over the summer to hammer out solutions to larger class sizes, dwindling supports for students with “hundreds” of educational assistants, speech language pathologists and other support staff “gone.”

All education contracts expired at the end of August, and talks typically extend for months past that before a deal is reached.

The high school teachers union and the province will resume bargaining Friday for its education workers, and Nov. 24 for teachers.

The Ontario government spent $42.7 billion on education in 2025-26. Although a historical high, a recent report by Ontario’s financial watchdog said that when inflation is factored in, funding is actually decreasing on a per-student basis.

Lane restrictions will be in place at the intersection of Huron Street and Highbury Avenue North starting Wednesday, November 18 while crews are doing maintenance on underground water infrastructure. This work is anticipated to be complete by Friday, November 20.

No scheduled water interruptions are expected as part of this work.

Drivers should follow posted signs and expect traffic delays and changing traffic conditions.

Visit theRenew London map for information about this project and other road and infrastructure projects in London.

stories.title: Billowing smoke and large flames seen from structure in southeast London, Ont.
stories.summary: A large response from first responders to a structure fire in southeast London, Ont. Monday night.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson, Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Crews remain on scene Tuesday morning after a large response from first responders to a structure fire in southeast London on Monday night.

Fire crews arrived to an address in the 3700 block of Old Victoria Road, between Bradley Avenue and Wilton Grove Line, to find a building engulfed in flames.

At it’s peak, there were about 20 personnel fighting the blaze with Thames Centre being called in for assistance to truck water.

About 10 firefighters remained on scene this morning.

There are no reports of injury to people or animals, and no details have been provided into the cause of the blaze or damage estimate.

stories.title: China and Canada expand tariff relief while Ottawa-Washington relations are strained
stories.summary: Shenzhen, China (AP) — The leaders of China and Canada agreed Tuesday on additional tariff cuts as they pledged for deeper ties and Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States.
stories.author: E. Eduardo Castillo The Associated Press
stories.content:
Shenzhen, China (AP) — The leaders of China and Canada agreed Tuesday on additional tariff cuts as they pledged for deeper ties and Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties.

stories.title: Flying out of Kelowna is about to get more expensive as airport fees increase
stories.summary: Travellers flying out of Kelowna International Airport will soon be paying more for parking and airport improvement fees.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Travellers flying out of Kelowna International Airport will soon be paying more for parking and airport improvement fees.

On Monday, Kelowna City Council unanimously approved a new fee structure that will see several airport charges increase, including short-term and long-term parking rates.

The changes take effect Dec. 1.

The hourly rate for short-term parking will move to a flat $3 per hour, replacing the current rate of $2.25 for the first hour and $3.50 for each additional hour.

But the daily maximum for short-term parking will increase significantly, climbing from $27 to $50.

Airport officials say the higher daily rate is intended, in part, to discourage travelers from using the short-term lot for extended stays.

Weekly parking in the long-term lot will also become more expensive, increasing from $88 to $100.

“I fly out twice a year and in between, so it’s not a good thing at all, ” said Penticton resident Rona Schwager.

Parking isn’t the only thing going up. The Airport Improvement Fee (AIF), paid by every departing passenger, will gradually increase from the current $31 to $39 over the next five years, an increase of approximately 26 per cent.

The first increase from $31 to $33 takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Kelowna International Airport’s CEO said the revenue is needed to help fund $423 million in planned capital investment projects over the coming years at the country’s 9th busiest airport.

“When you look at our growth rate of our airport, we’ve been amongst the busiest airports in the country,” said Sam Samaddar. “With that passenger growth, we, you know, we need different infrastructure investments to support that growth.”

Some of the major investments include terminal expansions, runway resurfacing and a new roundabout for easier airport access.

Samaddar said that a review of airport fees found the new rates are comparable to other similarly-sized airports.

“The airport improvement fee that I understand,” said Kelowna resident Colin Chatfield, who was concerned about rising parking costs. “Parking fees are already quite high.”

There is some good news for travelers who drive to the airport.

A new seven-storey parkade is nearing completion and will add more than 1,000 stalls to the parking inventory.

stories.title: Carney meets with President Xi in Shenzhen, China ahead of Apec summit
stories.summary: It's the second in-person meeting the two have held in China this year. The meeting took place in the high-tech hub in the Pearl River Delta megacity region in southeast China.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting in the metropolis of Shenzhen as Carney seeks to expand trade with China on everything from agriculture and energy to financial services and automobiles.

The meeting took place mid-morning on Tuesday in the high-tech hub in the Pearl River Delta megacity region in southeast China, where Xi will host the Apec leaders summit on Wednesday and Thursday.

It’s the second in-person meeting the two have held in China this year. In January, Carney travelled to Beijing for a meeting with Xi, marking the first official discussion between a Canadian prime minister and Chinese president in more than eight years.

Carney says there are “clear guardrails” about what is on the table with China and that discussions around the auto sector are also dependent on ongoing trade talks with the United States.

Canada’s turn to China is in part because of its pivot away from the United States, which under President Donald Trump has imposed wide-ranging tariffs and even threatened to annex Canada through economic coercion.

Carney has reinvigorated Canada’s economic relationship with China as part of his bid to expand Canada’s trade away from an overreliance on the United States.

Since that January meeting, Canada’s exports to China have surged 40 per cent as both countries agreed to drop various tariffs including on electric vehicles and some agricultural products.

Oil, canola and peas are among the products that have seen big jumps in exports to China.

Ahead of the trip, Carney said Canada could do more with China in terms of agriculture, clean and conventional energy, and financial services.

Carney is in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, or Apec. Earlier on this trip, he was in the Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, Cambodia for the Francophonie summit, and Ireland for a European Political Community meeting.

Carney said he expected to speak with Xi about “the evolution of the international system, China’s role in that and Canadian priorities.”

An overarching topic will be Chinese investments into Canada’s auto sector. Both countries agreed earlier this year to allow a limited amount of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada.

Carney has said he wants Chinese carmakers to set up shop, but only if they provide decent jobs, saying he is wary of plants where workers assemble cars using components mostly made in China. Canada has already said no to that as an option for the shuttered Stellantis plant in Brampton, Ont.

Carney said trade talks with Washington will shape how Canada approaches Chinese investment, and that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail.

Those comments prompted blowback from Trump trade adviser Peter Navarro.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S,” Navarro posted on X on Monday. “This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive — as it is already doing.”

Navarro went on to say Vancouver is not British Columbia, it’s “PRC” or People’s Republic of China.

The relationship between Canada and China had soured during the tenure of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, largely over accusations from Canada about foreign interference from China.

Before leaving Canada, Carney said he would raise foreign interference with Xi, prompting a Chinese government spokesperson to deny any such activities take place.

stories.title: Alert Ready will test national emergency alarm on Wednesday
stories.summary: Torontonians can expect to receive alerts over the phone, television and radio at 12:55 p.m. on Nov. 18.
stories.author: Megan Mills Devoe
stories.content:
On Wednesday, Alert Ready will be testing Canada’s national emergency alert system. Torontonians can expect to receive alerts over the phone, television and radio at 12:55 p.m. on Nov. 18.

Alert Ready is used to notify Canadians of emergencies such as Amber Alerts, environmental hazards, national security threats, major fires, natural disasters and other threats to public safety.

stories.title: Peloza pitches changing how London’s committee chairs and vice-chairs chosen
stories.summary: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza wants to change how the chairs and vice-chairs of three standing committees at city hall are chosen, in a move that acknowledges Strong-Mayor Powers, but would give individual councillors a voice in the process.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Coun. Elizabeth Peloza wants to change how the chairs and vice-chairs of three standing committees at city hall are chosen, in a move that acknowledges Strong-Mayor Powers, but would give individual councillors a voice in the process.

Among the Strong-Mayor Powers given to Mayor Josh Morgan by the provincial government last term, was the legislative authority to appoint the chairs and vice-chairs of city hall’s standing committees.

However, Peloza’s motion recommends each standing committee be asked to nominate its own choices for the roles for appointment by Morgan.

“The mayor does have, and has used, his Strong-Mayor Powers to appoint the chairs of these committees. My motion would allow for a vote by all committee members to make the selection of chair and vice chair themselves,” she told CTV News.

Her motion would be restricted to three standing committees at city hall, the Infrastructure and Corporate Services Committee (Icsc), the Planning and Environment Committee (PEC), and the Community and Protective Services (Caps) Committee.

Peloza believes giving each committee member a say in the decision would strengthen the sense of collaboration following last month’s election, “I believe this will help set the tone as the next four years for this council.”

Current policies require the deputy mayor to chair the Strategic Priorities and Policy Committee (Sppc), and the budget chair to lead the Budget Committee and Audit Committee.

Mayor Josh Morgan has responded to Peloza’s motion in a letter.

“I firmly believe it is important that Council and committee members have the opportunity to confirm their support for those serving in these roles,” he wrote prior to listing three councillors for consideration as standing committee chairs.

- Infrastructure and Corporate Services: Coun. Shawn Lewis

- Planning and Environment Committee: Coun. Skylar Franke

- Community and Protective Services Committee: Coun. Hadleigh McAlister

Morgan explained, “I am asking Sppc to consider and ratify these nominations before I formally exercise my appointment authority.”

He added, “I believe this motion allows chairs to know they have the support of their colleagues, and recognizes the importance of experience, stability and continuity as we begin a new term of Council.”

Peloza acknowledges the mayor has final authority, but believes her proposal is more collaborative.

“Recognizing Strong Mayor Powers are something he inherently has at any moment, [and] can use them or revoke any chair or vice chair, even if we decide to go this way,” she explained. “But it’s the spirit of collaboration I’m trying to get to.”

A council committee will consider Peloza’s motion, and the mayor’s letter, at a meeting on Wednesday, Nov. 17.

stories.title: Two senior Poilievre staffers decamp to BC Conservatives
stories.summary: Both say decision to join provincial team reflected desire to return home, have not lost confidence in Conservative Leader
stories.author: Stephanie Levitz
stories.content:
Two senior members of federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre ’s office are joining B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson’s team as the provincial Tories prepare take over the reins of government and Mr. Poilievre’s party struggles to gain momentum in opposition.

Mr. Poilievre’s director of communications, Micah Green, and his director of media relations, Sam Lilly, announced Monday they have taken positions with Mr. Doerkson’s government.

Both men have roots in British Columbia and said their decision to join the provincial Conservative team reflected a desire to return home. Mr. Green and his wife, Hayley Quipp – who also works Mr. Poilievre – are expecting their first child in the spring. The pair met knocking on doors for the federal party. Ms. Quipp is also leaving her job.

Both Mr. Lilly and Mr. Green said they have not lost confidence in Mr. Poilievre.

“Pierre has my full support. I believe he can win the next election, and I believe he would be an outstanding prime minister. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together,” Mr. Green said in a statement.

“This decision is about becoming a father, returning to my home province, and accepting an exceptional career opportunity.”

Staff switching between federal and provincial political parties isn’t uncommon, especially after an election.

But the exodus from Mr. Poilievre’s office also reflects the federal political landscape. Prime Minister Mark Carney now has a majority government, and the next chance for Mr. Poilievre to try for a victory with the electorate is likely three years away.

In a memo to caucus and staff sent late Monday announcing the staff changes, Mr. Poilievre’s chief of staff, Steve Outhouse, noted the pull of B.C. for federal staffers who hail from the province as he thanked the departing staff.

“Last month’s election of a Conservative government in British Columbia was exciting for the conservative movement,” he wrote in the memo, a copy of which was obtained by The Globe and Mail.

In addition to Mr. Green, Ms. Quipp and Mr. Lilly, Mr. Poilievre’s senior policy adviser Andrew Evans also announced his departure Monday for a role in the private sector.

Aaron Wudrick, Mr. Poilievre’s deputy chief of staff, told colleagues earlier this month that he’s leaving the office. Mr. Poilievre’s director of photography, John Lehmann, also departed this month.

The staff departures are on top of the loss of nine Conservative MPs since the 2025 election.

One MP stepped down so Mr. Poilievre could run in a by-election after losing his seat in the general election. Then, four crossed the floor to the Liberals, one quit and accepted a Senate appointment, one recently announced he’ll resign later this year, and two have already stepped down.

By-elections for the latter two seats – Yorkton–Melville in Saskatchewan and Brantford–Brant South in Ontario – are taking place next month.

The Saskatchewan seat is a Conservative stronghold, but the Ontario riding is expected to be a tougher fight for Mr. Poilievre’s party.

He appointed a candidate for the riding, but a long-time Conservative Party volunteer is running as independent, raising the potential for a vote split on the right.

Nationally, polls suggest the Poilievre Conservatives lag around 10 percentage points behind Mr. Carney’s Liberals.

Six Liberals have also resigned since the 2025 election, including former cabinet ministers Chrystia Freeland, Steven Guilbeault, Jonathan Wilkinson and Bill Blair. The latter two were given diplomatic appointments.

Mr. Poilievre’s staff are joining a team of seasoned operatives in British Columbia as the Doerksen government prepares to be sworn in on Friday.

The premier-designate’s chief of staff is Dimitri Pantazopoulos, a fixture in conservative politics for decades, and Angelo Isidorou is Mr. Doerkson’s principal secretary.

Mr. Isidorou served as executive director of the BC Conservative Party before resigning under the leadership of former party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

Ms. Findlay stepped down just ahead of Premier David Eby’s decision to call an election. Mr. Doerkson became interim leader and beat Mr. Eby’s New Democrats. The BC Conservatives’ campaign director was Katy Merrifield, who had previously served as Mr. Poilievre’s director of communications.

She was replaced by Mr. Green after she had left Mr. Poilievre’s staff.

stories.title: ERs report overcrowding as flu cases continue to rapidly rise
stories.summary: Alberta, British Columbia and Yukon have the highest levels of flu activity, with Manitoba, the Northwest Territories and Quebec close behind
stories.author: Alanna Smith, Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Influenza season is well under way across Canada, but experts warn that the worst is yet to come as case counts barrel upward.

Don Vinh, an infectious-disease specialist at Montreal’s McGill University Health Centre, said the flu has “its own agenda” and there’s no telling when cases will peak. He said hospitals across the country will remain under intense strain from the flu for at least several weeks, if not months.

“We don’t know exactly when we’re going to hit our peak or how long we’ll be at that peak before things quiet down,” Dr. Vinh said. “This is the unknown that can cripple already fragile health care systems.”

The flu virus has hit Canada hard and fast with cases rapidly rising since the season officially started in early October, forcing some provinces to adjust vaccination plans. Nearly 14 per cent of flu tests came back positive in the week ending Nov. 7, according to the latest update from the Public Health Agency of Canada.

Since Aug. 30, according to Phac, roughly 16,500 flu cases have been detected in Canada, the majority being Influenza A, which matches this season’s vaccine. Alberta, British Columbia and Yukon have the highest levels of flu activity, with Manitoba, the Northwest Territories and Quebec close behind.

Data on previous viral periods show that the 2023-24 and 2025-26 flu seasons began in late November, with peaks in early January. The 2024-25 season didn’t officially begin until mid-December and peaked in late February, underscoring how early this season is.

Emergency departments already overflowing with patients are now being packed further with flu cases. In Montreal, for example, hospital emergency wards were running at 150 per cent of their stretcher capacity on Monday, according to Quebec’s Index Santé website.

On Monday afternoon, Montreal hospitals had an intake of 654 patients requiring stretchers, but only had 435 functional gurneys. This left 219 people to wait on hallway stretchers. Non-urgent patients on stretchers had to wait an average of more than 18 hours at Montreal General Hospital and more than 39 hours at Lakeshore General.

Health authority Santé Québec issued a statement last Thursday acknowledging the impact of respiratory infectious diseases and urging sick people to consider other options in lieu of visiting emergency departments, such as calling medical hotlines.

Emergency physician Raghu Venugopal, who works at three Toronto hospitals, said Ontario’s situation is also dire. He said about 20 per cent of patients he has seen in recent weeks, both young and old, are presenting with influenza-like illnesses. Meanwhile, EDs in the region are seeing record-breaking numbers and what he called “insane” wait times.

“It is a train rolling to the cliff and the whole thing comes crashing down as usual between, say, Christmas and school starting again for the kids,” Dr. Venugopal said. “That period is going to be, I think at least in Toronto, where I’m most confident, extremely messy.”

Patients will have to wait even longer for care, he added, and some will leave without being seen, putting them at greater risk of harm. “Our cardinal sin remains, we just don’t have beds,” Dr. Venugopal said.

Ontario’s flu activity is still considered low in comparison with other provinces, reaching a 7.7-per-cent positivity for the week ending Nov. 7, according to provincial data. In neighbouring Quebec, the province’s public health institute reported a 12.2-per-cent flu rate for the same week.

Roughly one year earlier, Quebec’s flu rate was 3.6 per cent.

Quebec is the only Canadian province to end universal flu vaccine coverage this season. Only certain vulnerable Quebeckers – including people 65 and over, patients with certain chronic conditions, pregnant women and nursing home residents – can still get vaccinated at no charge.

Lower vaccination rates across Canada have contributed to viral spread, Dr. Vinh said. Making matters worse, vaccine campaigns launched a “little too late” this season, he said, as flu cases popped up earlier than expected.

Even when the vaccine became available in Montreal, appointments were booked up quickly, Dr. Vinh said, leaving some more vulnerable people at increased risk while they waited for their shot. Others aren’t getting vaccinated because they believe it isn’t effective, he added.

Dr. Vinh stressed that reports from Canada and the United States indicate this year’s vaccine is between a 95-per-cent and 100-per-cent match for the circulating strains. Even a mismatch – like last year’s vaccine – still protects against serious complications and hospitalization.

“If you have a time machine, I’d say go back a few weeks and get it,” Dr. Vinh said. “But if you don’t have a time machine, now would be the second-best time.”

Ontario’s flu activity is still considered low in comparison with other provinces, reaching a 7.7-per-cent positivity for the week ending Nov. 7, according to provincial data. In neighbouring Quebec, the province’s public health institute reported a 12.2-per-cent flu rate for the same week.
Roughly one year earlier, Quebec’s flu rate was 3.6 per cent.

Quebec is the only Canadian province to end universal flu vaccine coverage this season. Only certain vulnerable Quebeckers – including people 65 and over, patients with certain chronic conditions, pregnant women and nursing home residents – can still get vaccinated at no charge.

Lower vaccination rates across Canada have contributed to viral spread, Dr. Vinh said. Making matters worse, vaccine campaigns launched a “little too late” this season, he said, as flu cases popped up earlier than expected.

Even when the vaccine became available in Montreal, appointments were booked up quickly, Dr. Vinh said, leaving some more vulnerable people at increased risk while they waited for their shot. Others aren’t getting vaccinated because they believe it isn’t effective, he added.

Dr. Vinh stressed that reports from Canada and the United States indicate this year’s vaccine is between a 95-per-cent and 100-per-cent match for the circulating strains. Even a mismatch – like last year’s vaccine – still protects against serious complications and hospitalization.
“If you have a time machine, I’d say go back a few weeks and get it,” Dr. Vinh said. “But if you don’t have a time machine, now would be the second-best time.”

stories.title: Witness testifies that accused was angry with the victim moments before being set ablaze
stories.summary: When he testified, Robert Beasley told a London, Ont. courtroom that he had a close relationship with both 29-year-old Jonathan Graham and the accused in this case, 36-year-old Bradley Joudrey.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
When he testified, Robert Beasley told a London, Ont. courtroom that he had a close relationship with both 29-year-old Jonathan Graham and the accused in this case, 36-year-old Bradley Joudrey.

He said he was with them both on July 12, 2022, when they got into an altercation at an after hours hangout in east London, saying, “Jon and Brad got into a fight. I think it had something to do with a girl ... Jon punched Brad.”

He continued, “Brad takes it and is pissed off ... he had been drinking.”

Beasley said he ended up leaving and so did the accused.

When they met up later, he said Joudrey was on the phone with Graham’s brother saying, “That fer’s going to get it, that fer’s going to die.”

Beasley said when they got to Joudrey’s shared apartment on Hilton Avenue, he saw the accused doing something, “I went outside, I remember it smelled like gasoline at the side of the house.”

The Crown’s theory is that Graham and Joudrey met at a convenience store parking lot at Admiral Drive and Trafalgar Street minutes after the altercation.

The victim was doused with gasoline and set on fire. He died in hospital from thermal injuries.

Joudrey sped away and crash his vehicle along Royal Crescent.

Officers found his identification inside the silver Dodge Journey.

Within minutes, Joudrey was arrested and he has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder.

Earlier in the day, Tabetha Passmore testified that she rented her basement to Joudrey at the time.

She said the accused woke her up in the middle of that July night, “All he (Joudrey) was yelling was, ‘I crashed the car.’”

The trial, which is now into its second week, resumes on Tuesday.

stories.title: Recreation funding, ice rental fee increases criticized in Calgary’s proposed budget
stories.summary: The City of Calgary's upcoming four-year budget proposal includes potential increases to ice time fees for youth sports like hockey, figure skating and ringette.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
How much Calgary is planning to spend on sports and recreation, as well as some rising costs, has the upcoming four-year budget proposal drawing the ire of some minor sports organizations.

The criticism comes ahead of budget deliberations, which are set to begin with a public hearing on Nov. 23, after the spending plan was made public last week.

According to the city, the budget proposal includes $284 million to fund projects though the GamePLAN strategy including including the Forest Lawn recreation facility replacement, Kingsland and Belmont athletic parks and a reaffirmed commitment to the city’s portion of the Foothills Fieldhouse.

Another $66 million is earmarked to maintain arenas, aquatic centres and the Calgary Soccer Centre. However, the Calgary Minor Soccer Association (Cmsa) believes the budget misses the mark when it comes to addressing facility shortages across the city.

“We’re extremely disappointed not to see any funding for indoor facilities, in particular the Rocky Ridge Fieldhouse and design funding for the Southland Fieldhouse,” Cmsa executive director Carlo Bruneau told Global News.

The Rocky Ridge Fieldhouse is listed as one of 17 prioritized projects in the first wave of GamePLAN, the city’s investment strategy for recreation and sports facilities.

According to Bruneau, the city had already committed funding for preliminary design work for the project, and its construction costs are estimated to be just over $70 million.

“For Cmsa alone, it would allow 3,000 more kids to play soccer, it would allow us to have over 200 more soccer teams and over 1,500 more games per year,” he said.

“That impact for us is transformational, and really at the end of the day it’s a small investment for the city in the grand scheme of things.”

However, Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot said there’s limited room for additional investment in the budget proposal due to a lengthy list of projects and spending set to cost $21 billion over the next four years, for things like water infrastructure, roads, and transit.

“We are so leveraged out when it comes to our commitments that we can’t possibly take on any more,” he told reporters Monday.

“I know everyone wants us to do more, but the problem is we’ve already committed ourselves to too much.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I know everyone wants us to do more, but the problem is we've already committed ourselves to too much."

Chabot was part of the previous council that approved the GamePLAN strategy, including a funding commitment of up to $250 million annually for recreation infrastructure entitled “Making Waves.”

The representative from Ward 10, who instead voted for a lower funding stream of up to $150 million annually, said the commitment was “too far reaching.”

Ward 3 Coun. Andrew Yule, meanwhile, agreed the proposed spending in the budget falls short to address the capacity issues at local sports and recreation facilities.

“We’re not making waves with this budget,” Yule said. “Phase 1 of GamePLAN is barely scraping the surface of what we need for recreation in Calgary.”

The price to play could also increase under the proposed budget, with a number of fee increases scheduled over the four-year plan.

According to the proposal, rental fees for athletic fields and artificial turf field are set to rise nearly 10 per cent over the next four years.

Ice rentals are also set to increase with minor prime time slots proposed to jump from $230.30 to $270.83 in 2027, and minor non-prime time slots could rise from $82.30 to $133.33 next year.

Kevin Kobelka, executive director of Hockey Calgary, told Global News the proposed fee increases came as a shock, with no warning or engagement with city officials prior to the budget’s release.

Kobelka said city rates for ice times are typically lower than private facilities, but the move could have a significant impact on the organization, as well as for figure skating and ringette.

“Sixty-five to 70 per cent of the cost of youth hockey is ice costs, so we’ll have to pass this on,” he said. “We’re a non-profit organization — if there’s going to be a 17 per cent price increase on ice, then that’s going to have to go to the end user.”

When asked about the proposed increases, Chabot said the hikes that could impact youth sports “is not the direction to go.”

“When it comes to promoting active lifestyles, especially to our youth, those are the people we should not be targeting insofar as increasing their fees,” he said.

“Surely we can recover those costs from other user groups.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Surely we can recover those costs from other user groups."
