stories.title: Ex-CRA employee sentenced after pleading guilty to fraud, breach of trust
stories.summary: Mounties say Yoan Zola pleaded guilty to three of the charges — breach of trust, fraud and trafficking in identity information — last July
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Police say a former Canada Revenue Agency employee who pleaded guilty to three breach of trust and fraud-related charges will be serving his sentence in the community.

A statement from the RCMP says federal Mounties in the Pacific region conducted an “exhaustive” investigation into Yoan Zola starting in 2022 after the agency reported that an employee had compromised taxpayer information.

Zola was arrested in Vancouver in January 2026 and charged with breach of trust, trafficking in identity information, identity theft, fraud under $5,000, fraudulent personation, and use of a credit card obtained by crime.

Mounties say Zola pleaded guilty to three of the charges — breach of trust, fraud and trafficking in identity information — last July, while the other charges against him were stayed.

Zola was given a conditional sentence on Nov. 10 to serve two years less a day for the beach of trust and identity trafficking charges, and a concurrent two-month conditional sentence for the fraud charge, to be served in the community as long as he follows the supervision orders of the court.

Staff Sgt. David Grey with the Federal Policing Pacific Region’s cyber and financial investigation team says Zola’s actions undermined Canadians’ trust in public institutions and their employees who have access to sensitive personal information.

stories.title: Alberta tables legislation to force vote on changes to electoral map
stories.summary: Latest proposed boundaries have fuelled accusations of gerrymandering; provincial NDP has promised to challenge the map in court if bill passes
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith ’s government has introduced legislation that will force a vote on a proposed new electoral map that contains controversial changes to key provincial ridings and has fuelled accusations of gerrymandering.

Mickey Amery, the province’s Justice Minister, tabled a bill on Monday afternoon that, if approved, would finalize the shape of Alberta ’s electoral map for the next general election, scheduled for October 2027.

The Alberta NDP has promised to file a legal challenge to the map if the bill passes, a commitment party Leader Naheed Nenshi reiterated on Monday.

“If this passes, we’re challenging it in court,” Mr. Nenshi said at a news conference.

The new map has risen to the top of Alberta’s political agenda in recent weeks, largely because of a slate of changes it makes to ridings in Calgary and Lethbridge – regions that are tightly contested between the United Conservative Party and NDP – and Ms. Smith’s decision in April to reject a previous panel’s recommendations and restart the map-making process.

The latest proposals have been dogged by accusations of gerrymandering, the U.S.-style practice of drawing boundary lines that give an unfair advantage to the governing party.

If adopted, the new map would remain in place until the next scheduled redrawing in eight to 10 years.

The new map, expected to be debated this week, was drawn by a five-person panel. Alberta’s system dictates that the governing party selects the chair and two panelists while the Official Opposition picks the remaining two.

A recent analysis by The Globe and Mail showed that the new map would dilute urban voters’ power in elections, and widen population disparities between city and rural ridings. If approved, the average rural riding would be nearly 11-per-cent smaller than the provincewide average of 53,722 people. Calgary and Edmonton’s riding populations, meanwhile, would be roughly 6-per-cent greater than average.

In Lethbridge, the map proposes eliminating one of the city’s two urban ridings while creating three new districts that mix the city’s suburban neighbourhoods with swaths of rural southern Alberta, where much of the Ucp’s support resides.

And in Calgary, the battleground where next October’s election is likely to be won, a handful of ridings in the city’s northwest were merged with rural ridings.

Ms. Smith has said she rejected the first map because it would have eliminated two rural ridings because of massive population gains in Alberta’s major cities, Calgary and Edmonton. The new panel was given an additional two seats to work with.

Ms. Smith’s government has indicated it supports the new map, taking the first step toward implementing its changes last month by unanimously voting in favour of creating the bill tabled on Monday. (The Alberta NDP voted against the motion.)

On Monday, Mr. Amery, the Justice Minister, defended ridings that mix urban and rural constituencies, telling the legislature during Question Period that the new map satisfies the principles underpinning Canada’s electoral system.

“They were looking at the importance of making sure that they connect rural and urban constituencies together, because that’s how the world is going currently,” he said of the panel.

“Urban and rural communities are so interconnected today that it simply makes sense. It’s where the entire country is moving to, it’s where the panel recommendations are going, and we support them.”

When the NDP argued the map waters down urban voters’ power, Mr. Amery said: “Once again, that position is absurd.”

Should the map be proclaimed into law, it will be sent to Elections Alberta so it can be implemented ahead of the next provincial election.

But it is unclear how the Ndp’s legal challenge would impact that process.

Mr. Nenshi has refused to divulge the Ndp’s legal tactics. On Monday, he suggested that the challenge could lead to a “very quick trial on the merits of the application,” or result in an injunction that leads to “a very long court case.”

“I hate being vague on these things, but I also cannot give up our legal strategy before we’re in court, because it gives the other side an opportunity to prepare using taxpayer dollars,” Mr. Nenshi said.

Ms. Smith says she hopes the Ndp’s legal challenge doesn’t come to pass, but that her government will assemble a legal team if necessary.

Anaïs Bussiéres McNicoll, a director with the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, said in an interview that the legal challenge wouldn’t stop the map from being adopted, and that it would remain in place until a judge says otherwise.

Ms. Bussiéres McNicoll said it’s hard to predict whether the courts could reach a decision before next year’s election – a question currently weighing on Elections Alberta, which would have a short runway to incorporate the new riding boundaries if the bill passes. The agency said a legal challenge would make it even more difficult to be ready for next October’s vote.

She suggested that the case would likely look at the two controversial aspects of Alberta’s latest boundary redrawing: Ms. Smith’s decision to reject the first panel’s recommendations and restart the process, and the design of the map currently being debated in the legislature.

“It’s a case that’s interesting because both the process and the result of that process seem to be raising questions,” she said.

stories.title: Dale Hawerchuk’s son reflects on ‘surreal’ Scheifele record for Winnipeg Jets
stories.summary: "Sometimes life is stranger than fiction," says the son of Jets legend Dale Hawerchuk, as he reflected on Mark Scheifele becoming the franchise's all-time leading scorer.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The son of Winnipeg Jets legend Dale Hawerchuk says it was “surreal” to see Mark Scheifele pass his father to become the team’s all-time leading scorer.

Hawerchuk’s son, Eric, spoke with 680 Cjob Monday afternoon — days after Scheifele registered his career 930th point. Hawerchuk had held the title since December 984.

“It’s kind of surreal, the way it all shook out. Dale coached Mark in Barrie. Then, the Jets drafted him with the first pick, and he ends up being the guy that passes all his records,” Eric said.

“And I think that sometimes life is stranger than fiction. It’s a really, really cool, very emotional thing.”

Dale Hawerchuk died in August of 2020 of stomach cancer. His legacy as a playmaker, captain and community figure is recognized with a bronze statue near Canada Life Centre at True North Square in downtown Winnipeg.

When Scheifele broke the record Saturday, Eric sent a celebratory text message, saying “we’ll talk about the sappy stuff later.”

“A lot of these guys, when my dad first started coaching them, they (May have been) playing at a lower level. But he had a pretty good eye to find guys that really, really wanted it. And they kind of would bond over that,” he continued.

“They both really wanted to work hard and do whatever it took. And I think that’s where Mark and Dale really got along.”

Until recently, Hawerchuk’s record appeared to be set in stone. The original Jets franchise records were not connected to the franchise that relocated from Atlanta and took over the Jets name. The statistics were amalgamated before the start of this season.

“I do want to thank the NHL for doing the right thing and moving the records back to Winnipeg,” Eric said. “Those records were just sitting there with nobody to pass them.”

“I’m happy for Mark and I hope he passes the goal record tomorrow (Tuesday) night.”

The forward is one goal away from surpassing his mentor to become the franchise goals record holder as well. He holds several other Jets records, including career games played, overtime points and goals and 20-goal seasons, the team said in a news release Saturday night.

Scheifele was also named the NHL’s first star of the week for the week ending on Nov. 15.

More than anything, Dale would be pleased to see his student doing well, and the team winning, his son said.

Eric and his family are hoping to return to Winnipeg soon, he added.

“We’re hoping to come out there later in the season and do something special for Mark for passing these records.”

stories.title: Former CRA employee sentenced after pleading guilty to fraud, breach of trust
stories.summary: Vancouver — Police say a former Canada Revenue Agency employee who pleaded guilty to three breach of trust and fraud-related charges will be serving his sentence in the community.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Vancouver — Police say a former Canada Revenue Agency employee who pleaded guilty to three breach of trust and fraud-related charges will be serving his sentence in the community.

A statement from the RCMP says federal Mounties in the Pacific region conducted an “exhaustive” investigation into Yoan Zola starting in 2022 after the agency reported that an employee had compromised taxpayer information.

Zola was arrested in Vancouver in January 2026 and charged with breach of trust, trafficking in identity information, identity theft, fraud under $5,000, fraudulent personation, and use of a credit card obtained by crime.

Mounties say Zola pleaded guilty to three of the charges — breach of trust, fraud and trafficking in identity information — last July, while the other charges against him were stayed.

Zola was given a conditional sentence on Nov. 10 to serve two years less a day for the breach of trust and identity trafficking charges, and a concurrent two-month conditional sentence for the fraud charge, to be served in the community as long as he follows the supervision orders of the court.

Staff Sgt. David Grey with the Federal Policing Pacific Region’s cyber and financial investigation team says Zola’s actions undermined Canadians’ trust in public institutions and their employees who have access to sensitive personal information.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ecuadorian politicians warn about legal provisions in free trade deal
stories.summary: Ottawa - Twenty-five former cabinet ministers and former heads of parliament in Ecuador are warning the some provisions of the Canada-Ecuador free trade deal are putting the countries' economic relationship at risk.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Twenty-five former cabinet ministers and former heads of parliament in Ecuador are warning that some provisions in the Canada-Ecuador free trade deal are putting the countries’ economic relationship at risk.

The two countries signed a free trade deal in July. Several Canadian organizations and civil society leaders have warned that the deal threatens the environment and could exacerbate a human rights crisis in the South American country.

In a letter to International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, 25 Ecuadorian politicians object to the inclusion of investor-state dispute settlement provisions in the deal and urge the government to remove those sections before ratifying it.

The letter says the provisions, which would allow foreign investors to sue governments through an international tribunal instead of through domestic sovereign courts, are unconstitutional in Ecuador and have been rejected by Ecuadorian voters in several referendums.

“We are not opposed to Canadian investment in Ecuador or to closer economic relations between our two countries,” says the letter. “We write because we believe this agreement, as currently structured, places that relationship at risk.”

The Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives says the provisions were requested by the mining industry and opposed by human rights organizations during public consultations held in 2023.

Stuart Trew, the organization’s senior researcher, said investor-state dispute settlement provisions won’t enhance investment in either country.

“It just gives these companies a real sharp tool they can use to basically threaten countries away from policies they don’t want to see introduced,” said Trew. “We’re quite alarmed by what the Canadian government has done here.”

While the letter says Canada and Ecuador have substantial shared interests in trade, investment and development, it urges a cautious approach to what it calls “an instrument likely to be contested for the duration of its life.”

“An agreement built on sound legal and democratic foundations will serve the relationship between our countries considerably better than one that invites constitutional challenge from the day it enters into force,” says the letter.

Mujtaba Hussain, a spokesperson for International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, said in an email the Canada-Ecuador free trade agreement will support “long-term sustainable and inclusive bilateral economic growth.”

He said investor-state dispute settlement tribunals will not be able to repeal laws or regulations and will only be able to award monetary damages to investors in the event of a breach by either party.

“Canada considers that clear and balanced rules, supported by an effective dispute settlement mechanism, are key to a stable investment environment,” said Hussain.

Hussain said the Canada-Ecuador free trade agreement also makes arbitration proceedings more transparent and requires that arbitration hearings be open to the public and civil society.

“The Government of Canada expects all Canadian companies operating abroad to abide by all relevant laws, respect human rights in their operations, and adopt best practices and internationally respected guidelines on responsible business conduct,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Swollen B.C. rivers claim lives as boats, kayaks capsize
stories.summary: It was the fourth death in as many days in waters near the community, where three people died after a boat overturned in the swollen Squamish River on Thursday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Police say a kayaker has died after capsizing north of Squamish, B.C., while a man remains missing three days after a boat overturned in the Fraser River near Yale, following days of heavy rains throughout southwestern British Columbia.

Mounties in Squamish say they responded to a call to help paramedics after two kayakers who were part of a larger group flipped into the Cheakamus River on Sunday.

stories.title: Ontario tables law to more quickly deal with intimate image abuse
stories.summary: The proposed new statutory tort giving those victims access to civil remedies is contained in an omnibus bill introduced on Monday.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s government has tabled a bill that would create a new legal pathway for victims of intimate image abuse to have those images deleted.

The proposed new statutory tort giving those victims access to civil remedies is contained in an omnibus bill introduced today.

The legislation also includes new rules about long-term care placement data, electronic medical records, student financial aid at career colleges, and the child welfare system.

Michael Parsa, the minister of children, community and social services, also announced a host of child welfare regulatory changes that will accompany the bill, including stricter financial oversight.

The province launched a review in 2024 of children’s aid societies after Ford suggested they are being financially mismanaged, but the report released today by Parsa says the sector’s growing deficit is driven by staffing and placement cost pressures.

The report says cost pressures are highest for children and youth in out-of-home placements, where boarding costs grew by 50 per cent in four years.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - Health authorities say a resident at a long-term care facility northeast of Montreal is being treated after coming into contact with a bat infected with rabies.
stories.author: Katrine Desautels The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - Health authorities say a resident at a long-term care facility northeast of Montreal is being treated after coming into contact with a bat infected with rabies.

Nov. 16, 2026

By Katrine Desautels The Canadian Press

Santé Québec Montérégie-Est says the incident occurred during the night of Nov. 8 at the CHSLD Élisabeth-Lafrance in Sorel-Tracy.

The health authority’s director of public affairs couldn’t confirm whether the animal bit the resident, but said the contact was deemed significant.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Rabies is fatal once symptoms begin, but treatment can prevent the disease from developing in a person who has been exposed.

Pierre-Yves Séguin says the woman who was exposed is receiving the treatment, as are 15 more residents as a preventive measure.

He says the facility has had issues with bats dating back to 2017, but this is the first one to test positive for rabies.

Séguin says it wasn’t possible to kill the bats in the building since they’re protected by federal and provincial laws. He says the facility has tried to manage the problem through non-lethal means, such as sealing off entry points.

“We’ve captured and then relocated other bats. But now, with this new incident, we’ve reached a point where we need to take further action,” said Séguin.

Santé Québec Montérégie-Est has requested an exemption from the Ministry of the Environment to exterminate all the bats in the building, and Séguin says he expects it will be done by the end of the week.

He said there’s no exact count of the number of bats present in the long-term care facility, but thermal imaging revealed that there were several.

According to the government’s most recent data, there were 361 confirmed cases of raccoon rabies and 10 cases of bat rabies in the province since the beginning of the year as of Nov. 11. In an effort to control the spread of the disease, the Environment Department has carried out several vaccination campaigns this year by distributing vaccine baits.

stories.title: Air Canada says its flights ‘near normal’ 3 days after FAA ground stop
stories.summary: Thousands of flights to and from the U.S. were cancelled after the country issued its first nationwide ground stop to occur in 25 years.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
One of Canada’s major airlines says operations are “near normal” after a complete ground stop in the U.S. cancelled hundreds of flights to and from south of the border.

Air Canada said in a statement Monday that approximately 250 of its flights were cancelled on Friday, affecting about 27,000 passengers.

“As of Monday, Air Canada’s operations are near normal, with the recovery almost complete,” said Sean Davidson, director of media relations for the airline. “We are working as quickly as possible to accommodate the remaining affected passengers.

He added there were additional cancellations Saturday as aircraft and crews were “out of position across our network.”

Porter Airlines and WestJet both confirmed to Global News this weekend they had been affected by the ground stop. WestJet offered guests travelling to and from continental U.S., Mexico or the Caribbean with travel scheduled between Friday and Sunday the opportunity to make a one-time change or cancellation at no fee.

On Monday, Porter told Global News its operation was “back on track,” though added it could not provide more details.

Air Transat said its operations have returned to normal, though added due to the nature of its network only a small number of flights experienced disruptions. Currently, the airline’s only U.S. destinations are Fort Lauderdale, Miami and Orlando in Florida.

Global News has contacted WestJet and Flair Airlines for status updates.

The U.S. issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon after a communication failure hit air traffic control centres across the country.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy pointed the finger at a single router installed by government contractor L3Harris. He said Friday that the company was conducting routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fibre at at least one remote location.

It ended Friday evening at about 8:15 p.m. Eastern, but officials continue to look into the incident.

U.S. President Donald Trump broke his silence Sunday about the issue, saying the problems were the fault of old technology and criticized Democrats for the incident and that he doesn’t take any responsibility.

“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” Trump told reporters Monday morning.

A day earlier he called on Congress to provide more money to cover the cost of system improvements.

According to flight tracker platform Flight Aware, 9,155 flights within, to or out of the U.S. were cancelled Friday. The same platform showed more than 4,000 flights were cancelled by midday Saturday.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said on Saturday it expected schedules should recovery by Sunday but cautioned normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years would be slow.

— with files from Global News’ Rachel Morgan and The Associated Press

“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” Trump told reporters Monday morning.
A day earlier he called on Congress to provide more money to cover the cost of system improvements.

According to flight tracker platform Flight Aware, 9,155 flights within, to or out of the U.S. were cancelled Friday. The same platform showed more than 4,000 flights were cancelled by midday Saturday.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said on Saturday it expected schedules should recovery by Sunday but cautioned normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years would be slow.

stories.title: Faulty radon detectors could put Canadians at risk
stories.summary: Health Canada is warning that inaccurate radon detectors sold online could leave Canadians unaware of dangerous gas levels in their homes.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Health Canada is warning Canadians that inaccurate radon detectors sold online could leave households unknowingly exposed to a radioactive gas linked to lung cancer.

In a public advisory issued Monday, the agency urged homeowners to use approved testing devices, following several warnings and recalls involving electronic monitors that provided misleading readings.

Faulty readings raise health concerns

Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas released from the breakdown of uranium in soil and rock. It is invisible, odourless and tasteless, and can accumulate inside homes.

Long-term exposure to elevated radon levels is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada after smoking.

Health Canada said inaccurate detectors can provide readings that are either higher or lower than actual radon concentrations. The biggest concern is that homeowners could receive falsely reassuring results and remain unaware of dangerous exposure.

Previously flagged products include InkBird ⁠, Life Basis ⁠, Hanchen ⁠ and Spolehli ⁠ detectors, along with other devices sold on Amazon.CA.

How to test your home

Health Canada recommends testing during winter, when homes are more tightly sealed and radon levels are often higher.

A long-term test lasting at least three months provides the most accurate assessment of a home’s average radon levels.

Consumers should purchase electronic monitors that have passed performance testing by the Canadian National Radon Proficiency Program ⁠.

Anyone with a recalled detector should stop using it and dispose of it according to municipal electronic waste requirements.

More information is available in Health Canada’s radon testing guide ⁠.

stories.title: Community 'distraught' after copper Jesus statue stolen from B.C. school
stories.summary: Surrey - A Catholic school in Surrey, B.C., is praying that Jesus will help a group of thieves after they stole a life-size copper statue of Christ from the school's courtyard.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Catholic school in Surrey, B.C., is praying that Jesus will help a group of thieves after they stole a life-size copper statue of Christ from the school’s courtyard.

Silveria Roselli, president of the Saint John Paul II Academy Foundation, said the school community was “very distraught” to learn of the theft early in the morning on Nov. 11, when three people drove through a fence in a white van and cut the statue off at the knees.

“Some of the kids were very much devastated. It was like a death in the family,” Roselli said in an interview on Monday.

Roselli said one of the students suggested it was possible the thieves needed to find Christ, and she was praying Jesus would help them find what was missing.

“We hope that whoever did this will repent and that will bring Jesus back home,” said Roselli.

“As a school, we pray for them that they will find God and find Jesus.”

The theft was caught on the school’s security camera and has been shared on social media, but police have said the van used by the thieves was also stolen.

“An extensive initial search for suspects or a suspect vehicle was negative,” Surrey police said in a statement.

Police said officers received a report of the theft on Nov. 11 and visited the school to speak to staff and gather evidence.

“We understand this incident is impactful to the school and their community,” they said. “The investigation is ongoing.”

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson condemned the theft, describing it as a “disgraceful act against a community of faith and a school.”

“To the students, families and staff at the Academy: we stand with you,” he said on social media, urging anyone with information about the theft to contact police.

Roselli said the school would be boosting its security.

“We’re working with the police, and we will not let evil prevail,” she said.

The statue, entitled “The Last Supper,” depicted Jesus sitting before a plate and cup on a table, surrounded by 12 empty stools. It was donated by Canadian artist Timothy Schmaltz.

Joseph King, chair of the Saint John Paul II Academy Society, said the statue was an invitation for students, teachers and guests to sit and contemplate themselves as apostles of Christ and consider receiving the eucharist.

King said it was also a “beautiful” place to study or have lunch.

Roselli said the statue would be replaced as soon as possible with help from a fundraising effort.

A GoFundMe page, launched by Saint John Paul II Academy Foundation, asks people to help bring Jesus home.

“While the sculpture was made of copper, its true value was never in the metal, but in what it represented: the love of Jesus Christ and his presence among us,” the page said.

While the theft had left a sense of emptiness at the courtyard, Roselli said hearts in the community were full after seeing the support they’re receiving.

“It’s mainly beautiful to see the love, support of the community,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said the theft occurred on Nov. 1.

stories.title: I dusted off my old figure skates and rediscovered joy
stories.summary: Thursday night skating lessons helped me find the happiness I deeply craved
stories.author: Christina Heyding
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

My husband is joy incarnate. At 6:15 a.m., when he kisses me goodbye for work, he says, “Monday – the best day of the week!” It’s the same for each day. “Tuesday, the best day of the week!” Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, no matter the weather, no matter the traffic. It’s always the best day of the week.

Sometimes he leaves with a new little phrase he’s learned. (Fernando is Brazilian and started learning English later in life.) “See you later, alligator,” he says, then waits for me with a gleefully expectant smile, until I finish it off with, “In a while, crocodile.”

Before getting into the car, Fernando pauses to watch the world around him. He’ll admire a water droplet or take a picture of the sunrise.

I don’t know if his joy is born of nature or nurture. It’s probably both. His mom has the same disposition and so do many in his home country, from what I’ve observed. When Fernando’s Brazilian friends visit, our house must gleam from the street. They dance, they hug, they sing, they laugh. Even their language is joyful. It has the cadence of music with allegros and adagios.

I am not like my husband. I am prone to pointing out the annoyances in life. Monday is never the best day of the week and I find many reasons for even the best day to be a bad one. When I’m alone, life often turns a somber sepia, like Kansas before Dorothy lands in Oz.

This began to scare me. I realized how much I depended on Fernando to find joy, to feel joy. I needed to find my own wells of happiness.

Two winters ago, I started searching. There wasn’t much inspiration in a Toronto of concrete-coloured skies and dead leaves – a scene that puts into question T.S. Eliot’s cruellest month. But one night, I passed our neighbourhood outdoor rink on my way home from work.

When I got home, I found my old figure skates in the basement, scratched off as much rust as I could and walked back to the rink. It was empty except for me. When I pushed onto the ice, it felt like the exhale of a deep breath.

Once I got used to the feel of my blades, I dug into the ice to get speed. I used to be a competitive figure skater and I discovered that I still had that power. The wind on my face was amazing. Do you know the joy a dog emanates with his ears flapping through the open window of a car in the springtime? That’s what I felt, but in the dead of November.

It wasn’t the same joy as a samba or of carnival, but it was just as uplifting. So I signed up for skating sessions on Thursday nights.

Walking into the rink on my first night of ice time, I started to cry. The smell of the arena, like a cold Canadian Tire, brought back so many memories: my dad lacing up my skates, my mom helping me zip up my home-knit sweater, and my grandma and grandpa buying me a hot chocolate that would inevitably burn my tongue. So many small moments of joy.

My eyes welled up again when I got onto the ice. Zambonied ice is a thing of beauty. It’s like a thick piece of top-grade sketch paper and your skates are the charcoal pencil. It feels like anything is possible when you step out.

I did spirals and and lunges. I landed a Salchow and a loop jump. I fell on a Lutz. I got dizzy doing spins. I skated fast and stopped hard to make snow spray against the boards. I skated deep into my edges so that I could hear my blades carve the ice. I did three-turns and brackets and loops and rockers and counters, like doodles. I skated fast, forward and backward, forward and backward.

That first night back on the rink, it felt like something greater than me was joyful inside.

I’ve been skating for almost two years now, Mondays and Thursdays. I even choreographed two programs for myself.

I feel joy when I’m on the ice, not always when I’m off it. But it’s a start.

The rink is good practice for life’s annoyances like the lady who never moves for other skaters, the endless falls on my Axel and the sometimes overcrowded ice that feels like the DVP during rush hour. Still, I always feel joy there. And maybe, as I keep skating, that feeling will grow beyond the ice, until life feels like the rink. A place where there is always joy, no matter the day of the week.

Christina Heyding lives in Toronto.

stories.title: Former ambassadors caution tariffs May stay but say Canada-U.S. trade deal possible
stories.summary: Ottawa - A former United States Ambassador to Canada says he's optimistic a bilateral deal between the two nations is looming but cautioned Canadians not to expect a Democrat-controlled Congress to reign in President Donald Trump's tariffs.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - A former United States Ambassador to Canada said he’s optimistic a bilateral deal between the two nations is looming but cautioned Canadians not to expect a Democrat-controlled Congress to reign in President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

“I am saddened by where the relationship stands today but I really do remain optimistic about its future,” said David Cohen, who served as ambassador under former president Joe Biden.

“The ties between our countries run deep and I believe we have the foundation to rebuild trust, strengthen our partnership and move forward together.”

Appearing by video at the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and International Development in Ottawa Monday, Cohen said the U.S. midterm elections were a historic rebuke of the Trump administration’s policies.

But he’s worried about “unrealistic optimism” from Canadians after Democrats said ending Trump’s trade war with Canada will be a top priority when they become a Congressional majority in January.

Cohen said it will be very challenging for Democrats to convince enough Republicans to defy Trump over his signature economic policy in order to achieve the supermajority they need to bypass the president’s veto powers.

Other observers have said Democrats will likely only tackle one of Trump’s tariff tools — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — while leaving in place other duties still hammering parts of the Canadian economy.

The Canada-U.S. relationship has been shaken by Trump’s tariffs and threats of annexation but tensions rapidly escalated after negotiations between Ottawa and Washington broke down in August.

Trump used Section 338 to hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent levies and weeks later, using the same Depression-era statute, banned imports of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products. The president also signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.

Cohen said Carney was right to walk away from trade talks. While the prime minister has faced criticism domestically for not providing details of the possible deal, Cohen said strategically it is better to negotiate behind closed doors.

“I think Canada has conducted itself extraordinarily well under a very intense and, I think, unfair set of pressures that have been created by U.S. trade policy by the current administration,” Cohen said. “I think Prime Minister Carney has played the hand that Canada has extraordinarily well.”

Cohen said he is hopeful a bilateral agreement can be agreed by years end or in January.

Last month, Trump said he expects a trade deal with Canada soon. United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said he wants to deliver “arrangements” for Canada and Mexico to the president by the year’s end.

The Canada-U.S. relationship is durable but it May require a future U.S administration to apologize for Trump’s rhetoric, Cohen added.

Even if a temporary agreement emerges, negotiations over the future of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade will continue into next year.

The Trump administration in July chose not to renew the trilateral trade pact, known as Cusma. That triggered a rolling annual review for up to a decade, at which point the agreement will expire if the three countries cannot agree on an extension.

David MacNaughton was the Canadian ambassador to Washington during the first Trump presidency and had a front-row seat when Cusma was negotiated to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement.

The former ambassador told the committee that current negotiations are different because “the fact of the matter is (Trump) had advisers who were sane and were trying to build a relationship that was good for both sides.” Now the president is surrounded by people who will agree with whatever Trump wants, MacNaughton said.

The former ambassador said Greer, who played a role in Cusma negotiations, is professional but ultimately the decisions come out of the White House.

MacNaughton said Canada should look to make a deal and find a tariff off-ramp but the bilateral relationship has ultimately changed. He said Canada must diversify trade and boost domestic productivity.

“Let’s diversify our trade but also let’s find a way to get some kind of a long-term agreement with the United States back in place,” he said. “And thirdly, let us work on becoming more productive as a country because this does give us a chance.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

— By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

stories.title: Warm, sunny stretch ahead for southern Ontario
stories.summary: Monday’s cloudy conditions were the result of a temperature inversion trapping moisture from the Great Lakes near the surface.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
After a grey start to the week, southern Ontario residents can look forward to several days of sunshine and above-seasonal temperatures, according to CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Atchison said Monday’s cloudy conditions were the result of a temperature inversion trapping moisture from the Great Lakes near the surface.

“It’s feeling very November-like today with overcast conditions and an inversion setting up, which is trapping some Great Lakes moisture at the surface and keeping us cloudy,” Atchison said.

She noted temperatures were expected to rise a few more degrees through the afternoon as drier air gradually moves into the region, helping to break up the cloud cover.

The improvement is tied to a large area of high pressure that is expected to settle over the eastern seaboard and remain in place for much of the week.

“Nothing’s really going to be moving. A blocking pattern is developing, and we’re on the good side of the block,” said Atchison. “Western Canada will have a big trough, but eastern areas of the country will be soaking up beautiful sunny days and warming temperatures.”

A southerly wind is forecast to develop Tuesday, helping push temperatures above seasonal norms.

“We have a beautiful week setting up in southern Ontario with back-to-back days of sunshine,” Atchison said.

Overnight lows are expected to fall to between 0 C and 1 C Monday night, with slightly milder temperatures along the Lake Erie shoreline.

The forecast calls for full sunshine Tuesday through Thursday, with daytime highs ranging from 11 C to 13 C.

“Some gorgeous weather is on the way, and that looks to hold into the weekend,” Atchison said.

stories.title: What is Roshel, the company buying a Stellantis auto plant in Ontario?
stories.summary: Company says it wants to increase its capacity as Canada builds out its defence sector
stories.author: Daniel Johnson
stories.content:
Defence contractor Roshel is slated to take over the Brampton, Ont., assembly plant that has been idle for years after buying it from automaker Stellantis Stla-N .

While questions and criticism swirl about the sale and what will happen to jobs at the facility, Roshel says it wants to increase its capacity as Canada builds out its defence sector.

The Brampton-based company is a large manufacturer of smart armoured vehicles for both commercial and government organizations. Its trucks are used by military, law enforcement and security customers to protect occupants.

Roshel’s customers include government agencies such as Canada’s Department of National Defence, Nasa and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, along with law enforcement agencies such as the Peel Regional Police and U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Its security customers include The Brink’s Co. and GardaWorld Security.

Roshel is a privately held company founded by its CEO Roman Shimonov in 2016.

The sale of the plant has drawn the ire of the union representing Stellantis workers and government officials, but some defence industry experts say they are not surprised as to who is buying the facility considering Canada’s new-found appetite for building out its military and defence capabilities.

“As the sector expands, defence companies will need to invest in new facilities, expand existing ones, or repurpose industrial properties as they become available. This is a good example of that broader trend,” said Peter Graham, a national sector leader of aerospace and defence at Kpmg Canada, in a statement Thursday.

Canada and its Nato allies agreed in June 2025 to substantially hike their defence spending target to 5 per cent of annual GDP by 2035. The latest federal budget says Canada will reach 4 per cent by 2030. As defence spending rises, domestic companies like Roshel could benefit from military procurements.

Shimonov has said it’s looking to capitalize on these new opportunities.

“With the demand that is growing all around the world, we need more space, we need more capacity. And we also need the ability to create an infrastructure to address future need for companies that are willing to invest in Canada,” Shimonov said this week in an interview.

In February, the government outlined a new $6.6-billion defence strategy aimed at helping small- and medium-sized Canadian businesses break into the defence industry and reorient spending decisions to prioritize equipment made in Canada, instead of relying on foreign military contractors such as American firms. The document claims it will create 125,000 jobs over a decade.

“(Roshel) is buying (the plant) basically because defence spending in Canada is scheduled to go through a significant increase and what they’re trying to do is get some more capacity for defence manufacturing,” Jerry McGinn, the director of the Center for the Industrial Base, said in an interview.

In recent years, Roshel has been increasing its presence in the defence industry.

In October, it completed an acquisition of French armoured vehicle producer Centigon. In June, it signed a memorandum of understanding with Daimler to jointly develop and produce armoured military vehicles for Nato and allied customers.

In April, it signed a deal with Algoma Steel Group Inc. on a joint venture called Roshel Algoma Defence, which will produce ballistic steel for military vehicles as well as other industries. The partnership includes metal fabrication, forming, welding, and machining in Canada.

And in August of 2025, it partnered with Swedish steel company Swebor in a deal that allowed it to use Swebor’s intellectual property to produce ballistic steel in Canada. Ballistic steel is a special type of relatively lightweight, hardened steel that protects against blasts or bullets.

The company has previously faced criticism for its ties to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

U.S. government procurement records from November 2025 laid out plans for a rush order worth the equivalent of about C$10 million for 20 Senator Stang emergency response tactical vehicles made by Roshel. The purchase quickly drew criticism from arms control advocates and politicians in Canada due to the law enforcement agency’s alleged record of human rights abuses.

The company’s vehicles have also been sent overseas.

In 2023, then Defence Minister Anita Anand announced that Canada was sending an additional 200 armoured vehicles to Ukraine, which were purchased from Roshel at a cost of $90 million.

Stellantis announced the sale of its Brampton facility and associated equipment to Roshel for an undisclosed amount last Monday. The companies said they expect the transaction to close by the end of this year, however, it is subject to certain conditions, including government and regulatory requirements.

Shimonov said that the Brampton plant wouldn’t be limited strictly to defence.

“We want to continue looking for opportunities within automotive, not necessarily in defence, to create a brighter future, but it will be dependent on many other things that we are not certain of. We need certainty before committing to anything,” he said.

Shimonov added that the exact work being done at the facility will be dictated by the contracts it is able to secure.

With the facility changing ownership and possibly pivoting to defence, McGinn said other changes will likely be necessary.

“The processes might be similar but I just think the controls and the facility access, those kind of things will be a little different because they’re going be different regulations governing those for defence items versus automotive parts and the like,” he said.

stories.title: $110M long-term care home breaks ground in Seaforth
stories.summary: Ontario Minister of Long-Term Care Natalia Kusendova-Bashta said the project will help seniors remain close to their families while creating stable, well-paying jobs in a rural community.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A groundbreaking ceremony was held in Seaforth for a new $110-million long-term care home.

Ontario Minister of Long-Term Care Natalia Kusendova-Bashta said the project will help seniors remain close to their families while creating stable, well-paying jobs in a rural community.

The province is providing 85 per cent of the capital funding for the 256-bed facility, representing approximately $94 million in government support. The five-acre site was donated by the Seaforth Hospital Trust and Seaforth Development Trust.

“We know we have an older home that’s in transition, and we don’t know the final details of when or what’s going to happen with it,” said outgoing Huron East Mayor Bernie MacLellan. “We certainly didn’t want those residents to be moved out of the community. We didn’t want the employment to be moved out of the community.”

The home will be built and operated by Omni Quality Living, which operates 29 seniors’ facilities in Ontario and New Brunswick. The company is also constructing long-term care homes in Peterborough and Brighton.

“We definitely have the need, but now we have a government that supports this and is investing in the right places,” said Omni Quality Living president and CEO Raheem Hirji. “We’re building across the province, and we’re happy to be part of that initiative.”

The facility, which will be located near Seaforth Community Hospital, is expected to welcome its first residents in early 2029.

Kusendova-Bashta said long-term care projects help reduce pressure elsewhere in the health-care system, including hospitals that care for alternate level-of-care patients.

Hirji said Seaforth was selected because of both staffing opportunities and demand for long-term care beds in the region.

MacLellan said he hopes some of the facility’s future employees will choose to settle in the community.

“We’ve got building lots that are ready to go. We’ve got contractors that are already building neighbourhoods,” he said. “We’ve got spots for people to come and live here if they want to work here.”

stories.title: One hospitalized after fire at Montreal apartment building
stories.summary: The fire began around 3:30 p.m. in Montreal's Pierrefonds-Roxboro borough, ON Riviera Street at the corner of Riverdale Boulevard.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
One person was taken to a hospital after a fire broke out in Montreal on Sunday afternoon.

The fire began around 3:30 p.m. in the Pierrefonds-Roxboro borough, ON Riviera Street at the corner of Riverdale Boulevard.

About 150 firefighters responded to the blaze at the three-storey building, which contains 73 apartments.

Firefighters got control of the blaze at around 10:45 p.m., and ten people were taken in by the Red Cross.

Fire investigators are at the scene to determine the cause of the fire, which remains unknown.

The condition of the person taken to hospital was not immediately available.

stories.title: No complaint received by ombudsman after children allegedly confined in locker
stories.summary: Quebec's ombudsman's office says it won't be able to investigate or issue recommendations until a parent or student files a complaint.
stories.author: Patrice Bergeron
stories.content:
Quebec’s student ombudsman says it has not received any complaints regarding allegations that elementary school students were confined in a locker at a school in the Laurentians, north of Montreal.

The ombudsman’s office says it won’t be able to investigate or issue recommendations until a parent or student files a complaint.

The Cogeco media network reported last week that at least three children between five and seven years old were isolated and sometimes locked in a lightly padded metal locker in order to get them to calm down.

They also said four employees, including a teacher and the school principal, were suspended following the allegations.

The media report said the alleged confinement occurred at a primary school operated by the Centre de services scolaire des Mille-Îles, but did not name the school.

Local police, youth protection services and the education minister have all announced investigations.

stories.title: B.C. tribunal orders WestJet to pay, but only 50 per cent passengers' alcohol tab
stories.summary: Vancouver - A British Columbia tribunal has ordered WestJet to compensate two passengers over a cancelled flight that caused an overnight delay, although it cut the couple's alcohol expense claim in half.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A British Columbia tribunal has ordered WestJet to compensate two passengers over a cancelled flight that caused an overnight delay, although it cut the couple’s alcohol expense claim in half.

The B.C. Civil Resolution Tribunal decision dated Nov. 13 says Kevin and Susan Myles claimed $2,000 under air passenger protection regulations, along with delay-related meal expenses during their trip from Cancun, Mexico, to Kamloops, B.C., in 2024.

stories.title: Ontario’s medical regulator pauses safer supply drug changes after legal challenge
stories.summary: Ontario’s medical regulator is hitting pause on implementing a host of changes to the ways doctors prescribe safer supply drugs after it was served with a legal challenge.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Ontario’s medical regulator is hitting pause on implementing a host of changes to the ways doctors prescribe safer supply drugs after it was served with a legal challenge.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario says it was served Friday with the legal action, which includes a motion for an injunction to prevent the regulator from enforcing the new safer supply rules.

The changes were set to come into effect on Monday, but the college says it’s pausing enforcement to allow time to respond to the injunction.

The college approved sweeping changes to the safer supply prescription regime last month that would require doctors to prescribe safer supply drugs only in conjunction with opioid agonist therapy.

Safer supply drugs are medications given to people at high risk of overdose as an alternative to illicit opioids while opioid agonist therapy uses medications such as Suboxone and methadone to treat opioid addiction.

The new rules would also require patients to take their safer supply medications in front of health-care professionals, rather than take them home — a change that has raised accessibility concerns especially for patients in rural Ontario and those who work regular hours.

The medical regulator has said the changes were approved in an effort to reduce the amount of opioids prescribed as safer supply drugs making their way to the streets.

The chair of the regulator’s board, Dr. Patrick Safieh, has said police forces in Ontario are noticing patients’ safer supply drugs being diverted to the black market.

stories.title: Grey Cup festivities didn’t push Calgary’s water use beyond restriction threshold
stories.summary: City of Calgary officials say a surge in CFL fans in Calgary for the Grey Cup didn't overburden the water system, despite ongoing water restrictions.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
Officials say a surge in CFL fans in Calgary for the Grey Cup didn’t overburden the Calgary water system, despite ongoing water restrictions.

They say water use reached 490 million litres on Sunday, when the city and visitors watched the championship football game and closed out several days of celebrations.

Calgary is about halfway through three weeks of water restrictions, with a 500-million-litre per day usage threshold, as it repairs a water main that supplies treated water to more than half its residents.

The city’s goal with the restrictions is to ensure it doesn’t strain its water plant or risk running low on water to fight fires.

Mayor Jeromy Farkas says the city has stayed below its typical water use, despite welcoming about 35,000 visitors for the Grey Cup.

“The fact that we’re below where we were two years ago, despite the fact that we’re putting on the Grey Cup … that is an astonishing achievement,” Farkas said Monday.

— More to come…

stories.title: ‘I can shoot you dead’: Video captures confrontation outside Chinese Consulate in Toronto
stories.summary: A video showing an alleged assault against two Falun Gong demonstrators outside China’s consulate in Toronto has prompted renewed calls for Prime Minister Mark Carney to confront Beijing over alleged transnational repression in Canada.
stories.author: Judy Trinh
stories.content:
Toronto - Human rights advocates say a video obtained by CTV News is a flagrant example of transnational repression by China. The video shows a man tearing down Falun Gong banners set up outside the Chinese consulate in Toronto and threatening to “shoot dead” a female demonstrator and kicking another woman who was videotaping the incident.

Activists are calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney to raise the issue of China’s human rights abuses when he meets with President Xi Jinping on Tuesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen.

“It’s important that Prime Minister Carney raise this issue and put an immediate stop to this blatant transnational repression happening in Canada,” says Joel Chipkar, the spokesperson for the Falun Dafa Association of Canada.

“This is creating fear and insecurity for Canadians here who escaped (China’s) tyrannical regime and came here for a better life.”

The two women are part of a rotating group of volunteers who stand outside the consulate each day to draw attention to China’s persecution of Falun Gong practitioners.

Falun gong is a spiritual movement which has gained a mass following of millions in China and around the world.

According to human rights group, Safeguard Defenders, China has labelled Falun Gong one of “five poisons” including democrats, Taiwan, Tibet and Xinjiang that are considered threats to stability of the regime .

Chipkar told CTV News that one demonstrator was a Canadian citizen and that the other woman was a refugee who fled to Canada in 2024. Both women have families who have been imprisoned in China because of their religious beliefs.

“They feel the Chinese Communist Party has too much influence in Canada. We have people in our community who have been assaulted. They have been followed home, and their family members have been threatened in China.”

‘This is Chinese territory’

The Toronto incident that occurred on Sept. 22 is one of dozens of examples cited in a new Safeguard Defenders report, which alleges that Beijing has created a massive network of overseas associations, that Chinese Communist Party (CCP) agents are using to monitor and control its diaspora. The report claims that there are at least 18 illegal police stations in Canada.

The four-minute video reveals a confrontation on Toronto’s George Street in front of the Consulate-General of the People’s Republic of China.

It involves an altercation between two demonstrators and a man wearing a black jacket with the flag of China sewn on it.

Angered by the message on the protest banners, which drew attention to China’s repression of the Falun Gong, the man begins tearing apart the signs. The female demonstrator urges her friend to call the police, while the man tells someone off camera to start recording video as well.

A copy of the video has been sent to the Toronto Police Service. CTV News has independently verified the accuracy of the English subtitles on the video.

“These are illegal,” the man says, referring to the banners. “This is the entry to the embassy. This is Chinese territory – do you know that? You have violated China’s anti-secession law. I can shoot you dead.” He continues, pointing his finger at her: “I will make you fall to your death. Believe it or not. I will shoot you to death believe it or not.”

Later on in the video, the woman tries to grab him from behind to stop him from tearing down more signs. That’s when the man shoves her back, nearly knocking her glasses off. Then the man walks toward the woman recording the video and kicks her.

Chipkar helped the women report the incident to police. Witnesses were able to record the licence plate of the Uber vehicle the man got into. Chipkar says investigators were able to identify the man.

They found out through the Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) that he had returned to China.

“Police did tell us that if he returned, he would be detained at the border, charged for the assault, threats and mischief to property.”

Chipkar says that police are not releasing the perpetrator’s name.

It’s not clear if the suspect was a Chinese police officer or a diplomat.

Toronto police has confirmed to CTV News that there is an open investigation into the incident. A spokesperson said the Toronto Police Service is unable to provide more information until the lead investigator returns from leave.

CTV News has contacted the Chinese Embassy for comment but has yet to receive a response.

New Chinese law could lead to more transnational repression

Margaret McCuaig-Johnston, an advisory board member of the China Strategic Risks Institute, calls the incident “disturbing.”

She says the foreign affairs minister needs to summon the ambassador and “read him the riot act to ensure this doesn’t happen in Canada again and that there will be major consequences.”

She says the individual should be barred from returning to Canada.

McCuaig-Johnston is also concerned that China’s new “ethnic unity law” will lead to more cases of transnational repression in Canada and across the globe.

The new Chinese law , which came into effect July 1, grants China extraterritorial powers to act against organizations and people that it feels threaten the aims of the CCP.

The law, along with an expansion of the global network to monitor the diaspora, can be used to silence the voices of people advocating for minority rights such as those of the Falun Gong, Uyghurs or Tibetans.

Democracy activists from Hong Kong, or Taiwanese Canadians who are against unifying with China, can also be targeted.

“China thinks their law extends anywhere, including the streets of Canada,” says McCuaig-Johnston.

Other than the Toronto incident, McCuaig-Johnston says there are other cases of human rights abuses that Carney should raise with Xi. She points out that Uyghur Canadian activist Huseyin Celil has been imprisoned in China for 20 years.

There’s also Jimmy Lai, a Hong Kong media mogul who supported the democracy movement. He’s serving a 20-year jail sentence for collusion and sedition. The 78-year-old has family in Canada.

Before leaving for Asia, Carney said he would raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada with Xi.

The prime minister also said that the partnership between the two countries “is something that is deepening but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we’re involved.”

Former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig, who was detained for more than 1,000 days by China, says the prime minister needs to be pressed on what those guardrails are.

“The government needs to explain more to Canadians what the guardrails are, what they’re for, and how effective they’ve been, and what Ottawa is doing to strengthen them,” said Kovrig during an interview with Vassy Kapelos on CTV’s Question Period.

Kovrig, who now runs his own geopolitical risk advisory firm, says Carney should make it a “top priority” to bring up the findings of the Safeguard Defenders report, which claims that China May be operating at least 18 illegal police stations to control the diaspora in Canada.

“That is a violation of Canadian sovereignty, and it’s a threat to the rights of Canadian citizens. And so, I think that is a top priority, frankly, to raise with President Xi, and convey to him very clearly that that kind of thing is not acceptable, and that Canada will investigate it, and we will follow processes to ensure that Canadians are secure.”

Kovrig, who now runs his own geopolitical risk advisory firm, says Carney should make it a “top priority” to bring up the findings of the Safeguard Defenders report, which claims that China May be operating at least 18 illegal police stations to control the diaspora in Canada.

By The Canadian Press

Galloway’s lawsuit, originally filed in 2018, alleges that he was falsely accused of rape and assault by a former student, whose unproven allegations spread widely online after they became public in November 2015.

Several people originally named as defendants in the case settled before the trial and issued apologies to the author of the bestselling novel “The Cellist of Sarajevo.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

There are four remaining defendants, including a former creative writing student only identified as A.B., who alleged Galloway sexually assaulted her, though the trial heard that she was no longer asserting that Galloway assaulted her, rather that she reported he had done so.

The defamation trial has heard that Galloway’s writing career was destroyed, and his public suspension and firing by the University of B.C. was set off by the allegations, which he denies and were found unsubstantiated by a retired judge hired to investigate.

Galloway was awarded $167,000 in 2018 by an arbitrator who found the university, which was not a party in the lawsuit, violated his privacy rights and harmed his reputation.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Stellantis meeting ‘challenging’ but ‘productive’, Premier Ford says
stories.summary: The meeting came as Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly said the automaker can either keep its Brampton plant open or face a multimillion-dollar lawsuit from the federal government.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the federal government must be willing to mitigate emissions costs to keep the Stellantis auto plant open in Brampton, following a meeting with Ottawa and industry representatives Friday.

“We’re getting a little more insight. To keep the Brampton facility just open and warm — not production — is costing the clients about $135 million a year,” Ford told reporters following the meeting.

“Stellantis is paying about a billion dollars a year on gas house emissions basically, and that’s where we can mitigate it, buy a little more time, and focus on what they can put into that plant.”

The premier said the meeting was “challenging” but “productive.”

The meeting came as Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says the automaker can either keep its Brampton plant open or face a multimillion-dollar lawsuit from the federal government.

On Nov. 9, Stellantis announced it had signed a deal to sell the idled assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel .

Last week, the federal government served Stellantis with a notice of default on its 2022 funding agreement, in which Ottawa committed up to $529 million to help Stellantis retool its Brampton and Windsor facilities to produce electrified vehicles.

“They need to protect the workers. If not, we’ll get our money back,” Joly told reporters earlier in the day Friday during a separate announcement.

“If they go ahead and sell the plant, well then they will face legal recourses from the Government of Canada of hundreds of millions of dollars.

“And if they decide actually to protect their workers and not sell the plant — then we can work together.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "And if they decide actually to protect their workers and not sell the plant — then we can work together."

A letter from Joly said Stellantis breached conditions of the commitment by halting Jeep Compass production in Brampton, failing or refusing to identify a replacement vehicle, not maintaining any production at the facility and closing the plant.

Joly’s letter said Stellantis has 30 days to demonstrate it will “correct these conditions” or she will declare that the company is in default of its obligations.

It warned that if Stellantis remains in breach of its conditions, the company could face penalties including a requirement to repay all or part of the funding it has received, plus interest.

Unifor represents Stellantis autoworkers and following the meeting, the union’s national president Lana Payne said greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions costs are an “irritant” for the Canadian auto sector.

“If you manufacture and do full vehicle assembly in here, then the penalties around those GHGs should be waived,” she said.

“I often hear our government say, ‘there are things that aren’t in our control.’ This is one of the things that is in our own control — to take away what is a major problem for the auto industry at the moment.”

Ford said the cost of GHG emissions is a “big problem here” but also for other industries like steel.

“The federal government needs to listen,” he said.

On Thursday, the Brampton Board of Trade sent a letter to Joly asking her to approve the sale of the plant to Roshel, while still holding Stellantis accountable to its workers.

“Ottawa can pursue both objectives at the same time,” CEO Jaipaul Massey-Singh wrote.

“We urge Ottawa to use its leverage with Stellantis to secure fair compensation and company-funded retraining for affected workers, and to enforce the commitments Stellantis made in exchange for public support.”

But Massey-Singh said the consequences of the shutdown “extend well beyond the plant gates” and workers in affiliated industries “deserve a credible path back to an operating facility and an opportunity to compete for the work it generates.”

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023.

The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before the company paused the plan in early 2025.

It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois, leaving the plant idled indefinitely.

Beloved nine-year-old Fiona died from complications after ingesting a visitor’s knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo.

She had become a social media darling after being born prematurely and surviving against all odds.

The Toronto Zoo says it conducted the review to determine whether any additional measures were needed to prevent a similar fate to its animals, including at the river hippo habitat.

While the zoo said it found no structural or infrastructure changes that were required, it will be taking additional steps to remind visitors to refrain from throwing items into animal habitats.

The Toronto Zoo is home to one river hippopotamus, Perky II. It euthanized 39-year-old Petal back in October 2025 due to health issues.

The zoo also cares for three pygmy hippos, Kindia, Harvey and a calf named Maple that was born in August 2026.

stories.title: U.S. senator says Hegseth memo does not change military co-operation with Canada
stories.summary: Canada’s defence minister says he has not seen a memo from the U.S. secretary of war that reportedly restricts American defence co-operation with Canada.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
HALIFAX — A Republican senator says a U.S. defence department’s memo that reportedly placed restrictions on co-operation with Canada applies to things such as participating in think-tank conferences, not military operations.

Sen. Mike Rounds was responding to a Washington Post report on Friday that said Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth penned the classified memo putting restrictions on military co-operation with Canada last week. The paper reportedly said it had not seen the memo and offered no detail on its contents.

The senator said the memo does not affect any U.S. defence personnel in Canada today and does not impact the North American Aerospace Defence Command, North Atlantic Treaty Organization operations or the Five Eyes security alliance.

“It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance (defence department) objectives,” Rounds told reporters at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday. “(U.S. defence officials) must request permission for Canadian think-tank events or social engagements. And it is OK to attend any 9/11 events.”

Rounds said he and a delegation of U.S. senators attending the Halifax conference had just attended a meeting with Canadian officials and shared the information with them. Defence Minister David McGuinty told reporters hours earlier he was unaware of the memo’s contents.

“After listening to this, (Canadian officials) said it sounds like it’s nothing new, nothing different than what they’ve been really practising under for the last year-and-a-half,” said the South Dakota senator.

McGuinty said earlier in the day that it was “business as usual” between the Canadian and U.S. militaries and assured Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence was continuing.

“I’ve seen no evidence of (a change). I’ve checked with our top military folks, they’ve seen no evidence of change. We continue to co-operate. We continue to work together,” McGuinty told reporters.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a response to the story about the memo that the defence department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”

The statement, made late Friday, added that the department is prioritizing bilateral co-operation that strengthens the defence of the U.S. and “shared hemisphere” while also supporting Canada’s ability to meet NATO obligations.

“This guidance does not impact defense intelligence co-operation, our binational NORAD command, or our co-operation through NATO,” Parnell said.

Several U.S. senators at the Halifax event acknowledged their country’s standing around the world has been impacted by the aggressive policies of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Senator Tim Kaine, a Democrat, said the memo doesn’t help relations with Canada. He said he’s hopeful things will change when the new U.S. Congress takes office in January. Democrats took control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in this month’s midterm election.

“The tone is bad and it’s unnecessary,” said Kaine. “And we understand this actually goes back a ways and it is just the formalization of something that is now months and months old. I do think the new Congress is going to change the tone dramatically. ”

McGuinty also announced Saturday that Canada is formally becoming the 25th member of NATO’s Innovation Fund. Canada is contributing more than $100 million to the fund, enabling it to invest in Canadian startups.

Launched in 2022, the venture capital fund is designed to strengthen NATO by investing in cutting edge technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, biotech, space and communications.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.

Devin Stevens, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ottawa says it lost $2M from emergency drug stockpile after freezer malfunction
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Public Health Agency of Canada has reported losing another $2 million in pharmaceuticals from the national emergency stockpile because of the mechanical failure of a freezer.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan and Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The Public Health Agency of Canada has reported losing another $2 million in pharmaceuticals from the national emergency stockpile because of the mechanical failure of a freezer.

The figure is in the annual federal public accounts published earlier this fall, and comes after the agency had to write off $20 million in pharmaceuticals from the stockpile a year earlier after another freezer malfunction.

Sen. Mike Rounds was responding to a Washington Post report on Friday that said Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth penned the classified memo putting restrictions on military co-operation with Canada last week. The paper reportedly said it had not seen the memo and offered no detail on its contents.

The senator said the memo does not affect any U.S. defence personnel in Canada today and does not impact the North American Aerospace Defence Command, North Atlantic Treaty Organization operations or the Five Eyes security alliance.

U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds says a classified memo from Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth does not change the department’s co-operation with the Canadian military. Rounds was responding to a media report that said the memo placed restrictions on military co-operation between the two countries. (Nov. 21, 2026)

“It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance (defence department) objectives,” Rounds told reporters at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday. “(U.S. defence officials) must request permission for Canadian think-tank events or social engagements. And it is OK to attend any 9/11 events.”

Rounds said he and a delegation of U.S. senators attending the Halifax conference had just attended a meeting with Canadian officials and shared the information with them. Defence Minister David McGuinty told reporters hours earlier he was unaware of the memo’s contents.

stories.title: Ontario, Ottawa committing $250M to help fund new port in Sault Ste. Marie
stories.summary: Ontario and the federal government say they're committing $250 million to help build a new port in Sault Ste. Marie on the north shore of the Saint Marys River.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Ontario and the federal government say they’re committing $250 million to help build a new port in Sault Ste. Marie on the north shore of the Saint Marys River.

The province says the project will see the construction of two docking berths, a transload yard to transfer cargo from ships to rail, and other infrastructure to move goods between northern and southern Ontario, Quebec and overseas markets.

Ottawa is providing $125 million through the Trade Diversification Corridors Fund, a $5 billion fund aimed at doubling non-U.S. exports, while the province makes up the difference through a repayable financing loan.

In a news release, the province says the new port will serve as a gateway in the Great Lakes and support mining, steelmaking and critical mineral development in northern Ontario, including the Ring of Fire region.

The Hamilton-Oshawa Port Authority leads development of the project, which aims to be online by 2029 and reach full capacity by 2031.

The port authority signed a partnership last year with Sault Ste. Marie to advance the transportation hub and the city committed $15 million to the project in July.

The federal government says the port fills a vital gap in Ontario’s trade infrastructure, and is set to be the region’s first public, multi-user marine port between Thunder Bay and southern Ontario.

In a news release, Ottawa says the port is expected to be able to move more than 3.5 million metric tonnes of cargo annually once fully operational.

Premier Doug Ford is framing the project as a way to expand markets for Ontario businesses as the United States has become a less-reliable trading partner.

“With U.S. tariffs threatening Canadian jobs and industries, there has never been a more important time to build for the future and invest in infrastructure that will help Canadian businesses diversify,” Ford wrote in a statement.

Federal transport minister Steven MacKinnon says the project will “reinforce Canada’s position as a reliable and competitive trading nation.”
